paragraphs.text: 1- Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Blessed: O the happiness! In the Hebrew sense it takes a plural form, that is, an abundance of happiness and blessings.

1- He praises the man who did not accept the counsel of the hypocrites, that is, the thought of the wicked, whether he rejected it from the beginning, or erred a little and accepted it, and then repented of it. He progresses from thought to conduct in the way of sinners, and this too the spiritual man rejected, whether from the beginning, or he stood in the way and then repented and departed from it. In the end sin grows greater and reaches settled abiding in it, for he says "sitteth", that is, the spiritual man refuses to settle in sin, and even if he falls he hastens to repent. The wicked man progresses from thought to conduct, and then to settling in sin. The spiritual man rejected all of these.
2- Here he speaks symbolically about Christ, for He is the Man without sin who rejected the three degrees of sin.

3- And if the meaning is a rebuke of Saul the wicked king, who progressed through the stages of sin, namely thought, then conduct, then settling, then he rebukes him by showing the greatness of the one who rejects all the degrees of sin, perhaps that he might repent. This is a great courtesy on the part of David, if he is the writer of the Psalm, because this Psalm was not given a title, and many incline to the view that its author is David, as we have mentioned.
2- But his delight is in the law of the Lord; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.

1- If he praised the spiritual man in (v. 1) for keeping away from evil, here he praises him for his positive conduct with regard to the law of the Lord. The law of the Lord means either the conscience, or the Law of Moses, which was a preparation for the law of Christ, that is, the Holy Bible and all the teachings of the Church.

2- Here the importance of man's will and spiritual striving appears, in his inclination and desire to live by the law of the Lord. If human desire and readiness for striving are found, grace overflows to the man and helps him to carry out the commandments of the Lord.

3- He affirms the importance of spiritual striving in his repetition, that is, his meditation on the words of the Lord, because repetition confirms the meaning within the mind, and then, when it takes hold of the thought, it easily leads the senses, speech and conduct.
4- He declares that this meditation is day and night, that is, continually, that is, as long as he is awake, and in this state even his dreams are holy.

5- Day and night signify the time of rest and the time of affliction, and they also signify the times of life with God and the times of falling into sin; in both cases the spiritual man must meditate on the word of God.
6- Meditation on the word of God protects man from evil thoughts and draws him to heavenly things.
3- And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

1- He compares the spiritual man to a tree planted by the rivers of water, and this water signifies the Holy Spirit, and the tree gives its fruit in its season, that is, at the right time of bearing fruit that those around it need. These fruits are the virtues with which the spiritual man is adorned and which influence those around him.

2- In addition, the leaf of the tree does not wither, because the tree is filled with water, and its leaves are green and full of vitality, not dry so as to fall to the ground. The vitality of the leaf comes from the strong relationship with the Holy Spirit, who is the water. This leaf is the appearance of the tree, so it signifies the speech and appearance of the spiritual man; for his speech is from God, since the Holy Bible testifies that God gives His children from the Holy Spirit a mouth and wisdom (Lk 21:15). This speech is strong and firm and does not fall, ever influencing those around the spiritual man; indeed, his whole appearance influences those around him.

3- Likewise all the works of this spiritual man are successful, because God works in him, and successful means that they lead to his salvation and the salvation of those around him, and material success is not what is meant, because material success is sometimes tied to evil.

4- The tree can also signify Christ, planted by the rivers of water, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is His Spirit, and He gives His fruit, that is, salvation, in its season, that is, in the fullness of time He dies on the Cross, then rises on the third day, and founds His Church on the day of Pentecost. His leaf, that is, His word, is true and never falls, and everything He does is successful and leads to the salvation of mankind.

Take care that your words and deeds have a constructive aim that benefits you or benefits others. This is true success: that you draw near to God, or bring others near to God. As for words and deeds that have no aim, that is, that are vain, keep away from them.
(2) The wicked (vv. 4-6)
4- The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.
Chaff: that is, straw, yellow in color.
Driveth away: that is, scatters it. The word is taken from the winnowing fork, an agricultural tool used to separate the grains of wheat from the straw.

1- The writer of the Psalm shows the greatness of the spiritual man, who is compared to the tree planted by the rivers of water, by comparing him with the wicked, whom he likens to the opposite, that is, to light straw that is scattered by the wind far away so that it is found no more; he means the destruction of the wicked and their removal from God. But the spiritual man is firm in God.
2- The wind signifies the trials that test the wicked, so they fall and depart from God. The wind also signifies pride, into which the wicked fall and which destroys them.
5- Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.

If the previous verse showed the wicked's departure from God on earth, then likewise in heaven, on the day of judgment, they will have no resurrection and no glorified life with Christ, but destruction will be theirs. Nor can sinners have a place among the righteous around Christ, because they will be cast into eternal torment.
6- For the Lord knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.

1- The writer of the Psalm states in the end the sum of the matter, which is that God knows the way of the righteous, that is, He rejoices in them and they are with Him in the Kingdom, but the wicked, their portion is destruction, and they are far from the knowledge of God, meaning that they do not enjoy His love and His blessings of the Kingdom.

2- God knows the obedience of His children to His commandments and rejoices in it, and then His joy is complete if they complete their life on earth, and He gives them everlasting glory and complete joy with Him in heaven.

Be careful to memorize and repeat the words of the Holy Bible, so that they keep you in all your ways, and in this way God is in your mind and with you always, and you enjoy fellowship with Him on earth until your joy is made complete in heaven. Christ the King and the enmity of the nations "Why do the heathen rage" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, because the Apostles Peter and John ascribed it to him (Acts 4:25).

2- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, that is, those that speak about Christ the awaited Messiah, and it is considered one of the royal Psalms because it speaks about King David, who is a type of Christ.

3- And while the first Psalm speaks about man's choice of his way, if he chooses life with God, it requires that he believe in Christ the Savior, who gives him the new life in Him on earth and the Kingdom of Heaven.

4- The content of this Psalm is the sufferings of Christ, the world's rising up against Him, and His endurance of everything for the sake of our salvation, and how He conquered Satan and gave us authority over him, and the call to mankind, with all its great ones, to submit to Christ.
5- This Psalm is found in the Prime prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The nations' rising up against the Lord's Anointed

paragraphs.text: 1- Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?
Rage: gathered together and assembled for war.

1- This Psalm begins with a question that David asks of God, to know the reason for the rising up of the nations of the earth and the peoples against the awaited Messiah, for he sees with the eye of prophecy the rising up of the Jews and of the Roman state, which ruled the world, against Christ until they crucified Him.

2- He also asks about the nations' rising up against King David, who is a type of Christ, although God gave David victory over all the nations around him, and this appeared in his successive victories over the nations, so the rest of the nations ought to have submitted to him, and not tried to rise up against him or fight him.
3- He describes the thoughts of these peoples and their plots as vain, that is, without benefit.

4- This question may be one of astonishment and denunciation, as he asks how the nations and peoples dared to fight the Lord of glory Jesus, who has authority over everything, so the Jews fabricated false, lying and vain accusations against Christ Jesus. And the wonder is that they imagine a vain thing in killing the Source of life. Or how can it occur to him to fight King David, whom God supports, so that no one can overcome him? Consequently all their plots are vain.

5- This question may also be a rebuke, that is, David rebukes the nations and peoples for their insolence and daring to rise up against the Lord's anointed, that is, David, or the awaited Messiah; they have forgotten their weakness and the power of God who is before them.

entries.section: (1) The nations' rising up against the Lord's Anointed

paragraphs.text: 2- The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying,
Kings of the earth: Herod, who killed the children of Bethlehem, and Pilate, who crucified Christ.
The rulers: the chief priests and elders of the Jewish people.

The Psalmist continues his question about the daring of the rulers of God's people and the kings of the world, that they should try to destroy Christ and crucify Him. He affirms that these plots are not against the person of Jesus the man, who appeared before them in weakness, but against God, because He is God incarnate. Their plotting against David is also against God, who supports and protects him, for David is the Lord's anointed, that is, anointed with oil as king by the Lord, and is not like the rest of the kings of the earth, so whoever opposes him opposes God.

entries.section: (1) The nations' rising up against the Lord's Anointed

paragraphs.text: 3- "Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us."

1- The nations hostile to God cried out in rejection of His authority and of following Him, accusing Him that following Him lays on them heavy bonds and cords. In the Septuagint it says "fetters and a yoke"; the fetters are the bonds, and the yoke is the wooden beam that is placed on the necks of animals to pull farm implements behind them.

2- Although the yoke of Christ is easy and His burden is light (Mt 11:30), His commandments give rest to the soul and bring it salvation, whereas the bonds of sin and the lusts of the world humiliate man and lead him to destruction.

Do not be troubled by the plotting of the wicked or of anyone who threatens you, for they are worth nothing before the power of God that supports you. Only hold fast to God's commandments and remain firm in His Church.
4- He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.

1- God who dwells in the heavens laughs at the plots of the wicked, because they are worth nothing and do not hinder His salvation, which He offers to the world on the Cross; on the contrary, He turns their plots into a means of saving the world. By His death for mankind, they kill Him and He redeems them; they bury Him and He draws them to heaven: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me" (Jn 12:32).

2- The heavens can also be the souls of God's children and His saints, in whom He dwells because of their conduct being exalted above the world, for He is glorified in His saints, and the plots of the wicked fail to stop their relationship with Him; on the contrary, all the sufferings and torments they are subjected to make them cling to Him. And by their death for His sake they receive the crowns of martyrdom and the crowns of striving and service.

3- God derides the plots of the wicked in the world, for they are nothing before His power. The attempts of the scribes and Pharisees to ensnare Christ in a word showed His wisdom and power and at the same time their weakness. And when they crucified Christ and He died, He rose and gave His disciples, who were simple and ignorant in the eyes of the world, power, and they preached in His name and drew many in the whole world to Him. Thus God derides the false wisdom of this world and its vain power, and faith in Him spreads in the midst of tribulations and persecutions.
5- Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure.
Vex them: makes them tremble with fear.

After the Lord has laughed at them and derided them, He shows His wrath against them by rebuking them, as He rebuked the scribes and Pharisees and pronounced woes on them (Mt 23). But if they refuse to submit to Him through repentance, He frightens them and makes them tremble with His severe punishment of them, as He allowed the Romans to destroy Jerusalem and kill thousands of Jews in AD 70. And as all the wicked will tremble before Him on the day of judgment, and then He casts them into eternal torment.

The opportunity of life is for repentance and for enjoying the tenderness of God, even if it appears in the form of strong commandments or severe warnings. All this protects us from eternal punishment and destruction. May we not refuse God's hand stretched out to us every day to return to Him.

entries.section: (3) Christ the King, the Son of G

paragraphs.text: 6- "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion."
1- Here he speaks about God, who anointed David king over Israel and took as his capital Jerusalem, which is Zion.

2- God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, the eternal and everlasting, became incarnate in the fullness of time. The Father declares that Jesus Christ His Son He anointed in the Jordan on the day of His Baptism as King in Zion, that is, Jerusalem, the holy hill of God, where His great temple is, and it is a type of the Church, over which Christ was anointed King and Redeemer of all mankind. He called it the hill of His holiness because the temple is built on a hill, which signifies the loftiness of God's temple, and a type of the Church, which is the icon of heaven on earth, and the Church is built on the rock, which is Christ (Mt 16:18), just as the temple is built on the hill.

3- Christ was called King because the Magi offered Him among their gifts gold, because He is a king, and He spoke of Himself at the end of days, saying, "Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand" (Mt 25:34). And He confirmed the words of Pilate when he asked Him whether He was a king, and He said to him, "Thou sayest" (Jn 18:37); so He is a king, indeed the King of kings.

entries.section: (3) Christ the King, the Son of G

paragraphs.text: 7- I will declare the decree: the Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee.
The Psalmist David announces news concerning what God has decreed, namely the Incarnation of the Son in the fullness of time, to redeem mankind, and here he declares two things:

1- "Thou art my Son", that is, the hypostasis of the Father says of the Second Hypostasis that He is My Son. And He also says, "this day have I begotten thee", and "this day" represents the permanent present, that is, the Son is begotten of the Father from eternity and to eternity.

2- He speaks about the Incarnation, for by "this day" he also means the fullness of time in which Christ became incarnate for the salvation of mankind. And He said "begotten thee" and not "created thee", because He is begotten, not created, of one essence with the Father, as we say in the Creed.

3- This verse also applies to David: although the people asked for a king instead of God and He set Saul over them according to what pleased them in outward appearance, after this He sets over them a king who is a true son of God, whose heart is like the heart of God, and he is David. So He declares that he was begotten today, whether He means the day of his birth, or the day of his being anointed king by the hand of Samuel.

entries.section: (3) Christ the King, the Son of G

paragraphs.text: 8- Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.

1- The Father calls the Son, saying to Him, ask of Me and I will give You the nations of the world as an inheritance and a possession, however far away, even to the ends of the earth. The Father means that all that is His He gives to the Son (Jn 16:15), and this was accomplished when Christ died on the Cross and paid the debt for mankind, to save everyone who believes in Him and lives with Him.

2- By "Ask of me" he also means that there is a constant dialogue between the Son and the Father, that is, within the Divine Essence. If limited man has within his mind a stream of thoughts and dialogues, how much more so within the Divine Essence.
3- This verse shows the extent of love and unity among the hypostases.

4- "Ask of me" does not mean that there is incomplete knowledge or lesser power in the Son that He wants to receive and learn from the Father, but, as we said, it is an expression of dialogue, love and unity within the Divine Essence among the hypostases.

5- If we apply this verse to David, it applies only partially, for the kingdom of Israel in the days of David became as wide as it could be, and God's promise was fulfilled, which He made to the fathers, that He would give them the land from the river Euphrates to the river of Egypt, which is a seasonal river of torrents lying in the wilderness of Sinai. This did not happen except in the days of David and not before him.

entries.section: (3) Christ the King, the Son of G

paragraphs.text: 9- Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.

1- Christ is the King of kings, and the king has the scepter of kingship with which he shepherds his people, and because those who oppose Christ are created from clay, that is, weak human beings, He says of them that they are a potter's vessels, that is, vessels made of pottery.
2- And when He breaks them and shatters them, they turn into useless pieces, but if they repent He reshapes them and makes them vessels of honor and glory.
3- But if they insist on resisting Him, He punishes them with eternal torment on the day of judgment.

4- The meaning of this is that the scepter of Christ's kingship contains mercy and justice together: whoever responds to Him with repentance receives mercy, and whoever insists on his sins deserves justice.

We are children of God and have boldness to ask Him for our needs and for the forgiveness of our sins; as the Son asks of the Father, He encourages us to ask of God and to rejoice in His love and gifts.
10- Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.

1- David the king and judge calls the kings of the earth to walk in reason and wisdom, so that they believe in Christ the Savior and keep His commandments, and likewise the judges, to walk in discipline and good conscience, that is, to judge with justice, and so submit to the just God and His holy Christ.
2- And when the king and judge are wise and instructed, it influences his people and followers, so David by this calls the leaders to bring the peoples to faith in Christ and submission to Him.

3- Every spiritual man is considered a king and ruler over himself (Rev 1:6) and a judge, with justice, over his actions when he examines himself every day, for every believer who knows God's commandments passes God's judgment on himself before others. That is, David calls every man to submit to Christ and keep His commandments and live with discipline and reason.
11- Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling.

The prophet David continues his speech to the kings and judges, to call them to serve God with fear, that is, to offer repentance with contrition and tears before God, knowing that it is a great grace that God allows them, despite the multitude of their sins, to come before Him and serve Him, offering prayers of reverence before the King of kings and Lord of lords. He also calls them to rejoice, or to exult as the Septuagint (the Agpeya) says, with trembling before God. This means that they will rejoice in being in the presence of God, so they lift up their voices with shouting and exultation, but at the same time this joy is mixed with trembling, that is, they do not lose their fear and reverence before God, for they rejoice in their sonship to God, which He has bestowed on them although, because of the multitude of their sins, they do not deserve to be servants to Him. This is true repentance, bound up with bent knees, tears and contrite prayers, so the heart is filled with joy and consolation at the same time.
12- Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.

1- It was an ancient custom among peoples to declare their submission to the king by kissing his feet; therefore the Psalmist calls the kings and judges to kiss the Son, that is, to kiss His feet and submit to Him and keep His commandments. For if they do not submit, the wrath of God, that is, His punishment, awaits them, and this is not an emotional passion like that of human beings but His divine judgment on those who oppose Him, so they are cast into eternal torment for their insistence on sin. And this torment is what he calls perishing from the way, that is, from the life, that is, the Kingdom.

2- The Psalmist also warns that God's wrath is soon to be kindled, that is, the day of judgment, when Christ judges everyone who refused to believe in Him and did not keep His commandments. Therefore the Church has lived since its beginning in the apostolic age preparing for the day of judgment by repentance and spiritual striving, and if at times she grows weak and forgets this eschatological dimension, God alerts her through tribulations to return to the power of the age of the Apostles.

3- At the end of the Psalm the prophet David pronounces blessed the children of God who trust in Him, that is, those who believe in Him and keep His commandments. And as the first Psalm begins with a beatitude, the second Psalm also ends with a beatitude for the children of God, to encourage them to live with Him.

God's arms are open to you if you are repentant and reject your sins. However weak you are, and even if you accepted sin by your own will and even took pleasure in it, and then awoke after tasting the bitterness of the fall, return quickly with fear and tears, and you will receive mercies and consolations from God in the sacrament of confession that cannot be expressed. The salvation of the Lord A Psalm of David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son "Lord, how are they increased that trouble me" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

1- Its writer: the prophet and king David, when his son Absalom rose up against him to kill him, and he fled barefoot from Jerusalem and was suffering feelings of grief; for how hard it is when children rebel and rise up against their parents to harm them, even trying to kill them. This Psalm is also considered one of the Messianic Psalms, because it clearly prophesies the sufferings of Christ, His death and His resurrection, for example it says in (v. 5), "I laid me down and slept; I awaked."
2- This Psalm suits everyone who suffers pains, persecutions and frustrations from those around him, so his hope in God his Savior is renewed.

3- The Fathers consider the first and second Psalms an introduction to the Book of Psalms, as the first speaks about life with God and keeping away from evil, and the second Psalm declares clearly that this life is accomplished only through Christ the Savior and submission to His commandments.

4- As for this third Psalm, it suits everyone who begins his day with prayer, for after he lies down and sleeps he rises with Christ and awakes, relying on God his Helper. It is followed by the fourth Psalm, which many of the Fathers see as suitable for prayer at the end of the day, because it says "commune with your own heart upon your bed" and also says "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep." Therefore the Church arranged that the fourth Psalm be repeated in the prayer of the Veil, which is said at the end of the day.

5- The third Psalm is also repeated and said in the First Watch of the Midnight prayer, because it contains "I laid me down and slept; I awaked", and this is what happens with one who prays at midnight.
6- Some of the Fathers consider this Psalm a personal lament of David, in which he pours out his sorrows and pains over the rising up of Absalom his son against him.

entries.section: (1) The multitude of those who trouble him

paragraphs.text: 1- Lord, how are they increased that trouble me! many are they that rise up against me.
1- While David was fleeing in great humiliation from the face of his son Absalom, running barefoot with his head covered and weeping, he felt very deep sorrow, and wrote this lament.

2- And the beautiful thing is that in his great distress he did not grieve privately within himself, but took refuge in God in a humble prayer, in which he declares his weakness and the multitude of those who trouble and oppose him, because Absalom gathered behind him a great army, indeed all the Jewish people, not only to drive David out of his kingdom but trying to kill him.

3- Although God had foretold David what would happen (2 Sam 12:11) through the mouth of Nathan the prophet after his fall into adultery, David did not despair or surrender to evil, but raised his voice in faith toward God to rescue him from those who opposed him, and He had compassion on him and saved him.

4- And David here is a type of Christ, that is, this Psalm, as we said, speaks about the feelings of Christ when the Jews arrested Him, tortured Him and crucified Him, and the likeness between David and Christ in this situation appears in the following:
a- His son Absalom rose up against David, and the Jewish nation, His daughter, rose up against Christ to kill Him.
b- David's friend and counselor Ahithophel betrayed him, and afterwards hanged himself. And Christ was betrayed by His friend and disciple Judas Iscariot, who then hanged himself.

c- David had compassion on his rebellious son Absalom and charged his army to deal gently with him. And Christ had compassion on those who crucified Him and prayed for them on the Cross, saying, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).
d- All the tribes of the children of Israel rose up against David. And all the Jews rose up against Christ to be rid of Him.

entries.section: (1) The multitude of those who trouble him

paragraphs.text: 2- Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God. Selah.

1- When many people gathered behind Absalom and David fled before them, they said to him that he has no salvation in his God, because he had few with him, while Absalom had a great army with him. They forgot that power belongs to God and not to a great number. David, who was wronged, must be defended by God, and although He allowed this tribulation as discipline for him for his sin, He is merciful and accepts the repentance of His children and saves them if the wicked wrong them.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who was wronged like David, and the Jews said about Him, "let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him" (Mt 27:42). This verse applies to all God's children when they pass through tribulation and Satan tries to make them fall into despair, which is the hardest sin, but by their supplications they receive deliverance and victory from God. Satan may fight man with despair through the words of people, as Job's wife said to him (Job 2:9) and as Tobit's relatives said to him (Tob 2:16). Satan may also fight man with inner thoughts, but in every case by returning to God man finds his hope and strength.

3- After this verse there is the word Selah, which is a musical pause to give man an opportunity to reflect on the preceding words, that is, how hard the tribulation is and the doubts cast by human beings, so that this drives him to take refuge in God. The word Selah will come twice more in this Psalm (vv. 4, 8) for the same purpose.

Hasten to God in all your needs and tribulations, confident that He is very near to you and ready to keep you however much evils surround you. Do not believe thoughts of doubt and despair however logical they seem, for they are the lying words of Satan, because he tries to make you forget the power of God that is with you.
3- But thou, O Lord, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.

Shield: a defensive instrument in war, consisting of a piece of wood covered with leather and having a handle at the back, into which the warrior puts his hand, so that by moving his hand he can protect his head and body from the enemy's arrows.

1- David answered the doubts of his enemies by taking refuge in God, that is, he did not speak with them, because their speech is the speech of Satan, but spoke with God and said to Him, You are my shield, that is, my protection and my fortress, however much the enemies surround me, and You will also do a positive work with me, which is that You will glorify me and lift up my head. And this is what actually happened, for when Absalom dared to attack David, his army was broken and he died, and David returned with great honor to his throne.
2- The shield is the shield of faith (Eph 6:16); by faith David prayed to God, confident that He protects him from Absalom and those with him.

3- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, for the Son says to the Father, You are my shield and my protection, however much the wicked try to ensnare me in a word, or kill me, and after this You glorify me by the Cross, by which I accomplish salvation and redemption for mankind, and by my death I lift the sentence of death from those who believe in me, and then You lift up my head by the resurrection from the dead.
4- I cried unto the Lord with my voice, and he heard me out of his holy hill. Selah.
His holy hill: His temple, or the heaven of heavens, the place of His dwelling.

1- When David was driven out of Jerusalem, far from God's temple set on a hill, he was not troubled, because he was confident that his prayers and his cry toward God's hill would be answered by God and He would keep him, and even bring him back to his kingdom.

2- This verse, as a prophecy about Christ, means that the Psalmist, like every believer, cries out to Christ crucified on the hill of Golgotha, and He answers him and grants him salvation, and Christ is symbolized by the hill, as Daniel said that he saw a stone cut out without hands and it became a mountain (Dan 2:34, 35).
3- And we cry out in all our petitions to the Father through His Son Jesus Christ the Redeemer, crucified on the hill, in whom we trust, and He saves us from all our distresses.
4- And Christ cried out on the Cross and gave up the spirit, and God answered Him and raised Him from the dead on the third day.

5- Crying out is not only outward with the mouth, but can also be inward, as Moses cried out within himself and no one heard him except God, who said to him, "Wherefore criest thou unto me?" (Ex 14:15).
6- This verse carries the meanings of prayer, faith in God, His love and His answering us; therefore we find at its end the word Selah, to give man an opportunity to reflect on all this.
5- I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the Lord sustained me. 6- I will not be afraid of ten thousands of people, that have set themselves against me round about.

1- David felt that through his negligence he had lain down and slept in sin, when he sinned with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, but through repentance God removes his sin from him and raises him from it, and he awakes and returns to his sonship to God.

2- It is a clear prophecy about Christ, who lay down on the Cross and slept, that is, died, and by His lying down and His death gave rest and salvation to all who believe in Him, because sleep gives man rest. Christ died, and in Him we all died, to receive salvation with Him, as our teacher Paul the Apostle says, "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God" (Col 3:3). Then He awoke, that is, rose from the dead on the third day, to raise us in Him. So the believer does not despair if he falls into any sin and lies down in it, but believes that through repentance he receives justification from it and rises with Christ, to begin a new life in Him.

3- These words show the extent of the peace of heart: despite the severe tribulation and his exposure to death, he lay down and slept in God's hands, confident of His care, and then awoke in the morning, because the hand of the Lord upholds and sustains him, and he feels secure, whether in his palace inside Jerusalem or in the wilderness while pursued by Absalom. Consequently he does not fear the tens of thousands who follow Absalom from the people of the children of Israel, who have risen up against him to kill him; however ready and arrayed they are to fight him, with many weapons, all this is worth nothing so long as God protects him.
Remind yourself of God who is with you, by repeating prayers, to keep a calm heart, whatever problems surround you, because God is the one who protects you from them.
7- Arise, O Lord; save me, O my God: for thou hast smitten all mine enemies upon the cheek bone; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly.

1- Although David is reassured of God's support, he sees the multitude of the enemies and their strength; therefore he asks God, who has been long-suffering toward Absalom, to arise now to stop their attack, which has come near him. And he asks God to save him from the hands of his enemies, that is, to complete his salvation and keep them away from him. He trusts in God's power, so he asks Him to arise and stop the evil.

2- And David remembers the power of God, which formerly struck his enemies and all who tried to kill him, namely Saul and all who followed him, and God struck them on the jaw and shattered and broke their teeth, that is, removed their strength, and this means:
a- Their evil speech that they utter from their mouths against him.
b- Their strength, which is represented by their teeth, which want to devour him, but God shatters and breaks them, so they become worthless.
c- The jaw and teeth signify the power of those around Christ who persecuted Him and crucified Him, but they could not prevent His power, which bound Satan, and then His resurrection from the dead.

d- The jaw and teeth signify the innovations and heresies and blasphemies against the Holy Spirit that fought the Church, but God shattered them and stopped them by His power in the ecumenical councils and by the power of His holy children.
e- The jaw and teeth also signify the power of the demons that surround God's children in every generation, and God rescues His children from them.

3- God strikes the enemies on the jaw, that perhaps they may repent, but if they persist in their evil, He protects His children and His Church by shattering their teeth, that is, He deprives them of their strength with which they harm God's children.
8- Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people. Selah.
1- In the end David declares that salvation is from God alone and not from human power, so that no one depends on his own abilities or relationships, for no one will save him from evil except God.
2- He also affirms that God blesses His people and His children, and so long as God blesses them no one can harm them.

3- David asks salvation for himself from God, and also salvation and blessing for his people, whom Absalom led into the way of evil, for God is able to restore them to their peace and their life with Him. And this is what actually happened, for Absalom was killed in the war, and the people returned to God and submitted to David and restored him to his throne.

4- David ascribes the people to God, saying "thy people"; for he humbly sees himself as merely a small instrument in God's hand, and it is God who set him as king over this people, so he asks God with boldness to bless His people who belong to Him and to save David by His power, so that he may return to lead God's people.
5- "Selah", as we said, represents a musical pause, and it is an opportunity to reflect on the Lord who saves His children.

6- Thus we see that this Psalm begins with distress and ends with salvation; therefore the one who prays sings it at the beginning of the day, so that he is not troubled by any problems that may meet him this day, or those that are still with him from previous days, for God is able to save him from them and in the midst of them. This Psalm is also said at the end of the prayers of Great Friday, after Christ bore all our sufferings on the Cross, but by His death He saves us from all our sins.
Ask God with faith and be persistent with Him, for He is able to save you, and even to bless you, so that you lift up your heart in thanksgiving to Him always.
The life of righteousness To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm of David. "Hear me when I call" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, as is stated in the title.

2- We find a title for this Psalm that it is for the chief Musician, that is, it was sung by a large company of singers having a leader or conductor, so it is a Psalm for the people, sung before a large assembly, and this shows its importance.
3- We also find in its title that it is "on Neginoth", that is, it was sung to the accompaniment of an ancient stringed musical instrument called Neginoth, that is, having a number of strings.
4- In the Septuagint we find in its title "Unto the end, a Psalm of David."
The meaning of "unto the end" is as follows:

a- In (v. 1) he says "God of my righteousness", that is, God is the source of my righteousness, and "unto the end" means unto Christ, who became incarnate and in whom the righteousness of God appeared, and who is also the one who in the end reigns forever over the hearts of all who believe in Him, who sang and prayed to Him in their life on earth, so they deserve to sing with Him a new song in heaven forever.
b- Unto the end, that is, he sings throughout his life, because of the importance of the Psalm.

c- The end is David's victory over all his enemies surrounding his country and his subduing them to himself, and by this he is a type of Christ, who in the end subjects all His enemies, the demons, to Himself, for He bound them on the Cross, and at the end of days He casts them into eternal torment, declaring the victory of His children over them and glorifying them in heaven with Him.

5- The Fathers see that there is a connection between the third and fourth Psalms, for David feels sorrow in both; if the third Psalm is a lament of David when Absalom rose up against him, the fourth Psalm is an extension of it, because he says in it "How long shall my glory be turned into shame?" and "how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing?" (v. 2).

6- Some of the Fathers see that David said this Psalm during Saul's pursuit of him, when Michal helped him to escape (1 Sam 19:11-12), and God delivered him from the hand of Saul, so David thanks God, the God of his righteousness.

entries.section: (2) The call to mankind to the life of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 2- O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame? how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing? Selah.

1- David calls, with compassion, all mankind, first of them Saul, then Absalom, that they may not persist in their evils, turning his glory, because he is a king anointed by God, into shame by their pursuit of him, so that instead of being honored as a king he runs as a stranger everywhere, because he is threatened with death.
2- By this he speaks about Christ also, whom, instead of honoring Him, the Jews crucified on the Cross of shame; they did not honor Him as the King of kings but crucified Him as a wicked criminal.

3- David does not mean by this his own comfort, because he accepts everything from God, but he has compassion on sinners, the sons of men, for their separation from God and their wronging of His anointed, that is, David.

4- The cause of the evil of the sons of men is their love of lusts and pride and all the vain material things in the world. All of them are false and will pass away, but they will be called to account for their sins, so he calls them to repentance and not to persist in evil.
5- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause, so that man may review himself and repent of his sins.

6- He calls them sons of men so that they may reason as human beings and not be immersed in lusts like the animals, but he desires that they rise to spiritual thinking, care for the salvation of their souls, and live with God, so that they become like the saints, like angels on earth.

entries.section: (2) The call to mankind to the life of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 3- But know that the Lord hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the Lord will hear when I call unto him.

1- David alerts all mankind to an important truth, which is that God not only cares for David His godly one, or His chosen and holy one, as in the Septuagint, but also distinguishes him from the rest of mankind. This actually happened, for God rescued David from the hand of Saul, and gave him victory over him, since Saul fell into David's hand, and David pardoned him and did not harm him. In the end Saul died in the war, and David reigned in his place, and likewise God saved him from the hand of Absalom and gave him victory over him.
2- David here is a type of Christ, who lived as a man among mankind, but God distinguished Him by the working of miracles and powerful teachings, and then He died and raised Himself.
3- God always distinguishes His children and His people by His care for them and His work within them, so they enjoy God's presence with them on earth, as though they were in the Kingdom.

4- The prophet David declares another truth in this verse, which is that the Lord answers him when he prays to Him; prayer is a means available to God's children to enter into God's presence, and He answers them, and so they feel reassured however much tribulations surround them, and indeed they enjoy meeting God at all times.

5- David also declares to mankind that one of the most important means by which God shows His presence and power is His work in the one who fears Him and sanctifies his heart to Him. God declares Himself to those far from Him, either through creatures and the events of life, or through their seeing His work in His children, as David gave himself as an example in God's distinguishing him and answering his prayers, so that mankind may follow his example and believe in God and worship Him with all their hearts.

entries.section: (2) The call to mankind to the life of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 4- Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah.
1- The prophet David calls mankind to tremble, that is, to fear God, so that they do not sin; it is a call to keep away from sin and to fortify oneself in the fear of God.

2- In the Septuagint, that is, the Agpeya, it says "Be angry, and sin not", that is, let your anger be of the holy kind, in which there is no sin, as the Apostle Paul affirmed, quoting this same verse in (Eph 4:26). Holy anger is man's anger against his sins, his anger against evil and Satan, or his anger in the sense of firmness with those who err, until they repent.

3- He also calls mankind, if they have sinned in their anger, to regret it and repent when they go into their chambers before they sleep on their beds. The idea of repentance every day before man sleeps is an idea that every person needs, and David experienced it when he made his bed to swim every night with his tears (Ps 6:6); that is, it is good that man be still and examine his thoughts and the intentions of his heart every night and repent of them before God.
4- The verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for self-examination and repentance.

entries.section: (2) The call to mankind to the life of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 5- Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in the Lord.

After David called mankind to keep away from sin, then to pray to God, who answers and distinguishes His children, and after that to repent every day, he adds here a positive work, which is offering the sacrifices of righteousness, and they are:

1- Animal sacrifices on the altar of the Old Testament according to the Law of Moses, to offer repentance and love to God, all of which signify the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which we receive in the sacrament of the Eucharist, when we partake of the Body and Blood of the Lord, and so we are united with Him, and He works in us.
2- The slaughter of the predatory animals and the beasts within us, that is, sins, through repentance, so the heart is purified.
3- The slaughter of pride and self through humility.
4- Offering ourselves as sacrifices poured out in the service of others, so we bear with them and forgive them and labor and give ourselves for their good.
5- The sacrifice of emptying one's own will and relying on God and handing one's life over to Him, so we live reassured under His care.
6- The sacrifice of praise, which is the prayers and thanksgiving and praise lifted up before God from hearts and lips.
God awaits from you sacrifices of love in prayer, worship and service, so do not be negligent in seizing every opportunity to draw near to God and serve Him.
6- There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? Lord, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us.

1- God's goodness extends to all mankind, but the prophet David wonders that some murmur and say, who will show us goodness, as though God had done no good with them. There is another meaning, which is that the men of God and the prophets, in the Old Testament, longed to see the good things, which appear in the person of Christ incarnate in the fullness of time.

2- David answers the murmurers, who do not see God's goodness, and the righteous, who ask to see Christ, that God is able to lift up the light of His countenance upon His children, and in the Septuagint it says "The light of thy countenance, O Lord, hath shone upon us", and in the Greek translation "The light of thy countenance has been imprinted upon us", and this means that God shines and gives light upon His children with His light through the following:
a- The light by which man is distinguished from the rest of creatures through the spirit that is in him.
b- The light of faith in God and the enjoyment of His care and power.
c- The light of wisdom and discernment that He grants to His children, so they discern the good and reject evil and seek with love the depths of God.
d- The divine light and radiance, which is imprinted and pictured on the faces of God's children and shines upon others, so they see goodness through God's children who walk in righteousness.
3- The face of Moses was clothed with intense brightness when he met God, and so also God's children in every generation, God gives them grace and awe in the eyes of those around them.
7- Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased.

1- As a result of God's shining upon David's heart, he felt gladness and joy greater than any gladness man receives on earth; human beings feel gladness because of their possessions, such as wine and wheat, especially when they are abundant, but all the material things of the world pass away, so man is exposed to fluctuation between joy and sorrow, whereas the one upon whom God shines, He gives him lasting joy, which is higher and sweeter than every earthly joy.
2- This gladness in God's grace man receives through offering the sacrifices of prayer, worship and service, as we mentioned in (v. 5).
8- I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety.

1- Since David's heart is filled with gladness and peace, because he trusted in God to whom he cried out and by whose light he was enlightened, he is able to lie down and sleep reassured in God's hands; as he began his day with crying out to God in (v. 1) in the midst of tribulations, he trusts that at the end of the day he can lie down and sleep in rest, because he is in God's care, and therefore this Psalm is said in the prayer of the Veil at the end of the day.

2- Lying down and sleeping also apply to the repose of death; whoever lives with God a life of righteousness is in peace, so he does not fear death, but is alone and distinguished from other human beings in accepting death with reassurance in the hope of eternal life; thus in the Septuagint it says "Thou hast made me to dwell in hope."
3- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who lies down and sleeps in the tomb, alone among all mankind in that He will raise Himself on the third day.

4- This verse gives peace to man, for everyone who sleeps alone, away from people, sleeps reassured, because he is in God's hands and in the hope that He will raise him to pray and live with Him. It applies to everyone who lives among many who do not feel for him and for all that he suffers, but God is with him, so even if he lies down and sleeps alone and solitary, he is reassured that he will awake and live with God.

If only you would pray deeply at the end of every day to be rid of all your cares and feel God, so that you sleep reassured in the hope that you will awake to praise Him and live for your sole aim, which is the love of God.
The blessings of the righteous and the judgment of the wicked To the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David. "Give ear to my words, O Lord" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the Psalm.

2- In this Psalm David implores God for the sake of sinners, and shows God's delight in His righteous children and His blessings for them. On the other hand, it shows His distress at the wicked and His punishing them.

3- Some of the Fathers see that David wrote this Psalm out of distress over Ahithophel, who was David's counselor and then became counselor to his son Absalom, and gave counsel to kill David, so he is a traitor to his lord, whose service he enjoyed for many years. He is a type of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Christ, and also a type of the Antichrist, who appears at the end of days and opposes Christ.

4- This Psalm begins by speaking in the singular and ends by speaking in the plural, and this shows that everyone who prays has an individual relationship with God and at the same time is a member of the universal Church.
5- In the title of this Psalm we find "to the chief Musician", that is, it was chanted by the leader of the singers with a large company, and this shows the importance of this Psalm.
6- The title of this Psalm shows that it was chanted accompanied by wind musical instruments.

7- This Psalm is considered a lament of David before the betrayal of Ahithophel, and it suits everyone who suffers betrayal by his loved ones. But the Psalm ends with hope and blessing for the one who lives with God; therefore it is fitting that man pray this Psalm in the morning, so that he is encouraged and not hindered by the wrongs of others against him.

8- This Psalm is a morning prayer because it says "In the morning shalt thou hear my voice" ... (v. 3), that is, I rise early to You and pray; therefore the Church placed it in the prayer of Prime, so that man begins his day with it.
9- It also suits the believer who goes to church in the morning and bows down before God's sanctuary and says "But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy" ... (v. 7).
1- Give ear to my words, O Lord, consider my cry.

1- Since David feels severe distress, he speaks with boldness to God, asking Him to give ear to the words of his prayers, and also to consider, that is, to understand his cry; giving ear means to hear with attention, and then he asks Him to feel for him and understand what he is suffering, while the cry means prayers from the heart. In another translation it says "my thought" instead of "my cry", that is, he asks God to understand his inner thoughts, so it is an inner cry and not an outward one, that is, a deep prayer, like Moses, who was praying when he reached the Red Sea and saw Pharaoh and his army attacking him, and God said to him, why do you cry to me; because the prayer of Moses was from his heart like a cry (Ex 14:15).

2- David speaks with the boldness of a bride with her bridegroom, or a son with his father, so he does not beseech God to listen to him, but says directly, give ear, consider. He also speaks thus directly because he speaks as a father about his sinful children, and as a mother, who is the Church, about her children, so he speaks with boldness, that God may hear the prayers of all sinners who are in distress and have mercy on them.
2- Hearken unto the voice of my cry, my King and my God: for unto thee will I pray.
1- David also urges God to hear his prayer for himself and for his children, and for all who are tempted by betrayal or wrong from others.

2- In these two verses he gives God three titles: the Lord, my King, and my God, and perhaps this points to the Holy Trinity. He also asks God three times to give ear, to suffer and to hear, and this too is a symbol of the Trinity, and points to the persistence and boldness in David's prayer.
3- David asked God in his prayer for three things, which are:
a- Give ear, that is, listen with attention.
b- Consider; that is, understand after you have listened with attention.
c- Hearken; that is, do not neglect the words of prayer.
And that shows how much David needed God's intervention to support him and console him in his distress.

4- And when David says to God "my King", this is a declaration from David that God is the true King over His people and David is His deputy, and thus every person who has a position of leadership should understand that God is the Head and King, while man is His deputy who must walk faithfully, to give his account to the true King.
3- My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O Lord; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
In the morning: the early morning between dawn and sunrise.
1- David declares that he offers this prayer in the early morning, and the morning means that he begins with God before any other work and relies on Him before seeking the help of any human being.
2- The morning means activity, that is, man offers his best times to God, as the Scripture says, "those that seek me early shall find me" (Prov 8:17).

3- The morning also means spiritual enlightenment, as the Sun of Righteousness, that is, Christ, rises upon him, so he prophesies about Christ who comes with His wondrous light after the darkness of the night, which signifies sin and weakness; if man has fallen into sins during the night of his life, he awakes from his heedlessness and stands for prayer.

4- The morning means victory, because in it the resurrection of the Lord took place, who rose victorious and binding Satan. And in the morning the children of Israel looked and found the bodies of the Egyptians on the seashore, and they praised God (Ex 15). And in the morning the children of Israel, in the days of King Hezekiah, saw the bodies of the Assyrians of the army of Sennacherib, whom the angel had killed (2 Kgs 19:35).
5- And in the morning Christians offer their sacrifice, that is, the sacrifice of the Eucharist, in the Liturgies, which are the greatest of prayers.

6- David's faith appears in his waiting for God's answer when he directed his prayer toward Him, for he did not ask anyone else, because he trusts that God hears him and answers him. Perhaps by the spirit of prophecy he is speaking to us about Christ, whom he awaits to save mankind.

7- Here David makes clear that prayer is not only speech from one side, which is man toward God, but is also a dialogue, as man hears God's voice and His answer, whether through feelings within his heart, or verses that come to his mind, or in any other way; the one who prays ought to wait to hear the voice of God, and it is not right to leave without waiting for God's reply. This requires faith so that man may experience deep, true prayer.

God rejoices in your prayer when you offer it from all your heart, understanding what you utter, whether in the prayers of the Agpeya or your own spontaneous prayers, and be confident that He hears you and answers you, but at the right time for the salvation of your soul.

entries.section: (2) G does not take pleasure in evil

paragraphs.text: 4- For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee.

1- God did not create evil, but only good, and evil is the opposite of good, that is, when man separates himself from God, as Satan did, he becomes wicked, and does the opposite of God's commandments, just as night is the opposite of light; night is not something in itself, but merely the opposite of light, that is, when there is no light it is called night; so also evil is the opposite of good, and God is light and in Him is no darkness, and consequently He rejects evil. I cannot draw near to God while I keep evil within me, but I must hasten to repentance, that God may cleanse me.
2- The wicked man cannot draw near to God, since God does not accept him, and he too fears to approach Him, since he is going in another direction than the light.

3- The wicked man does not dwell with God, that is, he has no place in His Church, because he persists in evil. Therefore Paul commanded that the sinner of Corinth be set apart from the Church and put away (1 Cor 5:5).
4- It is understood, of course, that the wicked man has no place in eternity, for he does not dwell with God forever.

5- And if the wicked man does not dwell with God, then of course His children such as David cannot dwell with the wicked or mix with them in the close mixing that blends them together and influences them.

6- If the wicked are enemies of God, then I am not troubled if one of them wrongs me, for he is hostile to God; so I am reassured that God will defend me, and I continue to love him and ask Him to lift his evil from me, and if He wishes to discipline him that he may repent, let it be God's will.
When you commit sin, know that you have rejected God, and God has also rejected you; therefore hasten to repentance, so that you do not lose your place in His embrace and can also enjoy His care.

entries.section: (2) G does not take pleasure in evil

paragraphs.text: 5- The boasters shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity.

1- In this verse he adds a focus on a great sin, which is the root of many sins, namely pride; the proud person, or the one who boasts in himself, cannot draw near or stand before God. He also affirms God's hatred of the one who does evil, and he means God's hatred of evil, but He wants all the wicked to return to Him by repentance, so He accepts them and forgives them.

2- Pride blinds man's eyes to God and darkens his mind, so he thinks that what he does is right, and this makes him slip into many sins, and God hates all these sins; the tax collector received God's mercy by his humility and repentance, while the proud Pharisee added the sin of pride to his sins (Lk 18:10-14).

entries.section: (2) G does not take pleasure in evil

paragraphs.text: 6- Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the Lord will abhor the bloody and deceitful man.
In this verse he focuses on other sins after pride, which are:
1- Lying and deceit, which represent crookedness and deceiving others; whoever dares to deceive the image of God, that is, human beings, deceives God Himself, and he must perish.

2- The unjust and cruel, that is, the bloody man, is the one who wrongs the innocent, and this one too must perish, because murder is a terrible sin; therefore the Jews deserved destruction, because they killed the prophets who proclaimed the name of the Lord, and then killed Christ Himself, who came to redeem them.
3- This verse applies to Ahithophel, who plotted to kill his lord the king, and it also applies to Judas Iscariot the traitor, who delivered his Lord for the Jews to kill Him.

Whoever walks in evil against others not only makes enemies of them and of God, but is also an enemy to himself, because he condemns himself to destruction. It is spiritual blindness, which makes man not understand the gravity of the evil he is doing.
7- But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: and in thy fear will I worship in thy holy temple.

1- Although the wicked do not dwell with God, David, who believes in God, declares the conduct of the righteous, which is to draw near to the house of God, that is, the Church, which was symbolized by the Ark of the Covenant in ancient times, and then by the temple of Solomon. There David and every believer declare their submission by bowing down before God in reverence and fear, rejecting all evil from the heart, declaring their repentance before the holy God.
2- David declares that man is unworthy to enter the house of God, but it is God's mercy that allows man this great honor, because the house of God is the icon of heaven.

3- Bowing down means man's lowliness because of his sins, as he brings his head to the ground, but in confidence in God's mercies he rises from the prostration, that is, the metanoia, and stands before God in hope and with the boldness of sonship, as St. Basil the Great says.

4- Although David was driven out from before his son Absalom outside Jerusalem, in faith he is confident that he will return by God's mercy and enter His house and bow down before Him, as the prophet Jonah believed after him, while in the belly of the whale, that he would return and look upon God's temple (Jon 2:4).

5- Because of the greatness of this verse the Church arranged that every deacon and every worshiper who enters the church should say it, bowing down before the sanctuary and saying this verse, and many churches have even written this verse above their sanctuaries.
8- Lead me, O Lord, in thy righteousness because of mine enemies; make thy way straight before my face.

1- As David enters the house of the Lord and bows down, he feels his need for a life of righteousness, and he has no way to it except God Himself; indeed, he attaches righteousness to God, saying "thy righteousness", and distinguishes it from the righteousness of the world, that is, all that the world thinks to be good morals and right conduct, because God's righteousness is higher than all this, for it springs from man's entering into God's embrace, so he puts on God and is united with Him, and God leads him accordingly in the way of righteousness.
2- God's righteousness is being with Him, and consequently it is the Kingdom on earth; therefore we say in the Divine Liturgy "Guide us, O Lord, to Your Kingdom."

3- The wicked try to hinder David and every believer from the life of righteousness; therefore David asks God to remove the obstacles that the wicked placed in the way of righteousness, so that He makes his way toward God easy. Our enemies are the demons, who try to hinder us with evil lusts, preoccupations and problems, but they have no authority over us, because God is able to make our way to Him easy.

4- This verse shows David's longings for a life of perfection and the completion of his worship, so he asks for a way toward God in which He guides him, that he may reach the righteousness of God and not be hindered by all the hindrances of Satan.

Set your goal before you, which is the life of righteousness, have a spiritual rule, and ask God's help to lead you and support you, so that you enter every day into new depths in fellowship with God and live the Kingdom while you are on earth.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of G on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 9- For there is no truth in their mouths; their inward part is an abyss; their throat is an open sepulchre; they have polished their tongues. Polished: said of a sword or a knife, that is, making it sharp and smooth, and what is meant here is that the tongue is harmful.

Here the prophet David shows the gravity of the evil that his enemies do, and the enemies, as we said, are the demons and all who follow them in their conduct and slip into their evils, so he declares their gravity in the following:

a- "There is no truth in their mouths": that is, their speech is falsehood; they are deceivers, cheats, trying to lead God's children astray with hypocrisy, or wrong counsel, and with thoughts that seem good but contain the poison of death.

b- Their inward part is an abyss, that is, they are never satisfied with evil and injustice and wronging others, so they kill many with the arrows of their sins and swallow them up like a bottomless abyss. Consequently the demons cannot be appeased, but must be overcome by the power of God.

c- Their throat is an open sepulchre: the stench of death appears in their speech, like an open grave from which the foul smell rises. The meaning of this is that their speech harms God's children and leads them astray, like the heretics, or the proud and selfish, who harm those around them, and also the unjust, who suck the blood of the righteous, so they die, in order to achieve their personal interests.

d- They have polished their tongues, so their speech is sharp and painful to others, so they wrong God's children with insults and reproach, and also with hypocrisy and dissimulation, and they slaughter them as a sword wounds and slaughters and kills. And their tongues are polished, that is, trained in evil.

David shows the gravity of the wicked in order to ask great help from God, that He may protect him from them, and also to be careful to keep away from them, so that his heart is not influenced by their evils.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of G on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 10- Destroy thou them, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; cast them out in the multitude of their transgressions; for they have rebelled against thee.
1- In this verse David states the natural result of evil, which is that God will judge the wicked and call them to account for all their sins.

2- And when David says "Destroy thou them, O God" he does not mean personal vengeance for himself, but states a fact, which is the punishment of the wicked, perhaps this will alert the wicked, that they may repent.

3- David also declares that the wicked will fall into God's just hand because of all their plots that they devised against God's children. The plots of the wicked turn back upon their own heads and destroy them, as happened in the plot of Haman against Mordecai, for instead of Mordecai being hanged, the king hanged Haman on the same gallows that Haman had prepared for Mordecai (Esth 7:10).

4- Because of the multitude of the transgressions of the wicked, God will punish them by casting them into the abyss, that is, eternal torment, for every idle word man will give account of it in the day of judgment, how much more all his evil deeds.

5- Here David affirms that the evils of the wicked are rebellion against God, and not merely a wrong to a weak human being like David, and consequently the wicked await God's justice and His punishment.

Remember the punishment of sin, so that you keep away, not only from evil, but from everything that leads to it. And so long as you are striving on the way of repentance, be confident that God supports you and delivers you, however weak you are.

entries.section: (5) The blessings of G for the righteous

paragraphs.text: 11- But let all that put their trust in thee rejoice; they shall ever shout for joy, and thou shalt overshadow them; and they that love thy name shall be joyful in thee.

1- At the end of the Psalm David declares God's blessings for His children, and they are the opposite of the punishment of the wicked mentioned in the previous verse. God's children rejoice on earth in His care for them, and this is a pledge of their lasting joy in the Kingdom of Heaven. This joy is enjoyed only by everyone who trusted in God and not in himself or the powers of the world.

2- From the joy of God's children they shout, that is, they glorify God and proclaim His name before those around them; indeed, their joy in itself is the glorification of God in the midst of a world depressed because of sin.
3- The shouting is also the hymns of thanksgiving to God, which the Church lifts up every day and continues in forever, since the only work of God's children in the Kingdom is praise.

4- God's children also enjoy that God overshadows them, that is, He cares for them with His love and satisfies them with His presence with them. This too begins on earth, when they feel God's embrace and the warmth of His love, and then they discover new depths of His love in heaven.
5- Everyone who loved the name of God and trusted in Him and praised Him and lived for Him as his only goal is, of course, the one who will be glad and rejoice with Him forever.

6- For the sake of these joys and glories the Septuagint puts as a title for this Psalm "Unto the end, for her that inherits", that is, God's work in His children is completed unto the end, that is, forever in the Kingdom, and there He gives them their eternal inheritance.

7- We note in this verse that he speaks about the believers as a community, that is, the Church, and not as an individual, as he began his supplications at the beginning of the Psalm about himself and as an intercessor for his people, so he concludes the Psalm with the joy of God's children on earth and in heaven.

entries.section: (5) The blessings of G for the righteous

paragraphs.text: 12- For thou, Lord, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield. Shield: a piece of wood having a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand and moves this wood before his head and body, to protect himself from the arrows of the enemy.

1- In conclusion God declares His blessing to His children who hold fast to Him, and this blessing satisfies and suffices His children, so they need nothing from the world and are not troubled or disturbed over any gain or loss.

2- God surrounds His children and protects them, as the soldier protects himself with the shield; indeed, God is distinguished in His protection in that He is a shield on all sides, that is, complete protection. This shield results from God's favor toward them. And this shield is God's fatherhood and His love, which protect His children, so no one can harm them. And even if they walk in the midst of tribulations, God keeps their inner peace for them.

3- This shield, with which God surrounds His children, is also like a crown on their heads, which gladdens their hearts, as the Septuagint says, "Thou hast crowned us as with a shield of good pleasure."
4- And the shield, as Paul the Apostle says, is "the shield of faith" (Eph 6:16); everyone who believes in God and relies on Him, God surrounds him with His care.

If only you would look to the eternal recompense, so that your heart does not cling to the enticements of the world, but you bear tribulations and ask the help of God, who protects you and brings you to His Kingdom.

The acceptance of the cry of a penitent To the chief Musician on Neginoth upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David. "O Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, who lived the feelings of repentance in their deepest form.
2- This Psalm is the first of the seven penitential Psalms, which are (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143) as determined by St. Augustine.
3- It was prayed every day in the synagogues of the Jews, and is now prayed in the prayer of Prime in the Agpeya in the Coptic Orthodox Church, and is also prayed in the Latin Church.

4- The title of the Psalm shows that it was repeated by the chief Musician, that is, it is a Psalm for the people that the people repeat, and this is what happens in the Old and New Testaments, as we mentioned.

5- This Psalm was accompanied by a stringed musical instrument called Neginoth, which has eight strings; for the title of this Psalm in the Septuagint is Octave, that is, eight in the Latin language. Perhaps eight signifies the day of judgment, when God accepts the penitent and glorifies them with Him, especially as the Septuagint puts as a title for this Psalm "Unto the end", that is, unto the day of judgment.
6- At the end of the title of the Psalm it says "upon Sheminith", and the Sheminith is a degree among the registers of the voice.

entries.section: (1) The cry for help of a penitent

paragraphs.text: 1- Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.

1- David acknowledges that he is a sinner and deserves punishment, but he approaches as a penitent and with the boldness of sonship, asking that God deal with him in His mercy; he deserves rebuke and discipline, but if only it might be in God's mercy and not in His anger and displeasure, because God's anger and displeasure destroy the sinful man, since the wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23).

2- By this David's word does not contradict the saying of Paul the Apostle, "My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him" (Heb 12:5); indeed David himself said, "Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest" (Ps 94:12). David accepts discipline on earth but hopes that God will lift His anger from him on the day of judgment, for discipline by divine anger and displeasure is for the wicked on the day of judgment, whereas David, as a son, appeals to God's fatherhood to have compassion on him and rebuke him and discipline him with His love and mercy.

entries.section: (1) The cry for help of a penitent

paragraphs.text: 2- Have mercy upon me, O Lord; for I am weak: O Lord, heal me; for my bones tremble.

1- Here David confesses before God his weakness, and indeed the trembling of his bones, and bones are the strongest thing in a man's body, so he is no longer able to stand firm before God because of his sins, and this shows the extent of:
a- David's repentance
b- His sense of the fear of God.
2- David felt weakness in the following:
a- Spiritual weakness because of his fall into sin, which may be his fall with the wife of Uriah the Hittite.
b- Psychological weakness resulting from the fall into sin, "My soul is also sore vexed" (v. 3).
c- Bodily weakness represented by the trembling of the bones.
d- His fear of his enemies and those who trouble him (v. 7). Because of this weakness David asks God's mercy and healing with his whole being.

entries.section: (1) The cry for help of a penitent

paragraphs.text: 3- My soul is also sore vexed: but thou, O Lord, how long?

1- David asked for God's mercy and that He not discipline him in anger and displeasure in (v. 1) because of what he mentioned in (vv. 2, 3), namely his weakness and trembling and shaking. By this he represents the perfect penitent.
2- At the same time he urges God to answer quickly and not leave him in this hard state. But why does God delay in these situations and leave the penitent to suffer?
a- That their repentance may be completed with contrition, humility, tears and patience.
b- That they may be sure of the gravity of sin, and so keep away from everything that leads to it.
c- That their faith and hope in God and their spiritual fervor may increase.
d- That they may long for the life of righteousness, purity and spiritual loftiness.

entries.section: (1) The cry for help of a penitent

paragraphs.text: 4- Return, O Lord, deliver my soul: oh save me for thy mercies' sake.

1- At the end of his cry for help David expresses his intense longings for the return of God's tenderness and mercy upon him, that He not leave him in the torment of the consequences of his sin, but return to His former fatherly kindnesses toward him and rescue him from the sin into which he had cast himself, so that He mends his faults by divine mercy and saves him, that he may return to enjoy God's embrace and pray with joy and praise God.

2- David feels that sin makes him a stranger to God, so he asks God to bring him back to Himself after he had strayed, so he enjoys God's return to him in mercy, and is rescued and saved from all evil.
3- In God's return, which David asks for, there is the following meaning:
a- The return of His mercy to rescue him and save him instead of His anger and displeasure.
b- The bringing back of David, who had gone far away through sin, to return to God.
c- The return of God's appearing in David's life, that is, David enjoys, as a son, the sight of God.

In proportion to your repentance, humility and lowliness before God, His mercies overflow upon you. And do not be troubled if His answer is delayed, for His fatherhood wants you to complete your repentance in order to receive great salvation and joy.
5- For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?

1- David feels that sin separates him from God, so he is like one dead with regard to God, and like one who has fallen into the abyss of evil, so he cannot pray and praise God because of his immersion in sin.
2- Sin leads to eternal death if man does not repent of it, and consequently there in the abyss and hell no one can remember God and praise Him, because he receives his eternal punishment.

3- On the contrary, the bodily death of the righteous does not hinder them from continuing praise and prayer, but they set out in them with greater power, as we say in the Third Hoos and call the spirits and souls of the righteous who are in heaven to share praise with us (Dan 3:86, that is, the Additions to Daniel).

4- The meaning of this is that our life on earth is an opportunity for prayer and praise, but after death our opportunity for repentance, prayer and returning to God has ended, and what remains is facing eternal punishment.
6- I am weary with my groaning; every night I make my bed to swim; I melt my couch with my tears.

1- This verse shows the depth of David's repentance, which appears in his continual heartache over his sin, so that in the end he became tired psychologically and physically.
