It is clear that the repentance continued a long time, so that he said "I am weary"; in addition, he is still in the present making his bed swim and melting in his couch, that is, he continues in repentance. Repentance is not a moment but a life; however confident the penitent is of God's forgiveness, as a son he is deeply moved by what he did against his father through the sins he committed.

2- From the foregoing the importance is understood of man's examining himself every day, whether concerning a sin he committed recently or some time ago, so he finds his heart sighing and deeply moved, and so he lives the life of repentance.
3- His feelings did not stop at the limit of sighing, but his tears flowed abundantly, so that he said "every night I make my bed to swim", that is, he wept for many hours.

4- During the day King David was occupied with his responsibilities in running the kingdom, but his authority and works did not distract his heart from being alone at night to examine himself and stand before the just Judge, and so he wept much. For whoever can stand before God on the day of judgment, whatever his position, is nothing. Thus David was contrite with many tears, so he lived repentance in its depths and received countless blessings, and God led his life all his days. Although David defiled his bed once, he makes his bed swim every night. Although David committed his sin in the night and the darkness, he turns his night by the tears of repentance into a bright life with God, so he received God's countless mercies.

5- Repentance is considered a second Baptism; as man is immersed in the water of Baptism, so also man is immersed in a sea of tears that he pours out before God, when he examines himself and repents of his sins, so his life is renewed every day through the sacrament of repentance and confession. David did not say "I wet my bed" but said "I make to swim", and this means that his tears were very abundant, and his repentance consequently was deep.

6- David shows the multitude of his tears in that his bed was melting from the abundant tears, so he was not absorbed in his sleep but occupied with repentance every night, and on the contrary the lax soul, we express it in the interruption of sleep by the prayer of the Agpeya, that it is "cast down upon the bed of sins and negligent in subduing the body"; that is, David was on his bed as though in a sea, because the bed had melted from the multitude of tears, so David was swimming in these tears.
7- Mine eye is consumed because of grief; it waxeth old because of all mine enemies.
Consumed: sank in and was troubled.
1- David was angry with himself because of his fall into sin, so his tears flowed from his eyes until his eyes sank in with tears and were covered in deep repentance.
2- His eyes also sank in from his remembering God's anger against him because of his sin, so his tears flowed, seeking by repentance His forgiveness and mercies.

3- From the multitude of tears David's eyes were consumed, that is, his eyes became like the eyes of an old man, weak and wasted, as he remembered his spiritual enemies, that is, the demons who made him fall into sin, and he offered regret in many tears.

4- But the wonder is that David enjoyed peace of heart during this repentance and abundant tears, so he was able to continue in repentance all the days of his life, for he was confident of the word of Nathan the prophet that the Lord had put away his sin, but this did not keep him from seeing God, the fearful Judge, so there was mixed in his life intense regret, appearing in many tears, with the deep peace that God bestowed on him all his life. It is a peace that cannot be experienced outside repentance.

If, my brother, you need true peace, come with me, let us repent of our sins, and stand before the fearful God and let our eyes express what is within us, remembering the guilt of our sins, and so receive His forgiveness and His many divine blessings.
8- Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping.

1- When God gave peace in David's heart he became reassured and his faith was firm, so he called all his enemies the demons and all the wicked who followed them, who gloated over him and fight him, to depart from him. The power on which he relies is God, who heard his prayers, and even accepted his tears and his contrition before Him, and consequently God is with him, defending him and protecting him, after He accepted him and forgave his sins.

2- Here we see that weeping is a feeling of deep repentance that has a voice stronger than the ordinary cries of human beings, because weeping springs from heartfelt feelings, regretful and humbled before God.

3- And we see clearly the power of faith of one who repents and is contrite before God, for he speaks with confidence that God has heard the voice of his weeping, and this means that God gave him this confidence in his heart, until he uttered these words.
9- The Lord hath heard my supplication; the Lord will receive my prayer.

1- Supplications are prayers filled with humility and faith, for in them we lay hold of God, who cannot fail the one who clings to Him; therefore David said the Lord has heard, that is, in the past tense, for he is reassured that his supplications have reached God.
2- The humble receives God's mercies and tenderness, and God accepts his prayers and lifts him out of his tribulations, however great his weakness.
10- Let all mine enemies be ashamed and sore vexed: let them return and be ashamed suddenly.

1- David continues his speech in the faith of the penitent whose prayer God has answered, and he affirms that all the wicked and the demons will be ashamed and greatly afraid when they see God's power supporting him, since he has been changed from a rejected sinner into an accepted son, and his heavenly Father even protects him, all this through repentance.

2- Indeed all his labor in repentance and spiritual striving throughout his life becomes nothing before God's acceptance of him on the day of judgment, when He glorifies him with His saints, so all the long time he has passed through is not counted, for he says "suddenly", when he looks upon the glories of heaven.

3- On the other hand he makes clear that the demons around him, who rejoiced at his fall, depart and are ashamed and tremble when God suddenly appears and declares His acceptance of his repentance, for repentance transfers man from under the authority of the devil to the dignity and glory of God's children.
4- Perhaps David in this verse, when he shows the wicked their shame before God's power, is thereby calling them to stop their evils and repent.
Be confident that God hears your prayers and supplications and tears and that He is very near to you, to blot out your sins and strengthen you and raise you above the demons who made you fall.

God saves the innocent and punishes the wicked A Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the Lord, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite. "O Lord my God, in thee do I put my trust" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

1- Its writer: the prophet David, who had been exposed to evil speech and false accusations, so he said this Psalm, beseeching God to look upon his innocence and save him from the one who accuses him falsely.

2- Cush the Benjamite is a person whose name is not mentioned except in this place, and he is a known figure from the tribe of Benjamin, from which King Saul came, who pursued David and tried many times to kill him. It is understood from this that Cush was hostile to David, a follower, like most of his tribe, of Saul, and he said many words that were false accusations against David.

3- This Psalm shows David's supplication to God, who is able to rescue him from his enemies and show his innocence, because He blesses and rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked, and David believes in God and trusts in Him with all his heart.

4- We see in the title of this Psalm that it is a Shiggaion, from the word shajw, that is, sorrow, so it is a sorrowful lament that David offers to God from his soul affected by the wrongs of his enemies, and he takes refuge in God who is able to console him.

5- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, which prophesy about Christ the awaited Messiah, as it prophesied about the resurrection of Christ and His ascension, because David is a type of Christ, and it is also considered one of the royal Psalms, because it speaks about King David.
1- O Lord my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me.

1- We sense in David's words here his strong relationship with God, for he says O Lord, and by it he means Jehovah, the God of the whole world, and then he says my God, who is personally bound to him, and with whom he has boldness, and this encouraged him to ask in faith, despite the difficulty of the trials he is passing through.

2- Since David believed in God he relied on Him, and this gave him reassurance, despite the rising up of the wicked against him, so he prayed this prayer, seeking the help of God, who will certainly save him.

3- He asked for salvation and deliverance from those who pursue him, and perhaps by this he means Saul and his pursuits of him, or Absalom his son, who drove him out and removed him from his throne, and his emphasis on asking for salvation and deliverance shows:
a- The extent of the distress he is passing through.
b- His faith and his clinging to God.
4- We note David's love for his enemies in that he asked God to save him and deliver him from the hands of his pursuers but did not ask for vengeance on them.
2- Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver.
Rending: breaking violently.

1- If David spoke in the previous verse about his pursuers in the plural, in this verse he speaks about them in the singular, that is, the lion; because he is confident that Satan is his only enemy who moves the wicked against him. This helps David to love his enemies, and to be spiritually alert and rely on God, because his war is with Satan.

2- He used the comparison with the lion, since it is the king of the forest and the strongest of the animals, and he understands this well as a shepherd of sheep, guarding against the lion that snatches his lambs. On the other hand Saul, who pursued him, was a king, so he is like the lion. And Absalom also seized the kingdom from David, that is, both of them were kings.
3- And Peter the Apostle likens Satan to the lion, but David is confident that Christ, the true Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah, is the One able to save him from Satan.

It is good to know that your true enemy is Satan alone, so that you prepare with all your spiritual weapons of prayers, fasts and humility, and so defeat Satan easily, especially when you love the one who wrongs you and pray for him.
3- O Lord my God, if I have done this; if there be iniquity in my hands; 4- If I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me, and have plundered him that troubled me without cause.

1- David in his distress casts himself before God, declaring his innocence regarding his enemies, for he did not wrong them or do evil to them, and yet they rose up against him, pursuing him and trying to kill him. Consequently he beseeches God to save him, for the sake of his weakness and innocence. He satisfies divine justice by his innocence and asks mercy from the tender God, for the sake of his weakness.

2- David says "if I have done this" (v. 3), and he means pursuing and trying to kill any innocent person who did not wrong him, as Saul does to him, or if I have risen up against my father to kill him and seize his glory, as Absalom my son did to me.
3- David passed through the degrees of love in dealing with others, which are:

a- Meeting good with evil: "if I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me" (v. 4), and this is the degree of barbarism, that is, before the Mosaic Law, and even against the good human conscience.

b- Meeting evil with evil: "have plundered him that troubled me without cause" (v. 4), that is, he did not wrong the one who troubled him and wronged him. And this is the law of the Old Testament, that is, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth"

c- Meeting evil with good; this is what David did, for he asked for salvation and deliverance from the hands of his pursuers and did not ask for vengeance, but pardoned them, as he said to Saul after he fell into his hands (1 Sam 24:11), and as he asked Joab the commander of his army to deal gently with his son Absalom, who was trying to kill him (2 Sam 18:5). And this is the law of Christianity, that is, love of enemies (Mt 5:44).
5- Let the enemy persecute my soul, and take it; yea, let him tread down my life upon the earth, and lay mine honour in the dust. Selah.

1- David declares his deserving of humiliation and punishment if he has done the injustice and evils mentioned previously in (vv. 3, 4), for he is subject to divine justice and accepts God's discipline. But if he has not done evil, he asks God's mercies. David shows that if he had done these previous evils, he deserves what Saul or Absalom is doing to him, but if he has not done them, he is confident that the just God will save him.

2- Virtue is the new life with God, that is, David's love for his enemies and his doing good and not wronging without cause, so if David had done the opposite of these virtues, he deserves that his life be trodden down to the earth, that is, be humiliated and die. He also deserves to lose his glory as king.
3- By glory he also means his glorious eternal life, for he does not deserve it if he has not lived in virtue, and his glory is laid in the dust, that is, he goes down to hell.

4- And whoever does not practice virtues, his life is trodden down to the earth, that is, he becomes earthly and carnal, behaving like the rest of the wicked human beings, and has no glory before God.
5- The word Selah is a musical pause to reflect on the punishment of sin, to keep away from it and from all its sources.
Take care to examine yourself every day, to discover your sins, so you are purified and consequently deserve the divine mercies.
6- Arise, O Lord, in thine anger, lift up thyself because of the rage of mine enemies: and attend to me; in truth thou hast commanded.

1- When David felt the strength of the enemies who pursue him and their authority, his heart was not shaken because of his faith in the mighty God, whose power is above every power in the world. So he called upon the Lord in this prayer to arise in His anger, that is, to come out of His long-suffering to discipline the wicked, and declare His rejection of him, and thereby rescue David his son.

2- He also calls upon the Lord to lift Himself above the height of the anger of those who oppose him; if their anger is severe and has become rage, God's anger is stronger and rises above their anger to discipline them and show them their weakness, so that they do not persist in their evils.

3- The rising of God's anger against the opponents is not only to stop their anger and their opposition to David, but God is also able to draw them to Himself and turn them into believers in Him, submissive to Him, and consequently at peace with David, as God turned Abimelech king of Gerar to be at peace with Isaac and to make a covenant with him (Gen 26:26-30). And likewise Laban, submissive and at peace with Jacob and making a covenant with him also, so that Jacob would not harm him, because God was with him (Gen 31:48-52).
4- By David's prayer the battle was turned from a war between him and his opponents into a war between God and the wicked, and by this David was reassured, because no one can stand before God.

5- This verse speaks about Christ: "Arise" signifies the resurrection of Christ, which shattered the forces of evil, and "lift up thyself" signifies His being lifted up on the Cross to bind Satan, so the rising of God's anger above the anger of Satan, who opposes mankind, was accomplished on the Cross.
6- He calls upon God to attend to him, and this does not mean that God was heedless or forgetful, but he intends to move God's mercies, so that He rescues him from his enemies.
7- David relies on God's justice, so he says to Him: "in truth thou hast commanded", and here is David the innocent, wronged by his opponents, so he deserves God's mercies and help.
7- And the assembly of the tribes shall compass thee about: therefore return thou over it on high.

1- David speaks by the spirit of prophecy about the gathering of the peoples around God and His king David, and God's returning to reign over their hearts, and this is what happened after David reigned, and the kingdom in his days extended from the Euphrates to the river of Egypt, and the peoples submitted to him and to his God.
2- It is a clear prophecy about the faith of the tribes of the world in Christ, and not only the Jews, and His returning to reign over the hearts of those who believe in Him in the whole world.
3- It is likewise a clear prophecy about the ascension of Christ into heaven and His return to His glory, after He had completed redemption on the Cross and the resurrection from the dead.

4- Perhaps this verse signifies what will happen on the day of judgment, when Christ the Judge appears on high with all the nations of the world around Him, and He judges them, and then gathers His children who believe in Him, that they may surround Him in the Kingdom of Heaven and He glorifies them with Him.

Have a direct relationship with God in prayer, and cast all your problems upon Him, and be no more troubled by those who oppose you, because God is the one who protects you and defends you, and pray for those who oppose you, that they may return to God.
8- The Lord shall judge the people: judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me.

1- David the wronged hopes for God's justice to save him from his opponents, and he declares that God will judge all the peoples of the earth on the day of judgment. He does not fear the day of judgment, because he has reached a high degree of love for God, as the Holy Bible says, "perfect love casteth out fear" (1 Jn 4:18).
2- David as one wronged awaits his right which the unjust took from him, that God may compensate him for it, as a free grace, because there is no power in himself, but it is God's grace.

3- When David says "according to mine integrity" he means the relative perfection that he reached as a weak human being, that is, according to my obedience to Your commandments deliver me and reward me, that my heart may be comforted.
4- David hopes not only for earthly salvation from his enemies and opponents but for the eternal reward, where the heavenly glories are.
9- Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end; but establish the just: for the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins.

1- David asks God the Judge to judge evil and bring it to an end, and this is accomplished on the day of judgment, when God binds Satan and casts him into eternal torment, he and all the wicked who submitted to him.
2- David also desires that the wickedness of the wicked come to an end, and not the life of the wicked, that is, that God remove evil from them and they repent.

3- The purpose of David's request for the end of evil is that the just may not be shaken or exposed to going astray, and therefore David asks God to establish the just, and he means himself and every person who believes in God and lives with Him.

4- God the Judge does not need proofs like the rest of the judges, because He trieth the hearts and reins, that is, He knows the thoughts and intentions of every person, and He is the righteous and holy One, who easily uncovers any evil inside human beings and is repelled by it, so God judges evil.
5- The complete end of evil is the day of judgment, as we mentioned, and the complete establishment of the just is in the Kingdom of Heaven.
10- My shield is with God, who saveth the upright in heart.

1- In faith David declares that his protection is in God, and he likens this protection to the shield with which the soldier wards off the enemy's arrows from himself, for God is the One who protects His children from the arrows of the devil and his wars.

2- David is also confident that God is the Savior, but of those who believe in Him, and are upright, not only in their outward conduct but also in their hearts, that is, their thoughts and inner intentions.
Ask God's protection, confident that He loves you, and let your heart be upright before Him through repentance, so you are pure by His forgiveness and enjoy His love.
11- God is a righteous judge, and a God who is angry every day.
1- David reminds himself and all mankind that God will judge the whole world, and He is just, He will show partiality to no one, and He knows all the evils of human beings.

2- Because of the evils of human beings God is very angry every day, for human beings do not cease from wrongdoing, but He is long-suffering and does not punish them, giving them an opportunity for repentance. But if they are negligent He will be compelled to punish them, because He cannot abandon His justice.

3- Indignation declares the strength and sternness of God's anger; He is not silent because He is weak, but because He is merciful and long-suffering and wants everyone to return to Him through repentance.
12- If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready,

1- In His long-suffering God awaits the repentance of the wicked, and if they do not return to Him by repentance He draws His sword and whets it, that is, makes it sharpened and keen, ready to cut. This signifies God's warnings of punishment for the wicked. God is long-suffering; when He sees the wicked persisting in their evil He does not hasten their punishment, despite their disregard of His long-suffering, but also warns them with the words of the Holy Bible, that they may repent.
2- And to confirm God's warnings the prophet says that God bends His bow and makes it ready, to strike the wicked with His arrows.

3- God's word is the sword, which cuts off evil and strikes hearts like arrows, that they may be moved and return to Him by repentance. But if they insist on not returning, the sword or the arrows kill them. God was long-suffering toward King Saul, but he persisted in evil, so He warned him through the mouth of Samuel, and by his seeing David the righteous as an example of goodness, but Saul made light of all this, so he was killed in the war when he was struck by an arrow, and then fell upon the sword and died (1 Sam 31:3, 4).

4- The sword kills those who are near, while the arrows kill those who are far, so God warns the wrongdoers whose sins are visible and near and clear, and likewise those who hid their sins in their hearts, or were negligent and exposed to falling into sins that are still far from them, but will come to them and fight them.
13- He hath also aimed at him the instrument of death; he maketh his arrows burning.

God continues in His long-suffering, so He aims, that is, directs His fiery arrows, to kill and burn, that is, they must destroy and kill the wicked, but He has not yet sent them, but threatens to send them, that is, warns the wicked that they may repent, so His tenderness is wonderful beyond description, even toward those who oppose Him and disobey Him.
14- Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood.

1- In this verse he speaks about the stages of sin, which are conception, then travail, then birth, that is, evil increases and is perfected gradually, although the woman gives birth to a child, that is, a new life in the world, but the wicked gives birth to iniquity.
2- He put the stage of travail before conception, because the wicked person feels the pains of lust and evil within him from the beginning of sin.

3- On the other side, the just conceives and gives birth to the fruits of the Holy Spirit, and although he suffers the pains of travail, they are the labors of spiritual striving and with them are God's consolations, and in the end he receives great blessings.
15- He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. 16- His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.
Digged: dug.
A pit: a hole in the ground that fills with water from the rain, so it becomes like a pool.

The wicked digs a pit to make his brother fall, and he falls into it himself, that is, his evil returns upon his head. And this happened to many, such as Haman, who tried to kill Mordecai by hanging him on a gallows, and the king killed him and hanged him on the same gallows (Esth 7:9, 10); and likewise the two elders tried to kill Susanna, and the people killed them (Dan 14:28, 41); and also Absalom tried to kill David his father, and he was killed in the war (2 Sam 1:6-10); and Saul also tried to kill David and was killed in the war (2 Sam 18:9).

Do not think evil of others, whether by evil suspicion or by condemnation, lest God condemn you and the evil in you harm you, but make excuses for everyone, however they have erred, and pray for them.
17- I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness: and will sing praise to the name of the Lord most high.
1- David ends the Psalm with praise of God and thanksgiving to Him, because He delivers His righteous children and punishes the wicked.

2- It is beautiful that David begins the Psalm with reliance on God and ends it with praise, for this is the life of those who rely on God, that they rejoice in the end and give thanks to God, whatever the tribulations they passed through.
Let thanksgiving be an essential part of your prayer every day, that your heart may rejoice, and you may rejoice the heart of God, and His blessings upon you may increase.
The glory of God in man To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of David. "O Lord our Lord, how excellent is thy name" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears from the title.
2- It is a Psalm of praise and glorification of God.
3- This Psalm is sung before a large assembly, for we find in its title that it is for the chief Musician, that is, a group of singers sing it under the leadership of a conductor, or leader.

4- The repetition of this Psalm is accompanied by a musical instrument called the Gittith because it is taken from the city of Gath. By the Gittith may be meant a tune taken from the city of Gath, and it is the tune of this Psalm. By the Gittith may also be meant a winepress, because Gath is a Hebrew word meaning a winepress, and in the Septuagint the title of this Psalm is written "for the winepresses", and this points to Christ, who passed through the winepress alone and died for us, as appears in (v. 5), where it says "thou hast made him a little lower than the angels", that is, Christ in His death on the Cross was without honor because of His love for us.
5- This Psalm shows the position of man in the heart of God and God's honoring him, for he is the head of all creation.
6- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, because it speaks about the glorified Christ, who condescended by His Incarnation to redeem us.
7- The New Testament gives attention to this Psalm, for it quoted from it three times; Christ Himself mentioned it in (Mt 21:16) and Paul the Apostle quoted from it in (1 Cor 15:27), (Heb 2:6-8).

8- In the original Hebrew this Psalm has eight verses, and the name Jehovah is mentioned in the first and the eighth verse, and this points to the fact that Jehovah is the First and the Last, because the number 8 signifies eternity. (1) The greatness of G (vv. 1-3)
1- O Lord our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens.
1- God's glory is wonderful, appearing in all His creation that is on the earth.
2- God's majesty and greatness are above the heavens, for they surpass all creation, earthly and heavenly.

3- The earth signifies the human body, and the wonder appeared in the Incarnation of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, for He is higher than the heavens, which signify the spirits of human beings.

4- God's work shines in the earth, that is, the body of every person, and above the heavens, which are the spirits of human beings; and while God's glory is manifest in all His creation, His glory is magnified in man, with his spirit and his body.

5- The Lord is our Lord, that is, our Lord, we who believe, and He has a special glory in the spirits and bodies of His saints, for they are His children in a special way, so He gave grace to their spirits to cling to Him in prayers, and in their bodies, so they worked miracles, and even after their death the bodies of many of them did not decay.

6- When man feels the love of God, who is glorified in him, he praises Him, and his praises rise above the visible and perceptible heaven, and he joins with the angels in praising God, whose majesty is lifted above the heavens, that is, in the heaven of heavens.
2- Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou founded praise because of thine adversaries, that thou mightest silence the enemy and the avenger.
Adversaries: your enemies, that is, the devils.
1- Who are the babes?

a- The young in age who gathered around Christ and whom the disciples tried to keep away, but He said, "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me" (Mt 19:14). Indeed He praised them, for He asked His followers to become like them, saying, "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 18:3).
b- They are the humble, who are like children in their simplicity.
c- They are those born of the font of Baptism, that is, the beginner believers, of whom Paul the Apostle said, "I have fed you with milk" (1 Cor 3:1, 2).
2- Who are the sucklings?
They are those who suckle from the word of God in the Holy Bible.

3- This praise that rises from human beings silences the evil of the devils and binds them, for they are unable to fight the humble and the simple, and cannot take vengeance on them, because they love God and praise Him, and He protects them. A clear example is the babes in the eyes of people, that is, the disciples, for they were weak in their learning and position, but they believed in God, and He worked through them, and they preached in the whole world and brought many souls to Christ (1 Cor 1:27, 29).
3- When I behold thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast made;

1- David joins with the babes and sucklings in praising God, and declares that the reason for his praise is the works of God that He created, especially the heavens and what is in them of moon and stars, each of which has its course in which it travels with precision and does not collide with another, lest hard disasters occur.

2- The heavens signify loftiness, that is, the spiritual life that is high above earthly things and lusts, and the moon signifies the Church, and the stars signify the Apostles and the saints and all God's children, and all of them are lit by the light of the sun, which signifies Christ the Sun of Righteousness; therefore he did not mention the sun here, because it points to Christ.

3- God made the heavens with His fingers and all that is in them such as the moon and the stars, and he shows that He made them with precision and also with ease, because precision suits fingers, and he did not say with His hands.

4- The fingers of God signify the work of the Holy Spirit, as Luke the Evangelist expressed it (Lk 11:20). The Holy Spirit is the One who created the heavens and what is in them, and He is the One who raises the spiritual life and works in the Church and the saints, who are symbolized by the moon and the stars.

Contemplate the nature around you to see God clearly in it, and He speaks to you about Himself through it, as He spoke to the prophet David and he expressed it in (Ps 19). (2) The dignity of man (vv. 4-8)
4- What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?

1- David wondered at God's care for man in creating him in His image and likeness, and likewise His providence for him in ordering all his needs. In addition He made him head of all creation; God created it for his sake, to serve him and guard him and help him to reach salvation.

2- David saw God's spiritual care for man in arranging salvation for him after his fall, for He taught him the idea of sacrifice. And He was glorified in godly men, to be an example for mankind, such as Enoch, Noah, Job, Abraham ... then He sent him prophets and gave him commandments and a written Law, to call him to repentance and show him his need for salvation.

3- David saw by the spirit of prophecy the Incarnation of Christ the Son of Man, that is, His condescension in taking the body of a man to visit mankind, then His life among human beings, to be an example for them, and His redemption and resurrection and ascension into heaven, to prepare a place for man and take him up with Him. It is a care and visitation that surpasses understanding.
5- For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and splendor.

1- God created man with great glory, a little lower than the great angels who are in the heavens, because he has a material body liable to change and death, but if he lives in righteousness and repentance, he will be transformed into a spiritual body united with his spirit and will live forever like the angels. This lack in man is temporary in this life, but in eternity he will be in the glory of the angels.

2- God crowns man with the glory and splendor of the virtues, the good works, and every spiritual relationship with God that he acquires through his life on earth, especially during the tribulations that he bears with thanksgiving.

3- This verse is a clear prophecy about Christ, who condescended by His Incarnation, so that in form He became lower than the angels, but He showed His glory by His resurrection and His ascension into the heavens, and then was crowned with glory and honor, when He prepared a place for His children in heaven, and He, like a slain lamb, stands in their midst, as the Book of Revelation tells us (Rev 5:6), declaring His love poured out for His children.

6- Thou madest him to have dominion over the works of thy hands; thou hast put all things under his feet: 7- All sheep and oxen, yea, and the beasts of the field; 8- The fowl of the air, and the fish of the sea, and whatsoever passeth through the paths of the seas.
1- God alone is the possessor of authority, and He gives it to His creatures such as man.

2- God gave man complete authority over all animals and plants, but he lost this authority by his fall into sin. And when he repented God restored it to him in the New Testament, as the two lions submitted to St. Anthony and dug a grave for St. Paul the Hermit, and as the serpent submitted to St. Barsoum the Naked and lived with him in the cave.

3- Man was able to overcome wild beasts by hunting them with tricks and deceit, or by frightening them, as in the circus, or by killing them using various weapons; this is an incomplete authority, but it is completed if the holiness of this man increases, as in the examples mentioned previously.

4- This authority was given to man in completeness in Paradise, and he regains it partially in proportion to his holiness. But on the other hand these verses speak about Christ, God incarnate, who has complete authority over these creatures, because He is their Creator.
5- The creatures mentioned in these verses have spiritual symbols, which are:
Sheep: signify the flock of Christ that is subject to Him; or the Jews who believed in Christ.
Oxen: signify the leaders of the Jews who bore the yoke, that is, the responsibility; as it says, "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn" (1 Tim 5:18).
Beasts of the field: signify the Gentiles who believed and submitted to Christ, or the distant sinners who repented and returned to God.
Fowl of the air: signify the angels and the saints soaring in the heaven of spiritual things.
Fish of the sea: signify those who are tossed about amid the lusts of the world, but through their repentance they enjoy the salvation of Christ.

6- There is another reflection on these creatures, which is that the sheep and oxen and beasts signify the body and its lusts, while the fowl of the air signify self, boasting and pride, and finally the fish of the sea signify the circumstances around us that oppose us. Over all these God gave us authority to subdue them by our spiritual will and so enjoy His work in them.

If only you would subject your abilities to the love of God and His service, and not be troubled by the multitude of your falls and the wars of the devil; for you are able by the power of God to enjoy with your whole being the God who dwells in you.
(3) The glory of G (v. 9)
9- O Lord our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!

1- When man sees the grace of God that has been given to him in honoring him and giving him dominion over the various creatures, his heart is moved to thanksgiving and glorifying God, for glory is not for man but for God alone.

2- Thanksgiving and praise are man's life; the Psalm began with them and also ends the Psalm with the same words, for thanksgiving and praise are a life and not merely an event, nor do they have a set time, but are at all times.

3- If God has set man as head of all creation, his basic work that endures is glorifying God, and indeed leading all creation in glorifying Him, as is clear from the Third Hoos, which the Church prays every day in her Midnight Praise.

If only you would not forget to glorify God every morning and every evening, for praise is the true life on earth and is the only work in heaven. Taste praise here, that you may have a place among those who praise in heaven.
A hymn of victory To the chief Musician. On the death of the Son. A Psalm of David. "I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, and it was repeated by the chief Musician followed by a group of singers.
2- It is a Psalm of praise and thanksgiving that David said after one of his victories.

3- In the Beirut translation, taken from the Hebrew text (which we have in hand), there are two Psalms numbered 9 and 10, whereas in the Septuagint the two Psalms are joined in one Psalm, the ninth, for the following reasons:
a- The two Psalms are written on the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and the tenth Psalm is an extension and completion of the letters of the alphabet found in the ninth.
b- The meaning is connected between the two Psalms, for the ninth Psalm speaks about victory in external wars with enemies, and the tenth Psalm speaks about the internal enemies who wrong the poor.
c- The two Psalms speak about the struggle between good and evil.
d- The two Psalms speak about tribulations.
4- The title of this Psalm is "on the death of the Son", and this has the following meaning:
a- On the death of David's son by Bathsheba, or on the death of Absalom.
b- Since it did not specify who the Son is, it may be a prophecy about the only-begotten Son, that is, Christ and His death on the Cross and His redemption of mankind.
And in the Septuagint the Psalm is titled, instead of the death of the Son, the mysteries of the Son, that is, the mystery of redemption and all it contains of blessings for mankind.

5- In the Septuagint there is in the title "unto the end", or "to the consummation", and what is meant by it is that this Psalm speaks about the son, that is, the people of God, not only the Jews in the Old Testament but the Christian people who remain sons of God forever in the Kingdom, because they believed in Christ and lived for Him.
6- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- I will praise the Lord with my whole heart; I will shew forth all thy marvellous works.

1- Praise and thanksgiving from the whole heart, and this results from David's love for God with his whole heart; thanksgiving has degrees, the highest of which is thanksgiving from the whole heart, for a person can be thankful and at times murmuring, or give thanks seeking more gifts, or give thanks superficially, that is, with coldness and weak feelings of love.

2- It is clear that David is rejoicing because of his victory, and the first thing he felt was to thank God. This is the mind of the Church, that she always begins her prayers, like the prayer of the Divine Liturgy, with the prayer of thanksgiving.
3- As a result of praise and thanksgiving, man longs for others to join with him in giving thanks to God, so he tells them of His wonders, so that they love Him, and then they give Him thanks.

4- Whoever loves God with all his heart does not speak about some of the divine wonders but talks about all the works of God with zeal and power that influence those around him, and does not leave any opportunity without speaking in it about God.
2- I will be glad and rejoice in thee: I will sing praise to thy name, O thou most High.
1- Praise and thanksgiving necessarily produce joy within man and delight in fellowship with God.

2- The man who praises feels the loftiness of God and His elevation above human beings, not only in power but in love and perfection in all attributes, so he increases in zeal for praising Him and singing to Him.

3- Joy in God and praising Him gives man steady feelings of joy, so he continues praising God even within tribulations, and experiences new depths in fellowship with God that he does not see outside tribulations, because God rejoices greatly over the one who praises Him at all times and especially in tribulations, so He pours out on him consolations that cannot be expressed.

4- The joys of the world are temporary and leave within man a sense of deprivation and distress, but joy in God is settled within man and results in greater longings toward God and greater enjoyment of delight and gladness.
If only you would get used to thanking God in all your prayers and add to your prayers a portion of the hymns of the Church, to experience new depths in the love of God.
3- When mine enemies are turned back, they shall fall and perish at thy presence.
1- The enemies are the demons, or the wicked who follow the demons in their thinking.
2- At thy presence, that is, before the works of God and His power.
3- Satan's retreat before the face of Christ after He overcame him in the temptation (Mt 4:10); this is the retreat of the enemies backward.

4- And when Peter tried to prevent Christ from accepting suffering and death, to complete redemption, Christ rebuked the thoughts of Satan that were in him by saying, "Get thee behind me, Satan" (Mt 16:23); this too is the retreat of the thoughts of the enemies before Christ.

5- And when the officers of the temple came to arrest Christ in the garden of Gethsemane and He asked them whom they sought, and they said to Him Jesus of Nazareth, He said "I am he"; and they went backward and fell to the ground (Jn 18:6).
6- And when Christ, the second Adam, became incarnate and lived without sin, the first Adam, who fell through his weakness, retreated before Him.
7- When believers hold fast to Christ, Satan fears them and retreats and falls backward before the power of God that is in them.
4- For thou hast maintained my right and my cause; thou satest in the throne judging right.

1- In faith David spoke with God, who saves him from his enemies, and even gives him victory over them, and he thanks Him that He accepted his petition and gave him his right and victory, because he was wronged. God, seated on His throne in heaven as a just judge, gave judgment in favor of David the wronged.

2- David asks on behalf of every believer that God sit on His throne within his heart and judge and pass sentence on evil thoughts and every evil intention and feeling, so that the whole heart is God's and all darkness flees from it.

3- David looks by the spirit of prophecy and speaks in the name of the Church, asking Christ to sit on His seat or His throne, which is the Cross, so He binds Satan and passes judgment to free those who believe in Him, and brings them up from hell to Paradise. He takes Adam and his children, among them David, to enjoy with Him in heaven.

4- David also speaks by the spirit of prophecy about Christ the just Judge, who sits on His seat on the day of judgment and judges for the believers in their cases and their wrongs, and compensates them for everything in the Kingdom, and also passes the sentence of punishment on the wicked in eternal torment.

5- Thou hast rebuked the heathen, thou hast destroyed the wicked, thou hast put out their name for ever and ever. 6- O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end: and thou hast destroyed cities; their memorial is perished with them.

1- David thanks God, who gave him victory over his enemies, and rebuked them from before him, and destroyed them and caused their memory to cease despite their great power, for God supports the weak and gives them victory, because they are His children who believe in Him.
2- God dwells in the heart of His children and rebukes evil thoughts and destroys Satan, who is the wicked one, and annihilates him, that His children may love Him with all their hearts.

3- David also speaks by the spirit of prophecy about Christ crucified, who bound Satan and rebuked sins by His death on the Cross, and demolished Satan's fortresses and cities, that is, the great evils, and so abolished their authority over man, who believes in Him and lives for Him.

4- These two verses apply to Christ the Judge on the day of judgment, who rebukes the nations, that is, the wicked, and casts them into torment, and destroys Satan the wicked one by casting him into Gehenna, and blots out his name and annihilates him, so he has no place in the Kingdom.

5- God blots out the names of the wicked by their death and destruction, and likewise if man repents and believes in Christ He blots out his old life and gives him a new life, and this happens in the sacrament of Baptism, when the old man dies and a man with a new nature is born. Therefore many take care to give their children new names at Baptism. This change happened with Saul of Tarsus, when he believed in Christ, so he left his former life, and his name was even changed to Paul the Apostle, to live as a servant and apostle of Christ, after having been hostile to the Church.
7- But the Lord shall endure for ever: he hath prepared his throne for judgment. 8- And he shall judge the world in righteousness, he shall minister judgment to the people in uprightness.

1- God remains the Judge, seated on His throne forever, that is, to eternity, so He continues to reward the righteous in the Kingdom with glories rising without end. And on the other side He tortures the wicked with torment rising forever.

2- God judges the world and all the peoples in it with justice and uprightness, so He shows partiality to no one and calls every person to account according to what he received. He judges the Jews according to their Law, and the Gentiles according to their conscience. And every person according to his abilities and circumstances, for the one who knows more is required to give more.

3- God's sitting on the seat of judgment reminds us of the cover of the Ark of God's covenant, which was called the mercy seat, for God's justice is perfect and at the same time His mercy is perfect, because He has mercy on the penitent who return to Him, and receives them in His Kingdom.
If God is just, then you must repent, O my soul. Humility draws God's mercies, so He lifts your sins from you, and even supports you on the way of life so that you may enjoy His love forever.

entries.section: (3) The Lord the refuge and Savior

paragraphs.text: 9- The Lord also will be a refuge for the contrite, a refuge in times of trouble. 10- And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, Lord, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.

1- God is not only just but a fortress and refuge for those who believe in Him, so He protects them from evil, and although they live in the midst of the wicked world, they are in God's protection and no one can harm them except by His permission.
2- God protects only the humble, but the proud He abandons, because they reject Him and rely on themselves, as the tax collector was accepted, whereas the Pharisee received nothing of God's mercies.

3- God's protection appears clearly in tribulations, where people abandon one another, each one caring for himself, but God remains the tender One, who welcomes His children who take refuge in Him and protects them.

4- God is a refuge for everyone who seeks Him, but those who do not seek Him and do not move toward Him will not find protection, that is, the lazy and the negligent do not enjoy God's protection. But whoever holds fast to the name of God is in safety, as Solomon says, "The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Prov 18:10).
5- The one who is accustomed to repeating the name of God in prayer and praise finds it easy to rely on God, so he is not shaken before tribulations but takes refuge in Him with complete faith.
6- People in general, and believers in particular, are exposed to various tribulations, but they do not lose their peace, because they have God as a refuge and fortress, and so they rely on Him.
7- The one who takes refuge in a refuge hides in it; so the one who hides and denies himself and shows God is the one who enjoys divine protection.

entries.section: (3) The Lord the refuge and Savior

paragraphs.text: 11- Sing praises to the Lord, which dwelleth in Zion: declare among the peoples his doings. 12- For when he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble.

1- God is long-suffering toward the wicked and allows some of His children to be martyred, so He takes them to Himself and brings them up to heaven, but He requires of the wicked the blood of the righteous, as He required of Cain the blood of his brother Abel, when He said to him, "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground" (Gen 4:10).
2- God is long-suffering and delays the answering of prayers, but He does not forget or neglect any petition lifted up to Him.
3- Because of God's power and justice and love for His children, His children praise Him in every place and sing to Him.
4- God's children tell the people around them of God's works by means of:
a- Their righteous life, which gives light to others and shows God.
b- Their conversations with others, which show God in an indirect way.
c- When they meet people who suffer from problems they encourage them to take refuge in God.

entries.section: (3) The Lord the refuge and Savior

paragraphs.text: 13- Have mercy upon me, O Lord; consider my trouble which I suffer of them that hate me, thou that liftest me up from the gates of death: 14- That I may shew forth all thy praise in the gates of the daughter of Zion: I will rejoice in thy salvation.

1- David declares that sin humbles man, and the enemy Satan tries not only to humble man but to shed his blood, as in (v. 12), but God's mercy and His looking with compassion upon His children delivers them from the hands of Satan and lifts them from the gates of death, which are sins.

2- David was exposed to death in his war with the enemies, but his reliance on God saved him from their hands, so he is an example of the man who prays, believes in God and relies on Him, who does not fear tribulations.

3- David feels that his basic work, as a believer in God, is to praise Him in His temple that is in Zion, that is, Jerusalem, which signifies the Church in the New Testament, and also the Kingdom of Heaven.
4- This praise lifted up before God makes the believer joyful and a light to the world around him, since everyone knows that the cause of his joy is his relationship with God.

Be confident of the power of God that is with you, so that you are not troubled by the wars of the devil or your falls, but hasten to repentance and prayer, and you will find God's mercies and His protection, and He will lift you from every sin.
15- The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken.

David shows that evil is on the heads of the wicked, for while they devise schemes against the righteous they themselves fall into them. If they dig a pit for the righteous they themselves fall into it, and if they cast a net their feet are entangled in it and they cannot escape from it. This verse is a confirmation of what the Psalmist said in (Ps 7:15, 16).
16- The Lord is known; He hath carried out a sharper judgment: the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands. The striking of the strings. Selah.

1- David comments on the verse that shows that the evil of sinners comes upon their heads, so he says that the Lord is "known", and he means known by His justice, for He repays the wicked who wrong the righteous.
2- Sharper: very keen, so it is said "sharper than a two-edged sword"

What is meant by a sharper judgment is that God's judgment is severe on the wicked who persist in their evils, so He punishes them not only after their death, but also in their lifetime their evil comes upon their heads.

3- Here he affirms that the wicked is snared in the evil that he prepared for the righteous, that is, he faces divine punishment from the schemes that he devised, as the priests and elders of the Jews devised and sentenced Christ to crucifixion, and when He was crucified and redeemed mankind their evil came upon their heads, that is, the death of Christ condemned them, as it saved the penitent and those who believe in His name.
4- The striking of the strings here means that the strings are struck declaring the severity of God's judgment, followed by a musical pause expressed by the word Selah.
17- The wicked shall return to the abyss, and all the nations that forget God.

He states in conclusion that the punishment of the wicked is to be cast into the abyss, that is, eternal torment. Their being cast into eternal torment is a natural extension of their evils, for they lived in the pit of sin far from God, so they finally deserved punishment in the eternal abyss; they return to the abyss in which they lived during their life; death does not have mercy on them, because they rejected God and forgot Him in their lives, and it does not lead them to a better place, but to their natural place far from God.
18- For the needy shall not alway be forgotten: the expectation of the poor shall not perish for ever.
1- Here God's love and care for the weak and the poor and all who suffer injustice or distress appears.

2- God is long-suffering toward the wicked and sometimes does not vindicate the wronged quickly, until their crown is complete, and at the same time the cup of His wrath against the wicked is filled. But He cannot neglect or forget the weak who seek Him; therefore their hope is firm in God.
3- By the poor and wretched he also means the humble, that is, the poor in spirit; these God supports and prepares for them the Kingdom with all its glories, as He said in (Mt 5:3).
19- Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail: let the heathen be judged in thy sight. 20- Put them in fear, O Lord: that the nations may know themselves to be but men. Selah. Prevail: be arrogant.

1- David asks God to answer and arise from His long-suffering to stop the pride of the wicked who are proud because of their authority and their wrongs to the righteous, in order to show God's justice and so that the righteous do not faint and doubt.
2- David urges God to judge the wicked who are far from Him, that is, the Gentiles, and he does not hate the wicked but wants the declaration of God's justice, to establish the righteous.
3- He asks God that the wicked fear, so they know that God has authority over them, and that they are merely men like others, so they do not frighten or threaten others or wrong them.
4- The word Selah calls us to reflect on the power of God and the fear of Him, that we may repent and keep away from evil.

Do not persist in evil however easy it is, and do not wrong another in order to give yourself rest; for God the Judge sees everything, so return to Him by repentance lest He terrify you by His power, and have mercy on those around you to receive God's mercies. God rescues the poor "Why standest thou afar off, O Lord?" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

1- The Fathers consider this Psalm an extension of the previous Psalm, indeed it is one with the previous Psalm in the Septuagint, as we mentioned. Consequently its subject is the wronging of the poor and how God rescues them, for it deals with the problems that occur to God's people from within, after he told us in the ninth Psalm about the enemies' wars against God's children, that is, external wars.
2- Since this Psalm is an extension of the previous Psalm, its writer is the prophet David; consequently it has no title in the Holy Bible.
3- This Psalm suits everyone who suffers distress, or the Church when she passes through sufferings and cries out to God her Savior.
4- This Psalm makes clear that evil, or good, springs from the heart, so it must be purified.
1- "Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? Why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?"

1- David describes his feeling in affliction, which is that he does not sense God near to him, as though He had hidden Himself, although he trusts in His presence and nearness. But the feeling of affliction envelops a person and covers him, just as Christ on the Cross felt, as man, the severity of affliction and pain and the distance of God from Him, though He is God united with man. He expressed this affliction by saying, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Mt 27:46).

2- The feeling that God is far from a person in the midst of affliction may be because the person has distanced himself from God, and not the reverse. But whoever continues in prayer and crying out, like David, will surely feel God's nearness to him, as David expressed this in the same psalm in (v. 17).

3- God sometimes leaves a person for a time in the midst of affliction, not out of neglect, but to stir his feelings so that he cries out to God and receives greater blessings. In this way God tests his faith and blesses him with abundant blessings.

4- A person's feeling in afflictions that God is far from him makes him not only cry out to Him, but also leave his lusts and sins and renounce the world, so that he is purified from evil and filled with the grace of God.
Let the affliction you pass through be a motive for you to much prayer and crying out to God, so that you grow spiritually and experience new depths in the love of God.
2- "In the pride of the wicked the poor is burned; they are taken in the plot that they have devised."
1- The wicked man is full of evil thoughts and deeds, and in pride he persists in his evil to harm the poor and try to destroy him; that is, the wicked man has neither compassion nor love.

2- God allows the evil of the wicked only to the extent that benefits the poor. But He makes the evil of the wicked come upon his own head and his plots harm himself, as this meaning was confirmed in (Ps 7:15, 16; Ps 9:15). This meaning is repeated often in the Holy Bible, such as Babylon, which brought down many and was utterly destroyed, as the Book of Revelation tells us (Rev 17:5, 6; 18:6), and Ahab, who wronged Naboth, and the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, so the dogs also licked the blood of Ahab, as Elijah had told him (1 Kgs 21:19).

3- God disciplines the wicked by making his evil come upon his own head, to declare that evil is hateful before Him and that He does not want any of His children to walk in it; for evil binds its owner and keeps him away from God, from the good, and from every good work, and he becomes like a blind man who sees nothing but evil, just as the blind man sees nothing but darkness.

4- The wicked man seizes the opportunity of God's hiddenness in times of trouble, as (v. 1) mentions, and persists in his evil in pride. But God is longsuffering and gives him an opportunity to review himself; yet if he does not benefit from this opportunity, He turns his evil upon his own head.

5- David the poor man calls upon God and cries to Him for help, that He may save him and save all the poor who are burned by the evil of the wicked, and he asks for their deliverance. Of course God hastens to His children and does not neglect them, especially since the faith of some of them may be shaken and they doubt the swiftness of God's answer and support, so that they burn inwardly with these doubts, and so they need swift divine help.
3- "For the wicked boasteth of the desires of his soul, and the robber blasphemeth. He despiseth the Lord."

1- Here he mentions a second characteristic of the wicked man after pride, which is lust. The wicked man is immersed in bodily lusts and persists in them until he justifies these evil lusts, so that his persistence in them increases, and he reaches the point of boasting of them, and consequently advances in them without limit.

2- The wicked man's boasting of his lusts increases his pride, and he is often glorified by people, which increases his persistence in lust; because in his sight God is hidden in times of trouble, and people think that the wicked man is right, while the godly are poor and weak; that is, concepts and principles are turned upside down.

3- Those who praise him may be hypocrites seeking their own interest and benefit, but the wicked man is deceived by these words, so his pride increases, and in his lusts he falls also into another, third sin, which is greed. He seizes from others, that is, he steals, and it may be a forced theft, using his power and influence.
4- Through the wicked man's greed he falls into a fourth sin, which is injustice; he assaults the property of others and seizes their rights to satisfy his selfishness.

5- Then the wicked robber goes further and falls into a fifth sin, which is blasphemy against God, since he feels his power and authority over others through what he takes from them, so he insults God and describes Him with evil attributes, because he relies on his own strength in pride, neglects God's commandments, and feels no need of God, so he stands as an equal against God and blasphemes Him.
4- "The wicked, through the pride of his countenance, saith: He will not require it. All his thoughts are that there is no God."
1- The sixth sin of the wicked man is atheism; for in his pride and loftiness he says of God that He does not require it, and even says there is no God.

2- The cause of atheism is falling into the sin of pride, lust and greed, so that in his loftiness he lifts his nose above all who are around him, despising others; that is, he feels that with a puff of his nose he can destroy others, meaning that with a little strength of his he destroys the poor. Therefore he feels no need for the existence of God and abolishes His existence.

3- The wicked man's fall into atheism comes gradually; as he becomes great in his own eyes and domineers over others, he forgets God, then he grows insolent and describes God as weak and passive, because He will not demand the rights of the poor, as proved by the fact that he has been lording it over the poor for a period of time and God has not punished him. And in the end he reaches atheism by rejecting the idea of God's existence, so that he may persist in his evil without limit.

4- God rebukes a person and warns him many times to return, and when God's anger against the person increases, He abandons him, so that he may suffer the consequences of his sins and be pricked, perhaps he will repent, as it says of the wicked in the Epistle to the Romans, "God gave them over to a reprobate mind" (Rom 1:28).

5- The wicked man in his evil assaults people with injustice, contempt and domination. Then he goes further in his insolence to assault God Himself, and blasphemes Him, and in the end claims that God does not exist; that is, he falls into atheism.
6- Behind atheism stand not only lusts but also man's deification of himself, and in the end he falls into atheism, and this is what the Antichrist will fall into.
5- "His ways are always grievous; thy judgments are far above out of his sight: as for all his enemies, he puffeth at them."
Puffeth: blows, and what is meant is that he pours out his venom, his authority and his evil upon his enemies.
1- The wicked man lives in his uncleanness and evils and is firm in his evil ways, since he silences his conscience and justifies his faults, so he persists in his sins.

2- As the wicked man is immersed in evil and becomes accustomed to it, God becomes far from his mind and heart, and His commandments become high above him, which he cannot grasp, and he gives them no weight, so he neglects them completely.

3- Since the wicked man has put God away from his thinking and has become accustomed to evil, he directs his evils against the godly and the poor, so he harms them and regards them as his enemies, because by their righteousness they expose his evil; therefore he tries to crush them.

4- We see here a clear relationship between uncleanness and evil on the one hand, and the rejection of God and atheism on the other; the wicked man rejects the existence of God so that he may persist in his evil and no one may rebuke him for it.
6- "He hath said in his heart: I shall not be moved: for I shall never be in adversity."

When the wicked man persists in his evil he feels strong and secure, relying on material things, so he thinks to himself that no one can shake him or harm him; he deludes himself with security and happiness, although he knows that the whole world is changeable and that evil passes away, but he forgets reality and lives in illusions, that is, he lives an imaginary happiness although his heart is troubled within him, like the foolish rich man who trusted in his wealth, but was surprised that he would die that very night (Lk 12:19, 20).
7- "His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity."

1- The seventh characteristic of the wicked man is abuse; he is not content with blaspheming God, but curses and reviles the righteous who expose his evil by their righteousness. He does not repent, but on the contrary curses righteousness and the righteous.

2- The eighth characteristic is deceit; for the wicked man cheats those around him to reach his evil goals, and he is also a hypocrite and a pretender, so he speaks sweet words by which he deceives those around him and makes them imagine that evil is delightful and gives happiness, while he carries under his tongue, that is, he hides, the toil and torment that evil contains; whoever is deceived by the pleasure of sin suffers afterward from its troubles.

3- The sweet tongue of the wicked man may be in spiritual speech, but he hides under it innovations and heresies; his evil does not appear on his tongue but under it, to deceive by it the poor and the simple if they stray from God.

8- "He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor. 9- He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net." Lurking place: an ambush, a place where the wicked man hides to pounce on the innocent and destroy them. His den: the house of the lion.

1- The wicked man is characterized not only by deceit but also by violence, which is the ninth characteristic of the wicked man; he hides quietly so that the poor man scarcely suspects him, and suddenly he comes out of the ambush in which he was hiding to pounce on the poor man and devour him.

2- The wicked man watches the righteous not to learn righteousness from them or to care for them, but on the contrary to seize an opportunity and harm them, and if possible destroy them. His looks, his words and his deeds are all evil.

3- He cannot harm the righteous, because God protects them and does not allow harm to come to them except what benefits them spiritually, as happened with the martyrs. But the wicked man can seize the opportunity of the weakness of the righteous and make them fall into sin; therefore the children of God must constantly hold fast to His commandments and examine themselves every day.

4- This verse likens the wicked man to a ravening lion, that is, extreme violence and at the same time trickery, like the hunter who casts his net so that the innocent fall into it. This is what happened with the Church, which was and is exposed to the cruelty of persecution and also to the deception of heretics.
10- "So he is crushed, and bowed down, and the poor fall by his strong ones." (literally: the poor fall in his claws).
His claws: his talons.

1- Before the cruelty of the wicked man the righteous grow weary, carrying their cross for the sake of Christ, so they are crushed and bowed down to the ground under the weight of the cross, and even offer their lives as a sacrifice of the love of God.

2- Of the righteous, whoever grows careless and looks to earthly lusts, bending over them, the wicked man seizes this opportunity and makes them fall into sin, crushes them, and sinks his claws into them and destroys them. This wicked man is Satan and all the wicked who follow him, such as the Antichrist who comes at the end of days.
11- "He hath said in his heart: God hath forgotten: he hideth his face; he will never see it."

So that the wicked man may persist in his evil, he imagines and claims either that God does not exist, or that He is weak, so he accuses Him of forgetting and being occupied with something other than His weak children, and even that He will not turn to their prayers and their crying out to Him, and will remain far from them forever. In this way the wicked man numbs his conscience, because he cannot bear to remember the great punishment of judgment.

If a person accepts doing evil, or thinking about it even a little, evil creeps into his life, grows and gains control over him, so he justifies his faults and assaults God with evil words. So be careful to repent, that you may reject sin first by first, and return to God and gain the salvation of your soul.
12- "Arise, O Lord; O God, lift up thine hand: forget not the poor."

1- David calls upon God to end His longsuffering and forbearance toward the wicked, so that He may rescue His poor children and punish the wicked with the power of His hand, that is, with His divine might.

2- The hand of God is a type of His Incarnation; David, in the spirit of prophecy, calls upon Christ to rise from the dead, binding the power of Satan and rescuing His poor servants who believe in Him from the dominion of the devil.

3- David also awaits the rising of Christ on the Day of Judgment, to judge the wicked and glorify His righteous children who endured much on earth, so that they receive in return for it blessings in the Kingdom of Heaven.
13- "Wherefore doth the wicked contemn God? He hath said in his heart: Thou wilt not require it."

David the prophet denounces the wicked man's contempt for God and his claim that God will judge no one; this is considered a denial of God's existence and authority, and therefore he is severely punished by God.
14- "Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless."

1- David proclaims the truth against the claims of the wicked, so he addresses God and says to Him: You have seen the evil of the wicked and their injustice, and You have felt the troubles of Your poor children and their toil. And You are a tender Father who cannot bear injustice to Your children; as happened in ancient times when God had compassion on His people in Egypt, humiliated in the slavery of Pharaoh, and looked upon their toil and declared to Moses that He would come down and deliver them (Ex 18:8).
2- He declares that God will requite the wicked and punish them for their injustice to the poor, as He punished the nations that humiliated His people, such as Egypt, Assyria and Babylon.

3- The strong hand of God that punishes the wicked is the very hand on which the hope of His children depends, when they feel that they are poor and weak, and even fatherless, that is, without earthly father and mother to support them, so that You, O God, are a Father to them and a helper in their hardships.

Do not be troubled if you feel that you are alone, or weak before the powers of the world, or the wars of Satan, for God loves the weak and supports them. Take refuge in Him, confident of His power that saves you from every evil.
15- "Break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil man: seek out his wickedness till thou find none."
Break: shatter and crush.

1- David asks God to break the arm, that is, the power, of the wicked man, so that he may feel his weakness before God and his helplessness; he does not gloat over the wicked man or try to take vengeance on him, but wants the breaking of evil, so that the wicked may repent.

2- When God breaks the power of evil the wicked man can do nothing, and his works are of no use or effect upon the righteous poor, because God protects them; this strengthens the faith of the poor in God and calls the wicked man to repentance.

3- God's breaking of the power of evil is completed on the great Day of Judgment, when the devil and all his followers are judged, and in the Kingdom of Heaven they have no power, but the righteous poor live in perfect happiness with God.
16- "The Lord is King for ever and ever: the heathen are perished out of his land."

1- God reassures His children that He is King over His people and the hearts of His children, so He protects them from every evil, and even destroys the enemies, that is, the nations, from their land. But He says "his land", that is, He declares that the land of His people is His land and that He is responsible for them, which increases their reassurance.

2- If God is King over the hearts of His children and protects them, He also gives them the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, so that they are distinguished from the rest of mankind by the fellowship of God.
3- God is not only King now over His people, but also for ever and ever; He continues to give them enjoyment of His love and glory in complete stability, which increases and develops their joy.

4- The land is a symbol of the heart of man, and the nations are a symbol of sins; so when God reigns over His land, that is, the heart of His son and beloved who has believed in Him, He removes sins from him and helps him to destroy them, so that the whole heart may be God's, fulfilling the commandment that says, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart" (Mt 22:37).

5- The land is also a symbol of the Kingdom of Heaven, and the nations are a symbol of the demons and the wicked who have no place in the Kingdom, and thus the children of God enjoy perpetual joy with God, without the presence of the wicked with them.

17- "Lord, thou hast heard the desire of the humble: thou wilt prepare their heart, thou wilt cause thine ear to hear." (literally: the groaning of the meek you have heard, O Lord; you establish their hearts; you incline your ear)

1- The sufferings of the godly believers who live in meekness and quietness are very precious to God; not only does their crying out move Him, but their mere groaning makes Him hasten to hear them and answer them.

2- God's swift intervention and His condescension to incline His ear to them reassures the meek and gives them inner steadfastness and stability, so that they are no longer disturbed by outward afflictions, even if these continue for a time, but He gives them blessing, spiritual depth and inward delight during the affliction.

3- God's hearing of the groaning of the meek, who ask for His justice and equity for them in the face of the injustice of the wicked, is completed in the Kingdom of Heaven when He glorifies them with Him for ever, and punishes the wicked in eternal torment.

4- The meek in the Old Testament groaned to God to deliver them from the cruelty of the devil, so He became incarnate in the fullness of time and bound Satan by His Cross, and brought Adam and his children up from Hades to Paradise.
18- "To judge the fatherless and the oppressed, that the man of the earth may no more oppress."
1- God moves by His justice to do right and restore the rights of two groups:
a - The fatherless, that is, those without support and care, or those whom sin has deprived of their strength and who repent, so God becomes a Father to them and cares for them with His providence.
b - The oppressed, that is, the humble who seek God, so He rescues them, restores their rights to them and distinguishes them from others.

2- God gives His children their spiritual rights before their material ones, because inner peace and the relationship with God are the most important, and He gives them strength to face outward problems, and then in the end He gives them their distinguished right in the Kingdom of Heaven.

3- God's intervention frightens the enemies of His children, so they no longer terrify them and trouble them when they see God protecting them by His power. This is what happened with the saints, when Satan was afraid to come near their places and be burned by their prayers.
4- When the children of God see His punishment of the wicked, not only are they reassured, but they also fear God, so their repentance and their care for their spiritual life increase.
Faith and steadfastness. For the choir director. Of David. "In the Lord I put my trust"... (v. 1). Introduction:

1- Its writer: David the prophet, during Saul's pursuit of him, when the wicked frightened him and asked him to hide in the mountains so that Saul would forget him, but he preferred to trust in God and to be among his people and with his loved ones in the cities and villages.

2- This psalm is considered a hymn of steadfastness in God during afflictions, so that a person is not shaken, whatever evils surround him. It also applies to the whole Church, when it is exposed to persecutions, and stands firm in faith in God.
3- This psalm is among the psalms of faith, which call a person to faith in God and not to trust in the world and material things, and like it are Psalms (Ps 16, 23, 62, 125, 131).

4- In this psalm the providence of God for the world appears; He cares for His children and watches all their works in order to care for them, and examines them to purify them from evil, but the wicked He punishes severely because of their disobedience and rebellion against Him.
5- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- "In the Lord put I my trust: how say ye to my soul, Flee as a bird to your mountain?"

1- David's friends advised him to flee from the face of Saul, who was pursuing him, lest he kill him, and perhaps during that time he was still in Saul's service; but he refused, relying on God who protects him.

2- The meaning intended by the word "flee" in the Hebrew original is confusion and alarm, that is, flight in trembling and agitation, like a frightened bird that does not know where to flee. This kind of flight is rejected by the believer who trusts in God, who knows that his refuge is God.
