3- Flight is to be from evil and sin and all the snares of Satan, but at the same time a person accepts suffering and the bearing of the cross, as the martyrs endured. So David endured the heavy commands and demands of Saul, such as killing a hundred Philistines to present them as a dowry for marrying Saul's daughter, but he did not flee out of fear of Saul.

4- Flight is useful when it is aimed at not being hindered from life with God, like Christ's flight from the face of Herod, and as David himself fled from the face of Saul, and endured his pursuit and was not hindered from his goal, which is life with God, by clashing with Saul, but he was patient until Saul died in the war, as a divine punishment for him.

5- Although mountains are a symbol of strength and material steadfastness, the believer does not flee to them, but to God, who is the true mountain and the fortified refuge; a person must not rely on the material powers in the world, but on God.
6- David answered at once that the solution is trust in God, and he did not even discuss the idea of fleeing out of fear of the wicked, because his faith is firm.

7- David's friends said to him, "Flee," because they meant David and those with him, that is, the soldiers who followed him. But his trust in God caused Saul to fall into his hand twice, and David forgave him and did not kill him (1 Sam 24:4-11, 1 Sam 26:9-11).
2- "For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart."
Make ready their arrow upon the string: the notch of the arrow is its end, and to fit the arrow means to place its end on the string, in readiness to release it.
Privily: in the darkness of the night.
1- David's friends based their advice to him to flee on the fact that the wicked had prepared their weapons to do away with him, namely arrows.
2- Arrows are mostly used to hunt people and kill them when they are not prepared, that is, by trickery and deceit, and this shows the evil of the wicked.

3- Bending the bow and fitting the arrow means complete readiness to harm David, but they had not yet shot the arrows; this shows how near evil was to David, and therefore it was necessary for him to flee quickly.
4- David replies to his friends with three things:
a - that he has trusted in God, as mentioned in (v. 1), and therefore he is not shaken by the enemies.
b - that his enemies are wicked, and God does not answer or support the wicked, but is against them, so they therefore have no real power.
c - he is among the upright in heart, who are under God's protection, so the wicked cannot harm him.
5- The cruelty of the wicked appears in that they try to kill him secretly, that is, in the darkness; they are not open enemies, but deceivers.

6- These wicked people may be the heretics, who twist the word of God, and who are symbolized by the arrows that strike in the darkness, and also the time of persecution; that is, heretics and the wicked in general seize the opportunity of the persecution of the children of God to harm them. This is the goal of Satan, to destroy the children of God, but God does not allow him.
3- "If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?" (literally: if the pillars are overturned, what does the righteous do?)
1- David's friends continue their advice to him: if the pillars fall, what will be the condition of the righteous man? And what is meant by the pillars is:
a - The righteous kings and rulers who fear God.
b - The principles and values prevailing in society.
c - Respect for the spiritual leaders, such as the prophets of the Old Testament, or the bishops and priests in the Church.
d - The word of God and the teachings of the Church.
2- The fall of the pillars means the following:

a - The death of important persons in the Church; as happened in the Old Testament when Saul killed the priests dwelling in the city of Nob (1 Sam 22:17-19). What would David the righteous do without priests?
b - Their deviation from God and their preoccupation with the world.
c - Their falling into innovations and heresies.
3- The righteous man who is meant is:
a - David the prophet, in whose time King Saul and many of the rulers, teachers and people became corrupt, and they are symbolized by the pillars.
b - Christ our Lord, who sees that His teachings have been neglected, the righteous have fallen and the people of innovations have spread; what does He do, except judge them on the last day.

c - Any person who lives in godliness, when he sees the pillars falling, has nothing before him except to take refuge in God and be sheltered in Him, so that He establishes him in the faith to the end.

Do not be troubled in afflictions, for they are temporary; hold fast to your faith, trusting in God, confident that the end of evil is destruction, and that God will not leave you, but will support you and comfort you and gladden your heart during the affliction, and then you will enjoy complete joy in heaven.

entries.section: (2) The care of the righteous and the vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 4- "The Lord is in his holy temple, the Lord's throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men."

1- Since the pillars had fallen, and the wicked had aimed their arrows at David, and his friends had advised him to flee like a bird, David had nothing before him except to take refuge in God, the strong and just, who cares for him and keeps him, so he looks to God in His holy temple and in His heaven.
2- What is meant by the holy temple of God is:
a - The tabernacle of meeting, or, in the spirit of prophecy, the Church of the New Testament.
b - God in His heavenly Kingdom.
c - The just God, who dwells in heaven, who will judge all on the Day of Judgment.
d - The souls of God's children, where He works in them, so that they become a light to the world and condemn the evil of the wicked.

3- David looked to the Lord, whose throne is in heaven, to raise his thoughts, words and deeds to heaven and live spiritually, and to keep away from the enemy, Satan, who wants to bring him down to earthly things and make him live carnally. By this David wants to live in the light of heaven, while the enemy wants to fight him with darkness, as in (v. 2).

4- By David's looking to heaven to see the justice of God, he is not troubled by the spread of injustice on earth, and the persecution of the upright in heart and the righteous by the wicked, as in (vv. 2, 3). And by his looking to heaven he flees to God with faith and strength and not in trembling to the mountains like a bird, as his companions advised him (v. 1).
5- When the eyes of God look on mankind, this means:
a - Care and providence for His righteous children.
b - Condemnation of the wicked, with whom He is patient, but He destroys them if they continue in their disobedience.
6- The eyelids try mankind; because the eyelids of God are a symbol of:

a - When God opens His eyelids He sees with His eyes, His love and His care the life of His children, then He closes His eyes to the wicked, because they have left Him and neglected life with Him and insisted on evil, although He called them many times, so He abandons them, perhaps they will grow weary of their evils and return to Him.

b - When God opens His eyelids He declares His judgments to mankind, and at other times He closes His eyelids, that is, His judgments are hidden, not seen by mankind, but understood only by the righteous, when they lift up prayers to Him.

c - When God opens His eyelids He tests mankind with success, to see how thankful they are to Him, and when He closes His eyelids He tests them with failure and hardship, to see how steadfast they are in the faith.
7- The eyelids of God try the children of Adam, that is, all mankind, so that the righteous may be proved and the wicked may perish.

entries.section: (2) The care of the righteous and the vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 5- "The Lord trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth."

1- God cares for His righteous children so as to purify them from every evil that clings to them from the world, which is full of evil, so He tests them with afflictions until they return to Him, so that their faith is established and they keep away from everything that angers God.

2- God abandons the wicked because of their insistence on evil, and then they lose their peace and become distressed with themselves, and God allows this, perhaps they will return to Him, when they taste the results of their sins and see the peace of the righteous, so they are pricked in their hearts and repent.

3- The continuance of the wicked and those who love injustice in their sins will lead them to eternal destruction, and in the torment their souls will hate them; because they brought this destruction upon themselves.

entries.section: (2) The care of the righteous and the vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 6- "Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and a wind of poison shall be the portion of their cup."

1- The wicked, who by their evil deeds harm themselves, God leaves to the torment of their consciences throughout their lives, perhaps they will repent, and He allows them to fall into the snares of the evil they loved, whether the snares of evil lusts, or innovations and heresies. And if they do not return to God, nothing awaits them but divine punishment on the Day of Judgment. God allows them to fall into the snares, just as they also set snares for the righteous, but God delivered the righteous from them, whereas the wicked, because of their distance from God, fell into these snares and did not rise.
2- These snares which God allows are so many that He likens them to rain, and in this God gives the wicked many opportunities to repent.

3- If the wicked do not return to God they will deserve eternal torment, which is expressed here by fire and brimstone, and the severity of this fire cannot be measured by the fire we know; because it burns spirits and continues for ever. As for the brimstone, it is an expression of the speed of burning and also of the foul smell, and it is like the foul smell of sin, and all this shows the horror of eternal torment. God expressed this when He burned Sodom and Gomorrah with fire and brimstone, to be a lesson to all the wicked and a likeness of what will happen in the eternal torment.

4- By wind is meant spirits, and as for poison, it is known to be deadly; so God allows the spirits of the wicked to go astray and lead them to destruction, because they reject God, and they also submit to the spirits of the demons and their thoughts, which lead to eternal torment.

5- All these preceding punishments are the portion of the wicked, and He has expressed their portion by the cup, that is, the cup of God's wrath which they deserve. And the cups differ in capacity, that is, each wicked man receives his portion and the cup of divine wrath that he deserves according to his sins, not only on this earth but in eternity; for hell has degrees of torment, according to the evil of each one.

entries.section: (2) The care of the righteous and the vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 7- "For the righteous Lord loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright."

1- David begins the psalm with trust in God and ends it with looking to the just God; God is the beginning and the end, and therefore faith and steadfastness in Him is life on this earth and for ever.

2- If the upright meet afflictions in life and injustice from the wicked, God supports them and comforts them in the afflictions by their seeing God, as happened with the three young men in the fiery furnace, and as happens every day with the children of God who seek Him in affliction.
3- God must compensate the upright for their endurance of sufferings in this life, in eternal life, by shining upon them with His face, and they enjoy Him for ever. This is the perfection of justice.

Seek God in every affliction that meets you, confident that He is beside you and is able to comfort you with a joy that makes you forget the pains, so that you are strengthened, and even become an example to those around you and draw them to life with God.
The cry of the poor and God's intervention. For the choir director, on the "Sheminith." A psalm of David. "Help, Lord, for the godly man ceaseth"... (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: David, and he used to sing it through a group that had a director, or leader.
2- The occasion on which this psalm was said:
There are two opinions:
a - When David was serving Saul and there were rumors from Saul's assistants, who flattered him and spoke evil words against David, David cried out to God to rescue him and support him.

b - When the Philistines attacked the city of Keilah and plundered it, David cried out to God and asked for His guidance, and He told him to fight the Philistines and deliver Keilah. This was during his flight from Saul (1 Sam 23:1-6).
3- In the title of this psalm it says "on the Sheminith" (literally: on the octave), which is one of the degrees of the voice, on which this psalm is chanted.

4- In the Septuagint translation this psalm is titled with the words "to the end" or "for completion", which means that God's intervention and His rescue of the poor continue throughout the days, that is, throughout the life of mankind.

5- Also in the Septuagint translation this psalm is titled with the words "for the eighth" or "concerning the eighth", and this means that the words of the wicked come to nothing, while the righteous are those who remain with God to the eighth, which is a symbol of eternity, that is, the righteous remain with God for ever, while the wicked go to hell.

6- We find a relationship between Psalms 9, 10, 11, 12 and also Psalm 14, for all of them speak about the words and deeds of the wicked and God's intervention to rescue His poor children; they are suitable for times of affliction and injustice, so the children of God repeat these psalms to receive God's help.

7- This psalm is in the prayer of Prime in the Agpeya, and its number differs, taking number 11 in the Agpeya because Psalms 9 and 10 are joined into one psalm in the Septuagint translation from which the Agpeya was taken.
1- "Help, Lord; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men."

1- David remembers the injustices of Saul against him, and of the Philistines too, and every wrong that falls upon the children of God, so he cries out to the Lord saying "Help, Lord"; because there is no hope for the poor in affliction except God.

2- "The godly man ceaseth", that is, the number of those who fear God, who walk in righteousness, has become very small as a result of the wrong done to them by the wicked: some died and others feared people, so they abandoned righteousness. And the wicked try to wipe out the righteous so that they will not condemn them by their goodness, and so the wicked rid themselves of the pricking of conscience, since Satan makes them feel that the evil they do is the natural behavior of people.

3- "The faithful fail from among the children of men", that is, the number of the faithful in business dealings has become very small, as well as the faithful in holding fast to the faith and the creed, so that the majority has become tainted with strange ideas and doubts.

4- David asks for salvation because of the spread of evil in the world, and this salvation was accomplished in the fullness of time by the Incarnation of Christ the Savior. Elijah felt the same feelings as David, when he said that all had gone astray and he alone was left, and God reassured him that there were seven thousand knees that had not bowed to Baal (1 Kgs 19:18).

2- "They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak." Flattering: from flattery, which is showing something other than what a person holds within, in order to deceive the listener with false praise. A double heart: the wicked man has two hearts, meaning two faces, so he speaks deceitfully to the listener although inside him are opposite feelings.

1- The wicked are liars because they show other than what they hold within; they speak words of praise to others although they hate them in their hearts, or they reassure them when the matter calls for caution; this is so as to make them fall into the trap, for the purpose of the words of the wicked is to deceive the righteous and make them fall by malicious plots into many problems in order to be rid of them, and this is a continuation of what the first verse mentioned.

2- Jeremiah set forth the same meaning about the wicked in (Jer 9:4, 5), and Christ Himself rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy (Mt 23), and James the Apostle tells us of the danger of the tongue of the wicked (Jas 3:1-12).
3- "The Lord shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things."
Proud things: great sins.
1- The evil of the wicked reached not only to deceit, but to speaking shamelessly of great, shocking sins as though they were an ordinary matter.

2- David the prophet declares that there is a divine threat to the wicked, that God will uproot the deceitful lips and the evil tongue, that is, He will uproot the wicked if they do not repent; so it is a call to repentance, but a firm one, perhaps the wicked will take heed.
4- "Who have said, With our tongue will we prevail; our lips are our own: who is lord over us?"

1- He describes these wicked people as proud, whose might and power are in their tongue, although in truth they are deceivers of no worth before the power of God. And they declared that they are free and say what they want.

2- Throughout history wicked people have appeared who neglected the existence of God and were proud, such as Pharaoh (Ex 15:4), whose end was drowning with his army in the Red Sea, and Herod, who accepted praise as a god, so God struck him with worms and he died (Acts 12:23).

Do not be troubled by the plots of the wicked and their injustice, for it is temporary and will come to an end. Hold fast to your prayer, for God hears you and is near you, and the troubles He allows for you are for your good, so that you may be purified from your sins, but He keeps you and has prepared for you a great place in the Kingdom.

5- "For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the Lord; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him." (literally: I will set him in a wide place, him who is puffed at)
In a wide place: that is, in spaciousness and ease.
Him who is puffed at: him upon whom the wicked blow and pour out their wrath and harm him.

1- God is longsuffering toward the wicked, that they may repent, but their persistence in evil makes them use up their opportunity, especially when the poor cry out to God as a result of the injustice of the wicked, and God intervenes swiftly, for He says, "Now will I arise."

2- God does not merely stop the wicked, but also glorifies His righteous poor children and puts them in ease and a spacious, safe life. And this will be declared plainly before all, to strengthen those who fear God and to alert the wicked to repent. And in the Septuagint translation, that is, the Agpeya, it says "I will deal openly in salvation" instead of "I will set him in a wide place, him who is puffed at", that is, the salvation of the wronged poor will be plain before all.

3- This divine threat that God will arise to save the righteous from the hands of the wicked, God carried out many times, such as bringing His people out of the land of Egypt, and drowning Pharaoh and his army in the sea, and also delivering His people from Amalek in their war in the wilderness of Sinai. And delivering His people from the surrounding pagan nations many times, in the days of Joshua, the judges, Saul, David and Solomon.

4- This open divine salvation Christ accomplished in the fullness of time on the Cross, and He will also declare it with power on the Day of Judgment before all mankind, from Adam to the end of the ages.
6- "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times."

1- If the words of the wicked are deceit, flattery and hypocrisy, the words of God are pure, and they purify those who hear them, as Christ Himself said, "Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you" (Jn 15:3).

2- The words of God are pure like silver that is refined in the furnace seven times, that is, a complete refining. This shows how pure the words of God are, since they have no impurities. And Christ in His Sermon on the Mount spoke the first seven Beatitudes, which are found in the one who receives the eighth Beatitude, which is persecution; that is, one cannot reach the eighth Beatitude unless a person is purified by the first seven Beatitudes.
7- "Thou shalt keep them, O Lord, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever."

1- David the prophet declares that God keeps and guards His righteous children from the hands of the wicked, so no affliction befalls them except what God allows for their benefit; they are under God's protection throughout their life in this age, and this gives them reassurance, so they move freely in their relationship with God and their service to Him.

2- The prophet promises the humble righteous, that is, the poor, that God will keep them with Him for ever, and even give them the enjoyment of fellowship with Him in the Kingdom of Heaven, so they enjoy God throughout their life, and then in heaven. This is contrary to the wicked, who live in turmoil and when they die go to eternal torment. Therefore the title of this psalm says "to the end, for the eighth", that is, God keeps the life of the righteous on earth and gives them the enjoyment of the glories of the Kingdom, which the eighth day symbolizes.
8- "The wicked walk on every side, when the vilest men are exalted."
Walk on every side: they spread throughout the whole world.

1- After David concluded the psalm in the seventh verse with God's care for His children, he returns in the last verse, the eighth, here, and declares that the wicked will remain spread in every place in the world, and most of them will not repent, so that the righteous may not be shaken by the spread of evil, but stand firm and lean on God, who protects them.

2- The wicked will support one another when some of them take great authority in the world, so they encourage evil, and sins spread, and even become the law of the world, but all this does not make the children of God troubled; because Christ said, "The whole world lieth in wickedness" (1 Jn 5:19).

God hears your petition, especially when you are in severe affliction, and hastens to you, so do not despair, but seek Him with faith and persistence, for He is able to rescue you from every evil, however it surrounds you.
Taking refuge in God. For the choir director. A psalm of David. "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord?"... (v. 1). Introduction:
1- The writer of this psalm is David the prophet.
2- When this psalm was said:
There are three opinions:

a - When David was fleeing from the face of Saul, and Saul was placing watchers on him everywhere, and pursuing him with great armies to seize him, and at some times he almost seized him, but at the last moment God delivered him.
b - When David fell into his great sins such as adultery and murder, and felt severe distress, as though God had left him, and he cried out to Him.
c - When his son Absalom rose against him and drove him from the kingdom, and went out to fight him, trying to kill him.
3- This psalm is repeated collectively because it is titled "for the choir director", that is, a group of singers who have a leader.
4- It is a short prayer that the man of God cries out in severe affliction, and it includes the basic aspects of prayer, which are complaint, supplication and praise.

5- It speaks in the spirit of prophecy about the affliction that meets the people of God, which is the captivity and humiliation four times at the hands of the kingdoms: Assyria and Babylon, then Media and Persia, and after them Greece; therefore David repeats an important question to God, which is "How long", four times.
6- This psalm is a symbol of the afflictions that come upon a person from every side in his life, that is, from the four directions of the world, so we find that it repeated "How long" four times.
7- This psalm is said in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime.
(1) Complaint (vv. 1, 2:)
1- "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?"

1- David does not ask an interrogative question when he says "How long?", but implores God with all his heart and reproaches Him, since he feels that He has neglected him and left him, and even feels that He has hidden His face from him; because of his sin and weakness, or because problems and afflictions surround him.

2- David, despite his feeling that God is not with him because of the pressure of the affliction upon him, has hope in Him that He will save him; therefore he cried out to Him, "How long wilt thou forget me?"
3- A person in his spiritual lukewarmness feels that God has neglected him, although God withdraws a little so that the person may strive and seek after God, and so experience new depths of His love.

4- Satan fights a person in affliction, making him imagine that God may forget him utterly, or "to the end" according to the Septuagint translation, so that he falls into despair; but the beautiful thing about David is that he did not give in, but rose to pray in reproaching God, that He may rescue him from the affliction.

5- David had become accustomed to fellowship with God; therefore he felt that God had hidden His face from him, so he was greatly distressed and offered repentance and prayer to regain his sense of God, who is his life. But the person who is far from God does not feel these feelings and does not seek God with this persistence.
6- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who said on the Cross, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Mt 27:46), so from this aspect it is considered among the Messianic psalms.

7- We notice that David did not complain about Saul, or Absalom, or any difficult circumstances surrounding him, but directed his complaint to God, saying "How long wilt thou forget me?", since he feels that God's presence with him is enough for him and protects him and rescues him from any affliction; he is not distressed by people, but he needs God.
2- "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?"

1- After David reproached God in the first verse with the first reproach, which is neglect and forgetfulness, and reproached Him with the second reproach, which is hiding His face from him, here he reproaches Him with the third reproach, which is that his heart has been filled with cares and sorrow, as a result of his sin and the severity of the affliction upon him; David's thoughts, which Satan stirs up, press upon him, so that he is depressed under the weight of thoughts of care and fear.

2- David reproaches God with the fourth reproach, saying: why have You allowed my enemy, who is Satan, to prevail over me and humble me? This is a confession of his weakness and faith in the power of God, who is able to drive his enemy away from him.
3- David advances in his cry to God in four stages:
a - His feeling of God's neglect of him.
b - His sense of losing the sight of God and fellowship with Him; because He has hidden His face from him.
c - The filling of his heart with evil thoughts of cares and sorrow.
d - His distress at the enemy's triumph over him.

But despite all this he has hope in God, and cries out to Him to rescue him from all these troubles, which advanced gradually, as we mentioned; for a sin that advances gradually, God is able to remove it and all its results.

4- David represents the spiritual man, who finds rest only in the arms of God; whatever David's resources and strength, he seeks the face of God, who satisfies him and delivers him from all troubles, since fellowship with God is his life and there is no substitute for it in the wealth of the world or its power; for if he has all the resources and does not have God with him, he is in great affliction.
5- God does not forget man, but man in his sin feels that God has forgotten him, but through prayer he regains his sense of God.
6- Anxiety, care and the feeling of losing God is a natural result of sin, and this is considered a divine grace, since it drives the spiritual person to prayer, so that he regains his life with God.

When affliction comes upon you, seek God and press Him, until He intervenes and restores your peace and makes you feel His presence, whether by removing the affliction at once, or leaving it for a time, but you will rejoice in your sense that God is with you.
(2) Asking for the help of A (vv. 3, 4:)
3- "Consider and hear me, O Lord my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death."

1- David addresses God, "Consider", meaning that He should look upon his lowliness and need, the enemy's insolence against him, and his repentance, so that He may rescue him because he is His son, and he has no hope except in Him.

2- David believes that God is his heavenly Father, who will feel for him and answer his prayer; therefore he demands of Him, "Hear me", and says to Him "my God": You are the Lord, the master of all kingdoms, but You are also my God who loves me, and cannot bear to see me in this weakness and lowliness. You are able, O God, to do all things, and at the same time You love me with perfect love, and give me special care because I am Your son.

3- David also asks God to lighten his eyes, that is, to give him spiritual enlightenment, which is the knowledge of God, so that he may come out of his spiritual lukewarmness and be rid of his sin, which separates him from God.

4- This enlightenment is life for David and without it he dies, for there is no life without the knowledge of God. On the other hand he asks God to hasten to lighten his eyes, before he is swallowed up by sorrow and grows weak before his enemy and he destroys him, that is, he asks for the power of God and His light to protect him from the demons.

5- Spiritual enlightenment is able to restore confidence to David's soul, and spiritual zeal, and remove sorrows, and cast the enemy down under his feet, that is, it answers all four degrees of sin mentioned before in (vv. 1, 2).
4- "Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him; and those that trouble me rejoice when I am moved."

1- David demands that God intervene, lest the principles be overturned by the triumph of Satan, so that he thinks he is stronger than the children of God and that he has been able to shake them and drive them away from God. So he asks God to intervene for the following:
a - For the glory of God's name.
b - To rescue him from destruction.
c - So that the righteous may stand firm in righteousness and not doubt.
d - To put the wicked to shame so that they repent.

2- As heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents, the demons on the other hand rejoice at the destruction of one righteous man and shout for joy; therefore David demands that God intervene swiftly, to stop the joy of the wicked at the destruction of the righteous.

The devil has no authority over you, so if you fall, rise and ask God to drive him away from you and rescue you, and even raise you up, so that you experience fellowship with Him, and He lightens your eyes, and you make up for all that you have missed.
(3) Trust and praise (vv. 5, 6:)
5- "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation."

1- Since David pleaded with God in (vv. 3, 4) and asked for spiritual enlightenment, he placed all his trust in the mercy of God, so he became settled psychologically and spiritually and felt reassurance, and his heart found rest; because he did not trust in any human power, but in God, who is able to do all things and abundant in mercies, who forgives every sin.
2- After the reassurance, David felt joy at his sense of God's work with him, who rescued him from his enemy and from all his evil thoughts, and forgave his sins.
3- In the spirit of prophecy David saw Christ the Savior, and his heart rejoiced in the complete salvation on the Cross.
4- Here we see the power of prayer, which transforms a person from severe sorrow and complaint to God into supplication with confidence and asking for enlightenment, then trust, and finally joy.
6- "I will sing unto the Lord, because he hath dealt bountifully with me."
1- David felt the grace of God, His forgiveness, His support and His great kindness to him; therefore he lifted up his heart with thanksgiving, praise and song.

2- The faith of David appears, for although the affliction was not outwardly removed, he received peace of heart through his faith, so he thanked God and praised Him, and after this God's work in him was completed and He lifted him up and glorified him.

3- Although the psalm is brief and small, it includes all the feelings of a person in affliction, and the work of God in the heart, until He gladdens him in the end; so it is suitable for prayer in all afflictions.
How beautiful is the thanksgiving and praise that you offer to God when He works in your life, for it establishes your faith, and gladdens your heart, and gladdens the heart of God.
The danger of denying God. For the choir director. Of David. "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God"... (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: David, and he used to sing the psalm with a group of singers who have a director, that is, a leader.
2- The occasion of the writing of the psalm
a - A prophecy about Sennacherib, who reproached God and His people in the days of the reign of King Hezekiah.
b - A prophecy about Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who took the kingdom of Judah captive and reproached God and His people.
c - The rejection of the corruption of those who deny God in every generation.
3- The psalm shows the causes of the corruption of the atheists, and examines their psychology and their evils, and the saving power of God for His people from their hand.
4- This psalm resembles Psalm 53 and does not differ from it except in a few words, and perhaps the reason is the repetition of the idea in David's mind and his distress at the evils of the atheists.
5- Paul the Apostle quoted from this psalm (Rom 3:10-13), to show that the Jews and the Gentiles had both gone away from the knowledge of God and were immersed in evil.
6- This psalm bears a prophecy about Christ the Savior (v. 7), so it can be considered among the Messianic psalms.
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good."
1- Denying the existence of God is folly; because whoever denies God declares that his human nature is not immortal and will perish, so he lowers himself and makes himself like the animals.
And if God exists and he in his folly denies His existence, he exposes himself to punishment because of his corruption, so in both cases he is a fool.
2- The fool denies God in his thought, and feels this in his heart, whether he declares it with his tongue or not; in both cases he is an atheist and a fool.

3- The word "fool" in Hebrew is "nabal", or "withered", or "dry" like the leaves of autumn, meaning that he is worthless and his speech and life have no meaning; because he has lost God, the source of life.

4- Denying God permits the fool to be immersed in corruption and evil and to keep away from goodness. And a person's immersion in evil makes him deny God, to justify and acquit himself so that his conscience does not prick him.

5- The fool falls into weakness of mind and heart: the mind has not examined the Holy Scriptures and understood nature, so as to understand that God is behind it, and the heart has grown weak before the lusts of the world and become corrupt, that is, it has turned away from goodness and fallen into the abominations and filth of evil.
6- The fool falls into many sins, the most important of which are:
a - He longs for God not to exist, so that he may continue in his evil; therefore he says "in his heart", that is, he flatters himself with the wish and longs for it.
b - When the fool denies the existence of God, he rushes into evil and corruption, without restraint.
c - If the fool denies the existence of God, he will therefore not ask for His help and will continue in his corruption and be unable to be rid of it.
d - The fool justifies his corruption and considers it among the natural characteristics of man, so as to be rid of the pricking of conscience.

e - If the fool sees the conduct of the righteous and his conscience begins to prick him, then he harms them; because in his view they are deviant, and in truth he is trying to do away with them, so that they do not rebuke his evil.

f - Whoever denies the existence of God will naturally not keep His commandments; so he does not do the good to which the commandments call, and because he does not believe in divine reward and punishment.
2- "The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God."

1- Despite the spread of folly, David shows hope in God, who looks down from heaven, that is, watches the world; he expressed this in words that people understand, for God is the searcher of hearts and reins and does not need at any time to look down, because He always sees everything, but He gives us hope that God intervenes with perfect knowledge, and looks upon the folly spread in the world.

2- God looked down from heaven, that is, from His loftiness and perfection; He is present everywhere, but heaven declares His loftiness, as we call Him in the Lord's Prayer, "Our Father which art in heaven."

3- God seeks the person who knows Him with his mind, that is, who "understands", and longs for Him with his heart, so he seeks Him and searches for him, that is, "seeks", and so will find Him in the end. He looks with His divine eye upon His children who believe in Him and seek Him; they are not neglected in the midst of the many corrupt fools, and this shows God's care and concern for His children, even if their number is small.

4- "God looks to see if there are any that understand" shows the fewness of those who believe in Him, since people are influenced by one another and walk in the way of corruption and the denial of God, and this of course grieves His heart.
3- "They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one."
1- God saw that mankind in general had become corrupt and walked in evil and gone far from goodness, and there is not one of the atheists who does good.
2- This does not mean that there is no person on earth who does not seek God, but it shows how widespread evil is.

3- This verse shows that all mankind has fallen into evil, even the children of God, and needs the salvation which Christ offers in the fullness of time, whether these people are Jews or Gentiles, that is, believers in God or idol worshippers, as Paul the Apostle made clear in (Rom 3:10). That is, human nature has been corrupted by the Fall and needs the justification of Christ.

Remember the presence of God before you every morning, so that you may live in virtue and keep away from sin. And if you fall, hasten to repentance, for remembering God establishes His fear in your heart. Speak with Him in short prayers throughout the day, to remember His presence before you.

entries.section: (2) The enmity of the wicked toward the righteous

paragraphs.text: 4- "Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people as they eat bread, and call not upon the Lord."

1- David's question is not interrogative but denunciatory of the evil that the atheists do; indeed he rebukes them and threatens them with divine judgment upon them because of their evils in harming the righteous, and he answers them firmly in the next verse (v. 5).

2- The wicked's denial of the existence of God makes them harm the righteous people of God, so they devour them and destroy them with all cruelty; because the wicked have denied God and His punishment.

3- The wicked atheists go further in their cruelty, so they destroy the righteous in great numbers and with ease as though they were eating bread, and they feel no pricking in their consciences; because they have denied the existence of God and no longer call upon Him or pray to Him.

4- It is understood from this verse that weak prayers make the heart hard and liable to harm others, and on the contrary whoever prays much, his conscience is refreshed, so it is tender and does not hurt the feelings of any person.

5- Since the wicked do not call upon God they become proud and act on their own thoughts, which are evil, so they destroy everyone who does not please them, or seize his rights, because they have become without understanding or guidance from God.

6- These wicked people who persist in their evil are like the false prophets, or the heretics, who lead the people of God astray, so they destroy it, and do not pray and call upon God so that He may guide them and turn them back from their error.

entries.section: (2) The enmity of the wicked toward the righteous

paragraphs.text: 5- "There were they in great fear: for God is in the generation of the righteous."

The wicked feared God, despite their persistence in evil, since their consciences have not died, that is, the voice of God is still in them and they try to silence it but cannot, and this frightens them. Why?
1- Because He will take vengeance for all the evil they have done.
2- They fear the loss of their position, their power and their possessions on earth.
3- They feel the difficulty of repenting and being rid of their sins, in which they have lived a long time.
4- They see God in the righteous and their sins are exposed, that is, the light of God in the righteous shows up their darkness, so they fear what they have done.

entries.section: (2) The enmity of the wicked toward the righteous

paragraphs.text: 6- "Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge." (literally: you have contradicted the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge)
1- So that the wicked atheists may continue in their evil they reject the opinion of the children of God, which declares the truth, in order to persist in their corruption.
2- The poor man is the righteous man, who seems weak before the wicked, but is mighty and strong within; because God is his refuge.

3- The poor man is also the humble man, that is, the poor in spirit, whom the proud try to dominate; because he is stronger than they, since God dwells in him, and so by his humility he rebukes them for their pride.

4- This verse can apply to Christ, for He is the poor One who humbled Himself by His Incarnation and His Cross, and the priests, scribes and Pharisees contradicted His teachings; because they rebuke their evils.

Take refuge in God when afflictions come upon you, or when others trouble you, so that you may stand firm in your faith and God may support you, and so you are not shaken by evil, but remain in your prayers; so that you have compassion on the wicked and pray that they may repent.
7- "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! when the Lord bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad."

1- After David's review of the evil of the atheists he declares his longings for divine salvation by saying "Oh that", which comes from Zion, as God promised that from the seed of David the Savior would come.
2- This verse is a prophecy about the return from captivity, which God accomplished in a miraculous manner at the beginning of the kingdom of Media and Persia at the hand of King Cyrus.

3- The bringing back from captivity is not only from the Babylonian captivity but also from the captivity of sin, and this is accomplished through the salvation of Christ and the repentance of those who believe in Him and their return to Him.

4- The salvation that comes out of Zion is not only through Christ the Redeemer on the Cross and His Resurrection, but also on the Day of Judgment, when Christ saves the righteous, His children, from the world and raises them to the Kingdom of Heaven.

5- "Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad": this is a symbol of the joy of Jacob, who has not yet met God and wrestled with Him but lives with Him, controlling his lusts and striving on his way, and of Israel, who wrestled with God and prevailed and whose name was changed to Israel, the joy of meeting God and fellowship with Him (Gen 32:22-32). That is, Jacob is a symbol of the ordinary believer and Israel a symbol of the saints who saw God clearly. And Jacob is also a symbol of the person who walks with God but is still in weakness and falls into various sins, while Israel is a symbol of the strong spiritual person who triumphs over sin, so the weak and the strong rejoice in God and both have a place in heaven, but each one in his own degree.
6- The Jews believe that this verse is a prophecy about the Messiah the Savior and they are still awaiting Him until now; because they did not believe in the crucified Christ the Redeemer.
It is good that you ask for God's salvation from all your sins with faith and hope, whatever your falls, and thank God, who raises you up and forgives you and keeps you.
Dwelling with God. "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle?"... (v. 1). Introduction:
1- The writer of this psalm is David the prophet, as it is in its title.
2- When was it written?
a - When David celebrated the bringing back of the Ark to Jerusalem.

b - There is another opinion, which is that David wrote it when he was fleeing from the face of Absalom and Zadok the high priest came out to him, carrying the Ark, and he said to him, Take it back into Jerusalem, that it may keep the city, and if God wills for me to return to the kingdom, I will enjoy worshipping before Him; then he declared his longings for worship before the Ark during the period of his flight.

3- This psalm was said at religious celebrations before the temple of God, so the visitor to the temple would say the first verse, which is a question about who deserves to dwell in the house of God, and the doorkeeper, that is, the guard, would answer him with the rest of the words of this psalm.
4- If the previous psalm, that is, the fourteenth, speaks about the fool, this psalm tells us about the characteristics of the children of God, who deserve to enter and settle in His house.
5- This psalm resembles the words of Isaiah the prophet in (Isa 33:15).
6- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime as number 14, because Psalms 9 and 10 are joined in the Septuagint translation from which the Agpeya was taken.
7- David lists the characteristics of one who deserves to dwell in the house of the Lord, and these characteristics show the following:
a - Whoever worships God must have characteristics that confirm his purity and righteousness.
b - Some of these characteristics concern the feelings of the heart and some the tongue, and finally what concerns conduct.
c - David presents to us eleven characteristics of one who deserves to dwell in the house of God; six of them positive, mentioned in vv. 2 and 4, and five of them negative, mentioned in vv. 3 and 5.
1- "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill?"

1- When David thought of those who enter and dwell in the house of the Lord, since inside it there were chambers in which the priests lived, in the days of Solomon, or tents in the days of David, he felt that God dwells and abides inside His house, and therefore the one who will dwell in the house of God must be distinguished by purity, and he wrote its manifestations in the following verses.

2- When we feel God's dwelling in the Church of the New Testament inside His house we are filled with awe, and we even feel that no one can enter the Church except through the blood of Christ the Redeemer, that is, no one deserves to receive the Holy Sacraments unless he is a believer in Christ the Redeemer and has received His grace in the sacrament of Baptism. David speaks of all these matters in the spirit of prophecy in this psalm, looking to Christ, in whom the divine promises are fulfilled. For this reason, when the time for Communion of the Holy Mysteries draws near, the priest cries out in the Liturgy, declaring the awe and greatness of drawing near to God and receiving His Body and Blood, and says, "The Holies for the holy."

3- If the heavens are not clean before God and He charges His angels with folly, who can dwell in His house? This is what David felt, so he presented the utmost he could of the characteristics of the righteous man here on earth, and in this he prepares himself to enter the divine presence in heaven.

4- When David said "who shall abide in thy tabernacle" he meant a temporary stay; because the word "abide" in the Hebrew original means staying in a tent, that is, a temporary stay. But his saying "dwell" in the same verse means settling; because the word "dwell" in the Hebrew original is a verb meaning to settle. In this we understand that David is not repeating himself in this verse, but means that whoever stays in a tent beside the tabernacle of meeting, and then wishes to settle in the heavenly dwelling of God, must enjoy the following conditions. David does not mean only dwelling in the house of the Lord on earth, but also in heaven.

5- Staying in a tent is during war, and therefore the words of the psalm mean that during our life on earth in the tent of this body we shall meet wars from Satan, but after this life we shall be transferred to the heavenly dwelling, in which we settle and the wars of the demons cease.

6- David says "thy holy hill" because the mountain is a symbol of the summit of elevation above earthly things; whoever wants to settle in the house of God must rise above earthly things to receive heavenly things. And whoever has experienced staying with God in His house enjoys fellowship with Him, and so rises gradually up the mountain, and the summit of this mountain means the summit of the relationship with God, that is, dwelling with Him in heaven.
7- Descending is also a symbol of God's condescension in dwelling by His Holy Spirit in the dwelling of our body, so that He may raise us up and we may settle with Him in the heavenly dwelling.

8- If David wrote this psalm in celebration of the transfer of the Ark, perhaps he felt the greatness of God and the awe of drawing near to Him, as he was affected by the death of Uzzah, who touched the Ark (2 Sam 6:7).
2- "He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart." (literally: he who walks in perfection, and works the truth, and speaks the truth in his heart)
This verse includes three positive characteristics, which are:
1- He who walks in perfection, and this includes the following:
a - The first characteristic is a positive one and is also a practical conduct, and it means walking in all righteousness and not walking in one virtue.
b - And walking in perfection means the absence of blemish, as in the Septuagint translation (the Agpeya), and it means the absence of visible blemishes that cause others to stumble.

c - And the word "without blemish" in the Septuagint translation, in its Hebrew origin, was used in describing the lambs without blemish that were slain in the house of the Lord, and these lambs are a symbol of Christ the Lamb without blemish, and the meaning of this is that this characteristic means perfection and walking without blemish, that is, being like Christ in His life on earth.

d - He says "he who walks", and this means a continuing state; he continues walking in perfection and has not yet arrived at perfection, so he is careful to keep away from visible sins, and if he falls into them he repents quickly.
e - God is the Perfect One, so whoever walks in perfection is the one who lives in communion with God and strives toward Him every day.
2- He who works the truth: this is the second characteristic, and by it is meant the following:
a - The truth is God, so he works by the commandments of God and all that pleases Him.
b - Truth also means justice, so he works with uprightness in all his dealings, favoring no one and wronging no one, imitating God.
c - He who works the truth, it is certain that he believes the truth within him and worships God faithfully, and this appears in his walking in the truth.
3- He who speaks the truth in his heart: this is the third characteristic, and by it is meant the following:
a - That his heart is pure and he lives sincerely in the commandments of God and feels God within him.

b - He who lives with truth in his heart is pure and therefore deserves to see God (Mt 5), that is, to receive spiritual enlightenment, so God reveals Himself to him and gives him the enjoyment of fellowship with Him.

c - He who lives in his heart with truth, his speech is truthful, so his thought and feelings appear in his speech without hypocrisy, and then they appear finally in his deeds, that is, walking in perfection and truth.

And therefore he is not liable to fall into lying, as Gehazi fell when he lied to Elisha the prophet, because his heart was attached to the love of possessions, so he behaved badly by lying to Naaman the Syrian and took from him garments and silver, and then lied to Elisha (2 Kgs 5:25).
3- "He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour."
1- This verse includes three negative characteristics of the righteous man who deserves to dwell in the house of the Lord.
2- The fourth characteristic is "he does not backbite with his tongue", and this characteristic means the following:
a - He does not hunt for a fault in another and pass it on to others to set them against each other; he enjoys the love that covers others (1 Pet 4:8).
b - He does not slander a person with lies for the purpose of harming him, for this is a clear sin of lying, in addition to lack of love, as we mentioned.
c - A straightforward person who does not work with cunning in secret; he is bold and easy to deal with and therefore others love him.
3- The fifth characteristic is "he does not do evil to his neighbour" and it includes the following:
a - His heart is full of love and all his dealings are good with his companions and those around him.
b - An unselfish person; just as he does not accept evil for himself he cannot do evil to others.
c - A faithful person who cannot betray his friend and do evil to him.
4- The sixth characteristic is "he does not take up a reproach against his neighbour" and this characteristic means the following:

a - A loving and gentle person who does not accept hearing others reproached before him, that is, he refuses condemnation in all its forms against every person; because the neighbour, as Christ interpreted in the parable of the good Samaritan, is every person (Lk 10:29-37).
b - He does not reproach anyone else, that is, he does not judge others.
c - His heart is forgiving; if he hears a condemnation or reproach of another he ignores it and rejects it and prays for all, to keep the purity of his heart and his love for those around him.
4- "In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the Lord. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."
1- This verse includes three positive characteristics by which the one who dwells in the house of the Lord is characterized.
2- The seventh characteristic is "in whose eyes a vile person is contemned" and its meaning is the following:
a - He hates vice, that is, sin, and not the vile person, or the sinner, however enticing the sin.
b - The eyes of this righteous man are lifted toward heaven, so all the lusts of the world are despised and contemned before him.
c - He is not influenced by the position or authority of sinners and does not follow after them, but rejects their evils.
3- The eighth characteristic is "he honoureth them that fear the Lord" and what is meant by it is the following:
a - He cares for the saints and the virtuous, to learn their virtues, and glorifies them and honors them.
b - He encourages the godly who fear the Lord, when they hold fast to virtue and endure the mockery of the wicked.

c - He fears God, so he loves those who fear Him and clings to them and becomes a disciple at their hands, as the saints did in both Testaments, such as Elisha's discipleship to Elijah, and Timothy's to Paul.
d - He loves God and sees Him in those who fear Him, even if they are despised by the wicked; he honors God when he honors those who fear Him.
4- The ninth characteristic is "he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" and it means the following:
a - Swearing was permitted in the Old Testament, so whoever swears by something bears its consequence even if it brings harm upon him and does not go back on his word.
b - A truthful and faithful person in his speech, so others trust him and deal with him with reassurance.
c - He fears God, so he fulfills his oath, or his promise, whatever the sacrifice.
d - Not attached to material things, but the love of God and of others is better in his sight, whatever he spends or sacrifices.
5- "He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved."
1- This verse includes two negative characteristics, then a very comforting conclusion.
2- The tenth characteristic is "he does not put out his silver to usury" and its meaning is the following:

a - He does not give a monetary loan of silver, or gold, or any possessions to a poor man and expect profits; he has compassion on the needy and helps them, or at least lends to them without benefiting from them.
b - Giving silver, or money, for the purpose of profit to banks, or companies so that they may trade with it, and they gain a part and give another part, is not wrong.

c - Silver is a symbol of the word of God, and this means that whoever puts out his silver to usury, that is, trades in the word of God, like one who preaches to receive honor and glorification from others, this is very wrong and cannot be done by the righteous who dwell in the house of the Lord.
d - Not attached to the love of money, but uses money to meet his expenses and the needs of those around him.
3- The eleventh and last characteristic is "he does not take a bribe against the innocent" and it includes these meanings.
a - A just person who does not pervert justice because of a bribe (Ex 23:8).
b - A person who loves righteousness and encourages it, so he cannot harm the righteous, whatever the temptations of the bribe.
c - Not attached to the love of money, but loves the truth with all his heart.
4- He concludes the psalm with this comforting statement, which is "he that doeth these things shall never be moved" and it means the following:
a - Whoever is distinguished by these characteristics enjoys inner peace and lives in reassurance.
b - This peace helps him to grow in his relationship with God and in spiritual joy, so he is rooted and established in God.
c - He is not moved, or troubled, since the wars of Satan become weak before him, that is, the devil does not prevail against him.
d - He enjoys this stability not only in this life but it extends to eternity in the Kingdom of Heaven.

Thus David concludes the psalm, that whoever enjoys these characteristics not only dwells in the house of the Lord, but goes beyond this with steadfastness for ever, that is, the enjoyment of God in this life, and then in heaven.

The way to the Kingdom is clear; if you love to be with God in eternity, then naturally you must enjoy fellowship with Him on earth, by keeping His commandments and keeping away from evil, so that you keep your inner peace all your days.
God is my portion. A golden psalm of David. "Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust"... (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, and the New Testament also bore witness to this (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35).
2- When was it said?

When David was fleeing from the face of Saul, the spies of Saul told him the place of David and he hastened to him with a great army to seize him, and reached him. A mountain separated them, and David prayed, and there came to Saul one who told him of the Philistines' attack on the land, so he left David and went to fight the Philistines (1 Sam 23:19-29).

3- We see in the title of this psalm "golden", and in the Septuagint translation "golden, on a pillar", and the meaning of this title is that the psalm was written in gold on a pillar, or a monument; for a monument is erected as an indication of victory.

4- This psalm is considered among the Messianic psalms; if the second psalm, "Why do the nations rage", speaks of the eternity of Christ, then His birth in the fullness of time, and the eighth psalm, "O Lord our Lord"... speaks of the incarnate Christ, who glorifies man, then this psalm tells us how the risen Christ glorifies man.
5- This psalm speaks of the Resurrection of Christ and therefore of the resurrection of man in Christ, to live with Him in the Kingdom while on earth until he reaches Him in heaven.
6- This psalm is prayed in the prayer of Prime as number 15, and because it speaks of the Resurrection, it suits this hour, which symbolizes the Resurrection of Christ at dawn.
1- "Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust."

1- This psalm begins with prayer, as David asks God to preserve him from dangers and death, since David was often exposed to Saul's pursuit of him, in addition to his wars with enemies, and then his flight from his son Absalom.
2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who speaks in the name of the Church, and asks the Father to preserve Him; because He trusted in Him (Heb 5:7; Jn 17).
3- David's faith in God appears here in his trusting in Him, so he is not troubled whatever dangers surround him; he is confident that He is able to preserve him.
2- "I said unto the Lord, Thou art my Lord: my good is nothing without thee."

1- David feels that God alone is his righteousness and his Lord, and it is a prophecy about Christ, who speaks showing His humanity, saying "my Lord"; because Christ by His Incarnation took the form of a servant, so the word "my Lord" suits Him.
2- David sees that God is the source of his good things, so he hopes for none other, and feels his sufficiency in Him, while the world with all its delights cannot satisfy him.

3- In the Septuagint translation it says, "Thou hast no need of my goodness"; David's goodness is from God, and it is a declaration from David that he does not depend on his own goodness, or strength, or any resources he has, but depends on God alone, the source of all good and strength. And this shows David's humility.
4- God is David's good, not only by His gifts, but God Himself in His love is David's good; he contemplates His Person and praises Him and rejoices in fellowship with Him.
3- "But to the saints that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight."
The excellent: that is, the virtuous, who are distinguished by virtues.

1- David's love for holiness and virtue appears in his love for the saints, that is, those who sanctify their lives and hearts to God. And the excellent, who strive to acquire virtues, and by them is meant all believers who strive in the way of righteousness, that is, the people of God. So he is encouraged by their company and encourages them. David loves holiness and virtue, and therefore he is bound to those who love them, for he is the one who said, "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" (Ps 133:1).
2- If this verse is a prophecy about Christ, then Christ shows here that His delight, His desire and His joy are in His children who strive in the way of holiness.

3- In the Septuagint translation, that is, the Agpeya, it says "his land", that is, the saints live in the land of God; it is a feeling of the children of God that their life depends on God and is in His protection and they live for Him, therefore God rejoices in them, for they rejoice in their life in God, and God rejoices in their trusting in Him. And the Septuagint translation says, "He hath wrought all his pleasure in them", that is, the saints gave their life to God and trusted in Him, so God fulfilled His will in them.
4- "Their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god: their drink offerings of blood will I not offer, nor take up their names into my lips."

1- David shows the corruption of the way of the wicked unbelievers, who worship gods other than God, and declares that their sorrows are many, meaning the bodily and spiritual troubles that befall them; because God has abandoned them. Perhaps, if they believe, they will repent and return to God.

2- These wicked people are a symbol of everyone who today depends on the powers of the world, such as money, lusts, or positions, and does not trust in God, so psychological and spiritual troubles befall him, and even if at first he gains some material things, he cannot enjoy them because of his agitation.

3- David clearly declares that he does not share with these wicked idol worshippers in any sacrifices and does not pour out their blood before the strange gods, that is, the children of God today are not attached to lusts and do not share with those who love them, but trust in God.
4- And David also, to protect himself from evil, does not mention the names of these wicked people or their gods with his lips; so that his heart is not attached, or his thought confused, by evil.

5- God declares through the tongue of David that He does not permit or bless idol worship and the pouring out of the blood of their sacrifices, and He rejects these wicked people and does not mention their names, that is, there is no place for them in heaven with Him.

6- During Saul's pursuit of him, David was compelled to take refuge in the Philistine city of Gath and in the land of Moab (1 Sam 27:3; 22:3, 4) and lived for a time among them, in flight from Saul, but he did not share in their idol worship; so he justifies himself in this by his saying "I will not pour out their drink offerings of blood."
5- "The Lord is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup: thou maintainest my lot."

1- On the other hand David declares his faith in God and his looking to heaven, where his eternal inheritance is, and God is also his cup, that is, all that God allows him of sufferings or blessings. And if he has lost something of material things through Saul's pursuit of him, or others', God will compensate him for them and restore them to him; because He maintains his lot, that is, his inheritance is not only in this world, but in great blessings in heaven.
2- If we take this verse as a prophecy about Christ, we find that Christ says to the Father that His inheritance is in Him, so He declares as man that His hope is not on earth, but in heaven.
And He accepts the cup of sufferings which the Father allows for Him, that is, death on the Cross, and rejoices in the accomplishment of the salvation of mankind.

And the Father will restore to Him His inheritance, since He "maintains my lot", that is, keeps for me my inheritance, and it means the salvation of the souls of men so that they believe in Christ, and He rejoices in their salvation. That is, the inheritance of Christ is His Church, which He acquired with His blood.
3- We see that David does not rejoice in being king on earth, but rejoices that God is his portion and his lot.

If only you would focus on your love for Christ, for He is the most precious thing in existence, and when you are raised to heaven nothing will draw you except His beauty, and you will contemplate Him for ever; therefore take care today for prayer, praise and contemplation.
6- "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage."

Lines: plural of line, and what is meant is the measuring line with which the areas of lands were measured in ancient times. Pleasant places: the good condition, which is taken from grace, and what is meant is fertile land.

1- David speaks with confidence after trusting in God, declaring that God's gift to him on earth will be a good and goodly land, and he means that God will supply his needs and give him abundant material gifts.
2- The better inheritance and the divine gift to David is his place in heaven, in the new earth, for it is better than everything on earth.
3- David enjoys God here on earth, and He gives him spiritual gifts, which are peace of heart and joy; God's gifts to him are abundant and goodly.

4- If David expresses in the tongue of every spiritual person that his inheritance is God Himself, and this is the greatest thing in existence, God also rejoices in possessing the heart of David and of every believer. These souls are the inheritance of God, to whom He gives countless gifts on earth and in heaven, and the inheritance of God are the saints, who have loved Him with all their hearts.
5- He says "the lines are fallen unto me", that is, it is a divine choice and a free grace from God, and therefore it is a precious gift that fills the heart with joy.

6- If we look at verses 1-6, we understand that whoever trusts in God and rejects the lusts of the world and strange gods, his portion is God, so he lives reassured on earth and in great enjoyment in eternity. And the opposite is true, for whoever chooses the pleasures of the world is deprived of fellowship with God and the Kingdom of Heaven.
7- "I will bless the Lord, who hath given me counsel: my reins also instruct me in the night seasons."
1- David felt the grace of God upon him in His guiding him all day to the truth, that he might walk uprightly, so he thanked God and blessed Him; because He counsels him and guides him.
It is the work of the Holy Spirit, who worked in the Old Testament partially, and in the New Testament continually in the heart of every believer in the Church.

2- Thanksgiving, praise and blessing God establish a person in a strong relationship with God and pour out upon him more abundant blessings, so he hears the voice of God more clearly and He guides him in all his steps.

3- David does not tire of prayer, for he prays all day and in the night too, and even sits to contemplate God's works with him all day, and then he hears the voice of God from his depths, which his reins symbolize. So he is attentive all day by way of thanksgiving, and likewise at night he reviews himself, and so also hears the voice of God, and in this he keeps away from sin by day and by night.

4- The night is an opportunity in which David examines himself for his mistakes all day, and God guides him from within and warns him to repent of his sins, so that he used to weep and make his bed swim with his tears, as mentioned in (Ps 6).
5- The night is a symbol of the darkness of sin, and during it God stirs the depths of man, which alert him to repentance and return to God.

6- The work of the Holy Spirit appears in this verse; He counsels David and every believer who is submissive to God during the day, and at night His voice rises and the person hears it clearly in the form of strong warnings about the mistakes that occurred during the day, and makes him watchful all night, for he is under the protection of the Holy Spirit, and therefore lives uprightly.

7- The work of the kidney in the body is to purify the blood of toxins; therefore David borrowed it to express the work of the Holy Spirit in the depths of man, to purify him from every sin and lead him to repentance.
8- "I have set the Lord always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."
1- David sees that his life is not without God's being before him; therefore he strove to remember that God is always before him, to lead him in all his steps.

2- We understand from the word "I have set" the importance of man's will; he must strive to remind himself of the presence of God, and then God favors him with the sense of the divine presence. Thus Elijah also felt when he said, "As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand" (1 Kgs 17:1), and likewise Joseph, who felt the presence of God, so he did not accept sin with Potiphar's wife (Gen 39:9). And therefore we say in the Divine Liturgy, "Guide us, O Lord, to Thy Kingdom", and in the Coptic original we find the meaning more exact, which is "Take a way before us into Thy Kingdom", that is, God is the constant leader of the believer in all the steps of his life, until He brings him to the Kingdom.
3- Since David feels God's presence with him, supporting him, and says "at my right hand", that is, giving him all strength, naturally he is not moved, however much the world is troubled around him.
4- God is before me, that is, my guide, and at my right hand, that is, my support; God is everything in my life and with me at all times, so I am not moved.

5- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who completed His ministry on earth, setting the Father before Him and at His right hand, for He is in the Father and the Father in Him; therefore He was not moved by persecution of Him and endured all the sufferings of the Cross for our sake. The Father is at the right hand of the Son and the Son at the right hand of the Father (Mk 16:19); because the two are equal in essence.
9- "Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoiceth: my flesh also shall rest in hope." (literally: my spirit rejoiced; my body also shall dwell in security)
1- If God is always before David, then naturally he is in marvelous joy and peace continually.

2- The heart is a symbol of the feelings and depths of man, so the joy of the heart is the true, steady joy. And the spirit of man clings to God who satisfies it and rejoices, and then David feels that his body is in a quietness free from all anxiety and agitation.
3- David's body dwells in security, that is, settles in peace, and his spirit exults within him; because it enjoys the sight of God and fellowship with Him.

4- David's body dwells in security, that is, lies in the grave in security; because it awaits Paradise and the Kingdom. And the Septuagint translation in the Agpeya is clearer, for it says "my flesh also shall dwell in hope", and what is meant is the hope of the Resurrection.

5- If Christ is the speaker, that is, this is a prophecy about Christ, He feels that He has completed His striving and His endurance of sufferings on earth and His steadfastness in the Father who is before Him and at His right hand (v. 8). Now in this verse He rejoices, after dying on the Cross, that He has accomplished the redemption and the salvation of mankind, and His body lies united with His divinity, secure in the tomb in hope of His Resurrection on the third day, when His luminous body is united with His soul which is united with the divinity, and then He appears to His disciples.
10- "For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption."

1- With faith and steady hope David declares that God will not leave his soul in Hades (Sheol), but it is a temporary period after which he is transferred to Paradise, when Christ accomplishes the redemption on the Cross; for David sees the promises from afar and greets them (Heb 11:13).
2- David, who fears God, believes that he will not see permanent corruption, that is, eternal torment.

3- This verse is the clearest verse about Christ, whose soul will not remain in Hades, but He only went down to Hades and brought Adam and his children up to Paradise, after He had bound Satan by the Cross. And likewise the word "thine Holy One" means Christ, who was like man in everything except sin alone; His body will not see corruption in the tomb, but the divinity united with it keeps it until He rises on the third day.

4- The love of God appears in this verse, who blesses those who fear Him and crowns them with glories in heaven. And God shows His love for the saints by keeping the bodies of some of them without corruption to this day, such as the body of St. Anba Pishoy.
5- Peter used the words of this psalm in his sermon on the day of Pentecost, when three thousand souls believed and were baptized (Acts 2:25-31).
11- "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

1- Since David is reassured of God's presence with him and that his end will be with God in eternal bliss, he thanks God who has made known to him and makes known to him the spiritual means that give him life with God, that is, prayer, contemplation and love for all.
2- He also thanks God, who satisfies him so that he is not attached to the world or abases himself before it, so he is always filled with God, and this naturally gives him gladness and joy.

3- David sees that as long as he depends on God who is at his right hand and leans on His strength, not on himself or the resources of the world, he continues to enjoy the bliss of fellowship with God on earth, and then the eternal bliss after this life.

4- Christ, who rose and whose body did not see corruption, raises those who believe in Him to live with Him in a lofty life while they are on earth, and also gives them by His Ascension into heaven joy and bliss with Him for ever, which cannot be expressed and surpasses all human imagination.

5- "Pleasures for evermore" means that God will continue in the Kingdom to give us from the abundance of His favors and satisfy us, for life in heaven is living, renewed and growing in a spiritual way that surpasses our minds; it is not boring at all, but there is a joy that surpasses all our imaginations.

Remind yourself that God is before you at all times, so that you may be reassured and rejoice and at the same time fear Him, so that you keep away from sin and grow every day in knowing Him, until you set out to glories unspeakable in heaven. God, the giver of righteousness and salvation. A prayer of David. "Hear the right, O Lord, attend unto my cry"... (v. 1). Introduction:

1- Its writer: David the prophet, who was distinguished by many prayers, and this whole psalm is considered a prayer, therefore it is written in its title that it is a prayer of David. Although the characteristic of all the psalms is prayer, this psalm is filled with petitions and supplications from its beginning to its end.
2- When was it said?
a - When David was fleeing from the face of Saul.
b - When he fled from the face of Absalom.
3- This psalm comes from the heart of one who is wronged, who believes in God, who is able to do him justice and save him, and then he comes out reassured, triumphant by the power of God.
4- If the title of this psalm is "A prayer", there are four other psalms whose title is also "A prayer", which are 86, 90, 102, 142.

5- This psalm applies completely to Christ during His passion, so it is considered among the Messianic psalms. And the psalms from (Pss 16-24) tell us about Christ the Savior, and the clearest of them is (Ps 22), the beginning of which Christ said on the Cross ("My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"), and this psalm and the one before it, that is, (Ps 16), are very similar, so that the Fathers call them the twins.
