6- This psalm is suitable for the Church to say in every affliction, and for every believer, when any trial passes over him.
1- “Hear the right, O Lord; attend unto my cry; give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips.”

1- Since David finds injustice surrounding him, he looks to God, who is the Truth, confident that He rejects injustice because He is perfect in His justice, and he entreats Him to hear his complaint, which is a righteous one against the slanders and wrongs of his enemies.
2- David pours out feelings from the depths of his being because he is suffering and wronged, so his prayer goes up to God like a cry.
3- David affirms that his words and entreaties are pure before God, in contrast to the lies of his enemies, who have risen up against him.

4- David's faith in God appears in his persistence, as he repeats his cry and entreaties to God three times in this verse and throughout the Psalm when he says (hear, attend, give ear). His persistence also expresses how much he is suffering from injustice, and his asking God to turn to him and to give attention to the details of his prayer. Perhaps he is addressing the Holy Trinity, asking for help from God in all His hypostases.

5- David trusts that God loves righteousness and answers the prayers of the righteous, for “the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16). So he tells God that his prayer comes from “lips without deceit”, and by this he of course does not mean to boast.

6- This verse applies fully only to Christ, the Righteous and Holy One, whose lips are without hypocrisy, for it is He who said, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Jn 8:46). Here Christ intercedes for His whole Church as its representative before God the Father, to remove from it the injustice of Satan.
2- “Let my sentence come forth from thy presence; let thine eyes behold the things that are equal.”

1- David believes that God alone is the Judge of the whole world, and that all the judgments of men are void without God. So David's judgment comes forth from before God, and this makes David firm, so that he is not shaken by the lies of the wicked, however many or persuasive they may seem, because God searches the hearts and the reins, and everything is naked and open before Him; and, on the other hand, He shows partiality to no one.

2- God the Holy sees only the things that are upright, and rejects the crooked deeds of men. Therefore David is sure that God will look upon the uprightness of his conduct and deliver him from the wicked.

3- Because David loved God and clung to Him, he wishes that his words and his judgments, that is, his judgment of his people as a king, would come forth from before God. David truly has a heart like God's heart, and wants his will to be God's will, and consequently his eyes see only the things that are upright, as appears in the Septuagint translation, which says, “my eyes behold the things that are upright.”

4- The Septuagint translation says, “from before Thy face let my judgment come forth.” The face of God is Christ: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18). Christ is the just Judge and the Judge on the Day of Judgment (Jn 5:22).

5- When David asks for God's judgment, he trusts that His judgment is for the good of his enemies and not for their harm; even if God's judgment contains discipline for the enemies, it is so that they may repent and be saved. David loves his enemies and seeks their good when he asks for judgment from the face of God.
3- “Thou hast proved mine heart; thou hast visited me in the night; thou hast refined me, and shalt find no blame in me; my mouth shall not transgress.”
Refined me: examined me.
Blame: evil; it comes from the verb “to blame.”

1- David, who gives his life to God and submits to His commandments, examines himself every night, and finds that God through His commandments examines him and alerts him to his iniquities, so that he may repent of them and God may cleanse him from all evil.

2- David does not review himself only concerning his deeds and words, but also concerning the feelings of his heart and his inner intentions. God tries him every night, that is, God constantly visits him with examination through the accounting of the soul, and this shows that David always lives in repentance and purity; therefore his prayer, which comes from a pure heart, is made entirely of pure words. It seems that he spent a long part of the night in this repentance, because he says, “thou hast visited me in the night”: if he spent the day at work, he spent the night in repentance and in meditation on God's commandments in order to be pure.

3- David speaks with confidence to God, who purifies him every night, and he declares that there is no evil or wickedness within him. Yet he is not speaking with pride; rather he shows how perfect God's work is in purifying him. And in the sixth Psalm he affirms his deep repentance every night, saying, “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps 6:6).

4- When God tries a person, He examines him thoroughly, so that he becomes utterly pure. Here David attributes the purification to God when he says, “Thou hast proved mine heart,” so that the result is assured, namely purity.

5- He who is occupied by the lusts of the world during the day has his night filled with evil thoughts and dreams; but he who sets the Lord always before him (Ps 16:8), like David, spends his night with God. He hears His voice, which visits him and alerts him to repent, and he feels God's kindnesses and thanks Him, so that the night becomes a greater delight to him than the day, since his heart is free for prayer, as the holy Fathers said, “The night is set apart for prayer.”
6- God's visiting David is not only at night, but also during the day.
7- If an evil thought comes to David's mind, he drives it away at once and does not let it come out in words; therefore he says, “my mouth shall not transgress.”

8- In humility David attributes the whole purification to God when he says, “Thou hast proved mine heart,” then “thou hast visited me in the night,” and after that “thou hast refined me,” that is, You have examined me with all precision in hard trials, as gold is purified from impurities by fire, and You found me in the end pure: “thou shalt find no blame in me.” Consequently he beseeches God to hear him and deliver him from the wicked oppressors.

9- We notice that David does not speak of the evils of his enemies, but prays with a pure heart in which there is no blame toward any person. This is one of the conditions of accepted prayer, the remaining conditions of which we notice in the verses of the whole Psalm: he condemns no one, and he prays with a heart that bears no resentment against those who wronged him; therefore God hears his prayer.
4- “Concerning the works of men, by the word of thy lips I have kept me from the paths of the destroyer.”
The violent one: the harsh and cruel.
1- This verse shows David's concern for the words of God's lips, that is, His commandments; he meditates on them, obeys them, and lets them lead his life in his conduct with others.

2- He is not disturbed by the works of violent men who wrong him or others, but remains in his upright conduct according to God's commandments. He loves everyone and is not overcome by evil, but overcomes evil with good; the credit for David's upright works goes back to the word of God.

3- David enjoys a pure tongue, as he said in (v. 1) “from lips without deceit,” and likewise a pure heart (v. 3), for God proved his heart and found in it no “blame.” In this verse he tells us about his pure works, which are according to God's commandments, even if he lives among the wicked, the hard of heart, and is not influenced by their ways and conduct.

4- Even if the ways of the violent wicked carry evil speech against David, David the righteous was not driven to speak evil words against them or about them, because he is obedient to the word of God, who keeps him from evil. The word of God keeps the tongue of His righteous children, so that they do not slip into evil, even if the wicked say evil things about them.
5- “Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not.”

1- What are the footsteps of God but His works with mankind and in nature, all of which is good and for edification? David admired these footsteps, so he walked after God to do good to every person, even the wicked among them.

2- In this verse we see David's attachment to God and his trust, as a son, in holding fast to God's footsteps; he cannot walk on a road without God, that is, without God being a leader for him and a light for his path.
3- David's following after God kept him from following after evil, and consequently he was not exposed to slipping and falling into the sins of the wicked around him.

4- God's love appears in His care for His righteous children, as He places signs on the spiritual road that leads to the Kingdom, so that His children may walk by their guidance, and these are His footsteps. God does not leave Himself without witness (Acts 14:17), such as the righteous and the just who live among us, and likewise everything that happens in the events around us; even the wrongs that others do to us may be a sign on the road, that we may take heed not to slip into sin.

5- In the Septuagint translation it says, “Establish my goings,” instead of “my footsteps hold fast.” From this appears David's request for God's help, which establishes him on the road; even if the road is hard, he is able to cross it with God's help, and indeed to be firm on the divine road, not turning aside from it through the wiles of the devil.
6- This verse is a prophecy about the footsteps of Christ, who became incarnate and lived in our midst so that we might follow Him in all His life, as it appears in the four Gospels.
6- “I have called upon thee, for thou wilt hear me, O God: incline thine ear unto me, and hear my speech.”

1- David believes in God's fatherhood, and that He hears him and answers him, because He is also able to answer; therefore he calls upon Him and asks of Him all his needs in prayer, and he also trusts in His justice, for He does not accept injustice.

2- David likewise trusts in God's love and humility, and asks Him to condescend and incline His ear to his prayers. He knows that he has a place in God's heart which no one else fills, and trusts that God cares for him and hears his requests.
3- David has tested God in his life, for he sought Him often and He answered him; this gives him confidence and boldness to call upon Him today.

4- God's inclining His ear appears clearly in the Incarnation of His only Son, to declare His nearness to us and His care for our needs. Therefore this verse is a prophecy about Christ, because Christ is our Intercessor, since through His redemption our requests reach the Father.
7- “Show thy marvellous lovingkindness, O thou that savest by thy right hand them which put their trust in thee from those that rise up against them.”

1- David, who trusts in God's mercy, asks for distinguished and wondrous mercies for those who trust in God like himself, since he has none but God to support him, whereas the wicked adversaries rely on the powers of the world, that is, their influence, their money and their great numbers; and God in His wisdom and justice pours out countless mercies on those who trust in Him.

2- David trusts in God's mercy, so he asks that these mercies be from His right hand, that is, from the fullness of His power, so that they may be wondrous and great mercies, which will of course support those who trust in Him.

3- David asks God to answer his prayers because He is the Truth and Justice (v. 1), and also because He is righteous and so cares for the pure (v. 3); and then, thirdly, he asks that his prayers be answered by the merciful God, who has great mercy on those who trust in Him (v. 6).

4- God's right hand is a symbol of Christ, who sat at the right hand of the Father; here it is a symbol of the Incarnation of Christ, who has mercy on the believers who trust in God through His redemption.

5- David asks God to distinguish His mercies, meaning to show them clearly, lest some people think that they happen by chance and not from God. He wants all people to know that God is the source of mercies, and that He uses people and the events of life as instruments to show His mercies; but here David wants God's mercies to be so distinguished that a person cannot overlook them or doubt them, like the standing still of the sun for Joshua during his war (Josh 10:13), or the going back of the shadow to declare God's mercy in extending the life of King Hezekiah by fifteen years (Isa 38:8).

6- God's right hand, which supports a person and protects him, does not prevent the wars of the adversaries, but it supports him so that he overcomes them. In life we will meet trials, but our Christ promises us that “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Jn 61:33).
8- “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings,”
Apple (pupil): the round opening in the middle of the iris of the eye, which appears black but is transparent; light enters the eye through it, and it is in the center of the eye.

1- David is reassured by God's care and tenderness, so he asks Him to look after him and keep him, and he trusts in God's precise care, which looks after his weakness, as a person looks after his eye and closes his eyelids over it so that it is not exposed to dust or any foreign bodies. So God keeps him from every evil and from any problems greater than he, and shuts him in His embrace, so that he is at peace however much troubles surround him. God makes him close his eyes to evil sights, and feel God's works in everything good around him.

2- In humility David feels his weakness and asks for God's protection, which covers him with His wings, so that the sun, which is a symbol of trials, does not scorch him. In God's shadow he feels protection and peace, as the hen protects her chicks with her wings (Mt 23:37).

3- David trusts in his sonship to God, that is, God's love for him as a father for his son, and even higher than this, for he feels that he is the apple of God's eye (Zech 2:8), which He keeps with His care; and by this confidence of love he receives abundant blessings and care from God.

4- God created the human eye amid bones that surround it, called the socket of the eye, to protect the eye from any external injury. The eye is a very important organ in the body, through which a person sees all that is around him and so leads the whole body in the right way. God's care for the eye is care for the whole body, and God's care for David is care for all his people, because he is their shepherd.

5- God's keeping of the apple of the eye is to make it a single eye that sees God in everything around it and keeps away from evil, for God is the source of spiritual enlightenment, which He gives to the eye. The eye surrounded by the bones of the face resembles Jerusalem surrounded by the mountains, illumined by the Temple that is in its midst.
9- “From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about.”
Enemies of the soul: enemies of my soul.
Compass me about: surround me.

1- In the previous verse David showed his confidence in God's care, which is like the care of the apple of the eye and sheltering under God's wing; and here he declares that he is not disturbed by the wicked's attempt to ruin his soul, for they are worthless as long as he relies on God and takes refuge in Him. This is what happened with David when Saul's counselors incited him against David to kill him, but God was always protecting him.

2- The hideousness of Satan's wars appears in that he wants to ruin the soul of man; therefore there is no truce with Satan, but one must keep away from every evil and every semblance of evil, because the crafty Satan presents sin in an attractive form, to make man fall into the trap.

3- The wicked in their wickedness surround the righteous in order to make him fall; so if the righteous fortifies himself with God, in the form of spiritual practices such as prayers and fasts, he has built a wall around himself that the wicked cannot storm, for taking refuge in God is the only solution. Because of the wicked surrounding David, he pleads with God to hasten and protect him, for pleading with God is the only refuge and solution.
10- “They are inclosed in their own fat: with their mouth they speak proudly.”

1- David describes the wicked as having a fat heart, because they were concerned with satisfying their lusts and doing every evil, so they became extremely selfish, and consequently became unable to feel for those around them or to offer mercy and love to the needy. On the contrary, they closed their hearts and feelings to those around them.

2- From the wicked closing their hearts we understand that a person has the freedom to feel for those around him or to refuse to; whoever is busy fattening his heart will lose his feeling for people, so that he sees their needs with his eyes and his heart is not moved to help them. And he who has closed his heart with lusts will not feel God, and consequently will not feel others. Whoever does not love God will be unable to love others.

3- If selfishness and lusts lead to keeping away from works of mercy, they will also lead the wicked to what is worse, which is speaking with pride and troubling others, and even despising the weak. Thus we see that sin descends from the evil feelings of the heart to evil speech; whoever does not treat his inner thoughts and feelings will have evil increase within him, and it will show on his lips, and then in his deeds.

4- This verse applies to the wicked who surrounded David, such as Saul and Absalom the son of David, and everyone who tried to wrong David. It applies also to Christ, whom the scribes, the Pharisees, the priests and the high priests tried to ensnare in a word and to deliver into the hand of the Roman authority, and then attempts to kill Him, which ended in His crucifixion; by this they closed their hearts to listening to His words, and also spoke proudly against Him.
11- “They have now compassed us in our steps: they have set their eyes bowing down to the earth;”
Make us slip: make us fall into sin.
1- The wicked watch the movements of the righteous at every step in order to surround him and harm him; he therefore needs God's help, which protects him and delivers him from their hands.

2- The wicked prepare snares for us, so that we slip into them and are deceived by them, and fall into their hands, and then they laugh at us. They rejoice in evil, since they have no love; but the righteous strives to do good even to enemies, and therefore God protects him.

3- The righteous must beware of the snares that the wicked set, which are hidden or covered with attractive things, in order to deceive the righteous by them. The remedy is prayer and careful watchfulness.

4- If David in the previous verses spoke of the righteous in the singular, now in this verse he speaks in the plural, because Satan fights the whole Church, or the company of the righteous; it is not Christ only, but all His children.

5- The wicked try to make us fall into earthly things, that is, earthly lusts; but if our hearts are attached to heaven, their wiles will weaken and almost come to an end, since we use earthly things as food and clothing, but our hearts are drawn to heavenly things.
12- “Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places.”
Greedy: eager to prey.
His lair: his den, which is the lion's house.

1- David cries out to God for help, because the wicked one who stands before him, by whom he means Satan and all who follow him, is like a lion in his strength, and this lion longs and is eager to prey upon David, since his evil nature drives him to wrong others; he loves evil and rejoices in destroying the righteous.

2- The wicked one is also likened to a young lion: though he may seem small, he sits in his house waiting for the opportunity to crush the righteous; even if he suffers from some weakness now, he awaits the nearest opportunity to do harm to the righteous.

3- The wicked one in his wickedness has become like the beast of prey, the lion, that is, he has gone far from God and become like an animal; he does not understand love and spiritual values, but believes only in his lusts and in fulfilling them at the expense of others.

4- The wicked one is like the lion eager to prey upon whomever he meets. And it is known that the one who hunts is the lioness, that is, the mother who leaves her cubs in their den and goes out to prey on whatever she meets and brings the prey to be food for her mate and her young; and the lioness, in her anxiety for the young she has left at home, is fierce in her hunting, and on the other hand is seeking food for them lest they die of hunger. So the wicked one is always inclined to evil and in constant anxiety, and wrongs everyone he meets, especially the righteous, who are symbolized by tame animals.

5- The lion is distinguished by strength and also by cunning; he seizes the opportunity to attack the last animal in a large herd so that the herd will not tear him apart, and in this he is a symbol of the wicked one who watches for the opportunity to destroy the righteous if he strays a little from the rest of the flock, that is, the members of the Church, and grows careless in his relationship with God.

If the wicked are strong and deceitful and want to devour you, do not be disturbed, for your God is stronger than they. Do not look at your weakness, but at the power of God, and you will walk in peace among the wicked, and even love them and have compassion on them, and so win them and bring them back to God by your love.
13- “Arise, O Lord, disappoint him, cast him down: deliver my soul from the wicked, which is thy sword:”

1- David sees that he is weak in his confrontation with Satan through the wicked who want to destroy him, so he asks God to be a barrier between him and the wicked one, just as God went before and stood between the children of Israel and the Egyptians with the pillar of fire at the Red Sea, and separated them until the people of God had crossed before Pharaoh and his army, so that they did not touch a single person of God's people and were drowned in the Red Sea (Ex 14:29). So He prevents his wrongs to David, because God is stronger than all the wicked and able to protect His children.

2- David trusts in God's power, which is able to triumph and destroy Satan, that is, to subdue him and protect God's children from him. Thus evil returns upon the head of the wicked one, so that instead of his casting down the righteous, God casts him down. David here does not want vengeance on the wicked one, but vengeance on evil and the exposure of its vanity, to establish the faith of God's children.

3- David asks God to deliver him by His sword, which is the word of God, which satisfies the righteous and at the same time judges the wicked and condemns them and destroys them if they do not repent.

4- The wicked think that God's long-suffering means His neglect of men, or His weakness; therefore David calls upon God to arise, that is, to show His power, in order to stop the wicked from persisting in their wickedness, and to save his soul and all the righteous.

5- If God's sword is meant to be the word of God, it also symbolizes His authority and justice, as well as His wrath, as it declares the truth against the vanities of the wicked. And if God is silent for a time, it is to give the wicked an opportunity to repent, but He will certainly use His sword to destroy those who oppose Him, who want to destroy the righteous.

14- “From men which are thy hand, O Lord, from men of the world, which have their portion in this life, and whose belly thou fillest with thy hid treasure: they are full of children, and leave the rest of their substance to their babes.”
Treasures: precious riches and gifts.

1- David affirms his need of God to deliver him from the hands of men, the people of the world, that is, the wicked around him; he trusts in God's hand, which is able to protect him however many his enemies may be.

2- The wicked have as their portion their earthly lusts, which they obtain during their life on earth. But the portion of the righteous is God, with whom they live on earth, until He takes them with Him into the heavenly Kingdom.
3- The wicked forget that God is the source of all the blessings they enjoy, of food or drink or possessions, so they do not thank Him, but rise up against His righteous children to destroy them.

4- Among God's gifts to men is that He gives them children, and also gives them material blessings with which to be satisfied and to give the remainder to their children, so that they too are satisfied. In all this they do not ascribe the glory to God, and do not thank Him, and here the selfishness of the wicked appears, for they are satisfied first and then give to their children, and this conflicts with self-giving love.

5- God's hand symbolizes His tangible work among men, and the clearest picture of His work is His Incarnation to redeem mankind. David longs for the redemption of Christ, and speaks of it in the spirit of prophecy, that mankind may be delivered from the dominion of Satan.
6- The wicked, to whom God gave many treasures, are still in their wickedness wanting to prey upon others; they do not need to prey, for they are satisfied, but their love of evil drives them to it.

7- The wicked leaving their remainder to their children teaches the children the lust to prey and to destroy others, so they become wicked like their fathers. And this is the extreme of spiritual folly, that a man corrupts his children while he thinks it benefits them.
15- “As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.”

1- On the other hand, the righteous walks in an upright life with God, and by this uprightness and righteousness God rejoices in him, and reveals to him His secrets and His knowledge, so that he enjoys the sight of God. This is the Kingdom on earth which, if a person lives it, qualifies him for the heavenly Kingdom. And the more a person walks in righteousness, the more he discovers God in His works and sees Him clearly in all that is around him.
2- When a person beholds God, his heart is filled with the fear and love of Him, so he keeps away from evil and turns to good, that is, he grows in righteousness every day.

3- The righteous cannot begin his day except with prayer, to see God, so that he longs to be like Him in his works all day long. And when he becomes like God he rejoices and is satisfied spiritually with God's love, and God also suffices him in all his bodily needs.

4- Perfect righteousness is Christ, who lived without sin on earth: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18). Through Christ the Righteous we can see God the Father, and Christ declared this clearly when He said, “without me ye can do nothing” (Jn 15:5), and we end the Lord's Prayer in Christ Jesus, through whom we receive all our requests. And the most important request is that we see God, for if we see God our souls are satisfied, and we keep striving all our lives to be like Him, until we see Him always before us. And in the end we reach the Kingdom through the righteousness He has given us on earth. And there we see none but God, the everlasting satisfaction forever. From this we understand that this verse is a prophecy about Christ.

5- Righteousness is purity of heart, and Christ declared in His Sermon on the Mount, saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” (Mt 5:8); so in righteousness we behold the face of God.

6- If the wicked are satisfied with the lusts of the world and do not perceive God who gives them (v. 15), the righteous are satisfied by seeing God and being like Him, and they see that all the material things in their hands are a grace from God and speak to them of Him.
7- The righteous in righteousness beholds God all day long, and at night sees God in his dreams, and when he awakes longs to be like God in his thoughts, his speech and his conduct.

8- David concludes the Psalm by saying that the life of the righteous is in seeing God always through his continual prayer. And if he is distracted from God, he returns and takes heed and awakes from his heedlessness, and sees God and is satisfied with Him, and in his life is like God, that is, a true human being as God wants him, who created him in His image and likeness. And if he falls into sin he rises from it with the risen Christ, and returns and beholds God and enjoys Him.

Your life is God, and you can taste Him and behold Him through prayer; so never keep away from it, but seek God at all times, not only in your official times of prayer, but before every work and during it and after it, and you will enjoy seeing Him.

God is my deliverer and my strength. To the chief musician. For the servant of the Lord, David, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song in the day that the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul, and he said:
“I will love thee, O Lord, my strength” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: David, as we find in the title of this Psalm.
2- When it was said: there are two opinions:

A- The title of this Psalm mentions that David said it on the day God delivered him from his enemies. By the day is meant the end of the troubles David faced from Saul and many enemies, such as Ishbi-benob (2 Sam 21:15-17); this period in his view was as one day, and he accepted the sufferings for God's sake, who saved him, and he is in joy and thanks God for delivering him; that is, David wrote it at the end of his life, and this is the more probable opinion.

B- The other opinion is that David did not write this Psalm at the end of his life, but wrote it after he reigned over the whole kingdom of the children of Israel, when the wars of Saul were still clear in his mind, and before he suffered the fall of adultery and murder; because he speaks much of his righteousness and perfection, that is, he had not yet reached the age of forty.
3- This Psalm is found almost word for word in (2 Sam 22). From this it is clear that it was said at the end of his life, that is, about thirty years after he began to reign.
4- In the introduction to this Psalm David calls himself the servant of the Lord, and this shows his humility and his pride in belonging to God and relying on Him.
5- This Psalm is one of the Messianic Psalms, for it speaks many prophecies about Christ.
6- The Apostle Paul quoted from this Psalm twice, namely (Rom 15:9; Heb 2:13).
7- God's delivering David from his enemies is a symbol of Christ's victory over Satan by the Cross and His Resurrection, and then His reign forever.
8- This Psalm suits everyone who strives in his spiritual life, strengthening him and establishing his hope of victory.
9- In the Septuagint translation we find in the title of the Psalm “to the end,” by which is meant:
A- the complete deliverance of David from his enemies and his rest as king.
B- a prophecy about the completion of salvation on the Cross.
C- a prophecy about the acceptance of the Gentiles, that is, the offering of redemption to mankind, to the whole world.

10- David spoke this song to the Lord, as appears in the title of the Psalm, and it does not say that he praised or sang it; he said it without musical instruments, and it seems that this was because of his advanced age, so that he did not chant the Psalm with melodies or music.
11- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- “I will love thee, O Lord, my strength.”
1- This shows the extent of David's attachment to God and his love for Him.

2- It shows David's humility and his confession of his weakness, for the only source of his strength is God; he trusts in God and is at peace as long as God is with him, so he does not fear things to come, since in God is the fullness of strength.
3- This verse also shows the personal relationship and familiarity between David and God in his saying “my strength,” and this relationship is confirmed in the following verses of the Psalm.
2- “The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.”

1- David expresses God's power that supports him, so he likens God to the rock and ascribes it to himself, because he feels God's fatherhood toward him: God is his rock, and if God is his rock, who can prevail against him? The rock represents steadfastness, and David boasts in God, the source of his steadfastness.

2- God is also a fortress that protects David, so that none of his enemies can harm him, however they surround him, like Saul, who pursued him many times with large armies, while he felt that God was his fortress, that is, that He had given him constant protection that never ends. He points to the power of the salvation of Christ, offered on the Cross, which saves and protects His children continually.

3- If David sinned and went away from God, even a little, and went outside the fortress, God has compassion on him and delivers him; indeed, his enemies set many snares for him and God delivered him from them all.

4- David also expresses God's protection of him by saying that God is his buckler. The buckler is a defensive instrument of war with which the soldier shelters from the enemy's arrows, just as David and every spiritual person shelter in God from the arrows of the demons.

5- The salvation that David received and lives by is a mighty salvation, which he likens to the horn, because the horn is the strongest part of the animal, with which it can gore its enemies. David is able to overcome his enemies by the power of God, so he attacks them and triumphs over them. The horn is also used as a trumpet to proclaim war, so it symbolizes the proclamation of salvation and victory over Satan.
6- David affirms God's care for him: if he is exposed to any attacks from enemies he is not disturbed, but hastens to God, his refuge, and rests in Him.
3- “I will call upon the Lord, who is worthy to be praised: so shall I be saved from mine enemies.”
1- If God is everything to David, that is, his Savior, his strength, his rock, his fortress, his deliverer and his refuge, then He truly deserves continual thanksgiving and praise.

2- David's continual praise pours God's mercies upon him, so that He continues to protect him from his enemies. David loves God and delights in thanking Him, for his aim is to glorify God, and then God's fatherhood appears in an increasing protection of David.
4- “The cords of death compassed me, and the floods of destruction made me afraid. 5- The cords of hell compassed me about: the snares of death overtook me.”
Compassed me: surrounded me and embraced me.
Compassed me about: surrounded me.
Snares: traps.
Fastened (took hold): were driven in; the term is used of the claws of wild beasts when they seize the prey.

1- David was exposed to death many times by his enemies, so he expresses the seriousness of his condition, likening death to a strong man who has attacked him and bound him with cords that surround his body to crush it, but he is still alive.
2- If we take these verses as prophecies about Christ, He experienced all this on the Cross and in the tomb.

3- In the Septuagint translation we find “the pangs, or the birth-pangs, of death compassed me,” that is, David entered into sufferings from his enemies like the pains of a woman when she gives birth, but since he cried out to God he came out with greater strength and steadfast faith.

4- “The floods of destruction made me afraid” refers to the very many thoughts that attacked David like floods to terrify and frighten him, since he was on the verge of death at the hands of his enemies, but he was patient and endured, so God kept him and brought him out of his distress. David repeats this same verse in (Ps 116:3).

5- As David faced death at the hands of his enemies, he felt as if Sheol had surrounded him and embraced him and bound him like cords, but he called upon the Lord and He delivered him, as he said in (v. 6).

6- In facing his enemies David felt that death was like a set of snares that had been driven into his flesh, that he had fallen into them and could not get out, and he had no one before him but God to deliver him from them, so he prayed to Him, and He saved him from this great danger.
7- David describes the difficulty of his condition as he faced death, in order to show how great is the God who delivered him from it.
6- “In my distress I called upon the Lord, and cried unto my God: he heard my voice out of his temple, and my cry came before him, even into his ears.”

1- Before this violent distress in which David nearly died, he had nothing to do but take refuge in God his Savior and pray to Him; indeed he cried from the depths that God might deliver him. This shows David's faith in God, since in distress he has no refuge but Him.
2- David was assured that God heard his prayer and his cry to Him.
God's temple is the place of His dwelling, and what is meant is:
A- Heaven, where God dwells.
B- The Holy of Holies in the tabernacle of the congregation, where the ark of God's covenant is.
In sum, God cared for David's prayer and answered him. This shows God's love and care for His children, especially in distress.

3- The entering of David's cry into God's ears means God's comprehension of and concern for the distress of David His son. God cares for the needs of His children, and does not hear them merely as information, but takes them to heart, feels for His children and rises to deliver them from all their troubles.

Be at peace, for your God loves you and looks upon all your needs and hastens to answer your prayers, to deliver you from all your distresses. Be at peace however long the trial lasts, for God is beside you to keep you and save you from it, and even to turn it to your good.
7- “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken, because he was wroth.”

1- God's answer appeared in His moving to help His son David, and when God moved David felt that the earth was shaking violently, and the strongest thing in it, the mountains, began to tremble because of God's wrath against the wicked. Nature feared God, but unfortunately the wicked man remains immersed in his wickedness until he meets his destruction, as Saul did.

2- This disturbance happened in the kingdom of the demons when Christ became incarnate and preached His salvation in the world, and then was lifted up on the Cross, for the devil knew that Christ was able to bind him. David saw all this in the spirit of prophecy and wrote it in this verse. Therefore, as we have said, this Psalm is one of the Messianic Psalms.
3- This disturbance will also happen at the end of days, when the Day of Judgment draws near and God's wrath against the wicked appears.
8- “There went up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it.”

1- The appearance of smoke is a prelude announcing that fire is coming, or fire within, whose outward appearance is smoke: God's wrath is the fire and the shaking of the earth is the smoke; or the fire is the complete judgment, and the wrath is the afflictions that come upon the wicked so that they may repent.
2- The fire coming out of God's mouth is His words, which condemn the wicked and sentence them to destruction.

3- The stone kindled from the divine fire symbolizes the Apostles, who preached in the whole world, and so purified with fire the hearts of the believers and drew them to Christ, and condemned the wicked who refused to believe.
4- God tests us with fire in this life through afflictions, that we may repent; but if we refuse repentance, the fire of eternal torment awaits us.
9- “He bowed the heavens also, and came down; and mist was under his feet.”
Bowed: lowered and brought down.

1- The wickedness of the wicked and their attacks on the righteous stirred up God's wrath, but out of His tenderness He did not destroy them at once; He prolonged His long-suffering until the Day of Judgment. On the contrary, He condescended from His heavenly glory and became incarnate to redeem us, and to show us, through His life on earth, how a person ought to live.

2- Heaven comes down to earth through the Incarnation of Christ, so that He may make heaven and earth one in His Person, and lift up His children who live on earth into heaven, so that they become earthly angels, or heavenly beings living on earth, until they return to their natural place in heaven and live in it forever.

3- God's feet are a likening of Him to man; this symbolizes His Incarnation and His love and tenderness toward man, as the Monday praise says that God was overcome by His compassion and sent us His high arm, that is, the Incarnation of Christ.

4- The mist under His feet symbolizes His presence, as it appeared in many places in the Holy Bible at the appearances of God, whether in the Old Testament or the New. The mist indicates that the mysteries of God cannot be grasped by any man, but He reveals to us what we can bear to grasp. The mist proclaims His greatness and majesty. The mist also symbolizes God's holy children who surround Him on earth in His holy Church.
10- “And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind.”

1- God's movement and His descent from heaven was surrounded by His angels, so He flew from heaven and came down to earth. And though in appearance He is a man, at the same time He is God, all-knowing; therefore it says “he rode upon a cherub,” and the order of the Cherubim, or Seraphim, are those full of eyes, that is, of knowledge.
2- God's riding upon a cherub and flying also symbolizes His Ascension, after He had completed His redemption of mankind.

3- The winds upon which God flew symbolize the spirits of His holy children, upon whom He descended with His Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, and when they completed their striving on earth He lifted them up by His Spirit to heaven; and He moves over them with His Spirit and overshadows them with His love.

4- David's faith appears in his speaking of God, not only that He answered him and shook the foundations of the earth, that is, the wicked, however strong and firm they seemed, but that He came down in His love to earth to seize Satan and bind him with His Cross. David feels that God will do everything to deliver him, so He draws near to him and saves him from all the wicked.
11- “He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were the mist of waters and thick clouds.”

1- God made darkness His covering in His Incarnation, where He hid the divinity in the humanity, and the God who became man appeared as an ordinary man; but whoever looks closely with faith at His words and works discovers His divinity. He is a hidden God who cannot be seen except by faith and as far as man can bear, and even His angels grasp only a little of His glory, as Isaiah declared of God that He is “a God that hidest thyself” (Isa 45:15), and David himself said of Him in (Ps 97:2), “Clouds and darkness are round about him.”
2- God's pavilion round about Him is His Church, in which and by which He works, and in which He satisfies His children.
3- His pavilion is also His humanity, in which He hid the splendor of His divinity and His glory.

4- The mist of waters are the Apostles, priests and servants, who lift themselves by their lives to heaven, and may be called earthly angels. The waters are their words and teachings, or the word of God that they speak; that is, the heavenly mist turns into waters that quench the thirsty, just as the life of the Apostles and servants of the New Testament turns into light and teaching that satisfies souls and draws them to Christ. St. Paul called them a cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1).

5- The thick clouds, that is, the dense cloud in which it is hard to see what is within, yet which is high in the sky, symbolize the prophets of the Old Testament, who lived a heavenly life and proclaimed the voice of God and prophesied about Christ, but in prophecies and types that were obscure in the Old Testament and became clear when Christ became incarnate.

The thick clouds also symbolize the Holy Sacraments in the Church, in which the Holy Spirit works and quenches the thirst of the believers, such as the hiding of His Body and Blood under the appearances of bread and wine in the sacrament of Holy Communion.

12- “At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire. 13- The Lord also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice; hail stones and coals of fire. 14- Yea, he sent out his arrows, and scattered them; and he shot out many lightnings, and troubled them.”
1- It expresses God's love for His children in His haste to deliver them with His brightness that pierces the cloud, for He loves them and cares for their prayers and hastens to their help.
2- God the Mighty punishes the wicked who wrong the righteous, His children, so He rains upon them hail, which is sharp flakes of ice that kill whomever they meet.
And He also casts fire upon them that burns them, as happened in the plague of hail and fire upon the Egyptians (Ex 9:23), and likewise with the people of God in Sinai (Num 16:35).

3- The power of God coming down to deliver His children appears in the sounds of thunder that accompanied His descent; in this verse He wants to declare His divine power, which shook the foundations of Satan's kingdom when He became incarnate.

4- Perhaps the thunders point to the rejoicing of the angels at receiving Christ ascending to heaven, when He ascended before His disciples forty days after the Resurrection, victorious over Satan after binding him on the Cross. Perhaps they also symbolize the rushing mighty wind that blew on the day of Pentecost when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples (Acts 2:2), to declare God's power that works in His righteous children, so that they defeat the power of Satan.

5- With the hail and the fire was the voice of the Most High God to destroy the wicked, and it points to God's power that delivered David from his enemies, not by a visible heavenly power such as hail and fire but by a divine ordering, such as the killing of Saul in the war (1 Sam 31:4), and the killing of his son Ishbosheth by the hand of his servants, so that David might reign (2 Sam 4:7, 8). So also God intervenes in every generation by His divine ordering to deliver His children, as He made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots that troubled them so that they fled in the days of Elisha the prophet (2 Kgs 7:6).

6- The arrows of God that He sent out and His lightnings that troubled the wicked are His angels of light and His pure Apostles, who by their preaching aimed arrows at the hearts of the demons, and so snatched from them the souls that had been in the hand of Satan and believed in Christ. The arrows symbolize the power of the word of God, and the lightnings symbolize the luminosity of the servants of the New Testament, which exposed the wickedness of the wicked and troubled them.
15- “Then the channels of waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were discovered at thy rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils.”

1- When God declared His wrath against the wicked in order to save His righteous children, the depths of the waters in the seas and rivers appeared, as happened when He divided the Red Sea (Ex 15:8) to deliver His people Israel and drown Pharaoh and all his army, and as He divided the river Jordan so that His people might cross with Joshua to possess the Promised Land and cleanse it of all the uncleanness of the Gentiles (Josh 3:13), and as Elijah and Elisha divided the Jordan (2 Kgs 2:8, 14), so that Elijah might be lifted up to heaven, and Elisha might begin his ministry as a prophet to Israel and rebuke evil, that the people might repent.

2- The Lord's rebuke and the breath of His nostrils are His words on the lips of the prophets in the Old Testament, to condemn sin and bring His people back to Him. They are also His words by the Apostles and servants of the New Testament; God's wrath and His rebuke of sin expose the foundations of evil, so that man may be rid of it and live anew to God.

Let God's wrath be for you and not against you, so that it exposes to you the wickedness of sin, that you may repent of it, and so for your eternity, as long as you are repentant, and you will enjoy a new life in Him and rejoice in His fatherhood and tenderness.
16- “He sent from above, he took me, he drew me out of many waters. 17- He delivered me from my strong enemy, and from them which hated me: for they were too strong for me.”

1- God's fatherhood appears in His care for David, for He is not a God who lives in heaven, occupied apart from His children on earth, but feels for them and sends His power to pluck His children from the midst of dangers and death, so that the wicked cannot harm him; here God's power and His special love for His children appear.

2- The many waters are the wicked people surrounding God's children, and the pagan nations, or those far from God, or the cares of the world and its troubles and problems. God plucks His children out of all these afflictions, and even what is harder than they, because they are beloved to His heart.

3- If God delivered David from his enemies, this is a symbol of Christ, who delivered those who believe in Him from the demons by the Cross: He bound Satan, brought the believers in Him out of Hades and brought them up into Paradise, and delivers His children in every generation from the authority of Satan.

4- The power of Satan and the wicked appears greater than the power of the weak and poor righteous, but the power of God that He sends to help them saves them from every evil, and the power of Satan appears to be nothing before the power of God.
18- “They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the Lord was my stay.”

1- Satan's wickedness appears in his seizing the opportunity of the weakness of the righteous, and fighting them during their afflictions in order to keep them away from God; he is hard of heart, and therefore we must beware of his wiles, however much he seems to take pity on us by giving us the pleasures of sin, or thoughts by which we pity ourselves; he wants only to destroy us, and his thoughts must be driven out as long as they keep us away from God.

2- God cannot leave us in the day of our calamity, but supports us as He supported David, and delivered him from the wiles of Satan and from the hands of his enemies. Faith in God's support reassures our hearts however much afflictions surround us, as God delivered Joseph from the hand of Potiphar's wife and from the suffering of prison and humiliation and raised him to the throne of Egypt.
19- “He brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me.”

1- Despite the difficulty of the distress that nearly choked David, as he expressed in (vv. 4, 5), God by His power brought him forth into a large place, that is, the feeling of release and spaciousness, when he reigned over all the children of Israel.

2- In the midst of afflictions God brought David forth into a large place when He made him feel His presence with him, so he sang to Him many Psalms and was freed from the narrowness of the soul, because he experienced new depths in God's love, and the distress was turned into a spiritual largeness and an experience of the breadth of God's love.

3- David gives a clear reason for the Lord's delivering him, that He delighted in him, that is, delighted in his love for God, his care to carry out His commandments, and his pursuit of righteousness. God loves His children and lifts them up in the midst of afflictions and humbles the wicked under their feet, as He gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. Christ declared this in saying, “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Lk 12:32).

4- The Church, the Body of Christ, who loved Him and believed in Him, is one He delighted in; and as the Father declared His love for the only Son, in whom He was well pleased as He came up out of the waters of the Jordan after His Baptism (Mt 3:17), so He declares His delight in His believing children, born of the font of Baptism, and supports them and saves them and brings them out into the large place, which is the experience of fellowship with Him.

5- God's children suffer afflictions in this life, but God saves them because He delights in them, and brings them out into the largeness of eternal life, that they may range free in His love forever.

6- The Church suffered persecutions in its beginning, from the Jews in Jerusalem and then from the Romans, so that the Church was scattered because of the persecution, but it spread and grew wide and reached the capital of the Roman Empire that ruled the world, namely Rome, where Paul preached, as appears from the end of the Book of Acts.
20- “The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me.”

1- In faith David trusts that God will reward him with divine blessings, because he walks in righteousness, unlike the enemies who persist in evil and want to kill him. Here he is not boasting in pride, but assuring the righteous that righteousness has a reward, because God is just.
2- The just God punishes the wicked and recompenses the pure with blessings, to encourage purity and righteousness.

3- If the wicked, in attacking David, falsely accused him of various faults, as Shimei the son of Gera accused him of being a bloody man (2 Sam 16:7), here he justifies himself and declares his purity and righteousness.
4- If we apply this verse to Christ, it is plain, because there is no sin in Christ, and His reward is the showing forth of His glory in the Resurrection and the Ascension.
21- “For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not wickedly departed from my God. 22- For all his judgments were before me, and I did not put away his statutes from me.”

1- The ways of the Lord are His commandments, and David declares that he kept them, that is, applied them and lived by them and did not disobey them, so he enjoyed their working in him and walked in the upright way.
2- Keeping God's commandments made him keep away from evil lusts, and all the ways of the world, and the thoughts of the Gentiles, and set his heart on the love of God and submission to His word.

3- David enjoyed carrying out God's commandments, that is, His judgments, because he set them before him, as God commanded in His Law (Deut 6:1-9), so they were his chief occupation, and he even grew accustomed to them and so rejected the thoughts of the world and its sins.

4- What helped David keep God's commandments was his holding fast to God's statutes, that is, his worship according to what the Law of Moses prescribed, so he was occupied with the love of God and with offering Him repentance and continual thanksgiving.

5- God's judgments are also those that will be carried out on the Day of Judgment, so when David set God's judgment before him, he lived in the fear of God, and rejected evil, and pleased God in all his ways.
23- “I was also upright before him, and I kept myself from mine iniquity.”

1- David strives for perfection in keeping the commandments and carrying them out. What is meant, of course, is the relative perfection proper to men, because absolute perfection belongs to God alone. He strives to carry out all the commandments with precision, so that he pleases God with all his heart, and by this God is delighted.

2- David's striving for perfection will make him, of itself, take heed and keep away from iniquities, for the love of God drives out the love of sin. And the converse is true, that “the friendship of the world is enmity with God” (Jas 4:4).
24- “Therefore hath the Lord recompensed me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight.”
David affirms God's righteousness and justice, which he declared in (v. 20), in that He rewards the righteous according to their righteousness and purity.

Do not despair if you see the success of the wicked and the afflictions of the righteous, but hold fast to God's commandments, confident that He will reward you, even after a while, and compensate you for all your labors. As for the wicked, if they do not repent, a destruction awaits them that cannot be imagined.
25- “With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful; with an upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright;”

1- Here too he affirms the justice of God, who rewards the person who shows mercy to others with many divine mercies; He helps the one who strives on the way of perfection to acquire perfect virtues, and the one who lives in purity with a pure heart can see God. God is a treasure full of blessings that He gives to those who care to acquire them.

2- To bring them near to God, it is mentioned here that “with the crooked thou wilt shew thyself twisted,” and in another translation “with the wayward thou wilt show thy opposition.” The meaning of this is that the sinner who persists in his wickedness and walks crookedly with God and defies Him, God abandons him, so that he is exposed to many problems and is humbled before sin, that perhaps he may repent. God is also twisted with him, in placing obstacles in the way of the accomplishment of his evil, that perhaps he may take heed; for God is merciful to the righteous and the wicked alike.
27- “For thou wilt save the afflicted people; but wilt bring down high looks.”

1- If God is merciful to everyone who shows mercy to others, He also saves all His people if they are humble; God works with the individual and the community and saves the humble, because He does not give His glory to another, since the humble always ascribe the glory to God.
2- The high looks, that is, the proud, God brings down to the earth, because they forgot God the Holy One and exalted themselves against Him and ascribed the glory to themselves.

3- This verse is about Christ, who saves those who believe in Him, the humble, such as the Apostles and His followers, and puts the proud, such as the priests, the scribes and the Pharisees, in ignorance, because they were proud, as our Lady the Virgin declared in her song, “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree” (Lk 1:52).

Humility is the shortest way to the heart of God, so why do you hold back from it? It saves you from all sins, and pours upon you the mercies of God, so that you live in peace, rejoicing in God's work in you.
28- “For thou wilt light my candle: the Lord my God will enlighten my darkness.”

1- The light that is in man does not have its source in him personally, but its source is God. It is He who gave the dust the breath of life, so that it became a man, and it is He who enlightens the old man in Baptism, so that he is turned into a new man.

2- If God enlightens man's darkness, that is, saves him from his sins and problems, so that he becomes a spiritual man, then the devil cannot fight him, because the darkness of sin is repelled by the luminosity of this man, so this man lives with God and treads down all the power of the enemy.

3- Spiritual enlightenment turns the power of evil in man into a power for good; when Christ dwells in the heart, his desire becomes the love of God instead of uncleanness. And his love of possessions is turned into love for the lives of the saints and imitation of them, that is, the person turns from the way of darkness and walks in the way of light.

4- It is God who lights man's candle, and the meaning of this is that He gives him continual life and constant enlightenment. There was an ancient Eastern custom of lighting a lamp all night in the house to declare that there was continual life in it, that is, that God works in man at all times and gives him joy in Himself. David's men asked him, when the enemies were about to kill him in the war and they rescued him, not to go out with them to war again, and said to him, “that thou quench not the light of Israel” (2 Sam 21:17); David represents the presence of God, and by His care and love gives continual life to His people.
29- “For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall.”
Leaped over: climbed and jumped from over the wall.

1- As David trusts in the power of God that is with him, he declares that he is able to run through armies like the armies of Saul or the armies of Absalom, in addition to the armies of the Philistines and all the enemies of the people of God. He triumphed over them all, because the power of God surpasses every power on earth, however weak David was or few his men.

2- The enemies set walls and barriers around God's children, and Satan sets high walls of sin and of the circumstances that lead to it. But whoever trusts in God can leap over them and pass all the obstacles that separate him from God. Satan sets up many walls, but the power of God supports the spiritual striver so that he leaps over them all, to reach his goal, the Kingdom of Heaven.
30- “As for God, his way is perfect: the word of the Lord is tried: he is a buckler to all those that trust in him.”
Buckler: a defensive instrument of war used by the soldier to ward off arrows from his body.

1- God's way is perfect, that is, His commandments lead us on the upright road and bring us to eternal life, and there is in it no deviation or error, and consequently whoever walks in it is assured of stability, success and happiness.
2- God's perfect way is Christ, who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”; whoever believes in Him and lives with Him is assured of his joy and his eternity.
3- The word of the Lord is pure, so it cleanses man from every sin, and consequently he can see God and enjoy fellowship with Him.

4- Whoever lives by the word of God and walks in His way protects himself from the wiles of the devil and his various wars, and Satan cannot make him fall into sin, however weak this person is, because he is sheltered in God.

5- God's way is perfect in the eyes of those who believe in Him, who empty themselves of their own will and seek the will of God; but those attached to the world see God's way as hard and unsuitable for them, because it does not fulfill their desires, so they try to mix the way of God with the way of the world, and then God says to them, “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1 Kgs 18:21), “I will spue thee out of my mouth” (Rev 3:16).
31- “For who is God save the Lord? or who is a rock save our God?”
1- David declares that even if there are many pagan gods, they are not counted as gods, but the only God is the Lord, the God of Israel, to whom worship and honor are due.

2- God is the Rock, that is, the protection of His children, and the strength on which they lean against all the powers of the world. The rock is the source of life for His children, for from it water came forth, as in the days of Moses, and the Rock, as the Apostle Paul declares, is Christ, who accompanied the people everywhere and preserved their life (1 Cor 10:4).
32- “It is God that girdeth me with strength, and maketh my way perfect.”
Girdeth me: puts a girdle on me, which is a belt tied around the waist and below, and signifies readiness for work and war.

1- David speaks of God, describing Him as strengthening him and preparing him for war so that he may triumph over his enemies. He does not mean only earthly enemies, but rather the demons; as long as God's power is with him, he will surely triumph over them.
2- God also makes David's way perfect, removing the obstacles that hinder his walking and turning the obstacles into steps for his ascent of the ladder of glory, so that he grows in the love of God.
3- The way becomes perfect in Christ Jesus, who is the way, the truth and the life, so whoever lives in Christ passes over all afflictions successfully.
33- “He maketh my feet like hinds' feet, and setteth me upon my high places.”
The hind (stag): the male of the gazelle kind, which is distinguished by speed of running.

1- David thanks God, who gives his feet speed in running like the stag, whether in fleeing from his enemies or attacking them, as was mentioned in (v. 29) that he runs through armies and leaps over walls; it is a divine power that distinguishes David and gives him victory over the enemies. So also He gives the spiritual person speed in fleeing from sin, and speed in attacking evil by prayer and humility, so that he always triumphs.

2- David flees and goes up on mountains, or high hills, so it is hard for the enemies to attack him; God fortifies him with these high places, and his speed in running helps him in this. Whoever trusts in God, He gives him a strength that the devil cannot resist.

3- The stag in its speed attacks serpents and eats them, so it symbolizes the spiritual person who attacks evil with the power of God and triumphs over it. And when the stag eats the serpents it becomes very thirsty and drinks much, just as the spiritual person drinks from the springs of the Holy Spirit in the Church.
4- The high places on which God sets David are prayer, which establishes man like a mountain and lifts his heart on high, so that God's help continues with him.
5- The spiritual person is swift like the stag in taking refuge in spiritual things, namely prayer and meditation, so he enjoys more than others the spiritual loftiness on the high places.

6- My high places are the virtues that God gave me and that I loved, and when I hasten to God like the stag, He makes me grow in the love of virtue, so that it becomes a fortress for me from the wars of the demons.
34- “He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of brass is bent by mine arms.”

1- God supports David by teaching him how to make war, and when God teaches He gives all skill to the warrior, so that he can overcome his enemies by his skill and with God's help, and will surely triumph over him.

2- God gives a special strength to man, surpassing ordinary human strength, so that he can hold a bow of brass in his arms and bend it, and consequently this warrior is able to defeat many of his enemies.
3- This strength and skill God gives to spiritual strivers against the demons, whatever their wiles and strength; God's power supports His children so that they triumph in their spiritual wars.

4- When a person's hands are lifted up for prayer they are in the shape of a bow, and these two arms are able to draw down God's mercies and help, as happened with Moses in his war with Amalek, when Joshua prevailed over them because Moses' hands were held up in prayer before God (Ex 17:11).
35- “Thou hast also given me the shield of thy salvation: and thy right hand hath holden me up, and thy gentleness hath made me great.”

1- The shield, as we mentioned, is a defensive instrument in war, so this means that God protected David in his wars from the enemy's arrows, so he overcame them; he would strike the enemies, while God kept him. This is a great grace that the spiritual warrior enjoys when he prays and humbles himself before God, so that he enters into every work and service and succeeds; he treads on the demons and they cannot harm him.

2- The shield of salvation, as the Apostle Paul mentions to us, is faith (Eph 6:16). Faith protects David and all God's children from the arrows of the demons, so they are not disturbed by their doubts, and they continue the war and triumph.

3- God's right hand is His power that supports David, so the secret of the strength and greatness in David goes back to God, in His shield, His right hand and His gentleness; and this shows the humility of David, who ascribes every grace he has to God.

4- David feels that the greatness of the kingdom and his high standing among the surrounding nations result from God's tenderness and gentleness. In the days of David God's promise was fulfilled in the widening of the kingdom of the children of Israel, extending from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, all of this by God's grace.

5- In the Septuagint translation, “thy gentleness will instruct me”: David feels that God gives him strength before others, but teaches him with a father's gentleness and tenderness how to behave, and also teaches him how to be gentle with others.
36- “Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my heels did not shake.”
Shake: tremble.
My heels: my heel bones.
1- God gave David strength to advance with wide steps in his spiritual and material life, so he triumphed in all his wars with his enemies, and also triumphed in his spiritual wars.
2- David in his advance advances with steady steps, so what he gains in victories is not lost to him, but he completes his success, and his material and spiritual victories follow one another.

3- David's steadfastness declares the extent of his faith, for he was not shaken by the threats of his enemies or their attacks, but was strong and victorious, and even when he fell into his sin he rose with strong repentance and completed his spiritual striving and growth.

4- The spiritual striver at the beginning of his striving has narrow steps, but when he continues in the striving and grows accustomed to it his feet are strengthened and he becomes able to take wide steps with God's help, especially since God removes the obstacles from his way, and reveals them to him, and guides him how to pass over them, so his steps continue wide and his progress is great. This is what happens with the saints and children of God in every generation.

The power of God that supports you is enough for you to triumph in all your spiritual wars, so do not doubt because of your weakness or the strength of the devil, but persevere in your striving, leaning on the arm of God by prayer and humility.
37- “I have pursued mine enemies, and overtaken them: neither did I turn again till they were consumed. 38- I have wounded them that they were not able to rise: they are fallen under my feet.”

1- As David trusted in the power of God that supported him, he advanced with courage and overtook his enemies and destroyed them. This is what happened in David's various wars with the surrounding nations.

2- When God supports His children and reveals to them the weakness of the demons, they advance and triumph over them, as happened with the Fathers of the desert when they drove the demons out of it and filled it with prayers, so that monasteries spread in the deserts of Egypt from Alexandria to Aswan.

3- Because of David's trust in God he is not shaken however great the strength of the enemies, and he continues his war until he wipes out his enemies. He is not only courageous but persevering, so he completes his striving until he receives the crown and success.

4- David does not turn back until he consumes his enemies; this was not fulfilled except in Christ, who bound Satan and will cast him into eternal torment. But it is good for God's children to persevere in striving with all their strength, and not to be careless and leave an opportunity for Satan to fight them again by the same means, such as keeping an evil friend, or unsuitable places, or pictures ...

5- David persevered in his attack on his enemies until he crushed them, so that they were weakened and could not stand before him. This is what happened in his wars with the nations. And this is also what happens in spiritual wars when the spiritual striver, like David, perseveres in humility to crush the demons and tread them down, so they fear him and keep away from him.

39- “For thou hast girded me with strength unto the battle: thou hast subdued under me those that rose up against me. 40- Thou hast given me the backs of mine enemies; that I might destroy them that hate me. 41- They cried, but there was none to save them: even unto the Lord, but he answered them not. 42- I beat them small as the dust before the wind: I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets.”

1- David continues to explain the power of God that supports him in the war, affirming that it prepares him for battle, and by it he can destroy his enemies who were attacking him and trying to kill him. But their weakness appears when they fall under his feet.

2- He makes plain the weakness of the enemies in their swift flight from the battle, so that they give him the back and not the face, but David follows them until he wipes them out, as God promised in His Law to Moses (Ex 23:27).

3- When the enemies meet death they are afraid and cry out to their pagan gods, who do not answer. And if they cry out to God, the God of Israel, without faith, He does not answer them of course, because they are wicked. And if they were Jews, like Saul and Absalom and their armies, He also does not answer them, because they wrong David and their hearts are full of evil; David's success and victory depend entirely on his purity before God and God's help to him.

4- When David pursues his enemies he scatters them as the winds scatter dust, so that it spreads everywhere and has no resting place, while David remains steadfast by the power of God, pursuing them. Whoever lives with God enjoys steadfastness, and whoever disobeys God has no place and no rest.

5- David makes plain the humiliation of the enemies, likening them in his war with them to the mire of the streets, which is much trodden on, so they lose their dignity, and indeed their whole life. This is the natural result of sin.

6- David likens the enemies to dust and mire, because they are men created from dust and clay, whom God distinguished by His Spirit in them; but when they disobey God they return to their dust and the Spirit of God leaves them and condemns them.

7- The humiliation of the enemies also appears in their being cast out as the mire of the streets is cast out; David is a symbol of Christ, who casts Satan into the lake burning with fire and brimstone.
43- “Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people; and thou hast made me the head of the heathen: a people whom I have not known shall serve me.
44- As soon as they hear of me, they shall obey me: the strangers shall submit themselves unto me.”

1- When David came to reign he was exposed to opposition from the offspring of Saul, that is, his son Ishbosheth and the commander of his army Abner. This opposition and strife lasted seven years, but in the end Ishbosheth died, killed by the hand of two of his servants (2 Sam 4:5-7). As for Abner, he was reconciled with David, but Joab killed him (2 Sam 3:27); David was patient, trusting in God, until He subdued the whole kingdom to him. Whoever is patient for God's sake in his spiritual striving, the demons are subdued to him and the war is lifted from him.

2- If God gave David stability within his kingdom, He also gave him authority over the nations around him, so they were subdued to him and he triumphed over them in successive wars, such as his victory over the Philistines and the Moabites and his threat to Hadadezer king of Zobah and the Syrians (2 Sam 8:1-14).

3- David did not only triumph over his enemies, but became a head among all the surrounding countries, and the peoples were subdued to him and offered him tribute and gifts. So God glorified him in the eyes of all, because he was righteous and good. He is a type of Christ, who by His death on the Cross subdued death to Himself, and became the head of all His brethren, the human believers in Him, so that He became the firstborn among many brethren, and ascended to the heavens and prepared a place for them, that they might be with Him forever. And the Gentiles believed in Him and were subdued to Him.

4- David's greatness became very great, so all the surrounding nations feared him when they heard of his victories, and humbled themselves before him and offered gifts, seeking his favor lest he destroy them, after they had formerly troubled the people of God; but in the reign of David, as we mentioned, God's promise was fulfilled and the surrounding nations were subdued, so the kingdom of Israel extended from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

5- (v. 44) is a clear prophecy about Christ, of whom the Gentiles heard though they had not seen Him in the flesh as the Jews had, so they believed the preaching of the Apostles and were subdued to Him, leaving their idols and their former lusts.

6- David's overwhelming victory over his enemies appears in that they were wasting away, that is, perishing; and even those who fortified themselves in strong fortresses he defeated, so they fled and crept out of their fortresses, and He destroys them also.

Satan has no authority over you; rather, by the power of Christ you can overcome him, and he flees from you. So resist him and cast away all his evil methods until you tread them down with your feet, and trust that God will help you however weak you are, and you will regain your place as a child of God whatever your falls.
46- “The Lord liveth; and blessed be my rock; and let the God of my salvation be exalted.”

1- After David reviewed God's works with him and how He saved him from his enemies, and even gave him victory over them so that they fled from him or submitted to him, he now offers thanks and praise to God; that is, his experience with God increased, so his love and praise of God increased.

2- David felt that God is living, and feels for His children and supports them in all their afflictions; even if He is long-suffering for a time for a wisdom of His own, He certainly intervenes at the right time and delivers His children. He is unlike the pagan gods, which are stones, unable to help their followers.

3- He offers thanks and blessing to God because He is a rock and an unshakable fortress; everything in the world changes except God alone, with whom “is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17).

4- David feels that God, who saved him from his enemies, is exalted beyond measure above the pagan gods and all the powers of the world; He is lofty in His thoughts, His love, His dealings with men and His power. He deserves meditation and praise every day and forever. This verse shows the extent of David's attachment to God.
47- “It is God that avengeth me, and subdueth the people under me.”

1- David thanks the just God, who keeps the righteous and punishes the wicked; as He blessed David and glorified him, so He avenged him on his enemies, such as Saul, Nabal, Absalom and all the nations that rose up against him. How they all perished!

2- God did not only avenge David, but turned the enemies into friends, as they submitted to him, such as Abner the commander of Saul's army, who was reconciled with David, and like the nations that offered gifts and submitted to David.

3- This verse applies to Christ, who avenged Himself on His enemies the demons by binding them with His Cross; as for the Jews who persisted in opposing Him, they perished, and Jerusalem their city was destroyed in AD 70 at the hands of the Romans; and God subdued the nations that opposed Christ, so they became believers and joined the Church.
