48- “He delivereth me from mine enemies: yea, thou liftest me up above those that rise up against me: thou hast delivered me from the violent man.”
1- After thanking God the Living One, the Rock and the Support (v. 46), David thanked God who avenges him on his enemies (v. 47), and in this verse he thanks God who delivers him from his enemies.

2- David praises and thanks God because He delivered him from his enemies, such as Saul and the Philistines and Absalom his son. He has repeated the same meaning found in this verse in the previous verses of this Psalm, for he ascribes the glory to God in his victories over his enemies, and not to his own strength or anything else.

3- He thanks God also because He not only delivered him from his enemies but glorified him and lifted him above his enemies, that is, subdued them to him or destroyed them. This is what happens with everyone who trusts in God if he is patient in his striving.

4- This verse applies to Christ also, because the Father lifted Him above His enemies the demons by His death on the Cross and His Resurrection, and the priests, the Pharisees, the scribes and everyone who opposed Christ were put to shame when they faced the power of His Resurrection and the miracles that took place at the hands of the Apostles.
49- “Therefore will I give thanks unto thee, O Lord, among the heathen, and sing praises unto thy name.”
1- For all the works of God that he mentioned in this Psalm, David praises and sings to God; how beautiful it is for a person to remember God's kindnesses to him every day.

2- David was not content with praising God among his people, but also praises Him before the pagan nations, and by this he preaches to them indirectly, for he believes that the expected Messiah will offer salvation to the whole world, Jews and Gentiles. It is a prophecy about the acceptance of the Gentiles into faith in Christ.
50- “He is the tower of salvation for his king; and sheweth mercy to his anointed, to David, and to his seed for evermore.”

1- In conclusion David thanks God, who saved him from his enemies and gives him an opportunity to enjoy the true salvation, which is fellowship with God. David likens this salvation to a tower, that is, a permanent immunity, which King David enjoys. And everyone who reigns over himself, that is, controls his lusts, Christ gives him salvation and lasting joy.

2- In the midst of this joy and praise David does not forget his weakness, so he speaks with humility to God and praises Him for His mercy to him; for he, the one anointed as king, deserves nothing, but all that he has is grace and mercy from God.

3- David concludes the Psalm with great faith that all the preceding blessings God gives to him and to his seed after him, and to everyone of his seed who believed and lived with God and reigned on the throne of the kingdom of Judah, until it reaches Christ, who came from the seed of David and who reigns forever, and indeed makes those who believe in Him, who are of David's faith, reign with Him forever in His Kingdom.

Praise is a delight to which no delight in the world compares; it is a pledge of the Kingdom that you can taste from now, so do not deprive yourself of praising God in your private prayer every day, and you will live in joy forever. Nature and the word of God call us to perfection. To the chief musician. A psalm of David. “The heavens declare the glory of God” ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, as appears in the title of the Psalm.
2- When was it said?
After a quiet sitting or sittings of David in which he contemplated nature, and saw God in it, and enjoyed being in His hands. So he expressed his feelings in this Psalm.
3- This Psalm speaks of three matters:
A- God, who created nature and is shown through it if man contemplates it.

B- The word of God, which prepares man and leads him to bring him to the Kingdom, and the work of the word of God is manifested in the Incarnation of Christ, to redeem man and to show the way of the Kingdom in Himself, in His saying, “I am the way.”
C- Man's response to God as shown in nature and the word of God, in his pursuit of perfection in order to please God.

4- In the title of this Psalm in the Septuagint translation it says “to the end,” and what is meant is the perfection of God's manifestation in nature, and the perfection of the work of His word in man.
5- This Psalm encourages whoever wants to sit in solitude and meditate on God, so it is fitting for a person to repeat it when he is alone with God.
6- This Psalm is found in the prayer of Prime, to lead man at the beginning of his day to look to God and meditate on His creatures and His word.
1- “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.”
The firmament: the heavenly bodies and their courses.
1- David began with the heavens, which glorify God, because at the beginning of creation God created heaven first.

2- He mentions the heavens here in the plural, because the Holy Bible mentions to us a number of heavens and not one heaven, as Moses declared (Deut 10:14), and David (Ps 68:33), and Solomon (1 Kgs 8:27), and Nehemiah (Neh 9:6). And Christ Himself, when He taught us to pray, said to us, say, “Our Father which art in heaven” (Mt 6:9) (literally, in the heavens). And the Apostle Paul declared that he was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor 12:2). So all the heavens glorify God.

3- Nature, that is, the heavens and the firmament, declares the glory of God. How, when it cannot speak? Through its submission to God and the order He has set for it, so they do not collide with one another and carry out His will, and so declare the power of their Creator and His precision through their work, and not through their speech, as the verse mentions.
4- The heavens are the angels and the saints who are in the heavens, for they glorify God and praise Him at all times.

5- The heavens are also the souls of the righteous, who are the Apostles, the Evangelists and the saints everywhere in the world, who praise God, serve Him faithfully, and proclaim His name in their preaching, through their words and works, for their very conduct is itself a glorification of God's name. And the steadfastness of these saints in goodness is like the steadfastness of the heavens and the firmament throughout the ages since God created them.

6- When a person repeats this Psalm and says “The heavens declare the glory of God,” he lifts his eyes upward, and God reveals His works to him and his mind is enlightened, so he understands endless depths of God's love for him.

7- The heavens also symbolize the dwellers of heaven, and the firmament symbolizes the dwellers of earth, that is, the Church triumphant in heaven and the Church militant on earth speak of God and preach Him.
8- When a person looks at the sky and sees all that God has done for his sake, he rejoices greatly, and is humbled before God, who loved him and did all this for him.

9- The heavens symbolize the dwelling of God, so they represent the work of grace, and the firmament means the earth where man dwells, so it represents spiritual striving, and so the work of grace and striving are completed together that man may receive his salvation, and by them God is glorified.

10- This part of the Psalm (vv. 1-6) resembles the eighth Psalm, “O Lord our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!”; but this Psalm speaks of nature's glorification of God, while the eighth Psalm speaks of the relationship of the Creator with His creation.

11- From this part we see that God gave us two holy books. The first, the Holy Bible, is the one in our hands and includes the books from Genesis to Revelation. The second book is the nature around us, and the two books speak to us of God that we may love Him and glorify Him, and each of them completes the other and confirms it.

12- Every artist is known by his works, and according to their splendor and greatness he is great; how great, then, is God, when we see the nature He created with a precision and perfection in which no one equals Him.
2- “Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge.”

1- The day represents the daytime in which the greatness of God appears, and after it comes the night with its quiet, which confirms the greatness of God; their precise succession confirms God's power and His ordering of the universe.

2- The day is an opportunity for work and striving, and the night an opportunity for quiet and prayer and for receiving the work of God's grace more fully, so the day and the night symbolize striving and grace.
3- The day has light and symbolizes the shining saints, who make known the word of God through their lives and words.
4- The night symbolizes obscurity, for man knows of the mysteries of God only what the Holy Spirit reveals to His children who believe in Him, who watch with Him in prayer and praise.

5- The day symbolizes the periods of ease and relief that God gives His children. The night and the darkness symbolize the distress that comes upon God's children, and during both God works and gives His blessings.

6- The day symbolizes the New Testament, where Christ became incarnate and declared great mysteries and salvation for mankind, and the night symbolizes the Old Testament, where there are prophecies and types, which were declared and made manifest in the New Testament.

7- God makes known His knowledge by works visible in the day and in the daytime, that is, He utters speech. And also in the night He shows knowledge, so He declares deep mysteries about Himself to everyone who loves Him and watches with Him, for He always wants His children to know Him and enjoy fellowship with Him.
3- “There is no saying nor speech; their voice is not heard.”

1- The speaking of the sun, the moon, the stars and all the planets, through their submission to the order God has set for them, is stronger than the words of human languages; for any language is understood by some people, or races, or the educated, but the speech of the heavenly bodies can reach every person, and so proclaims the power of God the Almighty.

2- If the great heavenly bodies were to speak with the words of human languages, or with any voice, it would be an annoying voice that men could not bear. But their speaking without a voice conveys the meaning God wants quietly to every person, when he contemplates these heavenly bodies, and so glorifies God.

3- The Church throughout history, by its Apostles, its martyrs and all its servants, has spoken through their lives and conduct with a power that surpasses every human language and every sermon that moves people, because their lives were a practical application of Christ's commandments, and an example that cannot be resisted.
4- “Their speech is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun,”

1- The earth symbolizes the earthly who walk according to the flesh and not according to the Spirit; to these will come the voice of the heavenly bodies, which declare God to them, that they may believe in Him and walk by the Spirit, and so their concern for fleshly things will lessen.

2- The voice of these heavenly bodies will also reach, without a word, every place where any person lives, that is, God will call all mankind by means of these bodies, that they may believe in Him and leave their sins and live to Him.

3- The speech of these heavenly bodies symbolizes the preaching of the Apostles, which reached the end of the world, and Christianity spread in the world when it reached the capital of the Roman Empire, which ruled the world, and from it spread to all the lands.

4- The sun has a dwelling and a resting place among these heavenly bodies, and this symbolizes Christ the Sun of Righteousness, who dwelt in our flesh and walked among creatures as one of us, to redeem us and to be an example to us of pure and perfect conduct.
5- Our Lady the Virgin Mary is the dwelling in which the Sun of Righteousness dwelt, that is, Christ our God was born of her.

6- The Church also is where the Sun of Righteousness, Christ our God, dwelt, through His Holy Sacraments and all the work of the Holy Spirit in the believers. And the Church became manifest before the whole world, declaring that she is the house of God in which He dwells.
7- The Sun of Righteousness, our Lord Jesus Christ, dwelt likewise in those who believe in Him, so they became light for the world.

5- “Which is as a bride coming out of her chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race in the way.” The bride: what is meant is the bridegroom, because the Hebrew original of the word means both masculine and feminine, but here we see that the rest of the words of the verse are masculine (such as “coming out,” “rejoiceth”). The chamber: the private room of the bride and bridegroom.

1- He likens the sun to the bridegroom coming out of the marriage chamber (his chamber), by which he means the womb of the Virgin, from which He was born to redeem mankind, or the bosom of the Father, in which He was from eternity, and His bride, the Church, was in His heart before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4). The Bridegroom came out of His chamber joyful and rejoicing, and moved with power to complete our salvation, like the sun that moves as a strong man going out to the race, and no one can stand in its way.

2- As the sun is strong and its movement cannot be stopped, so Christ completed our salvation with power on the Cross, and the devil with all his wiles and wickedness could not hinder His salvation; on the contrary, when Christ died on the Cross He was in the fullness of strength, for by His death He bound Satan, and he no longer had authority to take those who believe in Christ to Hades.

3- Christ offered us a salvation full of exultation and joy, and at the same time a mighty, powerful salvation that crushes the evil in us and gives us a new life in Him, and by this we receive in Christ lasting joy and the strength to crush Satan, who fights us during our spiritual striving on earth. The might of Christ He gives to us in the strength and continuity of our striving, whatever Satan's hindrances.

4- Christ the Bridegroom, who prepared for us the chamber, that is, the place of the wedding, and we were in His heart before He created us, came in the fullness of time and redeemed us on the Cross, and ascended to heaven, and prepared for us a place, which is the chamber in which we shall enjoy His embrace forever; and out of the abundance of His love for us He lets us enjoy His chamber in part while we are on earth, when He reigns over our hearts and lets us enjoy fellowship with Him, that we may be encouraged until we reach the heavenly chamber.
6- “His going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid from the heat thereof.”
1- The sun symbolizes Christ the Sun of Righteousness, of clear power; from the end of the heavens to the ends of it, and His care for His creatures is clear to all, even if the atheists deny it.
2- The Incarnation of Christ was known in the whole world, and His redemption and His death on the Cross, but many neglected it and some denied it.
3- At the Second Coming of Christ He will appear, and the whole world will know Him from the end of the heavens to the ends of them.

4- God showed His action and power, not only by His light like the sun, but also by the heat of the work of His Holy Spirit, which affects people's feelings, and no one can hide from the work of the Holy Spirit, though he can refuse this work and try to quench this heat. And though a person may be unable to see the light of the sun, like the blind, yet he cannot keep away from the heat of the sun that affects him; God seeks everyone and calls everyone to believe in Him and repent.
5- The heat of the sun symbolizes the warmth of the divine love and mercy that God gives to men, and makes men show compassion to one another and love one another.

God calls you by means of all His creatures to love Him and worship Him and enjoy fellowship with Him, so always look at the nature around you and seek God in it, and then He will reveal Himself to you and let you enjoy seeing Him.
7- “The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the Lord is sure, making the ignorant wise.”
1- The sun covers the world with its light and heat, and likewise the word of God lights up a person's life, moves his feelings, cares for him and leads him on the way to God.

2- In this verse and the following verses he explains the work of the word of God in man in six actions, just as the days of creation, which were created by the word of God, are six. And as God rested on the seventh day, so the soul rests in the end by its being with God.

3- The law of the Lord is the Law of Moses and the Ten Commandments, and it is also the law of Christ, that is, the teachings of the New Testament. The law of the Lord is perfect because God is its giver, and it cannot be lacking in anything, and it calls men to perfection and turns souls back from the deviations of sin.

4- God's word is called, in addition to being a law, that is, an order and a statute, a testimony, that is, it testifies before man to the right way to God, and testifies against man if he sins that he deserves punishment, and testifies for the righteous that they held fast to the word of God.

5- Even if all men lie, the word of God remains true and faithful, and there is no falsehood in it. And because it is the word of God it can turn the ignorant from his ignorance to wisdom, so he walks in the way of God, keeps away from sin, and goes on the way to the Kingdom of Heaven.

6- The testimony of the Lord is sure because it testifies to the bitterness of sin and its corruption of man, and at the same time it testifies also to the truth of God's promises and the life-giving effect of His words in souls.
8- “The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes.”

1- God's commandments are upright amid the crooked, perverted teachings of the world, which lead to the ways of destruction, but God's upright commandments ensure arrival at God and enjoyment of fellowship with Him.

2- Those who incline to uprightness rejoice in God's upright commandments, because they help them reach God, and also make their will like the will of God, so they rejoice in the knowledge of God and the sweetness of the upright life.
3- Everyone who meditates on God's commandments discovers their uprightness and their loftiness above all the thoughts of the world, and as he walks in them he can see God, and his heart rejoices.

4- If the person who strives on the way to the Kingdom sins, and then looks at God's upright commandments, he finds them a help to him in reaching the way of the Kingdom, so he regains his joy with the tears of repentance.

5- The word of God, that is, His commands, is pure and clean with no purpose but the knowledge of God, so it can purify everyone who holds fast to it, and then his mind and his eyes are enlightened, so he sees God and enjoys fellowship with Him.

6- God's pure commands lift man above the thoughts of men, and God gives him spiritual enlightenment with all the wisdom, discretion and discernment they carry, so he discovers the sweetness of being with God and discerns sin, and so keeps away from all that leads to it.

7- Whoever lives by God's pure commands receives the wisdom with which he can guide others; the servant, and every father and mother and all educators need the word of God, which gives them wisdom, so that they can guide others.
8- God's pure commands are the conscience, that is, the voice of God within man, which enlightens his eyes, so that he sees God in all who are around him and in all creatures.

9- God's pure commands in their perfection are also the work of the Holy Spirit, who enlightens man's eyes and guides him in all his ways, and no one can twist the words of the Holy Spirit, as sometimes happens with the conscience.
9- “The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ever: the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether.”
1- The word of God plants the fear of God in the heart, so it keeps away from every sin and man is established forever, where he enjoys fellowship with God in the Kingdom.
2- The fear of God purifies man's heart from sin, so that he can see God, and by this he abides in God forever.
3- The fear of God purifies man's heart, so he sees everything as clean and sees God in it, so he lives with God and endures in Him forever, because he passes over sin and rejects it.

4- The word of God is His judgments, which judge everything in the world; it is the measure of what is right and exposes errors, so however crooked men's measures become, the word of God remains the sound truth declared to men.

5- The word of God is altogether righteous; it cannot show partiality to one person against another, whatever his circumstances, and it leads all to the salvation of their souls, and it is also the source of justice for everyone who seeks it; so to the extent that the laws and statutes of men submit to the word of God they become just laws.
10- “More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.”
Fine gold: pure, unalloyed gold.
The honeycomb (drippings): pure bees' honey, free of wax.

1- He describes the word of God as more to be desired and better than all the possessions of the world and the most precious of them, like pure gold; the word of God is the pearl of great price, for which the merchant sells all the pearls to acquire it.
2- Likewise the word of God has a spiritual delight that surpasses all sensual delights, for it is sweeter than honey and the honey drained of wax.

3- If sins and evil lusts have their pleasures, they are all corrupt; but the word of God is pure honey, indeed sweeter than it, because it is a delight refined of everything, by which man knows God and enjoys fellowship with Him.
11- “Moreover by them is thy servant warned: and in keeping of them there is great reward.”

1- God's commandments and His law warn David of sins, and by this he knows wrong things and keeps away from them, so he lives the upright life and does not turn aside from the truth. That is, God's commandment protects him from sin and leads him on the way to the Kingdom.

2- David's obedience and love for the commandment appear in his holding fast to it and keeping it. What is meant by keeping it is applying it in his life, and not only keeping it in the mind, that is, that he lives by it and tastes its sweetness, so he enjoys fellowship with God through it.
3- Also when David keeps God's word he receives the eternal reward and the great recompense, that is, the happy eternal life.

Be careful to read the Holy Bible and meditate on it every day, so that you can apply it in your life, and you will touch God's work and His blessing on all your works, and also on your words and thoughts, and you will feel the delight of divine fellowship.
12- “Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults.”

Errors (oversights): the sins to which a person does not pay attention, that is, they escape him and he does not notice them, either because of their smallness, or because it is not clear that they are sin.

1- David the prophet declares his weakness before God, and that he is unable to discover the sins of oversight, and asks for God's forgiveness and tolerance toward him for these sins; however much he keeps God's word he will overlook some sins, because God in His perfection charges His angels with folly (Job 4:18), how much more man's weakness and his falling into many lapses.

2- In the press of life, though a person knows the sins, he overlooks them and falls into them. And Satan may depict justifications for them to him, so that he feels they are not sin, and this is from man's weakness, but the merciful God forgives him if he is striving on the way of repentance.

3- Because of the weakness of his understanding, though he keeps the commandment, a person may not understand that some things are wrong, that is, in his practical application he falls into some sins without feeling it, and needs divine guidance and also forgiveness from God.
4- A person meets many things in his life that distract his mind, and during this distraction Satan slips in sins, so he needs divine warning.

5- Secret sins are sins hidden from the person himself, that is, he does not know that they are sin, so he needs guidance and clarification from God, and this is what happens when there is much reading in the Holy Bible and spiritual books: a person discovers every day some of these secret sins.

6- Secret sins may be hidden from people but known to the person himself, such as sins of thought and of the heart, and David asks God to forgive him for them; he offers repentance between himself and God, even if people do not see his sins.
13- “Keep back thy servant also from the proud; let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression.”

1- By “the proud” he means their sin, that is, pride, and so he asks God to keep him from it, and in the Hebrew original it says, “and also from the sins done in pride”; it is a continuation of the previous verse, that is, the oversights and the secret sins, and he adds the sin of pride, especially since what is done in pride a person may persist in and justify, so that it is hard to offer repentance for it.

2- David asks God with humility that if he falls into a sin in pride he may repent of it, and he calls on God not to let this sin have dominion over him; David's distinction is his haste to repent and his fear of sin, which makes him keep away from it.

3- David also hopes that he will not be a cause of another's falling into the sin of pride, or what is connected with it, such as judging, which was when he fell into the sin of adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite and exposed Uriah to be killed in the war; so he fears that he caused his people to stumble and made them fall into judging and pride.

4- Because of the seriousness of the sin of pride David feels that by being rid of it and all that follows it he walks in the way of perfection, because the sin of pride is the mother of many sins, such as anger, hatred and murder, so by being cleansed from the great sin of pride he is rid of many sins. He does not concentrate on the sin of adultery and murder despite their seriousness, but the more serious are the mother sins, such as pride.

When you examine yourself, be concerned to discover the cause of your sins, that is, the mother sin that made you fall into these sins, so examine the extent of your selfishness or your pride, to treat it, and you will be rid of the sins that result from it.
14- “Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, my rock, and my redeemer.”

1- At the close of the Psalm, after David showed his great care concerning the mother sins such as pride, he asks God that his words and thoughts may be according to God's will, that is, that what shows outwardly in him and what is within him may please God.

2- By the words of the mouth he means not only that in dealing with others he keeps God's commandments and law, but also that his prayers, that is, his speaking with God, be in the fitting manner that pleases God, that is, with humility, love and submission to Him.

3- If a person's thoughts and the intentions of his heart are pleasing to God, his words also become pure, for out of the abundance of the heart the tongue speaks, and finally his actions are upright.

4- The words of the mouth and the meditation of the heart include words, thoughts and inner feelings, and all of these are expressions of the prayer that man offers to God, whether by the tongue, or by thought, or by feelings, as St. John Climacus says, “Let your tongue be silent so that your heart may speak.”

5- In humility David thanks God, who is the cause of the purity of his words, thoughts and feelings, for he says to Him, “You are my rock,” that is, the cause of my strength, my peace and my steadfastness in living with You.
6- In the end David is assured that God is his redeemer, that is, his savior from sins, his defender, and the one responsible for his care, that he may live in purity all the days of his life.
God the Savior in distress. To the chief musician. A psalm of David. “The Lord hear thee in the day of trouble” ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, as we see in the title.
2- When was it written?

David the prophet wrote it before his war with the children of Ammon, whom the great army of Aram supported, and this army had many horses and chariots (2 Sam 10:6, 8; 1 Chr 19:7), and David triumphed by the power of God in this war.
3- When is it said?

When the kings of Judah went out to fight their enemies, or when their enemies attacked them, such as Sennacherib when he besieged Jerusalem, so this Psalm was said to King Hezekiah, that he might trust in the power of God who gives him victory (2 Chr 32). The people used to say this Psalm to the king when he offered sacrifices before God before going out to war (v. 3).
4- This Psalm is a prophecy about Christ, who went forth and triumphed over Satan, not only in the temptation on the mountain, but rather on the Cross, when He bound him by His death for us.
5- It is fitting for the Church, and every believer, to repeat this Psalm in the war with Satan, to trust and establish faith in God, who gives victory over Satan in all spiritual wars.
6- This Psalm can be said at the beginning of the new year to God, who reigns over the hearts of His children and triumphs over the demons and drives them out.

7- This Psalm is connected with the Psalm that follows it, that is, (Ps 21). The twentieth Psalm speaks to us of the king going out to war to triumph over his enemies, while the twenty-first Psalm is a prayer of thanksgiving after the victory over the enemies.

8- This Psalm shows the importance of prayer for others, especially the leader, that is, the king, and every person responsible in his place, because of the seriousness of the leader's position, and at the same time it shows his need for the prayer of those who follow him.
9- This Psalm is found in the Agpeya at the beginning of the prayer of the Third Hour, in which appears the work of the Holy Spirit, who supports man in his spiritual war.
1- “The Lord hear thee in the day of trouble; the name of the God of Jacob defend thee;”

1- Affliction is a hard thing and troubles a person, but in it he experiences the work of God and rejoices in fellowship with Him, so the distress becomes a cause of blessing and spiritual growth for the person, and even an experience of the Kingdom while he is on earth.

2- For affliction, or distress, to be lifted, a person must pray and strive, like Jacob the father of the fathers, who wrestled with God and received the blessing. God answers him who cries to Him, and not the slothful.
3- David prays to God during his distress, but he also needs the prayers of the people for him, so they say to him, “The Lord hear thee.”

4- The God who will give David victory, as He gave Jacob victory of old when he wrestled with Him, is a tangible and real God, who has a name; He is not imagination but a lived reality, experienced by the fathers throughout the generations, seen by Jacob, and felt by David when he killed Goliath (1 Sam 17:45).

5- This verse is David's confession of his weakness and his need of God, who is able to answer him and give him victory, as Jacob confessed his weakness before the strength of Esau and clung to God and He blessed him, and as he pleaded with God and He delivered him from the hand of his uncle Laban (Gen 31:24).
6- This verse shows the people's love for their king in their prayers for him, and this rejoices God's heart, that the leader loves his people and the people their leader, so He hastens to answer.

7- The day of trouble and affliction is the day of the Cross, while the victory that was accomplished on the Cross appeared in the Resurrection and the Ascension. And as we feel affliction in this life, we feel victory when God delivers us from sin, and then the victory is completed in reaching eternity.

8- David's prayer represents individual prayer, and the people's prayer represents communal prayer, and when the two are joined God answers and gives victory, for God rejoices in both kinds of prayer.
2- “Send thee help from the sanctuary, and strengthen thee out of Zion;”

1- God feels for you and sends you help at the right time, and if He delays it is so that your striving and your clinging to Him may increase, and you may afterward receive greater help and experience His love more fully.
2- God's sanctuary is heaven, where He dwells, and heavenly help is very strong help, which covers you and protects you, and no one can resist it.

3- God's sanctuary is the ark of the covenant, which symbolizes the Church, where the altar and the sacrament of the Eucharist are, and this is the greatest power that supports you against the wars of the devil.
4- Zion is also the Church, where the believers gather and lift up communal prayers, which support every striver among the members of the Church in his life and striving.
5- Zion is the human soul, for God strengthens man within him, so that he feels the power of God supporting him and is at peace even in the midst of distress.
3- “Remember all thy offerings, and accept (make fat) thy burnt sacrifice; Selah.”
1- God in love does not forget the former offerings that David offered; He forgets no love offered to Him, and stretches out to him His hand with blessing and help at the time of man's need.

2- God makes your burnt offerings fat, that is, He sees them as fat, even if they are small, but in His eyes they are great, as He saw the greatness of the gift of the widow with her two mites (Lk 21:3), and likewise the two fishes and five loaves (Jn 6:9), and also the cup of cold water, whose reward is not lost before God (Mt 10:42).

3- Sacrifices are what a person offers and others share with him, eating of them, so they symbolize a person's love for those around him; but the burnt offering is burned entirely to please God, so it symbolizes a person's love for God. God rejoices in our love for Him and our love for others.

4- When a person sees Christ crucified, he feels that he wants to offer his life as a sacrifice of love to God, indeed a burnt offering for Him, that is, to give his life in prayer, worship and service.

5- The word Selah is a musical pause, in which we lift our hearts to God that He may accept our worship, our striving and our small service, which He sees as great by His love and His fatherhood toward us.
4- “Grant thee according to thine own heart, and fulfil all thy counsel.”

1- The giver of every good thing in a person's life is God; so he must lift up his heart with thanksgiving to God at all times. It is good for a person to ask of God, but it is better not to forget to thank God after he receives the gift, so that he is not proud, or ascribes it to himself, or to others, or to circumstances.

2- God is ready to give you all that you desire, that is, according to your heart, if your heart desires and accepts the will of God; but if your will is contrary to God, He will not give it to you, because His will is the salvation of your soul, so if your will is contrary, that is, you seek the world that keeps you from God, He will not answer you.

3- If you have counsels and have begun to carry them out, do not worry about completing them, because God who loves you will complete for you what you began, as long as you hold fast to His commandments.

Be at peace, for God is your shepherd, and your heavenly Father is with you; He will not leave you, but gives you what you ask and what you desire. Only be submissive to Him, hold fast to His word, and be steadfast in His Church, and even if afflictions pass over you, you will come out of them with more strength.
5- “We will rejoice in thy salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners: the Lord fulfil all thy petitions.”
1- When God saves a person from distress he must sing and thank God, that is, express his joy in words of praise and thanksgiving to God.

2- Deliverance from distress is the first thing that makes a person glad, but greater than it is deliverance from sin and the enjoyment of eternal salvation, that is, he thanks God that He has prepared the Kingdom for him, and he receives it through the Church and its sacraments and means of grace.

3- There was an ancient Eastern custom that if a man killed another and then fled and sheltered in a city, or with some great person, and then reconciliation became possible between him and the family of the one killed, he would raise a banner in which he proclaimed his deliverance and reconciliation, and the pardon of those who had the right to take vengeance on him. So we raise a banner in the name of our God, who saved us from Satan, who wants to kill us and holds our sins against us. Christ lifted from us the sentence of death and gave us acquittal from sin; therefore we glorify Christ our God and lift up His Cross, which is our banner, our salvation and our victory.

4- If we began by thanking and glorifying God who saved us from distress, we must after this love Him and cling to Him, because we discover the extent of His love and care for us, so that we live in praising Him forever; so you love God the Giver more than the gift, and the One who gave us victory more than the victory and success.

5- In the spirit of prophecy David sees not only God who gives him victory over his enemies, but Christ the Redeemer, who comes in the fullness of time and saves mankind from the chains of sin and opens to them the closed gates of Paradise.
6- When a person feels at peace through praising God his Savior, he is encouraged and asks of God, who answers him and completes His gifts to him in all that he asks according to His divine will.
6- “Now know I that the Lord saveth his anointed; he will hear him from his holy heaven with the saving strength of his right hand.”

1- David felt that God is his Savior; his anointed means David the king, anointed as king by the pouring of oil on his head by the hand of Samuel the prophet. During his prayer he felt peace and rest that God is his Savior and will always save him, so it is a prayer full of faith and hope.

2- His anointed means also our Lord Jesus Christ, who was anointed by the Holy Spirit in the river Jordan at His baptism, and the Lord saved Him from death by His Resurrection, for He raised Himself by the power of His divinity.

3- Likewise the word “his anointed” applies to every believer in the New Testament, who has been anointed by the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Holy Myron; God saves him from all his troubles, and he feels rest and peace when he prays, so he is not disturbed by any distress that may come upon him in the future.

4- God rejoices in the prayers of His children and answers them from His holy heaven, that is, the heaven in which God's throne is, and this is a declaration of God's power and loftiness and His ability to answer our prayers. His holy heaven is also the womb of the Virgin, for she is the second heaven, which was sanctified by the divine conception, and by His Incarnation He saved us from our sins and redeemed us. Likewise His holy heaven is His temple, which is the holiest place in the world, or heaven on earth, for He rejoices in the prayers of His children in the Church and answers them.

5- God's power to answer mightily is stronger than we imagine, and He expresses this power by His right hand, which is able to save us from our troubles and give us depths we cannot imagine in His love and fellowship.
6- And at the right hand of the Father the Son sat, so here he prophesies about Christ the Mighty and Powerful, who offers salvation to mankind in the fullness of time.
7- “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the Lord our God.”

1- Here David speaks of the enemies of the people of God, whether the Egyptians under the leadership of Pharaoh (Ex 14:28), or the Syrians who fought David (2 Sam 8:6), or, in the spirit of prophecy, the Assyrians under the leadership of Sennacherib (Isa 37:36). All these enemies relied on strength in war, represented by horses and chariots. But the people of God relied on remembering His holy name, which overcomes the enemies however great their strength.

2- The chariots and horses symbolize the body, and this is what Satan fights; but the spirit lives and is strengthened by the name of the Lord, so it can overcome the lusts of the body, control them, subdue the body and lead it in the way of God.

3- This verse applies, in the spirit of prophecy, to the Apostles and servants of the New Testament, who by the name of the Lord overcame the power of the demons and spread Christianity among the pagans. It applies also to the monks of the desert, who cleansed it of demons by the name of the Lord and triumphed over the various lusts.
8- “They are brought down and fallen: but we are risen, and stand upright.”

1- When God entered the war with His people the enemies fell, and David the prophet says of them “they are brought down,” that is, they knelt and fell and were thrown on the ground. This is what happened with the Egyptians at the bottom of the Red Sea, when the water covered them and they drowned and died, because they relied on their strength and did not believe in God.

2- The people of God relied on the power of God, so they rose and stood upright and came out of the Red Sea with a great victory, and so in all the wars the enemies would fall and they would be exalted above them.

3- In the spiritual war the demons fall, but God's children by His power rise and come out of every distress, and if they fall because of their weakness God raises them, and they stand upright and thank Him.

4- If the beginning of the Psalm in (v. 1) mentions the trouble and distress through which Christ passed, which is His Cross, in this verse he declares that by the power of Christ the children of God bear the Cross, and they rise and stand upright by His Resurrection.

Trust, for you are a child of God and your natural position is to be standing upright; if you fall into sin, this is a position foreign to you, so repent and return to God, and you will rise and return to your natural position. And if the marks of distress appear in your life do not be troubled, because God who rose from the dead dwells in you, and comforts you, and strengthens you, and keeps your peace until the distress ends.
9- “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call.”

1- He concludes the Psalm with a call upon God to save whom? The king, the rulers, the teachers and all the people, for God is able to deliver all His people and save them continually from all enemies.

2- David addresses God and calls Him King, and this is the first time we find a man addressing God with this title, and after him Isaiah the prophet, who said that God is the King (Isa 6:5). So he asks God, who has authority, to answer him on the day he calls upon Him and seeks Him.

3- Whoever has God reigning over his heart, and controls his senses and thoughts, can respond to the requests and needs of others when they ask him for help, because he is rid of selfishness by God's reigning over his heart, which gives him the spirit of giving and self-sacrifice.
4- God is ready to answer if we ask Him, but if we are slothful, or our faith is weak and we do not ask Him, we will receive nothing.

5- It is our duty to ask on behalf of our kings and rulers, and all our spiritual and worldly leaders, that the Lord may give them grace and wisdom, so that we may live in peace. And because the wars of the demons are stronger against rulers, it is our duty to ask for them.

Ask of God all that you need, for He is your Father who loves you and hastens to meet your requests. And do not forget to ask on behalf of others and everyone who has responsibility, that God may support him in it.
“Victory”
To the chief musician. A psalm of David. “The king shall joy in thy strength, O Lord” ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- When was it written? After David's victory over the children of Ammon in the city of Rabbah (2 Sam 12:26-31).

2- When is it said? At the coronation of kings in the kingdom of Judah; the priest would repeat the words of this Psalm except verses 8 and 13, with which the people respond to the priest; all of this is said to the king.
3- This Psalm is one of the Messianic Psalms; it speaks of Christ after His victory over Satan, His Resurrection from the dead and His Ascension.

4- This Psalm completes the previous Psalm: if the twentieth Psalm speaks of David's distress before the battle, this Psalm speaks of his victory after the battle. And if the twentieth Psalm speaks of the distress of the Cross, this Psalm speaks of the Resurrection. And if the twentieth Psalm speaks of the distress in the life of any spiritual person, this Psalm speaks of his thanksgiving to God after his victory in the spiritual war.
5- This Psalm speaks of the gifts granted to the spiritual striver, or to the king who trusts in God.
6- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- “The king shall joy in thy strength, O Lord; and in thy salvation how greatly shall he rejoice!”

1- Who is the king but David, who rejoices in the power of God that saved him from his enemies the children of Ammon; and in his likeness every believer who reigns by his will over himself, controlling his senses, thoughts and feelings, rejoices in the power of God that supports him in his war with the demons and saves him from them.

2- David rejoices because the victory over the enemies is very great, despite their strength, and God saved him from them beyond human logical expectation, for the power of God surpasses the expectations of men because of His great love for His children.
3- David saw Christ, who would become incarnate in the fullness of time, and rejoiced in His power that triumphed over Satan and in His wondrous salvation, which He would offer to mankind.
2- “Thou hast given him his heart's desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips. Selah.”

1- The desire of the heart is a person's inner longings and feelings, and it precedes the request of the lips, that is, the requests a person asks of God; God gave David both, for He answered the desire of his heart and his requests.
2- God answers the desire of the heart and requests when they agree with His will.

3- This verse applies to Christ, who desired our salvation and loved us before the foundation of the world, and desired to eat the Passover with His disciples, and likewise asked the Father for our salvation and for our being kept from evil in the world (Jn 17).

4- At the end of the verse is the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditating during it on God's love for His children, who gives them the desire of their hearts and their requests, and which encourages His children to hope and to ask of God.
3- “For thou preventest him with the blessings of goodness: thou settest a crown of pure gold on his head.”

1- David asked God to deliver him from his enemies and give him victory over them, and because he asked nothing for his own glory God gave him the victory, and added to it other divine blessings, which are various good things, such as wealth and the widening of his kingdom. This is what God also did with the daughter of Solomon, who asked for wisdom, and He gave it to him, in addition to wealth, so that he was the richest man of his age.

2- David declares that these blessings go before the person who trusts in God, that is, God makes easy his way to reach the Kingdom, and makes easy also many aspects of his life, and he finds in every road he walks divine blessings awaiting him, so he feels God's hand generous to him in giving.

3- This verse applies to Christ in His going before with blessings of goodness, for before His Incarnation God declared many prophecies and types of Him, and it was said that Abraham saw the Incarnation of Christ and rejoiced (Jn 8:56). The men of God and the prophets in the Old Testament beheld the Incarnation of Christ and rejoiced in it; these are the blessings with which God poured out upon His children in the Old Testament as a preparation for His Incarnation.

4- God set a crown of pure gold on David's head, that is, he received material blessings and spoils in his victories, among them a very large crown of gold, belonging to the king of the children of Ammon, which they put on David's head after David's victory over the children of Ammon (2 Sam 12:30).
5- And symbolically this crown is placed on the head of Christ and means:
A- The crown of thorns, which represents the unlimited love of Christ, which appeared in His bearing all the sufferings for the salvation of His people.
B- The crown of the Resurrection and the Ascension; that is, the glory Christ received in the declaration of His Resurrection and His ascension to the heavens.
C- This crown is the twelve Apostles, of whom the Book of Revelation tells us as the twelve stars crowning the head of the woman clothed with the sun, that is, Christ and His Church (Rev 12:1).
D- The crown is the Church, which is the bride of Christ; as a virtuous woman is a crown to her husband (Prov 12:4), so the Church is the crown of gold that Christ acquired with His blood.
6- God set on David's head the crown of glory, which is that Christ would be born of his seed, and this is the greatest crown, that Christ is called the Son of David (Ps 110:1).
7- The crown is the crown of virtues that God places on the head of everyone who believes in Him in His Church and strives to acquire any virtue, and God crowns him in glory.
4- “He asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever.”

1- David was exposed to death many times, during the pursuit of Saul and Absalom and during his wars with the surrounding nations, so he asked life of God, and He delivered him and gave him life on earth, and then eternal life.

2- This verse applies plainly to Christ, because He alone is able to live forever, and before His death He asked for life when He said, “if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Mt 26:39). And God gave Him life by His Resurrection and Ascension.
3- This verse applies to every believer who asks for a spiritual life with God, and He gives him eternity.

4- Life is Christ, for He said, “I am the resurrection, and the life” (Jn 11:25); whoever asks for life, that is, Christ, on earth, God gives him eternal life, as Christ said, “whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die” (Jn 11:26).

5- David also said this verse as a prophecy about King Hezekiah, to whom Isaiah announced that he should set his house in order because he would die, so he asked life of God, and then He granted him an extension of his life of fifteen years, in addition to eternal life.
5- “His glory is great in thy salvation: honour and majesty hast thou laid upon him.”

1- David was the youngest of his brothers and a shepherd of sheep, and God took him and anointed him king, and magnified him with great glory, not only by his sitting on the throne of the kingdom of Judah, but also by the coming of Christ from his seed.
2- God delivered David with great glory from the hands of his enemies, and even lifted him above them, so that the surrounding nations were subdued to him and offered him gifts and tribute.
3- This verse is a prophecy about Hezekiah, to whom the nations came with gifts after God lengthened his life, and the Assyrians submitted to him after his victory over them.
4- Christ emptied Himself by His Incarnation and His redemption on the Cross, so God glorified Him by the Resurrection and the Ascension, after He had bound Satan.

5- Every believer who strives and reigns over his senses, his thoughts, his speech and his works, God blesses him and glorifies him in the eyes of people in this life, and then with great glory in eternity.
6- If the king enjoys glory and majesty, all this is grace from God and not from man.
6- “For thou hast made him most blessed for ever: thou hast made him exceeding glad with thy countenance.”

1- God does not only bless the king, or Christ, or the believing spiritual striver, but makes him himself a blessing to those around him, so that everyone connected with him receives a blessing, as Abraham the father of the fathers was a blessing to all around him, and likewise Joseph in the house of Potiphar, and in prison, and on the throne of Egypt.

2- “Thou hast made him blessings for ever”: this applies plainly to Christ, because He blesses His children who believe in Him on earth, and continues to give them the blessing forever; He is the focus of all eyes and the satisfaction of all in heaven.

3- God gives everyone who believes in Him the grace of joy and gladness, by which he is distinguished from all around him who are troubled and wretched because of sin, because they live for the world; but the mark of God's children is joy.
4- The cause of the joy of God's children is God's looking upon them and their fellowship with Him, for He is in them, and they rejoice at all times as long as they hold fast to Him.
5- Joy and gladness remain in the heart of God's children by His constant care for them and their remaining before Him, but if they go away from before Him they lose the joy.

6- The victory of the spiritual person in his wars against the demons, or the victory of the king over his enemies, makes him glad, but in order to continue victorious and in joy he must remain before God, that is, look to God as his only goal throughout his life.
7- “For the king trusteth in the Lord, and through the mercy of the most High he shall not be moved.”

1- The king draws his strength in governing his kingdom from God, in whom he trusted, and consequently succeeds in all his affairs, just as the person who reigns over his spirit and his body is successful by trusting in God.
2- He who relies on God is not troubled or shaken, but whoever trusts in the world and its power must be troubled, because he is exposed to falling and the passing of his kingdom.

Why do you weary yourself and are troubled on your way to achieving success, when the way is clear before you, namely trust in God, for through Him you receive grace and peace and ability to accomplish all your affairs? So hold fast to His commandments, and cast all your labors upon Him, and He is able to use your abilities at the right time and in the right manner to bring you success.
8- “Thine hand shall find out all thine enemies: thy right hand shall find out those that hate thee.”

1- God promises the king that His hand will find his enemies, and will bring them down and destroy them, that is, none of them will escape, and by this the striving spiritual person is turned from one defending himself into one who overcomes and rules over his enemies the demons, as we say in the prayer of thanksgiving, “He gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy.”

2- The king's hand strikes and so punishes the enemies, but his right hand, which symbolizes salvation, as the Psalm says of God, “The right hand of the Lord is exalted: the right hand of the Lord doeth valiantly” (Ps 118:16), strikes in order to save those who hate him, and this means that David, or Christ, or any spiritual person wants the salvation of those who hate him; if he disciplines them, he wants their salvation, as Joseph did with his brothers.

3- If the hand mentioned in the verse means the left, this means that if the spiritual person uses his right hand and his left in striving, that is, all his works are on the way of spiritual striving, he will certainly triumph over his enemies.

9- “Thou shalt make them as a furnace of fire in the time of thy presence: the Lord shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them.” Furnace: an oven, that is, the place where they kindle fire; it represents a huge mass of flames, whatever the kind of oven.

1- God declares to David that his enemies burn like a furnace of fire and the fire devours them, that is, their power is destroyed, and they become as nothing. This is what David did to the children of Ammon, when he made them pass through the brick kiln (2 Sam 12:31).
2- The fire declares God's wrath by distress, pain and the reproach of conscience in this life, and then eternal torment at the end.

3- David's enemies are God's enemies, so in the time of God's presence the enemies burn, and this is what supports God's children, that God fights for them, and as long as He is with them all the enemies fear and are defeated, and even burn.

4- God's wrath and anger and the fire that devours the wicked are not hatred on God's part toward them, but are the natural result of their works, which call for divine justice; the wicked have sentenced themselves by their wickedness, and deserved this destruction.
10- “Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.”

1- The enemies vanish from before David, or the spiritual person, or Christ, so that they have no power or effective deeds, that is, the fruits that are in the earth. By this David disregards their existence, and goes on in his positive, constructive works. Likewise the spiritual person goes on in the way of acquiring virtues, not hindered by the wars of the demons.

2- God destroys the seed of the wicked, that is, there is no man left to weary and trouble David. And the enemies of man are sins; and sins are of two kinds: the mother sins, that is, the great, “their fruit,” and the small sins that result from them, “their seed”; God helps the spiritual person to overcome both, and this helps him to be free for positive work.

3- The wicked who tried to kill David and his people God destroyed, that is, their sin came upon their own heads, and what they wanted to do to David came upon them. This is what happens with the demons, who fight God's children to destroy them, and God delivers them, and casts the demons into eternal torment.
4- If the earth symbolizes the body, then our holding fast to God destroys the fruits of evil, that is, the sins into which the demons try to make us fall.

5- This divine punishment of the wicked is a threat to them, that they may turn back from their wickedness, and it is a hard threat, because it includes their seed also; if they do not fear for themselves, their hearts may be moved because their children also will be destroyed.
11- “For they intended evil against thee: they imagined a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform.”
1- David's enemies tried to wrong him and do evil to him, and even set snares for him in war that he might fall into them, but God delivered him from all this, and no harm came to him.

2- The Jews tried to wrong Christ with evil words, and tried to kill Him, and then crucified Him, but all this turned to the glory of God, for Christ by the Cross accomplished our redemption, and then rose from the dead with great power. And the Jews tried to spread the rumor that His disciples stole the body, but their attempt failed, and Christ appeared to many.
3- The demons try to wrong God's righteous children, so they set snares for them, but God delivers them, and the demons are put to shame, and evil comes upon their own heads.
4- While the wicked devise schemes, God frustrates them before they are completed, so although their hearts are full of evil toward God's children, their schemes fail.
12- “Therefore shalt thou make them turn their back, when thou shalt make ready thine arrows upon thy strings against the face of them.”
Turn their back: run and flee.
Make ready: to place the arrow on the string to shoot it, meaning to aim the arrow.

1- The strength that God gives David makes his enemies fear him and flee from before his face. So also with Christ, when they tried to seize Him and He said to them, “I am he,” they feared and went backward and fell to the ground (Jn 18:6). And God's children who hold fast to Him are feared by the demons, who flee from them, as happened with the saints who cleansed the deserts. Thus the enemies turn from attackers to fearful ones and fugitives.

2- God aims His arrows at the wicked, that is, He threatens them that He will destroy them, that perhaps they may repent. This shows that God's justice is bound up with His mercy, for He seeks their salvation and their return to Him. But if they persist in their wickedness, punishment and destruction await them.

3- God shows His power in His children, as they defy the wicked and stand against their faces; meaning that He gives His children courage that frightens the enemies. This appeared in David and likewise in Christ, but those who refused to believe, their wickedness came upon them.

Do not fear the wars of the demons, for they are worthless as long as you hold fast to God in the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace, and humble yourself at all times and the demons will flee from you.
13- “Be thou exalted, Lord, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power.”

1- If Christ emptied Himself by His Incarnation, David sees in the spirit of prophecy the Resurrection of Christ and His Ascension, and asks Christ to be exalted before those who opposed Him and crucified Him, that perhaps they may repent and believe.
2- When God's children see His power and His victory over the enemies they rejoice and praise, singing spiritual songs; this is the conclusion of this great Psalm.

3- If the beginning of the Psalm tells us of the power of God (v. 1), its end is also sealed with His power and exaltation, as we end the Lord's Prayer by saying, “Thine is the power, the glory and the honor.”

Do not let your heart cling to the earthly glories you achieve, because they are changing and passing, but hold fast to your prayers and to doing good. This is what remains for you, and keeps you and lets you enjoy fellowship with God.
The sufferings and glories of Christ. To the chief musician upon Aijeleth Shahar. A psalm of David. “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” ... (v. 1) Introduction:

1- David wrote this Psalm, but the events mentioned in it did not happen in David's life; he speaks of another person, that is, he speaks of Christ in the spirit of prophecy, after God inspired him with the thoughts of Christ on the Cross and in His sufferings, and then after His Resurrection and His kingdom, and he recorded all that for us in this Psalm.

2- It says in the title of the Psalm “upon Aijeleth Shahar,” and Aijeleth is the time of the dawn, that is, the dark time just before daybreak, and at this time the Jews used to prepare the morning burnt offering, which is a symbol of Christ, who rose early at the dawn of Sunday, and whose sufferings and Resurrection this Psalm speaks of.

And the title of this Psalm is Aijeleth Shahar (the hind of the morning) because it contains the sufferings and Resurrection of Christ, who saved us from the darkness of the night and gave us the dawn of the new life; indeed it is said of Him that He is “the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). There is another opinion that Aijeleth Shahar was a tune to which this Psalm was sung.

3- What confirms that this Psalm is Messianic is that David did not mention in it his confession of any particular sin, or his justification of any particular sin, or ask for vengeance on his enemies; he tells us of the sufferings borne by a righteous man who committed no sin, so it applies to none but Christ. And although this Psalm speaks of the sufferings of Christ and His salvation, its title Aijeleth Shahar points to His Resurrection, because the aim of the sufferings and death of Christ is the Resurrection.
4- This is the first Psalm in the Book of Psalms that speaks of the sufferings of Christ, and the Fathers regard it as one of the greatest Psalms that speak of His sufferings.

5- Because this Psalm contains events that took place at the ninth hour, the Church chants it in the sorrowful tune (Adribi) at the ninth hour on Great Friday. And because it was customary that if one of the Jewish priests said the beginning of a Psalm the hearers would complete it, Christ uttered the beginning of this Psalm on the Cross at the ninth hour (Mt 27:46), so that the Jews standing beneath the Cross might complete it and know that this Psalm is a prophecy about Him, that perhaps they might believe.
6- This Psalm declares an important truth that the Jews forgot, namely God's acceptance of the Gentiles and their salvation (vv. 27-31).
7- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
The words of my roaring: words coming out with my breath, that is, my sighs; for roaring is the air that goes out when a person breathes.
1- This verse clearly applies to Christ, because He said it on the Cross. It is a clear prophecy of His sufferings, which David saw by the spirit of prophecy.

2- These words confirm the humanity of Christ, who truly suffered severe pain and expresses it by His cry to God, and confirms it by saying "my God" twice; that is, Christ took a real body like the rest of mankind.

3- In His saying "my God" the boldness of sonship appears; for He speaks to God on behalf of humanity as a man. And although He suffers from the intensity of the pain and says "thou hast forsaken me", at the same time He expresses the faith and the boldness that exist between Him and the Father, or as every spiritual person ought to behave with boldness toward God.

4- This verse is an expression of the purity and holiness of God, who cannot bear sin, which the Son bore on the Cross. Although He is holy, He bore the sins of the world; indeed, He who knew no sin was made sin for us (2 Cor 5:21).

5- The words of Christ here are not a question seeking an answer, nor a complaint, but an expression of the intensity of the sufferings He endures. These are not only the dreadful bodily sufferings and the psychological sufferings of everyone rising up against Him, so that even His beloved ones forsook Him, but the hardest of all these is the spiritual suffering of bearing, while He is the Holy One, all the sins of the world.
6- By saying this on the Cross, Christ gives support to everyone who suffers and feels as if he were forsaken by God; Christ assures him that He feels with him and that he is not forsaken by Him.

7- Christ said this verse in the Aramaic language, which the Jews understand, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani", in order to alert them that this Psalm, which the Jews memorize without understanding it, speaks about Christ, so that perhaps they might believe.

8- Sin is the barrier that separates man from God. So Christ, on the Cross, bearing the sins of the world, expresses this by saying "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" But when He completes redemption by His death, humanity obtains reconciliation with God in Him.

9- The saying of Christ, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?", is speech about humanity, which sinned against God, and on its behalf He speaks before the Father, although He is righteous and holy. He is a son of man but without sin, as He declared plainly to the Jews, saying, "Which of you convinceth me of sin?" (Jn 8:46), and therefore He does not deserve sufferings and death, but bears them for others, that is, fallen humanity, in order to save it from its sins. It is a declaration of His holiness, and that He did not deserve death or the Father's forsaking Him, but by His own will He accepts the sufferings. The hiding of the Father's face from Him is an expression of the divinity's distress at sin, in spite of its great love for humanity, which made Him become incarnate and unite with it, and suffer and die for it.

10- A heresy appeared that proclaimed interpreting this verse as meaning that the divinity departed from the humanity. This is, of course, wrong; His saying this is a communion between the Son and the Father that expresses all the meanings mentioned above, that is, the perfection of Christ's humanity and the divinity's distress at sin. This verse expresses the work of the Second Hypostasis, the Son, in suffering for the sake of humanity and bearing its sins, and it also expresses the work of the Father, the just Judge, in leaving the Son to bear the sufferings unto death.
2- O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and have no rest.
Rest: calm, or repose.

1- Here He affirms that He asks for God's help, but He does not answer Him, neither in the day nor in the night; that is, Christ's sufferings were continuous, whether in the day while on the Cross, or in the night while in the garden of Gethsemane, and He bore all this for our salvation.

2- Asking for God's help in the day signifies asking at the time of victory, so that the believer may stand firm in his victory; while the night signifies tribulation, and the believer asks God to bring him out of it and to save him from his sufferings and troubles.

3- God sometimes does not answer His children, because postponing their request is best, as in the case of Zacharias and Elizabeth, or because the request is not suitable for the salvation of the soul, such as the healing of St. Paul from his thorn; and at the same time He may answer the wicked, or even the demons, to their shame, as He answered the demons who begged that they might enter the herd of swine (Mt 8:31, 32). And in the case of Christ, the Father did not answer His prayer in the garden of Gethsemane that the cup of His sufferings might pass from Him, and left Him to bear the sufferings of the Cross, because the sins of humanity required that Christ bear these sufferings unto death, in order to redeem His children.
3- But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel.

1- Beginning with this verse, Christ presents a group of kinds of reproach to God for having forsaken Him. In this verse He reproaches God the Father, saying to Him: You are the Holy One in whom is the perfection of holiness and justice; how can You be content with injustice, and that the sins of the world be laid upon an innocent person?! This is an expression of the extent of the sufferings that Christ bears, confirming His humanity united with His divinity.

2- God the Holy One is praised by His angels in heaven, but He also rejoices greatly in the praises of His children on earth, who were at that time His people Israel, since His people were the only people who believed in God.

3- God is holy, that is, wholly holy, and therefore deserves praise from the heavenly and the earthly, for He alone is the Holy One. And all His holy children have received something of His holiness. These saints are the ones who appreciate holiness, and therefore they alone are the ones who praise Him. By the saints is meant everyone who believed in Christ and so became holy in Him.
4- Our fathers trusted in thee: they trusted, and thou didst deliver them. 5- They cried unto thee, and were delivered: they trusted in thee, and were not confounded.

The second reproach of Christ to God the Father, on the lips of David by the spirit of prophecy: that when the fathers of God's people trusted in Him, prayed and cried to Him, He answered them and delivered them from their afflictions, as happened with God's people in Egypt, when He struck the Egyptians with the ten plagues and then drowned Pharaoh's army in the sea, and as He saved the three young men from the furnace of fire, Daniel from the lions' den, and chaste Susanna from the hands of the two elders.
6- But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. 7- All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,
1- The third reproach that Christ presents to the Father is that He left Him until He became despised like the worm, which is trodden underfoot, and no longer had the dignity of a human being.

2- The worm appears to be a very weak creature, just as Christ appeared in weakness during His crucifixion. This is how He appeared before men and the wicked Jews, who did not understand that it pleased the Father to bruise Him with grief. Christ by His own will accepted death, and accepted to appear as having no form nor comeliness, for the sake of our salvation. And while He appeared weak before men, in Him was the perfection of power, and by His death He abolished death and bound Satan.

3- The worm, which appears very weak, is able to destroy the bodies of men, for it eats them after their death; and Christ on the Cross destroyed the old body, that is, the nature inclined to evil, and saved us from it and gave us the new nature by our birth in the sacrament of Baptism.

4- The worm is the source of a red dye called crimson, and Christ shed His blood on the Cross, and by His blood, which is red in color, He gave redemption to all humanity, that we may be dyed with His dye and receive a new nature by His death and resurrection.

5- There is a kind of worm called the hydra; if its body, which is formed of rings, is divided, each ring becomes able to live by itself. Likewise Christ, by His death, became the head of His body, which is the Church, and every member in it has its own independent life. Likewise, believers in Christ in the arenas of martyrdom become the cause of many believing in their God, and they too receive the crown of martyrdom.

6- Isaiah prophesied about the people of Israel and described them as a worm (Isa 41:14). So God's people appeared weak at the captivity, like Christ on the Cross, but because God's power was with His children, He brought them back from the captivity, and from them came Christ, the Savior of the whole world.
7- The worm comes out of the clay without mating; likewise Christ also was born like earthly man, but without the seed of man.

8- By Christ's accepting the Cross, He became despised like the worm, indeed a reproach of men and despised of the peoples, so that the Jews, while He was on the Cross, mocked Him (Mt 27:42). How then can man, who is of dust and whom the worm eats, be proud and think that he is something and ascribe glory to himself, although all that he has is gifts from God?!

9- The Jews who passed by the crucified Christ showed their evil and their contempt for Him, and mocked Him in every way; for they opened their mouths, "shooting out the lip", laughing at Him. They also "shook the head", that is, wagged their heads in contempt of Him (Mt 27:39). Thus their hard hearts were devoid of feeling and tenderness toward Him; moreover, their outward behavior was moved to abuse Him with the head and with the mouth. It is a marvelous hardness, especially because it came upon the Righteous and Holy One, who had wronged no one.
8- "He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him."

1- David the prophet foretold what the wicked Jews, who passed by the crucified Christ mocking Him, would say, saying that He is rejected by God; for if He were with God, let Him deliver Him from the sufferings of the Cross. Indeed, they said the very words that David prophesied (Mt 27:43).

2- Satan speaks on the tongue of the wicked, to cast doubt on the righteous about their conduct and their life. By the righteous are meant those who believe in Christ, for when they see the crucified Christ in weakness they leave their faith. This satanic doubting is repeated every day until now, but the faith of those who believe in Christ remains firm, bearing sufferings unto death, in order to receive the power of the resurrection, which they feel in their lives on earth, that is, they feel peace and joy in fellowship with God, and then in eternity they enjoy the glories of the Kingdom of Heaven.
3- The doubting of Christ was in two matters:
a - That He does not trust in God and does not believe in Him, otherwise He would have delivered Him from the Cross.
b - That He is not loved by God; He is not His beloved Son as He claims, otherwise He would have rescued Him from these sufferings.
9- For thou art he that drew me out of the womb: thou didst make me secure upon my mother's breasts.

1- In this verse David the prophet speaks by the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who makes the fourth reproach to the Father for having left Him to all these sufferings, although it is God who drew Him out of the womb and nursed Him at the breast of the Virgin His mother; so why does He forsake Him now? This confirms the humanity of Christ and that He bore real, hard sufferings.

2- The Father is the one who drew Him out of the womb, because the birth of Christ was wonderful, distinguished from the rest of mankind in that it was without the seed of man, and it did not dissolve the virginity of the Virgin; God drew Him out of the womb, and the virginity of the Virgin remained sealed. This is the divine miracle.
3- The Child Jesus nursed milk from His mother's breast, and was secure while nursing like any child, and this confirms His humanity and His need for nursing like the rest of mankind.
4- The womb from which the Father drew the Son is also the Jewish nation, and He came out of it to redeem it and to redeem the whole world.

5- If it is the Father who drew Him and set Him securely on His mother's breast, then He is responsible for His birth and His life on earth, and therefore He is responsible for the sufferings He endures; these insults from men are directed against the Father, and He trusts in Him. Likewise, a person who trusts in God feels that what he suffers, despite his good conduct, is directed at God, so he is not troubled; if God wills, let Him rescue him, or fight for him, and if it is for his good, He supports him to bear the sufferings.

6- This verse also applies to every believer in the New Testament, whom God draws out of the womb of the Church, which is the baptismal font, and nurses him securely at the breast of his mother the Church, that is, satisfies him with her prayers, her books, her history, and all that she contains of rites and doctrines.
10- I was cast upon thee from the womb: thou art my God from my mother's belly.

Here He confirms the fourth reproach mentioned above, which is that He trusts in God, so why does He leave Him to bear all these sufferings? And here He declares that He was cast upon God from the time He was in the womb, in the Virgin's belly; He trusted in God throughout His life, indeed before His life began, while He was in the womb.
11- Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help.

1- The reproach here turns into prayer, and Christ asks the Father not to be far from Him; for Christ as a man declares His need of the support of the divinity in order to bear the sufferings, just as every person in tribulation needs God in order to be able to bear it and pass through it.

2- The secret of the strength of the believer within tribulation is God's being with him, so he accepts the pain, and even rejoices in his fellowship with God during the pain, and the pain turns into joy.
3- Christ declares that trouble is near, and what is meant by it is death on the Cross, and this calls for divine help to pass through death, and then the resurrection.
