2- The pious who fear God live in righteousness, because they are influenced by the holiness and righteousness of God, and they are always occupied with the beauty of God, so they praise Him and always remember His holiness. And the more they bless God and remember His holiness, the more their hearts are drawn to holiness and righteousness in all their conduct.

3- Remembering the name of God and His holiness is the foundation of the dedication and blessing of any house. And this is the first reference to dedication in this psalm. And you also: the blessing of your life comes by remembering the holiness of God every day.

4- David, who experienced the life of praise and enjoyed it, was moved in his heart toward the rest of the believers, so he calls them to share with him in praise and in remembering the holiness of God; for he is a member of the people of God and cannot be separated from them, just as the Christian is a member of the Church and does not feel life apart from his brethren.
5- "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: at evening weeping lodgeth, and in the morning singing."

1- The tenderness of God, who desires that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, appears in that He is angry with His children for a very short time, expressed here as a moment, so that they feel the guilt of sin, and He disciplines them, and they turn away from it and reject it; then God's mercies and favor come in a complete, happy life that the believers in Him live. So God was angry with David when he numbered the people, and struck them with the plague, but He quickly returned and forgave them, and David offered a sacrifice in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite (2 Sam 24:25).

2- Life is in God's favor, but distance from Him is death; therefore the children of God seek to please Him by keeping His commandments, and when they please Him they receive His abundant blessings, so they thank Him and rejoice.

3- David speaks to us of weeping in the evening, that is, by a person's examining himself for his sins throughout the day, so that he regrets them and confesses them before God in tears, then sleeps quietly, and wakes to praise God who kept him through the night and granted him to begin a new day.

4- Christ died on the cross and was buried in the evening, and the Marys and all His beloved wept for Him, but on the morning of the Resurrection His beloved saw the tomb empty, and He even appeared to them, and they rejoiced in His resurrection.

5- The evening signifies our life in the world, where we suffer many pains and tribulations, expressed here as weeping, but in the morning of eternity, that is, when we enter the Kingdom of Heaven, we live in singing and praise forever.

6- In the evening Sennacherib the Assyrian reproached the people of God, and they were in grief and weeping, and in the morning the Jews were rid of the Assyrians, for they found them corpses after the angel had killed them, while the rest fled. And in the evening King Hezekiah grieved over his sickness that would lead to his death, and in the morning God gave him a new lifespan of fifteen years (Isa 36-39).
Do not forget to examine yourself every night, and as much as you regret your sins God gives you hope and forgives you your sins, and after this you begin with great spiritual vigor.

entries.section: (3) Asking the Savior and praising Him

paragraphs.text: 6- "And in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved."

1- David expresses his security in his earlier life, when he was tending the sheep, and felt the hand of God with him, and killed the lion and the bear. And when he saw Goliath he was not troubled but remained secure, and went out to him and killed him.
2- Adam also lived securely in Paradise with God, enjoying fellowship with Him, and was far from sin, so he felt that he would live in this security forever.

3- King Hezekiah felt security when God healed him of his sickness and prolonged his life, but in pride he opened his treasuries to show his greatness to the Babylonians who had come to congratulate him on his recovery, so he lost his peace, and God was angry with him, and his children were taken captive years after his death (2 Kgs 20:13).

4- Perhaps David, in his negligence when he went up to the roof of his house, felt a false security, and fell into adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite (2 Sam 11:1-5). And perhaps he also became proud when he numbered the people, and God's punishment came upon him in the plague.

entries.section: (3) Asking the Savior and praising Him

paragraphs.text: 7- "Lord, by thy favour thou hast made my mountain to stand strong: thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled."

1- David declares that the cause of his strength and might is God's favor toward him. And if the mountain signifies strength and steadfastness, David declares that his mountain, that is, his life, became steadfast and strong by God's favor toward him. In this he attributes the stability of his kingdom and his many victories to God's favor toward him. So David declares here his return to God and his reliance on Him, and not on his personal strength, because of which he fell into the sins of pride, adultery and the numbering of the people.

2- At the same time David makes clear his concern for God's favor toward him, for as much as he keeps His commandments and submits to Him, he is established in his spiritual life and in his kingdom and his leadership of the people and his victories over the nations.

3- The steadfastness of the mountain also applies to the kingdom of the children of Israel and its capital Jerusalem, which was built upon five mountains; if Jerusalem pleased God, He established it so that it became great and the nations were subject to it. But if it disobeyed His commandments it was disciplined by captivity and made subject to the nations, then if it returned to Him in repentance He brought it back from captivity and established it again.

4- David declares that he needs God's constant care, for if God forsakes him and hides His face he is in fear and terror, and his enemies overcome him; so he declares his constant need of God's care, which is the cause of his strength. And so all the children of God and His Church declare their constant need of His care, that they may live before Him. For this reason also Moses refused that God should abandon His people when they fell into the worship of the golden calf, and because of Moses' clinging to God, God forgave His people and led them in the wilderness (Ex 33:15-17).

entries.section: (3) Asking the Savior and praising Him

paragraphs.text: 8- "I cried to thee, O Lord; and unto the Lord I made supplication."

1- Since David believed that his life is in God's favor, and that if He turns His face away from him he is afraid and terrified, he cried out to God, because He is his only help, and in Him he finds his life.
2- Crying out is not by raising the voice, but by the entreaty of the heart, tears, and clinging to God; therefore God hears and cares and watches over, and indeed also lifts up His children.

3- Supplication to the Lord shows David's humility and persistence, for he feels that he is a servant begging his master, and he makes supplication to Him from the depth of his heart that He may rescue him. And God looks upon the prayer of the poor and the humble, and hastens to him.

entries.section: (3) Asking the Savior and praising Him

paragraphs.text: 9- "What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit? Shall the dust praise thee? shall it declare thy truth?"

1- David reproaches God with the boldness of sonship and says to Him, why do You leave me and not hear my cry? For without You I shall perish, and my life will end by my being put in the pit, or the dust, that is, the grave, and I shall lose my sonship to You and my enjoyment of fellowship with You forever in the Kingdom. In this he urges God to hasten to him to rescue him from every sin, and to support him in his life on earth.

2- David also reproaches God and asks Him to hasten to his aid, because he wants to praise God, and to go on praising Him forever in the Kingdom. But if he dies while far from God, he will lose the ability to praise God, and praising God is the hope of his life.

3- Those who do not pray and do not praise God are dead in the sight of God, although outwardly they are alive and move about on the earth, but the mark of the living is prayer and praise. And in proportion to one's concern for prayer, a person is alive.

4- The spiritual person always thanks God, and declares God's faithfulness and truth, because he loves God. And when he declares God's faithfulness and praises Him, he thereby calls others to love the faithful God in His care and love for His children.

5- Christ says to all the sinners who refused to believe in Him, what profit is there in my death on the cross and my going down to the tomb, that is, the pit? For you have not benefited from my death for you, and you, O sinners, have become dead, that is, dust, who do not pray, nor praise, nor declare my truth.

entries.section: (3) Asking the Savior and praising Him

paragraphs.text: 10- "Hear, O Lord, and have mercy upon me: Lord, be thou my helper."

1- David continued in his prayers before God, because he feels that He is his only refuge. So he repeats here his request to God to hear his prayer, and in this David is reassured, and even waits for God to answer him and make him feel His care, so that his heart rejoices.

2- David's asking for mercy shows his humility and his confession of his sins before God, and that he needs God's mercy in order to live. And in proportion to David's repentance and humility he receives abundant mercies, however great his sins. And so David sees Christ not as a judge, but as an intercessor and forgiver of sins.

3- Despite David's many experiences, he is confident that he has no success except with God's support and help, so he asks God to enter into every detail of his life, and in this he enjoys fellowship with Him, and secures the safety of his way and his success in all his steps, and this moves him to constant thanksgiving to God, so he enjoys true joy.

entries.section: (3) Asking the Savior and praising Him

paragraphs.text: 11- "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;"

12- "To the end that my soul may sing praise to thee, and not be silent. O Lord my God, I will give thanks unto thee for ever." Girded me: clothed me with a girdle, and the girdle is what is worn around the waist and extends to the upper thighs.

1- By David's offering repentance and asking God's mercies, he received His forgiveness, and God wiped away his tears, so his weeping turned into joy and spiritual dancing, that is, gladness of heart. For in repentance sorrow and joy mingle together at one and the same time in a wonderful way, so that joy covers the tears, and the feelings of regret melt away in the hands of the tender, forgiving God.

2- David in his abasement before God had put on sackcloth, which is coarse clothing that declares his weakness and his austerity from the world, and his seeking God. And when he continued in fasting and prayers, God stretched out His hand and took off from him the garments of abasement, and clothed him with garments of joy. And He strengthened him with joy, because one who is girded about the waist shows strength and readiness to set out, for his heart was filled with joy, and he became ready for every good work and every self-giving service; that is, filled with hope and readiness to make others happy.

3- Before the great works of God that David saw in himself, his spirit expressed its joy in singing and praise, after its silence for a long time because of its grief over its sins. And so life returned to his spirit, because prayer and praise are the delight of life.

4- At the end David's boldness before God appears, for he feels his sonship to God and calls Him "my God," for he feels that God is his Lord and his God and the One responsible for him, so he praises Him for His works, not only in this life, but forever. And this shows David's faith in the other life after death, and his confidence in the love of God, who grants him the glories of the Kingdom.
5- David's giving thanks to God forever indicates his joy in God his Savior, and his thanks to Him for all that he passes through in his life, and that this joy lasts forever.

Be diligent in prayer at all times, so that you see God as the tender Father who forgives your sins, and so you are encouraged however much you fall, and rejoice in God's love and thank Him continually.
My hope in God my Savior. To the chief Musician. A Psalm of David: "In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.
2- It is among the psalms of thanksgiving, which are (Pss 30-34).
3- When was it said?
a - When he was fleeing from the face of Saul, and probably he was in the region of Maon.
b - Another opinion is that he was fleeing from Absalom his son.
c - Perhaps when David sinned his sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, then returned to God in repentance and trusted in Him, he wrote this psalm.
4- This psalm calls to trust in God and to entrust one's life to Him, then to thank Him for His works; this psalm strengthens the faith of everyone who meets with troubles.
5- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- "In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed: deliver me in thy righteousness."

1- It appears from the words of this verse that David was exposed to troubles from his enemies beyond his capacity, but he believed in God and trusted in Him, so his heart was at peace and he was no longer troubled, despite the continued opposition of the enemies.
2- David's perfect faith in God appears in his confidence that God is able to support him all his life, until He transfers him from this life to the better life, that is, eternity.

3- David may have been exposed to a sin and repented of it, so God forgave him, and David trusted in Him to protect him from falling again; indeed, in confidence he feels that God is able to raise him always in a constant relation of love with Him.
4- Because of the harshness of the opposition of the enemies who wrong him, he asked God to deliver him in righteousness, for God is not pleased with injustice, and He supports His weak children.
2- "Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me."
1- David's humility appears in his saying "bow down thine ear to me"; he feels his weakness before the loftiness of God, and asks Him to incline His ear to him.

2- Perhaps the tribulation through which David was passing made him speak in a low voice, and this shows how much he suffered from the threats of the wicked against him. And since his voice was low, he asked God to condescend and bow down His ear to hear him.

3- It appears that David was in severe distress and strong threats from the enemies, who almost overtook him, so he asked God with the boldness of sonship to hasten to him, for he trusts in God's fatherhood and tenderness and His concern to help him.

4- Because of the multitude of enemies David needed to hide from them, and he had nothing before him but God in whom to hide as a fortress and refuge, and in this the Lord delivers him from his enemies.

5- It is a prophecy about Christ, the rock of the fortress and likewise the house of refuge, through His redemption of us on the cross. So whoever takes refuge in the cross of Christ is saved from the warfare of the demons.
3- "For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name's sake lead me, and guide me."
Fortress: stronghold.

1- David's hope is the name of God, which delivers him, and he trusts in nothing else, for he has no other power to protect him, and he does not depend on his own strength or the strength of his men; rather, his hope of salvation depends on the grace of God, which He pours out on him for the sake of His holy name.

2- David also depends in his conduct and movements on God, who guides him, and when God guides him his enemies cannot overtake him; for God hides him from their eyes and gives him an escape far from them.

3- The Church counsels that in our spiritual warfare we depend on the name of God and repeat it often, whether through the Jesus Prayer or the Absalis in the Midnight Praise, for it rescues us from the snares of the demons.
4- "Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me: for thou art my fortress."

1- God's protection of David does not mean only stopping the wars directed against him, nor does it mean preventing the possibility of his falling, but it means rescuing him if he falls, so that he does not perish. David trusts in God, his fortress, who will deliver him if he falls into the net.
2- It is a confession by David of his weakness and his need of God, when he said, "Pull me out of the net," and the humble person receives all of God's mercies.

3- David was exposed to many attacks from Saul, not only direct assault but also hidden snares, such as the trickery of some who showed friendship to David so as to deliver him into the hand of Saul, even though David had done good to them, as happened at Keilah (1 Sam 23:12); but David's prayers deliver him because God is his fortress, and God knows the unseen, so He rescues him from all evil.
5- "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord God of truth."
1- When David says "Into thine hand I commit my spirit," it means his complete reliance on God and his faith in God, who protects not only his body but his spirit from every sin, and keeps it in Him.

2- When David commits his spirit into the hand of God, it shows the extent of David's spirituality, who cares for the salvation of his soul more than the comfort of his body, so even if he is exposed to hardships and tribulations from Saul or others, his spirit is kept in the hand of God.

3- David's placing his spirit in the hand of God shows his faith and his heart's preoccupation with eternity, in which his spirit enjoys being with God; for if he longs to enjoy fellowship with God while he is on earth, how much more his longings to enjoy permanent being with Him in eternity.

4- David thanks God who rescued him many times from the hand of his enemies, for by logic David should have died, but God redeemed him and rescued him by miracles, so the arrows of the enemy did not reach him but flew in the air, and he remained kept in the hand of God.
5- It is God who redeemed David, and He is his God of truth; this means that David is wronged and innocent, and God knows this; therefore He rescued him from the hand of his enemies.

6- This verse is a clear prophecy about Christ; David saw with the eye of prophecy Christ dying on the cross and committing His spirit into the hand of the Father, to redeem David and to redeem all mankind. And Christ spoke these words on the cross just before He died (Lk 23:46).
6- "I have hated them that regard lying vanities: but I trust in the Lord."

1- David's enemies trusted in their strength, their position and their wealth, and all these are lying vanities, because they are nothing before the power of God, while David trusted in God alone and not in any other power; therefore he was at peace.

2- Although circumstances, in his flight from the face of Saul, made David take refuge by dwelling among the pagans, he refuses and hates their idol worship and their evil way of life, for in his eyes they are lying vanities, and the truth is God alone; therefore he trusted in Him.

3- David not only refused to rely on the powers of the world but also hated them, because his love for God made anything else rejected and hateful to his heart, for God had filled his heart and satisfied it.

4- All the people around David care for and regard lying vanities, worshiping idols, or caring for money, position and military power, like Saul, but David cared for the worship of God, repeating His holy name, and praying at all times, and this helped him to trust in God.
7- "I will be glad and rejoice in thy mercy: for thou hast considered my trouble; thou hast known my soul in adversities;"

1- When David committed his spirit into the hand of God (v. 5), he of course rejected every sin and was purified by repentance; therefore he received God's mercies and God brought him through the tribulation in peace, and even gave him the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, and for this reason he is in great gladness and joy.

2- David shows God's fatherhood and tenderness in His concern for him and His rescuing him from his adversities; for although He allows the trial, it is only for a time so that man may benefit from it, then He lifts it and compensates man with great tenderness.

3- David received and attained the aim of the trial, which is abasement before God, that is, humility and poverty of spirit and prayer with contrition, so the trial turned into a blessing, and then David experienced God's turning to him and looking upon him, for he is the object of God's love.

4- God allows trials, but in a set measure according to man's endurance, and God, who watches man and looks upon him, lifts the trial at the proper time, for He knows man and the extent of his endurance, so He cannot give him anything beyond his strength; God looked upon David's affliction and knew him in his adversities.
8- "And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room."
1- David thanks God that He delivered him from the hand of his enemies, so they could not seize him, or imprison him, or kill him, or harm him with any bodily harm.

2- At the same time he thanks God for widening the way for him to flee from his enemies, so that he could run far from them, throughout his life and in all his wars, and indeed He gave him victory over his enemies.

3- When David fell into the sin of adultery (2 Sam 11:4) or numbered the people (2 Sam 24:1), God gave him an escape from the hand of Satan, that is, He delivered him through repentance, and he returned to his first state, that is, his sonship.

God wants your salvation however great your weakness, so if He allows you tribulations do not be troubled by them, but seek Him and be confident that He delivers you from the hands of the demons, and even gives you the joy of beholding Him.
9- "Have mercy upon me, O Lord, for I am in trouble: mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly."
Consumed: spoiled.
Grief: sorrow.

1- David faced severe tribulations from Saul's pursuit, or other tribulations that pressed upon his soul and body, and even upon his discernment of what was around him, so he cried out to God to have mercy on him and save him from this distress and all its effects.
2- David's prayer to God means his severe suffering in body and spirit, and that he has no refuge but God, and this confirms two things:
a - His humility and showing his need of God.
b - His faith in God.

3- These words of David apply to the Church, which asks God's mercy because of the persecution and tribulations she passes through, so her eyes are spoiled; that is, many of her priests and servants, who are eyes for her, were martyred and tortured. The soul signifies all the spiritual saints, members of the Church, and the body signifies all the people. And when the eye or the soul is spoiled it affects the body; therefore the Church asks God's mercies.
10- "For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of my misery, and my bones are consumed."
1- David expresses the effects of the tribulations upon him, or of his falling into sin, and these effects are:
a - Inner sorrow.
b - Sighing.
c - Bodily weakness.

2- If problems and tribulations continue, the body and soul grow weary, and so David expresses his pains and takes refuge in God, that He may have mercy on him and lift his burdens from him; for he suffered hardships for many long years, which were the period of Saul's pursuit of him.
3- David's taking refuge in God by prayer and sighing is a humility on David's part that makes him receive God's many mercies.
11- "I was a reproach among all mine enemies, and especially among my neighbours, and a fear to mine acquaintance: they that did see me without fled from me."

1- When David fled from the face of Saul, those who knew him thought that he had sinned, and therefore Saul was angry with him, and he deserved death, so David became in their sight an example of shame, and they kept away from him.
2- When David's enemies learned of his flight from the face of Saul they rejoiced over him, and were sure that he was wicked and deserved punishment; indeed, perhaps they helped Saul to arrest him.
3- When David's neighbors and acquaintances learned of his flight from the face of Saul they feared for themselves, so they kept away from him and did not try to help him, lest Saul harm them.
4- These words of David apply to Christ, when the Jews seized Him and tortured Him, then crucified Him, and they apply also to our fathers the martyrs and everyone who endured severe persecutions.
12- "I am forgotten as a dead man out of mind: I am like a broken vessel."

1- It was very painful to David's soul to feel that his neighbors, acquaintances and loved ones, when they found him fleeing from Saul, did not move, and in time considered him lost and dead, so they forgot him and no longer felt for him. This extreme neglect was painful to his soul.

2- When David fled, his acquaintances considered him a broken vessel, that is, refuse and a worthless thing that has been thrown away and got rid of, so David had nothing before him but God, who feels for him and supports him and comforts him.
3- This verse too is a prophecy about Christ, whom they considered like a dead man, despised at His crucifixion and burial, and the world did not know that He is its Savior who died for it.
13- "For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life."

1- David's pains were not limited to his flight from Saul, who wanted to kill him, but he was also exposed to evil words and insults from others, who rejoiced over him and seized the opportunity of his flight to invent from their wicked hearts evil words against him, and he bore them for God's sake.

2- David's enemies cooperated with Saul to destroy him, and devised plots to seize him, but God delivered him from their hands for the sake of his righteousness, and because of their false accusations against him.
3- The threats of Saul and all David's enemies put those who accompanied David in fear; that is, fear came to be on every side around him, but he remained steadfast in his faith.

If tribulations come upon you one after another, stand firm in your faith, and lift up your heart in prayer, and be confident that God will not leave you and will surely turn the tribulations into blessings in your life, and bring you out after this into rest.
14- "But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God."
1- Before the tribulations that met David he found nothing before him but God in whom to trust and to feel peace in His hands.

2- David felt a boldness and a special relationship with God, so he said to Him "my God," and raised prayers to Him in which he poured out his soul before Him, and was at peace in His care and protection of him.
15- "My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me."
My times: plural of term, which is the end.

1- The terms are the ends, and David was exposed to death many times, and God rescued him and gave him a new lifespan, so he is assured that all the ends of his life are in the hand of God, and for this reason he devotes himself to prayer and to enjoying fellowship with God who protects him.

2- The terms are also the stages through which David passes in his life, some of which were heavy, like Saul's pursuit of him, and some lighter in troubles, like his reigning over the tribe of Judah and his wars for seven years with Ishbosheth the son of Saul, and some more restful when he reigned over all the children of Israel. In all these David feels that he is in the hand of God, so he lives in His fear, enjoying His love.

3- Since David is at peace in the hand of God, he asks Him in confidence to deliver him from the hand of Saul who pursues him, and from the hand of all his enemies, because God is stronger than all and able to protect him.
16- "Make thy face to shine upon thy servant: save me for thy mercy's sake."

1- David's heart is occupied with God; he wants to enjoy being with Him, and he is not troubled by the enemies because he is assured of God's protection. This shows the extent of David's attachment to the love of God.

2- The shining of God upon David and all mankind was fulfilled in the Incarnation of Christ, so David by the spirit of prophecy awaits the appearance of the expected Messiah, the Savior of the whole world, to enlighten the hearts of those who believe in Him.

3- In humility David says to God, I am Your servant, and save me by Your mercy; for David feels his unworthiness in everything, and at the same time he trusts in the mercy of God, which is able to save him from all who trouble him.
17- "Let me not be ashamed, O Lord; for I have called upon thee: let the wicked be ashamed, and let them be silent in the grave."

1- Since David raised his voice in prayer and enjoyed the shining of God, his heart rejoiced and he lived enjoying fellowship with Him; therefore he is confident of victory over his enemies on earth, then of the glory that awaits him in eternal life.

2- Prayer is being with God, and in it man tastes the foretaste of the Kingdom, that is, he feels the sweetness of fellowship with God, and after this it extends into unceasing prayer, which is eternal life. So whoever loves fellowship with God, God lifts him to permanent fellowship with Him in heaven.

3- The wicked who refused to be with God and preferred to be with sin await nothing but shame in hell, to receive the punishment of their sins, and there they feel deprivation of God forever, and this in itself is severe torment.

4- In hell the wicked are silent out of their fear and their shame, for they have nothing with which to justify their sins which they committed on earth, and they know for certain that they deserve this torment; therefore they are silent. And if they had a chance to speak with God on earth, they have lost it in hell, so they are silent and deprived of God forever.
18- "Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous."
Put to silence: be made silent, for the dumb is the mute.
1- David asks God, and wishes, that the tongues of the wicked be silenced, which ascribe evil to the righteous, lest they cause them to stumble and weary them.

2- In hell too the wicked lose the ability to speak the vain words that they spoke against the righteous, for they lied and accused them falsely, so the wicked feel their sin, but in despair, and they are silent in the torment.

3- If the righteous man has endured lies, contempt, insolence and pride from the wicked, he is comforted by the joys of heaven, which compensate him for all that he endured, but the wicked are tormented because of all these wrongs they did. The righteous enjoys the praise of God, and the wicked is silent in shame.

If you are enduring insults from others, seek God's help, and know that these troubles are temporary, and indeed, as you endure them willingly, God compensates you for them with great glories in heaven.
19- "Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee; which thou hast wrought for them that trust in thee before the sons of men!"
Laid up: stored up.

1- David thanks God for His blessings that He poured out on him, for He gave him consolations and peace in his heart, and even joy during the tribulation, so he was not troubled by Saul's pursuit and threats.

2- God's blessings to His children surpass the mind, so that David could not describe them, and said, "Oh how great is thy goodness." They therefore lift man above the tribulation and make him taste the sweetness of heaven while he is on earth.

3- God's blessings and goodness are given by God only to those who fear Him, and not to all mankind; for although God gives general blessings to all mankind, He gives those who fear Him great spiritual blessings, which are the feeling of Him and the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, and these surpass all material and spiritual blessings.

4- God loved His children who revere Him and fear Him; He loved them before the foundation of the world, and laid up for them from eternity countless blessings. This shows God's unlimited love for His children, which satisfies them, so that they need nothing.
5- Whoever fears God keeps away from every sin, carries out His commandments, trusts in Him, and lives at peace among troubled people, and so he is a light for the world and salt for the earth.
20- "Thou shalt cover them with the covering of thy face from the plots of men: thou shalt hide them in a pavilion from the strife of tongues."

1- God covers those who fear Him and trust in Him, and protects them from the plots of the wicked, and as long as God covers them no one can harm them with anything; it is He who preserved David from all of Saul's plots.

2- God covers His children with the covering of His face, so that during the tribulation they see nothing but the face of God, and enjoy His love and fellowship, as happened with the three young men, who praised God and did not feel the fire.

3- When God covers His children with His face and looks upon the plots of men, He spoils them and destroys them, so that they become worthless and do not harm His children, as He spoiled the plot of the wicked against Daniel, so the lions became tame animals and did not harm Daniel.

4- When God covers His children, He gives them wisdom and power in speech, so the wicked cannot overcome them, and all their adversaries become weak before them, as He promised in the New Testament to give His children a mouth and wisdom which all their adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist (Lk 21:15).

5- God in His love hides His children from evil and the plots devised against them in the pavilion of His care, which signifies the Church in the New Testament. Either He gives them wisdom in their speech with the wicked, or the wicked are not able to prove their words, or He keeps them away from His children in some way, so the children of God always feel God's care and His protection of them.
21- "Blessed be the Lord: for he hath shewed me his marvellous kindness in a strong city."

1- God's love for David the righteous appeared in His protection of him, as if he were in a fortified city, whose high walls cannot be stormed, and these are faith; and this city signifies the Church in the New Testament, surrounded by the angels and saints, and relying on Christ the Head of the Church, who feeds His children with His Body and Blood. It also signifies the perfectly fortified city in heaven, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, where the children of God enjoy fellowship with Him without any disturbance from the demons.

2- David thanks God and blesses Him because He worked miracles in protecting him from Saul's pursuits; for God's mercy made a wonder surpassing the mind, and even delivered Saul into David's hands twice, but David forgave him, so Saul felt shame and confessed it before David, and said to him, "Thou art more righteous than I" (1 Sam 24:17).
22- "For I said in my bewilderment, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee."

1- When Saul's pursuits of David increased, Satan fought him by casting doubt on God's protection of him, and he was preoccupied with Saul's plots, so he was bewildered and said to himself, has God forgotten me and no longer looks upon me?! So he was in spiritual and psychological distress.

2- But David did not continue in his bewilderment; rather, he returned to what he was accustomed to, which is prayer, and cried out to God, so he regained his peace, and felt God who is with him and protects him, and hears his prayer and supplications.
23- "O love the Lord, all ye his saints: for the Lord preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer."
1- David concludes the psalm with a call to the pious who fear God, that they may enjoy His love, for as they contemplate His love for them, their hearts are drawn to Him and they cling to Him.

2- God cares very much for the faithfulness of His children toward Him, so He blesses them and gives them peace, especially when they hold fast to faithfulness in keeping His commandments, however much tribulations surround them, and in the end He blesses them with many blessings, as happened with David, and made him a great king over all the children of Israel, and subdued his enemies to him, and as He kept faithful Joseph in the house of Potiphar and in the prison, then raised him to the throne of Egypt.
3- On the other hand, the proud wicked, who resist God and wrong His children, God punishes severely, as happened with Saul and his sons, who died in the war with the Philistines (1 Sam 31).
24- "Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all ye that wait for the Lord."

1- In the end David calls those who believe in God to be strong, that is, to stand firm in the faith and not fear the wicked, and likewise to take courage, so that they can attack their enemies with power, because victory is guaranteed to them by the power of God.

2- David calls the believers and styles them those who wait for the Lord, that is, those who are patient in tribulations and bear the pains of striving, for these enjoy God's work in them, which establishes them and encourages them, and as they feel God's support for them, they rejoice in His presence.

If tribulations surround you and Satan casts his doubts at you, do not be troubled, but hasten in humility to God, and seek Him and cry out to Him, for He is near to you, and hastens to your aid, and reassures you, and saves you from your enemies.
God's blessings for the penitent. Of David. A poem: "Blessed is he whose iniquity is forgiven" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its author is David the prophet.
2- When was it written?

After the fifty-first psalm, which begins with the words, "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness." David wrote these two psalms about a year after his fall into adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, when Nathan the prophet came to him and warned him, so he wrote the fifty-first psalm, then wrote this psalm.
3- This psalm is an encouragement to the penitent; if the fifty-first psalm is full of contrition before God, this psalm shows God's blessings to everyone who repents.
4- This psalm is one of the seven penitential psalms, which are (Pss 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).
5- This psalm is also considered, as we mentioned, among the psalms of thanksgiving, which are the psalms (Pss 30-34); here David thanks God who forgives sins.
6- A part of this psalm is mentioned in the sacrament of Baptism, because in it the forgiveness of the sins of the baptized is accomplished.
7- This psalm is considered one of the Pauline psalms, that is, those whose words and thoughts resemble the words and style of St. Paul the Apostle, and they are (Pss 32, 130, 143).
8- St. Augustine loved this psalm and was careful to repeat it until the end of his life.

9- This psalm is called in Hebrew "Asher," which is one of the tribes of the children of Israel and means "happy," because this psalm begins in its first two verses with the word "Blessed," that is, "happy."
10- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- "Blessed is he whose iniquity is forgiven, and whose sin is covered."

1- David shows his joy at the forgiveness of his sins after he had committed his abominable sin, which was adultery and murder, so he says, happy is the one whose sins God forgives, so that He lifts them and removes them from him, and casts them into the sea of forgetfulness.

2- God in His love covers the sins of the penitent, so they do not appear again, that is, He blots them out. And this is a divine love that surpasses the mind, because the thing that troubles man most is his sin. And God in His love removes it completely.

3- If the first psalm speaks to us of the happiness of the one who walks uprightly and keeps away from evil, this one speaks to us of the man who is exposed to falling during his life on earth, but who loves God and His commandments, so he returns to God in repentance, and then receives His forgiveness, and rejoices in this forgiveness.

4- From this verse we understand that forgiveness is a free divine gift that God gives to the penitent; God has compassion on His weak children if they sin and return to Him in repentance, and He blots out their sins from them as if they had not done them.
2- "Blessed is the man unto whom the Lord imputeth no sin, and in whose spirit there is no guile."

1- Happy and joyful is the one whose sins God forgives, and who consequently becomes pure, and in this purity stands before God and beholds Him, and no sin appears in him before all the heavenly beings, so it becomes his right to enjoy God while he is on earth, until he reaches Him in heaven.

2- As this man enjoys God's forgiveness and the purity of his heart, he feels the guilt of sin and the sweetness of purity, so he keeps away from all evil and all guile, that is, he is careful in his life and his spirit becomes pure, not wanting to sin because of its preoccupation with God.

3- Sin defiles man, and this defilement is first of the spirit, then of the body, because out of the abundance of the heart the tongue speaks. But harder still is for guile to exist in man's spirit, for he deceives himself, and not God of course. And this guile makes him persist in sin, so it dwells inside him and appears on his body, such as his speech, his glances and his actions; therefore whoever is purified from guile becomes truly pure.

4- St. Paul the Apostle quoted (vv. 1, 2) from this psalm and said them in (Rom 4:6-8), confirming the importance of the work of God's grace in the forgiveness of man's sins, and not the works of the Law.
3- "When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long."

1- After David fell he kept silent and did not confess his sin before God, nor before the priest, nor did he offer a sacrifice for his sin, nor before a prophet like Nathan; therefore his conscience pricked him, and he tried to flee from it, so he remained troubled, having lost his peace.

2- The reproach of David's conscience to him did not quiet down, especially since David is a spiritual man who knows God and His commandments well, and the reproach of conscience wearied David, not only in his spirit, which was troubled, but his body was also affected. And David expresses the depth of his pains and says "my bones waxed old," that is, he suffered many inner troubles until his bones, which are the strongest thing inside the body, almost wasted away and dissolved.

3- David's distress and his being affected by the reproach of his conscience appeared in the sighing of his aching heart every day and all day long, and he expressed this in that he was in pain with every breath that came out of his nose, that is, he was in constant pain, and perhaps this sighing was with a loud cry, either within himself or even in a loud audible voice, which those around him did not understand, or perhaps they thought he was suffering from something; so that some of them said that he was struck with a bodily illness from the great reproach of his conscience to him.

4- David's silence is silence from prayer and praising God, for sin keeps God away from us and separates us from Him, so we lose our enjoyment of Him, and our prayers weaken or stop, but by repentance the ability to pray can be regained.
4- "For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah."
Drought: dryness.
Summer: the intense heat.

1- The hand of God was a support to David, but when he sinned the hand of God became heavy upon him until he repented; for after he sinned with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and a child was born of the adultery, David prayed, but the child died, then Amnon the son of David sinned with his sister Tamar, and after that his brother Absalom killed him, then fled, and after his return he stirred up the people and removed David from his throne and drove him out of the kingdom. All this is the hand of God that became heavy upon David, that his repentance might deepen and he receive the mercies of God.

2- Because of the tribulations that God allowed to come upon David, his inner life turned from moisture, that is, the enjoyment of God's work in him, to severe dryness, so he felt distress and pressure, and then he took refuge in God, who forgave him and removed his sin from him.
3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical note, and means here the asking of God's mercies, because David is in distress and needs God's compassion and tenderness.
5- "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah."

1- David arrived at the solution of his problem, which is confessing his sin before God, and before his man Nathan the prophet, and in this he was rid of his sin, since God removed it and lifted it from him.

2- David overcame the barrier of shame and pride by confessing his sin and not hiding it, and his confession was a public confession, so that he even wrote it in his psalms, and he abased himself before God, since he felt the guilt of his sin, and his honor before people no longer mattered to him.

3- The confession that David made declares his rejection and hatred of sin, and the exposing of Satan who made him fall, and in this David regained his sonship to God, who forgave him and restored his purity to him.

4- God's lifting David's sin from him gave David inner peace, but God allowed him a punishment in the problems that he went through, which we mentioned in the previous verse. For although God had forgiven his sin, by this discipline He wanted to deepen the thought of repentance within David, so that afterward he would reject any sin.

5- God in His love wants to forgive the sins of His children, but He waits for their repentance and confession, and then He hastens to forgive, and restores them to their sonship to Him, so they enjoy His care. This is because when Nathan confronted David he confessed his sin at once, unlike what happened with Cain, whom God warned to confess the sin of killing his brother, and he answered insolently and said, "Am I my brother's keeper?" and so he was not forgiven (Gen 4:9). David and Cain both fell into sin, but David confessed with humility before God, while Cain answered God with shamelessness and pride.

6- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical note, and means here thanking God and rejoicing in His forgiveness. In this it differs from the word Selah that is in the previous verse, for the two notes are different according to the meaning of the verse preceding the word Selah.
6- "For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the flood of great waters it shall not come nigh unto him."
1- Because God is the forgiver of sins, every person who fears God and lives with Him believes in His love and hastens to Him with repentance to receive His forgiveness.

2- Prayer is not only for confessing sin and obtaining forgiveness, but whoever is godly and falls into sin feels that it keeps God away from him and weakens his prayer, so he hastens to repentance and regains his prayer, and it even becomes warmer because of his feeling of his need for God.
3- When the godly person feels repentance for his sin, at this time he can find the merciful God, to whom he prays confessing his sins, and so receives His forgiveness.
4- Whoever is always godly and fears God feels His constant presence, for God is present at all times, and therefore prayer is available to man at all times.

5- When severe tribulations pass over a person, until he almost perishes as happened in the days of the flood, he hastens to God with repentance, and no harm comes to him; rather, God rescues him, as He rescued Noah and his family.

6- The flood of great waters signifies the day of judgment, when the wicked ask the mountains and hills to cover them, but the children of God suffer no harm; rather, when God appears He takes them to Himself and satisfies them with His love.

The door of repentance and confession is the greatest grace that God gives us, so hasten to Him with repentance if you fall into sin, confident of His love and forgiveness, and in proportion to your sense of the guilt of sin offer prayers and tears before God throughout your life, and so your tears mingle with feelings of peace, joy and thanksgiving to God who forgave your sin.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who trust in Him

paragraphs.text: 7- "Thou art a covering for me; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah."
Compass me about: surround me on every side.

1- When God sees the repentance of His children He covers them, so they are not exposed before people; for if they expose Satan by repentance He covers them, but if they hide their sins they are exposed before people, especially on the last day.
2- God's covering of the penitent also means that He protects him from falling into new sins, whether the same sin into which he fell, or any other sins.

3- If tribulations pass over this penitent for his discipline, God keeps him in them, so that he does not fall into sin, but learns from the discipline and returns to God with all his heart, that is, lives a deeper repentance.

4- When God delivers the penitent from many sins, he rejoices and praises God and sings to Him, and so he enjoys prayer. And thus his heart is filled with joy, and joy also surrounds him, so it shows on his face as a smile and heart's peace.
5- The word Selah here is a musical note that means joy, praise and thanksgiving.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who trust in Him

paragraphs.text: 8- "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will counsel thee, mine eye being upon thee."

1- God promises David and all the penitent that He will teach him the way of life with Him, that he may walk in the new life, after being rid of his sin. And this walk of his gives him the enjoyment of fellowship with God, so he rejects sin, and in this He protects him from falling into many sins.

2- The second promise is that God will guide the penitent in the way in which they walk, so that the world cannot deceive them with its crooked ways, however great the world's doubts. And they also overcome all despair and discouragement which block the ways before them, and God guides them to the open way that leads to eternal life.
3- The third promise is that God will counsel him, that he may guard against falling again, and also that he may strive in the way of virtue, so that his fellowship with God increases.

4- The fourth promise is God's constant providence and care for him, so that His eye is on the penitent, to keep him from all evil and warn him of any satanic deceit, and to care for him in all his steps, and in this he is established in the way of righteousness.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who trust in Him

paragraphs.text: 9- "Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: with bit and bridle, whose adornment muzzles them, lest they come near unto thee." Bit: an iron piece placed in the mouth of the horse or the mule to prevent it from walking or running. Bridle: a strip of leather that ties the bit on both sides to control the movement of the horse or the mule. Muzzles: the bit is considered a muzzle, that is, a restraint placed on the mouth of the horse to control its movement.

1- God warns His children not to behave like animals, such as the horse and the mule, which are distinguished by pride and lust, but to be calm and humble, living in purity, that they may enjoy fellowship with God.

2- The bit and bridle are placed in the mouths of the horse and the mule to control them and prevent them from rushing, but in man God has placed the conscience to control him and prevent him from all evil. And in the New Testament He gave him the Holy Spirit, to prick his heart if he sins and to warn him of all evil.

3- The horse and the mule signify the proud, lustful wicked, and God restrains them, so that they do not approach His children and harm them; so He allows tribulations for the wicked, that they may not carry out their evils against the children of God, or He warns them with His commandments and frightens them with the last judgment, that they may keep away from evil.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who trust in Him

paragraphs.text: 10- "Many sorrows shall be to the wicked: but he that trusteth in the Lord, mercy shall compass him about."
Sorrows: calamities.

1- The wicked are exposed to many tribulations, whether external tribulations, such as diseases, problems and external calamities, or inner tribulations, which are the reproach of their consciences to them, for they are always without peace, even if they laugh and indulge in various lusts.

2- The person who lives with God and trusts in Him and repents of his sins receives God's mercies, and in proportion to his repentance God surrounds him with many mercies and blessings, so his trust in God and his enjoyment of His love increase. And God protects him from the snares of the demons, so that he does not fall into the various sins.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who trust in Him

paragraphs.text: 11- "Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye righteous: and shout for joy, all ye that are upright in heart."

1- David concludes the psalm with a call to the children of God to rejoice in God, who protects His children and forgives their sins, and pours out many blessings on them, so that they thank Him and enjoy His blessings.

2- The one who enjoys joy is the one who has acquired a pure, upright heart, then the pure intentions of his heart appear in good conduct, which is the conduct of the righteous; for outward righteousness comes from inner purity, and therefore the joy of the righteous is inward and is not taken away from them, because it is inside their hearts, while the joys of the wicked are outward and passing.

3- If joy is the portion of the righteous, this is divine justice, because the portion of the wicked is sorrows, as in the previous verse; so none can enjoy inner peace and true joy but the children of God, who fear Him.

4- This psalm begins by pronouncing blessed the one whose sins are forgiven, and ends with the joy of the righteous and the upright in heart. This shows the importance of repentance, which lifts man's sins and fills his heart with joy, so that he thanks God at all times.

If repentance gives all these blessings, would that we hasten to it every day, indeed immediately after falling, so that we humble ourselves before God, and He pours out on us His mercies and blessings.
The shout of victory "Shout for joy in the Lord, O ye righteous) "... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: there is no title for this psalm in the Hebrew text; therefore it is among the orphan psalms, but the Septuagint attributes it to David.

2- When was it said: after David's victory in a battle with the Philistines, in which he was exposed to death at the hand of one of the Philistine champions called "Ishbibenob," but God rescued him with the help of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, the son of David's sister (2 Sam 21:16, 17).

3- A liturgical psalm: this psalm was sung in the temple, especially at the feasts, and the choirs would repeat this psalm in response to one another, each choir repeating a verse or several verses, then at the end they would conclude with verses repeated by all together; and these are the last verses in this psalm.
4- A psalm of thanksgiving: this psalm is one of the five psalms of thanksgiving, which are Psalms 30-34. And the beginning of this psalm is connected with the end of the psalm before it.
5- A teaching psalm: because it teaches that God is the strongest power in the world, and the victor over the nations; therefore His people glorify Him.
6- This psalm is not among the psalms of the Agpeya.
1- Rejoice in the LORD, O ye righteous: for praise is comely for the upright.
The righteous: the upright.

1- Shouting for joy is the highest expression of rejoicing. It is not an inward rejoicing in the heart, but it expresses itself with a loud voice. Those who rejoice are the righteous, whose lives are marked by constant joy in God.

2- The shouting, the rejoicing and the joy are in the Lord, whereas the wicked rejoice in sin, and the carnal rejoice in passing material things. But the righteous rejoice in God; and even if they rejoice in some material thing, they regard it as a gift from God for which they thank Him, and their joy is not in material things in themselves.

3- The upright in heart is the one who keeps God's commandments and rejects evil, so his heart is enlightened and he sees God, and consequently he is drawn to praise Him, and even delights in this praise, for it is the most fitting thing for his life. Indeed, his works and his words in every aspect of life are a testimony to God and praise to His holy name, and not only the words of praise.
2- Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings.
The harp (oud): one of the oldest stringed instruments. It is a large wooden box with holes in its face, over which the strings are stretched, five pairs of strings.
The psaltery: a stringed instrument consisting of a small wooden box over which ten to twelve strings are stretched. In ancient times the strings were played with the fingers or with a bird's quill.

1- David calls us to thank God for His gifts and kindnesses, and to accompany this thanksgiving with melodies played on the harp. Jewish worship was accompanied by musical instruments, because the spiritual level of the Jews needed musical instruments; but in the Church of the New Testament praise became free of musical instruments, as the saints such as St. John Chrysostom and Didymus declared. Musical instruments did not enter Christian worship until the thirteenth century, when the Catholic Church accepted them, and then the Protestant Church. The Orthodox Church, however, still relies on the human throat, and there are only percussion instruments to regulate the voices, namely the cymbals and the triangle.

2- The musical instruments signify man's use of his body and soul, or his tongue and mind, in praising God. As for the ten strings of the psaltery, they signify the name of Jesus, which begins with the letter iota "I", which is the number 10 in Coptic and Greek.
3- The ten strings signify the body and the soul, because the body has five senses and the soul has the inward senses, so the sum of the two is ten; that is, man praises God with his whole being.
3- Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
1- The new song presents God, because God's mercies are new every day; therefore we offer Him a song and praise that is renewed every day.
2- The new song is a symbol of the praises of the Church in the New Testament, and also a symbol of the praise of the heavenly ones, as the Book of Revelation tells us (Rev 5:9; 14:3).

3- We hear in the Book of Psalms that all creatures praise God: the mountains, the rivers and all created things. This is a new praise, that is, the submission of all creation to God its Creator, and thanking Him for His kindnesses and His care for it, and man leads this praise.

4- David also calls for the skilful playing to be accompanied by a shout, which is the highest expression of joy and rejoicing, that is, praise with a loud voice. This signifies the praises of the New Testament and their loud cry from the heart, for with spiritual growth man exchanges loud voices for lofty feelings. In the Old Testament we find pictures of this powerful speech of the heart, as when the Lord said to Moses at the Red Sea, when he saw Pharaoh and his army following him and Moses was silent, praying deeply within himself: "Wherefore criest thou unto me?", though he had not opened his mouth (Ex 14:15).
4- For the word of the LORD is right; and all his works are done in truth.
1- The word of the Lord is the Second Hypostasis, Christ our God, and He is right, that is, there is no crookedness in Him, but He is true and perfect.
2- The word of the Lord is right because it teaches us uprightness by means of His commandments, so that we walk uprightly in all our works, in addition to our thoughts and intentions.
3- The word of God draws us and leads us to God, who is uprightness, so that we believe in Him and live with Him in uprightness.
4- The upright word of God makes our inside like our outside, so that we are faithful like God and have no hypocrisy or pretense.

5- All the works of God, that is, His creatures, He made with precision and faithfulness, and all of them testify to Him that He is their Creator, so they call man to believe in God. Whenever he looks at them, he glorifies God.
5- He loveth righteousness and judgment: the earth is full of the goodness of the LORD.

1- God is the Righteous and Holy One, so by nature He loves righteousness, that is, purity and goodness, and consequently He loves all His children who walk in righteousness, and if they sin, they return by repentance to purity.
2- God is perfect in His righteousness and perfect in His justice, so He rejects sin and is repelled by it.

3- Although He is kind to the weak and has mercy on them if they repent, and even calls them to repentance by His mercy, yet He cannot bear the rebellious, the licentious and the sinners who justify their faults and so persist in them. And although He is long-suffering toward them, in the end they must face His justice on the Day of Judgment, to be punished for their sins.

4- God is also perfect in His mercy, and His mercy is unlimited; it is wider than all the sins of mankind and able to forgive all who repent. God comes forward with His mercy toward all the righteous and the wicked, to call them to Himself, but those who enjoy the overflow of His mercies are the righteous.
5- Mercy results from God's love for mankind, so it reaches out toward all; but people, because of their sins, move God's justice to punish them. God is perfect in His mercy and His justice.
6- By the word of the LORD were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
The breath of his mouth: the air that comes out of His mouth, that is, the mouth of God.
1- God made the heavens by His command, that is, by His word. With all ease and with His perfect power He made the heavens, and He did not need anyone to help Him in that.
2- By the breath of the mouth of God, that is, by His Holy Spirit, He made the host of the heavens. What is meant by their host is:
A - The stars and suns that move with precise order in perfect obedience to God, like the soldier who is bound by the orders of his commander.
B - The angels, who obey God's orders and do everything He asks of them.

3- The Holy Trinity, who created the heavens and what is in them, appears in this verse. It mentions the Lord, that is, the Father, His word, that is, the Son, and the breath of His mouth, that is, the Holy Spirit.

4- The Holy God created the heavens holy, so that man might dwell in them after he completes his striving on earth and becomes pure and holy, fit to dwell in heaven. The righteous are heavenly people who live with the mind of heaven while they are on earth, so in the end they deserve that God glorify them in His heavenly Kingdom.
7- He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses.
As an heap: a heap is a mound, or a hill.
The waters: much water.
The sea: the ocean.
The depth: the deep waters.
Storehouses: storage places.

1- This verse shows the power of God, who controls the earth and the seas, just as heaven is under His authority. He is able to gather the waters in heaps. This is contrary to the nature of water, as happened when the Red Sea was divided by the hand of Moses, and a road was made between two walls of water, and His people crossed on dry land.

2- The deep seas are very frightening, so that some in ancient times thought them to be the dwelling of Satan; but these depths, that is, the deep waters, God gathers in His storehouses, and He controls them, and even fills them with good things that benefit man, such as fish.

3- The sea signifies the world, which is under God's authority, and He controls it for man's good, so the children of God do not fear the troubles of the world, because God protects them, for He is the Ruler of all.
8- Let all the earth fear the LORD: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him.
9- For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.
1- David calls all people to the fear of God, because He is the Creator of all, the life of all is in His hand, and He is also the Ruler of all; therefore the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God.

2- God's greatness appears in that He created everything by His word, and His word is the Second Hypostasis, Christ our God. As soon as God commands, creation comes to be with all its goodness and beauty; therefore all creation ought to glorify Him and all people to praise Him.
10- The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect.
11- The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations.

1- God created all His creation good and excellent, but after man's fall the wicked thought evil and devised their schemes. God saw how they turned aside and went step by step into evil, but He intervened and brought their plots to nothing when these plots were directed against His godly children, and He rescued them from them, as He brought to nothing the counsel of Ahithophel against David and rescued him from the hand of his son Absalom (2 Sam 17:23), and as He brought to nothing the plot of Haman against the people of God in the days of Esther and Mordecai (Esth 7:10).

2- God's counsel is His thought and His providence. The counsel is that on which people gather in a conference, and here we find God, in His Holy Trinity, having a thought, and this thought is fixed and cannot be changed, and no one, however strong, can bring it to nothing, even if people think that God goes back on His word and changes what He declared, as happened with the people of Nineveh (Jon 3:10). But God's thought is fixed, for He planned to threaten the people of Nineveh and then to return and forgive them when they repent, since God, by His foreknowledge, knows everything, and consequently His thought is fixed.

3- Since God's thoughts are fixed, and the counsel of the wicked can be brought to nothing, the children of God are not alarmed, but pray in every affliction, and God rescues them and brings to nothing the counsel of their enemies, as happened in the days of Hezekiah when Sennacherib attacked him and his army perished.

4- When God created mankind and the whole world, He did not neglect them and leave them afterward, but He placed in His plan the providence and care of His children, so He does not leave the wicked to rule over them; that is, He is able to keep His children in the midst of afflictions and to destroy the wicked. And if His children endure sufferings, or die for His name, He rewards them with eternal life and punishes the wicked.
If God is the Ruler of all and orders everything for your good, why do you worry? ..! Rely on Him, ask for your needs and be persistent with Him, for He will order everything for your good.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: 12- Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD; and the people whom he hath chosen for his own inheritance.

1- God greatly values man's freedom, so the nation that of its own will seeks God as its God receives a great blessing, because God will lead it in the way of salvation, protect it, and let it enjoy His blessings.

2- God also pronounces blessed the one whom He has chosen to be His people, and this choice is based on the people's response to God and their faith in Him. For God knows the hearts, and everything is naked and open before Him.
3- God's choice of His believing children is a choice to give them glories on earth and in heaven. They are His inheritance; He blesses them and establishes them with Him forever.

4- The people of God are His inheritance, for they are the people who loved God out of the whole world. God rejoices in them, because they responded to His love. They alone live for Him, so they are His inheritance.

5- Perhaps in his speaking of the nation there is an allusion to the entry of the Gentiles into the faith, when they choose God as their God, and this is what happened in the New Testament when they believed in Christ our God.

6- We notice that the blessing is due to faith in God, and to the people of God who chose Him as their God, and not to self-righteousness or to personal works apart from faith, that is, the works of the Law.

7- God's choosing of some people means that many were not chosen. This calls us to hold fast to God and to stand firm in the faith, that we may be among the chosen. For if our worship is superficial, or we are lax with sin, we lose our place as children of God.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: 13- The LORD looketh from heaven; he beholdeth all the sons of men.
14- From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth.

1- God looks from heaven, for He is higher than all creatures, but His love calls Him to care for His creatures; by His nature He seeks us and condescends to draw near to us, to shepherd us and to care for us. The greatness of His love appeared in His Incarnation, when He united with us and lived among us, to be an example for us of how to live before Him.

2- God sees all people, and nothing is hidden from Him, and He pours out His good things on all; and at the same time, since everything is open before Him, we must fear Him, and if we sin we must hasten to repent to Him, to regain our sonship and enjoy His blessings.

3- God looks into the depths of man, and not only his outward appearance, for He knows the inward intentions of everyone, so He rewards the righteous and also repays the wicked, the pretenders and the hypocrites.

4- The place of God's habitation is not only in heaven, as a declaration of His loftiness, but in His humility He dwells also in the hearts of His children, and He looks upon people who do not believe in Him in order to reveal His light through His children, so that when people see the good works of His children they glorify Him.
5- God's looking at us is a looking of care and love, to look after us by means of His angels, whom He sends to us to declare His love for us and His concern for our salvation.

6- God's looking at us is not mere looking for the sake of knowledge, that is, a passive, useless look, but a positive looking, to care for us and encourage us. When He sees His believing children in His Church, He rejoices in them and leads them in the way of salvation, that they may attain His Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: 15- He fashioneth their hearts alike; he considereth all their works.

1- God is the Fashioner, that is, the Creator of the heart, and He knows man's feelings and inward intentions that move his whole being, and consequently nothing is hidden from Him, so no one can be a hypocrite before Him.

2- God observes all man's works; He sees the upright among them and the crooked. He will surely bless and reward with good the one who walks uprightly. This calls us to carefulness and spiritual striving, however much the wicked surround us.

3- Because God is the Creator of the heart, He is able to create in it the conscience, that is, His voice, to call people to live with Him. He is also able to put His Holy Spirit in them, so that He draws them to faith and works in them with all His power.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: 16- There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.
17- An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength.

1- David shows that military power is not in the multitude of soldiers, nor in the courage of the commander and his soldiers. Nor is it in the war equipment, the most important part of which is the horses, but in the power of God alone. Sennacherib had many soldiers, and Goliath was very courageous, and Pharaoh in the days of Moses had chariots and many horses, and God destroyed all of these by the hand of His children.

2- Satan comforts the wicked with reliance on the multitude of soldiers, or their courage, or the horses they own, or any material power on which they rely. All these signify Satan, who is nothing if the believers rely on the power of God. Therefore the law of Moses commands not to multiply horses (Deut 17:16), and one of the sins of Solomon was his multiplying of horses, which distanced him from relying on God (1 Kgs 4:26).

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: 18- Behold, the eye of the LORD is upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy;
19- To deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine.

1- David concludes his words in this part about God's blessings to His children by speaking of His care for them. He shepherds them and supplies all their bodily and spiritual needs; therefore they live in tranquility, satisfaction and joy, and praise Him continually.
2- Whoever enjoys God's care must have two conditions:
A - The fear of God.
B - Reliance on Him.
For whoever fears God keeps away from every evil, and whoever relies on Him declares his faith in Him.

3- The children of God do not fear death or any affliction, because God is able to deliver them from it; He repels the enemies from them, satisfies them in famine, and solves all their problems; therefore they live in constant security.

4- The satisfaction that God gives them is first of all spiritual satisfaction, before bodily satisfaction. This is by the word of God and His commandments, which rescue His children from spiritual death. And in the Church of the New Testament He satisfies them, above all this, with His most holy Body and Blood.

God's blessings are very abundant, and they await you if you rely on Him with true faith. If the fear of God is before your eyes, it will protect you from evil and lead you to repentance if you fall, so that you do not lose your sonship to God, and so enjoy fellowship with Him and your eternal life.
20- Our soul waiteth for the LORD: he is our help and our shield.

Our shield: the shield is a defensive instrument that the soldier uses to ward off arrows from himself. It is a piece of wood with a loop at the back, in which the soldier puts his hand and moves it in front of his head and body to protect himself with it.
1- David declares the importance of spiritual striving by saying "we waited for the Lord." He strives relying on the help of the Lord, which must support him and give him victory in the end.

2- In our spiritual warfare God gives us a positive power, which is His help, and a defensive power, which is the shield, so He protects us from the wars of Satan by humility and fasting, and gives us power to overcome him by prayer and all works of goodness.
21- For our heart shall rejoice in him, because we have trusted in his holy name.
1- Reliance on the name of God is reliance on God Himself, for He is a power above every power, and is able to overcome all the powers of the enemies.

2- Repeating the name of God fills the heart with power, and even steadfastness, so that it is not alarmed before the wars of the demons, but conquers them, as we say in the Midnight Praise: "Everyone who says, O my Lord Jesus, is like one who has a sword in his hand and strikes down the enemy" (Monday Psali).

3- Confidence in the power of God during our spiritual wars, and victory over the enemy Satan, gladden the hearts of the children of God, so they hold fast to their striving and experience the renewed work of God in them, and so taste the Kingdom while they are on earth.

4- Reliance on passing material things produces turmoil in the soul, but reliance on God gives steadfastness and inward peace, and consequently enjoyment of fellowship with God, and no alarm at the many wars of the demons.
22- Let thy mercy, O LORD, be upon us, according as we hope in thee.

1- God's mercies have no end; they are very abundant, and God grants them to everyone who strives and relies on Him in proportion to his labor and his holding fast to God, so he enjoys fellowship with God, thanks God in constant praise, and rejoices with inexpressible joy.

Do not fear the wars of the devil, for he is very weak before the power of God. Rely on God and ask for His help, for it is very near you and seeks to help you in all the details of your life; indeed, through it you taste a new sweetness in fellowship with God, and so advance with great strides toward the Kingdom.

Thanksgiving to God who cares for His godly ones. By David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, who drove him away, and he departed. "I will bless the LORD at all times" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.

2- When he wrote it: when he was fleeing from the face of Saul and went to the king of the Philistine city of Gath, who was "Achish", or Abimelech (a title of the kings of the Philistines, like the king of Gerar (Gen 20:2)). His servants advised him to seize David, because he was their enemy, so David feigned madness, and Achish disregarded him, and David afterward went to the cave of Adullam (1 Sam 21:10-14) and thanked God for his deliverance.
3- This psalm was written according to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, so each verse begins with one of these letters.
4- This psalm is considered the last of the five psalms of thanksgiving that began from Psalm 30.
5- The Apostle Peter quoted from it in his first epistle (1 Pet 3:10, 11).

6- The psalm tells us of God's help to those who seek Him and fear Him. Perhaps David prayed when he went to Gath, and when he felt the danger of falling into the hand of Achish, and God guided him to feign madness and made Achish despise him and leave him, because in ancient times they feared madmen, believing that a strange spirit was in them. So he escaped from the hand of the Philistines, and wrote this psalm in thanks to God who rescued him; therefore this psalm suits everyone who meets an affliction or a problem with no solution, and seeks God, who is able to deliver him, and then thanks Him for his deliverance.
