7- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Third Hour in the Agpeya, where we remember the descent of the Holy Spirit at this hour, and we thank God who pours out His Holy Spirit on those who seek Him and fear Him, and on everyone who is godly toward Him.
1- I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth.

1- David felt the hand of God that had rescued him from death, so he lifted up his heart in thanksgiving and praise, and felt that God's work with him called him to praise Him throughout his life, indeed at all times, perhaps to repay God something of what He deserves; it is gratitude, and a sense and appreciation of God's grace.

2- The constant praise results from David's sense of God's continual care for him; indeed it is a feeling of God's being with him, and a desire on David's part to enjoy His presence always. Therefore he praises Him at all times, in the time of affliction or in the time of ease, declaring that God is the secret of his happiness and joy.

3- Perhaps David realized that the work of the heavenly ones is praise, so he wanted to share with them in praising God, out of longing for eternity and in preparation for it, and enjoying it as a pledge while still on earth.
4- Pleasing God in every work that man does, and not only in the words of praise, is obedience to God and occupation with Him, and this is counted as continual praise throughout the day.
2- My soul shall make her boast in the LORD: the humble shall hear thereof, and be glad.

1- Every person needs to boast in something. The children of God boast in God, but the children of the world boast in themselves, and this leads to pride, or they boast in evil, and so go on further in their sins.
2- Boasting in the Lord gives man confidence in himself, because God is with him, fills his heart with peace, and moves him to bear all responsibilities and to succeed in them.

3- It is easy for the humble man to boast in God and glorify Him at all times, and he feels God's gifts, so he thanks Him and praises Him continually; but God has no need of people's boasting in Him, because He is perfect in Himself.

4- When the humble, who are the gentle and full of peace, hear of the humble David's boasting in God his Savior, they rejoice; for the humble boast in God, and they rejoice when they hear of any person who boasts in God, and they are even stirred and increase in boasting in God and praising Him.
5- Boasting in God and glorifying Him fills the heart with joy, for it feels God's love, and even His being with it, so it holds fast to Him and increases its enjoyment of fellowship with Him.

6- Man boasts in God, but as for himself he boasts in his weaknesses, which lead to the intervention of God, who completes his lack and is glorified in him, as happened with the Apostle Paul (2 Cor 11:30).
3- O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together.

1- When David's heart was occupied with praising God, he felt responsible for others, so he called them to magnify the Lord and praise Him with him, that they might enjoy with him being in His presence.
2- David's call to the children of God to glorify and praise Him shows David's faith in communal worship in the tabernacle of meeting, which signifies the Church of the New Testament.

3- Exalting the name of God is not an addition to His holy name, because He is perfect, but it is a showing forth of His glory and thanksgiving for His kindnesses, so that man enjoys the knowledge of God and delights in fellowship with Him.
4- Magnifying God is accomplished in five stages, which are:
A - In the mind and thought, that is, thinking of God's greatness and His works.
B - In the heart, when man's feelings are moved with love toward God.
C - In speech, with words of praise and thanksgiving.
D - In works, by obeying His commandments, especially in affliction.
E - In calling others to share in glorifying Him.

How beautiful is the praise of God! For when you join with those who praise, you are lifted up to heaven and are with the angels and the saints. So do not deprive yourself of praise every day, even with a small part of the Midnight Praise.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who seek Him

paragraphs.text: 4- I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.

1- David's faith appears when he recalls what confirms his faith, namely the situations in which he sought God and He answered him. Whenever man's faith is confirmed he is encouraged, so he asks of God with confidence at every time, and trusts that God hears him and answers him.

2- God does not answer because people do not ask, or ask with doubt, or ask for bad things, or in their ignorance do not know what is to their advantage, or their good. Indeed the good may be the opposite of what they asked.

3- In affliction Satan fights with doubts and fears within man. So when God answers and rescues man from his enemies, Satan can continue in his casting of doubts, but God's power appeared in driving all these fears out of David's heart.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who seek Him

paragraphs.text: 5- They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed.

1- David turns here from speaking about himself to speaking about the children of God, who seek Him and take refuge in Him in their afflictions, to affirm that he is not the only one who lives with God, but many enjoy fellowship with God.

2- When the children of God ask of Him in affliction, they receive a great blessing, which is their being with God, so their hearts and minds are enlightened, they know God and are filled with peace, and they receive the ability to discern the truth in order to walk in it. This is greater than the removal of the affliction. The affliction may remain for a time, but they will have received spiritual enlightenment.

3- The spiritual enlightenment that those who seek the Lord receive gives them boldness and peace, so they approach with confidence in prayer, and ask and press upon God, and their relationship with Him increases, and God also gives them favor in the eyes of those around them. And in the end He makes them succeed and grow spiritually, so they are not put to shame.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who seek Him

paragraphs.text: 6- This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles.

1- By the poor man David means himself, that is, the humble one who cried to God, and He heard him and answered him, because God loves the humble, and listens to them attentively and answers them quickly.

2- The poor man suffers many afflictions and hardships, but God loves him and hastens to him, and He is able to deliver him from all his hardships, so God is glorified in him, and he thanks God and glorifies Him.

3- Perhaps David, in the spirit of prophecy, speaks of King Hezekiah, the poor man who implored God in humility to rescue him from the hands of Sennacherib, and God heard him and answered him, and sent His angel, who destroyed the army of Sennacherib and rescued his people from his hands.

4- The angels hear David's words and rejoice and support them, because heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents more than over ninety and nine just persons who need no repentance. The angels rejoice over the humble who cry to God, so He hastens to them and rescues them from their enemies. Perhaps David felt that the angels repeat this verse in heaven in joy at the salvation of sinners.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who seek Him

paragraphs.text: 7- The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
1- God cares for those who fear Him, and by this David declared his faith and reliance on God: God cannot leave him, but delivers him from all his afflictions.

2- The demons help the wicked and stir them up against the righteous who fear God; therefore God must support His holy children, so He sends them angels to protect them, and these are stronger than the demons, because they have the power of God with them.

3- God has assigned an angel to everyone who fears Him, and he never leaves him; for he encamps round about those who fear Him, that is, he remains steadfast in guarding the one whom God has charged him to look after, and he alerts him and encourages him in the spiritual life.

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who seek Him

paragraphs.text: 8- O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.

1- Hearing reports about God is not enough; therefore the prophet David calls all who love God to come forward, to gain practical experience in knowing God by tasting His sweetness. Just as talking about honey is not enough to know its sweetness, but it must be tasted, so too God's sweetness is known only by tasting it through prayer and reading.
2- If man tastes God's sweetness he will need to see Him, that is, to contemplate Him, and God reveals to him something new of Himself, and he enjoys new depths in fellowship with Him.

3- Whoever tastes God's sweetness knows the extent of His fatherhood and His power, so he relies on Him and is at rest in His embrace, and enjoys an inexpressible inward peace that encourages him to continue tasting God's sweetness and contemplating Him.

4- This tasting and contemplation continue and grow throughout life, then deepen further upon entering eternity, and there man continues to enjoy tasting God in a new way whose beauty cannot be expressed, so that whoever has experienced it cannot express the extent of its sweetness, like the Apostle Paul, who could only say of God's sweetness in eternity that it is what "eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man" (1 Cor 2:9).

entries.section: (2) Blessings for those who seek Him

paragraphs.text: 9- O fear the LORD, ye his saints: for there is no want to them that fear him.
10- The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing.
Want: need.

1- Why does David ask the saints to fear God and revere Him? Because the saints care about the worship of God, so they know Him and fear Him. This is a call to go deeper in the fear of God as their knowledge of God and their attachment to Him increase, for God reveals to them His greatness and how hard it is to be far from Him, as St. Pachomius, the father of koinonia, desired to see hell, and he saw it, and his hatred of sin increased, and the fear of God also increased in his heart.
2- The saints always look to God, and consequently His fear is established in them, and this moves them to grow in the life of godliness.

3- Whoever looks to God and suffers much in God is satisfied by Him, so he is not exposed to hunger and need. The meaning is not material need, though God provides that for His children, but rather spiritual need; they do not suffer spiritual want, that is, they are constantly satisfied by God.

4- A thirst for righteousness is generated within the children of God who fear Him, for the fear of God purifies them from sin, so their longing for God increases; but this hunger is not accompanied by a sense of deprivation, but on the contrary by a spiritual satisfaction that works in them with constant longings for more and more satisfaction.

5- All creatures are exposed to want and need, even the young lions; for the lion is the king of the forest, yet his young can be in need of food. But whoever seeks God cannot be in need, since God Himself cares for him and provides for his needs.
In summary, God's blessings to those who seek Him are:
1- Deliverance from fears (v. 4).
2- Spiritual enlightenment (v. 5).
3- Freedom from shame (v. 5).
4- He surrounds us with His angels (v. 7).
5- The sweetness of God (v. 8).
6- He supplies our needs (vv. 9, 10). And in order to receive these blessings we must turn to God with the following:
1- We seek (v. 4).
2- We look (v. 5).
3- We humble ourselves (v. 6).
4- We taste (v. 8).
5- We trust (v. 8).
6- We fear (v. 9).

God is very rich, and He is ready to satisfy you from His riches as much as you ask, so do not be distracted from Him by the passing things of this world, or let your requests be only material requests; but seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, that is, let God reign over your heart and satisfy you, that you may enjoy His inexpressible fellowship.
11- Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.
12- What man is he that desireth life, and loveth many days, that he may see good?
1- These two verses show David's concern for the fear of God, which is the entrance to the spiritual life and to all blessings on earth and in heaven.
2- The fear of God is a very important matter and needs to be learned, and we see here David's concern to teach his people this fear, which needs definite exercises in order to acquire it.

3- No one cares to learn the fear of God except His sons and those who love Him, since they are bound to Him and want to feel His awe in order to go deeper in knowing Him; as for those far from God, the matter does not concern them.
4- David calls those who want to learn "children" for the following reasons:
A - It is a word full of love, for the father loves his children and wants them to be in the best condition.
B - The son feels that he is smaller than his father and needs to learn, so he comes to hear and obey what he learns from him.
5- The blessings of acquiring the fear of God are:
A - Acquiring spiritual vitality.
B - The days of his enjoyment of fellowship with God increase.
C - He receives many good things, beginning on earth and extending into eternity in an inexpressible way.

6- The life that man desires is not meant to be life on earth and many days in one's lifetime, because animals, trees and inanimate creatures such as the stars enjoy these. But man is distinguished from all of them in that he receives eternal life, whose days are without number, so the many days are meant to be eternity, and there he enjoys inexpressible good things.
13- Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.
14- Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.

1- To acquire the fear of God one must keep away from evil, whether in speech or in deed: "Keep thy tongue" - "depart" (that is, keep away). For evil blinds man's insight so that he does not see God and does not hear His voice, and the fear of God grows weak in the heart. This calls for keeping away from association with the wicked who cause stumbling.

2- It is also necessary, on the negative side, to keep away from guile, because in it is the twisting of the heart, which appears in deceitful words or works. God does not accept guile and lying, so guile must be rejected in order to acquire the fear of God.

3- On the positive side, doing good establishes the fear of God; for how can I find someone in need and not help him? And what shall I say to God who sees me? One who fears God seeks all works of goodness, as Christ went about everywhere doing good (Acts 10:38).

4- Whoever fears God seeks peace, to be a son of the God of peace, who is Christ our God, who made peace between heaven and earth, and also between the Jews and the Gentiles, and likewise between the spirit and the body.

If only you would seek peace, for it is the most precious gift that you receive from God and offer to those around you, whatever concessions you make, for nothing equals peace. Your right to peace is more precious than all material and moral rights. And in the end the fear of God and His love are established in your heart.
15- The eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry.

1- The eyes of the Lord mean His watching, His care and His concern. And because God is the searcher of hearts and reins, His eyes see the inside of His children, and not only the outside. All this is to supply their spiritual, psychological and bodily needs.

2- God is concerned for and cares for the righteous, because they are His children who obey His commandments, and their good works confirm their sonship to Him. So God gives them special care, more than the rest of mankind.

3- The cry of the righteous quickly reaches the ears of God, that is, God is deeply moved by the needs of His children and their suffering, so He hastens to their aid. And if He is sometimes long-suffering and delays the answer, it is so that their repentance may be completed, and His blessings that He pours out on them may increase, because of their endurance and their love for Him.

4- God leaves man freedom of movement and choice of what suits him, but He watches over him with His eye and listens to his words and his cry, as a mother cares for her child. This shows God's concern for man's freedom, and also His concern for his care, which gives man security.
16- The face of the LORD is against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth.

1- The face of the Lord here means His anger at the wicked and His judgment of their deeds. He is against them and not with them, just as His eyes looked from afar with tenderness, love and care upon the righteous.
2- The wicked's continuing in their evils means that they are walking toward their certain destruction as a result of God's anger against them, for the wages of sin is death.
17- The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.

1- Those are the righteous of whom he spoke in v. 15. When afflictions met them, they cried to God, because they believe that He is their God and their Father, who provides for all their needs and solves all their problems. Crying means severe need, for their only refuge is God.

2- God's hearing the cry of His children means not mere ordinary listening, but concern for their requests and full readiness to rescue them from their troubles and supply all their needs. But it is at the proper time which He sees to be for their good, for He is able to do everything at any time, but He chooses what is most suitable for their spiritual salvation.

3- God rescued His children from all their hardships, because He is able to do everything; but if He postpones rescuing them materially for their benefit, He must rescue them spiritually and psychologically, for He gives them patience, and even comfort and spiritual delight during the affliction, so that His children hardly feel the weariness of the affliction because of the abundance of consolations, in proportion to how much they cry to God and continue to hold fast to Him.
18- The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

1- He tells us in this verse about God's feelings toward His children who cry to Him, and declares His special concern for the humble, and that He is near to them, that is, He feels their troubles and is ready to support them in all that they suffer.

2- The broken-hearted is the one who accepts the afflictions that God allows, and even feels that they are because of his many sins, so he does not murmur or blame God. But he humbles himself before Him, seeking His help, and so receives the overflow of God's mercies.

3- The broken-hearted also accepts God's chastenings, which lead him to repentance and the reform of his life. And by his humility and obedience he fulfills God's plan for his salvation, so God supports him and rejoices in him.

4- The broken-hearted is the servant, the father and the shepherd who is moved by the fall of his beloved ones into sin, so he prays for them and strives that God may remove from them the circumstances that help toward sin. When God sees his prayers, fasts and prostrations (metanoias) for them, He declares that He is very near to him, appreciates his labors, and rewards him for them with countless blessings.

5- God is exceedingly high above all people, so if man exalts himself in his thinking, searching for God and relying on his mind, he feels that God becomes more and more exalted the nearer he approaches Him, until in the end he feels his inability to know God. But if he is crushed in great humility and his heart is broken before God, then God has compassion on him, draws near to him and reveals Himself to him. He is near to the humble who seek Him, and He reveals His secrets to them.

6- The contrite in spirit is the one who gives his life for God. Contrition means that nothing is left to him in himself, for he has been crushed and ground and become dust, and then he receives blessings and a salvation that surpasses the mind. For when he becomes nothing, everything is in God, who fills him and satisfies him and gives him complete salvation. This is the truly humble.
19- Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the LORD delivereth him out of them all.
20- He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken.

1- Afflictions pass over all people, the righteous and the wicked, but they are more upon the righteous, because they are different from the people of the world, so Satan opposes them; but in the end complete happiness awaits the righteous in the Kingdom, while eternal torment awaits the wicked. In addition, there are God's consolations to the righteous during all their afflictions, and His support of them, so they do not grow weary of the afflictions.

2- God delivers the righteous from all afflictions: He removes them from him, ends them, and compensates him with many blessings. In addition, He delivers him during the affliction through his sense that God is with him, so his heart rejoices, as it was with the three youths in the midst of the furnace.

3- The bones are the strongest thing in man, around which the flesh, muscles and skin gather, so they signify the spirit within the body, which believes in God and all His commandments and spiritual principles. Afflictions cannot change or break the faith of the children of God, even if the body is exposed to torments or afflictions.

4- God allows afflictions for His children, and despite their many number He delivers them from them all, and does not allow one of their bones to be broken, so He keeps them in faith in Him, however great their bodily and psychological suffering.
5- This verse was fulfilled in Christ on the Cross, when not a bone of Him was broken, to signify the firmness of His mind, and the salvation that He offers us by His death and resurrection.

6- If Christ is the Head and the Church is His body, then the bones are the believers in Him. God keeps all of these so that they are not broken, but establishes His children in His Church and gives them eternal salvation. This psalm is prayed at the Third Hour, in which the Holy Spirit descended upon the Church, and in this hour it was founded.
21- Evil shall slay the wicked: and they that hate the righteous shall be punished.

1- The sins that man commits harm him first before they harm others, for they tense his nerves and fill his heart with spite, so his blood changes and is filled with poisons that harm his body. And as these sins continue, man is affected and dies because of his evils.
2- If sins affect man in his life on earth, they affect him even more in the other life, for eternal torment awaits him, which is hard to grasp.

3- Also the wicked man, because of his evils, sometimes dies in a hideous way, like the death of Herod and also of King Antiochus, whom worms ate (Acts 12:23; 2 Macc 9:8, 9) while they were alive, and likewise the death of Arius, when his bowels came out of him as he entered the latrine.

4- Although the righteous endures the one who hates him, and God is long-suffering toward these wicked, in the end those who hate the righteous must be punished, because they rejected righteousness, their hearts were filled with hatred, and they were proud, relying on their strength. In the end nothing awaits them but divine punishment in eternal torment, in addition to various earthly punishments, such as the punishment of the Jews who crucified Christ by the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and the killing of huge numbers of them.
22- The LORD redeemeth the soul of his servants: and none of them that trust in him shall be punished.
1- God redeemed His servants who believe in Him by His Incarnation in the fullness of time and His death on the Cross for them.

2- Although the children of God sin and deserve punishment, and the penalty of sin is death, God redeems them by giving them life, while others die because of their persistence in evil, as the children of Israel sinned in Egypt and worshiped idols, so He allowed them to be humiliated in forced labor, but He struck the Egyptians with the ten plagues, and then Pharaoh and all his army were drowned in the Red Sea, while the children of Israel crossed in safety to the wilderness of Sinai. Likewise God redeemed Isaac with a ram because of Abraham's faith and his love for God.

3- Every person who has trusted in God, despite his many sins, God accepts his repentance for the sake of his faith and his reliance on Him, so he is not punished in the other life, but enters the Kingdom of Heaven.
God cares for you throughout your life, so do not be alarmed by afflictions, because they are temporary, and God keeps you during them, supports you and comforts your heart.
God is my Savior from my enemies. By David. "Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author is David the prophet.
2- When he wrote it: when he was suffering from Saul's pursuit of him.
3- This psalm is related to the previous psalm, and was written after it because:
A - Both psalms speak of the angel of God and his work (Ps 34:7; 35:5-6). These two psalms are the only ones among the psalms that speak of the angel of God.
B - The previous psalm speaks of the afflictions of the righteous (ch. 34:19), and in this psalm he explains them in detail.
4- Every section of this psalm ends with hope, so it is an encouraging psalm in the face of the enemies' cruelty.
5- This psalm is an encouragement and support for the children of God in their afflictions; it is fitting for a person to repeat it when he meets an affliction.
6- In this psalm David asks the just God to defend him, but at the same time he bears no hatred toward his enemies.
7- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms that speak of the sufferings that Christ met.
8- Perhaps David, in the spirit of prophecy, felt what Jeremiah would suffer because of his enemies, and expressed that in this psalm (Jer 18:20, 22; 23:12).
9- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 1- Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me: fight against them that fight against me.

1- David asks God to stand as an adversary against his enemies. David feels the strength of the enemies and his own personal weakness, but he trusts in God's power as a fighter and adversary, so that He frightens the enemies and drives them away from David.

2- David's enemy was King Saul with all his power and authority, so David had nothing to do but take refuge in One who is stronger than the king, and he took refuge in God, the King of kings. Our enemy is Satan, and our war is with the spiritual hosts of wickedness; therefore we take refuge in God, who is stronger than all.

3- David did not ask for vengeance on his enemies, but asked only - in his refuge in God - that God stand before him and protect him from the enemies. He does not want the death of the enemies, but that God defend him.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 2- Take hold of shield and buckler, and stand up for mine help.
Shield: a large buckler.

Buckler: a defensive instrument that the soldier held in ancient times to defend himself. It is a rectangular piece of wood with a loop at the back, in which the soldier puts his hand and moves it in front of his head and body, to ward off the enemy's arrows with it.

1- David asks God to go out to war before him, holding a shield and buckler to protect him from the arrows; he wants to hide behind God, and he believes that God's power is able to repel everything from him.

2- He asks God to stand up; and God, of course, is not a man who carries something or rises from place to place, but David means that God should show His power, so that the enemies are afraid. That is, He should frighten the enemies in any way, whether by David or by any other person, and turn the enemies away from him, so that David suffers no harm.

3- What is meant by the buckler is the shield of faith, that is, David's faith in God, so that he is not alarmed by the strength of the enemies, and then God will repel them from him. The weapons are spiritual and not material, and the shield is God Himself, not a material instrument.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 3- Draw out also the spear, and stop the way against them that persecute me: say unto my soul, I am thy salvation.
Draw out: bring out and aim the spear.

1- David asks God to ready His spear to frighten his enemies, and God does not use the spears known among men, but David means the word of God, which exposes the demons, conquers them and frightens them.

2- David also asked God to stop his pursuers, and did not ask for vengeance on them, for he needs God's protection and loves his enemies. Saul fell twice into David's hand, and he let him go and did not harm him, so David is an example of love for enemies.

3- David also asked God to say to him that He is his Savior. He did not ask to obtain salvation, but to hear a word from God, because he believes that the word of God is effective and powerful and must be fulfilled at the proper time. This is evidence of David's faith and reliance on God.

4- David was exposed to many pursuers, the first of whom was Saul, who pursued him for many years and kept pursuing him until Saul died in the war. Likewise the Edomites, the descendants of Esau, used to raid him and fight him, since they lived south of his country, and pursued him, but God used to strengthen him and protect him from them, and even to defeat them before him. Likewise his son Absalom drove him from his throne and tried to kill him. In addition to all the peoples who tried to oppose and pursue him, and also Abner, the commander of Saul's army, who fought him for seven years and afterward was reconciled with him. David was exposed to many pursuers.

5- When did God need a spear to fight with? Only when He needed a body in order to redeem us. This is a symbol of the Incarnation of God in the fullness of time, to save us and die for us on the Cross, and to repel from us the wars of the devil, who pursues us to make us fall into his snares.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 4- Let them be confounded and put to shame that seek after my soul: let them be turned back and brought to confusion that devise my hurt.

1- Because of David's steadfastness in faith, relying on God, his enemies fear him and feel shame because of their weakness and inability to oppose him. These words apply to those who were enemies of David on earth, or to the demons who were fighting him.

2- David also asks that his enemies draw back because of their feeling of weakness before him. All this is based on the appearance of God's power in him to the degree that it frightens the enemies. David does not want to gloat over his enemies, but that God's power appear and be glorified.

3- This verse applies to Christ on the Cross, and at the hour of His arrest, for He asks for the shame of the wicked who oppose Him. Satan was put to shame when Christ bound him by His death on the Cross, and likewise when the Jews tried to arrest Him in the garden of Gethsemane, and He said to them "I am He," and they were afraid, went backward and fell to the ground (Jn 18:6).

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 5- Let them be as chaff before the wind: and let the angel of the LORD chase them.
Chaff: a dry leaf of a plant that the wind can carry because of its lightness.
Chase them: pursue them and defeat those who pursued him.

1- David asks that his pursuers be like chaff before the wind, that is, that their extreme weakness before the power of God appear. The wind signifies the Holy Spirit, and the chaff signifies extreme weakness, that is, that they become as nothing, and in the Hebrew original "splendor."

2- The angel of God shows the power of God, who is able to defeat all the power of men, as the power of God appeared in the angel who killed 185,000 of the army of Sennacherib (2 Chr 32:21), and as the angels surrounded Judas Maccabeus to protect him from the arrows of the enemies, and he defeated them (2 Macc 11:6-8).
3- The angel who defeats the enemies of the children of God is Christ, as He is called the angel of the covenant (Mal 3:1); it is He who defeated the devil and bound him by the Cross.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 6- Let their way be dark and slippery: and let the angel of the LORD persecute them.
Slippery: a road on which the one walking on it slips easily.

1- To show the seriousness of evil, David asks that the way of his pursuers be dark and slippery, so that they cannot see the road, and fall in it, and do not reach their goal, which is to harm the children of God. Here too he does not want vengeance on them, but to hinder them from doing evil. This happened in the plague of darkness upon the Egyptians in the days of Moses (Ex 10:22), and in the angel of the Lord who appeared in the form of a pillar of fire and troubled Pharaoh's army at the Red Sea; but Pharaoh insisted on following the children of Israel, so he and all his army were drowned (Ex 14:19, 24).

2- When the angel of God chases David's pursuers, he prevents them from carrying out their evils, and shows them the power of God, that perhaps they may repent; so David asks for the salvation of their souls and at the same time for his protection from their evils.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 7- For without cause have they hid for me their net in a pit, which without cause they have digged for my soul.
8- Let destruction come upon him at unawares; and let his net that he hath hid catch himself: into that very destruction let him fall.
Catch: entangle.

1- The wicked do evil and wrong the righteous without any cause, that is, the righteous have done nothing to wrong them, but because the nature of the wicked is evil, they incline to evil in all their dealings, and wrong others without cause, and therefore their punishment from God is great.
2- The wicked are hypocrites; they show affection to the righteous, then hide for them plots and calamities to make them fall into them. This confirms their malice and evil.

3- God intervenes and turns the evil so that it comes upon the head of the wicked man who prepares the traps by digging pits and covering them with nets so that the righteous fall into them, but the wicked forget the places of these pits and fall into them themselves. And God turns the evil so that it does not strike the righteous but comes upon the wicked, as Ahithophel tried by his counsel to kill David, though he had formerly been David's counselor; but when Absalom rejected Ahithophel's counsel he was greatly vexed and hanged himself, and died (2 Sam 17:23), while David was kept by God, and neither Absalom nor Ahithophel harmed him. Likewise Absalom tried to kill his father, and he was killed and David escaped (2 Sam 18:15). And Judas Iscariot betrayed Christ to die and then hanged himself (Mt 27:5) and perished, while Christ, after He accomplished redemption on the Cross, rose from the dead. And Satan wanted to kill Christ and bind Him on the Cross, but was surprised that Christ bound him by His death on the Cross, and abolished his authority over the children of God.
4- Just as the wicked man prepares a hidden plot for the destruction of the righteous, so he too is destroyed without knowing it, while the Lord delivers the righteous.

5- The nature of the wicked is to do evil, and the nature of the righteous is to do good; therefore evil comes upon the head of the wicked, and good comes upon the head of the righteous, that is, every person's work returns upon him; perhaps this is a warning to all people, that they may repent of their sins and do good.

entries.section: (1) Taking refuge in the mighty Defender

paragraphs.text: 9- And my soul shall be joyful in the LORD: it shall rejoice in his salvation.
10- All my bones shall say, LORD, who is like unto thee, which deliverest the poor from him that is too strong for him, yea, the poor and the needy from him that spoileth him?

1- The joy of the children of God is in God Himself, and not because He delivered them from the enemy's plots; or it is joy and occupation with God who delivered them, that is, occupation with His Person more than with anything else.
2- The bones represent the inside, that is, man's heart thanks God, and not only his tongue; all of man's members, his feelings, and every pulse within him thank God.

3- The children of God see the wonderful works of God that surpass the mind, so they say to Him, "Who is like unto thee," that is, no one can be found who loves us like You and cares for all the details of our life. God's love was perfected in His death on the Cross for us; this is the greatest love, the like of which is not in the whole earth, and perhaps David, in the spirit of prophecy, saw the redemption of Christ and said, "O God, who is like unto thee."

4- When God intervenes to rescue the poor man, who is the poor and weak one, from the one who dominates him, robs him and exploits him, the poor man feels that he is stronger than all the strong of the world by God's support of him, so he thanks Him and says to Him, "Who is like unto thee." Perhaps this poor and needy man is David, who suffered much from Saul's pursuit of him, where Saul used his authority as king in pursuing David, but God delivered him.
Be at peace as long as God is with you, however much the wicked surround you and threaten you, and even if they are able to wrong you, God will compensate you and lift you up, while they will perish.
11- False witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I knew not.
12- They reward me evil for good to the bereaving of my soul.
Bereaving: loss, or deprivation of children, and here it means humiliation.

1- The servants of Saul rose up and informed against David to King Saul, and questioned him and investigated him concerning what they accused him of, though they were all false accusations, and David tried to convince Saul of his innocence and not to listen to these false witnesses, but Saul in his wickedness continued to pursue David.
2- False witnesses rose up against Christ, and the high priest investigated Him, and could not find any fault in Him.

3- Saul repaid David evil instead of his good; for David used to play music for Saul so that he would be calmed when the evil spirit came upon him, but instead of thanking him, Saul rose up to pursue him and try to kill him. Saul fell twice into David's hand, and he did not harm him, and Saul confessed to David that he was more righteous than he, and said to David, "Thou art more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil" (1 Sam 24:17).

4- David's enemies tried to make his soul bereaved, that is, without children, meaning to humiliate him, kill him, and blot out his name and any offspring of his; but God delivered David, and he lived and reigned over the children of Israel, and even became an example of godliness and righteousness, and from his seed came Christ.
5- The Jews tried to kill Christ and blot out His name, but He rose from the dead, and the Apostles preached Him in the whole world.

6- Perhaps David saw in the spirit of prophecy Christ, who went about everywhere doing good, and the Jews rose up against Him and demanded His crucifixion, and even crucified Him, and repaid Him evil for good.
13- But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth: I humbled my soul with fasting; and my prayer returned into mine own bosom.

1- Although David's enemies tried to kill him, he had done them much good. When they were sick, or in affliction, he prayed and humbled himself for them, and even put on sackcloth, which is rough clothing for humbling oneself before God, and fasted that God might intervene and have mercy on them; perhaps this happened when Saul was afflicted with an evil spirit that came upon him, and David served him to give him rest.

2- David prayed for his enemies, but his prayer returned to his bosom, that is, God rejoiced in David's prayer and blessed him with good, but did not answer his prayer because of the evil of his enemies.
3- The return of the prayer to David's bosom moved his heart to pray again, and so he lived in what is called constant prayer, so that he said of himself, "but I give myself unto prayer" (Ps 109:4).
4- Christ prayed for those who crucified Him while on the Cross, that God would forgive them, but they did not benefit, because of their persistence in evil and unbelief.
14- I behaved myself as though he had been my friend or brother: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother.

1- David continues to explain his feelings toward his enemies whom he loved, and sympathized with in their afflictions and sicknesses; he says that he counted his enemy as his relative or his brother, so he felt his pains, was moved by his sufferings, and prayed for him with all his heart.

2- David's feelings toward his enemy increased, so he counted him as his mother, because the relation of a son to his mother is one of the strongest relations. So he used to weep for his enemy in many prayers and was moved by his condition, like a person weeping over the loss of his mother.

3- David also expresses his sorrows for his enemy, saying that he bowed down with grief, that is, he no longer looked at food and drink and clothing and all the adornment of the world. Indeed his sorrows increased, so he wept and bowed toward the ground, because he was moved by his enemy's suffering. These feelings show the extent of his love for every person, even one who is hostile to him.

4- Christ wept over Jerusalem, which He knew would rise up against Him and crucify Him; so despite the Jews' enmity toward Him He loved them, and wept over them and counted them His brethren (Mk 3:35). David, in his grief for his enemy, signifies Christ's grief over Jerusalem (Mt 23:37).
15- But in my halting they rejoiced and gathered together; they gathered together against me, reviling, and I knew it not; they tore and ceased not.
My halting: halting is limping.

1- David's love grows greater toward his enemies, because they wronged him greatly. When David was suffering his heavy pains he would groan as though limping from their weight; sadly, they gloated over him and rejoiced in his weariness, and this shows that their hearts were filled with evil.
2- David's enemies gathered against him and conspired to wrong him, which is a persistence on their part in evil and a cooperation in wronging him.

3- David's enemies were not content with wronging him in their hearts by rejoicing at his troubles, but went further in their evil, and reviled him when they gathered in his absence, and David did not know at the time, but he learned afterward.

4- David's enemies went still further in their evil, and committed greater wrongs, "they tore," that is, they wronged him and harmed him and continued to harm him, and this means the absence of any pity for David.

5- All that happened with David was a symbol of what happened with Christ when the Jews gloated over Him during His sufferings; they scourged Him, divided His garments, crucified Him naked, and rejoiced at His calamity, while Christ loved them and died for their salvation.
16- Among the profane mockers for the sake of a cake they gnashed upon me with their teeth.
Mockers: plural of a jester, who is one who jokes and scoffs with little shame.
Gnashed with their teeth: ground their teeth (gnashed upon them) out of rage.

1- David shows that his enemies are wicked, going further in their evils, for they wronged him without limits; and he endured for God's sake, because he was innocent, that is, he was wronged and endured.
2- These enemies also mocked him without manners, and directed hard words at him that increased his pains, and he endured and remained holding fast to his faith.

3- These wicked also persisted in their evils and harbored evil toward him, and when the opportunity did not come to them to carry out their wrongs they would be enraged and grind their teeth, and David did not fear them and stood firm in his faith.

4- When God did good to David, providing for him, for example, his needs of food and drink, even if it was little, which is symbolized by a cake, this enraged his enemies, so they gnashed their teeth upon him, since they wanted David to die of hunger and want.
5- What David's enemies did to him was a symbol of what happened with Christ, when the Jews and the Gentiles rose up against Him and wronged Him, and wanted to kill Him, and in the end crucified Him.

When you meet injustice, or wrongs from others, know that your Christ endured more than this for you, and He feels with you and is able to deliver you, so be at peace and ask for His help, and He will support you and comfort you.
17- LORD, how long wilt thou look on? restore my soul from their destructions, my only one from the young lions.

1- David reproaches God and says to Him, why do You look on, that is, watch and see Your son David suffering and being fought by the enemies, and You are silent despite the abundance of the wicked's injustice? He calls to Him to intervene and rescue him from the hands of the wicked. This shows David's faith in God and his boldness with Him.

2- David asks God to restore his soul from the destructions of the wicked, because David beholds every day death and destruction at the hands of the wicked, so he is as good as dead; therefore he asks God to restore his soul, that is, to give him life and bring him out of their hands, and keep them away from him, that he may live and glorify God.

3- David feels that he has one soul that he wants to live for God, and he fears for it from the cruelty of the enemies, whom he likens to wild animals, namely the young lions, which also signify the demons, so he asks God to rescue his soul from all evil, that he may stand firm in his faith and his life with God.

4- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom the Jews rose up and whom they tried to kill many times, so He asks the Father to rescue His only one, that is, His soul that is different from the rest of the souls; for after He died on the Cross, Satan tried to seize His soul, but was surprised that Christ had seized him and bound him so that he would not harm His children for whom He died. And Christ descended to Hades and brought up Adam and his sons to Paradise. Christ alone is able to overcome Satan and deliver His children from him, and the Father preserved His soul because the divinity is united with the human spirit, so He descended to Hades and ascended with His children who believe in Him.
18- I will give thee thanks in the great congregation: I will praise thee among much people.

1- David feels his oneness with the rest of the believers of the people of God, so he praises God and thanks Him with the rest of his people, and this establishes and builds up his faith, because communal praise strengthens the soul.

2- Any blessing that one of the people of God receives gladdens the rest of the people, because they are all members of one body, which is the Church, and when one praises, the whole congregation rejoices; thanksgiving from one affects the rest and gladdens and encourages them, so that they too rise up and praise God.

3- David's praise not only makes him feel his fellowship with the rest of his people, and makes his people feel him, but by praise he also joins a great people, not only on earth but also in heaven, namely the angels who praise God at all times.

4- David's praise of God in the midst of the congregation shows David's faith and his boasting in glorifying the name of God; this not only encourages others to praise, but becomes a cause for receiving many blessings from God for the sake of his faith.
5- The great congregation and the mighty people are a symbol of the entry of the Gentiles into the faith, and this is what happened in the Church of the New Testament, so that all praised God.

19- Let not them that are mine enemies wrongfully rejoice over me: neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause. 20- For they speak not peace: but they devise deceitful matters against them that are quiet in the land.
21- Yea, they opened their mouth wide against me, and said, Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it.
Opened wide: opened their mouths in contempt and mockery.
Aha: an expression indicating mockery.

1- David asks God to rescue him from his enemies, so that they may not gloat over him by achieving their purposes and their injustice to him. What is meant is not only the earthly enemies, but even more the demons.

2- The words of the verse (v. 19) were spoken by Christ Himself when He said, "But this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause" (Jn 15:25). So this verse is a clear prophecy of what happened in Christ.

3- David also asked God to stop the hypocrisy and deceit of the enemies, who treated him with outward love but harbored evil toward him. So after acting out a deceitful love they wink with their eyes at one another, confirming their evil and their spite toward David.
4- David's enemies want evil, and to create disturbances and anxiety, and they use every deceit or craft to achieve their aims, and they rejoice in harming the quiet and peaceful, like David.

5- David's enemies express their hatred of him by mockery, ridicule and contempt, especially when they succeed in wronging him in any way. All this injustice David places before God to move Him to compassion, that He may deliver him from the hands of his enemies.

6- The wicked used all their abilities for evil; they used their tongues, their thoughts, their mouths, their eyes and their hearts, and this means their being filled with evil and their complete subjection to Satan.
7- These three verses apply to Christ, whom they mocked and insulted during His sufferings and crucifixion, and He endured all this out of love for us.

22- This thou hast seen, O LORD: keep not silence: O Lord, be not far from me. 23- Stir up thyself, and awake to my judgment, even unto my cause, my God and my Lord. 24- Judge me, O LORD my God, according to thy righteousness; and let them not rejoice over me.
25- Let them not say in their hearts, Ah, so would we have it: let them not say, We have swallowed him up.

1- As David calls God to witness all the injustice that has befallen him, he implores Him not to be silent and not to be long-suffering any longer, because David is weary and needs God's swift intervention to rescue him. This shows the extent of David's suffering, and also the extent of his trust in God and his reliance on Him.

2- The mighty David was able to turn the wrongs of others toward him into prayers and supplications to God, so he did not become angry with them or condemn them, but took refuge in God, and his love for Him increased.

3- David trusts in God's power, but he sees God silent as though asleep, or heedless and not attentive to what is happening with David, so he presses Him to intervene. Here appears the importance of persistence in prayer - which God loves - because it is evidence of David's clinging to God alone to rescue him.

4- David walks in uprightness, and his enemies wrong him; therefore he asks for God's justice, that God may judge and rule on his requests so as to remove the injustice from him. And everyone who walks in uprightness is a person who fears God and asks for God's intervention, and He rescues him and glorifies him.

5- David also asks God to stop the mockery ("Aha") and the gloating of the enemies over him, because they thought they had deprived him of all ability, and fulfilled their desire by taking vengeance on him, so that he became like one dead in their sight, as though they had swallowed him; but despite David's apparent weakness before people, his heart was still strong, steadfast in the faith that God would intervene and rescue him.

6- The Jews thought that they had got rid of Christ by His crucifixion and death, but David - in the spirit of prophecy - calls Christ to awake and rise from the dead, so that the demons see that His life was not swallowed up by death, but on the contrary He trampled death, and rose to give new life to all who believe in Him.
26- Let them be ashamed and brought to confusion together that rejoice at mine hurt: let them be clothed with shame and dishonour that magnify themselves against me.

1- God intervenes when David prays, and his enemies who gloat over him are turned to shame, because they see God's rescuing him and honoring him. And God allows them this shame as a chastening, that they may repent and know that God supports the righteous and shames the wicked.
2- Shame and confusion cover the proud also, for pride is one of the chief characteristics of the wicked, while the humble God gives His peace and His joy.
27- Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the LORD be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant.
1- David implores God to gladden the hearts of the righteous, who wish for David's deliverance from his enemies, and then they glorify God and praise Him.

2- This verse applies to Christ, who was in the form of shame when they insulted Him and crucified Him, and because He emptied Himself and became like a servant; but by His resurrection He declared His divinity and authority, and everyone who believed rejoiced in Him and enjoyed the blessings of salvation.
28- And my tongue shall speak of thy righteousness and of thy praise all the day long.
1- In the end, before the great works of God which David believed that God does with him, he thanked God and praised Him, and even kept praising Him all day long, that is, throughout his life.
2- By the constant praise that extends all day long David means continuing in praise forever, where the day does not end in eternity, so that man lives in eternal joy.

3- The stars praise God at all times without speaking, by their work, and so also man can praise throughout his life on earth, not only with words of praise, but by his faithfulness in the works he does for God's sake.

4- As long as man's life has become praise, God in His fatherhood embraces him, defends him, and stands before his adversaries, that is, the demons and everyone who walks in evil, following the demons.

He that endureth to the end shall be saved; therefore continue in your prayers with persistence, confident of God's power, and He will reveal Himself to you and deliver you from all evil, and you will praise Him continually.
The works of the wicked and God's blessings to His children. To the chief Musician. By David the servant of the LORD. "The utterance of the transgression of the wicked" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

1- Its author: David the prophet, who describes himself in the title as the servant of the Lord, and this means that the writer writes with authority from God, because he is His servant and near to Him, so he understands Him. The description "servant of the Lord" is repeated only in the eighteenth psalm.
2- The psalm speaks of the characteristics of the wicked, meaning by this the wicked in general, and it may mean Saul specifically, because he did many evils against David.
3- When it was written: David wrote it when he was being driven out by King Saul, or by Absalom.

4- This psalm is divided into two parts, each the counterpart of the other; the first part is the first four verses, and it speaks of the wicked and their characteristics. The second part contains the rest of the psalm, and speaks of the characteristics of God, who is just, the Shepherd of His children, and the tender Father to whom His children make request, and He cares for them.

5- This psalm establishes the faith of the children of God, for it lifts them up to contemplate His attributes, so they are not alarmed however much the wicked surround them, and they keep away from the wicked and hold fast to their life with God.
6- This psalm is not found among the psalms in the Agpeya.
1- The utterance of the transgression of the wicked is within my heart: that there is no fear of God before his eyes.
The utterance: a groaning, or a sigh, or an aching in the heart.
1- David's heart aches when he looks at the sins of the wicked, which all result from their neglect of the fear of God; for since they do not fear Him, they rush easily into any sin.

2- When the wicked neglect the fear of God they fall into the fear of men, so they care for the outward appearance of their lives, while their insides are evil; that is, they become hypocrites and pretenders.
3- Because the wicked do not fear God, they neglect His commandments, and this makes it easy for them to fall into sin.

4- David's fatherhood appears in this verse; not only toward his obedient, righteous children, but also his fatherhood toward the wicked, so his heart aches for them, and he longs that they return to God, that they may fear Him and keep away from every sin.
2- For he flattereth himself to himself concerning the finding out of his iniquity and the hating of it.
He flattereth himself: that is, he deceives himself and honors himself beyond what he deserves.

1- One of the characteristics of the wicked is that he is deceitful; he deceives others, but the harder thing is that he deceives even himself, deluding himself that he is upright and behaves well, and consequently he keeps entirely away from repentance, since he does not feel his sin; so how can he repent of it?
2- The wicked man flatters himself because of his pride; he does not want to imagine the truth, nor does he accept it, for his pride is built on delusions with which he has deceived himself.

3- The wicked man justifies to himself the evils and iniquities he commits, and likewise his hatred of others, so he imagines that his iniquities are not evil, and pictures to himself that his hatred of others is merely not feeling at ease with them, and that the others are the cause of that.
4- The wicked man also deludes himself that he hates evil and loves what is upright, and by this he finds in himself no sin or hatred to repent of.

5- The wicked man begins by justifying himself in small sins, then justifies himself in greater sins, until he does the greatest evils without realizing it, because he is far from repentance; thus he does not hate his iniquity, because he does not feel it.
3- The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit: he hath left off to be wise, and to do good.

1- The wicked man has made deceit permissible, and as he continued deceiving himself and deceiving others, he believed the evil he says, so he moved away from the truth and from wisdom, and lost discernment.
2- The wicked man's departing from wisdom is by his own will, because he deceived himself and so kept it far from understanding and upright conduct.

3- If the wicked man is immersed in his sins and departs from wisdom, he departs from everything good and from helping others, because he does not feel for them; so how can he help them or do good with them? He is selfish, occupied with himself and his pride, and consequently he loses God's mercy and the love of others for him.
4- The wicked man's continuing in deceit will stop the work of the Holy Spirit in him, so his heart will not be convicted, nor will he repent of his sins, and he remains far from God.
4- He deviseth iniquity upon his bed; he standeth in a way that is not good; he refuseth not evil.
1- When the wicked man enters the place where he will sleep, instead of examining himself and repenting like the rest of mankind, he thinks about evil, so he remains deceived and far from God.

2- Since the wicked man has lost his discernment, he no longer keeps away from evil, but on the contrary stands in the way of evil and sits in the seat of the scornful and the sinners, and consequently goes further in his sins and remains in his error.

3- Because of the wicked man's great deceiving of himself, and his words full of iniquity and deceit, he loses his ability to resist evil, so he falls easily into any sin, and thus becomes a slave of Satan, who controls him as he sees fit.
4- The wicked man in secret thinks about evil, so he surrenders to it inwardly, and it becomes easy for him to do wicked deeds by day, because he is premeditating the doing of evil.

5- The wicked deeds that the wicked man does lead him to think about evil when he lies down to sleep. Man reaps at night the fruit of his deeds during the day. But for the righteous the night is an opportunity for repentance, prayer and praise.

Look at the hideousness of your sins and their effects on you, that you may reject them by repentance and take refuge in God in the sacrament of confession, that He may forgive them for you and cleanse you, and you come out with a new nature inclined to the love of God and of others.
5- Thy mercy, O LORD, is in the heavens; and thy faithfulness reacheth unto the clouds.

1- God's mercy is great and cannot be measured because it is in heaven; it is unlimited, and man cannot enumerate it. Therefore man's heart is reassured that however many his sins, God's mercies are wider and cover them.

2- God's mercies are higher than the thoughts of men, for He seeks the salvation of their souls, and not merely the supplying of their material needs; therefore mercy may allow the chastening of the children of God for a time, until they return to Him.

3- God's mercies and faithfulness are higher than man's understanding, and they are hidden in the clouds; therefore it is fitting for man to believe in God and submit to Him, and let Him give him the blessings in their season.

4- God's faithfulness is in His promises to mankind. Just as He promised Noah not to destroy the world again with a flood by the appearance of the sign of the rainbow in the sky when the sky rains heavily, so too God's promises are many, protecting His children and reassuring them, for God wants all to be saved, and seeks all sinners that they may repent.
5- God's mercy is in those who walk a heavenly walk, for it is in the heavens, that is, in the saints and the heavenly children of God in their life on earth.
6- Thy justice is like the mountains of God; thy judgments are a great deep: O LORD, thou savest man and beast.

1- God's justice is firm and strong like a mountain; it does not waver or change like the justice of men, that is, God's principles are fixed, and He cannot be deceived, and He is the searcher of hearts and reins. This reassures the righteous, frightens the wicked, and calls all of us to repentance.
2- God's judgments and commandments are very deep like the depths of the sea, and everyone who contemplates them is satisfied and rejoices and lives by them, and so tastes the Kingdom while on earth.
3- God's judgments do not conflict with His justice, for He has mercy on sinners and is long-suffering toward them until they repent, so they are not punished by divine justice.
4- God's judgments and commandments are too deep for man to understand; he grasps only a little of them, and the solution is to submit to them and let God order our lives by His good will.

5- God's deep judgments, like the deep sea, testify to His greatness, for He is unlimited in His wisdom; therefore how beautiful it is for man to keep God's commandments and repeat them, so that they become a source of blessings and constant satisfaction for his soul.

6- God in His love cares for His children, and likewise for the rest of the creatures for their sake, so He saves, that is, He cares for the beasts, the plants and all creatures for the sake of man. God cares for His children and for the whole world for their sake.
7- How precious is thy mercy, O God! therefore the children of men take refuge under the shadow of thy wings.

1- God's mercy is greater than any other mercy, because His mercy is unlimited, generous in its giving, and suits every person; for it is that which created man, so it understands him, and is able to cover all mankind, especially as the word "God" means the God of the whole world, and not only the children of Israel, who mostly use the word "LORD."
2- Because God's mercy is wide and distinguished, all the children of men take refuge in it, to protect them from every evil, forgive them their sins, and care for all their needs.
3- What is meant by the children of men are the believers in God, who seek God and trust in His protection.

4- God's wings represent protection; as the hen protects her chicks under her wings, and as the two cherubim cover with their wings the cover of the Ark of the Covenant, which is called the mercy seat; the two wings signify God's fatherhood, His care and His love for the children of men, and they also signify the Old and New Testaments.
8- They are satisfied with the fatness of thy house, and thou givest them drink from the river of thy pleasures.

1- God's care appears in His concern for the needs of His children; He satisfies them and feeds them, not only with material food and drink but rather with the spiritual; for they hunger and thirst after righteousness, and they are satisfied with His unlimited love.
2- God feeds His children generously; He does not give them ordinary food, but rich food, which makes them need nothing of all that is in the world.

3- The house of God is the Church, and its fatness is its holy sacraments, which surpass the mind. David, in the spirit of prophecy, sees the Church of the New Testament and union with God through its sacraments.
4- The river of grace is the Holy Spirit, who works in the being of those who believe in Him through the sacraments, the means of grace and the manifold gifts, and so waters all.
5- The river of grace signifies the water and the blood that came out of the side of Christ on the Cross, to water all who believe in Him.
9- For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.

1- The Holy Trinity appears in this verse: in his saying "with thee," that is, the Father, and "the fountain of life" is the Son, and "the light" is the Holy Spirit. God in His three hypostases cares for the man who believes in Him.
2- The light also signifies the word of God, which enlightens the eyes of our hearts amid the error and evil of the world.

3- The light of God signifies the Incarnation of Christ, by whom we see the light, that is, the Father; for "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (Jn 1:18). We see this verse repeated in the New Testament in speaking of Christ, "In him was life; and the life was the light of men" (Jn 1:4).
10- O continue thy mercy unto them that know thee; and thy justice to the upright in heart.

1- Those who know God believe in Him, and know that He is righteous and holy, so they repent of their sins before His holiness, and as they humble themselves God pours out on them His forgiveness and mercies.

2- When God continues His mercy to those who know Him, this helps them to grow in the knowledge of God and to hold fast to Him, so God's mercies upon them increase, and thus God's mercy leads to spiritual growth. And when man grows He pours out on him more mercies.

3- God's mercies cover all mankind, like His sun that shines on the righteous and the wicked, and His air, and His water ... but those who know God take notice, appreciate these mercies and thank the Lord for them; therefore God's mercies continue upon them and become more varied than for those who do not appreciate these mercies.

4- Whoever walks in uprightness wishes that God's justice would prevail, so that evil may not increase, but that all may know that the upright is rewarded and the wicked is punished. Justice does right by the upright and blesses them.

5- The upright in heart is a person who believed in God, relied on Him and kept His commandments, and consequently accepts His will and does not murmur at any affliction; therefore divine justice does right by him and rewards him.
11- Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the wicked remove me.
12- There are the workers of iniquity fallen: they are cast down, and shall not be able to rise.
1- David, who walks in uprightness and lives with God, wishes that the proud Satan would not attack him and make him walk in the way of pride; therefore he said "the foot of pride."

2- As long as David walks in the way of goodness and lives with God, he asks that the hand of Satan, that is, the works of the wicked, be kept away from him, so that he is not moved from his upright way and the doing of good.

3- David asks that he not walk by his own will, that is, with his foot, in the way of weeping, and that outward wars not be extended to him, that is, the hand of the wicked, to remove him from God's way.

4- Whoever does not humble himself and walks in the way of pride, or responds to the works of the wicked, will fall into sin and be separated from God, as Adam did in the garden of Eden when he wanted to become like God.

5- If man continues in the way of pride and wicked deeds, the devil will triumph over him, and his end will be destruction and eternal torment, where he falls and cannot rise. What is meant by the word "there" is that far from God is the fall, and then eternal torment.

Endure the labors of keeping the commandment so as to walk in uprightness, and then God's mercies will pour out upon you, and His justice will keep you to a happy eternal life, and you will escape all the devil's plots.
The recompense of the righteous and the wicked. By David. "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.
2- When it was written: in the last part of David's life, that is, about three years before his death, for it carries the sum of his experience of God's dealing with the righteous and the wicked.
3- It encourages the righteous in any afflictions that meet them, so that they are not troubled by the temporary success of the wicked.
4- It is one of the Messianic psalms, for it speaks of Christ and the blessings of the Church of the New Testament.
5- This psalm is didactic, for it is full of counsels, and resembles Psalms (73, 94), and also resembles the books of Job, Proverbs and Jesus son of Sirach.

6- This psalm is arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, meaning that every verse, or two verses, begins with one of the letters of the alphabet, and the forty verses fall under twenty-two Hebrew letters. This is the third of the psalms arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet.
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.
2- For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb.

1- These are the first two counsels that David gives to the children of God, that they may stand firm in the upright faith, and they are the first of the eight counsels that he sets out in this passage. He counsels the righteous not to be dazzled by the temporary success of the wicked, and not to fall into jealousy and envy.

2- Jealousy and envy are two sins into which the prophet David warns us not to fall, whether toward the wicked or toward any person, because they show that we are not content and satisfied with God, and also our lack of love for the others whom we envy.

3- The success of the wicked is temporary, and he likens them to grass or green herb, which grows quickly in the ground, then dries up and vanishes before the heat of the sun. But the righteous the Holy Bible likens to the palm tree with deep roots, which flourishes and blossoms, and to the trees of Lebanon, and all strong trees with a deep root (Ps 92:13).

4- The success of the wicked does not last long, and even if it continues throughout life, it ends on the Day of Judgment, where there is no rest for them but torment, for the hypocrites will not stand in the judgment (Ps 1:5).

5- The material success of the wicked is accompanied by turmoil in the heart, so they cannot have inward peace, as the prophet Isaiah said, "There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22).
6- The likening of the wicked and those occupied with the world to grass and herb is used in the Holy Bible in both Testaments (Isa 40:6-8; Jas 1:11).
3- Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and feed on faithfulness.

1- The third counsel is reliance on God. Whoever believes in God knows that He has perfect power and unlimited love, and consequently He is the only One on whom man relies with all confidence, and so receives rest and peace.

2- Whoever keeps away from attachment to the material things of the earth and the success of the wicked, so that he neither envies them nor is jealous of them, finds it easy to fix his gaze on God, so he sees His beauty and power and relies on Him.

3- If man clings to God and relies on Him, he becomes positive, and so he is able to carry out the fourth counsel, which is doing good. For whoever loves God and relies on Him is able to love people and strive to serve them.

4- If man is occupied with doing good, God helps him, so he feels God's love and care, and increases in doing good, and thus grows in the love of others; for he is gradually freed from his selfishness, and becomes a flame of love that lights and warms the whole world.

5- The natural result that the one who keeps away from jealousy and envy, relies on God, and is open in love toward others receives is that God grants him settlement in the land, so that he dwells in it, but on condition that he carries out the fifth counsel, which is faithfulness in all his works on earth and his dealings with others, so that he is settled in his life and works, and is faithful in cultivating the land or fulfilling his duties toward others, and God is pleased with him and blesses him.

6- Dwelling in the land may mean - as St. Jerome said - dwelling in the land of the living, that is, the Church, so that he is nourished by its holy sacraments and the means of grace, on condition of faithfulness in carrying out God's commandments.

7- Dwelling in the land can also mean dwelling in eternity, that is, receiving the eternal inheritance for those who were faithful in their life on earth; for the one who is faithful over a few things, that is, his earthly life, God makes ruler over many things, that is, his eternal life (Mt 25:21).
4- Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.

1- The sixth result is delighting, rejoicing and enjoying God, and it is built on the previous counsels; for whoever lives in fellowship with God and relies on Him, does good and is faithful in everything, God's mercies and gifts pour out upon him, so he thanks God and rejoices in fellowship with Him. What is meant by joy and delight is that man be aware of God's gifts, and look at His beloved Person, so that he rejoices in Him, that is, rejoices in being with God and enjoys His gifts.

2- We notice here in this counsel that David moves us from delighting in God's gifts and relying on Him to discovering God's beauty and contemplating Him, and this is the true joy and complete delight.

3- The result of rejoicing in fellowship with God is that God gives those who love Him the desires of their hearts, and he says here the desires of the heart, and not the requests of the mouth, that is, what man wishes, even if he does not utter it. The wishes of the heart are deeper than the wishes of the lips, but God, the rich and generous Giver, gives His children the desire of their hearts. The Apostle Paul asked for healing from the thorn in the flesh, that he might be able to serve God with all freedom, and God did not answer his request for healing, but He gave him the desire of his heart, so he preached more than all the Apostles, and wrote more books of the Holy Bible than all.
5- Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
6- And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy right as the noonday.

1- Here he confirms the third counsel, which is reliance on God and committing life to Him, so that God Himself leads man's way, guides him in all his steps, and protects him from stumbling, until He brings him to the Kingdom.

2- When man believes in God and commits his life to Him, God brings all his affairs to pass uprightly; that is, He works in his life, so he is able to carry out God's commandments, behaves well, and feels God's being with him, so his heart rejoices in God's companionship throughout his life.

3- The wicked are troubled by the righteousness of the righteous, so they fight him, accuse him falsely, and wrong him with bad words, and the righteous endures all this for God's sake, and then God intervenes, and the righteousness of the righteous appears like the light after the darkness of the bad words that the wicked said about him; that is, God - on whom the righteous relied - declares, "This is my son, and I am with him," and this divine glorification is a pledge of the glory of the Kingdom of Heaven.

4- If the wicked take away the right of the righteous, whether his material rights or his dignity, God intervenes after this and declares his right, and blesses him with many blessings that are strong, as the rays of the sun are strong at noonday. God rewards the righteous for his endurance, as He appeared to the righteous Abraham, who left everything for His sake, and that at noonday, and was host to God with the two angels (Gen 18:1), and as Joseph honored his brothers with a delicious meal at noonday, showing them his love (Gen 43:16), and as Christ declared His perfect love for mankind when He was hung on the Cross to redeem them at noonday (Lk 23:33, 44).
7- Wait for the LORD and be patient for him, and fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.

1- The seventh counsel is patience. When afflictions follow one another and the wicked man goes further in his wrongs toward the righteous, the righteous grows weary, but God counsels him through David's mouth to be patient and wait for God's salvation; for God watches everything, and will surely intervene and reward the righteous, and indeed during the affliction He supports him, giving him peace and establishing him in the upright way.

2- In order for the righteous to be able to be patient he must hold fast to God's commandments and promises, so that he is not shaken by Satan's casting of doubts upon him, and does not fret over the success of the wicked, because they do evil and plots in order to achieve their successes.
3- In order for man to be able to be patient he needs divine help, so he lifts up his heart in prayer at all times to receive help at every time, and his heart is comforted during the affliction.
