4- Patience means that man accepts afflictions with contentment and thanksgiving and does not murmur. The word "be patient" in the Hebrew original means "be silent and do not murmur," so God rejoices in his faith and steadfastness and rewards him for his patience.

5- Whoever waits for the Lord does not set Him a time to intervene in his life, but trusts in God's wisdom and only waits for Him, as Judith declared to the people of her city and reproached them that they had not been patient for God, confident of His salvation; and because of her faith God intervened and rescued her country from the enemies by her killing Holofernes, the commander of the armies of the Assyrians (Jdt 8:11-14).
8- Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil.

1- The eighth and last counsel is not to be angry; for anger means murmuring against God and against people, in addition to wronging others and man's losing his peace, so he is far from God and cannot pray with purity, and loses his fellowship with God.

2- If man is lax with the sin of anger it increases and turns into severe anger, which is wrath, and if man does not restrain himself from wrath it turns into the doing of evil, like the rest of the wicked. Therefore the sin must be cut off at its beginning, which is the thought of anger.

3- God gave man His commandments and promised to help him fulfill them however heavy they may seem, so why should man be angry and not continue his striving? God did not promise us the easy way and the wide gate, and therefore we should accept afflictions and not be angry.
9- For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth.
10- For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be.
11- But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.

1- The wicked are cut off from before God, that is, their occupation with material things and the doing of evils is temporary, and after a little while they are not, that is, their life on earth ends, and they are removed far from God and cast into eternal torment.

2- The righteous inherit the earth, and David repeats the inheriting of the earth in this psalm six times. What is meant by the earth - as we said - is the Promised Land, that is, the land of Canaan, and likewise the righteous enjoy their life on earth because God is with them and blesses them.

3- The earth is also meant to be the Church of the New Testament, the land of the living, where the believers receive the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace, and enjoy even more fellowship with God.
4- The earth is also meant to be the new earth, or the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the eternal inheritance, so the believers remain in fellowship with God and enjoy seeing Him in the Kingdom.

5- The meek are those who live with God, so He gives them His inward peace, and they are not troubled by any material gain or loss. This peace is abundant in their hearts, and increases in the Church of the New Testament, then is completed in the Kingdom of Heaven, where it is abundant without limits, that is, they live in peace forever.
6- The meek are the righteous who meet many afflictions and endure them for God's sake, so He gives them His inward peace, and they are approved before Him, and He also gives them eternal life.

7- The abundance of peace is for the meek however much afflictions surround them, because the unlimited God is the source of peace, and He gives it generously to His children. And peace increases as they grow spiritually, until it is completed in the Kingdom.

The way of righteousness is the way of happiness, so hold fast to it and keep God's commandments, and you will receive His blessings, and even possess God in your heart and taste the Kingdom while you are on earth, and then you will make light of afflictions and not be troubled by them.
12- The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth.

1- The wicked man has plotted evil against the righteous since the beginning of creation; this is what Satan did with Adam and Eve, then made them fall, and Cain did with Abel, and it continues until now.

2- If the wicked man fails to harm the righteous he is enraged, so he gnashes on him with his teeth, that is, grinds his teeth in rage, because the righteous held fast to God and His commandments, and so escaped from the hand of the devil.

3- These evils that the wicked man stirs up against the righteous are temporary in this life, but God removes them from the righteous for many periods, and then removes them completely in the Kingdom of Heaven.
13- The LORD laugheth at him: for he seeth that his day is coming!

1- The Lord laughs at the wicked man who devises conspiracies against the righteous, trusts in his power and wrongs others, because all this is temporary and will soon end with the end of his life, and also the Lord can end him by exposing his plans and protecting the righteous from him. God is stronger than the wicked man, but He is long-suffering toward him, that perhaps he may repent.

2- As the wicked man laughs at the righteous and harms him, or tries to harm him, God laughs at the wicked man and stops his evil, and even ends his life, so he goes to eternal torment; as the wicked man does, so it is done to him. What is meant by these words is that every person should take heed and not do evil.

3- The coming day is the Day of Judgment, where the wicked man is judged for every evil thought, word or deed; therefore the righteous who fears God and remembers the judgment keeps away from evil and keeps God's commandments.
14- The wicked have drawn out the sword, and have bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy, to slay the upright in their way.
The upright in their way: those who walk in the upright way of the Lord.

1- The sword and the bow are two instruments of war that show the conspiracies of the wicked against the poor righteous man, who is without weapon. This shows the extent of the wicked's injustice and cruelty, and their exploiting the righteous man's material weakness, so they conspire against him.

2- The sword represents the visible instrument of war with which the wicked man attacks the poor man, and the bow represents the hidden instrument of war with which the wicked man throws arrows from afar, and they strike the poor man; the wicked man uses all wicked means to destroy the poor man. Therefore their punishment from God is severe.

3- The righteousness of the children of God provokes and exposes the evil of the wicked, so instead of repenting and returning to uprightness they are enraged, and attack the righteous to get rid of him, so that their evil is not exposed by his holiness.

4- The wonder is that God returns the evils of the wicked upon their heads, so He protects the righteous, and the conspiracies return upon the wicked, so their swords strike their hearts, that is, destroy them, and if they remain alive their hearts are tormented by evil. And God shows the weakness of their bows, so they are broken, that is, their conspiracies fail. God means by this to establish the righteous in their faith and to call the wicked to repentance; but whoever does not repent, his evil harms him, as Haman perished and was hanged on the gallows on which he wanted to hang Mordecai (Esth 7:10), and as King Saul perished in the war, he who wanted to destroy David (1 Sam 31:4), and as Absalom perished and died in the war, having wanted to destroy his father David (2 Sam 18:15).
16- A little that a righteous man hath is better than the riches of many wicked.
17- For the arms of the wicked shall be broken: but the LORD upholdeth the righteous.
Arms: plural of forearm, which is the arm.
Upholdeth: supports and strengthens, that is, the one who strengthens man's upper arm, which is his arm.

1- Although the righteous man possesses little, yet by God's blessing it suffices him and overflows; but as for the wicked man, however great his wealth, he does not benefit from it, but his heart remains troubled and he does not enjoy his life.

2- The power of the wicked is temporary, and their arms are broken, that is, they are unable to work, whether during their life on earth or by the end of this life, so they find no rest in eternity, because they are cast into eternal torment.

3- God upholds and supports the righteous; therefore their power is mighty and without limit, because it is from God Himself, so no one can overcome them as long as they are with God, as Pharaoh and his mighty army were broken before the children of Israel by the ten plagues, and then by drowning in the Red Sea.

4- God supports His children, not only in this life, that they may stand firm in faith in Him and keep His commandments, but He supports them forever in the Kingdom, where He lets them enjoy His great glory.
18- The LORD knoweth the days of the perfect: and their inheritance shall be for ever.
19- They shall not be ashamed in the evil time: and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied.
The perfect: the complete ones.

1- The perfect are those who loved God, and realize that they are the image of God and His likeness, so they imitate Him in His perfection, in spiritual striving, rising above material things and honor, and occupied with being with God and doing good with every person.

2- God knows everything, so why does he mention here that He knows the days of the perfect? What is meant is that He is concerned with caring for the days of the perfect, that is, He looks after the life of His children who strive on the way of perfection, for He loves them because they imitate Him.

3- God knows the days of the perfect, that is, He notices their striving and their labor on the way of perfection, and prepares for them a great place in the Kingdom, to compensate them in it for their labors on earth. This is the eternal inheritance.

4- God cares for His perfect children during afflictions, which are the days of evil and famine, and it is not necessary that He remove the affliction from them, but He is able to keep them within the affliction, as He kept Elijah during the famine (1 Kgs 17:4, 9).

5- During the days of evil and famine God satisfies His children spiritually, so they are not troubled by the lack of food or the pressures of life, though these pass over them, but their occupation with God gives them peace and rest, so they pass through the affliction quietly.
20- But the wicked shall perish, and the enemies of the LORD shall be as the splendor of the pastures: they are consumed; like smoke they are consumed.

1- The wicked are the enemies of God, who keep away from His commandments because of their occupation with doing evil. Because they are separated from God and hold fast to evil, their end must be destruction.

2- He likens the wicked to herbs that grow quickly and dry up and wither quickly too. They represent the superficial life, and have no fruit, therefore they quickly perish, and have no enjoyment of God, even if their life on earth is long; but in eternity they perish, that is, their material enjoyment ends with the end of dominion, and then they are in torment forever.
3- He also likens the wicked to smoke; for although the fire appears great, it too goes out, and leaves nothing but the smoke that rises up and fills a large space, then scatters and vanishes.

4- Even if the wicked are found in the pastures, which signify the churches, they are merely herbage that quickly perishes because their life is superficial; but the pastures are filled with flocks of cattle, that is, the churches are filled with their children who are full of spiritual richness and enjoy fellowship with God.
21- The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous is compassionate and giveth.

1- The wicked man is greedy; he is not content with what he has and borrows from those around him to satisfy his lusts, but because God's blessing is not with him he remains needy and is unable to repay what he borrowed, so he constantly feels deprivation, in addition to troubling those around him, for he takes from them and does not give to them, and this is what God's law declared by the hand of Moses (Deut 28:44).

2- The wicked man has taken much from God, but he does not pay what he owes God, so he neither thanks God nor helps others; he always wants to take and not give, because he is selfish and refuses to do good.

3- King Saul made use of David in killing Goliath, and as a military commander who defended his country against the Philistines, his enemies, but Saul did not thank him, but pursued him and tried to kill him throughout his life, until Saul died. Likewise Judas Iscariot took much from Christ and gave Him nothing in return, but on the contrary sold Him to the Jews for pieces of silver, and his end was destruction, because he was selfish. And the Jews benefited from Christ in His miracles, but did not thank Him, but rose up against Him and crucified Him, and they perished when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

4- The righteous children of God enjoy God's blessing even if what they have is little, and they thank God for it and are inclined to give, since their hearts are full of compassion for the poor, so they help and give to every needy person, and God's blessings to them increase, as the Law said (Deut 15:2).

Thank God for His gifts to you, and He will increase them for you so that you can help those around you. For God's gifts are not for you alone, but for all those around you, that is, that you may give from them to every needy person.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 22- For such as be blessed of him shall inherit the earth; and they that be cursed of him shall be cut off.

1- Whoever pleases God, He blesses him, so he inherits the earth, that is, he receives blessings and good things on earth, and thanks God for them, so He pours out on him many blessings, and thus he lives in God's blessing and thanksgiving.

2- The one blessed by God inherits the earth, that is, he sees God on earth in all His gifts, so he enjoys fellowship with Him and possesses God, because he feels that God is the whole world, and he is the son of God, so he enters into His embrace, and sees Him in all the virtues of others and in all that is on earth, and so lives in constant joy.
3- The one blessed by God inherits the new earth, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, because he lived faithfully on earth, so he deserves eternal life with Him.

4- The wicked lose God's blessing, so nothing remains for them but the absence of blessing, that is, the curse; these are deprived of seeing God and feeling Him, so they are cut off from being in His presence, and live in the darkness of sin, which leads them to the darkness of eternal torment.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 23- The steps of a man are established by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way.
24- If he fall, he shall not be cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand.
1- God loves His children who hold fast to His commandments, so He helps them in their spiritual striving and establishes their steps on the way to the Kingdom.

2- Because of God's fatherhood and love He does not leave anyone else to care for His children, but He Himself cares for them, because He alone knows the secrets of their hearts, and consequently knows what suits them; He feels with them and establishes them in His way however great the obstacles. For God is able to remove them, or to bring them over them.

3- God rejoices greatly in His children's response to Him and their holding fast to Him, and God's joy in His righteous children gladdens them and drives them into greater striving to enjoy fellowship with Him.

4- The children of God are exposed to temptations like the rest of mankind, but God does not let the temptation dominate them and cast them to the ground, so that they lose their ability to strive spiritually, but He stretches out His hand and supports them, that they may continue the way with Him to the Kingdom.

5- The children of God are also exposed to falling into sin, but if they fall they take refuge in God by repentance, and He forgives them and supports them, so they are not cast down in sin and do not surrender to it. And by God's power they overcome sin, and even rush into greater striving that makes them grow in the love of God.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 25- I was young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.

1- David offers a personal, practical experience, which is that the righteous children of God cannot be forgotten by God, but He cares for all their needs, and even provides for the needs of their children; for the blessing of the righteous extends to his offspring, so they are godly, and God blesses them, and they lack nothing.

2- St. Augustine sees that David speaks with the tongue of the Church, which from its beginning was "young," and until the end of days "is now old," and God has not forsaken any of her righteous children nor their offspring.

3- The righteous is the one who loved God and was occupied with Him, and so sought the heavenly Kingdom before anything else; God provides for his needs, his and his offspring's, as Christ declared this clearly in His Sermon on the Mount, "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mt 6:33).

4- God's care for the righteous is to satisfy him spiritually. And the bread that He gives to his offspring is the spiritual food, for this is more important than material food. Although God does not forget his material needs either.

5- There are righteous men who have been hungry, such as Abraham and Isaac, who went to Gerar for bread (Gen 26:1), and Paul, who was exposed to hunger (2 Cor 11:27), but God did not forsake them, and they did not die of hunger.

6- The righteous is distinguished by tenderness and compassion, for he feels the needs of those around him, and as God loved him he loves those around him, so he helps them, and if they need to borrow from him he lends to them.

7- The whole life of the righteous is an occupation with doing good; his whole day he has compassion on those around him in different kinds of service, and indeed throughout his life he keeps doing good.

8- The offspring of the righteous walk in the way of the Lord like him, so they receive the Lord's blessings in their lives, and also care to bless those around them, helping them and doing good with them.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 27- Depart from evil, and do good; and dwell for evermore.
1- David declares that the characteristics of the children of God are two things, which are:
A - Keeping away from evil.
B - Doing good.

It is not enough to do one of these two commandments; the two commandments must be complete together in the life of the children of God. Whoever keeps away from evil only and does not do good is a person who does not show his sonship to God who loves goodness, and whoever does good and does not depart from evil is a person who limps between the two sides and is not a true son of God.

2- The reward of the children of God who depart from evil and do good is the greatest reward, which is eternal life and dwelling in it, that is, settling forever in the Kingdom, in addition to God's blessings in this life, such as the grace of inward peace.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 28- For the LORD loveth truth, and forsaketh not his godly ones. They are preserved for ever: but the seed of the wicked shall be cut off.
1- The Lord loves truth, which is virtue and the doing of good, and this is what the righteous and the just do; therefore God loves them and blesses them with many blessings.

2- If Satan supports the wicked in doing evil, all the more God does not forsake His righteous children, so He blesses them in their life on earth with many blessings, and if they are exposed to sufferings in the present life, He compensates them for them with inexpressible glories in the Kingdom of Heaven.

3- The wicked may flourish in the present life and enjoy some material things, but they have lost their peace, and then in the eternal life they are cut off from God's presence and cast into eternal torment.

4- As for the righteous, they enjoy their life on earth in fellowship with God, and then inherit eternal life. By this we find the inheritance of the earth repeated six times for certain groups, namely: first, those who wait for the Lord and rely on Him (vv. 3, 9, 34), second, the meek (v. 11), third, the blessed (v. 22), and finally the righteous (v. 29). And we find that in the fourth time he mentioned the righteous, who are those marked by the three previous characteristics.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 30- The mouth of the righteous meditateth wisdom, and his tongue speaketh truth.

1- Meditating is murmuring, that is, repeating a thought and a feeling about something, and this belongs to the heart, then appears on the mouth. The mouth of the righteous meditates wisdom, that is, his heart, his mind, his tongue and also all his works are marked by wisdom.
2- Wisdom is the word of God, and its work by the Holy Spirit in man's heart appears in the tongue, then in works. So man speaks the word of God and the will and desire of God at all times.
3- The truth is God, so whoever lives by wisdom, that is, the word of God, will of course speak the truth, that is, everything sound, and will declare God in his speech.
4- This is the first time in the Book of Psalms that the word wisdom is mentioned, so whoever repeats the psalms much is filled with wisdom and speaks it.

5- Man's mouth is an instrument for glorifying God, and therefore the Book of Psalms mentions the mouth and the tongue often (seventy-five times) to call the children of God to sanctify their tongues by repeating the words of God, so that Satan, who wants to use their tongues for evil, keeps away from them.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 31- The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide.

1- The heart of the righteous is occupied with God's Law, so he enjoys meditating on it, then it appears in his conduct, that is, his steps; he lives by God's Law, and whoever lives by it does not turn aside from God's way and is not shaken by the evils of the world, but walks with earnest steps toward his goal, which is the Kingdom.

2- God's Law, that is, His commandments and judgments, is a support for man on his way to the Kingdom; it is not heavy on him or restricting of his steps, but on the contrary encourages him, leads him in God's way and fills him with inward peace.

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 32- The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him.
33- The LORD will not leave him in his hand, nor condemn him when he is judged.
1- The wicked man uses his authority in this age to wrong the righteous, because the wicked man is full of evil, and because the light in the life of the righteous exposes the wicked man's evil.
2- The wicked man watches the righteous not to learn from him, but to wrong him, because evil has blinded the wicked man's eyes, so that he wants to get rid of the righteous.

3- God intervenes to rescue the righteous from the hand of the wicked, however great the wicked man's power, as He delivered David from the hand of Saul, Mordecai from the hand of Haman, and chaste Susanna from the hands of the two elders (Dan 13). In some cases God wants to give the righteous a greater crown, so he endures the wicked man's wrongs throughout his life, and God does not leave him, but gives him greater glory in the Kingdom of Heaven, in addition to consolations, peace and joy on earth.

4- When the righteous stands before God on the Day of Judgment he is not condemned or judged; first because he is repentant of his sins. And second, God disregards the false accusations that the wicked man directed at him in life, for they are void in God's sight, and on the contrary He compensates him for his endurance of the wicked man with great blessings in heaven.

5- The scribes and Pharisees tried to destroy Christ many times, and they used to watch Him to catch Him in some fault; this prophecy applies to Him, and He said to Pilate, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above" (Jn 19:11).

entries.section: (3) The protection of the righteous is assured

paragraphs.text: 34- Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he shall exalt thee to inherit the land: thou shalt look on till the wicked are cut off.

1- In the end this part tells us about God's protection of His righteous children; God calls His children to wait for Him and keep His way, that is, to hold fast to His commandments and walk uprightly, and not to be troubled by the cruelty of the wicked and their domination, because it is temporary and passing.

2- God declares the reward of the righteous, which is their being lifted up to heaven, to dwell in the new earth, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, to receive rest and blessing in place of all that they endured on earth.

3- To this reward is added that the righteous see with their eyes the passing away of the glory of the wicked, and even their separation from God and their being cast into hell. And these rewards are a divine gift from God, who lifts them up and gives them in heaven what surpasses the mind.
Hold fast to God's commandments and do not doubt God's way, however much you see the success of the wicked, but pray for them, that perhaps they may repent.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of the wicked and the reward of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 35- I have seen the wicked mighty, and spreading like a flourishing, fresh tree.
36- He passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found.
Mighty: powerful.

Spreading: describing a tree that extends, with many branches and leaves and wide shade. Flourishing: a tree that grows in its native land and by the courses of rivers. It is a natural tree that grows strongly in its original soil.
Fresh: full of vitality.

1- The wicked man becomes great in much glory on earth as a mighty man, and has great authority like the spreading tree that overshadows others, but all this is temporary, and ends quickly during his life on earth, that is, his condition changes, and he loses his greatness and becomes lowly, as happened with Nebuchadnezzar the great king of Babylon when he was driven from his kingdom and lived like the animals. His greatness on earth may extend throughout his life, but torment will be his in eternity, and he will not be in God's presence.

2- The wicked man appears strong like the tree that grows in its native land, drinks from the waters of the rivers near it and is full of vitality, but all this is outward, because within the wicked man there is turmoil; he has lost his peace despite his outward glory.

3- The life of the wicked man, if measured against eternity, is nothing, and is like a person who passed quickly and disappeared; he is worthless before God, though he dazzled the people around him in his life on earth, but he has no existence before God, because he did not know God, nor did he live purely, nor did he do good. Likewise the righteous pays no attention to the wicked man, however great his glory, for he sees his wicked deeds that neither build up nor benefit.

4- Whoever is proud and exalts himself, his life ends quickly and his weakness appears, like the Pharaoh of Egypt in the days of Moses, who was proud against God, so God struck him with the ten plagues, and then he was drowned in the sea.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of the wicked and the reward of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 37- Observe the perfect and behold the upright: for the end of the man of peace.
38- But the wicked shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off.
The end: the conclusion.

1- David calls for observing the righteous man who walks in perfection and uprightness, for he lives with God, and his life is an example to those around him, and he deserves that others be discipled at his hands.

2- The end of a person shows the nature of his life and conduct; the righteous who enjoyed peace and made peace in all his steps, his end is eternal happiness in the Kingdom. But the wicked who was immersed in his evils perishes, and God destroys him and casts him into eternal torment, and he enjoys nothing of the glories of the Kingdom.

entries.section: (4) The punishment of the wicked and the reward of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 39- But the salvation of the righteous is of the LORD: he is their stronghold in the time of trouble. 40- And the LORD shall help them and deliver them: he shall rescue them from the wicked and save them, because they trust in him.

1- Although the righteous are exposed to many afflictions, and this appears in front of the wicked, God intervenes by His power and grace, and saves them; therefore they are at rest however much the wicked surround them, because God cares for them and saves them.

2- The salvation of the wicked [sic] is not meant to be salvation from material afflictions, for these are the lesser matter, but rather salvation from sin and the devil's plots, for God delivers them as long as they take refuge in Him.
3- God's protection of the righteous is like a stronghold that cannot be stormed; it is constant and strong protection, and therefore the righteous enjoy inward peace.
4- The time of trouble is the time of falling into sin, so the righteous takes refuge in God and He delivers him from it, and if he falls he repents, and God returns him to His embrace.
And the time of trouble is our life in the world, where we meet afflictions, but God delivers His children from them and turns them to their good.

And in the end the time of trouble is the Day of Judgment, when God becomes a stronghold for His children, takes them to the Kingdom, and protects them from the authority of the devil. But the wicked go to eternal torment.

5- Though afflictions exist in this world and the wicked surround the righteous, God becomes a stronghold for His children throughout life until He takes them to the Kingdom, while the wicked are sent to destruction, like the wheat and the tares that grow together, and the wheat is gathered into the barns, but the tares are burned with fire (Mt 13:30).

Take refuge in God with confidence in all your afflictions, and in all the wars of the devil with which he fights you, for He is able to deliver you however great your weakness, and to protect you however much threats surround you.
Repentance and the seeking of salvation. "O LORD, rebuke me not in thy wrath" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet, as the title of the psalm states.
2- When it was written:

After David's fall into the sin of adultery with Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and after the killing of his son Amnon for his adultery with his sister Tamar, and after his son Absalom rose up against him and drove him out of the kingdom. Some think that he was also struck with a bodily illness; all this reminded him of his sin, so he wrote this psalm full of feelings of repentance.
3- This psalm shows us the hideousness of sin and its effects, so that we hate it and Satan does not catch us with its temporary pleasure.
4- Although this psalm carries many sufferings, and the Fathers count it a lament of David, it ends with hope.

5- This psalm is liturgical; it used to be repeated with the offering of the oblation, with which incense was also placed and burned on the altar (Lev 2:2); it reminds the one presenting the offering of his sins and their effects so that he may repent of them. The Ashkenazi Jews (those from Eastern Europe) used to pray it on the evening of the third day of every week.

It was also prayed in the second century before Christ, in the days of King Antiochus, for the whole nation of the Jews on the Sabbath, and therefore we find in the title of this psalm in the Septuagint "for a remembrance, concerning the Sabbath."
The Sabbath is the day of rest which signifies eternity, and this psalm is a reminder of sin as a preparation for eternity, for eternity cannot be reached without repentance.
And when we pray with this psalm and praise God we ourselves become a sacrifice of love before God, that is, we ourselves become a remembrance before God that gladdens His heart.
6- This is the third of the seven penitential psalms, which are, as we mentioned, (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).
7- This psalm is counted among the Messianic psalms because it contains many verses that signify Christ (v. 6, vv. 11-14).
8- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- O LORD, rebuke me not in thy wrath, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure. 2- For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore.
Thy wrath: thy severe anger.
Stick fast: are fixed.
1- David does not refuse God's rebuke or chastening, but implores God's tenderness and love, that the chastening and rebuke not be in wrath; for who can bear God's wrath?

2- Though I deserve punishment for my sins, yet rebuke me first, and give me an opportunity to repent before You are angry with me, O Lord, and punish me; for the punishment of sin is destruction. But rebuke and chastening lead to repentance and return to You and life with You.
3- This is the beginning of the sixth psalm, which is a psalm of repentance, so there is a similarity between the two psalms in meaning.

4- David felt that the words of Nathan the prophet, whom God sent to him to rebuke him for his sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, were strong in their effects on him, so that he likened them to the arrows that stuck fast in him, and to God's strong hand that came down and pressed on him. This shows that David, despite his fall into sin, loves God and is greatly moved by His words.

5- God's arrows that stuck fast in David may be the bodily and psychological pains that struck him when Nathan rebuked him, and they resemble the bodily pains that struck Job to call him to repentance, and Job called them the arrows of the Almighty (Job 6:4).

6- The coming down of God's hand upon David is divine pressure to lead him to repentance, and at the same time it is help to assist him in repenting, and to protect him from despair, and also from laxity; it is the hand of God the tender Father who wants his salvation.

7- God's arrows indicate God's promises, for Nathan told David, when he confessed his sin, that the Lord had put it away from him (2 Sam 12:13). So God's arrows are strong promises that stuck fast in David's heart, and gave him a hope mingled with the tears of repentance.

8- These arrows signify Christ's love, which was offered on the Cross; it sticks fast in the heart of every sinner to wound him, so that he is moved and returns by repentance to God. And so he receives forgiveness of his sins. Christ is the Father's arrow that caught us sinners and brought us back to life in Him.
3- There is no health in my flesh because of thine anger; there is no soundness in my bones because of my sin.

1- When David felt God's anger against him because of his sin he was greatly affected spiritually, psychologically and also bodily, because he fears God and loves Him, so he felt the guilt of his sin, and his health was affected, so he was in bodily weakness. He declares his humbling before God, his humility and his repentance of his sin.

2- By David's bones is meant his inside, for the bones are the deepest thing in man's body, and they support the body and give it form; that is, David's inward being, his mind and his feelings and all that is in him was greatly affected, and even lost its inward peace because of his sin, so he declares his need of God, that He may forgive him and restore his peace to him.

3- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, and in it He speaks of His sufferings that He endured because of our sins, for He bore in His body on the Cross the consequences of the whole world, and suffered and died to redeem us.

4- This verse shows the hideousness of sin, which shakes man's being; David, who was not terrified by the lion and the bear that he killed, nor by Goliath whose head he cut off, was greatly disturbed as a result of his fall into sin.
4- For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me.
Gone over: covered and risen.

1- David reflected on his sins and found that they were many; for though he had fallen into adultery and murder, he thought that his sins had many effects. He caused the wife of Uriah to stumble and fall, and likewise his sin was a betrayal of his wives, in addition to the fact that he sinned against God and against his own body, and also became a bad example to Joab the commander of his army, and to many around him who knew of the matter, and he wronged one of the commanders of his army, who was Uriah, and also caused Joab to stumble and made him share with him in killing Uriah, and betrayed his army that fought for him ... so he felt that he had not sinned two sins only, but many sins had risen over his head and covered his whole being. He is truly a man repentant with all his heart, who knows how to judge himself.
2- Sin, which seems sweet in its moment, presses upon man, pricks his conscience and affects his whole being. The wise man guards against any sin however attractive it is.

3- The humble man bows his head, so he does not grow weary under the weight of sins, but God has mercy on him and lifts them from him. But the proud man feels their weight upon him and cannot bear it.

4- When the iniquities covered David's head, that is, the thoughts of sin, they took away his discernment and understanding, so he was led without understanding and fell into sin; therefore beware of haste in any action, lest lust drive us into many sins.
5- My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness.
Corrupt: pus flowed from them.
Wounds: a wound that has not healed.

1- David feels that his sin affected him like a disease that produced wounds and pus, and some think that a bodily disease actually struck him after his sin, but here he speaks rather of the effects of his sin; that they are like wounds and pus that wearied his body so that he suffered bodily, in addition to the psychological and spiritual pains.

2- Sin is the result of foolishness and stupidity; it appears in the sinner's sight as pleasure and gain, but its reality is the demolition and destruction of man. But when he repents he understands all this; David at the hour of his sin saw that his sin was right, but when he repented he felt its hideousness and that it was a stench, a wound and folly.
3- If sin causes stench, wounds and pains, then good works produce a sweet fragrance before God, the building up of the soul, spiritual growth, and rest of the body.
6- I am twisted; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long.

1- One of the effects of sin on David is that it made him twisted, so he was no longer standing erect in uprightness, glory and greatness, but became crooked, and it also made him writhe from its pains that squeeze his body and soul, and thus he felt the guilt of sin.
2- David's twisting is the result of the fear and terror that sin caused him, whereas purity of heart gives strength, peace and uprightness.

3- Sin also made David bow toward the ground in shame before God, so that he cannot lift up his head before Him, but is in shame and disgrace like the tax collector who could not lift up his eyes toward God, and bowed his head because of the shame of his sin (Lk 18:13).

4- If the sin of adultery and murder carries behind it the sin of pride, after committing them David felt his evil, so he bowed toward the ground in repentance and seeking forgiveness, for pride is a lifting up, and repenting of it needs humility and looking to the ground. For God protects the humble from falling into sin.

5- David's sins are lusts that he carried out; he acted carnally, looking to the earth and its lusts; therefore the result was that he bowed toward the dust of the earth, to know the result of his sin.
6- Sin caused David exceedingly great grief, to the utmost, whereas virtue gives joy and peace.

7- Man's twisting and bowing toward the ground, that is, his abasement and shame, continue all the day long, that is, throughout life, unless he repents, in which case God forgives him, lifts him up and glorifies him.

8- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who said that His soul was sorrowful even unto death, and who fell "bowed down" to the ground under the weight of the Cross; all this Christ endured for our sins.
7- For my loins are filled with burning, and there is no health in my flesh.
My loins: my sides.
1- One of the effects of sin is that David suffered hard pains in his loins, like one who suffers from severe renal colic, and by burning he means that they are pains beyond endurance. This shows:
A - The hideousness of sin.
B - The extent of David's remorse.
2- David declares that his pains are hard and have no healing, "there is no health in my flesh," and the only solution is to return to God by repentance that He may remove his sin from him.
8- I am benumbed and crushed to the utmost; I groaned from the sighing of my heart.
I am benumbed: I lost my feeling and grew weak.

1- David was greatly affected when he fell into sin, so he lost his feeling toward God and his will was loosened, and he became like a person who has been anesthetized and become unconscious, and so rushed toward sin.

2- Sin shattered David and crushed him, so he lost his spiritual being and his enjoyment of God's presence; his being crushed to the utmost means that he became like the dust of the earth, or the sand of the seas, or in the extreme of weakness, and lost his ability to walk in God's way, for here sin dominated him and he fell into it.

3- David felt remorse after his fall, so he offered repentance not only with his lips but from all his heart, and sighed with a deep groan, which is expressed here by the sighing of the heart, that is, a continual groaning with every breath he breathes out. This made God grant him forgiveness.
9- Lord, all my moaning is before thee; and my sighing is not hid from thee.
1- Here David affirms his deep remorse by two things, which are:
A - Moaning, which is sounds coming out of his mouth.
B - Sighing, which is a groaning that comes out of his depths.

2- David's moaning and sighing are before God, seeking His forgiveness, and not moaning and sighing between himself and his own self, because the latter produces despair, whereas the former is before God, and so establishes his hope in God's mercies and forgiveness.
3- The moaning and sighing before God is prayer, and it is a prayer marked by the following:
A - A deep prayer with the heart and the tongue.
B - A continual prayer, because the sighing is continual.

And by this David offers a constant prayer full of hope, because it is offered to God who knows the secrets of hearts, and nothing is hidden from Him. And by these prayers David receives not only forgiveness but peace, and his heart is attached to God, and consequently keeps away from sin.
10- My heart throbs; my strength hath left me, and the light of mine eyes also is not with me.
Throbs: shaken and troubled.

1- When David fell into sin his heart was affected and shaken much, and its beats became rapid, because he did something foreign to his nature, which is sin, and also fell into disobedience to God, and the pleasure of lust turned into bitterness, pain and turmoil.

2- David's rushing toward sin with force dropped him into extreme weakness, so he felt that his strength had left him, that is, God's strength working in him, because he was separated from God by sin, and became like one dead.
3- Likewise by falling into sin David lost the light of his eyes, that is, his spiritual enlightenment and his ability to discern, because sin is error and spiritual blindness.
4- David's feeling of all these effects of sin, and his confession of it, confirm his judging himself and his repentance, and consequently his receiving God's forgiveness.

11- My loved ones and my friends stand opposite my stroke, and my relatives stand afar off. 12- And they that seek my soul set a snare, and they that seek my ill speak corruptions, and all the day long they mutter deceit.

1- Sin is evil and troubles people; all the loved ones and friends who knew that David was a man of God were greatly troubled and kept away from him, because he had kept away from God. For the secret of David's strength, which made his loved ones gather around him, is his love for God.

2- Sin destroys the close relationships of man, so even his relatives keep away from him. For sin is loathsome, and consequently it makes man lose the support of those around him, and he feels isolation; if he is a wise man he hastens to repent, and so feels God's support, and then his loved ones and his relatives return to him.

3- David was surprised that his loved ones turned against him, and this was wounding to him. David had served King Saul by playing music for him when the unclean spirit came upon him, and Saul rose against him and tried to strike him with the spear several times (1 Sam 18:11). And David brought Ahithophel near to him as a counselor, and he turned against him and devised a plot to kill him, and even his son Absalom rose up against him and drove him out, and tried to kill him.

4- This verse applies to Christ, who was left by all His loved ones at the hour of His arrest and in His sufferings, and He said "and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me" (Jn 16:32); His disciples scattered from Him, and His nation stood against Him when they tried Him and handed Him over to Pilate.
5- When we commit sin we are scattered from Christ, and even stand against Him, though He is the Beloved who died for our salvation; thus we are turned from loved ones into enemies.
And when we commit sin our loved ones, the angels and the saints, are scattered from us. While when we repent of our sins, the friends of evil stand far from us.
6- David was exposed not only to his loved ones' forsaking him, but to the enemies' rising against him, who wronged him with many evils, which are:
A - They tried to kill him, and set snares to catch him, as Saul, Absalom and Ahithophel did.
B - They spoke corruptions against David, and words of deceit and falsehood, as Shimei the son of Gera did, and all the followers of Saul.

7- Christ was exposed to false testimonies from the Jews in His trial, in addition to false accusations, such as accusing Him of being a blasphemer, an evildoer, an agitator of the nation, and of cooperating with Beelzebub the prince of the demons.

Beware of the glitter of sin that tries to draw you, for it carries poison within it. Remember its pains and that it will destroy you, so repent and return from it, and from everything connected with it, whatever the cost, for your salvation is more important than anything. And rely on God and lean on Him, for He is able to give you victory and save you from it.
13- But I am as a deaf man; I hear not, and as a dumb man who openeth not his mouth. 14- And I am like a man who heareth not, and in whose mouth is no argument.

1- David heard many false, void accusations, but was not disturbed by them, but was like a deaf man who does not hear, that is, he kept his inward peace and the steadfastness of his faith, and even prayed for the one who wronged him.

2- Likewise David did not answer the false accusations that Saul's servants raised against him, but only affirmed his love for Saul in practice, when Saul fell twice into his hand and David did not harm him. And David did not answer because he did not want to enter into useless argument; he speaks when there is benefit in his speaking, so he was like a dumb man, or one who has no argument although he is able to answer, but he speaks only at the proper time.

3- What helped David in his silence was his occupation with his repentance, so he did not answer Shimei the son of Gera, and accepted his wrongs as though they were chastening from God (2 Sam 16:11, 12).

4- Christ was completely silent before the accusations, the false testimonies and the useless discussions, whether from the scribes and Pharisees, or the chief priests during His trial, or before the civil rulers, such as Pilate and Herod.
15- For in thee, O LORD, have I waited; thou wilt answer, O Lord my God. 16- For I said, lest they rejoice over me; when my foot slipped they magnified themselves against me.

1- David was patient with the wrongs of his enemies and the forsaking of his loved ones, because he believed that God is a just judge and will not let his right be lost, so he endured for God's sake, and God lifted him up and glorified him on earth and in heaven, and this is evidence of David's firm hope in God.

2- David's silence was accompanied by prayers that he trusted God would answer at the proper time, and this confirms David's faith in God's love, and in His ability to answer for him against the wrongs directed at him.

3- And he asks God to intervene quickly so that his enemies do not gloat over him, for he is silent before their wrongs and accusations, waiting for God's intervention and defense of him, and this also confirms his hope in God.

4- David's enemies, and even more the demons, exploited David's fall into the sin of adultery and murder, so they magnified themselves and were proud against him, exploiting his weakness; but he was wiser than they, for he humbled himself and took refuge in God by repentance, so He put his sin away from him and forgave him.
17- For I am ready to halt, and my pain is continually before me.
To halt: to limp.

1- The slipping of David's foot - that is, his falling into sin - made him exposed to other falls and wars from the devil, so the slipping turns into constant weakness, that is, he keeps limping throughout his life, and what is meant is the continuation of his falling into sin.
And here David's humility appears, and his seeking God's help and His swift intervention to rescue him from the hand of Satan.
2- David declares here that his pain - that is, his sin - is before his eyes at all times, and this means the following:
A - Constant remorse and contrition before God.
B - Constant guarding against sin so as not to fall into it a second time.

C - It confirms David's holding fast to the fear of God; for he feels the guilt of his sin before God's righteousness, and although he is confident that God has forgiven him, he thanks God at all times for His forgiveness.

3- This verse applies to Christ, who is ready to endure sufferings unto death to complete the salvation of mankind; Christ draws near to the crucifixion and says "I am ready to halt," that is, to be crucified, "and my pain is before me," that is, the sufferings of the crucifixion before His eyes. This confirms that Christ had a true body, and endured all the sufferings for us to redeem us.
18- For I will declare mine iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin.
1- David declares his confession of his sin before all peoples in this psalm, and this is great courage, because he is concerned for the salvation of his soul whatever the cost or disgrace.
2- The cause of David's grief is his sin, which he remembers at all times, and not any affliction or punishment that comes upon him; repentance is his chief concern.
3- David's repentance and confession of his sin are what enabled him to pray, asking God's help, and so he received His mercies.
19- But mine enemies are living, and they are mighty: and they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied.

1- David met a problem, which is that his wicked enemies were full of vitality and strength, and even grew great in their position, power, authority and wealth. All this did not affect David, because he held fast to his faith, confident of God's power that supports him. He was not troubled by their strength and greatness, because he believes in contentment and detachment, and did not doubt because of their greatness, because he is confident of God's power with him, and that God is able to compensate him with inward peace and joy better than all the delights and powers of the world.

2- Among the problems that David met also was that his enemies who hate him and seek evil for him increased in number, but he did not doubt his faith and his conduct, even if he remained alone, but kept living in purity and love toward those who hate him, so he forgave Saul and did not harm him although he fell twice into David's hand. He is an example of steadfastness in the faith.
20- And they that render evil for good are mine adversaries; because I follow the thing that good is.

1- It is strange that a person should repay good with evil; for the natural man, not the spiritual, repays good with good and evil with evil, but the wicked alone is the one who repays good with evil. But David, who held fast to goodness, remained in his upright conduct, and did not answer evil with evil, but answered evil with good, so he did good to King Saul and did not harm him. Likewise he was tender toward his son Absalom, who drove him out and tried to kill him, and he used to say to his army going out to fight Absalom, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom" (2 Sam 18:5). He is an example of the love of enemies that Christ proclaimed in the New Testament, but David lived it in the Old Testament.

2- The wicked repay good with evil, because the light of the righteous exposes the evil of the wicked, so instead of the wicked imitating the righteous and correcting their ways, they are enraged and wrong the righteous, to put out their light, that they may continue in their darkness.

3- This verse applies to Christ, who came for the salvation of the world, and went about everywhere doing good, and the Jews rose up against Him and crucified Him, and repaid His good with their evils, while He died for their salvation. It is the love that surpasses the mind.
21- Forsake me not, O LORD my God: be not far from me. 22- Make haste to help me, O LORD my salvation.

1- Before the strength of the enemies David took refuge in God with faith, asking Him not to forsake him, because he trusts in God's power that is able to protect him, declaring by this his need of God. He is truly a humble man.

2- The psychological pressures that fell on David from the forsaking of friends and loved ones, and the rising of enemies against him, made him feel that only one support was left to him, which is God's being with him, and this is very sufficient and satisfying to him; therefore he urges God not to go far from him. And within God's embrace he is satisfied, rejoices and is strengthened.

3- David's enemies had surrounded him and almost destroyed him, so he asks for swift help from God, and he feels boldness with God, so he says to Him, "O my God." And he asks for God's swift intervention and believes that God is his Savior; He will surely deliver him; therefore David lives at rest however much the enemies surround him.

4- Though David fell into sin, and declared to us at the beginning of the psalm its results and its pains, yet when he looked to God and lifted his heart to Him, he was strengthened, empowered, and filled with peace and joy. The repentant prayer moves us from death to life, and from weakness to strength.
Give enough time to prayer, that you may enjoy your relationship with God, be rid of your sins by repentance, and lean on God in all your steps, and so live a calm life full of divine love.
A lament of a stranger. To the chief Musician. To Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. "I said, I will take heed to my way, that I err not" ... (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.

2- Jeduthun led the singers with this psalm, and this Jeduthun is most likely Ethan the Ezrahite, who with Heman the Ezrahite was chief singers, assistants to Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David. The name Jeduthun is repeated in the title of Psalms 62 and 77.
3- When it was written:
A - Either in the days of David's flight from the face of Absalom.
B - Or during David's flight to the Philistine city of Gath to Achish its king.

4- This psalm is considered a personal lament of David, in which he declares his labors and pains, and it is related to the psalm before it and the one after it. It is one of the greatest laments of David.
5- This psalm is also full of hope and faith, so it is a help to those who pass through afflictions.
6- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

paragraphs.text: 1- “I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a muzzle, while the wicked is before me.”
1- When David saw the success and strength of the wicked, he was troubled within himself and almost spoke words of murmuring, but by the power of God he was able to restrain his tongue from sin.

2- David's restraint of his tongue enabled him not to fall into evil conduct, since evil speech gives birth to evil deeds. Thus David's taking heed to his way enabled him to control his tongue, his thoughts and his actions.
3- This verse shows a dialogue within David's soul, that is, he holds himself to account before God so that he may not slip into his faults.

4- This verse shows the danger of the tongue, which is able to kindle evil within the whole being of man and in his deeds, so that it needs a muzzle, as though the tongue were a predatory beast that of necessity needs restraint, especially when it is provoked by the events of life and the conduct of the wicked.

5- David's tongue was liable to condemn the wicked, or to justify himself, or to murmur against God. It was exposed to many faults, from which David was able to free himself, even if he had fallen into them in thought or in heart; yet this shows David's striving and his attempt to control himself.

6- David's taking heed to his way, that is, his control of his thoughts and conduct, also made his tongue unable to err, because out of the abundance of the heart the tongue speaks; so when his inside became pure, his speech became pure.

7- David feels that the wicked man is before him and not against him, so David does not treat him as an enemy or condemn him, but only feels that the wicked man is different from him in his conduct in evil. Therefore David keeps a loving heart toward him and prays for him; indeed he was gentle toward his son Absalom, although Absalom wanted to kill David. Thus David charged Joab, the commander of his army, to deal gently with Absalom.

entries.section: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

paragraphs.text: 2- “I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; and my sorrow was stirred.”

1- David was able to control his tongue and keep silent, so he did not sin with an evil word; and he also held his peace from good speech, so he did not say a kind word. Yet the distress was still within him, that is, in his thoughts and feelings, and he continued to suffer from these pains until his heart grew calm.
2- David's silence is a great striving that God praises, but he was not able to do good to the wicked man who was before him, and so the pain continued within him.
3- If a man keeps silent from hearing the voice of God, he will lose his ability to do good, and so the pains of sin stir within him.

4- When Shimei cursed David, David kept silent and did not answer him, whether by words or by allowing Joab to kill him; but he held his peace from doing good or speaking kindly, and then David blamed himself and suffered, because his love toward Shimei was not perfect, since he ought to have been silent about the evil and also to speak good in the face of Shimei's curses.

5- David kept silent from evil speech, but he was not able to speak good, since the wicked man does not accept good speech; so there was a struggle within David, and pains because he was unable to speak the word of God, for the wicked man refuses to hear holy speech.

entries.section: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

paragraphs.text: 3- “My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue:”
Musing (lahaji): repeating the thought or the speech.

1- When the wicked wronged David, his heart was moved within him, and he was distressed because they wronged him while he was innocent. Then the thoughts were repeated within him until his heart was kindled with distress at those who wronged him. Finally he spoke with his tongue and rebuked them for their wrong to him although he was innocent, as he rebuked King Saul twice when Saul fell into David's hand and he did not harm him (1 Sam 24:11; 26:23).

2- This verse may also mean that David's heart, when it heard the wrongs of the wicked toward him, had pity on them because they sinned against God; for he wants the salvation of all and loves even the one who wrongs him. Prayers for those who wronged him were repeated within David until his heart almost burned with the fire of love for them. And David's tongue spoke about the wrongdoer, or to him, seeking an excuse for him, as he did with Shimei the son of Gera, when he declared that Shimei's wrong was a divine direction to David (2 Sam 16:10).

3- There is a third interpretation of this verse, which is that when David heard the wrongs directed against him, he was distressed by them, and his heart grew hot within him because of them. But he turned his heart to God in prayer, asking His help, and was kindled in crying out to God to deliver him and comfort him, and David's attachment to God increased. David's occupation with speaking to God made him keep silent, so he did not answer the wrong of the wicked with any word of wrong, because God gave him peace and tranquility, and even forgiveness. So he was content with his speaking to God with his tongue and with the prayers of love for God that drew his heart, and he left off thinking about the wrongs of others.

entries.section: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

paragraphs.text: 4- “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am.

1- David asks God to make him know that his life on earth is short and will end and he will pass away from the earth, and so he is not troubled by the wrongs of the wicked but bears them, because they are temporary and will end with the end of his life on earth, and in place of them he will receive heavenly glories.

2- David feels that the afflictions he passes through have an end, so he asks God to make him know their end and the number of their days, and how he will pass away from the earth; and so he hastens to acquire virtue and to do good in preparation for eternity, and is not occupied with the wrongs of others, but is even able to let the wrongs push him to repent of his sins and to cling to God and eternity. David does not ask to know the number of his days on earth, or the days of his trial precisely, but he wants God to remind him that his days are limited, so that he may be occupied with eternity.

entries.section: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

paragraphs.text: 5- “Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah.”

1- As David looks toward eternity, he sees that his life is very short, which he expresses as handbreadths, not a long period, but a breath and not a great wind, and then he sees it as nothing, for the days of life pass and are not remembered afterward. Thus this leads to David's humility and his non-attachment to material things, as he feels that he is a stranger on the earth.

2- As David feels the shortness of his life on earth, indeed that it is nothing in itself, he is careful to live with God so that his life may have value and extend into eternity in unspeakable happiness.

entries.section: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

paragraphs.text: 6- “Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.”

1- David likens the life of man to a phantom and not a tangible reality, and to loud noises (tumult) that then end, and you cannot hold on to them. Also man hoards many material treasures, then dies and takes nothing of them. Therefore the wise man does not cling to this passing world and all his possessions.

2- This world is full of tumult, that is, disturbance, and the wise man is the one who lives with God, so his heart is filled with peace, and indeed he possesses God within him, so his life becomes a true reality and not a phantom, and he increases in the knowledge of God and every virtue instead of the passing material things. And thus every day he prepares for eternity in which he will remain.

May the sojourning of the world be fixed in your heart, so that you do not waste your time in argument and quarrels with others over passing things, and be careful to possess God within you through many prayers.
7- “And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee.

As David sees the vanity of the world and its passing, and that the life of man is short and will end, he therefore waits for nothing in the passing world, but the only One whom he waits for is God. He is the only hope in this life, that man may live with Him, and He alone remains forever; so he hopes in Him and places all his hopes in Him.
8- “Deliver me from all my transgressions: make me not the reproach of the foolish.”

1- The sins and transgressions that man commits separate him from God, so he loses God's presence in his life. Therefore David asks God to deliver him from his transgressions, and thus he becomes pure and worthy for God to dwell in him, and he enjoys fellowship with Him.

2- Transgressions cause Satan, who is the foolish one, and all who follow him, who are the wicked, to rejoice at the fall of the righteous. So David asks God to forgive him his sins even if he needs divine discipline, but God must take his sins away from him, so that the foolish one may not rejoice at David's fall, and thus David may not go to eternal torment, but on the contrary may have enjoyment with God in the Kingdom.
9- “I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it. 10- Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand.”

1- David submits to God in all His disciplines, because David is repentant and submissive to the will of God, so he keeps silent and accepts all God's arrangements for his life. Thus he enjoys God's guidance of him and His care for him.

2- David expresses his suffering from God's discipline of him, so he begs Him to remove His stroke from him, that is, His disciplines, whether they were wrongs from others, or God's forsaking him so that he was exposed to falling into sins; he begs God to stop His stroke upon him and to have pity on him, because he is very weary, until he is near to perishing. By this humbling before God, David obtains His forgiveness, His love and His care.
11- “When thou with rebukes dost correct man for iniquity, thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth: surely every man is vanity. Selah.”

1- When God allows disciplines for His children so that they may repent, He makes them feel that the world is passing; for as the moth consumes woolen clothes and possessions, so God consumes the desires and possessions of man, so that he may not cling to the world, and may feel that his life is short and small, like a breath, and so becomes a stranger to the world and clings to God.

2- Because of the importance of being a stranger to the world, David places a musical pause, which is the word Selah, after this verse, as it was placed after the fifth verse of this psalm, to confirm the sojourning of the world within the heart of everyone who chants this psalm.
12- “Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.”

1- At the end of the psalm David begs God to listen to his prayer and his crying out, and even if he is unable to speak and express himself, God looks upon his tears and intervenes, removes his pains and forgives his sins. For David feels that his sins are the cause of God's disciplines and of all his pains.

2- David also begs God to answer him, because he is a stranger in the earth, like his fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who lived in tents as strangers all their days on earth. And because the stranger has no attachment to earthly things, his hope is his relationship with God and his eternity.
13- “O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence, and be no more.”

Recover strength (atabalaj): from the breaking of dawn, that is, the appearing of the light of dawn and the rising of the sun; the intended meaning is that I may shine forth, find rest and be enlightened.

1- The repentant David accepted God's discipline in all the pains he passes through, but he felt the weight of the pains upon him, so he asked God to remove His disciplining hand from him, that he may find rest and his life may shine anew, and so enjoy his life with God before his age comes to an end.
2- In the Hebrew original the word “spare” means “forgive,” so David wants God to assure him that He has forgiven his sins; then his face will shine and he will rejoice before he leaves this world.

You have boldness with God as His child, so ask of Him, indeed persist with Him to hear your prayer, and support you and give you rest, and delight you with His presence with you, so that your hope may be renewed and your faith in Him made firm.
Cry for help and longings: “Judge me, O Lord, and plead my cause” (v. 1) Introduction:

1- Most students of the Holy Bible see that this psalm is a continuation of the previous psalm, that is, the two psalms were one psalm that was divided. This psalm must have been written by David, because before David the Tabernacle was not in Jerusalem, and there were not two dwellings of God, “Thy tabernacles” (v. 3); and after David, that is, in the time of Solomon, there was one temple built in Jerusalem, and there were not two dwellings, or two tents.
2- When was it said?

When Jonathan, the son of Saul, saw the evil in his father's heart toward David, he warned David to flee so that no harm would befall him. This was mentioned in the title of this psalm in the Septuagint.

3- This psalm expresses the sufferings that David expects from Saul, and asks God's help to rescue him and bring him back from the places to which he fled, that he may enjoy worship in the temple of God.
4- This psalm expresses the feelings of every person surrounded by threats and problems, whose hope is firm in God, and whose longings are bound to the Church and her sacraments.
5- This psalm is a prophecy about the captives in the Babylonian captivity, who are surrounded by idolaters and long to return to Jerusalem, to enjoy the worship of God in His temple.

6- This psalm is also a prophecy about Christ, whom the Jews surrounded, trying to kill Him, but His hope was firm that He would accomplish the redemption of mankind, and die for it, then rise, to raise it up in Himself.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Third Hour, because it speaks about the Holy Spirit who enlightens the lives of the children of God and guides them to worship Him in the Church (vv. 3, 4).
1- “In waiting I waited for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.”

1- It is clear that David was subjected to many wrongs from those who wronged him, but he bore them and waited a long time. He confirms this by his saying “In waiting I waited”... and this confirms David's faith, his hope in God and his reliance on Him. For he kept silent and did not murmur, and surrendered his life to God and awaited His intervention, because of his confidence that He would surely deliver him.

2- God's tenderness and humility appear in His inclining toward David and His care to hear his prayers and his cry; He did not neglect him because He loves him. And David here is a type of Christ, who bore the sufferings for our sake and awaited the revealing of His glory after the torments and the Cross, and appeared in His Resurrection.
2- “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.”

1- David likens his suffering and afflictions to being in a pit, that is, a deep hole from which he cannot get out. He also says that this pit is full of mire, from which he cannot get out, but if he tried to get out he would sink deeper in it; so he surely needs the intervention of God, who stretched out His hand and brought him up.

2- Falling into the pit and the mire expresses David's falling into sin, and his inability to get out of it by his own strength although he had repented of it; so God stretched out His hand, brought him up from it and forgave his sins.

3- God was not content to bring David up out of the pit, but lifted him onto a rock, that is, solid ground and not like mire. So David was able to triumph with confidence and strength, and even to walk with strong steps, advancing and succeeding; because God, when He saw his striving, established his steps so that they became stronger. And the rock is a type of Christ, on whom His children lean throughout their lives (1 Cor 10:4).
3- “And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.”

1- In addition to God's delivering David from the pit, He pushed him onto the path of positivity, by teaching him a new song that expresses new feelings, and a great joy that David felt, so he praised God, who cares for His children, rescues them from all problems and dangers, and forgives them all their sins.

2- When the people saw God's wonderful work with David they feared God, since they felt that He is stronger than all the gods, that He is able to do all things, and that He alone can be relied upon in all situations; so David's faith and reliance became an example to all around him.
Wait for the Lord when a problem befalls you, and persevere in your prayers, confident that He is near you and will surely intervene and rescue you, whatever the threats of the wicked.
4- “Blessed is that man that maketh the LORD his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies.”
The proud (ghataris): the singular is ghatris, meaning the arrogant and conceited.

1- David glorifies the man who relies on God, in order to call all people to rely on God, and by this man he means himself, so as to strengthen all the righteous in the face of the wrongs of the wicked.

2- David supports and blesses the man who relies on God, so that he may not look to the proud and lying wicked, nor to the great ones of the world who have authority, but may trust in God, in whose hand are all things.

3- Whoever does not rely on God meets misery instead of blessedness; for when the people of God did not rely on Him, and feared the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, God deprived them of entering it and they died in the wilderness of Sinai (Num 14:22, 23).

5- “Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered.”
They cannot be reckoned up: they cannot be counted.

1- David meditated on God's care for him and for His people throughout history, and found that God's works are wonderful, surpassing the mind, and so many that he cannot count them. And His thoughts and arrangements toward His children are very great.

2- David's purpose in meditating on God's works is to tell of them to others in order to glorify God. But he found it impossible to count them, and therefore was content to speak of some of them, which is what he was able to enumerate and speak about.

6- “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. 7- Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me.”
Volume (scroll): a piece of skin or papyrus on which writings were written in ancient times.

1- David made clear that God asks for obedience to His commandments before the offering of sacrifices. And God opens David's ears to hear and obey, because obedience is better than the offering of sacrifice. And offering sacrifices without obeying God's commandments profits nothing. The meaning is not the rejection of offering sacrifices, because God commanded them, but He wants to declare that obedience to God's commandments surpasses every sacrifice, whether a burnt offering or a sin offering. For by obedience man sacrifices his own will and prefers the will of God to what he himself wants.

2- David spoke in the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who says to the Father that He took no pleasure in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, because they were merely a type, but His pleasure was in the coming of Christ and His Incarnation, for He is the sacrifice that was prefigured, who would be offered on the Cross, as mentioned in the volume of the book, that is, the prophecies of the Old Testament. And the Incarnation of Christ is the obedience of the Son to the Father, so Christ's obedience is better than the burnt offerings and sin offerings, and Christ's coming by His Incarnation is the fulfilment of the Father's will; therefore He said, “Lo, I come.”
8- “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is in the midst of my bowels.”

1- David loved God, and God's law became his delight; so he held fast to it and applied it in his life, and he took pleasure in carrying it out, because it had become in his heart and bowels, that is, he felt it, and afterward it appeared in his conduct. So the believers feel in every generation, and the word of God becomes lived in their hearts and conduct, and their life becomes a lived Gospel.

2- This verse is a clear prophecy about Christ, who became incarnate to fulfil the pleasure and satisfaction of the Father and to do His will, which is the redemption of mankind. And God's law was in His bowels, that is, His depths; for He is the Word of God, the Second Hypostasis, who became incarnate that we might see in Him how the law is applied in practical life.

9- “I have preached the Lord in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, O LORD, thou knowest. 10- I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation.”

1- David declares that he has preached God in the midst of his people, who are the great congregation, whether by killing Goliath, or by his service with King Saul, or by his bearing Saul's pursuit, or when he reigned over the people of God and continued to hold fast to God's righteousness, so he spoke with his lips and taught love to all around him. And God knows David's heart, that it is with God, and not merely words he utters with his lips (Acts 13:22).
