2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who preached not only among the Jewish people but among the Gentiles also, for He offered righteousness and love on the Cross in His death, being the Righteous One without sin, for the redemption of all mankind. And He preached in His life on earth with His lips, which signify justice and mercy, which are perfected in His Incarnation and redemption and all His words. And the Father knows how the Son is the Righteous, the Holy One.

3- Christ still speaks of His faithfulness and salvation through the Apostles, the priests and the servants to this day by the work of the Holy Spirit, not only in the words of the Evangelist, but also in the lived life of His children. And He also does not conceal His mercy and His truth, that is, God's forgiveness and support of His children, in addition to His warnings so that His children may repent. This is in the great congregation, that is, in the whole world for Christians, that they may live in purity, and for the whole world, that it may believe and repent.

Proclaim the voice of God to all around you by holding fast to God's commandments, keeping away from all evil, and offering your love to every person, so that you become light to the world and salt to the earth.

entries.section: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

paragraphs.text: 11- “But thou, O Lord, withhold not thy compassion from me; let thy mercy and thy truth always help me.”

1- David's humility appears in his asking God to have compassion on him; he is like the tax collector who humbly asked for God's mercy and obtained His forgiveness, and this confirms the importance of humility in the spiritual life.

2- David relies on God's mercy in forgiving his sins and supporting him, in addition to God's truth, that is, His justice, which is firm in the way of righteousness and judges evil to be void; so by mercy and truth David triumphs over Satan and lives with God unshaken by the success of the wicked, and even arrives at complete victory in eternal life.

entries.section: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

paragraphs.text: 12- “For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me.”
Taken hold (haqat): encompassed.

1- David remembers the wrongs of his enemies toward him, and declares that evils have compassed him on every side, and that the cause of this is his sins which have compassed him. This shows that David is a repentant man, who attributes the afflictions to the multitude of his sins, and by these feelings of remorse he obtains God's mercies and forgiveness.

2- When David's sins multiplied they took away his ability to discern, so that he no longer saw God, and also his feelings, that is, his heart, left him, that is, he no longer felt God as he used to in the past; so he is in severe suffering because of the multitude of his sins, but when he repented he regained his spiritual enlightenment.

entries.section: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

paragraphs.text: 13- “Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me: O LORD, make haste to help me.”

1- The verses from this verse to the end of the psalm are repeated in Psalm 70. We find in them a supplication from David to the holy God to condescend and be pleased to deliver him from his many sins to which he referred in the previous verse. So David continues in his humility and self-abasement before God, but in a firm hope that He will lift from him the continual afflictions that surround him.

2- Because of Job's great distress over his sins, he declares his swift need for God's intervention, that He may lift them from him and restore to him his sonship and his relationship with God; so He supports him lest he fall a second time.

entries.section: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

paragraphs.text: 14- “Let them be ashamed and confounded together that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be driven backward and put to shame that delight in my hurt. 15- Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha.”
Let them be desolate: let them fear and tremble.
Aha, aha: an expression of gloating.

1- David prays for the wicked who want to destroy him, not asking for vengeance on them, but that shame and disgrace may overtake them, so that they may know the result of their evils, and turn away from evil and repent, and thus return to God; he prays for them and does not gloat over them. Rather, he asks that they be driven backward from their sins, that is, that they repent of them.

2- When the demons see the shame of the wicked, who tried to harm and destroy David, they fear and tremble, for they see that their earlier gloating over David, by their saying “Aha, aha,” profited nothing. So they gloated of old over Adam at his fall, but Christ became incarnate and redeemed mankind.

entries.section: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

paragraphs.text: 16- “Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: let such as love thy salvation say, ‘The LORD be magnified.’”

1- David believed that God is his Savior, so he desired that all the children of God who seek Him share his joy. David feels his membership in the congregation of the people of God, and wants them to share together in joys and sorrows. And in the midst of these joys and their enjoyment of salvation they magnify the Lord, the giver of this salvation.

2- David's love for those who seek the Lord appears in his calling them to joy, “rejoice and be glad,” in God, and to take refuge in Him in all their needs, “all those that seek thee,” then they praise God and magnify Him, “The LORD be magnified,” and finally they long for His eternal salvation, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, “such as love thy salvation.”

entries.section: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

paragraphs.text: 17- “But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God.”

1- David concludes his psalm with humility, declaring that he is poor and needy, that is, he has no hope or strength except in God his helper. And because of his humility he obtains God's great mercies, unlike the demons and their followers, the proud and gloating wicked, who are put to shame and disgrace.

2- David also concludes his psalm with prayer, asking God's help quickly, because the affliction still surrounds him, and he trusts that God will intervene, because David has a personal relationship and boldness with God, so he says to Him “my help and my deliverer .. my God.” So also Moses concluded his song after crossing the Red Sea with prayer and the glorifying of God (Ex 15).
To the extent that you humble yourself, your prayers reach God and you obtain all help, and He even hastens to you more than you imagine.
The blessed and the traitors, to the choirmaster. A psalm of David “Blessed is he that considereth the poor” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer is the prophet David.

2- When was it written? During the rebellion of Absalom against his father David. It appears that David was ill, and his illness helped Absalom's betrayal of him, since the management of affairs in the country was shaken, and Absalom exploited it to win people to himself and carry out a revolt against his father. And the psalm speaks about Ahithophel, the betrayer of David.
3- This psalm calls for care for the poor.

4- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the wicked's opposition to Christ, the sufferings of Christ, the betrayal of Judas, and the Resurrection of Christ. Christ cited this psalm when speaking about the betrayal of Judas (Jn 13:18), and the Apostle Peter also cited it (Acts 1:16).

5- There is a similarity between this psalm and the first psalm, since both speak of the wicked's opposition to Christ, or their opposition to the righteous, and the victory of the righteous in the end.
6- The psalm is considered a personal lament of David.
7- This psalm was chanted in the temple, so it is one of the liturgical psalms.

8- This psalm is the last psalm in the first section of the Psalms (Ps 1-41), according to the division of the Jews, who divided the Psalms into five sections. And this psalm ends, like the end of the four sections, with the word Amen in its last verse.
9- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Third Hour.
1- “Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble.”

1- The poor man is the needy and the materially poor, or the sick. He is also the humble who bears pains or distress for the sake of God, and likewise the one who is spiritually needy, that is, who needs the word of God and someone to help him draw near to God. In addition, it refers to David himself, who humbled himself before God and was also sick, and his son Absalom rose against him in revolt. And finally, this poor man is Christ Himself, who humbled Himself by His Incarnation to save us from our sins.

2- Whoever considers, or shows kindness to, or has pity on the poor man, God rewards him by delivering him in the time of trouble. By the time of trouble is meant the day of affliction, and also the day of the last judgment. So God delivers him from troubles and punishment and supports him, and blesses him with unspeakable blessings.
2- “The LORD will preserve him, and keep him alive; and he shall be blessed upon the earth: and thou wilt not deliver him unto the will of his enemies.”
Be blessed (yaghtabit): to rejoice and be glad.
Will (maram): desire, or purpose.

1- This verse mentions God's blessings for whoever shows mercy to the poor: God preserves him from all evil, that is, He keeps evil away from him, and even if evil surrounds him it does not harm him, because God protects him, since he did a work of mercy with one in affliction, so God in his affliction rescues him from all evil. And He preserves him also on the day of judgment, for He forgives his sins and gives him to enjoy the Kingdom. And God gives him the spiritual life here on earth, so he enjoys fellowship with Christ, in addition to his obtaining eternal life full of glory.

2- In addition to God's preserving him and his obtaining life, God also gives joy to the poor man on earth, although there are many sorrows surrounding him, but God keeps for him his inner peace, the joy of his heart, and his enjoyment of fellowship with God.

3- Man's enemies are the demons and all the wicked who follow the demons; these want to wrong, and even destroy, the poor man who relies on God, but they cannot, because God protects him and does not give his enemies an opportunity to harm him.
3- “The LORD will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness.”
Will strengthen him: will support him.
His bed (madja'ahu): his couch.
1- Among the blessings of sympathy toward the poor is that God supports the merciful man if he is afflicted with some illness, and heals him, and turns his bodily weakness into strength.

2- Also among God's blessings to the merciful man is that He supports him in his spiritual weaknesses and strengthens him, and develops him spiritually. And this strengthening is either by the healing of the body and its comfort in health, or the opposite, the merciful man is exposed to afflictions, so he is not immersed in bodily comfort but lifts his heart to God, and is strengthened spiritually; in addition, God gives this merciful man a smoothed bed, not only on earth but also in heaven, that is, He gives him eternal rest.

Be careful to feel for those around you, to sympathize with their needs, to encourage them and to serve them, confident that whoever shows mercy to another, God shows mercy to him. To the extent that you are occupied with the comfort of others, God comforts you, so that you enjoy fellowship with Him.
4- “I said, LORD, be merciful unto me: heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee.”

1- David declares his need for God's mercy, and that he is sick and needs divine healing, and even declares that the cause of his illnesses is his sin, so he asks God's forgiveness. All this shows David's repentance and humility.

2- David asks spiritual healing for his soul, which is more important than bodily healing, for the forgiveness of sin and the purification of his heart is the divine mercy that he asks. By this he is able to feel God and live with Him, and even reach eternity. So whoever shows mercy to another obtains God's mercies, on condition that he is repentant and concerned for the salvation of his soul; but if the wicked man gives alms, that is not enough for his salvation, like the heretics who, if they give alms for the glory of men, it profits them nothing, and they die in their sins.
5- “Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish?”

1- In the previous verse David began by declaring his weakness and his need for forgiveness in clear humility, and after this he declared the cruelty of his enemies, who speak against him with evil words, intending his destruction and extermination. So he suffers from the evil of his enemies, but he ascribes the cause of his suffering first to his sins and weakness, and then adds and complains of the cruelty of his enemies; that is, he holds himself to account before he holds others to account, and inclines to repentance and not to the condemnation of others.

2- Ahithophel's counsel against David and all the words of the wicked for his destruction was a type of what happened with Christ and Judas's betrayal of Him, when he agreed with the priests of the Jews, and they seized Him and crucified Him, and tried to exterminate His name; but Christ rose, and the Apostles preached Him in the whole world (Acts 4:31).
6- “And if he come to see me, he speaketh falsehood: his heart gathereth iniquity to itself; when he goeth out, he speaketh.”
7- “All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt. 8- An evil thing, say they, is poured out upon him; and now that he lieth he shall rise up no more.”

1- Among the hardest things is for enemies to appear in the form of loved ones, as happened with Ahithophel, who was David's counselor and of course saw him in his illness and weakness; but the subsequent events showed that he had a strong relationship with Absalom, so he would see David's weakness and report it to Absalom, and when Absalom rose against his father Ahithophel joined him and tried to destroy David, but God rescued him. Likewise Judas clung to Christ like the rest of the disciples, and ate with Him, but he went out to carry out his plot, to inform the Jews and have Christ seized. So both of these traitors, Ahithophel and Judas, spoke falsehood, that is, speech against love, which was an attempt to destroy David and Christ, and they devised plots against them.

2- All David's friends who deceived him and joined Absalom took counsel how to destroy David. Likewise the priests, scribes and Pharisees tried to trap Christ in a word and failed, and their aim was to be rid of Christ, so they crucified Him and He died, but He rose on the third day.

3- Those who betrayed David carried out their plots, and Absalom attacked with a great army to destroy David, and they said among themselves that an evil thing had been poured out upon David, and that he would die and not rise up. But God scattered their counsel, so Absalom died and David was saved. So also the priests of the Jews carried out their plots, and crucified Christ, and by this supposed that an evil thing had been poured out upon Christ, and that they had been rid of Him and He would not rise, but they were surprised by His Resurrection on the third day.

4- David used the word “lieth,” that is, sleeps, to declare the possibility of his rising from the dead, and this is what Christ fulfilled when He raised Himself from the dead quickly, like a sleeper who rose from his sleep, and as Christ declared when He raised the daughter of Jairus and said that she was asleep (Mt 9:24), and likewise Lazarus before He raised him (Jn 11:11). And we too shall rise in the Resurrection like one who was asleep and rose from his sleep.
9- “Yea, the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.”

1- David speaks of those who betrayed him, meaning Ahithophel, or any servant among David's counselors who lived with him for many years, and whom he honored, and then turned against him and joined Absalom and drove David out of his kingdom and tried to kill him. And at the same time he speaks in the spirit of prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who was one of Christ's disciples, and betrayed Him and delivered Him to the Jews; so David describes this traitor as follows:

A – The man of his peace: that is, he lived in peace with him and was one of those close to him. So that Judas, when delivering Christ up, kissed Him, that is, there was between him and Christ a very warm friendly relationship.

B – I trusted in him: Ahithophel was one of David's chief counselors, and likewise Christ entrusted the money box to Judas, and this shows Christ's trust in Judas, that He entrusted him with the money.

C – Who ate my bread: Ahithophel was very close to David, and likewise Judas was one of the twelve disciples, and both of them ate at the table of their master. And Christ dipped bread in the dish and gave it to Judas apart from the rest of the disciples, that is, he was distinguished.
These three characteristics confirm the Master's love for this traitor, and therefore increase the guilt and heinousness of the betrayal.

2- Of this traitor David said “lifted up his heel against me,” that is, his foot, to trample me and crush me; for Ahithophel's counsel aimed at killing David while he was a fugitive and exhausted. As for Judas, his betrayal led to the crucifixion of Christ and His death, and indeed he sold Him for a paltry sum. All this shows the hideousness of the evil in the traitor's heart.

May you value the love of others, and respond to their love with greater love, and not act as a result of pressures you pass through, and so wrong another, especially those who are close, lest you become a traitor to love like Judas.

entries.section: (3) The victory of … for His children

paragraphs.text: 10- “But thou, O LORD, be merciful unto me, and raise me up, that I may requite them.”

1- David asks God to be merciful to him, that is, to rescue him from the plot of the wicked and the traitors, and to heal him of his illness, and this is a declaration of David's humility and his need for God's mercy and help. And it is a prophecy about Christ, who in humility became incarnate, and asked the Father to be merciful to Him, that is, that the divinity support the humanity in the accomplishing of redemption.

2- David asks God to raise him up, so that he may requite the wicked, and exalt and establish justice in the kingdom; he does not seek vengeance on the wicked, but the establishing of justice, since as a king he is responsible for the firmness of justice in his kingdom. And it is a prophecy about Christ, who asks the Father to raise Him up, that is, that the divinity raise the humanity, and requite Satan whom He bound by the Cross, and cast him into eternal torment at the end of the days. And everyone who persists in evil is also cast into hell, for refusing repentance. As Christ requited the Jews who refused to believe in Him, so that they were no longer His people, and their city was destroyed by the hand of the Romans in AD 70, and many of them were killed.

entries.section: (3) The victory of … for His children

paragraphs.text: 11- “By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me.”

1- David rejoiced that God was pleased with him, so King Saul did not triumph and shout over him, nor Absalom, for both died and God saved David from their hands, indeed from all David's enemies from the surrounding countries, and David triumphed and took possession of their lands.

2- The Father declared that Christ is His beloved Son, and was well pleased with Him when He was baptized in the River Jordan. And Satan was not able to make Him fall in the temptation on the mountain, but Christ triumphed over him. Likewise on the Cross the Father smelled His sacrifice as a sweet-smelling savour, and Satan was not able to seize His spirit after His death, but on the contrary Christ seized Satan and bound him, triumphing over him.

entries.section: (3) The victory of … for His children

paragraphs.text: 12- “And as for me, thou upholdest me in my perfection, and settest me before thy face for ever.”

1- David ascribes the perfection in which he lives to God; it is a grace given to him to walk in the way of perfection, and he thanks God for this, especially since he kept his perfection in the midst of difficult circumstances, such as the enmity of Saul and Absalom toward him. And he thanks God also that He raised him from his sin, and established him in the way of perfection, purity and love in which he will live forever, that is, not only in this present world, but he declares his hope in eternity, in which he remains standing before God in this perfection.

2- This verse applies to Christ, who lived perfect while in the flesh, and said, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Jn 8:46). Then He rose from the dead and raised mankind in Himself to reign with Him forever in the Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) The victory of … for His children

paragraphs.text: 13- “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.”

1- David concludes the psalm by glorifying God, the God of Israel, who is worthy of all honor from everlasting to everlasting, forgetting all his sufferings, then asks Him to answer all his requests in this psalm, and confirms this by saying Amen, and Amen.

2- There is an opinion that this verse was added by one of the elders of the Jews at the end of the last psalm of each of the first four sections of the Psalms, but to the fifth and last section of the Psalms this verse was not added, because the last psalms are all glorification of God (see the introduction to the Book of Psalms).

God is your supporter, so advance in your spiritual life and your service, and do not be troubled by the wars of Satan, because God is able to give you victory over them. And He is also able to adorn you with many virtues, and then give you the happiness of eternity.
God the Disciplinarian and Savior. To the choirmaster, for the sons of Korah - a poem “O God, we have heard with our ears” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer and the time of its writing:
A - The prophet David, when the Edomites attacked the tribe of Judah, while David was occupied at that time with other wars, and they destroyed many of the Jews.
B - One of the sons of Korah wrote it in the days of King Hezekiah, when King Sennacherib of Assyria fought him and took possession of many places in Judea, and killed many of them.
C - An unknown person wrote it in the days of the Maccabees, when they fought the Greeks and triumphed over them, after the Greeks had destroyed many of the Jews.

2- Its subject: the believing people of God, who rejected idolatry, were subjected to attack from their enemies, but they cried to God, and He rescued them, saved them, and gave them victory in the end over their enemies. So it is a communal prayer of supplication to God, that He may have mercy on His people and not leave them in the hands of their enemies.
3- This psalm suits every person who suffers afflictions and persecutions but holds fast to his faith, so he seeks God with importunity, that He may rescue him and lift his pains from him.
4- This psalm resembles Psalm 60.
5- This psalm is a prophecy about the Apostles in the Apostolic age, and the martyrs in the ages of the martyrs, who faced many persecutions, but God supported them with miracles and glorified them.
6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.”
The hart: the buck of the mountain goat, resembling the gazelle.

1- The hart is swift in movement and attacks snakes, kills them and eats them, which makes its inside hot, and it needs to drink much water, and if it does not drink it is exposed to destruction, so the hart longs greatly to drink water.
2- As the hart is marked by its inclination to drink water, so the writer of the psalm feels that his soul longs for God and cannot live without Him, and will perish if it does not find Him.
2- “My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?”

1- The writer of the psalm feels that he longs for God, and man cannot live without drinking. So he is in spiritual thirst for God, and describes God as living to distinguish Him from the dead pagan gods, which are idols that do not move, for God is the source of life.

2- The longing of the writer of the psalm is not to pray to God in just any place, but to appear before Him, that is, in His temple in Jerusalem, because the writer is estranged from Jerusalem. This shows the importance of prayer in the Church, in addition to prayer in every place.
3- “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say unto me every day, Where is thy God?”

1- The enemies reproached the writer of the psalm that his God had left him, since he is estranged from Jerusalem, expelled and exiled, so he is in affliction and God has not helped him. So they make him doubt the existence of his God, or the power of his God to rescue him.

2- The faith of the writer of the psalm was not shaken, but he continued in his prayers by day and by night, and his prayers were from his heart, so they were mingled with his tears, which express his longings for God and his grief over the affliction from which he suffers. So longings and griefs were mingled together in a wonderful way, and were mingled also with his faith, so his prayers continued. And he was not distracted from these prayers by talking with people, or by the works of life that are done in the daytime, nor did they stop with sleep during the night. Rather the longings of his heart continued, and covered everything in the day and the night. And from the excess of his sense of the importance of prayer and tears they became necessary to his life like bread, so that he cannot do without them. And he said “my bread” and not my water; for whoever eats bread while thirsty, his thirst increases; likewise the more his prayers and tears continue, the more his longing toward God increases.

4- “When I remember these things, I pour out my soul upon me: for I used to pass along with the throng, I went in procession with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, a multitude keeping holyday.”
I pour out my soul upon me: I meditate and look deeply into myself and pray with fervor and tears.
I go in procession: I go up the steps of the mountains leading to the temple.
The throng: the congregation of worshipers.

1- When his enemies reproached him they increased his present griefs, so he remembered the past days in which he enjoyed being in the temple of God. And he did not remember them with a feeling of deprivation and despair, but with the hope that he would return and enjoy them. For although there are griefs in the present, his past enjoyment stirred in him longings for the future, to enjoy worship in the temple of God.

2- When he remembered the past joys he poured out his soul upon himself, and was not enraged at his enemies who drove him out, but turned to meditation and prayer deep within, so he rejoiced in God's past blessings and longed for them, and his prayers became satisfying to his soul.

3- The writer remembered when he used to go up the mountain with the congregation of believers to worship in the temple of God, and he would lead them in beautiful songs, perhaps the Psalms of Ascents (Ps 120-134).
5- “Why art thou bowed down, O my soul? and why dost thou groan within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him for the salvation of his countenance.”

1- David, or the writer of the psalm, reproaches his own soul because it was bowed down, or broken and weakened, before the reproach of the enemies, who said to it “Where is thy God.” Indeed from the abundance of distress it came to groan and ache, and this does not agree with faith and hope in God; the soul must bear affliction with contentment and steadfastness in faith. So the problem is in his soul because of the weakness of its faith, for if it were steadfast in faith it would not have weakened before the reproaches of the enemies.

2- He calls to his soul to hope in God, and David reveals the sweet side within him that struggles with the groaning, so he says, I still praise God and thank Him for all that He allows for me, even if it is affliction. And I see the face of God, so I see my salvation which must be accomplished, and this affliction ends; indeed my preoccupation with my spiritual salvation lifts me above the toils of the affliction so that I forget them.

It is good that you review yourself every day to discover your weaknesses and recover your faith and your spiritual principles, so that you return to God by repentance, and raise up your soul, to live with God and enjoy fellowship with Him.
6- “O my God, my soul is bowed down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar.”

The mountains of Hermon: mountains that extend from the north toward the south and in which are the sources of the River Jordan, and the mountains are called “Sirion” (Deut 3:9; Ps 29:6) or “Senir” (Deut 3:9) or “Sion” (Deut 4:48). They are high mountains, whose height is nine thousand two hundred feet above sea level, and they have three peaks. And these mountains lie north of Palestine, where the tribe of Dan dwells, and in ancient times were the possession of Og king of Bashan.
Mount Mizar: one of the peaks of the mountains of Hermon.

When David found his soul still bowed down within him, he treated it by taking refuge with God, so he remembered God in his exile, which was at the sources of the River Jordan, the mountains of Hermon and Mount Mizar. And by remembering God he began to regain the strength of his faith, and hope revived within him. And because he was in affliction he was humble when he prayed to God, so he obtained divine grace and spiritual support.
7- “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy currents and thy billows have covered me.”
Deep: deep waters that cover whoever enters them.
Thy waterspouts: thy waterfalls.
Thy billows: thy waves.
Covered me: overwhelmed.

1- David in his exile at the sources of the River Jordan saw the overwhelming waters following one another as they came down from the mountains of Hermon, where the snow melts and the waters flow with force; indeed he heard the strong sound of the waterfalls, and saw the waves dashing and covering everything in their path. So he meditated on them and saw that in this affliction of his it was as though his soul were in the midst of the River Jordan, and these waters, currents and waves were coming upon him, so he felt that they express what he suffers in his affliction.

2- It is beautiful that David feels that all that happens to him is by divine arrangement, so he accepted it from the hand of God in submission, and at the same time he had a firm hope that God would lift from him all that he suffers during his affliction.
8- “In the daytime the LORD commands his mercy, and in the night his praise is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.”

1- David feels that he enjoys all day long the mercy of God, which He commands His angels to pour out upon men, and especially His children; therefore he thanks God for His mercy, but in the night, when people sleep and life grows quiet, David devotes himself to praising God, to whom his heart clung, until he felt that God is his life, so he continues all night praising God, as the Fathers said, “The night is set apart for prayer.” So David prays to God by day and by night; because He is his life, so in the daytime he awaits His mercy, and in the night he praises Him for these mercies.

2- The night is a symbol of the life we live on earth, for it is darkness when measured against eternity, where we do not see God except as in a mirror, as the Apostle Paul said (2 Cor 3:18). And in this night David praises all his life. But the day, which is a symbol of eternity, in it David obtains the mercies of God, who commands His angels to give him to enjoy his life with them.

3- The day is also a symbol of life in the light of God, for God supports His children with His mercies in their striving to speak to Him, and these mercies continue all day long. But the night is a symbol of the wars of the devil, who wants to make us fall into sin, during which we do not see God as in the daytime, but we do not stop our praise of God; because He is our life, without whom we cannot live.
9- “I will say unto God my rock, Why hast thou forgotten me? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?”

David, who enjoys fellowship with God by day and night, trusts that God is his rock, and his strong support able to rescue him, but he suffers pains in the affliction, which he expresses by saying why hast thou forgotten me and why do I mourn because of the reproaches of my enemy. He is not despairing, or doubting God's support of him, but he expresses his severe pains, as Christ on the Cross expressed the depth of His pains by saying, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46).

10- “With a crushing in my bones my oppressors reproach me, saying to me every day, Where is thy God. 11- Why art thou bowed down, O my soul, and why dost thou groan within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.” The reproaches of David's enemies were very severe during his affliction, and they made him doubt that God had left him because he is wicked, so that his spirit was crushed within him, and he expressed this by saying that his bones were crushed; because the bones are the strong part that gives the body firmness and rigidity, especially as the enemies continued to reproach him, so the crushing continued in the bones. But his hope was still strong in God; because he called to his soul that was bowed down and broken within him not to groan but to hope in God, as we explained earlier in the verse (v. 5).

Do not let afflictions keep you from God, but continue in your prayers and your praise of Him, confident of His love for you and His nearness to you, and that He will intervene at the right time with great power.
The glories of the King and the Queen. To the choirmaster “according to the Lilies.” For the sons of Korah. A poem. A song of love “My heart overflows with a good matter” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer:
A - The sons of Korah, as is written in the title of the psalm.
B - David, and he gave it to the sons of Korah so that they might chant it, and this is the more probable opinion.
2- The psalm was chanted “according to the Lilies,” as in the title of the psalm, and what is meant by the lilies:
A - A musical instrument.
B - A musical tune.
3- This psalm is Messianic, because it speaks clearly about the Messiah the King.
4- This psalm speaks about the Incarnation of Christ; therefore it is read on the Feast of the Nativity in the Hoos of the feast.
5- This psalm also speaks about the bride, who is:
A - The Church
B - The Virgin Mary
C - The human soul that loves Christ.
6- This psalm is a song of love as in its title; because it is praise and love of God, then a love offered to the Church that clings to Christ.
7- This psalm shows the greatness of life with God, and His children's enjoyment of blessings on earth and glories in heaven.
8- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Third Hour, when the Holy Spirit descends upon the Church and gives her to enjoy glory with her Bridegroom, Christ the King.
1- “Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against a nation that is merciless: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man.”

1- David cries for help to the just God to judge in the circumstances through which he is passing, which are the agitation of Saul with his whole kingdom trying to kill David; indeed he asks God to stand as an adversary in his place before Saul who contends with him, to ward off from him every evil that Saul tries to direct. And David's asking for God's meeting shows:
A - David's faith in God who loves him and shepherds him.
B - David's uprightness, so that he is not afraid of God's judgment and justice, for he is wronged, and cries to God for help.

C - He did not mention the name of his enemy who wrongs him, and this shows God's kindness. For he wants nothing but God's defense of him, and protection from the evil coming upon him, although he is innocent.

2- This verse applies to Christ, whom the scribes and Pharisees tried to trap in some error, and the priests tried to kill, and stirred up the nation of the Jews against Him, until they crucified Him in the end, aided by the treacherous, deceitful disciple Judas Iscariot, who is “the deceitful and unjust man.”

3- This verse also applies to the Church, against which the world rises and which it persecutes, and some try to flatter her with deceit to reach evil goals. So the Church asks God to rescue her from the wicked and from the evil world surrounding her.
2- “For thou art the God of my strength: why hast thou cast me off? why go I mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?”

David believes that God is his protection and his permanent fortress. This reassures David's heart, but he asks why God rejected him, since by his flight from Saul he went far away and was deprived of offering worship in the temple of God, and this led to grief in his heart. Therefore he asks God, “Have you forgotten me? Or how does your protection of me and your love agree with your depriving me of worshiping you in your temple?!” And this matter, that is, God's setting David aside and neglecting him, pained David's heart greatly; therefore he repeated it in many psalms such as (Ps 3; 10; 73). But despite David's grief he did not lose his hope, for he walked on, that is, he continued in his life and spiritual striving until God lifted these griefs from him.
3- “O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles.”

1- The light of God and His truth, that is, His justice, is the Holy Spirit, who enlightens David's life and supports him in his affliction, since he is wronged, and prepares his way to return to the holy hill of God and His dwellings, that is, the Tabernacle, to enjoy the worship of God. And the hill of God is Mount Zion, on which the city of Jerusalem was built. And the writer says His dwellings, because in the days of David there were two dwellings of God: the first dwelling, or the first tent, in Jerusalem, in which was the Ark of the Covenant, and the second tent in the city of Gibeon, in which were the rest of the contents of the Tabernacle (1 Chr 16:37-39). And David says “let them lead me and bring me” because David was walking sad, continuing his striving, but he was unable to reach the temple of God except with the help of the Holy Spirit.

2- The light and the truth are Christ, who said, I am the way, the truth and the life, and said, I am the light of the world. And by His redemption He brings up all mankind that believes in Him, to enjoy worship in His Church, and after this brings them up to the heavenly Jerusalem, to the Kingdom of Heaven.
3- The prophets in the Old Testament await the Messiah, who is the light and the truth, to lead them with all mankind, to enjoy His redemption and His salvation which He accomplished on the Cross.

4- “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God the gladness of my joy, and I will praise thee with the harp, O God my God. 5- Why art thou bowed down, O my soul, and why dost thou groan within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

1- When David comes to the temple of God and His altar he can be free of his griefs; because he enjoys seeing God in his worship, and this is what makes him glad and joyful. He has no joy in the world and all that is in it, but his joy is only in God, who comforts his heart for all he has borne of pains. And then he can sing to God with the harp; for how can he sing and rejoice far from God, as the captives in Babylon felt, so they said, How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land (Ps 137:4).

2- David asks his soul, after this hope of rejoicing in the hands of God in His temple; and says, why art thou bowed down, O my soul, and groanest within me, hold fast to God your hope, who will compensate you for all your toils (see the explanation of Ps 42:5).

May you look to Christ, your hope and your joy, when you pass through any affliction or griefs, and know that they are temporary, and after them Christ will compensate you with a peace and consolation that fills your heart, which cannot be expressed. Meditate on His past love for you, which will overflow upon you shortly, and your soul will grow calm and be at rest.
Thanksgiving and a request for salvation. To the choirmaster. A psalm of David “I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David.
2- When was it written?
A - The first opinion: at the end of the period of Saul's pursuit of him, that is, shortly before David's reign.
B - After David's victory over Absalom and his return to his throne.

3- After bearing many pains David thanks God in this psalm, declaring his obedience to Him, and asking the continuance of His help. So it is a psalm of thanksgiving, suitable for the children of God when they feel God's work with them.
4- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms; because it speaks with many allusions about Christ.
5- The Apostle Paul quoted from this psalm in his Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb 10:5-10).
6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
1- “We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old.”

1- The writer of the psalm declares about himself and the congregation of believers with him that they heard assured words, for he said we have heard with our ears words about God in the ages before them, by way of the fathers and the prophets, who had a strong connection with God. And the reports were handed down from fathers to sons.

2- When he says “we have heard with our ears” this signifies the Incarnation, for he tells us about the tangible God in the Old Testament by way of the fathers and prophets, who appeared plainly in the fullness of time by His Incarnation.
2- “Thou hast uprooted the nations with thy hand, and planted them; thou hast shattered peoples and spread them out.”
Spread them out: gave them expansion and breadth and dominion over many lands.

1- The work of God appears in shattering and uprooting the pagan nations that dwelt in the land of Canaan, who were strong peoples; because they worshiped idols and were immersed in evil lusts. And on the other side He planted and established His children, and gave them possession of this fertile land flowing with milk and honey, and extended their hands to take dominion over lands that were not theirs. For God removes evil and establishes good, that is, His children who believe in Him and live by His commandments.

2- The Incarnation of Christ also appears in this verse by his saying “with thy hand.” And by this He removed our mortal evil nature, which is signified by the nations that He uprooted and shattered. And He gave us the new nature inclined to good, which is signified by His children whom He planted and spread out in the land of Canaan.

3- “For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them.”

1- Here he confirms that the power of victory which was with the people of God, which made them overcome their enemies, drive them out, and possess their land, was not due to their weapons or their human strength, but its source was God, who struck Egypt with the ten plagues, split the Red Sea, drowned Pharaoh and his army, stopped the sun for Joshua, and brought down the walls of Jericho ... because God was pleased with His people and loved them, since they believed in Him and kept His commandments. This is the communal salvation that God gave to His people.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the incarnate Christ, who is signified by His right hand and His arm and the light of His countenance, for He is the source of the strength of those who believe in Him, and defeats their enemies the demons, and even gives them possession of the places of the demons who fell, so that they reign with Him in heaven.
3- This verse also applies to the Apostles and their preaching, for they did not uproot idolatry and shatter it by a sword or human strength, but by the word of God and His power.
4- “Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob.”

The writer of the psalm feels God's strength supporting him, so he submits to Him, and God reigns over his heart, until he calls Him with boldness, O my King. And with this boldness he asks Him for salvation for all his people. This salvation is accomplished by God's command, that is, by a mere word from Him, so he is rid of his enemies and defeats them.
5- “Through thee we push down our oppressors: through thy name we tread down those who rise up against us.”

As the writer of the psalm felt God's strength and salvation, he was encouraged to storm the enemies and the opponents, and to gore them like a horned animal and destroy them, and the horns signify strength, and after he throws them on the ground he tramples them and crushes them. And this is what the children of God believe in the New Testament, that they have authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. So the believer feels the power of God within him, and does not fear sin, or Satan, or the wicked, but attacks them by the power of God, and triumphs over them.
6- “For I do not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me. 7- But thou hast saved us from our oppressors, and hast put to shame those who hate us.”

The writer of the psalm declares that he will do his duty in the war, and arm himself with the bow and the sword, which are the weapons known in war at that time. But his reliance is on the power of God which gives him victory, and not on weapons. And as God saved the fathers of old from their enemies (v. 3) He will save His people, for the writer relies on God, and trusts that He will save all his people and give them victory.
8- “In God we boast all the day long, and praise thy name for ever. Selah.”

1- The writer believed in the power of God which has worked, and will continue to work with him and with his people. For this reason he raised his voice in thanksgiving, praise, and boasting in the work of God all the day long, that is, all his life, and even forever, and this confirms his faith in the eternal life that God has prepared for him. And the writer boasts in the work of God, whether periods of rest or affliction pass over him; because he trusts that after the affliction he will obtain God's victory in him, for the day includes the daytime and the night, that is, rest and affliction.

2- This verse is the voice of all the believers in the New Testament, who give thanks to God through the Sacrament of Thanksgiving, that is, partaking of the Holy Mysteries, and enjoy His constant work in them, and their victory over the demons, until He brings them to the Kingdom.

3- At the end of this verse there is the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditation on the power of God that supports His children, and that we may lift up our hearts with thanksgiving and praise to Him.

Rely on God at all times, confident of His power and His support which gives you victory in all your spiritual wars, and thank Him always for His past works, so that His work in your life extends forever.
9- “But thou hast rejected us, and put us to shame; and goest not forth with our armies.”
After God supported His people and gave them victory over their enemies, He returned and forsook them, and rejected them; why?
1- So that they may discover their sins and repent of them, and God returns and gives them victory.
2- So that they may be sure that their strength is from God, and not from their weapons or their personal strength.
3- So that their faith and steadfastness in God may be tested despite defeat and shame.

And this happened after Joshua's victory over the inhabitants of Canaan; they returned and were defeated before them in the days of the Judges (Judg 2:21-23). And as the Jews triumphed in the days of David and Solomon, they returned and were defeated and were taken captive to Assyria, then Babylon. And as they triumphed in the days of the Maccabees, but they returned and were defeated before the Greeks, and after their repentance they regained their victory.
10- “Thou makest us turn back from the enemy, and those who hate us plunder for themselves. 11- Thou hast made us like sheep to be eaten; thou hast scattered us among the nations.”
Thou hast scattered us: dispersed us.

When God forsook His people the enemies triumphed over them, so the people turned back defeated, and the enemy even seized the spoils that were with the people of God, and took from them slaves for himself, and slaughtered many of the people of God, as sheep are slaughtered, and the rest of the people of God the enemy scattered everywhere on the earth. This is what happened in the days of the Assyrian captivity, then the Babylonian, and as happened with the Christians in the Jewish persecution in the days of the Apostles, when they killed many of them, and the rest were scattered in the various countries of the world. And this divine forsaking may be because of the pride of the people of God, so God allows them weakness before their enemies, that they may be humbled, and repent and pray, and He returns and rescues them and glorifies them.
12- “Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase thy wealth by their price.”

The writer reproaches God, who forsook His people, so He sold them to their enemies, without profiting anything from selling them; because the cause was the sin of His people, that they might repent. Although it is a reproach of God, it is at the same time the writer's reproach of his people, to let them know that the cause of their discipline is their sin, so that they repent; and if it is not because of sin, they obtain approval, strength and grace from God.
13- “Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us. 14- Thou makest us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.”
A shaking of the head: shaking the head in mockery and contempt of another.

God did not only forsake His people and leave them to be defeated before their enemies, but He also humbled them among their neighbors, who saw their former glory, and now see them fleeing and their cities ruined. And God allowed this humiliation so that the people might be humbled and return to God. This reproach of God shows the writer's faith, his holding fast to prayer, and therefore his readiness for repentance, or it is, in other words, calling his people to repentance, after their neighbors from the nations mocked them and despised them. And these neighbors are the peoples of Palestine, Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon, and the Edomites would even seize the Jews who fled and deliver them to the Babylonians (Obad 1:10-14).
15- “All the day my confusion is before me, and the shame of my face hath covered me, 16- From the voice of him that reproacheth and gloats, from the face of the enemy and avenger.”

1- The people of God were affected by their enemies' contempt of them and their vengeance on them, and the people were in shame and disgrace for a long period, which is the period of the captivity that lasted seventy years. But this divine humbling led to repentance, so they enjoyed returning from captivity and building the temple.

2- These two verses and what precedes them apply to Christ (vv. 13-16), who bore our sins and suffered for us, and bore the cross of shame and disgrace to redeem us. And by His death for us He saved us, then rose in glory to raise us up in Him.

3- These verses apply to the Christians whom the pagans around them reproached, for their worship of the person of the Crucified, weak, in shame and disgrace, but God glorified them with many miracles while they bore the torments, then gave them crowns of glory in heaven.
Accept God's discipline, for it is profitable for your salvation, to purify you from your sins and approve you, so that you obtain great blessings and are made worthy of the Kingdom of Heaven.
17- “All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant. 18- Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way.”

1- Despite the divine disciplines that the verses mentioned from (vv. 9-16) the children of God remained holding fast to their faith and their covenants with Him, as happened in the days of the Maccabees when the Greeks persecuted them and tried to force them to worship idols, and wronged them, but they held fast to their faith (1 Macc 1:65, 66), and as the saints stood firm despite the afflictions surrounding them in captivity, such as Tobit and Daniel and the three youths...

2- These verses are a prophecy about the Christians who bore persecutions, and stood firm in the faith, and bore torments to the point of martyrdom in the days of the Jewish persecution, or the Roman, or any later persecutions.
19- “Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death.”
Dragons: plural of dragon, a strong and very predatory animal. It was known in ancient times, and does not exist now, and it is used to refer to any predatory animal.

The place of dragons is the hardest place in which human beings can be found; because they are exposed to being crushed by these dragons in their ferocity and violence. This is what the writer of the psalm wants to express by the extent of the distress into which the people of God entered, and he also expressed this distress as the shadow of death that covered the people of God, and despite the severity of the afflictions they did not leave God.
20- “If we have forgotten the name of our God, or stretched out our hands to a strange god; 21- Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart.”

The writer confirms the purity of his heart, and declares that he and his people could not have betrayed God, or forgotten Him and neglected Him, or lifted their hands in prayer to another god; because God searches everything, and knows all secrets. He does not only know that they worship God, but knows that their hearts love Him, and they hold fast to their faith. So the writer has no need to show God that his people believe in Him; because God knows everything.
22- “Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.”

1- The love of the people of God and their steadfastness in faith appear in their readiness to die all the day long, and by the day is meant all the days of life, that is, their constant readiness to bear all pains even to death. And in this they are like sheep led to be slaughtered, which are ready for the slaughter at any time. And this is a love above which no other love can rise, and this is what Christ accomplished on the Cross.

2- Every person who strives spiritually against sin gives up and strips himself of many things, and humbles himself. These are kinds of death for the sake of God, and likewise everyone who serves God laying down his life for him to bring His children back to Him, for service is a kind of death. In sum, the spiritual man who strives is ready to die for the sake of God all his life. And this is martyrdom, for the martyrs are not only those who were tortured and slaughtered for the sake of God, but everyone who strives in his spiritual life, and toils in service, as the Apostle Paul said (Rom 8:36).

Be steadfast in your faith, and keep God's commandments however differently the people around you behave and think of you. And bear their doubts, provocations and opposition to you, for your steadfastness is of very great value before God.

entries.section: (4) A cry for help and self-abasement

paragraphs.text: 23- “Awake, why dost thou slumber, O Lord? Attend, cast us not off for ever. 24- Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and forgettest our affliction and our oppression?”
Dost thou slumber: be not in a doze, that is, do not sleep, and leave us in our distress.

1- The writer of the psalm expresses his suffering in the affliction with all his people, and calls on God to hasten to their aid; because God in His silence and long-suffering seems as though He were asleep and inattentive, or rejecting His people, or hiding His face from them, or neglecting and forgetting their toils. All this shows the severity of the people's suffering and its great need for God's intervention to rescue it, for it is a kind of reproach, with the boldness of sonship, from the people to God.

2- These two verses resemble the words of the disciples in their reproach of Christ asleep in the hold of the ship, while the winds almost sank the ship (Mt 8:25). Every spiritual person needs to awaken the Christ who sleeps within him, to ward off from him the winds of trials and the wars of the devil, and to rescue him from every sin.

entries.section: (4) A cry for help and self-abasement

paragraphs.text: 25- “For our soul is bowed down to the dust: our belly cleaveth unto the earth.”

The writer expresses the extent of the abasement and humiliation to which the people of God had come, saying that their souls were brought low until they clung to the dust of the earth, and likewise their bellies, that is, they were in a spiritual and psychological abasement because of the afflictions through which they pass. So this verse shows the bitterness of their souls, and their great need for God's help. And their request in humility that God raise them up and lift them.

entries.section: (4) A cry for help and self-abasement

paragraphs.text: 26- “Arise for our help, and redeem us for thy mercies' sake.” The writer declares clearly that the only solution to rescue the people of God from their abasement is for God to intervene with His help, indeed that God come forward and redeem His people, that is, rescue them from the hands of their enemies, and destroy the wicked. And this verse is a clear prophecy about Christ the Redeemer, who justifies those who believe in Him, and binds Satan.
When the affliction increases and weighs heavily on you, trust that God your Redeemer is able to lift it from you; indeed when the affliction grows heavier, it means that its solution has drawn near.
Longing for God. To the choirmaster - a poem for the sons of Korah “As the hart longs for the water brooks” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer:

A - Some see that they are the sons of Korah who did not die with Korah in his murmuring against the priesthood (Num 26:11), especially since some of them were exposed to exile at the River Jordan, as mentioned in (v. 6). And the writer of this psalm was accustomed to lead those going up to the temple in singing (v. 4).

B - David is its writer and the sons of Korah are those who set it to music, and this is the more probable opinion, by the evidence that the writer of the psalm speaks in the singular, and mentions the word “my soul” as in (vv. 1, 2). And the places mentioned in (v. 6) were places where David was exiled during King Saul's pursuit of him, and it is thought that David wrote this psalm when Absalom drove him out of his kingdom.

2- This psalm shows man's longings for the temple of God, and for being with God, and his suffering at his distance from the communal worship in the temple, as he feels that God alone is able to quench the thirst of his soul.

3- This psalm is linked to the psalm that follows it in its subject, to the point that some scholars thought the two psalms to be one poem, especially since the first section and the second section in this psalm each end with the same verse, which is also the same verse with which Ps 43 ends (Ps 42:5; Ps 43:5), and therefore it was considered a refrain repeated in this one poem, which is considered a personal lament, expressing the pains of the past, present and future from which the writer suffers.
4- The eight psalms from Ps 42 to Ps 49 are of the composition, or setting to music, of the sons of Korah.

5- This psalm may be a prophecy about the griefs of the captives in Babylon, who long to return to Jerusalem, and it is also a prophecy about the longings of the believers in the Old Testament for the Church of Christ in the New Testament, and represents all the believers who are strangers on earth, and who long for the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.
6- This psalm is the first psalm of the second section according to the division of the Jews, which begins with this psalm and ends with Psalm 72.
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 1- My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.

1- David speaks a good word, which comes not only from his thought but from his feelings, that is, from his heart. By the work of the Holy Spirit in his heart he uttered these great and good words. He is speaking to the King, that is, the King of kings, God, and not an earthly king; he certainly does not mean himself. And he says that his tongue is like the heart of a ready writer, that is, that the Holy Spirit overflowing in his heart moves his tongue, so that he writes and utters these words. He senses that the Holy Spirit has turned his heart into a rich spring, overflowing with these words about God.

2- This psalm speaks to us about Christ, God incarnate. God the Father overflowed with His Word, who is the incarnate Christ. This is evident from the description of Christ's attributes in the following verses.

3- David, by the spirit of prophecy, saw Christ and was amazed by Him, and began to speak by the Holy Spirit, as far as he was able, with the expressions we shall see in the following verses. He could not express everything, but only as much as he was able.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 2- Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever.

1- David saw that Christ is fairer than all men. Although He became incarnate and became man like the rest of mankind, His beauty and perfection surpass all, not of course in the form of the body but in righteousness and holiness. His words were all by divine grace, overflowing from His Holy Spirit, poured out to satisfy those who hear them.

2- Christ is the Savior of those who believe in Him throughout the generations, and forever He gives them joy in the Kingdom through His salvation, with blessings that cannot be expressed. Likewise the Apostles, the priests and the servants speak the words of Christ throughout the generations and God blesses them, so that they become a blessing to all who hear them, and He glorifies them with Himself in the Kingdom forever.
3- The grace poured into the lips of Christ gave us and prepared for us the enjoyment of Him in:
a- Partaking of the Holy Sacraments.
b- Delighting in His word, which gives us spiritual illumination, so that we are satisfied by it all our days.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 3- Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty, with thy glory and thy majesty.

1- The sword is the word of God and the thigh is the body, so the girding on of the sword and its being joined to the thigh point to the Incarnation of the Second Hypostasis, the Word. This union between divinity and humanity surpasses the human mind, and none can accomplish it but God the Mighty One. The Incarnation revealed glory and majesty, that is, the greatness and light of the Father. For no one has seen God at any time, but the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared Him (Jn 1:2).

2- The sword is also a type of the Cross. By Christ's being fastened to the Cross He proclaimed His might and authority, for by His death He bound Satan and trampled down death, and the greatness of God appeared in His crucifixion. He freed the captives in Hades, Adam and his children, and raised them up to Paradise, since He paid the debt that was upon them. Thus in the weakness of the Cross Christ proclaimed His might and the perfection of His power by delivering His children, and He showed this to us in His Resurrection.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 4- And in thy majesty ride prosperously because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things.

1- David asks Christ to storm the kingdom of Satan in order to free His children from the dominion of evil, and to ride upon the Cross, He who is the righteous, the truth and the meek, and by the power of His right hand to make Satan afraid and bind him.

2- Christ the King, entering the battle, does not fight like other kings to exalt Himself, but is perfect in His greatness, so He storms in to reign over the hearts of His children ("ride"), and removes from them the dominion and reign of Satan, that they may walk in truth, righteousness and humility like Him by the power of His Holy Spirit. Indeed, He gives them by His right hand to make the demons afraid and to trample all the power of the enemy, as He trampled Satan by His Cross.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 5- Thine arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; whereby the people fall under thee.
Nibal: arrows.

1- The sharp arrows, that is, the keen, strong, piercing ones that destroy whomever they strike, are a type of the Cross, which bound the demons, who are the enemies of the King. The arrows are also the preaching of Christ by the hands of the Apostles, and then of the priests and servants throughout the generations. They may also be a type of the Romans who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70 and destroyed the enemies of the King, that is, the enemies of Christ, who are the Jews.

2- The peoples who fell under the hand of Christ are the demons whom Christ bound by His Cross, or they are the Gentiles and the Jews who believed in Christ and fell under His hand, that is, His authority, believing in His salvation.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 6- Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.

1- The writer here speaks directly about Christ, saying to Him, "Thy throne, O God," is lasting for ever and ever, and no king can reign forever except Christ. The throne of God is the Cross on which He was crucified, that He might reign over the hearts of His children forever. Therefore the Church chants this psalm in a distinctive long melody on Great Friday and on the Tuesday of Holy Week.

2- The sceptre of Christ's kingdom is the Cross, and it is a right sceptre because He is the only King who does not err. He is upright in His tenderness and in His discipline, and with His sceptre He guides us to the upright life.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 7- Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.

1- Because Christ alone is without sin, and is the righteous and holy One who hates evil, He alone was able to redeem mankind. So He was anointed with the Holy Spirit in the River Jordan, and the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. Christ did not need this anointing for Himself, but the Spirit came upon Him, that is, the coming of the Holy Spirit upon His head was shown to us, so that He might accomplish our redemption; it is a descent on our behalf. By this Christ takes His steps toward the joy set before Him, which is the accomplishment of our salvation on the Cross. Therefore the verse says that the anointing was with the oil of gladness, and to express the work of the Holy Spirit in all the children of God who will believe in Christ the Redeemer, as the Holy Spirit fills them with joy.

2- The coming of the Holy Spirit upon Christ was a complete, hypostatic indwelling, and He appeared in the form of a dove. But the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles and the believers was in the form of divided tongues of fire, that is, a partial indwelling, according to their ability to bear it, so that He works in them and through them in service.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 8- All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad.
Myrrh: a gummy liquid extracted from one of the trees abundant in the West, with a fragrant smell. The Magi presented it to Christ.
Aloes: sometimes called balm, a gummy liquid that flows from one of the trees abundant in Palestine, with a sweet smell. It was used as a perfume and in the burial of the dead.
Cassia: bark taken from one of the trees resembling the cinnamon tree, with the taste and smell of cinnamon. Ivory: the tusk of the elephant, with which palaces are adorned because it is costly.

1- This verse speaks to us about Christ, whose garments, that is, His body, were perfumed with the fragrances of myrrh, aloes and cassia, because He bore sufferings for our sake, which are what myrrh signifies. Likewise He founded His churches, the palaces adorned with ivory, by His death on the Cross, because the tusks of ivory are not taken from the elephant except after its death.

2- The garments of Christ are His churches and His children who cling to His body. These believers in Him are perfumed with many fragrances, which are their virtues, which they acquire when they carry the Cross and bear sufferings like Him. These sufferings are signified by myrrh, and the perfumes, that is, the virtues, are the sweet fragrances of myrrh, aloes and cassia. The palaces of ivory, as we mentioned, are the churches adorned with white ivory, which signifies splendor and glory. And the souls of the believers who are in the churches, by their praise of God, make Him glad and rejoice Him; therefore it says, "whereby they have made thee glad." The fragrances mentioned above are different, but all are beautiful; likewise the virtues and the fruits of the Spirit are different, but they adorn the souls of the believers.

entries.section: (1) The power and glory of the King

paragraphs.text: 9- Kings' daughters were among thy honourable women: upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir.
Honourable women: the women who are near, beloved and honored.
Ophir: a region in the south-east of the Arabian Peninsula, today's Yemen, distinguished by mines of the purest kinds of gold.

1- The kings' daughters are the daughters of the great ones of the world, or the souls of the rich and those of high position, whose positions and wealth did not keep them from believing in Christ, so they became believers, drawn near to God, and among the honourable women, who are all the souls of those who believe in Christ, whether rich or poor, from the Jews or the Gentiles; for the love of Christ and His redemption will draw the souls of believers from the whole world in all its classes.

2- The queen is the Church, or the Virgin, or the human soul that believes in Christ. Christ the King has set her at His right hand. The right hand signifies power and blessing, that is, Christ gave her grace and power more than all mankind, because she was adorned with the pure gold of Ophir, which signifies heaven, spirituality and lofty virtues.

3- The gold of Ophir signifies the precious price that Christ paid to purchase His Church, that is, His blood shed on the Cross, the most precious thing in the world, which He offered out of love for His bride the Church; therefore the Church loves Him very much for giving His life for her.

If Christ calls you to draw near to Him to give you many blessings, and even gives you the love of a bridegroom for his bride and adorns you with every virtue, do not be lazy, but hasten to Him eagerly, and seize every opportunity to be with Him, so that you may enjoy His fellowship.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 10- Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father's house;

1- God calls to the Church, or the Virgin, or every believing soul and says to her, "daughter," for He is the Father who cares for her, and He is Christ who redeemed her. David also calls to the Virgin who would come from his seed, that she may hear his spiritual guidance.
2- God asks four important actions of every soul that believes in Him, which are:
a- "Hearken": that she hear Him attentively so as to obey His commandments.
b- "Consider": that she look at His beauty and contemplate it, so that as Christ lived, the believing soul imitates Him.

c- "Incline thine ear": that she be humble and incline her head toward the ground, as Christ carried His Cross and bowed His head to the ground for her sake, and as He washed the feet of His disciples.

d- "Forget thine own people": that is, that she leave behind all her old life in evil and all material attachments, so as to empty her heart for the love of God, and He becomes her Father who cares for her, and she submits to Him with all her heart, as Abraham left his family and his kindred and went out into the wilderness to live with God (Gen 12:1, 4), and as Ruth left her family and went with her mother-in-law to the land of Israel to worship God with His people (Ruth 1:16), and as the Apostles left everything and followed Christ (Mk 10:28).

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 11- So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty: for he is thy Lord; and worship thou him.

1- When the Church, or the human soul, leaves her old life full of evil, that is, repents and believes in God, she becomes beautiful, because God forgives her and she becomes pure. And the wonder is that Christ the King desires her for her beauty which He Himself gave her, for she acquired her beauty from His beauty.

2- On the other hand, Christ is the Creator of this soul, so He is her Lord and Master, and she is a queen and does not belong to anyone else. Therefore the soul submits to Him, responds to His love, and so she also desires Him, rejoices in her life with Him and praises Him.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 12- And the daughter of Tyre shall be there with a gift; even the rich among the people shall intreat thy favour.

1- Tyre was the greatest commercial center in the world, and it was near the land of the Jews, lying to its north on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. It was rich, but unfortunately it was immersed in corruption and idolatry. The daughter of Tyre means the souls that believed in Christ, left behind their wealth and their evils, and drew near to the Church seeking her favor.

2- The drawing near of the daughters of Tyre, that is, its people, is a type of all the Gentile peoples who believed in Christ and offered Him their gift, which is faith and repentance. By this they pleased the Church, and she received them into her membership. On this pattern the Magi went and came to Christ, being among the great and the rich of the world, and offered Him gifts.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 13- The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold.
Her chamber: the inner room of the bride.

1- He describes the bride, that is, the Church, or the believing soul, as having all her glory within, as the glory of the Tabernacle was within it, where the golden Ark of the Covenant, the altar, the lampstand and the golden table of the showbread were. As for the outside, it was skins of badgers, with no appearance, just as Christ Himself had no form nor comeliness (Isa 53:2), yet He is God the Savior of the world. Likewise the soul that believes in Christ has her beauty in her inner virtues, and does not seek to speak of them lest she fall into pride, and she lives a hidden life, that God may glorify her with glories that cannot be expressed in heaven, and she enjoys a hidden, secret relationship with Christ through the Holy Sacraments. Her outward appearance seems to be suffering, stripped and despised, but within her is joy and satisfaction in her heavenly Bridegroom.
2- The garments of the bride are woven with gold, as in the Tabernacle and the Temple of Solomon.

Gold signifies heaven, so the bride lives a heavenly life and is adorned with virtues; indeed she is the temple of the Holy Spirit, and her heart is fixed on heaven, where her Bridegroom is, who is concerned to look upon her heart and her inner beauty.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 14- She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee.

1- The king's daughter, that is, the souls that enter into the faith and live with Christ, wears embroidered garments, that is, her life is adorned with virtues. She does not come forward to Christ the King empty-handed, but with virtues and good works, because she loves Him and her heart is attached to Him, and she expresses her love through these works. Love is expressed through spiritual striving, as it says, "shall be brought."

2- And behind the souls that began with Christ in faith, that is, behind the first Church that was founded on the disciples and the Apostles and those who believed on the day of Pentecost, many came forward to the faith; they believed through the hands of the Apostles and the preachers and came forward to Christ, so the Church expanded and spread throughout the whole world. Did the Apostles believe that all these priests and servants would come after them throughout the generations?! And likewise St. Stephen, the first martyr: did he imagine the multitudes of martyrs who would come after him until today?! And St. Anthony, the father of monks: did he imagine that all these monks in the world would come after him?!
All these souls are virgins, meaning spiritual virginity, that is, hearts consecrated to God, with no place for evil within them. They reject idolatry and keep away from all evil by repentance.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 15- With gladness and rejoicing shall they be brought: they shall enter into the king's palace.

1- The souls that believed in Christ rejoiced and entered to Christ the King in His Church, to live a life of constant joy through their relationship with Christ the King, and through the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace.
