These souls came forward of their own free will, and with joy, to live with Christ, enjoy His love, and express their joy by constant praise of Him.

2- The souls of the believers enter into the palace of the King, that is, they are near Him to enjoy His love. And as they are faithful in their love for Him inside the earthly palace of the King, inside the Church, they become worthy of the heavenly palace, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 16- Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth.

The king's daughter does not apply to the Jewish nation, for it did not have children in place of its fathers who became princes in all the earth. It applies only to the Church, which in place of her fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and all the fathers and prophets, has sons who are princes over the whole earth, namely the bishops and priests, who led the Church and the whole world in the way of life with Christ.

entries.section: (2) The queen, the bride, and her glory

paragraphs.text: 17- I will make thy name to be remembered in all generations: therefore shall the people praise thee for ever and ever.

1- David ends the psalm with a covenant which God offers, namely that he will remember God and glorify Him and live with Him all the days of his life, indeed from generation to generation. By this he means that his seed of believing Jews will continue to remember the name of God, and then whoever of them believes in Christ will continue to praise His holy name through the days. When the believer remembers the name of God he enjoys fellowship with Him and lives in His fear, so he keeps away from every sin, and then becomes an example to those around him, as they see the power of God in him and believe in his God. And the psalms that David wrote are chanted by the believers from generation to generation, that is, they pray and praise with them throughout the ages until today.

2- In this verse David declares a prophecy about the faith of the Gentiles by saying, "shall the people praise thee," that is, the Gentiles who will believe in Christ in the whole world and remember His name like David, so they enjoy all the spiritual blessings, and continue to remember the name of God throughout the generations on earth, and then extend in praising the name of God forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

Delight in remembering the name of God many times every day, that your mind, and then your heart, may be lifted up to Him; this will give you peace, and then God will reveal His secrets to you and give you joy in His fellowship, and you will live in joy forever.
The Lord of hosts our refuge. To the chief musician, for the sons of Korah, upon Alamoth, a song: "God is our refuge and strength ... v. 1"
Introduction:
1- Its writer: the sons of Korah, that is, one of the descendants of Korah, who were Levite singers.
2- When was it written?
a- A prophecy about the victory of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, over three peoples who attacked him, the children of Ammon, Moab and Edom (2 Chr 20:20-24).
b- A prophecy about the victory of King Hezekiah over the army of Sennacherib by the angel of the Lord (2 Kgs 19:35).
c- A prophecy about the victory of Christ by the Cross over Satan, his binding, and the occurrence of an earthquake, which happened at the ninth hour on Great Friday (Mt 27:51).
3- The title of this psalm is written "upon Alamoth"; the Alamoth is a high vocal range similar to what is now the soprano range, in which the singers sang in the days of David (1 Chr 15:20).
4- In the title it also says of this psalm that it is a "song," that is, a hymn of praise said in the Temple.

5- This psalm is connected with the psalm before it. In the forty-fifth psalm we see the union of the bride with her Bridegroom and His glorifying her, that is, Christ's glorifying the Church. In this psalm he makes clear that the Church will meet tribulations, but God supports her, establishes her and gives her victory.
6- This psalm is a song of praise, or a hymn of thanksgiving, and the two following psalms, 47 and 48, agree with it in this purpose.
7- Some churches pray this psalm on the Feast of the Theophany (Epiphany), on the feast of the wedding at Cana of Galilee, and at the consecration of new churches.

8- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Third Hour, which reminds us of the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Church, because it speaks to us about the power of the Holy Spirit who supports, establishes and gives victory to the Church.
1- God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

1- The Church and every soul that believes in God face war from the demons, in addition to the visible enemies, who are the wicked stirred up against her by the demons; but God offers His protection to the Church in three forms:
a- Refuge: that is, a fortress in which His children take shelter, so that no one can harm them, however strong he may be.
b- Strength: so that the children of God can conquer all their enemies through Him.
c- Help: that is, a supporter of His children spiritually, psychologically and physically, so that they remain steadfast in the battle and are never shaken.

2- The Church's past experiences with God confirm her faith, for God has been found exceedingly strong in troubles, that is, a supporter of His children throughout history and a deliverer of them from troubles that could not be passed through by reason; indeed He also glorified them, and they praised God.
2- Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea;

1- The writer of the psalm affirms the steadfastness of the children of God, whatever changes occur around them, even if they are powerful natural changes, such as earthquakes that move the earth; yet the children of God remain steadfast, and whatever the circumstances change, or the principles and values around them are shaken, they continue in their faith and their sound spiritual conduct.

2- Then he presents a natural change that is hard to imagine, namely the overturning of the mountains, which are the strongest and most stable thing on earth. If these mountains were to fall into the midst of the seas, the children of God would remain steadfast in their faith; that is, if the strongest powers of the world were overturned and sank in the seas, or if the great ones, even the religious leaders, were plunged into the lusts of the world and drowned in them, the true children of God would remain in their spiritual steadfastness, as happened when religious leaders fell into heresies, such as Nestorius, Eutyches and Arius.
3- The removal of the earth is a type of the earthquake that occurred at the crucifixion of Christ, announcing the turmoil of the world and its need of the Redeemer and Savior.
3- Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof. Selah.
Roar: the voices of the waves rise.
Be troubled: the waters surge and run so swiftly that they hinder the passage of ships and boats.
Swelling thereof: its rising and greatness.

1- The writer of the psalm affirms that our God is our refuge even if the earth is removed and the mountains are overturned. Likewise he says in this verse, even if the waters of the seas move with great force and their voices rise, as happens in floods, and even if the mountains become greater in their great height, all this will not shake the faith of the children of God who take refuge in Him, for He is their refuge and strength.

2- The mountains are a type of the mighty and the great ones in this world, and the waters are a type of the multitude of people, or of the multitude of armies, such as the Assyrian army which attacked Jerusalem in the days of King Hezekiah. All these cause no turmoil in the hearts of the children of God who are steadfast in faith in Him.

3- He says the word Selah at the end of the verse, which is a musical pause, so that a person may contemplate the power of God, the fortified refuge, and no longer be disturbed by the turmoil of the world.

Take refuge in God when things are in turmoil around you, so that your heart is not shaken with them, but stands firm in your faith and remembers the power of God that supports you; and as your prayers increase you will experience the help of God and feel His presence with you.
4- There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High.

1- The children of God who take refuge in their God, who is their refuge, are not troubled by the shaking of the world around them, but enjoy the work of the Holy Spirit in them, who is a river whose streams make glad the city of God. These streams are the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit, who works in the believers within the Church, which is the city of God. The Church is the holiest place in the world; in her the Most High God dwells, and He abides and dwells in His believing children who are united to Him through His holy sacraments. This verse is a prophecy about the work of the Holy Spirit in the believers in the New Testament (Jn 7:37-39).

2- The Holy Spirit, who is the river, has as His streams the Apostles, the priests who are their successors, and the servants, who preach the word of God and make glad the city of God, which is the Church. The river's water is sweet and flows quietly, unlike the salty sea whose waters roar and surge; so the work of the Holy Spirit is calm and restful within believing souls, and He works in service with spirituality and calm.

3- The Holy Spirit, who is the river, continues to work in the Church until He raises her to heaven, where the dwellings of the Most High God abide forever, and there the believers enjoy God with an enjoyment that cannot be expressed. And they delight in holiness in the holy place of the tabernacles of the Most High, that is, the place that the Holy Spirit sanctified, that the children of God may dwell in it forever.

4- The streams are also the baptisms which the Holy Spirit has granted to His churches, so that the souls of the believers rejoice in the new members, and are sanctified as dwellings of the Most High God, and are established in His Church forever.
5- God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early.

1- God's dwelling in the midst of His Church keeps her from being shaken before the world's opposition and persecutions against her, because God in her midst protects her and strengthens His children who live in the world yet remain holding fast to His commandments, however much evil opposes them.

2- God helps His children in the Old Testament until the morning comes, which is the incarnation of Christ the Savior, so that they enjoy His salvation, in the hope of which they lived and died. He also helps all who believe in Him "right early," that is, Christ in His Second Coming on the day of judgment, when He justifies them by His blood. So God helps them on the way of their spiritual striving until they reach the Kingdom.
6- The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted.

1- The pagan nations, headed by the Roman state, tried to resist Christianity, and persecuted the Church after the Jewish persecution, but God turned the persecutions into strength which the Church received. On the other hand the kingdoms melted, that is, the Roman Empire melted within the Church when Constantine ascended the throne of the Roman state, and attended the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea.

2- When Christ cried out on the Cross and said, "It is finished," the earth melted, that is, an earthquake occurred, the veil of the Temple was torn, and the tombs were opened, because Christ had accomplished the redemption (Mt 27:51; Mk 15:37, 38).

3- The nations resisted the Church but submitted to her after this. Then Christ comes in His Second Coming and utters His voice to judge the world, and the earth melts before Him, and the wicked try to hide from His face; then He glorifies His children in His Kingdom, and casts the wicked into eternal torment (2 Pet 3:10).
7- The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah.

The writer ends his words about the steadfastness of the children of God by reassuring them that God is very strong, because He is the Lord of hosts, meaning the heavenly hosts, of which only one is able to kill the army of the Assyrians in the days of King Hezekiah. The mighty God is the refuge of His children and His people, who are Jacob, or Israel, and then the Christians in the New Testament. He ends this verse with the word Selah, so that the reader may contemplate God, the supporter and the one who establishes His children.

The Holy Spirit dwelling in you is able to establish you and support you in all situations, however difficult; so do not worry, and do not think about tomorrow, because God who supports you dwells in you forever.

8- Come, behold the works of the LORD, what desolations he hath made in the earth. 9- He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.

1- God, who dwells in the midst of His people, triumphed over the nations around them and laid them waste, broke their weapons and burned them with fire, and crushed the armies of the enemies, so the earth around His people became quiet. This happened in the days of David and before him, that is, the days of Joshua and Moses. Thus God's superiority over all the gods of the pagan nations appeared, and His victory over them. Therefore the writer calls all peoples, and even the children of God themselves, to contemplate the power of God, victorious over the enemies.

2- In a moment, when Christ died on the Cross, He bound Satan, laid waste his kingdom, and broke and burned his weapons, that is, they became worthless before the power of God dwelling in His children, because the Holy Spirit dwelt in them through the sacrament of the Holy Myron, and by this the earth became calm and the children of God lived in peace. The souls that believe in Christ are not disturbed by the wars and weapons of Satan, because God who dwells in them lays waste these lusts which fight against them, and gives His children virtues in their place.

3- On the day of judgment Christ nullifies the power of the demons and utterly lays waste his kingdom by casting him into eternal torment, and His children dwell with Him in the Kingdom, enjoying His fellowship forever.
10- Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth. 11- The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah.

1- At the close of this psalm the writer asks the believers to cease from base lusts, and also from fear of the demons and their wars and all the powers of evil, for they are worthless before the power of God; and to cease also from relying on the passing and weak powers of men, that their reliance may be on God alone.

2- He also asks the believers to be lifted up with Christ who was crucified and then ascended into heaven, so that they leave their earthly concerns and busy themselves with the heavenly life, that is, that they have a spiritual way of life.

3- He affirms at the end of the psalm that God, the Lord of hosts, is with us, and that He gives victory to His people in every generation. We have already explained the last verse in the explanation of (v. 7).

That you may conquer your enemies the demons, may you fix your eyes and your heart on Christ, so that you are not disturbed by the power of the enemies; lift yourself up and leave your evil lusts by repentance, and you will behold the work of God in you and rejoice in it. The shout: God the King of the earth. To the chief musician. For the sons of Korah. A psalm: "O clap your hands, all ye people") ... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the sons of Korah.
2- When was it written?
a- When David brought the Ark of the Covenant back to Jerusalem (1 Sam 6:19-21).
b- A prophecy about God's victory over Sennacherib and his army (2 Kgs 18:13-19:37).
c- A prophecy about the redemption of Christ, which was accomplished on the Cross, so that He reigned over all who believe in Him from among the Gentiles and the Jews.
d- A prophecy about the ascension of Christ into heaven (v. 5).
e- A prophecy about the Second Coming of Christ on the day of judgment, to reign over those who believe in Him from the whole earth.
3- The Jews used to chant this psalm at the Feast of Trumpets (Num 29:1) and their great feasts.
4- In the Coptic Orthodox Church the priest recites it after the end of the Liturgy, as he goes around the altar and claps his hands to glorify God.
5- Some churches recite this psalm on the feasts of the Theophany and the Ascension.
6- This psalm is suited to every soul that loves God and longs for Him to reign over her, so she praises Him that longing for Him may be renewed in her heart.
7- This psalm is one of the psalms of praise, like the psalm before it and the one after it.
8- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms.

9- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Agpeya at the Third Hour, in which the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, in order to glorify God who reigned over His Church and those who believe in Him.
1- O clap your hands, all ye nations; shout unto God with the voice of triumph.
1- The writer of the psalm calls the whole world to believe in God and praise Him, and to express its joy by clapping its hands, and also by shouting, that is, praising with a loud voice.

2- Clapping of hands is a type of good works, by which the believer expresses his love for God, and when people see his good works they glorify God, so that the believer's words are mingled with his works, and when others glorify God they love Him and submit to Him; that is, the believer can draw those around him to the worship of God.
2- For the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth.

In this verse he describes God as high, that is, exalted above all the pagan gods, all men and all heavenly and earthly creatures. He describes Him also as terrible, that is, feared by those in heaven and on earth, and he likewise names Him a great King over all the earth, that is, everything is under His authority; and there is no king on earth to whom all the nations have submitted except Christ, in whom many have believed from every place in the world.

You are a light to the world, and you must glorify God in your life by your good works and your upright speech, and by this you draw souls to God; and take care lest you be a stumbling block to anyone, and drive them away from God.
3- He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet.

1- By the Cross Christ accomplished redemption, so all the peoples of the Jews, that is, their tribes, submitted to Him, namely the believers converted from the Jews. Likewise many of the pagan nations believed in Him. All these submitted to the preaching of the Apostles, who led them in the way of faith, so they learned humility, abandoning their philosophies and boasting in their lineages.

2- Likewise Christ gave His disciples and those who believe in Him authority over the demons, so that they tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Lk 10:19), and cast out the demons who held sway over men; in addition to giving the believers power to repel all the thoughts of the demons.
3- The submission to God of the peoples and nations increases in the souls consecrated to Christ, whether in the priesthood, or monasticism, or any service.
4- He shall choose our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved. Selah.

1- God chose His people to give them His promises, and out of His love He chose for them their portion, which is God Himself, and poured out His blessings on them; He gave them the land of Canaan, and blessed their crops, their cattle and all their possessions, so they were distinguished from the other peoples by God's dwelling in their midst and His protection of them.

2- God chose His people, the descendants of Jacob, who loved the birthright, that is, heavenly things. But Esau preferred the lentils, that is, material things. So Jacob boasted in God and God boasted in him, and Jacob became the portion of the Lord, and God became an inheritance for him.
3- The writer ends the verse with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for contemplating the love of God, and consequently the response of His people to Him.

How beautiful it is that your portion should be the Lord, so that you think of Him and are occupied with Him, and repeat His psalms every day, and taste the sweetness of fellowship with Him, and even enjoy seeing Him in your life, and live the Kingdom while you are on earth.
5- God is gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet.
The trumpet (shofar): a musical instrument, a horn made from the horn of an animal, that is, a wind instrument used in worship.

This verse is a clear prophecy about Christ, who conquered death, rose from the dead, and ascended into the heavens before the eyes of His disciples, who worshipped Him and then returned to Jerusalem with great joy, glorifying and praising God (Lk 24:21-53). And when Christ was lifted up into heaven the angels received Him with joy, which is expressed here by the sound of the trumpet. And at His Second Coming the angels will sound the trumpet, announcing His arrival (1 Thess 4:16).
6- Sing praises to God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises. 7- For God is the King of all the earth: sing a poem.

1- Because of the greatness of the divine ascension into heaven, which means the possibility of mankind's ascending and entering the places that were closed since the expulsion of Adam, so that it becomes the right of those who believe in Christ to enter Paradise and then the Kingdom, for all this the psalm calls all readers to sing praises to God, who is King over all the earth. But at the same time it calls Him in (v. 6) "our King," that is, although He is King over all the earth because He created it, He especially gives the believers in Him the enjoyment of His reign over their hearts, to give them His special blessings, the most important of which is His dwelling in their hearts.

2- This singing is to be in the form of a poem, that is, melodious verse with great meanings, so the writer asks that the singing be with understanding, and he repeats the word "sing praises" four times in (v. 6), which is a type of the four corners of the world, that is, he calls the whole earth to sing praises to God; and this draws the hearts of those who believe in Christ to the heaven into which He ascended, and consequently they live a heavenly life.

Praise lifts your heart to heaven and looses your chains that bind you to the lusts of the world; so be diligent in hymns and praises, that you may live with God and glorify Him, and He may bless you.
8- God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness.

1- God reigned on the Cross when He died to redeem all mankind, and He reigned over the hearts of those who believed from the pagan nations, as He reigned over the hearts of those converted from the Jews. For God sanctified and purified the hearts of those who believe in Him by Baptism, and sat in them, so they are the throne of His holiness.

2- The throne of God's holiness is the four living creatures who are not incarnate; this is the heavenly throne. But Christ in His humility was born in the manger and crucified on the Cross, and by this humility of His He made the heart of the least believer in Him a throne on which He sits. And the reigning of God means that He takes care of the whole man and blesses him, and sitting means continuance and permanence in the heart of man.

9- The princes of the people are gathered together, even the people of the God of Abraham: for God is the shield of the earth; he is greatly exalted. Shields: plural of shield, the large buckler. The shield is a defensive instrument which the soldier uses in war to ward off arrows from his body.

1- The princes of the people are the great ones of the peoples who believed in Christ, and many of them became servants and preachers. These gathered together, and with them also those converted from Jewish origin; all these are the people of the God of Abraham, because Abraham is the father of the Jews and the Gentiles, and everyone who lived by the faith of Abraham and did his works and accepted faith in Christ enjoyed the salvation of Christ.

2- God in His love is a shield, that is, a protection for the whole earth. What is meant is protection for all who believe in Him in the whole earth. And God is greatly exalted, that is, above all the pagan gods and likewise the earthly kings; therefore whoever believes in Him enjoys complete protection and no harm touches him.

God is able to protect you from any things that harm you, so why are you disturbed by the changes of the world? Take refuge in Him and hold fast to Him always, and He will turn everything to your good and nullify the plot of the demons directed against you, and if you fall He raises you up and supports you.
The city of God. A song and psalm for the sons of Korah: "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised") ... v. 1) Introduction:
1- The writers of this psalm are the sons of Korah.
2- It speaks about the city of God, that is, Zion, which is a type of the Church of the New Testament, and it contemplates her beauty and her great attributes.
3- Perhaps this psalm is a prophecy about the defeat of Sennacherib before the walls of Jerusalem, which God protected (vv. 4-6).

4- Perhaps this psalm is also a prophecy about the victory of Jehoshaphat over three kings, the children of Ammon, Moab and Edom, who were terrified before the city of God, while the people of God were praising and glorifying God (2 Chr 20:1-30).

5- It is a psalm of praise and thanksgiving to God like the two psalms before it: Psalm 46 speaks to us about God the refuge, Psalm 47 speaks to us about God the King, and this psalm speaks to us about God in His great city.
6- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in the mountain of his holiness.

1- The writer first glorifies the builder of the city, who is God, and describes Him as great and worthy of praise and thanksgiving for His care and keeping of His children, and for all His great and good works.

2- He describes Jerusalem and names it the mountain of God's holiness, since it is built on five mountains and in it is His holy Temple. He also describes it as the city of our God in which He dwells and which He blesses, and this means the special relationship with God, for He is our God, and the beauty of God appears in the greatness of His city and in His Temple. And the mountain of God's holiness, by the spirit of prophecy, is the Church, and the soul of every believer.
2- Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King.
The writer speaks about the attributes of the city of God, and describes it as follows:

1- Beautiful for situation: it is elevated because it is built on mountains, and this elevation is beautiful, not only because it draws the eyes of people to its great Temple, but also because it is a type of its being raised above earthly and material things, and its drawing near to heavenly things, for it represents holiness, spirituality and loftiness.

2- The joy of the whole earth: it gladdens the hearts of all who believe in God in all the earth, who come to worship in His holy Temple, and from it Christ would come, the joy and salvation of all the earth.
3- Mount Zion: it is firm like the mountain, strong like Mount Zion on which it is built, because God establishes it by His dwelling in it.

4- The joy of the sides of the north: it is the joy and salvation of the pagan great ones who come from the north, namely the Assyrians, the Babylonians and Persia, who attacked Jerusalem. These believed in Christ who came forth from Jerusalem, and submitted to Him and rejoiced in His salvation.
5- The city of the great King: it is the dwelling place of God the great King, because He dwells in Jerusalem His city and gladdens it with His blessings.

These five attributes are enjoyed by every soul that has believed in Christ and in which He dwells: she is lofty, joyful and firm, her heart is open to all, and she enjoys the dwelling of Christ in her.
3- God is known in her palaces for a refuge.

1- The palaces of the city of God are its great buildings which God blesses, so that they become a refuge for its inhabitants, who take shelter in them because God is with them. This is what happened to Jerusalem as long as she was firm in her faith, but when she forsook God and worshipped idols the Babylonians destroyed her.

2- The palaces are the souls of the believers in which God dwells, so that they become a refuge to which all people take shelter, to take of their peace and joy, and to learn from them how to live with God. So she is a refuge for them in the midst of the wilderness of the world.

God wants to beautify your soul, and raise it above the world so that it may be a light to every person; so submit to Him and hold fast to His commandments, that He may dwell in you, satisfy you, gladden you and work through you.

4- For, lo, the kings were assembled, they passed by together. 5- They saw it, and so they marvelled; they were troubled, and hasted away. 6- Fear took hold upon them there, and pain, as of a woman in travail. 7- Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind.
Tarshish: a famous commercial city in the ancient world, located in the south of Spain.

1- The writer of the psalm tells us about the assembling of kings to attack the city of God, Jerusalem, but strangely, after their assembling they departed and could not harm the city. Why was that? He declares the reason, which is that these kings saw something that amazed them, so they marvelled greatly, then feared with a great fear, and fled quickly. They felt terrible dread, and even suffered from their fear as a woman suffers when she is giving birth, as the pains of travail come upon her suddenly; thus they suffered intensely and fled far away. The sudden, intense terror of these enemies is likened to what happens when a strong east wind blows upon the great ships of Tarshish and breaks and ruins them.

2- This did in fact happen more than once with the city of Jerusalem. The kings of Moab, Edom and the children of Ammon assembled to attack Jerusalem in the days of King Jehoshaphat, who prayed to God and He reassured him; and Jehoshaphat went out with his army with the companies of praisers at the head of it, and when the allied armies of the enemies saw them they were struck dumb and marvelled greatly at this praise, but they were seized with great fear when a group of soldiers who had been hiding in ambushes rose up against them, and panic covered them and they fled. Perhaps these ambushes were angelic soldiers (2 Chr 20:22). It also happened when the commanders of the Assyrian armies assembled and besieged Jerusalem under the leadership of Sennacherib in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, who prayed to God, and Isaiah the prophet reassured him. And in the night the angel of the LORD appeared with his drawn sword to the armies of the Assyrians, and they were struck dumb, then feared greatly, especially when the sword of the angel began to work upon their necks, so that 185,000 soldiers of the enemy armies fell, and the rest fled (2 Kgs 19:35).

3- These verses show that however great the power of the enemies, and their pride and greatness, like the ships of Tarshish, God, when He sees them wishing to harm His city Jerusalem, frightens them, so they are troubled, and suffer, and flee. And the east wind is a type of the Holy Spirit, who shatters the power of the unbelievers who attack the city of God, and even turns some of them to faith, while the rest flee in great fear.
8- As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish it for ever. Selah.

1- The writer declares that God's protection of His city was fulfilled in the days of the fathers, and we heard of it from them, such as the ten plagues in Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea, and also the parting of the Jordan, the crossing of the people of God, the fall of the walls of Jericho, and all the victories of God in the land of Canaan. In addition to this the writer says we have seen with our own eyes the works of God, and His protection of His children in our generation, for the works of God are renewed every day, for He is "the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8). And He is the Lord of the invincible heavenly hosts, and He protects His city and establishes it for ever. What is meant by being established for ever is the heavenly Jerusalem, where the children of God reign with Him forever; for the earthly Jerusalem was destroyed more than once, but that which is established for ever is the heavenly Jerusalem.
2- At the end of the verse is the word Selah, which is a musical pause for contemplating the greatness of the city of God, and His mighty work in her, that we may glorify Him and praise Him.

Believe in God and hold fast to His commandments however much troubles or threats surround you; they cannot harm you, and God keeps you and establishes your faith, until He transfers you to heaven and gives you joy with Him in His Kingdom.
9- We have thought of thy lovingkindness, O God, in the midst of thy temple. 10- According to thy name, O God, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth: thy right hand is full of righteousness.
1- After we heard and saw the greatness of God in (v. 8), now in this verse we remember and speak of His great works.

2- Being in the Temple of God makes us feel His presence, and makes us remember Him, and remember His mercy and His great works. Just as His name is holy, so all His works are holy, and great, and good. And the highest form of God's mercy appears in His condescending to give us His Body and Blood on the altar every day for forgiveness, comfort and satisfaction of His children.

3- It is the nature of God to do righteousness, and His right hand, that is, His power, appears in the abundance of His righteousness. And the greatest form of His right hand is the Incarnation of His only-begotten Son Jesus Christ to redeem mankind and fill the world with righteousness by His good works. All this makes those who believe in God praise Him continually.
11- Let mount Zion rejoice, let the daughters of Judah be glad, because of thy judgments.

God, who governs the world by His wisdom, created all things and set for them laws by which they proceed, in addition to His commandments and judgments, which He gave to His children to live by, leading them to the Kingdom. In all this His city Zion rejoices, that is, Jerusalem, established by His power like the mountain, and she is a type of the firm Church of the New Testament and of the heavenly Jerusalem, firm forever; and the daughters of Judah who worship God in Jerusalem also rejoice, and they are a type of the souls of those who believe in God, for they rejoice in His presence in their midst, and in His judgments and commandments which guide them on their way.
God calls you to joy if you meditate on His commandments and His word, so be satisfied with the Holy Bible every day, and praise His holy name, and your heart will be filled with peace.
12- Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof. 13- Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following.

1- Zion is the most important of the mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built, so the writer calls the believers to walk about and go round the city, to contemplate its beauty and see its firmness. This was a custom of the ancients after the end of a war, to make sure of the soundness of the city's walls and towers; and by this going about they discovered the power of God and His protection and glorified Him, just as a person needs to go round his life and contemplate it after every spiritual battle, that is, to examine himself, to be reassured of his safety from any evil, and to glorify God who brought him through the trial.

2- The towers are the places of watching during war to protect the city from the enemies, the bulwarks are the walls built for the inhabitants to take shelter behind, and the palaces are the greatest buildings within the city. The towers are a type of the saints, the bulwarks a type of the means of grace, and the palaces a type of the virtues with which the Church and every believer are adorned. Therefore every person should examine himself, and how firmly he holds to holiness and the means of grace, and his striving to acquire virtues, and thank God for all His blessings, and tell of them to his children, that they may be firm in the faith and enjoy the work of God in the Church.

14- For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death. At the close of the psalm the writer declares an important truth, which is that God, who founded and preserved this city and its Temple, is our God whom we worship with all our hearts, especially since He walks with us on the way of life, and guides us to the Kingdom all our lives until death, and even continues with us in the Kingdom forever, to give us joy in His fellowship.

May you examine yourself every day, to know how often the enemy made you fall into sin, and how God kept you from many evils, and review how active you are in striving toward virtue, that you may be fortified in it. And as God sees your concern He supports you, blesses you and establishes you.
The inevitability of death. To the chief musician. For the sons of Korah. A psalm: "Hear this, all ye people") ... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the sons of Korah.
2- A wisdom psalm, that is, one full of words of wisdom, resembling the books of Job, Proverbs, Wisdom, and Jesus the son of Sirach.
3- It clarifies an important idea, which is that the rich who are great in the earth are not better than the poor, because the end of all of them is one, which is death.
4- Many wise sayings and counsels are drawn from this psalm, the most important of which are:
a- The importance of uprightness in life.
b- Trust in God.
c- The strangeness of the world (our being strangers in it).

5- This psalm is the eighth of the psalms which bear the title "for the sons of Korah," which are the psalms (Ps 42-49), to which four other psalms for the sons of Korah are added, namely (Ps 84, 85, 87, 88), so that the total of the psalms bearing "for the sons of Korah" in their titles is twelve psalms.
6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) A call to all to listen

paragraphs.text: 1- Hear this, all ye people; give ear, all ye inhabitants of the world:

The writer calls all peoples and those who dwell in the world, whether great or lowly, rich or poor, that is, all peoples, including the Jews, to hear and listen attentively to the truths he will mention in this psalm. By this he shows the importance of what he is about to say.

entries.section: (1) A call to all to listen

paragraphs.text: 3- My mouth shall speak of wisdom; and the meditation of my heart shall be of understanding. 4- I will incline mine ear to a parable: I will open my dark saying upon the harp. Meditation of my heart: recurring feelings that take hold and dominate.
I will incline mine ear: I will listen humbly.

1- The writer makes clear that what he declares in this psalm is wisdom and counsel uttered by his tongue, springing from feelings that recur within him. He feels every word he speaks, because they are important truths and basic concepts that every person needs.

2- The writer also humbles himself, listening to the beating of his heart, and then expresses it in a parable that confirms the truth he wants, because parables affect the hearer more than the direct truth, and are easy to understand. He also explains the counsels he declares, which seem hidden like a riddle, and presents them set to music, accompanied by a musical instrument, the harp, so that the hearer may accept them more easily.

May you listen attentively to the words of God and the guidance of your father of confession, for they are the direct voice of God to you, to act on, so that you live reassured and take steady steps toward the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 5- Wherefore should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels shall compass me about?
My heels: that is, my two heels, which are the two heel bones at the bottom of a person's feet.

1- The writer asks why I should fear the days of evil, that is, the days in which disasters and trials come. There are no evil days, but he means days that bring him troubles. For God uses these trials for his good, the purification of his soul, and his preparation for eternity.

2- What should frighten a person in the days of evil, which means the day of judgment, is only that his iniquities and sins, for which God will hold him to account, compass his feet; therefore a person should repent of his sins and prepare for the day of judgment.

3- The iniquity of my heels is the ancestral sin, the sin of Adam, which pursues me to the day of judgment, but through Christ the Redeemer I am freed from it in the water of Baptism. The iniquity of my heels is also the iniquities which I commit at the heel of my life, that is, the end of my life, and do not repent of; these condemn me on the day of judgment.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 6- They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches; 7- None of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him:

The writer rebukes the rich for trusting in their money and boasting in it. It cannot remove their sins from them, or stop the trials that come upon them, and consequently wealth cannot redeem a man after death or guarantee him a happy eternal life. And a man, or an upright brother, cannot redeem his wicked brother, and the upright cannot give God a ransom for his wicked brother, but each one is judged according to his works.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 8- (For the redemption of their soul is precious, and it ceaseth for ever:) 9- That he should still live for ever, and not see corruption. Ceaseth: remains preserved.

The writer turns in his speech to the poor, the lowly and the despised, and encourages them that their souls are very precious in the sight of God, and that they will live forever and ever. They must live looking to eternity, and not to this short life with its misery, which ends quickly in death, so that they are not disturbed by the toils of this life, nor by death and the grave; for if their precious souls live with God He will glorify them and give them rest in eternity.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 10- For he seeth that wise men die, likewise the fool and the brutish person perish, and leave their wealth to others. 11- Their inward thought is, that their houses shall continue for ever, and their dwelling places to all generations; they call their lands after their own names.

1- Death is seen by the wise, and they prepare for it by an upright life; but the fool, who has the information and knowledge of this world but is a fool in the spiritual life and immersed in lusts and the love of money, and likewise the brutish person, who does not understand the sciences of this world and does not know the importance of preparing for eternity, both of them, the fool and the brutish person, die and leave their wealth, and find no rest in eternity.

2- The strange thing is that the fool and the brutish person have strange thoughts within them, for they believe they will live forever in rest and greatness; that is, their outward greatness in their houses and their fame, as they give their names to houses, streets, squares and cities in order to immortalize their names, and they believe that this will continue forever although it is passing. The conclusion is that money and fame in this world do not benefit in eternity.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 12- Nevertheless man being in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts that perish.

The writer continues here his speech about the rich man who was occupied with the lust of the love of money and gained honor among men because of his wealth; he declares here that he does not abide in honor, that is, honor does not follow him after death, but he goes to Hades and loses his honor, because he dies and is buried like the beasts, which represent animal lust, for they have no honor in eternity and do not live forever in the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 13- This their way is their folly: yet their posterity approve their sayings. Selah.

In this verse the writer declares that those who relied on their wealth, and likewise their descendants who imitated them and lived occupied with the lust of money, die and are buried without honor like the animals, as we mentioned in the previous verse. Then he mentions the word Selah, a musical note, so that the reader may contemplate the vanity of wealth and the honor of this passing world.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 14- Like sheep they are laid in the grave; death shall feed on them; and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning; and their beauty shall consume in the grave from their dwelling.

1- The rich who were occupied with the lust of money die and are buried like the beasts, as we mentioned in the two previous verses. And their portraits which they hung on the walls, and likewise their power and their glory during their life in the world, wear away and vanish after death, because they dwell and settle in the grave, that is, Hades. Then judgment awaits them, where God judges them. And the upright have dominion over them, that is, they judge them, because they lived in the world like them but feared God. By "the morning" he means early after death, that is, the judgment, when God shines with His light and takes the godly into the Kingdom, and casts the wicked into eternal torment.

2- Those who were occupied with the love of money are shepherded by death, and lose all their honor, because they refused the care of God during their life, and left the commandments of God, and loved the world; therefore they face humiliation and disgrace in Hades after death.

entries.section: (2) Death, the end of all men

paragraphs.text: 15- But God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. Selah.

1- The hope of the upright is that God will redeem them from Hades. Those who died in the hope of the expected Messiah awaited His redemption, which was accomplished in the fullness of time, and He redeemed them, brought them up from Hades and moved them to Paradise.

2- The writer's faith in God appears in that he hopes for the redemption of Christ after he goes to Hades, so that He brings him up with the believers to Paradise. Then he ends with the word Selah so that the reader may contemplate the great redemption of Christ for those who believe in Him.

Do not be occupied with the lusts of this passing world, because they are perishable; and do not be disturbed if one of your material rights is lost, but be concerned first for your relationship with God, and keep your peace, looking to the heavenly glories in which God will compensate you for all that you lost in the world.

16- Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; 17- For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him. 18- Though while he lived he blessed his soul: and men will praise thee, when thou doest well to thyself.

1- Do not fear the rich who have great possessions and material power, for the glory of these rich is tied to their passing possessions, which they will lose by death, and so they become without glory, especially since they cared for money and relied on it to glorify them; for he says "the glory of his house," and not his glory.

2- These rich have no other glory, meaning spiritual glory in their faith in Christ, and they also accepted praise from the hypocrites and the self-interested around them, who saw the rich blessing their souls, that is, indulging themselves in the various material lusts. By this these rich increased in deceiving themselves, and drew away from God.
19- He shall go to the generation of his fathers; they shall never see light. 20- Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.

1- This rich man, who was occupied with his wealth, the worldly lusts, and the praise of others, will leave all this and die, and join his fathers whose life he lived, occupied with the love of money, and he will enter Hades, where there is eternal darkness, the reward of his distance from God, the true light.

2- The writer ends this psalm by saying that God gave honor to every person, and even increased His giving and honored the rich with many possessions, that they might use them in almsgiving to the needy. But in selfishness they kept them for themselves. And the ordinary person did not live as the image of God. Likewise those to whom God gave His knowledge, such as the Jews, and who did not use this knowledge to believe in Christ, all these die like the beasts, that is, they lose the heavenly glory and go to Hades and torment, just as the beasts have no heavenly glory.

If wealth is vain and passing, take care to use it for the glory of God; take what you need and use the rest in doing good. Do not be occupied, like others, with gathering money, and do not be attached to it, for it is only a means that helps you live, so that you may enjoy a strong relationship with God, until you reach your great heavenly place. God the Judge: "The God of gods, the LORD, hath spoken") ... v. 1) Introduction:

1- Its writer: Asaph, who was the chief of the singers in the days of the prophet David, and was of the tribe of Levi, and was assisted by two of the chief singers, Heman the Ezrahite and Ethan the Ezrahite (1 Chr 15:19). He led all the companies of praise in the Temple on the holy feast days. He was called the seer (2 Chr 29:30). The sons of Asaph also served in the ministry of singing, and continued in their service after the captivity, for one hundred and twenty-eight of them returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:41). Asaph wrote twelve psalms, the first of which is this psalm, then the psalms (Ps 73-83).

2- When was it written? It was written in the days of the prophet David, and he was speaking about the greatness of Jerusalem and her beauty, and perhaps he wrote it by the spirit of prophecy about Jerusalem after the division of the kingdom, specifically in the days of Hezekiah or King Josiah.
3- This psalm tells us about God the Judge who will judge His people, and also the wicked, and about God's preference for worship of the heart, and not formal worship.
4- The writer of the psalm directs our eyes to the importance of loving God and praising Him, and likewise of loving others and not judging them.
5- This is a didactic psalm in which God speaks to direct His people to right worship.

6- The psalm tells us about the first coming of Christ in the fullness of time, incarnate and coming forth from Jerusalem (vv. 1, 2), then about His Second Coming on the great day of judgment (v. 4), so this is considered
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- The mighty God, even the LORD, hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.

1- The writer prophesies about the incarnation of Christ and His coming in the fullness of time, for He is the Lord who is above all the pagan gods. Christ, the Word of God, spoke and called men from every place in the world to hear the good news of salvation. For He appeared in Jerusalem, which he describes as the perfection of beauty. Jerusalem is built on five mountains, the most important of which is Mount Zion, and therefore it is sometimes called Zion, as in this verse. The Jews and the Gentiles heard His good news in Jerusalem, and then the news of His preaching spread through the Apostles in the regions of the world from the rising of the sun to the going down thereof.

2- He describes Zion as the perfection of beauty because in it is the Temple of God, which is a type of the Church, where the Holy Spirit gives the salvation which Christ accomplished on the Cross, and bestows it on the believers in the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace.

3- Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him. 4- He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people.

1- God came with fire and tempest when He descended on the Apostles and the Church on the day of Pentecost, and spoke on their tongues in languages they had not known, and they began to preach to the people of God who came from all nations. And God called the heavens and the earth to judge His people, because the heavens are a type of the prophets who are in Paradise, and the earth is a type of the godly Apostles, who all declare that the Messiah has come and redeemed His people, and who judge the Jews who did not believe and call them to faith. And three thousand souls of the Jews did believe and were baptized by the hands of the Apostles on the day of Pentecost.

2- These two verses also speak about the fearful Second Coming of Christ on the day of judgment with fire and tempest, and He calls heaven and earth to witness, that is, He calls the angels and saints who are in heaven, and likewise the godly who are still living on the earth, and all of them judge the people of God who did not believe, and they are driven to eternal torment.

3- Fire is a type of the power of the work of the Holy Spirit and of the word of God, which burns up sins within the one who believes in Christ. The tempest is the work of the Holy Spirit that shakes the soul and returns it to its Creator. Fire and tempest also signify the tribulations that come upon the believers in order to draw them to God.
5- Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice. 6- And the heavens shall declare his righteousness: for God is judge himself. Selah.

1- God asks His angels to gather to Him the believers in His holy name, who have made His covenant upon the sacrifice of the Cross offered on the altar of the Church, His most holy Body and Blood; to gather them from the regions of the world to enter His heavenly Kingdom. These are those who lived in the fear of God and walked in godliness all the days of their lives.

2- When God gathers His godly into His Kingdom, the angels who are in the heavens declare His justice in rewarding the righteous with eternal life. But the wicked He puts far from Him in the outer darkness, that is, eternal torment. Thus God the Judge completes His judgment of all mankind.
3- The word "Selah" at the end of the verse is a musical pause that calls us to contemplate the justice of God and His fear, that we may keep away from every sin and keep His commandments.
May you place the day of judgment before your eyes every day, to prepare for it by repentance, prayers, love for all around you, and forgiveness toward everyone.

entries.section: (2) God asks for sacrifices of praise

paragraphs.text: 7- "Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God.
God calls His people the children of Israel to hear Him. Several things appear from His call:
1- His concern to warn His people so that they do not continue in their sins.
2- Although they have sins, before everything else they are His people for whom He cares.
3- He reminds them that they are the descendants of Israel (Jacob), their father beloved by Him, so they are encouraged that they are near to the heart of God.
4- That He is their own God, who cares for them, for He says "thy God," so they are under His care and providence, and they trust that they are near to His heart and beloved.
5- God begins by encouraging and showing His love for His people before He testifies against their faults and rebukes them for them; it is a gentle method for drawing the hearers to listen.

entries.section: (2) God asks for sacrifices of praise

paragraphs.text: 8- I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, to have been continually before me.

God bears witness that His people are committed to offering the sacrifices and offerings that worship requires. Therefore God does not rebuke them for any shortcoming in worship, but rebukes them for the formality of worship, which is not accompanied by feelings of the heart, such as repentance, humility and love for God; and God wants the love of His people, and their feelings, before outward worship. God accepted the sacrifice of Abel for his good feelings, and did not accept the offering of Cain because of his evil, and He rejoiced in the widow's two mites more than in all the gifts of the rich.

entries.section: (2) God asks for sacrifices of praise

paragraphs.text: 9- I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he goats out of thy folds. 10- For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills. 11- I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field are mine. 12- If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof. 13- Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? He goats: what is meant is the male goats, or the kids.
The forest (wilds): the desolate place, or uninhabited, or mountainous.

1- God declares that He has no need for man to offer Him many sacrifices as formal worship. God is not in need, for He owns all the animals which He created, which run on the mountains and in the wilds and fly in the sky. God does not hunger or need, because He is perfect in Himself, but He asks only for the heart of man and his love, and if this accompanies his sacrifices the sacrifices become accepted and beloved by God. For God rejoices to see His children coming to worship Him, loving Him.

2- Perhaps these verses are an indication that animal sacrifices will cease, after Christ offered His blood on the Cross, and there was no longer need for the animal sacrifices that were a type of the sacrifice of Christ.

entries.section: (2) God asks for sacrifices of praise

paragraphs.text: 14- Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High:

1- God asks for sacrifices of praise, which are the prayers and hymns that man offers from the heart and lips, for God asks for man's love, and not formal worship. Likewise good works and the labors of service are sacrifices of praise. And the greatest sacrifice in the New Testament is the sacrifice of the Eucharist, that is, thanksgiving, which is Communion from the Body and Blood of the Lord.

2- God also rejoices in the paying of vows, because they are an expression of man's love for God, and declare that man is not attached to material things but is attached to God, in addition to the fact that these vows help the needy. And the paying of vows is the fulfillment of man's love for God, and the carrying out of promises, and at the same time a becoming a stranger to the world and material things.

entries.section: (2) God asks for sacrifices of praise

paragraphs.text: 15- And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me."

1- If you love God by offering sacrifices of praise and offering vows, He opens His door to you to ask of Him what you want, especially during tribulations. And trust that God is able to deliver you from the hardest tribulations, so that you thank Him and glorify Him.

2- The day of trouble is the day of judgment, on which man takes refuge in God to save him from destruction, and He answers him, because he loved God all his life by sacrifices of praise and the paying of vows, and brings him into the Kingdom to live praising God forever.

May you be aware of and understand the meanings of the prayers of the Liturgy when you take part in them, and so prepare your heart and move it on the way of love; and when at the end you partake of the Body and Blood of the Lord you receive power and blessing, and God rejoices in you.

entries.section: (3) God rebukes the hypocrisy of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 16- But unto the wicked God saith, "What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?

1- God reproaches the wicked, because in appearance they are servants of God, but in truth their hearts are evil; in their outward show they have made a covenant with God to be His and serve Him, but they speak about the statutes of God without the speech coming from their hearts, because they do not live in them and in their spirit, and consequently it has no effect on others, but seems heavy, because the Spirit of God is not in it.

2- Why is a person concerned to hear the opinion of others about him, and neglects the more important, which is the opinion of God?! It is more fitting for him to hear the voice of God in him, to change and amend himself by repentance, and then after he is purified he can live by the commandments of God, and it is easy for him to teach them. Then the covenant of God turns from words on his mouth to living words in his heart and in his life, and people accept his teachings.

entries.section: (3) God rebukes the hypocrisy of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 17- Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee.

1- God rebukes the servants who do not act on His commandments, saying to the servant: you have hated My word which reveals your weaknesses, and asks of you My orders that you may live by them. You have hated to be instructed by them and to carry them out, and even neglected them, that is, cast them behind you.

2- This wicked servant used to accept the easy word of God, but the hard commandments of God he rejected and neglected. He is not faithful in his submission to all the word of God, but chooses from it what pleases him; the conclusion is that he refuses instruction, that is, the commandments of God that instruct him.

entries.section: (3) God rebukes the hypocrisy of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 18- When thou sawest a thief, then thou consentedst with him, and hast been partaker with adulterers.

1- When a person neglects the commandments of God he is stripped of righteousness, so it becomes easy for him to fall into any sin, and its enticements draw him. So when he sees a thief who tempts him to join him, he consents with him and steals with him. And if he sees adulterers he clings to them and commits adultery like them.

2- The servant who does not act on the commandments of God, and only speaks of them, is unfaithful to these commandments, that is, a thief of the power of the word of God, and does not let it work in him. He is also a betrayer of the word of God by refusing to act on the commandments of God, for he speaks the commandments of God with his tongue, while his heart is occupied with the concerns of the world and attached to them, and this is what is called spiritual adultery; this deserves the rebuke of St. Paul the Apostle in (Rom 2:21-24).

entries.section: (3) God rebukes the hypocrisy of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 19- Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit. 20- Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother's son.

1- Another sin into which the wicked servant falls is speaking evil, and deceit and lying, as the Jews did with Christ, for they accused Him of false and vain accusations. For the wicked speaks what is within him, that is, evil, because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh (Mt 12:34).

2- The impudence of the wicked increases, so that by his evil speech he wrongs his brothers and the sons of his mother. By brothers is meant all men, and by sons of the mother those close to him, such as the Christian who wrongs Christians, or his relatives in the flesh. By this he wrongs everyone without restraint or limit, that is, evil has taken control of him.

entries.section: (3) God rebukes the hypocrisy of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 21- These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself: but I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes.
22- Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver.

1- God rebukes the wicked because he commits many sins while God is silent and long-suffering, to give him an opportunity to repent. But the strange thing is that the wicked thinks this is weakness on God's part, or that God agrees with his evil: "thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself."

2- God threatens the wicked that if he does not repent nothing awaits him but the punishment of the day of judgment, on which God sets his sins before his eyes, that is, exposes him and discloses his sins before all men. And likewise He tears him in pieces and no one can deliver him from the hand of God. What is meant is that God, after He judges the wicked, casts him into eternal torment, in which no one can intercede for him, and he does not come out of the torment forever; and God means by this threat to warn the wicked, perhaps he will repent. God may also use this tearing in pieces during life, by way of trials, to call the wicked to repentance, as He tore His people in pieces by the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity.

entries.section: (3) God rebukes the hypocrisy of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 23- Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God."

1- The psalm ends with praise of the righteous who offer sacrifices of praise, which are the sacrifices of the lips that praise God, or those who strive against sins and raise many prayers in toils and vigils, and all these are sacrifices of praise; in addition to all good works and service, and also every condescension, obedience and detachment, for these are man's sacrificing of his own will and his submission to God. So the sacrifices of praise are by word, and also by deeds.

2- God also praises the righteous man who orders his way through repentance and spiritual striving to change his conduct and acquire virtues. By this striving he glorifies God, because he seeks the Kingdom and rids himself of the lusts and preoccupations of the world.

Be obedient to the commandments of God and submit to them, whatever toil they cost you, trusting that God will support you in carrying them out. And if you fall, rise quickly, and also thank God for all His gifts, and your heart will rejoice, and you will advance toward the Kingdom.

1- Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.

1- David felt that his two sins, adultery and murder, deserved death, and he no longer had any chance of escape from divine justice except by asking for the mercies and compassions of God. By this David humbly declares his weakness and his sins.

2- David's repentance for his two sins mentioned before drove him to repent of all his sins, and to ask God's forgiveness. His insistence in asking for divine mercy declares his faith in God's love and in His ability to forgive all sins; indeed, this shows that David looked by the spirit of prophecy to Christ who would come in the fullness of time to take away all sins from the penitent and those who believe in Him.
2- Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.

1- David expresses his evils with three words: the first, transgressions (v. 1), which in the original Hebrew means a turning aside from God; iniquity (v. 2), which means the justification of faults; and sin (v. 3), which means the evil intention accompanying the deeds. Therefore for the remedy he used three words: blotting out for the transgressions, washing for the iniquities, and cleansing for the sins.
2- Because David feels that his faults are many, he asked for a thorough washing of his iniquities. And this washing is accomplished by the following:
a- Trials, that a person may keep away from sin and hate it.
b- The blood of Christ the Redeemer, which David saw by the spirit of prophecy to be partaking of the Holy Sacraments, which forgive and strengthen a person against sin.
c- Repentance and confession.
3- The washing refers to the water of Baptism, which purifies the baptized from his sins.
3- For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.

David confesses his transgressions, and by this he receives forgiveness for them. His sin he set always before his eyes, to offer repentance for it at all times. And when he did this God helped him by sending Nathan to him and pricking his conscience, that is, the feelings of remorse increased within him, for he truly deserves the mercies of God.
4- Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
Be clear when thou judgest: to be just, upright and praised in Your judgment.

1- David feels that his sin is directed against God before it is directed against a man, because God is his Creator, and He is the one who holds him to account if he does not walk uprightly. And even if those around him flatter him and praise him because he is king, he does not forget that God is the one who will judge him. Here David affirms his confession of his sin and does not justify himself, but shows the enormity of his sin, because he did it with contempt and defiance in the sight of God. Consequently there is nothing before him but repentance to receive the mercies of God.

2- David's confession of his sin shows the justice of God, and that He is clear in His judgment. For when God punishes David, David deserves it, and it is not injustice. And if God forgives him, this is a great mercy from Him which David does not deserve. God's gifts are many, for He raised David from shepherding sheep and made him king, and taught him His commandments; but David sinned, and consequently deserves divine justice and punishment. David is a sinner and God is righteous and true in His promises.
5- Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.

1- David was raised with a godly mother who was a servant of God (Ps 116:16); he does not mean that he was born of adultery, but he means the ancestral sin with which all men are born, when he mentioned the iniquity and sin in which he was born.

2- David's mention of his being born in sin shows his humility and contrition before God, and consequently draws out the compassionate mercies of God, who has pity on those who plead to Him. By this verse David lives in the contrition of repentance and abasement before God, and at the same time enjoys God's tenderness and forgiveness, as God makes an excuse for him because he was born in sin and is exposed to falling into it.
6- Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.
The hidden part: the secret place.

1- David feels the love of God, who was pleased that the inward being of David, and his innermost parts, incline to truth and good, and not to doing evil, and that the sin into which he fell was a plot of Satan; that is, David feels that God loves him and makes an excuse for him.

2- David also feels the kindness of God, who did not rebuke him before the people for his sin, but sent to him in secret ("the hidden part") Nathan the prophet, and made his sin known to him, so David declared his repentance, and Nathan told him that God had forgiven it.

3- David by the spirit of prophecy saw the Truth, who is the Word of God, the Second Hypostasis, that is, Christ, in whom the Father was well pleased, and he also perceived in secret, that is, between himself and his own soul, that Christ is the true Wisdom, and he knew of the Incarnation and its mysteries, which would be accomplished in the fullness of time, and would give him and all believing mankind true salvation, purity and cleanness, unlike the Mosaic law, which was practiced in the days of David, for it is all a type of Christ who would come in the fullness of time to forgive his sins.
7- Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

Hyssop: a wild plant with a long stem having dense leaves at its end, like palm fronds. In ancient times they used it to clean their bodies of dirt and sweat. The Jews put vinegar on it and lifted it up to Christ on the Cross to drink (Jn 19:29).

1- David asked God to cleanse him with hyssop, which was used for purification according to the law of Moses (Num 19:6, 18; Lev 14:6). This shows David's sense of the multitude of his sins, and on the other hand his trust in God who is able to cleanse him whatever his sins.

2- The Jews used hyssop to smear the lintel and the two side posts of the door with blood, that the destroying angel might pass over them (Ex 12:22). So hyssop is a type of Baptism, since it is used for washing away dirt and for purification, and at the same time the blood put on it is a type of the blood of Christ, which cleanses from every sin. David longs for purification in all its dimensions, whether in the Old Testament or when it is perfected in the New Testament.

3- David longs to be washed by the hand of God, so that he becomes pure, dazzling white like snow, and this expresses his faith and hope in the new, pure life in which he wants to live after God forgives his sins.
8- Make me to hear joy and gladness; that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice.
1- Although sin disturbed and grieved David, the grace of God, His love and His forgiveness restore his peace to him, and even gladden his heart, because his joy rests on his sense of God's presence.

2- God broke David's bones, because when David fell he remembered the fear of God, so he repented greatly and felt the guilt of his sin. But God's tenderness did not leave him in his sorrows, but restored his gladness to him when he repented. Sin produces sorrow, but joy is of the fruits of the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to His penitent children.
9- Hide thy face from my sins, and blot out all mine iniquities.
1- As David feels the enormity of his sin, he asks God to hide His face from his sins, that is, to forget them, and look upon David with an eye of compassion, and restore to him his sonship.

2- When David fell into the two sins of adultery and murder, he awoke and repented of these two sins, and since his remorse was intense he examined himself concerning all his former sins, and offered remorse for all of them, and hoped of God that He would blot them out and forgive them, that he might become completely pure; for if David were to keep one sin without repentance, he would lose the Kingdom.

Take care to offer repentance for every sin, that you may receive the forgiveness of God; for if you try to hide it and cover it and do not confess it, God will judge you for it, but if you repent He will forgive it for you and hide His face from it, and you will live in joy on earth, and then in heaven.
(2) Renewal and service (vv. 10-13:)
10- Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
1- After David's fall he felt that his thoughts and feelings had all been defiled, and therefore he needed new, pure feelings, so he asked God to create in him a heart that desires life with God.

2- David also asked for the renewal of his spirit, by which he means his conscience and all that God distinguished him with as a human being from the rest of creation. And he asked for a right spirit that has no aim but the love of God, so that his innermost parts become longing for God and lead his body on the way to the Kingdom.
11- Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.

1- David lived enjoying fellowship with God from the time he was a boy shepherding sheep, and he used to seek God in every tribulation, and He rescued him and supported him, as when he killed the lion and the bear, and afterward Goliath, and then hundreds of the Philistine enemies. But after his fall he was sure that he was not worthy to enjoy seeing God, yet when he repented the longings for fellowship with God were renewed within him, so he implored Him not to cast him away from His presence, because seeing God and fellowship with Him is life for David.

2- The Spirit of God who dwelt in David and gave him prophecy, and also the wisdom to lead the kingdom as king, the strength for war and victory, and the wisdom to apply justice in judgment, David was no longer worthy of enjoying all this because of his falling into sin. But he is still a king, a military commander and a judge, and indeed as a spiritual man he needs the Spirit of God who guides him, and pricks him if he errs, and gives him gifts and abilities that he necessarily needs; therefore he implored God not to take His Holy Spirit from him.
12- Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.
Free spirit: a spirit obedient by free will.

1- Sin produced sorrow in David's heart, and he lost all the feelings of joy he had lived with God, so as he repents he implores God to restore to him the gladness and joy of salvation from sin, that he may live with Him anew.

2- By the spirit of prophecy David sees that complete salvation is accomplished by the redemption of Christ, and this salvation is able to fill the heart of man with joy, so David longs that man regain his joys which he lived in the garden of Eden by receiving the salvation of Christ.

3- David also asks God to uphold him by renewing his spirit, that it may be obedient to the commandments of God, and so go forth in freedom and its own will, resting on the grace of God, to enjoy being with Him.
13- Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.

1- Since David tasted the bitterness of sin and repented, he longed to warn all who had fallen into sin, that they may repent like him and enjoy peace in the hands of God. And as he caused others to stumble by his sin, now he calls every one who has fallen into sin to repent; for he who has experienced the bitterness of sin and repented is the person most able to call others to repentance.

2- The sinners and transgressors whom David means are all his senses and faculties which were defiled by sin, so as he repents he teaches and trains his thoughts, senses, body and all his faculties not to turn aside from God, but to keep His commandments and walk in His ways.
