When you fall into sin do not be content with sorrow or settle into despair, but rise quickly in hope, and ask humbly before God that He have mercy on you and forgive you, and even support you by His power to make up for all you missed, and by this the devil will not gloat over you, and God will rejoice in your repentance.
(3) Humility and praise (vv. 14-17:)
14- Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness. 15- O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.

1- David asks God to remove from him the effects of his sin, which are the blood of Uriah the Hittite whom he killed, and the blood of all who were killed with him from the army. By bloods he also means all who were made to stumble by David, the first of them the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and everyone who knew David's sin and stumbled at him. He asks that God forgive him all these bloods, because he trusts that God loves him, so he calls Him "God of my salvation," that is, the one who cares for me and is concerned for my salvation from every sin. So with faith and great hope, and by the spirit of prophecy, he sees Christ, the true Savior in the fullness of time, who saves him and saves mankind from its sins.

2- When David is purified from sin, and God forgives him its effects, he can praise God the righteous, the holy, who justified him and forgave him his sins. So he stands before God and utters words of praise and glorification, which confirm his faith and fill his heart with peace.

3- Sin closes man's heart to God, and also shuts his mouth, but repentance returns man to his natural state, and he enjoys the grace of God, which opens his lips, so he sets out in praise, thanking God who received him and forgave him. For God is the mover of the feelings and words of praise in His children and those who love Him.

16- For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. 17- The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

1- Although David was committed to the law and to offering sacrifices, such as the sin offering and the trespass offering which a person offers if he errs, he makes clear here that the offering of sacrifices is not sufficient, not only because they are a type of the sacrifice of Christ, but because God stipulates that they be accompanied by a humble, penitent heart. If the solution were to offer sacrifices, David would have offered many of them, especially since he is a king and able financially to do so, but he declares clearly that this alone does not please God, but He stipulates a spirit that is contrite in repentance. The meaning of this is that God despises sacrifices not accompanied by true repentance, but rejoices in the humility of the hearts of the penitent.

2- The greatness of humility lies in its being a sacrifice of dignity, a sacrifice of man's own will, and a readiness to endure insults, and God greatly rejoices in humble hearts. Humility was perfected in Christ, who was crushed on the Cross and in the sufferings for our redemption; here the good pleasure of the Father is perfected.

I ask You, Lord, to keep me from causing others to stumble, lest I be called to account for their blood. And give me, Lord, humility to keep Your commandments and to accept sufferings for Your sake, and then You will keep me in Your right hand from every evil, and fill my heart with peace and joy.
(4) Acceptable worship (vv. 18, 19:)
18- Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion: build thou the walls of Jerusalem.
Zion: the most important of the five mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built. The name Zion is used in many places to denote the city of Jerusalem.

1- After David tasted the sweetness of God's forgiveness of him, he asked Him to bless Jerusalem with His good pleasure toward her, and to build her walls, that is, that she become a strong, fortified city. This shows the extent of David's love for the holy city Jerusalem, and the dwelling of God in it. He feels his membership with the people of God, and asks on behalf of all the believers who worship God in this holy city.

2- By Zion and Jerusalem David also means himself, that is, he asks God to bless him and fortify him against the attacks of the devil, that he may remain in the love of God, and that God may show His kindness and good pleasure in His incarnation for the redemption of mankind. By Jerusalem he also means the Church of the New Testament, and the walls are the Apostles, who kept the faith and preached it to the whole world.
19- Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.

1- When God blesses Jerusalem, His holy city, and all the believers who come to her, these believers rejoice and are encouraged, and offer to God sacrifices of righteousness and perfect offerings, that is, the feelings of their hearts, their thoughts, hymns of praise going forth from their mouths, and works of righteousness that bear witness to God, so that He is glorified in them.
2- After hearts are moved on the way of the love of righteousness, the sacrifices become acceptable "bullocks," and even please God, because they proceed from hearts filled with love for Him.

3- David sees by the spirit of prophecy the Church of the New Testament, which, after enjoying the redemption of Christ, the believers in her offer sacrifices of righteousness and the perfect offerings of their hearts; indeed their tongues meditate on the praise of God, and their works glorify Him, and in the end they offer bullocks, which are the giving of their lives in spiritual striving and service, and then it is completed in martyrdom.

Express your love for God, who blesses you every day with many blessings, by offering the sacrifices of your lips, which are your prayers and hymns, and then complete them with works of mercy and service, out of your love for your Redeemer who gave His life for you.

The conduct of the wicked and the righteous. To the chief musician. A psalm of David the prophet, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, David is come to the house of Ahimelech: "Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man?") ... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, as appears from the title of the psalm.
2- When was it written?

At the beginning of David's flight from the face of Saul, after David went to Ahimelech the high priest in the city of Nob, in which the priests lived, where he ate the showbread and took the sword of Goliath, and Doeg the Edomite saw him there, and told Saul, and stirred him up against Ahimelech, so Saul killed Ahimelech and all the priests, and only one of them escaped, Abiathar (1 Sam 21).

3- Doeg the Edomite was of the descendants of Esau and joined the Jewish people, and rose to be the chief of the herdsmen responsible for the flocks of Saul, and he is a wicked man, inclined to shedding blood, so he carried news to Saul, which were facts, but supported by provocations to Saul, and all of it lies, as he showed Ahimelech cooperating with David against Saul, and this did not happen. And when Saul ordered the killing of the priests, all the servants of Saul were afraid of that, so Doeg came forward and slew them all with the sword; Doeg is wicked, and boasts in evil; therefore he is a type of the Antichrist, the opponent of the truth.

4- This psalm shows that the power of the wicked, however overbearing it may seem, is quick to pass away, and nothing awaits the wicked but divine punishment. But the righteous God blesses and rewards, and this establishes the believers in the life of righteousness.

5- This psalm is considered one of the eight psalms whose title states that David was driven out and fleeing from the face of Saul, and they are called "the psalms of the fugitive," and they are (Ps 7, 34, 49, 52, 54, 56, 57, 142).
6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The characteristics of the wicked man

paragraphs.text: 1- “Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? The goodness of God endureth continually.”

1- Doeg the Edomite loved evil, practiced it and persisted in it. To win the favor of King Saul he committed many evils, such as lying; he held the lives of the priests cheap and killed them without pity, and even destroyed everyone in their city, women and children alike. He boasted that he did evil, and this is the first characteristic of the wicked man.
He represents ungodliness and is a type of the antichrist. The Holy Bible shows examples of such ungodly men who boast in evil, like Rabshakeh and Sennacherib.

2- The mercy of God is every day: it halts the evil of the wicked, and it keeps and delivers the righteous, or promises them eternity, as happened with the priests of Nob (1 Sam 21). God, the Almighty, sets limits to evil by His mercy. Thus in this verse we see a contrast between the evils of man and the mercy of God, and this is the idea of the whole psalm.

entries.section: (1) The characteristics of the wicked man

paragraphs.text: 2- “Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs; like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.”

1- The second characteristic in Doeg, or in the wicked man, is lying and devising mischiefs. He made Saul believe that Ahimelech was cooperating with David against Saul. So that Doeg might draw near to Saul, he lied to achieve his aim. He was also deceitful and a cheat: he joined the Jews and was circumcised. He did this and pretended, but in truth he did not love God and His worship, as the hardness of his heart shows, and his rush to kill the priests, whereas the true Jews, the servants of Saul, could not bring themselves to kill the priests.

2- David likens Doeg to “a sharp razor,” which removes all the hair with ease, just as Doeg killed the priests and destroyed their city with ease. He thinks of evil, hastens to it and does it easily, because it is of his nature, and consequently he persists and goes on in it. In the same way a sharp razor wounds and cuts quickly anyone who is not careful of it; the wicked man is deceitful and cannot be trusted.

entries.section: (1) The characteristics of the wicked man

paragraphs.text: 3- “Thou lovest evil more than good; and lying rather than to speak righteousness. Selah.”

1- The third characteristic of the wicked man is that he loves evil more than good. Doeg loved lying and inciting Saul against the priests more than finding an excuse for Ahimelech in helping David, for example that he did not know of any problems between David and Saul. In his love of evil Doeg used lying and hardness of heart, and slaughtered the priests.

2- In the wicked man’s love of evil, he loved every evil word that destroys others and deceives them. The wicked man clings to the wicked and loves their evils, which makes him persist in his evils without limit.
3- At the end of verse 3 we find the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause, so that man may contemplate the gravity of evil and keep away from it.

Take care lest the devil provoke you and you persist in any evil, however small or hidden from the eyes of people, for he wants to turn your heart to evil so as to separate you from God. When God warns you, hasten to repentance, so that you may regain your sonship to God, your nature may be purified, and you may return to doing good.

entries.section: (2) The recompense of the wicked man

paragraphs.text: 5- “God shall likewise destroy thee for ever, he shall take thee away, and pluck thee out of thy dwelling place, and root thee out of the land of the living. Selah.”
1- “Likewise” means therefore: as a result of the evil characteristics the wicked man held fast to, God brings many punishments upon him, namely:

a- He will destroy you: that is, God will shatter you and strip you of every show of your strength. This destruction lasts throughout his life, that is, for ever, so that he is cast into eternal torment.

b- He will take you away: the divine punishment comes suddenly. After God has been long-suffering toward the wicked man, who persisted in his evils for a long time, the divine punishment comes upon him suddenly and snatches him away from all his pleasures and his pride, and strips him of all ability and strength.

c- He will pluck you out of your dwelling place: however deeply rooted the wicked man is and however firmly he has established himself, and whatever power, connections or wealth he has, God plucks him out of his secure dwelling place, as a plant is plucked out of the ground, and casts him out to wither and be burned with fire. That is, he loses everything he built up for himself and is cast into the eternal fire.

d- He will root you out of the land of the living: the wicked man loses his life, either by death, or he is considered dead in the sight of God because he has separated himself from Him, and he has no place in the land of the living, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven. Because he rejected life with God on earth, he becomes dead for ever, that is, he does not feel God, and is tormented for ever, since the knowledge of God is life, and distance from Him is eternal torment.
2- The verse ends with the word “Selah,” a musical pause for meditating on the punishment of the wicked man, so that man may keep away from evil.

entries.section: (2) The recompense of the wicked man

paragraphs.text: 6- “The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him.” 7- “Lo, this is the man that made not God his strength; but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness.”

1- When the righteous see the wicked man, who did not rely on God and did not make Him his stronghold, but trusted in his possessions and in his evil means by which he gains material things, and when the righteous see all this, they fear God. For they have grown accustomed to seeing God, so they feel His feelings and how His heart is grieved by evil. They fear for themselves lest they grow careless and fall into some of these evils, and so they become more watchful and careful, always remembering the fear of God.

2- The righteous also laugh at evil, that is, they scorn it and feel that it is a bad, trivial and passing thing, so it does not entice them to do it, but they loathe it, and their clinging to God increases.

Remember the fear of God at all times, so that it may keep you from sin and bring you near to God, and you will enjoy seeing Him, and He will even reveal to you the treasures of His knowledge, and you will rejoice in fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (3) The conduct of the righteous man and his reward

paragraphs.text: 8- “But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever.”

1- When the righteous man sees the sins of the wicked man, he keeps away from him; this is the negative side. But on the positive side, the righteous man enjoys, as he expresses in this verse, the following:

a- He likens himself to a green olive tree, that is, a tree that bears fruit, because the spiritual man has spiritual fruits. It also produces the oil that the believer needs to fill his lamp, and this oil is good works. The olive tree is green, that is, full of life through God who works in it. The olive tree also signifies peace, as in the story of Noah, because the righteous man makes peace and inclines to it, and God fills his heart with peace.

b- “In the house of God”: the secret of the strength of this olive tree is that it is planted in the house of God, that is, it has a very strong relationship, deeply rooted in the worship of God, and so it receives all the blessings mentioned before, and no one can pluck it up; that is, the wicked and all their sins do not affect it.
2- The steadfastness of the righteous man depends on his trust in God, who establishes him, keeps him, defends him and blesses him in this life and then in eternity.

3- David likens himself to the olive tree planted in the house of God, though he was driven out and excluded from the house of God, because his heart was attached to God and to His house. For this reason we read this part of the psalm on the eve of the feast of St. John the Baptist (2 Thout), who lived in the wilderness, driven out by Herod, yet whose heart was attached to the house of the Lord and to His Christ more than all the people of the Jews.
4- The green olive tree signifies Christ, for all the meanings mentioned above are fulfilled in Christ.

entries.section: (3) The conduct of the righteous man and his reward

paragraphs.text: 9- “I will praise thee for ever, because thou hast done it: and I will wait on thy name; for it is good before thy saints.”

1- At the end of the psalm David thanks God and praises Him, because He has given him the blessings mentioned in this psalm. This is God’s work in him; he appreciates the work of God and thanks Him, and so he remains in a deep relationship and constant love for God.

2- This praise produced in David’s heart longings toward God, which he expresses by saying that he waits on the Lord, that is, he hungers and thirsts for God, and God gives him blessings and joy in Him. As David’s life is enlightened, he becomes an example to God’s saints, who also wait on the Lord, and they are encouraged in their striving toward God. In David’s waiting on God’s name he bears the toils of life and the devil’s wars with joy, confident of God’s support for him and of the blessings He will give him, because those who believe in God are exposed to many wars, and God permits them, but at the same time He grants His children patience and support, and even more than this, the experience of His fellowship in the midst of tribulations.
Your trust in God gives you support and steadfastness in your spiritual life, so do not be troubled by the changes of life or the devil’s wars, and continue in your spiritual growth.
The salvation of the Lord. A psalm of David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son: “LORD, how are they increased that trouble me!” (v. 1) Introduction:
a- This psalm is a repetition of Psalm 14, but why is this psalm repeated in a single book?
1- Because their writer is one, David the prophet, they are very similar.

2- The first psalm, which is Psalm 14, was placed in the first group according to the Jewish division, which includes (Ps 1-41), the group that speaks of the salvation of the individual; it shows the turning aside of man’s heart after evil, and for this reason Christ became incarnate to redeem him. The second psalm (Ps 53) was placed in the second group, which includes (Ps 42-72), the group that speaks of the salvation of the community, or the Church, which as a whole is exposed to turning aside and corruption, and all of which needs salvation.

3- The idea of this psalm, that man’s heart is exposed to corruption, evil and betrayal, is an idea repeated throughout the generations. The purpose of the repetition is to alert man to the gravity of this corruption so that he may guard against it, especially since every man, however near to God, is exposed to falling, as happened with Judas, the disciple of Christ.

4- Despite the repetition of the psalm, there are some differences between the two psalms, and this confirms that the writer wrote each of them separately, so the writing comes out slightly different and not an exact copy; this psalm is not a copy of the other psalm. This confirms that the Holy Bible has not been corrupted: the hand of man did not interfere to delete one of these psalms so that no one would object to this repetition.
b- The differences between the two psalms:
1- In (Ps 14:1) we find “they have done abominable works,” while in (Ps 53:1) we find instead “have done abominable iniquity.”
2- In (Ps 14:2) we find “The LORD looked down from heaven,” while in (Ps 53:2) we find instead “God looked down from heaven.”
3- In (Ps 14:3) we find “They are all gone aside,” while in (Ps 53:3) we find instead “Every one of them is gone back.”
4- In (Ps 14:4) we find “Have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge?” while in (Ps 53:4) we find instead “Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge?”

5- (Ps 14:5, 6) tells us of the fear of the wicked toward the righteous, despite their opposing and resisting them and the humble man, as we explained in detail in (Ps 14). But (Ps 53:5) speaks of the fear of the wicked where there was nothing to fear, and God scattered the strength of those who besieged the righteous man and put them to shame, because they are wicked and God has rejected them, as He removed the strength of Sennacherib and his army, who besieged Jerusalem in the days of King Hezekiah. That is, (Ps 53:5) is a merging of the meaning of verses (5, 6) in (Ps 14).

6- We notice that the numbering differs after this between the two psalms, that is, (Ps 14:7) corresponds to (Ps 53:6). The certainty of divine salvation. A poem of David when the Ziphims came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us? “Save me, O God, by thy name” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David, as mentioned in the title.
2- When was it written?

When David was driven out by Saul and reached the hill country of Ziph, which lies in the tribe of Judah south of Jerusalem and Hebron. The Ziphites went to Saul and told him that David was hiding with them, so that he might come and seize him. This shows the extent of their fear of Saul and their attempt to please him, but God rescued him from Saul’s hand, and the Ziphites tried again and told Saul that David was in the wilderness of Ziph, and God rescued him again (1 Sam 26:1-25). Most likely David wrote this psalm after God’s first rescue of him, when he was in En-gedi and Saul had besieged him and was about to seize him, but news came to him of the Philistines’ raid on the land of the children of Israel, so he left David and went to face the Philistines (1 Sam 23:41-29). So David thanked God, who allowed this raid in order to rescue him from Saul’s hand.

3- In this psalm David asks God to save him, and God intervenes and saves him, so he thanks Him for his salvation and praises Him. It is a psalm of thanksgiving for everyone who has passed through tribulation and prayed to God, and He delivered him.
4- It is one of the eight psalms whose titles say that David was driven out by Saul, and they are called the psalms of the fugitive.

5- This psalm completes the psalm before it, because Psalm 53 shows the resistance of the wicked to the righteous man, and this psalm shows God’s support for the righteous man and His rescuing him from the hands of the wicked.

6- This psalm is found at the beginning of the prayer of the Sixth Hour in the Agpeya, the hour in which Christ is crucified for the world, and David suffers pains and shares Christ’s cross, then offers the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving to God; that is, we glorify the sacrifice of Christ on the cross with thanksgiving and praise. Therefore the Western Church reads it on Great Friday in remembrance of the crucifixion of Christ.
1- “Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy strength.”

1- The name of God saves His children and breaks His enemies. Therefore the Church has cared to repeat the name of God since the first centuries of Christianity, in the Jesus Prayer and also in the daily psalis of the Midnight Praise.

2- Because David walks in uprightness, he asks for God’s just judgment to rescue him from his enemies. He trusts in God’s justice and in his own (David’s) upright conduct, and believes that God does not reject the prayers of those who seek Him; therefore the Church asks Christ, her Savior, whatever tribulations befall her, confident of His power and protection.
2- “Hear my prayer, O God; give ear to the words of my mouth.”
David prays from his heart without words, and opens his lips with audible prayers; with his heart and his tongue he asks God to rescue him from his enemies. Of course God cannot leave him.
3- “For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul: they have not set God before them. Selah.”
1- David divides his enemies into two groups:

a- Strangers: by them he means the Ziphites, though they are Jews and of his own tribe, the tribe of Judah, but they became strangers to him and did not love him, and tried to kill him by delivering him into Saul’s hand.
b- The oppressors: by them he means Saul and his soldiers, who wanted to kill David and tried to do so many times.
These two groups did evil because they disregarded the existence of God, so there was nothing within them but their own evil human thoughts, but God is able to rescue David from their hands.

2- The Church meets enemies in every generation, whether from her own children who have become strangers to her by falling into heresies, or pride, or various lusts, and sometimes strangers who are not children of the Church. These seek the help of the strong ones of the world to harm the Church, and they have no fear of God before them, but the mighty God rescues His Church however much the wicked increase against her.
3- This verse ends with the word “Selah,” a musical pause for meditating on the name of God, who keeps us, protects us, strengthens us and satisfies our souls.
Do not fear the wicked and their threats, however strong or many they are, because God is able to protect you. Only seek God and press upon Him, and you will obtain His mercies and blessings.
4- “Behold, God is mine helper: the Lord is with them that uphold my soul.”

1- Although David began the psalm by asking God for salvation, he returns to thank God who supports him and to praise Him, and this is David’s habit in all his psalms. Here he declares that the Lord is his helper, even his supporter; therefore, if God is helper and upholder, who can stand against David? This shows David’s faith and his peace of mind in God’s hands.

2- And when he says that the Lord is with them that uphold his soul, he does not mean that He is merely one of the supporters, but that He is the true, principal supporter, even if there were some people supporting David. In addition, God’s presence among the supporters encourages these supporters in their support of David.
5- “He shall reward evil unto mine enemies: cut them off in thy truth.”

1- In the spirit of prophecy David foretells of his enemies that their evil will return upon their own heads, and that by God’s truth, that is, His power, these enemies will be cut off. In this the divine justice is established, and the righteous are not troubled by the abundance of evil. Perhaps the remaining wicked will repent and believe in God.
2- By the enemies he may mean the demons, whose end is eternal torment.

3- David does not mean vengeance or gloating over his enemies, for David’s forgiveness is clear, since he pardoned Saul his enemy twice, though he was able to destroy him. So of course here he does not mean to take vengeance on his enemies, but to show the corruption and futility of evil.
6- “I will freely sacrifice unto thee: I will praise thy name, O LORD; for it is good.”
Freely: willingly, and of good will.

1- Since David believed in God, his helper and supporter and Deliverer from all his tribulations, his heart was moved with love toward God to offer Him sacrifices of thanksgiving as an expression of his love, and not to seek a reward, for he had already received peace of mind and peace through God’s support for him. These sacrifices are not obligatory for David but freewill, out of love from him, because David was excluded and driven out, far from the Temple, and could not offer animal sacrifices, so he offered the freewill sacrifices of the lips, as praise to God. What moves David to thank God is his constant contemplation of God’s goodness, care and continual gifts to him.
7- “For he hath delivered me out of all trouble: and mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies.”

1- God’s goodness appeared plainly in rescuing David from every tribulation, and even in God’s swift intervention in striking the enemies, so David saw his victory and was encouraged to stand firm in his righteousness. Therefore he continued to thank and praise God, for he always recalled what his eyes had seen of God’s works with him and His rescue of him from the enemies.

2- It may be that God granted David a vision of the defeat of his enemies, or their eternal destruction, so that he would not be troubled by them; therefore he was encouraged and stood firm in his faith and thanksgiving.

Look to Christ, your God and Savior, and your heart will be encouraged before any difficult circumstances; you will even become brave, fearing no one, and enjoy the experience of God, so that you praise Him always.
God saves those who trust in Him. To the chief Musician on stringed instruments. A poem of David: “Give ear to my prayer, O God; and hide not thyself from my supplication” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.
2- When was it written?

When David was fleeing from the face of Absalom his son; for Absalom kept stirring up the city of Jerusalem against his father for two years and winning the people over to himself. Then he went to Hebron, gathered an army and attacked Jerusalem, and David fled lest his son Absalom kill him, by the counsel of Ahithophel, who was one of David’s greatest counselors and betrayed him and joined Absalom, and devised a plot to drive David out and then kill him (2 Sam 15:7-13).
3- This psalm, as the title indicates, was sung to the accompaniment of stringed instruments, which are musical instruments with strings, each of which has a single string.
4- This psalm resembles Psalm (41) in that both speak of the betrayal of a friend.

5- Because this psalm speaks of the betrayal of a friend, it is a prophecy about Jeremiah and the betrayal of his family and those who loved him (Jer 12:6), and also a prophecy about the betrayal of Christ by Judas Iscariot (Mt 26:14).
6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 1- “Give ear to my prayer, O God; and hide not thyself from my supplication.”
Hide not thyself: do not neglect and ignore.

David felt that he was in distress, so he asked God to listen attentively to his prayer and not to neglect his supplications, which are prayers made in lowliness and contrition before God. All this shows how much David felt his need of God, because he was in great distress.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 2- “Attend unto me, and hear me: I mourn in my complaint, and make a noise.”
My complaint: my severe distress.
1- David faced severe distress, so that his heart was troubled and he did not know what to do. He hastened to God, lifted up his prayers, and asked Him for two things:
a- That He condescend and hear him, that is, that God lay aside His greatness and listen to lowly man, and this shows David’s humility.
b- That He answer him, because he has no deliverer but God, and this shows David’s faith and his need of God.

2- David here is a type of Christ as He approached the Cross, when He was in the garden of Gethsemane and asked that the cup of suffering pass from Him. For He was in perplexity between His holiness and righteousness on the one hand, and on the other the necessity of bearing all the sins of the world upon His head.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 3- “Because of the voice of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked: for they cast iniquity upon me, and in wrath they hate me.”

1- David explains that the voices of his enemies were raised against him with false accusations and rose up against him in anger, so they wronged him though he was innocent, whether his son Absalom, or his friend and counselor Ahithophel, in addition to his people whom David had shepherded, loved and defended for many long years. Thus they all rose up against him, drove him out and deposed him from his throne.

2- David here is a type of Christ, against whom the priests and chief priests rose up, as did the scribes and Pharisees, and His traitor disciple Judas came forward and handed Him over to the priests, who tried Him in unjust trials and pressed Pilate to sentence Him to crucifixion.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 4- “My heart is sore pained within me: and the terrors of death are fallen upon me.”

David showed the extent of his suffering of pain, picturing his heart as a woman suffering the pains of childbirth, which are called travail. And as the woman expects her child, he expects a dreadful death for himself and for those around him, and he expresses these horrors as the terrors of death. That is, his feelings were in severe pain and in expectation of sudden troubles, for after his son turned against him, what was left to him? There is only God, his sole refuge.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 5- “Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me.”
Overwhelmed me: covered me.

David continues to describe his feelings in his distress when he heard of Absalom’s turning against him. He said that fear covered him and surrounded him on every side, and also trembling, that is, intense fear, and horror, that is, violent agitation. All this shows the harshness of the trial, but in the midst of this intense pain God’s saving power toward David appears.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 6- “And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest.”

1- When evil surrounded David on every side, he wished that God would deliver him from it, and imagined that the solution was for God to give him the wings of a dove, so that he might fly and get away from this evil and be at rest. He chose the dove specifically because it signifies innocence, simplicity and forgiveness: even if doves quarrel with one another and strike one another with their beaks, they return after a little while and eat together in one love.

2- Perhaps David, in the spirit of prophecy, saw the Holy Spirit, who appears in the form of a dove, and wished that God would give him the wings of the Holy Spirit to rise above the tribulations surrounding him. Even if he did not get away in his body, God would keep his spirit in peace in the midst of the severe tribulation, and he would be occupied with the love of God, and his heart would be filled with peace.

entries.section: (1) Fear and a cry for help

paragraphs.text: 7- “Lo, then would I wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Selah.” 8- “I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest.”
Tempest: a violent wind that causes disturbances in the sea.

1- Before Absalom’s attack with many men to drive out and kill David, who in this represent the windy storm and tempest, David was forced to flee to the wilderness and lodge there. The barren wilderness is safer than the fortified city of Jerusalem, which was filled with evil because of Absalom, but in the wilderness and its quiet he sees God and rests in His hands.

2- David used the words “lodge in the wilderness,” which means sleeping at the time of darkness, to express his severe distress and the blackness of his life, in his exposure to destruction at the hand of his son and the betrayal of his friend, but his hope and his stronghold is God.

3- The spiritual man flees from the turmoil of the world and its violent currents to the wilderness, to be alone with God, to regain his peace, to feel God’s supporting power and to be satisfied with His love.
4- He puts the word Selah at the end of verse 7; it is a musical pause in which man contemplates the importance of keeping away from evil and being alone with God.

5- Christ would go out to the wilderness to pray and be alone, and so the monks through the ages left the world and devoted themselves to prayer in the deserts, and they supported the Church with their prayers, their love and their knowledge.

Do not deprive yourself of enjoying solitude with God, in which you contemplate His love and so praise Him and thank Him, and at the same time see your sins in the light of His love when you examine yourself, and so you repent with contrition, and God forgives you and purifies your heart.
9- “Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues: for I have seen violence and strife in the city.”
Destroy: scatter their counsel, or make them confused.

1- David felt the betrayal of Absalom, who began winning the people over to himself against his father David with lying words. David was moved and asked for God’s help to divide their opinions and scatter their counsel. He means Ahithophel, who had been David’s counselor and friend, and then turned against him and sided with Absalom.

2- David saw violence spread in the city, that is, they wronged David, who was innocent, with false accusations spoken by Absalom, such as that his father David delayed justice in cases (2 Sam 15:2-4). He also saw strife in the city, for many turned against David and others defended him, so he asked God to calm the city and remove violence and evil.

3- So also in the days of Christ, when the priests stirred up the people against Christ while some continued to praise Him because He worked miracles among them, Jerusalem was filled with strife and violence against Christ.
10- “Day and night they go about it upon the walls thereof: mischief also and sorrow are in the midst of it.” 11- “Wickedness is in the midst thereof: deceit and guile depart not from her streets.”

The city of Jerusalem was filled with slanders against David, and they spread everywhere and surrounded all the people, and many of the leaders of the city fell into this plot and followed Absalom, and corruption spread in the city, even in its squares where the judges gather and show justice; all this was lost, and the squares became a place for stirring up the people against David with lies.

12- “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him:” 13- “But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.” 14- “We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.”

1- David explains the extent of the distress that befell him, because the betrayal and the wrong came not from an enemy known for his enmity to David, but from a friend and companion who loved David, his counselor Ahithophel, whom David treated as a brother, not as a king with one of his servants, and David used to enjoy sitting with him, and sharing spiritual practices, whether ordinary visits to the house of God or at feasts and occasions. How then could betrayal, turning against him and lying come from this intimate friend? It is a thing of the greatest difficulty that wrongs should come to a man from where he does not know and does not expect.

2- David said these words in the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who took Judas Iscariot as a disciple, even as a friend and companion, for He entrusted him with the money box and with arranging all the needs of Himself and the disciples, that is, He gave him a greater place among the disciples, yet he betrayed Him and handed Him over to the Jews to kill Him, and they crucified Him.
15- “Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them.”

1- This is a prophecy from David about what would happen to Ahithophel, for he saw in the spirit of prophecy that death would take him by surprise and he would go down to Hades, where there is perpetual torment. Perhaps he was moved by the opening of the earth to swallow Korah, Dathan and Abiram and those with them (Num 16:32), and because Ahithophel persisted in evil and betrayed God and his master King David without cause. This actually happened: after David’s flight and Absalom’s seizure of the throne, with Ahithophel at his side, Absalom chose the counsel of Hushai and abandoned the counsel of Ahithophel, and Ahithophel was greatly distressed and in despair hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23).
2- This is also a prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who, after handing Christ over to the priests, felt his sin, but in despair, and hanged himself (Mt 27:5).

Betrayal is very hard, and if it happened to you, you would be upset. So do not betray God by your sin, grieve Him and defy Him. How can evil come from you toward God, that is, from a son toward his father, and from a friend toward his friend? But there is hope: return and repent quickly, for He is tender and will forgive you, as if you had done nothing.
16- “As for me, I will call upon God; and the LORD shall save me.” 17- “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.”

1- After David showed his distress at the bitter betrayal, the violence and the corruption that filled the city of Jerusalem through Absalom and Ahithophel, he took the right direction, that is, he turned to God in prayer. And because the pain of his heart was severe, he cried out. The greatness of David’s faith appears in his saying that the Lord will save him, for he trusts that his cry reaches God and that God will surely save him, though the salvation had not yet been accomplished and David had not returned to his throne.

2- This cry began at the end of the day when David was alone with God in long prayer, which may have extended for hours during the night, and after sleeping a little he rose to continue his prayers in the morning and at noon, that is, throughout the day. He prays constant prayer by night and by day, and pours out all his feelings in complaint, weeping and appeal to God, who cannot turn away His children and those who seek Him.

3- This is a prophecy about Christ, who in the depth of His suffering in the garden of Gethsemane cried out to the Father that this cup might pass from Him. And He was confident that He would save Him. This was accomplished: though He bore all the sufferings for mankind, and died, He rose on the third day. David, the type of Christ, bore in part the sufferings from his loved ones, but Christ bore all the sufferings, and truly died, and rose, to raise us in Him.

18- “He hath delivered my soul in peace from the battle that was against me: for there were many with me.” 19- “God shall hear, and afflict them, even he that abideth of old. Selah. Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God.”

1- Absalom attacked with a mighty army gathered from all the tribes of Israel, that is, with a very great number, but David, who trusted in God, had his God intervene and redeem him and rescue him from the hand of Absalom, and Absalom died in his place, because God heard David’s cry and prayers, and humbled those who rose up against David, and they were defeated before David’s men. This is because those who rose up against David, that is, Absalom and Ahithophel, do not fear God and do not accept repentance and change; they are determined on evil, and therefore both perished: Ahithophel hanged himself and Absalom was killed in the war.
2- The word Selah in (v. 19) is a musical pause, so that man may contemplate the power of God, who protects His children, and so keep away from evil and repent of his sins.
3- The Jews stirred up the priests and asked Pilate to crucify Christ, but the Father heard Christ’s cry and delivered Him from death by His resurrection from the dead.
20- “He hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him: he hath broken his covenant.”

1- Here David spoke of the traitor Ahithophel, who cast upon David and all who were with him, who were at peace with him, the evil with which his hands were filled, and broke the covenant of love and friendship and his duty as counselor and servant to his master King David. These words apply also to Absalom, who rose up against his father who loved him and was at peace with him, broke the covenant of sonship, and wished to destroy his father.

2- These words are also a prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who cast his evil upon the most important person who loved him, embraced him and made him a disciple, namely Christ, with whom he lived in peace for more than three years, and he broke the covenant of love and submission to his teacher. It is also a prophecy about the Jews who testified to Christ that He is a good teacher, and asked Him as a Savior to reign over their hearts when they received Him as He entered Jerusalem, for they rose up against Him, broke the covenant of love and demanded His crucifixion.
21- “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”

1- Here David describes the hypocrisy and dissimulation of Ahithophel, and of Absalom. Ahithophel would show love as David’s counselor and friend, while his heart harbored evil against him and wished to destroy him. The verse likens his mouth to soft butter, but in truth he is a warrior, that is, one who destroys others, and likens him also to soft oil though in truth his words are drawn swords.

2- These words are a prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who pretended to love the poor and objected to the pouring of the ointment on Christ’s head, though he intended to steal from the box in which the contributions given to Christ were put (Jn 12:6). And when he went to Christ in the garden of Gethsemane he kissed Him, so the kiss, which is a sign of love, became a means and a signal that Judas gave to the Jews so that they might seize Christ.
Do not show love to those around you while your heart harbors evil against them. And if you notice bad thoughts within you toward any person, hasten to repentance so that God may free you from them.
22- “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.”

1- If human beings are exposed to falling into betrayal, you will not find a son or a friend to depend on, and nothing will remain for you but God, on whom you trust and cast your cares, and He is sure to uphold you, provide for your needs and keep you.

2- If God permits some tribulations for His righteous children, or if they sometimes fall into grave sins and repent, God will not leave them, but removes the tribulations from them, as He removed them from David and restored him to his throne. And if they have sinned like Peter and denied Christ, Christ rebukes them, forgives them and restores them to their first place.
23- “But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee.”
1- Everyone who walks in evil and does not live with God is exposed to two things:

a- He does not live out half his days, that is, he does not enjoy his life on earth in peace and joy with God; he has wronged his earthly life and filled it with misery and depression, even if he is immersed in material lusts.
b- His end is eternal torment, and so he loses his earthly and eternal life, because he walked in evil and held to it all his life.
2- David affirms that he has chosen the better way for himself, which is trusting in God and enjoying fellowship with Him, so he lives secure and happy.

Remember Christ at the beginning of each day, and before any matter you enter into, to seek Him and cast your affairs upon Him, and you will enjoy His care, and this will move you to praise Him at all times.

The blessings of trusting in God. To the chief Musician upon the silent dove among strangers. A golden psalm (Michtam) of David, when the Philistines took him in Gath: “Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.

2- When was it written? When David fled from the face of Saul and was forced to go to the Philistine city of Gath, one of the five great cities of Philistia in ancient times. There he pretended to be mad, scrawling on the doors of the gate of the city and letting his spittle fall down upon his beard, and the king thought him mad and disregarded him (1 Sam 21:14).

3- David expresses his distress, since he finds no place to hide from the face of Saul, so that he was even exposed to being seized by the enemy Philistines, and therefore he cries out to God, who is able to deliver him, because God delivers those who trust in Him. Therefore this psalm suits everyone who is exposed to severe tribulation and takes refuge in God to rescue him.

4- There is a resemblance between this psalm and Psalm 34, because the title of both psalms shows that they were spoken in Gath, so they are alike in thanking God, who rescued David from his enemies, and in boasting in Him.
5- It appears from the title of the psalm that it was said “upon the silent dove,” which is a quiet musical tune that suits the sorrowful words David felt and expressed.

6- The title of the psalm also has “among strangers,” because David the prophet spoke it while he was a stranger among the enemy Philistines, but God kept him and delivered him from their hands, so he wrote this psalm to thank God and boast in Him.

7- We find in the title of the psalm “a golden psalm (Michtam) of David,” and this means that this psalm is one of the important, distinguished psalms that David wrote, and some say that in ancient times they used to write it in gold ink.

8- This psalm is a prophecy about the enemies who would meet the people of God in the days of the captivity, or afterward in the age of the Maccabees, when King Antiochus persecuted the people of God.
9- This psalm was sung by the people on various occasions, especially when they passed through tribulation, so it is a liturgical psalm.
10- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 1- “Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up; he fighting daily oppresseth me.” 2- “Mine enemies would daily swallow me up: for they be many that fight against me with pride.”
Would swallow me up: is about to devour me.

1- David takes refuge in God and complains to Him about Saul and those with him, who pursue him and are hostile to him though he is innocent, and try to fight him and destroy him, and keep on pursuing him all the day, that is, all the time, because Saul kept pursuing David for many years until the end of Saul’s life. David’s taking refuge in God declares his faith in God’s power, which is able to protect him, and that however strong man is, he is weak before God, and however much this man feels his pride and strength, he is nothing before the greatness of God.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about the enemies of the people of God in every generation, such as Sennacherib in the days of King Hezekiah, Nebuchadnezzar in the days of King Zedekiah, and King Antiochus in the days of the Maccabees; indeed, it is a prophecy about the Jews who opposed Christ, and in general about the devil and the demons who fight men throughout time. All of these are marked by pride, cruelty, a tendency to shed blood, continual fighting, and seeking to destroy the innocent.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 3- “What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.”

When David went to Gath to hide from the face of Saul, he feared that the Philistines would discover that he was David, who had killed Goliath years before, but he trusted in God, who is able to protect him even in the midst of enemies. Here two things appear:
a- David’s courage in confessing his fear.
b- David’s faith in God and his trust in Him, and not in any other power in the world.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 4- “In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.”

Since David trusted in God, who is able to do all things, he no longer feared earthly, limited men, but on the contrary believed God’s promises and trusted them, that God is able to protect him, and he boasted, that is, he praised, thanked and glorified God, because He is his great God, able to do all things.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 5- “Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil.”

1- David’s enemies tried to twist his words, that is, to interpret his words with other meanings he did not intend, and to catch some wrong word against him. Their hearts were evil toward him, so they watched him and tried to accuse him with false accusations all day long, that is, they kept on presenting him in a bad light, and stirred Saul up against him (1 Sam 24:9), and Saul himself stirred up the Jews against David in order to be rid of him.
2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom the Jews, throughout His ministry to them, tried to catch some wrong word, and accused Him with many false accusations.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 6- “They gather themselves together, they hide themselves, they mark my steps, when they wait for my soul.”
1- David’s enemies were not content with twisting his words, but resolved to destroy him, and so they did the following:
a- “They gather themselves together”: so that their number would be large and it would be easy for them to seize him.
b- “They hide themselves”: to surprise him when he is unprepared and destroy him.
c- “They mark my steps”: they watched David’s movements through spies.
d- “They wait for my soul”: they prepared to destroy me.
2- All this too is a prophecy about Christ and what the Jews did to Him.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 7- “Recompense them for their iniquity. In anger bring down the peoples, O God.”

In the spirit of prophecy David saw what would befall the wicked, namely that God will punish them for their iniquities and show the wrath of God the Judge upon them, so that they are brought low under the strong hand of God in eternal torment. God may also punish them in their life on earth, that they may perhaps repent and return to Him. The Philistines attacked Saul many times, killed many and seized some of the cities of the children of Israel, that perhaps Saul would take notice and repent, but he did not repent, and died in the war.

entries.section: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

paragraphs.text: 8- “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?”
Thy bottle: the bottle is a vessel made of skin, also called a waterskin, in which wine was kept in ancient times, or in which water was carried.
Thy book: thy writing.

1- Though the enemies watched David to catch him by a word or to destroy him, at the same time David was confident that God watches his movements and his flight from place to place from the face of Saul, in which he appears as one wandering, that is, that the eye of God watches him, tends him and protects him, and therefore his enemies cannot harm him.

2- In the midst of the many tribulations David passed through, he lifted up his prayers to God and his tears flowed; he even wept for the wicked who did not repent, and wept at the loss of his loved ones, and even of those who were hostile to him, namely Jonathan, Saul, Abner and Absalom, and he also wrote a lament for them (2 Sam 1:23; 2 Sam 3:33, 34; 2 Sam 18:33). And he wept most of all over his sins (Ps 51). All these tears carried and expressed strong feelings from the depths of David, so he asked God to accept them, keep them with Him and care for them.

3- Though people do not care about his tears, and may despise him because of them, or at least may make light of them, he is confident that God does not neglect them. So he asks Him to keep his tears in a bottle with Him, that is, every tear has great value with God, because God says to every soul in the Song of Songs, “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me” (Song 6:5). Tears draw out God’s mercies and stir His tenderness, and He even writes their memorial in a special book with Him, to reward David, and everyone who weeps before God, with great blessings on earth and in heaven. This, of course, is different from the tears of people shed over the loss of material things or worldly attachments they were attached to; these tears are not for God’s sake, and God does not keep them with Him, because they take people away from God.

4- The Jews kept wine in a bottle, and wine signifies joy, so this indicates that God rejoices in the tears of His children poured out before Him, and gives them peace and joy on earth, and then joys in heaven that cannot be expressed.

Be confident that God cares about all your prayers and your crying to Him, and regards your tears with great regard, because your feelings are precious to Him when you direct them to Him. So do not listen to the doubts of Satan, who tells you that God has forgotten you, for He gathers your prayers and your tears and rewards you for them at the time that is right for you.

9- “When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back: this I know; for God is for me.” When David noticed that God takes care of him and tends him, his heart was assured that God is for him and not for his enemies, and that He will protect him and keep the evils of his enemies away from him. If they try to attack him they will be defeated and turned back, since God’s power defends him. What matters is that David keep praying and calling upon God, and so be assured of God’s protection and care for him.
10- “In God will I praise his word: in the LORD will I praise his word.” 11- “In God have I put my trust: I will not be afraid what man can do unto me.”

These two verses repeat (v. 4) in this psalm; it is like a refrain repeated in this psalm, or this spiritual hymn, to confirm the purpose of the psalm, which is the praise of God, on whom His children trust, and so enjoy blessings beyond counting. The two verses were explained before at (v. 4).
12- “Thy vows are upon me, O God: I will render thank offerings unto thee.”

David believed that God would save him from his tribulations and bring him back to Jerusalem, and even crown him king, because He had anointed him by the hand of Samuel, and would save him from his enemies, so he made promises of the following:
a- Fulfilling the vows to God, which it seems he had made while fleeing from the face of Saul.

b- Offering thank offerings to God, which are peace offerings, as the Law of Moses prescribed. David fulfilled this when he brought back the ark of the covenant of God and offered sacrifices in abundance (2 Sam 6:13) and was in great joy.
13- “For thou hast delivered my soul from death: yea, my feet from slipping, that I may walk before God in the light of the living.”
a- Because God delivered him from certain death to which he was exposed many times.

b- God also delivered him from slipping into wrong conduct or corrupt opinions that take him away from God and deprive him of the Kingdom, especially since his tribulations were severe, and he even lived among the pagans for a time, fleeing from Saul.

c- Walking in the way of light, that is, holiness, and carrying out God’s commandments: this is the light of the living with God, whose end is the perfect light of the living for ever in the Kingdom, where there is full enjoyment of the light of God. The light of the living is also the light of the living saints in heaven, whose way of life we imitate and who help us by their prayers.

God wants you to live in the light of the living all your days, so look to Him, for He is the true light, and make friends with His saints, for they are the first to be enlightened by Him; then you will be able to remain steadfast in His Church, enjoy her sacraments, and love prayer and meditation, so that you live enlightened and are alive before Him for ever. Thanksgiving to God my Savior. To the chief Musician, Al-taschith (Destroy not), a golden psalm (Michtam) of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave: “Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.

2- When was it written? When David was fleeing from the face of Saul and hid in a cave in the wilderness of En-gedi (1 Sam 24), and while he was hiding Saul entered and slept at the mouth of the cave, but David did not kill him; he cut off the skirt of his robe, and thanked God, who had rescued him from Saul’s hand, and even delivered Saul into his hands, and then David forgave him.
3- This psalm suits every person who passes through many tribulations and is surrounded by his enemies, and lifts his heart to God his Savior, and after He rescues him thanks God and praises Him.

4- The words of this psalm were set to a tune called “Destroy Not,” and the two psalms following this one, (Ps 58, 59) and also (Ps 75), were set to the same tune. The words “Destroy not” may refer to a musical instrument with nine strings that accompanied the presentation of the psalm.
5- This psalm is considered one of the distinguished psalms that David composed; therefore it is called a golden psalm (Michtam), and the Jews used to write it in gold ink.

6- This psalm was sung by a group of Levites led by a leader called the chief Musician. So it is a liturgical psalm sung by the congregation of the children of Israel gathered in the house of God, especially in times of tribulation and pain.

7- This psalm is counted among the Messianic psalms, because it tells us of many events in the life of Christ, such as Christ’s resurrection early at dawn on Sunday (v. 8), and it tells us of His ascension to heaven (v. 5).
8- The last part of this psalm (vv. 7-11) is repeated in (Ps 108:1-5).

9- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ was crucified; therefore it tells us of the tribulations that Christ met, but after He died He rose from the dead.
1- “Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast.”
1- David asks God for mercy twice, because of his great need of His help and protection. Asking for mercy twice indicates the need of the Jews and the Gentiles for mercy.

2- David asks for God’s protection under His wings, and God likened Himself to a hen gathering her chicks under her wings (Lk 13:34). God’s protection is complete and protects from all calamities and problems. The wings of God may signify His incarnation in the fullness of time. The two wings are marked by the ability to protect and to snatch away quickly one who needs protection, that is, they indicate the speed of God’s answer to those who seek Him.
2- “I will cry unto God most high, unto God who defends me.”
1- Because of David’s great need of God to save him from Saul’s pursuit, he cried out to Him, and this cry also confirms his faith in God, who is able to protect him.

2- In the spirit of prophecy David cries out to Christ the Savior, crucified at the Sixth Hour, to save him with the rest of mankind who believe in Him. Indeed, Christ who cries out while on the Cross proclaims the need of mankind to cry out to God to save it.
3- “He shall send from heaven, and save me, he reproacheth him that would swallow me up. Selah. God shall send forth his mercy and his truth.”

1- Saul pursued David and tried to kill him, but God kept David, and on the contrary made Saul fall under David’s hand, and then David’s virtue appeared, which is forgiveness. Here the God who saves appears, who sent and arranged from heaven David’s salvation, and reproached and showed the weakness of Saul, fallen at David’s feet. So the one who wanted to devour David was turned into a weak person fallen at David’s feet. Thus appeared God’s mercy, which rescued David, and His truth and justice, which made Saul fall weak at David’s feet.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the incarnate Christ, whom the Father sent to save mankind, and who reproached the devil and even bound him by the Cross, and mercy and truth were fulfilled in the person of Christ, who redeemed mankind and condemned Satan by His Cross.

3- The word Selah is in this verse, after the reproaching of the enemy and the proclamation of salvation from heaven, so that in this musical pause man may contemplate the power of God, who saves His children from the hand of the demons and the wicked.
4- “My soul is among young lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.”
Set on fire: the wicked, inflamed with the fire of evil.
Spears: the plural of spearhead, which is the weapon of the lance, that is, its pointed end.

1- David likens Saul and his company who pursue him to young lions, whose teeth are like the points of spears and arrows, and whose tongues are like swords, to show the fierceness of his enemies, their violence and their plots. But all this did not make David troubled; he slept among his enemies, who were set on fire with the fire of evil, in security, because God protects him, so that no one can come near him, and on the contrary he made his enemy Saul fall at his feet in the cave.

2- This verse is also a prophecy about the plots of the Jews, which ended in the crucifixion of Christ, but He slept at rest on His Cross at the Sixth Hour, and then rose to offer redemption to mankind.
5- “Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth.”

1- David asks God to be exalted above the heavens, that is, to show His glory above all the angels, and while He shows His greatness above the heavens, He lifts up David and all who love God to enjoy fellowship with Him. His glory is also exalted over the earth, that is, God’s glory appears above all the glories of men and their works, which are great in their own sight, and the weakness of men appears and their evils become nothing before His glory and power.

2- David speaks in the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who is exalted above the heavens and over the earth, for after hiding His divinity by His incarnation He rises from the dead and then ascends to heaven, that is, is lifted above the earth in great glory until He is hidden among the clouds, to draw the hearts of His children to heaven, so that they pray at all times.
6- “They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down: they have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves. Selah.”
1- While David’s heart is attached to the great, glorified God, as appeared in the previous verse, the other side appears, which is the wicked’s dealing with him, and it appears in the following:
a- The snares that the wicked prepared for him during their pursuit of him for many years.
b- The threats and the continual attempts to destroy him had a very strong effect on him, so that he expressed it by saying that his soul was bowed down under these pressures.
All this shows the violence of the enemies and the extent of the pain David suffered.

2- The snares that Saul set for David to seize him turned into a snare for Saul himself, for while Saul was pursuing David, he entered and rested in the cave where David was staying, and so the enemy pursuer, Saul, became an easy prey, and David came forward to cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe, and he could have destroyed him, but he forgave him. So Saul fell into the pit he had dug for David, and the pursuer became prey, while the pursued, David, became a mighty man by the power of God.

3- This verse applies to Christ, for whom the Jews set many snares, and bowed His soul with grief throughout His ministry on earth, and in the end dug a pit for Him, the Cross, and destroyed Him, and His power appeared; for by His death He bound Satan, because He paid the debt for mankind who believe in Him, and so He made Satan fall into the pit, and Satan could not bind Christ, but he himself was bound, and after the Cross he can no longer cast the children of God into Hades.

4- At the end of this verse we find the word Selah, a musical pause in which the psalmist contemplates the power of God, who changes situations and rescues His children until He saves them from all their enemies.

Look to Christ your Savior and your stronghold and contemplate His beauty, and He will captivate your mind, gladden your heart and give you peace, and the plots of the demons or all the tribulations that pass over you will no longer disturb you, because your heart is occupied with God. Thus you will be lifted up to heaven while you are on earth.
7- “My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise.”

1- When David’s heart was attached to God, who is exalted above the heavens, his heart was assured and became steadfast in God, not troubled by the enemy’s threats or the changes of life, and this steadfastness became a motive for his quiet spiritual growth, so that he enjoyed fellowship with God.

2- The continued steadfastness of David’s heart moved him to praise God; because David is settled, his eyes were enlightened and he saw God clearly, and so he sang and chanted to Him, and then God revealed His glory to him, and he shared with the heavenly ones in their praise.
8- “Awake up, my glory; awake, rebab and oud: I myself will awake early.”
Early: the early morning is the end of the night, just before dawn.
Rebab: musical instruments each of which has a single string.
Oud: a stringed musical instrument still known today.

1- David believed that God would rescue him from his enemies because he had seen God’s works with him; though he was still pursued by Saul, God had rescued him several times, so his heart was assured, and he felt that his glory is God. In his solitude he called his glory, God, to awake within him, and felt the strength within him, and praised God with the rebab and the oud; indeed, his heart was so attached to God that he awoke at the early morning to praise God before dawn.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the resurrection of Christ, to whom “my glory” refers, so we praise Him with musical instruments, and even awake at the early morning to praise Him, because our hearts have been attached to Him.
3- This verse is also a prophecy about the Holy Spirit, to whom the word “my glory” refers, so we praise Him with power and at all times.
4- The early morning refers to the whole of life that we live on earth, in which we ought to awake to praise God, before the dawn of our life rises, which is eternal life.

5- The Talmud mentions that when David went to sleep he would hang an oud above his bed, and in the middle of the night, when the north winds blew, they would move the strings of the oud, which produced beautiful melodies that woke him from his sleep to read in the Law of God, and then praise and glorify His holy name until the early morning.
9- “I will praise thee, O Lord, among the people: I will sing unto thee among the nations.”
1- David cannot do without God, so even if he fled to the Philistines from the face of Saul he keeps on praying, chanting and thanking God, because God is his life.
2- This verse is a prophecy about the acceptance of the Gentiles into faith in Christ, so that they chant David’s psalms, believe in Christ and praise Him.
10- “For thy mercy is great unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds.”
The clouds: the dark clouds.

1- David felt that God’s mercy had covered those who believe in Him, and forgave them their very many sins, and lifted these weak ones to heaven in their conduct, purity and exalted life, and the glories of heaven await them.
2- God’s truth, which is His justice, shines forth to the clouds, that is, the heavens, where the righteous are glorified with God, while the wicked are cast into torment.

11- “Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: let thy glory be above all the earth.” Here David repeats the verse found in (v. 5), to confirm his longing that God be glorified, and that this glory appear in the heavens and on the earth. And mankind enjoys the glory of salvation in Christ Jesus, as we explained before at (v. 5).

How beautiful it is to awake early to pray and begin your day with speaking to God. Take care to pray before any other work. Ask your guardian angel to wake you early, and know that God your Father is waiting to hear your prayer and rejoices in it.
God the just Judge. To the chief Musician, Al-taschith (Destroy not), of David. A golden psalm (Michtam): “Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation?”… (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, as mentioned in the title.
2- When was it written?
When David was exposed to flight from the face of Absalom and saw evil coming upon him, he asks God, the just Judge, to rescue him and save him.
3- This psalm is sung to the tune “Destroy Not,” and “Destroy not” may be a musical instrument that accompanies the psalm, as we mentioned in the previous psalm.

4- The subject of this psalm is the attack on unjust judges and rulers, that perhaps they will repent, and reminding them of the destruction that awaits them, while on the contrary blessing and joy await the righteous.
5- This psalm is one of the distinguished psalms and so is called a “golden psalm (Michtam),” and it may have been written in gold ink.
6- This psalm is sung by a group of singers who have a leader, or director; therefore it is written in the title “to the chief Musician.”

7- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the wicked Jews rising up against Christ and crucifying Him, but He rejoiced that He had accomplished the salvation of mankind.
8- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
(1) Rebuke of the wicked (vv. 1-5:)
1- “Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?”
Mute righteousness: righteousness that is suppressed, which is neither proclaimed nor carried out.

1- David the prophet asks the wicked rulers and officials: do they speak righteousness in their judgments? Or do they suppress righteousness and not carry it out, or speak deceitful words that seem right but are false, as Absalom sympathized with the people and their cases, wishing that if he were king over the people he would do them justice? He was flattering his people so that they would love him, and then he rose in revolt against his father. He continued for two years until he had won many to himself, and rose in his revolt and drove out his father David (2 Sam 15:2-6).

2- He confirms his first question of reproach with another like it, asking the officials, do you judge uprightly? For in their judging they gave unjust judgments, as the Jews did with Christ, and obtained an order from Pilate for His crucifixion, relying on false accusations.

3- David marvels that these unjust rulers claim that they judge by righteousness and uprightness, while they wish to kill him though he is innocent, for this injustice that fell upon David reveals their evil and their cunning. And he reminded them of their weakness, for he said to them, “O ye sons of men,” that is, that God the just Judge has all authority in His hand, to prevent their injustice and their evil directed at him.
2- “Yea, in heart ye work wickedness; ye weigh the violence of your hands in the earth.”

David makes clear to the unjust rulers that their desire and the intention of their hearts is evil, and then they turn their desire into an act that they do with their hands. They weigh the violence, meaning that they prepare it and know its measure and its weight, and they are aware of the evil they do. This shows their insistence on evil and their persistence in it.
3- “The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies.”
David describes these wicked judges as estranged from the womb and going astray from the belly.

What is meant is not that they went astray as embryos, for an embryo does not go astray, but that from the beginning of their lives they learned evil from their fathers, and when they grew up they lived in it and spoke lies. This shows the importance of sound spiritual upbringing.
4- “Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear;” 5- “Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.”
Poison: the source of venom in the snake’s body.
Adder: the serpent.
Charmers: the plural of snake-charmer, one who gathers serpents so that they do not bite people.
Charmers (chanters): the snake-charmers recite incantations and call to the serpents, to gather them and neutralize their harm to people.

1- David describes the influence of these wicked men as like poison that has no cure, and also describes them as like the serpent that does not hear, because they do not hear the voice of God and stop their ears to Him. On the other hand they do not listen to the cries of the wronged, that is, they are hard of heart, without mercy on anyone, and so they are children of Satan, who is known in the Holy Bible as the serpent that mercilessly brought down the human race. Saul, for example, did not merely pursue David but tried to kill him, like the poisonous snake that kills its victim, and there is no cure for its poison. At the same time Saul was deceitful like the serpent: he first showed his love for David and that he wished to grant him the favor of marrying his daughter, and then asked of him as a dowry the killing of a hundred Philistines, in order to be rid of him.

2- He likens the wicked not only to poisonous serpents, but says that they refuse to respond to the charmers, the chanters, who try to neutralize their poisons; that is, these wicked men refuse to respond to any advice to stop their evil.

If only you would respond to the voice of God on the tongue of the Church’s teachers and of everyone who advises you, so that you do not fall into evil, and if you fall into it, do not persist, lest your heart harden.
(2) The punishment of the wicked (vv. 6-9:)
6- “Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O LORD.”
Break out: shatter.

1- David likened his enemies to beasts with sharp teeth that wish to devour him and tear him, and to young lions with great teeth able to grind his bones, and perhaps he remembered the lion and the bear over which God gave him victory when he was a shepherd of sheep (1 Sam 17:36). If in (v. 4) he likened his enemies to serpents, that is, enemies who fight him with craftiness and cunning, here he likens them to fierce young lions that attack him openly, for David is fought in every way, in secret and in the open, and this shows the difficulty of the war and the extent of his suffering.

2- He asks God to break the sharp teeth, which signify the enemies’ sharp, wounding words, and to break out the great teeth, which signify the enemies’ crushing strength. But above these enemies is God, who protects him and is able to break and remove all the enemy’s strength; therefore David is at peace as long as he prays.

3- This psalm is a prophecy about Christ, who was fought by His enemies with the cunning of serpents, in attempts to catch a word against Him, or attacked violently and sought to be destroyed, as they cried, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Lk 23:21).
7- “Let them melt away as water, let them go. When he aims his arrows, let them turn aside.”
Aims: prepares the arrow for shooting.
Let them turn aside: let them swerve from their target.
