1- David asks God also to blot out the power of his enemies, and likens them to water that falls on the ground in the desert and is swallowed up and vanishes, leaving no trace, that is, the enemies’ power is nullified and does not affect him.

2- David also likens his enemies to arrows that are prepared to be shot at the target, and swerve from it, that is, do not hit David. In this God protects David, however great his enemies’ strength and their threats against him.
8- “As a snail which melteth as it goeth: like the untimely birth of a woman, let them not see the sun.”
Snail: a soft-bodied animal that lives in a sea shell.

1- Likewise David likens the enemies to a small sea creature called the snail, which lives inside a shell, and when it comes out of it and finds an enemy it changes its color from red to a pale white, then secretes a sticky substance on which to slide, and reaches its hiding place inside the shell and seems to have melted. So God makes David’s enemies weak, afraid, and they vanish from before David’s face, because God’s power is with him.

2- David likens the enemies with a new comparison, the untimely birth of a woman, that is, the embryo whose growth was not completed to become a child, so it falls from the womb and dies, that is, it does not become a newborn enjoying the sun and the air.
9- “Before your pots can feel the thorns, whether raw or burned, he shall sweep them away.”
Sweep them away: drive them before him with force.

1- David gives another new comparison for the swiftness with which the enemies vanish. He imagines pots set on thorns in which a fire has been lit, and before the pots feel the heat given off by the thorns, whether these thorns are raw and unburned, or part of them has burned, that is, before the contents of the pots are affected by the heat given off by the thorns, the enemies vanish, and the storm winds sweep them away, and they are not found. All this shows God’s power, which quickly puts the enemies away from David.
2- The pots do not feel the thorns, whether raw or burned (green or dry), that is, David does not feel the troubling of his enemies, because God quickly puts them away from him.

3- The storm wind signifies the wrath of God, which puts the enemies away from David, whether they are raw, green thorns, that is, having vitality, or burned, that is, in weakness; in both cases they do not stand before God’s wrath.

If your God is perfect in His power, do not be troubled by the strength of the demons who fight you, for they are nothing before His power, even if they have made you fall into sin many times. Rise, leaning on God in prayers and striving, confident of your victory.
(3) The joy of the righteous (vv. 10, 11:)
10- “The righteous shall rejoice when he seeth the vengeance: he shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked.”
Vengeance: that is, retribution, meaning by it the wrath of God and the punishment of the wicked.

1- God takes vengeance on David’s enemies; therefore David, that is, the righteous man, rejoices in God’s vengeance, not out of hatred for the enemies or gloating over them, but for the victory of righteousness and the showing of the futility of evil, and in this he remains steadfast in righteousness and in life with God.

2- There was an ancient custom in wars that after victory over the enemies they would wash their feet in the enemies’ blood. David uses this comparison to show the completeness of the victory of righteousness and the joy of the righteous man. This makes David take warning from the destruction of the wicked man, keep away from evil, and tread down all the corruption of the world.
11- “So that a man shall say, Verily there is a fruit for the righteous: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth.”

1- David sums up the whole psalm in this verse, for when the righteous man sees the punishment of the wicked mentioned in (vv. 6-9), he trusts in the justice of God the Judge, who governs the world, and so is not troubled by the strength of the enemies however much they exalt themselves.

2- The faith of David and of all the righteous in God’s just judgment moves them to stand firm in righteousness and to adorn themselves with its fruit, which is the virtues, for they live secure and so advance in the life of righteousness.

If only you would look every day to Christ, the Holy and Righteous One, so that you may stand firm in the life of righteousness and even grow in it, and learn from the saints, and so pass through the world and its evils in peace, even with joy.

The call to God the Savior. To the chief Musician, Al-taschith (Destroy not), a golden psalm (Michtam) of David; when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him: “Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.

2- When was it written? When Saul sent messengers to kill David in his house, but his wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, warned David and let him down through a window of their house before they arrived, and put the teraphim in his bed, with a pillow of goats’ hair at its head, and covered it, and when Saul’s messengers arrived to seize David, Michal told them that he was sick, but Saul told his messengers to bring him even though he was sick, and when they rushed into the house they did not find him (1 Sam 19:12-14). This psalm is counted among the oldest psalms that David wrote.
3- This psalm was sung by a group of Levite singers who had a leader, that is, a chief.

4- This psalm was sung to a musical tune called “Destroy Not,” or an instrument called “Destroy Not” with nine strings. Some of the Fathers see that the words “Destroy not” also mean that God did not allow David to be destroyed and delivered him from Saul’s hand.
5- This psalm is one of David’s great, precious psalms; therefore it is called a golden psalm (Michtam), and it was written in gold ink.
6- The idea of David’s escape by being let down through the window was repeated in the New Testament when they let St. Paul the Apostle down through the window to escape from Damascus (Acts 9:25).

7- This psalm is counted among the Messianic psalms because David here is a type of Christ: as Saul’s messengers watched David’s bed and thought he was sleeping on it, and then rushed in and found only his clothes, so also the guards stood at the tomb and thought that the body of Christ was inside the tomb, but were surprised by His resurrection, and that there was nothing in the tomb but the grave clothes.
8- This psalm expresses a man who suffers distress, and prays, and the Lord delivers him, and so he praises Him and thanks Him.
9- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 1- “Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God: defend me from them that rise up against me.” 2- “Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men.”

1- When David felt that Saul wanted to kill him, while he was still living in his house in Jerusalem with his wife Michal, he cried out to God to deliver him from his enemies and protect him from their evil. And since he prayed, he was assured that he had put himself in God’s hand, which is able to keep him and protect him, and God intervened in a miraculous way, for He made Saul’s daughter stand against her father, and Michal said to David, Flee quickly lest my father kill you, and let him down through a window of her house, and he fled without Saul’s spies, who were watching the door of the house, noticing. David believes that it was God who rescued him, using Michal, and this made his faith in God firm.

2- It appears that Saul wanted to slaughter David; therefore David asked God to deliver him from bloody men. The Church asks God at all times to rescue her, protect her, deliver her and save her, and the Lord answers and keeps His Church throughout the generations.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 3- “For, lo, they lie in wait for my soul: the mighty are gathered against me; not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O LORD.”

1- David declares how Saul and those with him laid an ambush for him to kill him; they are strong and David is weak, but his strength is in his reliance on God, and because he walks in uprightness he is innocent, and they want to kill him.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, whom the Jews tried many times to catch by a word so as to seize Him and kill Him, relying on their strength and their connection with the Roman authority, though He is without sin and they know this, and nothing moves them but their evil and their love of holding on to leadership, for fear of Christ and His popularity, as Saul clung to the love of power and feared the growth of David’s popularity lest he take the throne from him.
3- The mighty are the sinners and the demons, who with cunning and craftiness lie in wait for the innocent children of God to make them fall into sins.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 4- “They run and prepare themselves without my fault: awake to help me, and behold.”

1- David makes clear to God that his enemies are crowding together and running toward him, that is, hastening to destroy him. They are preparing the plot to kill him, knowing that he is innocent; therefore he calls on God to look at him and rescue him. Though they gathered around his house by night, he trusts in God, who is able to rescue him; therefore he says to Him, Awake, for they surround me, and do not wait, O God, until the morning lest they kill me. And indeed God moved Michal, and she let him down by night through the window, and he escaped from the hands of his enemies.
2- David asks God to look upon his innocence, to rescue him from the wicked who wish to destroy him.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 5- “Thou therefore, O LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel, give heed to visit all the nations: be not merciful to any treacherous transgressor. Selah.”

1- When David felt the enemies drawing near to him to kill him, he cried out to God, in whose power he trusts; therefore he called Him the LORD of hosts, who is at the same time the God of Israel, for His power is for the benefit of His people and His children. Therefore David asks Him to give heed, that is, to prepare to intervene to rescue him from death. And because Saul and his helpers went on in evil in their attempts to kill David, they are like the nations in their evil, and deserve God’s visitation, that is, His calling them to account and punishing them for their treachery and iniquity, for the punishment of persisting in evil is destruction.

2- This psalm is fit to be repeated by the people of God in their wars with the nations around them, since it mentions here the word “nations,” and by it he may mean the nations around the people of God, so he asks the mighty God, the LORD of hosts, the protector of His people Israel, to give heed and call the nations to account and punish them without mercy, for their rejection of God and their persistence in evil.
3- He ends this verse with the word Selah, a musical pause for meditating on God’s power that supports His children.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 6- “They return at evening: they make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city.”
They make a noise: the voice of the dog that shows its weakness, which is different from the barking that shows its strength.

1- David describes his enemies as like dogs that come at evening and make weak sounds. Men actually came and watched David’s house by night, and they spoke to one another in low voices so that no one would notice them. And they go round about the city of Jerusalem to spy and learn news of David, and to make sure that he is in his house so that they can kill him.

2- The gathering of the wicked in the evening, where there is darkness, shows their inclination to evil that they do in the dark, and they spend their night in anxiety and in devising plots, whereas God gives the righteous man quiet sleep by night.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 7- “Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords are in their lips: for who, say they, doth hear?”
They belch out: they speak evil.

David continues describing his enemies with three things: first, that they speak evil words; second, that they wrong people, for their words wound and destroy, and therefore he called them swords; and third, that they make light of God’s long-suffering toward them, and think that He does not hear their evils. All this means that the enemies went on in their sins, not profiting from God’s long-suffering as an opportunity for their repentance.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 8- “But thou, O LORD, shalt laugh at them; thou shalt have all the nations in derision.”

David lifts his eyes to God and turns them away from the wicked men’s attempts to destroy him, and sees God in His power deriding all their evil plots, for He is able to nullify them in a moment and deliver His son David. This shows the extent of David’s faith and his trust in God.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from the enemies

paragraphs.text: 9- “Because of his strength I take refuge in thee: for God is my refuge.”

When David looked at the strength of his enemies he felt his weakness, so he hastened to look to God, who is stronger than all, and took refuge in Him to protect him from the enemy, because David had grown accustomed to taking refuge in God and being fortified in Him, so that he lives secure however much evil surrounds him.

Get used to looking to God at all times, so that you depend on Him, and are not shaken by the turmoil of the world around you, and it is easy for you to seek Him, and He nullifies all the devil’s plots, and when you are at peace you enjoy fellowship with God and service of Him.
10- “The God of my mercy shall go before me: God shall let me see my desire upon mine enemies.”

1- Since David was assured that God is his stronghold and refuge, he began to describe his God with humility, saying that His mercy goes before him, that is, that he lives by God’s mercy, because he is a sinner, weak and falling short.

2- God, who protects David, shows him the weakness of his enemies and how God disciplines them and punishes them because they wronged him, and also guides him how to deal with them, and so David enjoys seeing God and hearing His voice.
11- “Slay them not, lest my people forget: make them wander by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield.”

Make them wander: make them stray, that is, be scattered, dispersed and dispersed abroad, and not know their way. Our shield: the shield is a defensive implement that the soldier used in ancient times; it is a piece of wood with a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand, and he moves it before his face and body to protect him from arrows.

1- David asks God not to destroy the enemies of his people, but to make them wander, that is, in weakness, not knowing how to walk or act, and to bring them down, that is, to lower them from their pride, so that they feel their weakness. In this David’s love for his people and for his enemies appears, in the following:
a- God protects His people from the enemies who have become weak and cannot harm His people.
b- When the people of God see their enemies in weakness, their faith is made firm in God, who is their shield and defender.
c- The people of God remain ready for war and for defending their country, that is, they are not careless, because the enemies are still present, but weak.
d- An opportunity for the enemies to repent, believe and return to God, and this shows David’s broad heart, loving even his enemies.

2- This verse applies to Christ, against whom the Jews rose up and crucified Him, yet He did not take vengeance on them and kill them, as Peter wanted to kill with his sword those who came to seize Christ, and He told him that if He wished He could ask for twelve legions of angels to fight for Him, but He wants to redeem mankind (Mt 26:53). And after His resurrection He did not kill the Jews, but scattered them in the countries of the world after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, so they became weak, as Cain, after killing Abel, became a wanderer in the earth; for the result of sin is always wandering and weakness (Gen 4:12-14).
12- “For the sin of their mouth and the words of their lips let them even be taken in their pride: and for cursing and lying which they speak.”
1- David identified his enemies’ sins as two sins:
a- Their speech, for they fell into sins of speech, such as cursing, that is, abuse, and lying.

b- Their pride, for they felt that their plots must succeed, and trusted in their personal strength. For these two sins God took them, that is, called them to account and punished them, so Saul and his sons perished in the war, and the throne passed to David.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom the Jews rose up with pride and with evil words, demanding His crucifixion, and imagined that they had been rid of Him by His death on the Cross, but the truth is that He rose from the dead and drew them to faith, and they submitted to Him.
13- “Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be: and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah.”

1- In the spirit of prophecy David declares that God will consume his enemies, and he repeats the word “consume” twice, because they will perish on earth, and then in the other life. And by this consuming, that is, when the existence of these wicked men ends, God is glorified in His people, the children of Jacob, that is, those who believe in Him, because He kept His children and consumed the wicked who trouble them, so the faith of the righteous is made firm, and the rest of the wicked fear, perhaps to return, believe and repent.

2- This verse was fulfilled in the Jews who resisted Christ, whom He consumed on earth by the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 at the hand of the Romans, and then He will consume them on the Day of Judgment, in eternal torment.
3- This verse ends with the word Selah, a musical pause for meditating on God’s power, which is glorified in His children and punishes those who resist Him.
14- “And at evening let them return; and let them make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city.”

Verse (14) is a repetition of (v. 6), but with another meaning, for it speaks of the wicked in eternity, and describes their life as being at evening, that is, in the outer darkness, and in weakness they make a noise like dogs, and go round about, that is, in wandering, and they remain so for ever in this torment and perplexity, as the position of the rich man in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus expressed (Lk 16:19-31).
15- “They shall wander up and down for meat, and if they be not satisfied, they shall stay the night.”

David continues his description of the state of the wicked in eternal torment, that in their wandering they suffer hunger, and remain, that is, stay the night in this hunger for ever, while the righteous are satisfied with the divine love in the Kingdom.

Do not rejoice in the gains you achieve by breaking God’s commandments, for they are all temporary and passing, and even call for judgment in the end; and on the contrary, if you fall into sin, hasten to repentance to obtain God’s mercies.

16- “But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble.” 17- “Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, and the God of my mercy.” Morning: early dawn.
Refuge: a place of shelter.

1- Although David began his psalm by crying out to God to save him, in faith he ends the psalm by praising the mighty God who saved him from his enemies. And he chants in the morning after his deliverance from their hands and the end of the trial, because God was his refuge. And he thanks God for His many mercies that are hard to count.

2- David prophesies about the resurrection of Christ at dawn on Sunday, “the morning,” and praises the mighty and merciful God, who died and rose to raise His children in Him, and to be a refuge for them continually.

3- This verse applies to the feelings of David and all who believe in Him in eternity, who praise God in the morning, which is the dawn of the new life, and thank His power and His mercy that kept them all their lives and was a refuge for them.

Thank God every day for His care for you, and for His rescuing you from the many evils that you know, or from which He kept you without your knowing, and by your praising Him your faith is made firm, and you keep away from sin and enjoy fellowship with Him.

God our helper. To the chief Musician upon Shushan. A testimony. A golden psalm (Michtam) of David, to teach; when he strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, when Joab returned, and smote of Edom in the valley of salt twelve thousand: “O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast broken us down” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.
2- When was it written?

a- When the children of Israel were fighting Aram-naharaim, who lives in northern Iraq, and Aram-zobah, who lives west of Aram-naharaim, that is, in northern Syria, and met strong resistance from them. At the same time Edom, south of the kingdom of Judah, struck, so David sent Abishai, and he killed six thousand of them, and then Joab, and he killed twelve thousand of them, that is, they killed 18,000 of the Edomites (2 Sam 8:13). That was in the valley of salt, which is called the Ghor; the valley of salt is a deserted valley lying south of the kingdom of Judah, on the border of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

b- There is another opinion that completes the previous one, which is that David also remembered what happened to him when he was driven out by Saul, and when he reigned for seven years over the tribe of Judah, and Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, was fighting him, so David bore much suffering, but God gave him victory, and he reigned after that over all Israel.
3- This psalm was sung to a tune called Shushan (lily), and there is another opinion that Shushan is a musical instrument resembling the lily flower with its fragrant scent.

4- This psalm is considered a testimony from David to God’s help and His power that supports His children. And by this psalm David means to teach God’s children in every generation to believe and trust in Him. The Levites used to repeat this psalm as a congregation with a chief, to teach the people not to be troubled by tribulations but to be patient, to strive and to offer repentance for their sins, and then God intervenes and gives them victory over their enemies, so they thank Him and glorify Him, because He alone is the cause of their victory. How beautiful it is to present teaching in the form of praise and thanksgiving to God.
5- This psalm is a golden psalm (Michtam) of David, that is, one of David’s great, precious psalms, and it was written in gold ink.
6- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms, because David in it is a type of Christ, who bore the sufferings for our sake, and then triumphed over all His enemies the demons by the Cross.

7- This psalm is considered a prophecy about the Assyrian captivity, then the Babylonian captivity, and then the greatness of God is revealed in the return of His people from captivity, the rebuilding of the Temple, and rejoicing in God’s grace and glorifying Him.
8- This psalm suits every person in distress, and helps him to be patient until he obtains God’s victory and passes through the tribulation, and so praises Him.
9- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- “O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast broken us down, thou hast been displeased; O turn us again.”
Displeased: very angry.

1- David reproaches God because He cast off His children and broke them down, that is, entered among the ranks of the army, divided it and scattered it. He was also displeased with it, that is, disciplined it with severe anger. All this shows God’s forsaking of His people, so they were exposed to the violence of the enemy armies. But David’s faith and his hope in God appear in his saying “turn us again,” that is, return Your care to us, and let us return to Your embrace, that You may shepherd us with Your fatherhood and love.

2- This verse is a prophecy about what happened in the Assyrian captivity and then the Babylonian, when God forsook His people and disciplined them with captivity, and the enemies broke into them, ruined their land and took them as slaves. But the people of God repented, put away the idols and lusts, and asked Him to bring them back from captivity, and He restored them with great honor, and they built the Temple.

3- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who was rejected and broken in upon, and on whom the divine displeasure came in the sufferings and the Cross for our sake, because He bore the sins of the whole world, but He returns with power in the holy Resurrection.
2- “Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof; for it shaketh.”
Broken it: split it and divided it.

1- David shows what happened to his army when he was fighting the Arameans, and likens what happened to an earthquake that split the ground under their feet, so the enemies attacked them, and therefore he asks God to mend the breach that occurred in the army; God answered, and he overcame the Arameans, and also the Edomites in the south.

2- This verse is a prophecy about what happened to Jerusalem in the Babylonian attack, which he likens to an earthquake that split the land and shook it, and he asks God to mend its breach, and this is what happened when God brought His people back from captivity, and they built the Temple and worshiped God in it.

3- This is a prophecy about the crucified Christ, at whose crucifixion the earth shook, but He rose and brought calm back to the souls that believed in Him, so they lived in peace, and He mended every weakness in them.
3- “Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of staggering.”
Hard things: distress.
Staggering: swaying and shaking as happens to one who is drunk with wine.

1- What happened to the army of the children of Israel before Aram David describes as hard things, and likens it to intoxicating wine, which makes the one who drinks it stagger, that is, the army of the children of Israel became weak before Aram, but when God was sought it regained its strength and defeated the enemies, and even defeated Edom, which took advantage of the opportunity and attacked the south of the land of the Jews.
2- This hardship and wine of staggering is what has happened to Christians from the beginning of the apostolic age until today, but God does not leave His people who cry out to Him in repentance.
4- “Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah.”

1- Here David shows God’s answer to the cry of His people, whom He had disciplined and who returned to Him; then God had compassion on His people who fear Him and gave them a banner, the banner of victory, for it was customary in ancient wars for armies to raise a banner of victory. This banner is raised to proclaim the truth, who is God, the supporter of His people, so that He defeats their enemies.

2- The first banner that God gave to His people to reassure them was the rainbow, to confirm to them that He would not flood the world with a deluge again, and this banner is still raised today when the rain comes down heavily.

3- The people of God in Egypt in the days of Moses raised the banner over their houses, which was the blood with which they smeared the upper doorpost and the two side posts when they slaughtered the lamb, and the destroying angel passed over their houses, because they were under the protection of the blood, which signifies the blood of Christ.
4- In the war with Satan the banner is the crucified Christ, who is the truth, who bound Satan by the Cross; our banner is the Cross. The Church confirms this verse in the Friday psali.
5- The word Selah is a musical pause for meditating on the power of God that He gives to those who fear Him, who love the truth.
5- “That thy beloved may be delivered; save with thy right hand, and hear me.”

1- The banner of victory that God gave to His beloved, His children and those who fear Him, delivers them from the hands of the enemies, and they are saved from every tribulation by the power of God, that is, His right hand, so David rejoices, because God answered his prayers and delivered his people.

2- David here asks for his people and not only for himself, for he feels his responsibility and fatherhood toward all his people, so he prays for them that God may give them complete victory, because God’s right hand is able to do all things.

Take care to pray for everyone around you, for you are responsible for them before God to guide them and encourage them in their relationship with God, and if you cannot speak, at least lift up your prayers, and be an example to them.

entries.section: (2) Joy in the victory of God

paragraphs.text: 6- “God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.”
Shechem: a city lying west of the Jordan River, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, now called Nablus, in which Jacob dwelt in ancient times.
Succoth: a region lying east of the Jordan River, south of the Jabbok River, in which Jacob dwelt in ancient times.

1- God commanded by His holy word and promised David to give him the whole kingdom of Israel, which dwells east and west of the Jordan River, that is, the land of Canaan and everything around it. And God rejoices and is glad at this, and divides the land and measures its borders and gives it all to His people over whom David reigns.

2- These words apply also to David, who rejoices in God’s promise to him, and so possesses the land east and west of the Jordan River, and the nations around him submit to him. This land is where the first fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dwelt and blessed it.

3- God in the fullness of time spoke by His holy Son, who became incarnate for our redemption. And God is glad because His Son is the object of His pleasure. And He divides and measures the land, which signifies the blessings of the New Testament given in His Church in the form of the Holy Sacraments, the means of grace, and the fruits and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (2) Joy in the victory of God

paragraphs.text: 7- “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the helmet of my head; Judah is my scepter.”
Gilead: the grandson of Manasseh, a wide region lying east of the Jordan River, in which half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt.

Ephraim: the largest of the tribes in the northern kingdom of Israel, and its first line of defense. Judah: the tribe from which King David came, and whose descendants continued to reign over this tribe until Christ came from his descendants.
My scepter: the golden staff that the king holds, which represents his authority and his kingship.

1- God declares that He has the region east of the Jordan, which is Gilead, where half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt with the tribes of Reuben and Gad; that is, God settled His people east of the Jordan River, and settled them also west of the Jordan River, where the tribe of Ephraim, large in number, reigned, which held a wide region and represents the great power in the northern kingdom of Israel; therefore He called it my helmet, that is, the protection of my head, for it is the first defender of the kingdom of Israel. As for Judah, it is also a large tribe dwelling in the south west of the Jordan River, and from it came King David and his descendants who reigned over the kingdom of Judah.

2- Though God permitted His people dwelling east of the Jordan, and in the kingdom of Israel, to be taken as slaves in the Assyrian captivity, and the kingdom of Judah also to be taken with the Babylonian captivity, yet they are all His children whom He brings back from captivity and keeps, because they believed in Him and lived with Him.

entries.section: (2) Joy in the victory of God

paragraphs.text: 8- “Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast my shoe: O Philistia, shout thou over me.”
Moab: a son of Lot; a people hostile to the people of God, who dwell east of the Dead Sea.
Edom: the descendants of Esau; a people hostile to the people of God, who dwell south of the kingdom of Judah.
Philistia: a people hostile to the people of God who dwell south-east of the kingdom of Judah.
My washpot: a vessel for washing off filth.

1- After David showed God’s grace given to him in possessing the land of Gilead, with the tribe of Manasseh dwelling in it, the strength given to the tribe of Ephraim, and the wisdom given to the tribe of Judah that kings might come out of it, he spoke in this verse about the hostile peoples who resist the children of Israel. And he showed his wishes that Moab become a washpot for him, that is, be brought low, he and his pagan gods, so that the people of God are not drawn to them but despise them. As for Edom, proud in its dwelling in the mountains, it will be brought low, and David and the children of Israel will tread it with their shoes. As for Philistia, which humbled the children of Israel greatly, David will subdue it, so that it shouts over him and cries out in pain at what he will do to it when he triumphs over it.

2- God, who graciously gave His people possession of the land of Canaan and what is around it, also gave His people to overcome the nations around them so that they would not resist them, and this actually happened in the days of David, and then Solomon.

If God is with us, who is against us. Do not be troubled by tribulations or threats, but always remember the power of God that is with you, which supports you and even glorifies you and gladdens your heart.
9- “Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?”

When David looked at the capital of the land of Edom, high on the mountains and fortified by them, so that it is very hard to reach and subdue, he cried out to God and said, expressing his weakness, who will lead me to it; and this shows David’s humility and his declaring his need of God, especially before the power of the enemies, that is, Edom.
10- “Is it not thou, O God, who hast cast us off, and goest not forth, O God, with our armies?”

David continued his prayer and said to God, there is none but You, O Lord, who brings me to Edom, so that I may triumph over it by Your power, and I know that You cast us off and did not go out with our armies for a time, to discipline us, so that we may trust that the strength is from You and not from us, and so be humbled and repent of our sins.
11- “Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man.” 12- “Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.” Valiantly: with strength.

1- In conclusion David declares that man is unable to save himself and must need God’s help. Man’s strength appears strong outwardly, but it is temporary and weak before the changes of life. The solution is to take refuge in God and ask His help.

2- David says that if we trust in God, He intervenes with mighty power and defeats our enemies and treads them down, so that they have no strength before us, whether the demons or the wicked who follow them, because God’s power cannot be resisted.

Do not be troubled by your helplessness and the weakness of your strength before the demands of life, because your God is able to make up every lack in you, and even supports you so that you become stronger than those around you and distinguished, and so glorify God.
Thanksgiving to God the stronghold. To the chief Musician upon stringed instruments. A psalm of David: “Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.
2- When was it written? When he fled from the face of Absalom his son, and then David’s army defeated the army of the children of Israel, and Absalom was killed.
3- This psalm was sung by a group of Levites led by a chief, that is, a leader.
4- The repeating of this psalm is accompanied by a musical instrument called the stringed instrument, an ancient stringed instrument resembling the oud and the rebab.
5- This psalm shows David the man of prayer, the believer, who trusts in God and is full of hope and loves His worship.
6- This psalm is a prophecy about the feelings of the captives before their return from captivity to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple.
7- This psalm is counted among the liturgical psalms, for the congregation of the people of God repeats it in tribulations, and when praying for the king, or the high priest.
8- This psalm is also counted among the Messianic psalms, because it speaks in the spirit of prophecy about Christ the King, who reigns for ever (vv. 6, 7).

9- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ offered Himself on the Cross for our salvation; therefore this psalm cries out to God the King to deliver us from all our tribulations, make us steadfast in Him and give us complete salvation.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God the refuge

paragraphs.text: 1- “Hear my cry, O God; attend unto my prayer.” 2- “From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.”
Overwhelmed: lost consciousness; here it means weakness, and in the Hebrew original it means suffering and writhing.

1- David felt that he was far from Jerusalem, the holy city, and from the ark of the covenant of God, so he felt isolation and that he was at the end of the earth; therefore he cried out to God with fervent prayers, and hoped that God would hear him, especially since he was in great weakness that overwhelmed his heart and made him suffer severely and writhe, especially as he was isolated and driven out by his son. And he asked God to lead him to a high rock, “higher than I,” and firm, that he might climb upon it, and his faith was that his rock is God and that God would lift him upon this rock, that is, make his faith firm, raise him above all his sorrows and pains and give him assurance and peace; so David was asking God not only for His protection but to raise him above his toils.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about the captives of the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity who pray while far from Jerusalem, scattered in the world and suffering, but their hope is the return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple, where God is their rock.
3- Christ is the rock who appeared in the Old Testament with Moses, of whom David speaks here, who is the hope of mankind, that is, the Cross that offered salvation to the whole world.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God the refuge

paragraphs.text: 3- “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy.”

1- David remembers God’s protection of him throughout his former life, and is filled with trust and faith in God, and says, “Thou hast been a shelter for me.” So ought every person to remember God’s former works and thank Him for them, so that his faith grows and is made firm.

2- God was to David not only a shelter but a tower from which he watches the enemy and discovers the hidden and concealed enemies, and strikes them with arrows. So God did not only protect David but gave him strength to attack his enemies, and they feared him. So also the demons fear the holy children of God.

3- Christ is a shelter for His children who protects them from every sin, and He is a strong tower by which they discover all the schemes of the demons, and even attack them with humility, the acquiring of virtues and the doing of good, and He also repels from them the hidden enemies, that is, the demons, and overcomes them.

4- 1- Since David, in his exile from the face of Absalom, was sure that God is his refuge and his strength, he wished to dwell in God’s tabernacle, that is, His Temple, for ever. What is meant, of course, is not to live inside the Holy Place or the Holy of Holies, but to live beside the Temple of God, as the Hebrew original of the word means, so that he could offer continual worship to God. Indeed, out of his love for the house of God he wished to dwell in his heart, that is, to enjoy God’s dwelling in him throughout his life.

2- David wished that God would protect him with the covering of His wings, so that no one could harm him, because God surrounds him with His care and love, as the cherubim spread their wings over the cover of the ark of the covenant of God; therefore the cover was called the mercy seat, and the glory of God appeared on the cover of the ark. That is, David wishes to receive God’s mercies when He overshadows him with His wings.

3- What is meant by God’s dwelling is Jerusalem, where the ark of the covenant of God is, so David wishes to offer the worship of God throughout his life. God’s dwelling is also the heavenly Jerusalem, so David wishes to live for ever with God.
4- The verse ends with the word Selah, a musical pause in which man meditates on God’s love, care and mercy.

Do you long to be in the Church so as to enjoy seeing God, be nourished by His Holy Sacraments, and cast all your toils into His embrace, so that your heart is at peace and you walk securely in all your steps?!
5- “For thou, O God, hast heard my vows: thou hast given me the heritage of those that fear thy name.”

1- Since David’s heart was attached to the house of God, he wished in his exile to offer vows to God, and mentioned them in his prayers, and God rejoiced when He heard them because they express David’s longing for the house of God and his faith in God’s power, which is able to bring him back from his exile to Jerusalem. And he reminded God of the blessings He gave to him and to all who fear God, which is the promised land from which his son drove him out, but God is able to bring him back to it. This land is a pledge of the inheritance of eternal life.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who offered Himself as a vow for us before the Father, when He said in His intercessory prayer, “For their sakes I sanctify myself” (Jn 17:19), and we respond to Christ’s love and sanctify ourselves to Him throughout our lives; for we have become God’s heritage and His possession in Christ, and so we live for Him, consecrating our hearts on earth, and then enjoy fellowship with Him in the Kingdom for ever.
6- “Thou wilt prolong the king’s life: and his years as many generations.” 7- “He shall abide before God for ever: O prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him.”

1- By faith David saw that God would bring him back from his exile to his throne in Jerusalem, and so his days and years as king are extended, and he remains seated on his throne before God, and God keeps him, working by mercy and truth, that is, justice, so that he governs his people with uprightness. In addition, he reigns for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

2- These two verses are a clear prophecy about Christ the King, who reigns for ever, that is, to eternity, and His rule is by mercy and truth. For He fulfilled divine justice, that is, truth, on the Cross by His death for us, and His mercy appeared in the forgiveness of our sins and the renewal of our life in Him. And when we walk in uprightness and reign over ourselves by controlling our lusts and directing our energy to God, God is glorified in us and reigns through us, and by our being kings we are an extension of His kingdom.
8- “So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever, that I may daily perform my vows.”

1- As a result of God’s works that David mentioned in the previous verses, he thanks God at the close of this psalm, and keeps on thanking Him throughout his life, and even wishes to enter the heavenly Kingdom to continue in this thanksgiving for ever. Thus David moved from the appeal and cry to God because of his need of Him, which he mentioned at the beginning of the psalm, and began to thank Him at the end of the psalm, and even entered into a life of constant thanksgiving.

2- David was not content with thanksgiving but promised to perform his vows that he offered to God while in his exile, and promises to perform them day by day. By this he does not mean only a specific, determined vow, but continual worship of God that he offers every day.

If you ask and press upon God to supply your needs and solve your problems, do not forget to thank Him after He intervenes and shows His love for you, because by thanksgiving you delight in His gifts, and your faith and your joy in God grow. Trust in God the Savior. To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun. A psalm of David: “Truly my soul waiteth upon God” (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.
2- When was it written?
When David was fleeing from the face of Absalom his son.

3- David wrote this psalm and gave it to a chief of the singers named Jeduthun, who is most likely Ethan the Ezrahite, one of the three chiefs of the singers in David’s days, for he was with Asaph and Heman the Ezrahite (1 Chr 15:17). The name Jeduthun is also found in the title of Psalms (39, 77).
4- This psalm shows David’s courage, his trust and his hope in God; it is an encouraging psalm that supports everyone who passes through distress.
5- This psalm also teaches patience, which controls anger and pride.
6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation.

1- Despite the severity of the affliction David suffered, being driven from the face of Absalom and threatened with death, his faith in God his Savior did not waver. He lifted his eyes toward Him, awaiting His salvation; indeed he waited upon God alone, as the verse means in the original Hebrew.
2- Here David prophesies of Christ, the only Savior of all humanity, apart from whom there is no salvation, by his saying, "from him cometh my salvation."
2- He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.

1- David feels that God is his refuge, and he likens Him to the firm, strong rock; and so, since David held fast to God the Rock, he stood firm in his faith. Although at the beginning he was a little disturbed, his hope was to return to his place in Jerusalem. However strong a man may be, he is weak and liable to be disturbed. The beautiful thing is to see David's clinging to God: his disturbance did not last, and he felt God his Savior with him.
3- How long will you attack a man? You all destroy him like a leaning wall, like a falling fence!
Leaning wall: a wall that is collapsing.

1- David addresses his enemies and says to them: How long will you attack the man and try to shatter him like a wall, or a broken or collapsing fence? The man here means David, and this shows the extent of David's suffering, so that he was shaken a little (v. 2); at the same time it shows the extent of his faith in God who steadies him, so that all his enemies cannot prevail against him.

2- The man also means Christ, against whom all rose up, Romans and Jews, rulers and people; yet He bore all this for our sake and died on the cross, but by the power of His divinity He rose from the dead.

3- The enemies here signify the demons, who attack the spiritual person and try to demolish him, so that he suffers afflictions in his life and may fall into some sins; but through repentance God raises him up from them.
4- They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah.

1- David continues to describe what the wicked do to the righteous man: they try to turn him away from faithfulness and from the worship of God. This is the excellency, and they do this because they are children of the devil, so they love evil and hate good; therefore they try to remove righteous David from his righteousness.

2- In addition to this, the wicked cast false accusations at the righteous man, and they delight in this because they are liars and also hypocrites. They bless the righteous man with kind words, but in their hearts they curse him and revile him. So did Absalom and Shimei the son of Gera to David.

3- The righteous man is also Christ, whom the Jews tried to ensnare with a word, to make Him fall into error, and whom they charged with false accusations. They showed Him affection while their hearts wanted to kill Him, as Judas Iscariot did with Him, who betrayed Him with a kiss.
4- This verse ends with the word "Selah," which is a musical pause for meditating on the hideousness of evil, so that a person may keep away from it.

Walk in goodness and do virtue, holding fast to God's commandments, for this is a proof of your sonship to Him. Keep away from evil so that you may not be a son of the devil. The more you love righteousness and strive toward it, the more your heart is filled with peace, and an inexpressible happiness awaits you in the Kingdom.
5- My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.

In answer to all the plots of the wicked against David, we find that he does not speak with them, but speaks to himself, calling upon his soul to submit to God, to bear these sufferings from the wicked, and to wait for the Lord, its hope. This means two things:
1- David's surrender of himself to God, his reliance on Him, and his acceptance of all sufferings for His sake.
2- His faith and hope in God, who will surely intervene and rescue him from the hands of his enemies, and this is what indeed happened, for God restored David to his throne.
6- He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved. 7- In God is my salvation and my glory: the rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.
1- David describes God as:
a- My rock: so he relies on Him, because the rock is firm and strong.
b- My salvation: for he has no deliverer from all his enemies and his afflictions except God, who is able to do all things.
c- My refuge: so he takes shelter in Him and is fortified against all the plots and attacks of the wicked.
d- My glory: for God does not only protect me, but also gives me glories that I taste in part on earth, and then fully in eternity.

2- At the beginning of the psalm David declared that he was shaken only a little (v. 2), but after he trusted in God, placed his hope in Him and felt that He was his rock, he became firm and never shaken.
8- Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
1- David sums up his counsels to the children of God who believe in Him in three matters:
a- Trust in God: for He is the only support in life, and trusting in Him is not only in time of affliction but at all times, so that a person lives secure from the enemy's attacks, open and hidden.

b- Pour out your heart: that is, pray with contrition and supplication to God, that He may intervene in one's life. Pouring out also means emptying the heart of every sin and worldly concern, that is, repentance, so that the heart becomes pure and ready to be filled with God.
c- Take refuge in Him: for He is the strong fortress inside which a person is secure and in which he remains always, in order to live in security.
2- This verse ends with the word "Selah," which is a musical pause calling us to think about God, our hope, in whom we trust.

If only you would accustom yourself to prayer every day. Then your feelings will stir toward God and you will trust in Him, as you feel His power with you, and your heart will rejoice and be filled with His grace that overflows upon you.

9- Surely the sons of Adam are vanity, the sons of men are a lie; in the balances they go up; they are altogether lighter than vanity. David describes the strength of men as vain, for it is nothing before the power of God. The measures of men are also vain, because the true measure is God, not money, or health, or social relationships. Therefore David does not fear those who are hostile to him, because their power is vain, and he is confident in his God, who is able to protect him, and even to restore him to his throne with power.
10- Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.
1- David counsels his people in two matters:
a- Not to be attached to the love of money and wealth, because it is vain and does not support a person; rather, strength is from God.

b- Not to resort to oppression, because it is a means of coveting the possessions of others and seizing them from them; oppression is a means to unlawful wealth, and this increases God's anger against a person. The Jews were angry with Christ because He drove the sellers out of the Temple, and so prevented their trade and the means of their wealth; for they loved money more than prayer, so much so that they defiled the temple of God with their trading.
11- God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God. 12- Also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy: for thou renderest to every man according to his work.

1- David says that God spoke once, meaning that His word is one and does not change. David heard it twice, because God repeats His word many times, so that a person may not forget but may take heed; yet the content of the word is one.
2- God has two essential attributes which must be present in a judge, and they are:
a- Power: that is, authority, ability and strength.
b- Mercy: that is, compassion and tenderness toward all.

For this reason, since God bears these two attributes in perfection, He alone is the Judge of the whole earth, and He will repay every person according to his works on the day of judgment, rewarding the righteous in the Kingdom and punishing the wicked in eternal torment. Neither of the two attributes in God can be neglected, that is, relying on His mercy without fearing Him, so that we become lax toward sin, or fearing His authority and forgetting His mercy, so that we fall into despair.

Always remember the fear of God so that you may reject sin, or rise from it quickly if you fall. Remember also His mercy, so that you may be encouraged however much the devil fights you and your weakness appears before him; for your God loves you and has mercy on you, and at the same time protects you by His fear from every sin.
Thirst and joys "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David.

2- When it was written: a- When David was fleeing from the face of Absalom in the wilderness of Judah (2 Sam 15:23). This is the more probable opinion, because it mentions that the king rejoices in God (v. 11).

b- When David was fleeing from the face of Saul in the wilderness of Judah (1 Sam 23:14), after Samuel had anointed him king, but he had not been proclaimed king over the people because Saul was on the throne.
3- This psalm is a prophecy about the captives in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity, and those thirsting for God and for worshiping Him in His temple in Jerusalem.
4- This psalm contains a prophecy about the destruction of Saul, or Absalom (v. 9).
5- This psalm suits every person who feels a longing for God and a need to be in His house.

6- The Church prays this psalm at the beginning of every day in the Prime prayer of the Agpeya, because it shows the longings of the praying person for God at the beginning of the day. The Church then prays it again in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ said on the cross that He was thirsty, not only for water, but for the salvation of humanity, and humanity answers Him that it is thirsty for His love and His redemption. (1) Longings and praise (vv. 1-7:)
1- O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;

1- David's longings toward God with his soul and body made him wake early to pray. The word for rising early in the original Hebrew means the time of the dawn watch, that is, before daybreak, because David's heart was so occupied with God that he could sleep only a little, and then he would wake up to pray.

2- David was in the wilderness, where there is thirst because there is no water, but the thirst of his soul for God was stronger. When he prayed, his soul was refreshed. His thirst for God was not only for praying in his chamber, but a thirst to be in the presence of God before the ark of the covenant, to offer worship in Jerusalem, for he was far from it because of Absalom.

3- The dry land without water cannot yield fruit, and this is a description of David's soul, which had become dry through its distance from God. The solution is prayer, so that it is refreshed and bears the fruits of the Spirit.
2- To see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary.

1- As David had experienced seeing God and sensing Him in Jerusalem, when he offered worship in the midst of the crowds before the ark of the covenant, he now longs to see God's power and glory while in the wilderness; for God fills every place, and he is unable to go to Jerusalem and needs God's power and glory, not only to satisfy him, but also to support him against the evil of his enemies. David loves the prayer he was accustomed to in Jerusalem and cannot do without it in any place.
2- When we say that David saw, he expresses his longings to see God's power and glory in His Incarnation, which was to take place in the fullness of time.
3- Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee.

1- David feels that life with God, and enjoying fellowship with Him, is better than all the delights of the life of the world; and likewise, before the greatness of God's mercy, his lips burst forth in praising God and thanking Him. His lips cannot praise God except by His help and mercy.
2- Life with God and the enjoyment of His mercy, even for a short period of life, is better than a long life far from God.

3- Perhaps this verse is a prophecy about the feelings of the captives in Babylon, as they feel that enjoying God's mercy and worshiping Him in Jerusalem is better than all the grandeur of life in Babylon, and there in Jerusalem it is sweet for them to praise before the temple of God.
4- Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name.

1- Since David enjoyed seeing God and felt His hand supporting him, he declared a clear promise to God to bless Him in his life, meaning throughout his life and in all the times and aspects of his life; for God is the cause of every blessing, success and security in his life.

2- Lifting up the hands is an expression of prayer, supplication and thanksgiving to God, and it is the body's sharing with the spirit in prayer. The lifting up of the hands and the love of prayer are both by the help of God, who encourages us to pray. Indeed, the prayer and the lifting up of the hands are directed to the name of God, that is, His person, because the heart has clung to God and risen to Him along with the body. This shows the extent of David's longings for God, so that they lifted him up to heaven and raised him above many sins because of his preoccupation with the love of God. The lifting up of the hands is also a symbol of victory over Satan, as Moses lifted up his hands and Joshua prevailed over Amalek (Ex 17:11). The lifting up of the hands also means a promise to God that David would continue in prayer, just as God promised His people and lifted up His hand, declaring His promise of the land of Canaan as an inheritance (Ex 6:8).
5- My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips:

David declares that just as the body is satisfied with marrow and fatness, so also his soul is satisfied with the richness of divine love, so he blesses God and praises Him with joy. When he prays, his satisfaction and spiritual growth increase, as the body grows by marrow and fatness. Marrow and fatness give food a good taste, and likewise prayer and praise give delight to life; indeed the soul tastes the sweetness of eternity while still on earth, because the whole Kingdom is delight in prayer and praise.
6- When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
Night watches: sleeplessness and inability to sleep.
Meditate: I repeat and recite the name of God.

1- David began the psalm by saying that he rises early to pray, because his soul is thirsty for divine love; and he continued all day speaking with God, and when he went in to sleep he kept speaking with God and remembering His name, and when he slept a little from the weariness of the day, he arose and began repeating His holy name, although the dawn had not yet broken. In the Septuagint translation, David awoke in the hours of the night watches; he rose early to God from the time of the dawn watch, while darkness covered the earth and people were asleep, and his heart could not sleep, and he woke to pray and continued until the dawn broke and his day began. Truly David expressed himself when he said, "But I give myself unto prayer" (Ps 109:4).

2- "Upon my bed," that is, in the time of my rest, and "in the night watches," that is, in the time of affliction and sleeplessness, I was praying and meditating on the name of God; for David prays in all circumstances, whether rest or affliction.
7- Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice.

David fled from the face of Absalom, and before that from the face of Saul, and God helped him, for He did not allow his pursuers to seize him or kill him. So David felt that he was under God's care and that He was shading him with His wings, and he came to great joy, not only because of God's care, but because he delighted in and was satisfied with the love of God. It may be that God gave him joy by a sense of Him in some way, as it is recorded of the three youths that they saw God in the midst of the furnace, and Daniel saw the angel in the pit (Dan 3:25; 6:22). So David enjoyed fellowship with God, and this is the reason for his joy.

If you feel a longing for God, do not delay, but rise to prayer and praise, or read in your Holy Bible and meditate on it, and you will find God clearly and enjoy fellowship with Him, and your heart will rejoice.
(2) Joy and boasting (vv. 8-11:)
8- My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me.

1- From the intensity of David's longings for God he was not content with His care or with seeing Him, but clung to God in love, so that he enjoyed Him continually. And when God saw David's love, He supported him and upheld him with His right hand, that he might remain firm in this love. Whoever seeks God with longing and clings to Him enjoys the power of God, which brings him into the depths of God, so that he experiences inexpressible things, that is, tastes the Kingdom while still on earth.
2- God's right hand signifies Christ, who is the power of God, which appeared in the Incarnation; so whoever seeks God enjoys the salvation and redemption of Christ.
9- But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth. 10- They are delivered to the hand of the sword; they become the portion of jackals.
Jackals: an animal resembling the fox, in size between the fox and the wolf, and it is one of the beasts of prey.

1- After David presented his enjoyment of God as an example of the happiness of the children of God, he presented on the other side the fate of the wicked who want to destroy him, and he defined it in three points:
a- They go into the lower parts of the earth, that is, eternal destruction awaits them, and they are cast into hell for their insistence on evil and for killing the innocent such as David.
b- They are delivered to the hand of the sword, that is, they perish, and this is destruction on earth, meaning that they perish on earth and in the other life, where there is eternal torment.

c- They become portions for jackals: the lion - which signifies Satan - when it attacks a prey kills it, eats part of it and leaves the rest to other beasts of prey, such as jackals. So these wicked men are tormented by Satan, as are the rest of the wicked on earth who attack them; that is, the wicked turn upon one another, and the shame of everyone who follows evil and relies on it appears. Everything that happens to the wicked confirms the faith of the righteous, so they are not troubled by the wrongs of the wicked or their temporary success, because their end is dreadful.
11- But the king shall rejoice in God; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: but the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.

1- David concludes the psalm by saying that the king, that is, David, rejoices in God, to whom he rose early in prayer, and whose fellowship and care he enjoyed. Indeed David becomes an example to others, so the righteous glory because of their faith in God, and their adherence to Him increases, and they swear by His name and not by the names of strange gods; for swearing in the Old Testament was a declaration of a person's faith and his allegiance to God, or to pagan gods. So when God protects David, the righteous who believe in God are confirmed in their faith, and even boast of their God by whom they swear.

2- On the other hand, all the wicked who speak evil, which is lying speech that carries injustice against the innocent, and wrongs that are all temporary and worthless, all this is made void, and God stops the mouths of the wicked when they see God's care and protection of His children, and that the evils of the wicked do not touch the righteous.
Contemplate God's work in His saints, and also in His children around you, and your faith will be confirmed and you will grow in your love for God ... Truly the stories of the saints are delightful.
God's vengeance for the plots of the wicked. To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. "Hear my voice, O God, in my prayer" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet, as appears from the title of the psalm.
2- When it was written:
a- When David was pursued by Saul, who devised many plots to destroy him.
b- When he was pursued from the face of his son Absalom.
3- This psalm is considered a personal lament of David, showing the extent of his suffering, but at the same time his trust and faith in God.
4- This psalm suits every person who is fought by those around him and for whom plots are devised; for this psalm confirms his faith in God.
5- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, since most of its verses speak of clear events in the life of Christ.
6- This psalm does not occur in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 1- Hear my voice, O God, in my prayer: preserve my life from fear of the enemy.

1- David sensed the plots of the enemies devised against him, so he took refuge in God with a complaint, asking for His help, not only to nullify these plots, but also that He might remove fear from his heart, so that he would not fear the enemies; for God is with him, and no one can overcome him. He also asks that God remove from his heart the fear of the demons, for they are nothing before God's protection of him.

2- This cry to God is a prophecy about Christ on the cross, as He asks the Father to hear His prayer, and this proves the humanity of Christ. This cry is also a prophecy about the cries of the martyrs and of the suffering Church in every generation.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 2- Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked; from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity:

1- David asks God to protect him and cover him, so that the plots of the enemies may not strike him, especially since their numbers are great and they are a multitude larger than he; but his reliance on the power of God reassures him.

2- David also asks, on behalf of every believer, that God cover him from the nakedness of sin and its shame, so that the multitude of demons, who want to make him fall and destroy him, may not gloat over him.
3- The plots of the Jews against Christ were many, and they gathered in a great crowd; so this verse is a prophecy about Christ.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 3- Who whet their tongue like a sword, and bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words:
Whet: said of a sword, meaning to make it sharp; it means here that their tongues are strong and sharp in hurting him.
Bend: to fix the arrow on the string, ready to hit its target. It means here the strength of their tongues, which direct violent words to strike David.

David describes the words of his enemies, and their tongues, as a whetted sword, very sharp, and as an arrow aimed precisely at its target; he also describes their words as bitter, and this shows the extent of David's suffering from the harsh words of his enemies against him.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 4- That they may shoot in secret at the perfect: suddenly do they shoot at him, and fear not.

1- David's enemies were lying in wait for him everywhere; even when he hid from their eyes they would go to him and shoot him with their arrows, that is, they never left him in rest, but pursued him everywhere and fell upon him suddenly to destroy him, and they did not fear God, though he was righteous and perfect and had not harmed them in anything; but they are wicked, and their nature is evil, so they do evil even to the righteous.

2- This verse applies, in the spirit of prophecy, to Christ, who hid His divinity and walked in righteousness, but the wicked Jews devised plots against Him and fell upon Him with their words and their embarrassing questions, and even cried for His crucifixion after they attacked Him suddenly in the garden and seized Him, and they did not fear God in all that they did.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 5- They encourage themselves in an evil matter: they commune of laying snares privily; they say, Who shall see them?
Encourage themselves: they embolden and strengthen themselves.
Laying: burying.

1- David showed that his enemies were encouraging themselves to wrong him by evil deeds. They would set snares for him, hiding them in the ground and covering them so that they would not appear, in order that David might fall into them. And while they dug these snares they said within themselves that no one sees us, because they did it in secret, forgetting that God sees them and will repay them for their evils.

2- The buried snares are either an ambush to fall upon David and kill him, or evil lusts that entice people with their pleasures, as Satan devised for David the snare of the wife of Uriah the Hittite, so he fell with her, and then repented and turned back.

3- This verse is a prophecy of what happened to Christ, when the Jews agreed to kill Him and tried to ensnare Him with a word, then cried "Crucify Him, crucify Him," and devised a plot to seize Him by means of Judas Iscariot, His disciple, who gave them the sign of the kiss to betray Him. They did all this and forgot that God sees them and will repay them for their deeds; so Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70 at the hands of the Romans, and a huge number of Jews were killed.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 6- They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, is deep.

1- David continues to describe the wicked who are hostile to him, saying that they devise varied evils, and their inventions were precisely planned to entrap David and every righteous man, such as the revolt of Absalom, David's son, against his father, his driving him out and his attempt to kill him; this is an invention that would not occur to anyone's mind, that a son should attack his father and try to destroy him. Likewise Satan made David's friend Ahithophel devise a plan to kill David. So we see the heart of the wicked man is deep, full of evil, and inventions of iniquity.

2- This verse also applies to Christ, for the people whom Christ fed, whose sick He healed and from whom He cast out demons, rose up against Him and demanded, "Crucify Him, crucify Him." Moreover, Satan caused Christ's own disciple Judas Iscariot to rise against Him, to sell Him to the Jews and betray Him to them.

Even if the plots and schemes of the wicked are precisely planned and hidden so that the righteous may fall into them, do not be troubled; for everything is naked and open before God, and He is able to uncover these snares and rescue you from them, for He is your God who loves you and cares for you, and you will glorify Him for rescuing you.
7- But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded.

1- God was long-suffering toward the wicked, so they devised many plots, including varied evil inventions, and God bore with them to give them an opportunity to repent; but if they persist in evil He takes vengeance on them, and shoots them suddenly with a deadly arrow, as He punished King Herod, whom the people of Sidon called a god, so he became proud and thought he was a god; then God struck him with worms and he died (Acts 12:22).

2- We see this verse in the life of Christ, whom the wicked tried to kill and were indeed able to crucify, and He died on the cross; but by His death He trampled death and saved all who believe in Him, for He lifted from them the debt of sin and gave them new life.
8- And they make their own tongues fall upon themselves: all that look upon them shake the head.
Shake the head: to wag the head in contempt and mockery at what one sees.

If the wicked speak harsh words against the righteous, God makes their tongues come upon their own heads; that is, their evil words and their attempts to ensnare the righteous, they themselves fall into, as divine vengeance upon them. So everyone who passes by them marvels, and even mocks them, because their evil has come upon them.
9- And all men shall fear, and shall declare the work of God; for they shall wisely consider of his doing.
Wisely consider: understand.

1- After God punishes the wicked and their shame appears before people, all understand the power of God that supports the righteous, that is, David, and they understand God's providence and His care for His children.

2- This verse appears in Christ, over whom the Jews gloated when He was crucified and died, but they understood God's dispensation when they saw that He had risen from the dead, appeared to His disciples, and then ascended into heaven.
10- The righteous shall be glad in the Lord, and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory.

1- In conclusion David declares that the righteous man, that is, David, rejoices in God's work with him, and His protection of him, and how He nullified the plots of the enemies and rescued him from them. He also punished them, in order to confirm David in his faith, and indeed all the righteous; for God established righteousness and showed the vanity of evil.

2- This verse applies to Christ, for He is the righteous One who rejoices in the completion of the mystery of redemption, and all His disciples rejoice in His resurrection and are strengthened, because God protects them.

Be confident of your principles and of your adherence to God's commandments, even if the temporary superiority of the wicked appears; but in the end believe that God will reward you with peace on earth and marvelous joy in heaven. Praise to God for His benefits. To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. A Song. "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.

2- When was it written? It is not known precisely, and some think that David wrote it when he brought up the ark of the covenant of God from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it stayed three months (2 Sam 6:13-16).

3- This psalm is liturgical; the children of Israel used to recite it at the feast of firstfruits (Lev 23:9-12), when the fields are clothed with wheat (v. 13). The Church prays its first and second verses on the feasts of the Cross and on Palm Sunday, because through the cross and salvation Christ opened the door for the whole world to believe in Him and praise Him. Likewise in the funeral prayers verse 4 is said, and also on the Feast of Nayrouz verse 11 is prayed.
4- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it is a prophecy about Christ the Savior, who forgives the sins of those who believe in Him (v. 3).
5- This psalm, with the three psalms that follow it, offers praise and thanksgiving to God, and there are the two words
6- This psalm does not occur in the prayers of the Agpeya.
1- Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed.

1- David declares that God deserves praise in Zion, where His great temple is, and there vows are paid to God, that is, worship and offerings of love, and the promises made to God are fulfilled; because He is a God able to do all things, and He alone is the Savior of man, and His love and care deserve our thanks and praise.

2- Zion means the high hill on which Jerusalem is built, for praise lifts us up to the heavenly things, so that we live a spirituality that rises above the evil thoughts of the world, and we offer praise in the Church of the New Testament in preparation for offering unceasing praise in the heavenly Jerusalem.

3- The Babylonians tried to make the Jews praise God in Babylon, but they refused, because praise and worship are only in Jerusalem, in the temple of God, that is, in Zion. Perhaps the Jews in captivity used to say this verse: that praise should be in Zion only and not in any other place, since there is only one God whose temple is in Zion.
2- O thou that hearest prayer, unto thee shall all flesh come.

1- Since David and all the believers offered their praises in Zion, God heard and answered them, and this encouraged people in the whole world to believe in God, pray to Him and praise Him. This is a clear prophecy about the faith of the Gentiles; for though the Jews used to reject this, David, as a spiritual man, had the faith of the Gentiles revealed to him by God.

2- God's hearing of prayers shows His love for people, and David's wishes that all people come to God show the breadth of David's heart and his love for the Gentiles; for David's heart was filled with the love of God through the abundance of his prayers.
3- Iniquities prevail against me: as for our transgressions, thou shalt purge them away.

David considers that his sins have become heavy upon him, because the burden of sin is the heaviest burden a person suffers. But David hastened to God with repentance and confessed his sins and his suffering from them. At the same time he declared his faith that God alone is able to atone for these sins and forgive them. This is a clear prophecy about Christ the Redeemer, who atones for our sins.
4- Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple.

God's love appears in His offering heavenly glory to whoever believes in Him, prays to Him, praises Him and confesses his sins.
