The prophet David shows that heavenly glory is given to the chosen, that is, those who have believed in God; God brings them near to Himself on earth, lets them enjoy His blessings through their worship of Him in His temple, and satisfies them with His love. This satisfaction is a symbol of what Christ gives in His Church to those who believe in Him, where He gives them the fruits and gifts of the Holy Spirit and satisfies them with His Holy Mysteries and the means of grace. All that they receive in the Church is also a pledge of what they will enjoy forever in the Kingdom; therefore the Church bids farewell to her departed beloved and recites this verse in the funeral prayer.

The great salvation that Christ accomplished for us on the cross, and offers to us in the Church on the altar every day, as true Body and Blood, deserves thanks and praise from you every day. And when you give thanks, your enjoyment of God's blessings and gifts increases at all times.
5- By terrible things in righteousness wilt thou answer us, O God of our salvation; who art the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea:

1- God's fearful justice appeared when the Father offered the greatest gift to the world, giving His only-begotten Son on the cross. This justice was fearful to the demons, whom Christ bound by His cross, and by this justice God answered His children who confessed their sins to Him and granted them His salvation. When the world saw God's fearful justice they feared and believed in Him, because they saw His miracles and His power, for He glorified those who confessed His name and destroyed sinners, such as Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1-11). He is the Savior of His children, like the Apostles whom He strengthened, so that the world feared them despite their personal weakness, and they spread the preaching in the whole world, opening the door of salvation through Christ to everyone who believes in Him.

2- As for God's wonderful salvation and His fearful justice, the Gentiles sensed it, and that there is no God but Him alone, so they believed in Him and trusted in Him, not disturbed by the agitation of the wicked or the changes of life.
6- Which by his strength setteth fast the mountains; being girded with power:
Girded: one who ties on a girdle, which is a belt placed around the waist.

1- God's power appears in that He sets fast the mountains, which are the strongest and most firmly rooted things on earth, that is, they are fixed and not shaken. He is also the one who sets fast the moral mountains, meaning His holy children, such as the Apostles, the martyrs and the fathers of monasticism, who stood firm against all the wars of the devil. On the contrary, everyone who relied on his own strength, such as the kings of the earth and the great kingdoms, were all subject to perishing and overthrow.

2- God is able to do all things, and David likens Him to a man who has girded himself with power; for whoever prepares for any work girds his clothes in readiness for the work, but God has complete power over all things, and nothing is too hard for Him, and therefore He is able to save us.

3- If God is the one who sets fast the mountains and is girded with power, then everyone who believes in Him and holds fast to His commandments is firm like the mountain and is girded with the strength of God, so he gains power to do great works and overcomes Satan.
7- Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people.
Noise: the loud sound of the dashing waves.
Tumult: uproar and shouting.

1- God's power appears in stilling the loud sounds resulting from the dashing of the waves, which terrify the passengers of ships because they threaten them with drowning. The seas signify the world, and the noise of their waves is the loud sounds arising from the disturbances and changes of the world; these God stills in the ears of His children, so they are not troubled by them. Likewise the tumult of the people, that is, the pride and agitation of men against the children of God; He intervenes and stills the power of evil and protects His children. God permits the agitation of the world, for this is its nature, but He intervenes to protect His children, so they live in safety and peace in the midst of disturbances, because of His care and power.

2- This is what Christ did when the waves rose and nearly sank the boat in which He was riding with His disciples, and He arose from His sleep and commanded the winds and the waves to be still, and they obeyed Him, all by the authority of His divinity.
8- They also that dwell in the uttermost parts are afraid at thy tokens: thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice.

1- Before the signs of God, such as the ten plagues and the parting of the Red Sea (Ex 7-14), the Gentiles look on and fear the God of Israel, so that some of them believed and joined the people of God, such as Rahab (Josh 6:25). The greatest sign is the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption, as the prophet Isaiah declared (Isa 7:14).

2- All nature rejoices in its Creator and Ruler, and David chooses from it the sun at the outgoing of the morning when it rises, and the time of evening when it sets. The evening signifies the time of the cross and the death and burial of Christ, and the outgoing of the morning signifies His resurrection. The morning and evening also signify the east and the west, that is, the whole world, meaning that Christ by His redemption and resurrection gladdened the whole world, east and west.

Contemplate God's power in nature and in the Holy Bible, and you will sense His greatness. This produces in you the fear of Him and the love of Him; fear leads you to repent of your sins, and love leads you to cling to Him and enjoy fellowship with Him through prayers and readings.
9- Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it.

1- God's care for man appears in His concern for the cultivated land that feeds man, as He gives it water from the rivers and springs to water its crops. This water is so abundant that it fills the channels that water the land, so man is not in need and does not go hungry. God's visiting the earth reassures man that his life is in the hand of God, who cares for him. We see in the East great rivers, such as the Nile, the Jordan, the Tigris and the Euphrates, and if the water in these rivers falls short, prayer to God makes Him fill them, as happened in Egypt at the beginning of the nineteenth century, in the days of Muhammad Ali, when Pope Peter El-Gawli prayed. This water signifies the work of the Holy Spirit, who waters the believer, that is, the crop, so that he is firmly planted in the earth, that is, the Church, and lives with God.

2- God's preparing of the earth is not limited to the water of rivers, but He also prepares the earth and waters it with rains, as in the land of Canaan, so God gives His children the early and the latter rain to water the plants, so they eat their food in abundance. In the rains we see the blessings of heaven, which prepare the food of His children, not only material food, but rather spiritual, for He always satisfies them with His love and His fellowship, so they cling to Him and trust in Him.
10- Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof.
Ridges: plural of the furrow, which is the cut of the plow in the earth in which the seeds are placed.
Furrows: plural of the trench, which is an elongated cut in the earth, and the farmer needs to level it so that he can sow the land.
Showers: rains.
Springing: its crops, such as wheat and barley ...

1- In His concern for man's food, God cares for the cultivated land, so He prepares the earth and makes it level, and it is rid of its trenches and becomes fit for sowing. When the plow cuts it and makes furrows in it, and the farmer puts the seed in it, God waters it with rains and softens the clods of earth, that is, breaks them up, so the crops grow in it and give their yield abundantly by the blessing of God, to satisfy man's bodily needs.

2- So also God cares for the soul: He prepares it, that is, removes from it the results of sins and makes it level; He softens it, that is, examines it through repentance and examination of the soul, then waters it with the waters of the Holy Spirit and nourishes it with His Body and Blood, so it grows spiritually and bears fruit, and He blesses these spiritual fruits.
11- Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness.

1- So we see God's goodness and mercies blessing the whole year with all the crops sown in it, whether winter or summer. The earth is filled with the greenery on which the animals feed, and the effects of the blessing of the cultivated land appear in animals that give milk and meat full of fatness.

2- God also speaks to the spiritual man with His mercies and goodness throughout the year, that is, throughout his life, and keeps him, causes him to grow and blesses him; likewise the effects of His care for him appear, for He gives him grace in the eyes of those around him, and he becomes an example to others, and so influences them. Thus the fatness of the work of grace in him appears.
12- They drop upon the pastures of the wilderness: and the little hills rejoice on every side.
Drop: overflow.
Little hills: hills.

1- When God blesses the earth He cares for all its kinds: the plains, or the valleys in the wilderness, He gives crops that the animals eat, so they become pastures, and when these animals are satisfied they give fatness of meat and milk. Likewise the hills are filled with pastures and the animals feed on them, so that all are in gladness and joy.

2- The plains of the wilderness signify the humble and all believers, while the hills signify those advanced spiritually, who are raised toward heaven, that is, all believers rejoice. The wilderness also signifies the Gentiles, who were barren and were filled with greenery by the grace of God, and the hills signify the Jews who knew God and rose to Him from the days of the fathers, who rejoiced and were glad when they believed in Christ.
13- The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing.
Covered over: wearing a cloak (a coat), that is, clothed.
Corn: wheat.

1- The prophet David continues to describe the blessings of God, who shepherds His people, so He blesses His land and makes the meadows fill and be clothed with flocks, and the valleys likewise are covered with wheat. Man and animal eat, and therefore all shout for joy, because they are satisfied and give thanks to God.
2- The flocks signify those advanced spiritually, and the valleys signify the beginners; all are clothed and satisfied and give thanks to God, praising and glorifying Him in joy.

If only you would thank God every day for His gifts and His blessings to you, spiritual and material, then your heart will be at peace and rejoice, and God's gifts to you will even increase, so you become a light to the world, calling them without speaking to life with God, as they see in your life calm, peace and happiness.
All praise God. To the Chief Musician. A Song. A Psalm. "Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- The name of the author of the psalm is not mentioned, so it is counted among the orphan psalms, whose author is unknown; it may be that David wrote it, or someone else.
2- This psalm is liturgical; it offers praise to God and calls the Gentiles to praise Him.
3- This psalm is a prophecy about what happened in the days of King Hezekiah, at the defeat of Assyria before him, and about the victory of the Maccabees over the Greeks, and their praising God.
4- This psalm is a clear prophecy about the faith of the Gentiles in Christ, and the praise of Him by the whole earth, Jews and Gentiles.

5- This psalm also carries a prophecy about the resurrection of Christ, the Giver of life (v. 9), and in the title of this psalm in the Septuagint translation there is the phrase "for the resurrection."
6- This psalm does not occur in the prayers of the Agpeya.
1- Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands: 2- Sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious.

1- The author of the psalm calls on all people to shout to God, that is, to declare their joy with jubilation and praise, and to sing forth, that is, to continue in prayers of joy, glorifying God for His great works, whether His forgiveness of their sins if they offer repentance, or their rescue from afflictions, as He brought the captives back from Babylon to Jerusalem and they built the temple, or for the resurrection of Christ from the dead, to proclaim to humanity victory over the devil and new life.

2- The singing and the shouting are for the glory of the name of God, not for our personal glory, and singing is the highest of prayers, because it asks nothing for man, but is only for the glory of God. Singing is with the lips, and also with good works.
3- Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies flatter thee.
Terrible: more fearful and great.
Flatter thee: deceive thee and lie to thee.

1- The author of the psalm teaches people, when they shout to God, to say to Him, How terrible are Your works, and how great, whether in His great creation or in His rescue of His people, such as bringing them out of Egypt with the ten plagues, their crossing of the Red Sea, and how He provided for them with manna and quail from heaven, and water from the rock!

2- When the pagans see the great works of God they fear Him greatly, so they flatter Him, that is, they lie, declaring their submission to Him, and then draw back from this outward faith, as Pharaoh declared his submission to God during the ten plagues, and then went back and hardened his heart.
4- All the earth shall worship thee, and shall sing unto thee; they shall sing to thy name. Selah.

1- All the earth means all humanity, that is, Jews and Gentiles. This is a prophecy about the faith of the Gentiles, who will come and worship in submission to God, declaring their faith. Then they will be able to sing to His holy name.
2- This passage ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on the greatness and glory of God.

Do not deprive yourself of the joy of praising God, so that you rise above earthly things and are drawn toward the love of God, and feel His presence with you and long for heaven, and walk spiritually in your steps on earth.
5- Come and see the works of God: he is terrible in his doing toward the children of men. 6- He turned the sea into dry land: they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him.

1- The author of the psalm, by the Holy Spirit, calls on those who have believed and praised God to look with their hearts at the great works of God that He did with His people, such as the parting of the Red Sea and turning its bed into dry land, and likewise the parting of the river Jordan and making its bed also dry land, so that the children of Israel were able to walk on it with their feet and cross to the other bank. The Holy Spirit always calls us to see with our hearts, and to recall and remember with our minds God's works with us. This brings us into a wonderful feeling of joy, so we rejoice as God's people rejoiced of old when they crossed the Red Sea and the river Jordan. This crossing is a symbol of Baptism, by which we crossed from death to life, so we remain in constant joy.

2- When we remember God's great works in parting the sea and the river we rejoice, although the event did not happen to us, and it is supposed that those to whom it happened rejoiced; but all of us who believe in God rejoice together, so we rejoice in God's works of old, and the present ones that happen with us, and even those of the future, that is, we rejoice in the faith of those who have not yet believed, and this shows the unity of the Church through the generations.
7- He ruleth by his power for ever; his eyes behold the nations: let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah.

1- It appears from the preceding verses that God has power and authority over the whole earth, and if some do not believe in Him and resist, God's eyes watch them, so that if they rebel He punishes them, as happened with Pharaoh when he increased his humiliation of God's people and became very proud, and God struck him with the ten plagues and then drowned him in the sea. One who rebels against God cannot exalt himself above God, but God is long-suffering and gives him an opportunity to repent, and if he does not repent He takes vengeance on him.
2- At the end of this passage there is the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on the power and authority of God, so that we may fear Him and keep away from every sin.

When you read the Holy Bible and see the great works of God, offer Him thanks and glorification, confident that God is the same yesterday, today and forever, so your heart will be at peace and rejoice, and your praise of Him will increase.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Chastener and Healer

paragraphs.text: 8- O bless our God, ye people, and make the voice of his praise to be heard:

The author of the psalm calls on those of the Gentiles who have believed to bless God, our God, that is, the God of the Jews who believe in Him, and then asks those of the Gentiles who have believed to make the sounds of their praises heard by those around them, whether those who have believed, that they may be firm in their faith, or those who have not yet believed, that they may call them to faith. Making their voices heard is not only with the lips, but rather with works, and also with proclaiming God's works and His wonders with them.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Chastener and Healer

paragraphs.text: 9- Which holdeth our soul in life, and suffereth not our feet to be moved.
Moved: slipping and falling.

God gave man life when He breathed into him the breath of life, and created him from dust, and then gave him the commandment to live by. When he fell, He gave him the promise of life, that the seed of the woman would bruise the head of the serpent (Gen 3:15). Then He fulfilled the promise of life by His Incarnation, His redemption and His resurrection, so Christ became our life, and by His power He protects us from falling into sin, and if we fall He raises us up. By our constant steadfastness in Christ our Rock our feet will not slip.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Chastener and Healer

paragraphs.text: 10- For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried. 11- Thou broughtest us into the net; thou laidst affliction upon our loins.
Loins: our backs.

1- In His concern for His children, God permits trials for them to purify them from all evil, as silver is refined to separate it from impurities and dross, so that the children of God become pure from all the filth of sin.

2- Likewise God permits afflictions for His children, that they fall into the net of the enemies, and He also lays heavy burdens on their backs, until they almost fall from the weight of the load, as He permitted His children to be humiliated in Egypt before He freed them by the hand of Moses, and likewise the humiliation of captivity in Assyria and Babylon before He brought them back to their land.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Chastener and Healer

paragraphs.text: 12- Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place. Continuing God's chastening of His children, He permitted their enemies to rule over them, as happened in Egypt in the days of Moses, when the enemies rode over the heads of the children of Israel and humiliated them; but the grace of God intervened, and after they were almost destroyed, drowning in the humiliation of forced labor and the fire of slavery, God brought them out with a high hand, after He struck the Egyptians with the ten plagues and made His people pass through the Red Sea, and they were not drowned, but Pharaoh and his army were drowned, and they crossed the wilderness of Sinai, and He brought them into the land of Canaan, the fertile land flowing with milk and honey.

Bear afflictions, for they are temporary and many blessings follow them; they also deliver you from your sins, and you live in repentance, and you learn virtues from them, such as humility, faith and prayer.

entries.section: (5) The praise of those who fear God

paragraphs.text: 16- Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul. 17- I cried unto him with my mouth, and he was extolled with my tongue.
Extolled: exalted.

1- The author of the psalm speaks to those who fear God, because whoever fears God keeps away from sin, is purified, and is able to praise God. The author tells them of the works of God, not only those He does with His people, such as the crossing of the Red Sea and the crossing of the river Jordan (v. 6), but he also tells them of God's works with him, so he cries out praising and glorifying God with his tongue; that is, the works of God are ancient and contemporary, and in every generation His children feel His great works with them and glorify Him.

2- He tells those who fear God of God's works with him, that they may join him in glorifying God, because the power of God is the cause of every blessing in the life of the author of the psalm and of all who fear God, and therefore God must be glorified.

entries.section: (5) The praise of those who fear God

paragraphs.text: 18- If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me: 19- But verily God hath heard me; he hath attended to the voice of my prayer.
Regard: keep and hold to.

1- The author of the psalm declares a necessary condition for the answering of prayer, which is repentance from every sin; but whoever persists in sin, or is lax with it, or justifies it, so that it remains in his heart, God does not answer him. Man's weakness does not hinder God's work, but persisting in sin and treating it as permissible is what angers God, so He does not listen, and God does not answer such prayers.

2- When the author here does not regard iniquity in his heart, this is not out of pride, but because he walks in the way of God, so he repents at once of every sin. He entreats God with humility, need and repentance.

entries.section: (5) The praise of those who fear God

paragraphs.text: 20- Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me. In conclusion the author of the psalm blesses God for two things:
1- His acceptance of prayers.
2- God's mercies that He poured out upon him, which include his inner peace, his love for God, and his rescue from many troubles ...
The acceptance of prayers is also part of God's mercy, and therefore at the end of every matter we must thank God and bless Him.
Hold fast to the fear of God so that you may be purified from your sins, and your prayers may rise to God and He answer them, and you may enjoy His abundant mercies.
The joy of the Gentiles in salvation. To the Chief Musician on Neginoth. A Psalm. A Song. "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author is unknown, and it is therefore classified among the orphan psalms, but some attribute it to David.
2- It is sung by a group of singers who have a leader, or chief.
3- The recitation of this psalm is accompanied by a musical instrument called the stringed instrument, which is a string instrument like the lute.
4- We see in the title of the psalm that it is a song; it is thanksgiving and praise to God from His beloved who believe in Him, and an invitation to the whole world to join in praising Him.
5- This psalm is a clear prophecy about the faith of the Gentiles in Christ and their praise of Him.

6- This psalm is considered liturgical, for in the Old Testament it was recited at the Feast of Harvest, or Pentecost, and it was also recited at the Feast of Tabernacles. It was called the psalm of blessing, since the word blessing is repeated in it three times.
7- The first verse of this psalm is recited at the conclusion of the Evening and Morning Raising of Incense.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayers of Prime and the Sixth Hour, so that the day may begin with blessing, and likewise in the Sixth Hour the world received the blessing through the crucifixion of Christ and His redemption of it.

entries.section: (1) The knowledge of God offered to all people

paragraphs.text: 1- God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us. Selah.

1- The author of the psalm asks for himself and for his people God's compassion, His mercies and His blessings, and as he comes forward with humility and need, he finds before him not God's judgment and justice, but His compassion and blessing. God shines upon him, so He sanctifies him, blesses him, and gives him spiritual understanding and the knowledge of the person of the great God.
2- When a person receives God's blessing and compassion, he is able to give light to others, and is changed into a spiritual person, who shows compassion and mercy to those around him.

3- These mercies and this enlightenment are accomplished in Christ incarnate in the fullness of time, who changes those who believe in Him into earthly angels who know God and convey the knowledge of Him to others.
4- This verse ends with the word "Selah," which is a musical pause for meditating on God's tenderness, His blessings, and the knowledge with which He favors all.

entries.section: (1) The knowledge of God offered to all people

paragraphs.text: 2- That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.

1- When God pours out His mercies on the world and shines upon it with His face, the world knows His way, that is, His commandments, and His salvation offered to all, the Gentiles in addition to the Jews, which is the cross and redemption.
2- The way is Christ, who said, "I am the way" (Jn 14:6); it is He who saves those who believe in Him and brings them to the Kingdom.

Contemplate the love of Christ on the cross, for He strives for your salvation and your spiritual enlightenment. And when you contemplate, your heart is filled with reassurance, joy, and longings to know God and enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (2) The faith and praise of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 3- Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee.

When the peoples of the world, that is, the Gentiles, received the salvation of Christ, they raised their voices in praise and thanksgiving to God, and began to offer worship to God with the rest of the believers. All this was accomplished in the fullness of time, by the redemption of Christ, and this verse speaks in the spirit of prophecy about the spread of faith in Christ among the Gentiles.

entries.section: (2) The faith and praise of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 4- O let the nations be glad and sing for joy: for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah.

1- The Gentiles who believed in Christ and worship Him remain in a state of continual joy in fellowship with Him, especially since they enjoy the guidance of God, who is upright in judgment, so He judges them and governs them with truth, unlike the people of the world, who are liable to error, deviation and partiality.

2- God seeks the Gentiles who have not yet believed, preaching to them to guide them to Himself, that they may believe and join the rest of those of the Gentiles who have believed in worshiping God and praising Him. And when the day of judgment comes He judges them righteously, so they receive the glories of the Kingdom, but the wicked and unbelievers are cast into eternal torment.
3- This verse ends with the word "Selah," which is a musical pause for meditating on God, the Pantocrator, before whom we shall stand on the day of judgment.

entries.section: (2) The faith and praise of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 5- Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee.

After the joy of the Gentiles who believed in Christ over His salvation and worship of Him, they were also reassured that the just Judge on the day of judgment is Christ Himself, their God, who will bring them into the Kingdom, so they thank God every day for all that He has prepared for them in heaven.

If only you would thank God every day for His salvation, and for the Kingdom He has prepared for you, so that your heart rises above sin and the material things of the world and clings to the love of God, who gave you Himself on the cross, and gives you to taste His sweetness on earth, and will give you what you cannot imagine in the Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) The blessing of God and the fear of Him

paragraphs.text: 6- Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us.

1- This psalm was written at the time of harvest; therefore the author of the psalm declares that this yield is the blessing of God given to His children to satisfy their needs. It shows God's care for His children.

2- The earth signifies human beings, and the yield is their faith in Christ; this is the true blessing that God gives to people. The earth also signifies human beings, among whom is the Virgin Mary, so the yield is the fruit of her womb, that is, Christ who was born of her.

entries.section: (3) The blessing of God and the fear of Him

paragraphs.text: 7- God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him.

1- When people see that God is the cause of the blessing that gives them life, they trust that their life is in His hand, so they fear Him, and the fear of Him keeps them from sin and purifies their hearts, so they behold Him while still on earth and enjoy fellowship with Him.
2- When people enjoy God's material blessings on earth they thank Him, incline to every good work, prepare for the day of judgment, and live every day in the fear of God.

What is the yield you produce? It is the spiritual fruits, so examine yourself: do you carry out the commandment, and does it appear in your life? Then you will be a light to the world and the salt of the earth.

God the Savior of His people and the avenger on His enemies. To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. A Song. "Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.
2- When was it written?
a- When David brought up the ark of the covenant of God from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite (2 Sam 6:12-15).

b- David wrote it in the spirit of prophecy about future events such as God's victories in the days of King Hezekiah over Sennacherib (2 Chr 32:20-23), or the last years of the Babylonian captivity, or the victories of the Maccabees in the second century before Christ.
3- Moses, when moving the tabernacle of meeting and journeying from one place to another, used to recite the beginning of this
4- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the life of Christ on earth and His resurrection and ascension.
5- St. Paul the Apostle quoted (v. 18) in the Epistle to the Ephesians (Eph 4:8).
6- The beginning of this psalm (v. 1) is quoted in the Litany of the Assemblies in the Divine Liturgy, and is also found at the beginning of the Midnight prayer.
7- This psalm does not occur in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The joy of the righteous in God the Victor

paragraphs.text: 1- Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him.

1- Moses used to recite this verse when the ark of the covenant of God and the tabernacle of meeting were moved from one place to another in the wilderness of Sinai, declaring the power of God, in whom His people believe, and of whom His enemies are afraid, who did not believe in Him but know His power, chiefly the demons, the pagan gods, and the peoples who follow them.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who rises from the dead on the third day, binding Satan, and it is also a prophecy about the second resurrection and the day of judgment, when those who hate God hide from His face (Rev 6:16).

entries.section: (1) The joy of the righteous in God the Victor

paragraphs.text: 2- As smoke is driven away, so drive them away: as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God.
3- But let the righteous be glad; let them rejoice before God: yea, let them exceedingly rejoice.
Driven away: scattered and dispersed.
Exceedingly rejoice: leap.

1- The wicked have no power before God, and by the wicked are meant the demons and all who follow them. He likens them to smoke that the winds disperse, or to chaff that is tossed and flies in the air, away from the grains of wheat. So the smoke is not found and the chaff is scattered.

2- He also likens the wicked to wax that melts with the heat of fire, and even flies away so that it is not found. Fire signifies the work of the Holy Spirit, who burns sins out of a person so that he is purified; this is for the righteous, but as for the wicked, or the demons, all their works are burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit and are not found.

3- When the righteous see the power of God that scatters the wicked and their works (which He likened to the divine wind and the fire that at the same time purify the righteous), they rejoice, and with the purity of their hearts they behold God, so their gladness increases, and indeed their feelings are stirred, and they leap, rejoicing and praising God for His power and His great works with them, and how He protects them from the evils around them.

entries.section: (1) The joy of the righteous in God the Victor

paragraphs.text: 4- Sing unto God, sing praises to his name; prepare a way for him that rideth through the deserts by his name Yah, and rejoice before him. Deserts: wastelands in which there is no water, nor plants, nor man.
Yah: short for Yahweh, which is the name of God.

1- The prophet David calls on the children of God to shout His name, and perhaps he was bringing the ark of the covenant of God from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite; for God rides in His ark of the covenant after it had been a stranger among the Gentile Philistines, and now returns by the hand of David to Jerusalem, His holy city. His being among the Gentiles is signified by the deserts, but His being among His children is thus within the good land, where His children sprout and bear good fruit, and His name Yahweh is clear and proclaimed among His people; therefore they prepare His way with shouting and glorifying, so they rejoice and make the heart of God rejoice.

2- God who rides and comes from the deserts is Christ incarnate, who declared the holy name of God; for no one has seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared Him (Jn 1:18); therefore the angels shouted, and the believing children of God such as the Virgin, for His great Incarnation.

entries.section: (1) The joy of the righteous in God the Victor

paragraphs.text: 5- A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.

1- When a person is far from God he is like the orphan, that is, one without a father, and like the widow, that is, one without a husband and support; but by faith a person acquires God within himself, and God sanctifies him and dwells in him, so the person becomes the holy dwelling of God, that is, God cares for His weak children who need Him, so He satisfies them, lifts them up and sanctifies them, and they are higher than the whole world, because He dwells in them, after He has saved them from Satan who controlled them when they worshiped idols or were immersed in lusts, and He changed them from orphans into believers proud of their Father, and from widows into His bride.

2- God's holy dwelling is also Jerusalem where the ark of the covenant of God was, and it is also His Incarnation in the fullness of time, and likewise it is the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Kingdom, in addition to the human soul in which God dwells, as we mentioned before.

entries.section: (1) The joy of the righteous in God the Victor

paragraphs.text: 6- God setteth the solitary in a house; he bringeth out those which are bound to prosperity: but the rebellious dwell in a scorched land.
Prosperity: goodness and success.
Scorched land: land that is dry and hot from the intensity of the sun's heat.

1- The solitary are those who have no one to care for them, and who are separated from others, and by them He means His people the Jews, who separated from the world and worshiped God, so He settles them in His house and dwells in their midst. The solitary are also the orphans and widows, and every person who suffers weakness, whom God cares for, giving him stability and even distinction, as he is settled in God's hands. And everyone who was enslaved to sin and became its captive God frees, as long as he has believed in Him and repented, and gives him success in his life.

2- On the other hand, those who rebel against God and reject His commandments and faith and life with Him, God keeps in Gehenna and eternal torment, where the fire is not quenched, and they are completely deprived of seeing God and enjoying Him.

The sweet God is available to you to enjoy the sight of Him and fellowship with Him, so do not be distracted from Him, and know that your sins that separate you from Him you can be rid of through repentance, however much they have mastered you. Trust that He will help you and free you from your sins, and even make you succeed in all your steps, and give you inner stability, and you will delight in being with Him.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 7- O God, when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst ascend in the wilderness; Selah.

1- David tells us about God's going forth before His people to free them from the slavery of Egypt: He walked before them in a pillar of cloud by day to shade them from the heat of the sun, and in a pillar of fire by night to light the way for them, and He crossed the Red Sea, and walked with them in the barren wilderness, that is, Sinai; He fed them, gave them water and kept them until He brought them to the land of Canaan. And God continued to go forth before His people through His great works with them, and He still does so to this day.

2- Christ went forth before His Church and crossed with her from death to life by His cross, and after His resurrection ascended into the heavens, rising above the wilderness of this world. And everyone who believes in Christ sees Him as his leader in the world, until He brings him up into the heavens. God appears to His children who believe in Him, and not to the whole world. The people of God of old, and the Church today, enjoyed God's care and leadership; even if their appearance is one of distress, they are in truth victorious and joyful because of Christ's presence in their midst.

3- If God goes forth before His people of the children of Israel, He also goes forth before the Gentiles, who are signified by the wilderness because they were far from faith; when they believe, faith lifts them up to a lofty life with God, then to glories in heaven, so the believers, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles, are one in Christ, and ascend through Him to the glories of heaven.
4- He closes the verse with the word "Selah," which is a musical pause for meditating on God, who leads His people and leads your life to keep you and care for you.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 8- The earth shook, the heavens also dropped at the presence of God: even Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God, the God of Israel.

1- When God appeared on the mountain with smoke, mist, thunder and fire, the earth quaked, and the wilderness of Sinai, "Sinai itself," quaked, and the heavens dropped with the Ten Commandments, the Law of God, and the design of the tabernacle of meeting; for God appeared to declare His power and love and His readiness to dwell in the midst of His people, and to give them His commandments and Law, that they might live by them.

2- At the crucifixion of Christ the earth quaked and the rocks were split, and after His resurrection many of those who slept came out, that is, the heavens dropped, and some lofty spirits of the saints came and entered their bodies and appeared after the resurrection of Christ, to confirm His resurrection and call people to faith. The redemption of Christ shook the kingdom of Satan, that is, all the powers of Satan do not stand before the believer in Christ, but shake before him.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 9- Thou, O God, didst pour out a plentiful rain; thine inheritance, when it was weary, thou didst restore.
Pour out: overflow and rain.

1- The plentiful rain that He granted to His people in the wilderness of Sinai is the manna and the quail, and also His commandments and His Law. And when He found sins in His people, who are His inheritance, such as murmuring, He restored them by His grace and purified them, so all the murmurers died in the wilderness of Sinai, and only His innocent children entered the land of Canaan.

2- The prophet David says to God that his inheritance is from God, that is, the people of God, whom David shepherded faithfully, but David declares with humility that he is a sinner and weak, and was not able to shepherd the people of God perfectly, but the tender God intervened and repaired the results of David's mistakes. David sinned by adultery and murder, but God made him repent at the hand of Nathan, and he sinned by numbering the people, but God punished him and punished the people, and he and his people returned to God with repentance.

3- The plentiful rain is also the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church, "thine inheritance," and God's restoring of His people by means of convicting them by the Holy Spirit, repentance and confession, and every Church discipline, in addition to partaking of the Holy Mysteries. Thus God's special care for His people appears because of their submission to Him. For God pours out many gifts, which are like the plentiful rain, upon everyone who loves Him and clings to Him.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 10- Thy congregation hath dwelt therein: thou, O God, hast prepared of thy goodness for the poor.

1- David continues his discourse about the people of God, describing them as God's flock, and He is their faithful Shepherd, so He settled them in the wilderness of Sinai, where it is difficult for a human being to dwell, and even fed them, gave them water, kept them in their wars, and delivered them from all the hardships of the wilderness, because they are His people, and He is responsible for them.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 11- The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
1- God gave His Law and His commandments to Moses by angels, and Moses preached and taught them to his people through the priests and the Levites, who are also the great host.

2- In the New Testament God gave His Word to humanity, which is the Incarnation of Christ, and accomplished the redemption of humanity on the cross, and the "great host" proclaimed the salvation of Christ, who are the Apostles and priests and all the servants of the New Testament.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 12- Kings of armies did flee, did flee: and she that tarried at home divided the spoil.

1- The children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai, and then in the land of Canaan, were exposed to facing trained armies led by kings, whereas the children of Israel were not trained for war, and by the power of God they defeated the enemies, who fled before them, and the children of Israel took their spoil, which was very great, and it was not divided only among the fighting men of the children of Israel, but they also gave to the women, and to all the sick and the old who stayed at home because of their inability to fight, so each one took his share of the enemies' spoil.

2- God gives His children victory over the armies of the demons and their chiefs, so the demons flee before them, and the children of God take much spoil from the hand of God, which is virtues and the fruits of the Holy Spirit, and everyone who stays at home, that is, the Church, receives it. And in the end, after this life, God's holy children take the spoil of the demons, as they reign in their place in the heavens.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 13- Though ye have lien among the sheepfolds, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold.

1- Lying among the sheepfolds means taking possession of the promised land which God promised to the fathers, and Joshua divided it among the tribes of the children of Israel; so when you possess the land you enjoy a life with God, simple and innocent like the dove. You need to be committed to the word of God and His commandments, which silver signifies, and you are like gold which signifies heaven, that is, you have heavenly spiritual longings.

2- Lying among the sheepfolds signifies settling in the Church, the house of God, and being nourished by the word of God, in addition to enjoying the blessings of redemption, all this is signified by silver, and your life is lifted up in longing for eternity and the Kingdom of Heaven. In addition, the dove returns to its home, as Noah's dove did when it returned to him, and this signifies the souls which, when they go out into the world, must return to the Church, their home, where they settle with God.

entries.section: (2) Crossing the wilderness and entering Canaan

paragraphs.text: 14- When the Almighty scattered kings in it, it was white as snow in Salmon.
Salmon: one of the peaks of Mount Gerizim, which lies beside Shechem, south of Samaria, among the northern tribes of Israel.

1- If God settled His people and gave them the enjoyment of the land of Canaan, on the other hand He scattered the pagan kings who dwelt in the land of old, that is, God triumphed over these kings and drove them out of their lands.

2- Mount Salmon is known in the land of Canaan as a dark and gloomy mountain, and this signifies the dark pagan life of the peoples who dwelt in the land of Canaan. This mountain God clothed with snow, so it became white and beautiful, a symbol of the pure life of the people of God who dwelt in the land of Canaan, of whom we spoke in the preceding verses, over whom the silver and golden dove hovers, with the spiritual meanings we explained.

3- Christ by His cross transferred humanity from the life of darkness, which Mount Salmon signifies, to the pure, enlightened life, which the snow that covered the mountain, especially its peaks, signifies.

If only your stability were in the Church, so that you come to her often to cast all your burdens and troubles on God in her, and enjoy seeing Him; this will encourage you to pray at all times and to walk in His commandments.

entries.section: (3) Dwelling in Zion, and ascending to heaven

paragraphs.text: 15- The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan; a humped hill is the hill of Bashan. 16- Why look ye with envy, ye humped hills, at the hill which God desired for his dwelling? yea, the Lord will dwell in it for ever.
Bashan: a very fertile region lying east of the river Jordan, in which there is much cultivation and animals full of fatness.
Humped: from hump, the triangular protuberance on the back of the camel, which is full of fat.

1- David addresses the mountains of the fertile region of Bashan, each of which has several peaks resembling the humps of camels full of fat, like the abundant animals and crops of Bashan. And he says to these great mountains full of greenery and richness: Why do you watch Mount Zion on which the city of Jerusalem is built, in which is the ark of the covenant of God, and after this the temple of Solomon? For the mountain of God, the mountain of Bashan, which God filled with richness and greenery, looks at a small mountain, Mount Zion, and counts it blessed because it received the blessing of God's dwelling by the presence of the house of the Lord in it.
2- Mount Bashan signifies the Gentiles who entered into faith, and look to Jerusalem, built on Mount Zion, and see their salvation through Christ incarnate for the redemption of humanity.

3- If high mountains that God endowed with richness like Bashan admire the greatness of little Mount Zion, because it is distinguished by God's presence in it, then it is not right for the people of God to sacrifice in any place other than the house of the Lord, as many erred at different times and sacrificed on mountains that were not the mountain of God.

4- The mountains of the world are rich and great, but the Church of God, that is, His house, even if she seems small, like Mount Zion, is greater than any place in the world because God dwells in her, not only in this world, but after the passing away of heaven and earth He remains dwelling in her, that is, in the Kingdom of Heaven, where the triumphant Church is.

entries.section: (3) Dwelling in Zion, and ascending to heaven

paragraphs.text: 17- The chariots of God are ten thousands, thousands upon thousands: the Lord is among them, Sinai is in the sanctuary.
Ten thousands: plural of ten thousand.

1- David shows the greatness of God, whose glory appears among His angels who carry His throne. He shows that their numbers are very great, for they are thousands of thousands and ten thousands of ten thousands, as he says they are repeated, meaning millions of millions, all these angels praise God and glorify Him. And as God reigns over His angels, His reign is also repeated over everyone of mankind who believes in Him.

2- If God is surrounded by myriads of His angels in heaven, He also appeared among His people at Sinai, and dwelt in the tabernacle of meeting, which He sanctified for Himself, and continued to sanctify the temple of Solomon and the city of Jerusalem; for He works in all generations, as He worked with His people by the crossing of the sea, the manna and quail, and the water from the rock. And He sanctifies His Church throughout time, and every human soul that believes in Him and loves Him and submits to Him, so that His kingdom may be in heaven among His angels, and on earth He dwells in His children who believe in Him.

entries.section: (3) Dwelling in Zion, and ascending to heaven

paragraphs.text: 18- Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts among men; yea, for the rebellious also, that the Lord God might dwell among them.

1- In this verse David prophesies about Christ, who rose from the dead and ascended into the heavens, and brought up those who believe in Him who were in Hades, and brought them into Paradise, that is, the souls that were under the authority of the devil He freed, and they became His followers, for He bought them with His blood, so they became servants to Him, and He took them captive by His love. These captives are the gifts that Christ the Son received from the Father, and some of these souls were rebellious against God and walked in evil for a time, but they believed in Christ, and became a dwelling for God, and St. Paul the Apostle quoted this verse in (Eph 4:8).

2- Christ in His Incarnation humbled Himself and received gifts from people, such as the gifts of the Magi, and those who used to put money in the box that Judas Iscariot kept, to provide for the needs of Christ and His disciples, and Mary the mother of Mark, who hosted Christ in her house in the upper room, and those who gave the colt and the donkey to Christ; for He received gifts from them to encourage them to give, and He gave them life by His redemption, which is the greatest gift.

Christ ascended to heaven in order to raise you in Him to the glories, so remember that you are a stranger on earth and your place is in heaven, that you may keep away from every sin and live a spiritual, heavenly life.
19- Blessed be the Lord, who day by day bears us up, even the God of our salvation. Selah.

1- God's care for His children appears in that He carries them throughout their lives in His hands, that is, He keeps them, provides for their needs, and cares for them; not only material care, but rather spiritual care, that is, He is concerned for the salvation of their souls. This care takes place every day; therefore His children bless Him and glorify Him every day.
2- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on God's love and His care for us every day.
20- He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto God the Lord belong the issues from death.

Our God is our Savior from all the afflictions of our life, even if they are hard, reaching to death. As Christ rose from the dead, so our God is able to raise us from afflictions, even if they bring us to the point of death. "The things which are impossible with men are possible with God" (Lk 18:27). Therefore we live in reassurance always, however many afflictions surround us.
21- But God shall crush the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses.
Scalp: the crown of the head.
Hairy: having much hair.

If God cares for His children, at the same time He rejects evil and punishes it; whoever is proud and vain of his hair like Absalom awaits nothing but destruction, indeed God holds the wicked to account for every sin they commit, because He knows every sin, even if it is small like a hair. And whoever lifts up his head against God and lords it over others and wrongs them, God crushes all these heads that exalt themselves against Him.
22- The Lord said, Return from Bashan, return from the depths of the sea: 23- That thy foot may be dipped in blood, the tongues of thy dogs have their portion from the enemies.

1- God continues His discourse about His vengeance on the wicked who rebel against God; God seizes them even if they try to flee from Him, and climb the mountains, such as Mount Bashan, or flee into the depths of the sea; for He gathers them and gives His people victory over them, and the dogs lick up their blood, as the dogs licked the blood of Ahab and Jezebel. Thus the weak people of God trample their strong enemies, and their feet are dyed with the blood of the enemies, and it was an ancient custom in wars that the victor would dye his feet with the blood of the enemies. What is meant is that God gives His children victory, however weak they are, and however much their enemies exalt themselves against them.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who bound Satan by the cross, and passed through the winepress alone, and His garments were dyed with blood. Thus by shedding His blood on the cross He won a great victory over Satan.

24- They have seen thy goings, O God, the goings of my God, my King, in the sanctuary. 25- The singers went before, the players on stringed instruments followed after; among them were the damsels playing with timbrels. 26- Bless ye God in the congregations, the Lord, ye that are from the fountain of Israel.

1- When David brought the ark back from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite to Jerusalem he rejoiced greatly, and all the children of Israel rejoiced with him, and held fast to God's commandments and His ways, that they might live to God, and declared their submission to God that He might reign over their hearts. The singers from among the Levites and the maidens sang before the ark and played musical instruments, such as the stringed instruments and the timbrels, as they sang with timbrels after crossing the Red Sea.

2- Then David calls on those who believe in God, who were refreshed with the waters of grace in the midst of the people of God, that is, from the fountain of Israel, to bless God and praise Him with a common praise.

3- These verses are a prophecy about the Apostles and those who believe in Christ, who saw the life of Christ on earth and learned His ways and commandments, to shout and sing to God. And the Christians are those who came forth from the people of God the Jews, that is, from the fountain of Israel, because they are the new Israel. And even now the Church still praises God every day with songs of thanksgiving and glorification.
27- There is little Benjamin, their ruler, the princes of Judah, all of them, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.

1- David completes his discourse about the procession of joy and victory of the children of God, and mentions four of the tribes of the children of Israel; among them Benjamin, which was a small tribe, but from it came the first king of the children of Israel, Saul the son of Kish. Judah was a large tribe, and these two tribes dwelt side by side, and opposite them dwelt the two tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. By this he means that all the tribes rejoiced in God's care and His work in them.

2- From these four tribes came most of the disciples of Christ: from Benjamin came Paul, from Judah came Peter, Andrew, James and John, and most of the rest from Zebulun and Naphtali; that is, the Church with her Apostles rejoices in the work of God in her.
28- Thy God hath commanded thy strength: strengthen, O God, that which thou hast wrought for us.
Thy strength: thy glory and thy power.

David reassures the people of God and says to them that God has commanded your strength, so do not be troubled by the power of the enemies and their threats; because your God, the Pantocrator, protects you, and has promised you glory and power, and therefore the people of God ask Him to support them in all their works that they may be blessed and prosper. And this is a prophecy about the preaching of the Apostles, as they ask God to strengthen them in it.
29- Because of thy temple at Jerusalem shall kings bring presents unto thee.

This verse is a clear prophecy about the faith of the Gentiles in Christ, as they come to the temple of the New Testament in Jerusalem, where Christ accomplished His redemption, for the temple is Christ, God incarnate, crucified for the world, and they declare their faith in Him, and even bring gifts, like the Magi, the kings of the East, who came with gifts for Christ. And every believer is a king over himself who offers his gift to Christ, which is his love and submission and obedience to His commandments.

30- Rebuke the beast of the reeds, the herd of bulls with the calves of the peoples, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war. 31- Princes shall come out of Egypt; Cush shall soon stretch out her hands unto God. Beast of the reeds: in the land of the Jews there grew a thicket, or reeds, in some marshes, in which beasts of prey dwelt. It may mean the crocodiles that live among the reeds in Egypt. What is meant by these beasts is the enemies of the children of Israel.
Herd of bulls: that is, a flock or gathering of bulls.
Cush: Abyssinia or Ethiopia.

1- David asks God to rebuke the enemies of His people who have savage natures, who are either the surrounding Gentiles, or the heretics present among the people of God, whom he expresses as the beast of the reeds. He also rebukes the herd of bulls, by which are meant those characterized by pride, that is, the proud enemies of the people of God who resist God. In addition to the calves of the peoples, that is, the peoples of the Gentiles who are led and submit to faith in Christ, and offer gifts such as silver. Silver also signifies redemption, that is, they seek Christ the Redeemer. Among these peoples are the great ones of the Egyptians who are distinguished by learning and honor, and likewise the people of Abyssinia who stretch out their hands and submit to the faith.
2- David also asks God to scatter and drive away the peoples of the Gentiles who do not want to believe, so that He protects His people from them.

If only you would not resist God's commandments for the sake of your personal aims, but submit to Him and hold fast to them, then you will find your life, and rejoice in God's work in you; for He wants your salvation, and He must give you the joy of fellowship with Him, and grant you His treasures.
32- Sing unto God, ye kingdoms of the earth; O sing praises unto the Lord; Selah.

1- David calls on all the Gentiles to praise God, meaning those of the Gentiles who have believed in Christ, or who have heard about Christ. He calls them to believe, and then to praise God, declaring their joy in Him as a Lord to them who reigns over their hearts and lets them enjoy His care.
2- The verse ends with the word "Selah," which is a musical pause for meditating on the greatness of God so that we may praise Him and glorify Him.
33- To him that rideth upon the heavens of heavens, which were of old; lo, he doth send out his voice, and that a mighty voice.

1- He describes God as reigning over the highest of the ancient heavens, that is, those He created at the beginning of creation. Here he points to the eternity of God, and that He is the Creator of all creation.

2- He also speaks of the mighty voice of God, and this is not only through thunder and lightning and strong winds, but also through the mighty words of Christ, who rebuked the winds and the waves, cast out demons and raised Lazarus ... and likewise through His mighty word that terrifies sinners, as Paul spoke with Felix the governor about judgment and Felix trembled (Acts 24:25). This verse also points to the mighty voice of God on the day of judgment, when sinners tremble and the righteous rejoice.
34- Ascribe ye strength unto God: his excellency is over Israel, and his strength is in the clouds.

1- David also asks the Gentiles who have believed to glorify the great God, who is exalted above all gods, and whose greatness and majesty appear over His people Israel, so they glorify Him continually, and He protects them and subdues their enemies, as He struck the Egyptians with the ten plagues, and drowned Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, and at the same time kept His people, and brought them across to the wilderness of Sinai, and freed them from slavery.
2- God's power also appears in the cloud and mist rising in the sky with its beautiful white color, and this signifies His saints who live on earth a lofty, heavenly, luminous life.
53- O God, thou art terrible out of thy holy places: the God of Israel is he that giveth strength and power unto his people. Blessed be God.

1- David also speaks of the great fear of God in His holy places, which are the places of worship around the ark of the covenant of God in Jerusalem, and also the other parts of the tabernacle that were in Gibeon during David's life. And likewise the holy places are all the souls that have been sanctified to God and worshiped Him with all their heart, for He gives awe to His children in the eyes of others; because the world sees in them the power of God and the greatness of carrying out the commandment.

2- God is the source of the people's strength, and therefore He protects His people who worship Him and subdues their enemies, so that His power appears in them, since they have no source of strength except God, and so they bless Him and praise Him continually.

Contemplate the greatness of God and the fear of Him so that your heart may be reassured, for He is your God who protects you, and at the same time reject every sin so as not to anger Him, and your heart will be purified and free to praise Him at all times.
God the Savior of the afflicted. To the Chief Musician upon Shoshannim. Of David. "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.
2- When was it written?

When David was fleeing from the face of his son Absalom, then war broke out between them, and Absalom died, and before David returned to his throne. He was living and remembering his sufferings which he had passed through and was still suffering from, while a stranger to his throne in Jerusalem.
3- This psalm is sung upon Shoshannim, which is:
a- A special tune.
b- A musical instrument resembling the lily flower.
4- It is considered one of the Messianic psalms because it speaks clearly of the sufferings of Christ.
5- This psalm resembles Psalm 22 in speaking of the sufferings of Christ.
6- Many verses are quoted from this psalm in the New Testament; it is one of the psalms most quoted (Mt 27:35; Mk 15:24; Jn 15:25; Acts 1:20; Rom 15:3).
7- Many parts of this psalm are prayed in the prayer for the departed in the prayer of the Third Hour.
8- This psalm does not occur in the prayers of the Agpeya.
1- Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul.

1- David feels that sorrows have increased upon him, so that they became like waters that rose until they covered his whole body up to his neck and nearly drowned him. Therefore he asks God for salvation, to lift these events from him, since his tribe Judah was slow to bring him back to his throne, at the very time when it ought to have been the first of the tribes to be blamed for this; for Jerusalem lies in the tribe of Judah, while the rest of the tribes wanted to bring him back, and an expected conflict arose between the tribes and the tribe of Judah. All this while David was driven out, a stranger to his city Jerusalem, far from the ark of the covenant of God, and suffering because of what Absalom had done to him, and the betrayal of many. Therefore he asked God to save him from all these psychological troubles, in addition to the bodily troubles, since he was not living honored as a king.
2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, upon whom sorrows gathered in the last week of His life, especially when He was praying in the garden of Gethsemane before He was arrested.

3- This verse is also a prophecy about the Babylonian captivity, for these are the feelings of the Jews at their captivity. It is also a prophecy about the prophet Jonah, for these are his feelings while in the belly of the whale.
2- I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
Floods: a strong current of water.

1- David depicts the extent of his sufferings as though he had sunk in deep mud and could not find a place for his feet to stand, but sinks endlessly, that is, he is exposed to destruction. Then he depicts himself as having entered deep waters, with strong currents of water covering him, so that he nearly drowned; so also are his sorrows and sufferings, especially since he finds no way out of them and no support to lean on, and there was nothing left before him but God his Savior.
2- This is also a prophecy about Christ, in the last week of His life, sunk in His sorrows and sufferings for the redemption of humanity.
3- I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.
Fail: grow weary.

1- David expresses his many pains that took in all his members: his feet find no place to stand, as in the previous verse, and in this verse we find that his throat is weary and dry and he is no longer able to continue crying out. As for his eyes, they have grown weary from looking so much to God, while He is slow and does not answer. This verse expresses the extent of David's sorrows and his great need of God. It is a kind of entreaty and insistence upon God to have compassion on him.

2- Perhaps this verse depicts part of the sufferings of Christ on the cross, where His throat dried, as He said, "I thirst," and His eyes grew weary as He bore the cup of God's wrath on behalf of humanity, and asked that the cup pass from Him, and it did not pass, and He completed the redemption to redeem us by His wonderful love.
4- They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head: they that would destroy me, being mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty: then I restored that which I took not away.

1- David shows the great number of those who wronged him and hated him, saying that they are more than the hairs of his head, and that they tried to consume him with their many evils in order to be rid of him, and in all this he was wronged and had done no evil, and he restored to them what he had not seized, namely the throne of the kingdom; for God was the one who anointed him by the hand of Samuel, and the people made him king. Those who rose up against David were so many that it is hard to count them, such as Shimei the son of Gera and Ahithophel.

2- This verse also applies to Christ, against whom the Jewish people, the scribes and the Pharisees rose up, and tried to ensnare Him in errors but were unable, and He restored what He had not seized, for He was crucified as a sin offering for us though He had not sinned, and He restored Adam, whom Satan had seized and made fall into sin, and brought him back to Paradise.

If you suffer pains and sorrows, know that your Christ suffered before you, though He did not err, so ask His help and He will support you, and even compensate you for what you have borne with abundant blessings.
5- O God, thou knowest my foolishness; and my sins are not hid from thee.

Although David declared in the previous verses that he was wronged and exposed to many troubles, he returns and confesses his foolishness and sins. There is no contradiction between this verse and the previous verses, because there is no person without sin, whether voluntary sins, even if few, in addition to the sins he commits without knowledge and in ignorance. This shows two things:
1- David's carefulness and his repentance of every sin.
2- David's humility in declaring his weakness by saying "my foolishness"; for if God charges His angels with folly, how much more do human beings fall into various follies.
6- Let not them that wait on thee, O Lord God of hosts, be ashamed for my sake: let not those that seek thee be confounded for my sake, O God of Israel.
7- Because for thy sake I have borne reproach; shame hath covered my face. 8- I am become a stranger unto my brethren, and an alien unto my mother's children.

1- While David was suffering and bearing the pains of being driven out of Jerusalem and exposed to death, his heart took pity on all who believe in God, and who see in King David an example for themselves, lest they doubt the way of righteousness and leave God. He enjoys God's care for him and is spiritually satisfied, but with a wonderful fatherhood he has compassion on his children, that is, his people, lest they stumble because of the following:
a- The shame and disgrace that covered David in his fleeing barefoot from the face of Absalom, and people's reproaching him, such as the reproach of Shimei the son of Gera (2 Sam 16:7, 8).

b- His brothers the Jews treated him with contempt, indeed with enmity, and considered him as though he were a foreigner and stranger to them, and rose up in a great army to destroy him and all who were with him.

2- These verses apply to Christ, who bore the disgrace and shame of the cross and the false accusations directed at Him, but He asks the Father not to allow all who await the coming Messiah to stumble; so that if they see Him in weakness they do not doubt Him, but learn from Him endurance, and love for those who wrong them.
9- For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me.

1- Although David was driven out of Jerusalem, his heart was attached to the house of the Lord, that is, the tabernacle in which was the ark of the covenant, and he is zealous for the house of the Lord with a good zeal and fears that the wicked may wrong this house; indeed he longs to be beside the house of the Lord every day, to offer holy worship to God.

2- Everyone who resists God and whose heart is filled with evil reproached David and resisted him, because he walks in uprightness; in addition, everyone who resisted God, or reproached Him, grieved David, because David was attached to God and did not want anyone to wrong the name of God.

3- The zeal of God's house ate up the heart of Christ, so He drove the sellers out of the Temple, and said, "My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves" (Mt 21:13), in addition to His bearing many reproaches and accusations from the Jews and the priests. All this He accepted for our salvation and redemption.
10- When I wept, and chastened my soul with fasting, that was to my reproach. 11- I made sackcloth also my garment; and I became a proverb to them.
Sackcloth: coarse garments worn in self-abasement before God.
1- David makes clear what he bore of the toils of spiritual striving, and they are:
a- Weeping with prayers before God, which carries the meaning of repentance, and asking for help and salvation.

b- Fasting and abasing himself before God, but David's enemies considered his weeping and fasting weakness and disgrace, yet he did not care about their opinions, and held fast to his striving for the sake of God.

c- Wearing sackcloth and abasing himself before God after his fall into sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and after she bore him a child and it fell sick and was exposed to death (2 Sam 12:16, 17).
d- David became a proverb to those around him, who mocked him, and he bore them. And he was a type and symbol of Christ.
All this shows the extent of David's faithfulness in his spiritual striving, and his bearing the reproaches of his enemies.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who grieved over Jerusalem (Mt 23:37) and fasted forty days, and put on our body, which was to Him like sackcloth, and became a byword of mockery and shame at His crucifixion; all this He bore for our salvation.
12- They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards.

1- After David had been the king sitting on the throne and the judge who governs his people, he was changed into a man driven out of the city, judged by the elders sitting beside the gate in the city square, that is, he became weak and accused, his case examined, although in truth he was innocent, and moreover the drunkards began to mock him with songs full of derision.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, whom the scribes, the Pharisees and the chief priests accused with many false accusations, and tried at the end of His life on earth, and the soldiers, drunk with sin, mocked Him, and so they reviled the Lord of glory who is without sin.

If you are liable to fall into various sins, then at least offer repentance with striving and self-abasement before God, and He will lift them from you, and even comfort your heart and bring you back to His embrace.
13- But as for me, my prayer is unto thee, O Lord, in an acceptable time: O God, in the multitude of thy mercy hear me, in the truth of thy salvation.

1- Before all the afflictions that faced David, he could do nothing but direct his prayer to God with humility and self-abasement. This is what God asks, in order to be pleased with a person; for He loves the humble who cry to Him, and His mercies overflow upon them and He answers them.

2- Christ also prayed in the garden of Gethsemane with humility and fervor, and then offered Himself as a sacrifice on the cross for us; all this pleased the Father, and He answered Him and accepted His sacrifice, and by His death He redeemed us and we received great mercies.

14- Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink: let me be delivered from them that hate me, and out of the deep waters. 15- Let not the waterflood overflow me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me.

1- David asks God to deliver him from the mire so that he may not sink and drown in it, and from the waters so that he may not fall into their depths and drown. What is meant by the mire and water is the wicked who hate David and try to destroy him though he is innocent. His request for deliverance also includes that God keep him in righteousness so that he is not led along with the wicked in their evil. And consequently, in the end, he does not enter the pit and have it close its mouth upon him, that is, he does not come out of it forever; for he has hope in the awaited Messiah, who is able to bring him out of the pit and lift him up to Paradise.

2- These two verses apply to Christ, for the mire and water mean the sins that Christ bore for us, that is, the sins of all humanity, and because of them He was crucified and died, and went down to the pit, that is, Hades. But the pit could not hold Him, but He brought out Adam and his children, and all who died in hope, and brought them up to Paradise.

16- Hear me, O Lord; for thy lovingkindness is good: turn unto me according to the multitude of thy tender mercies. 17- And hide not thy face from thy servant; for I am in trouble: hear me speedily. 18- Draw nigh unto my soul, and redeem it: deliver me because of mine enemies. 19- Thou hast known my reproach, and my shame, and my dishonour: mine adversaries are all before thee.

1- David pleads with God to include him in His mercies, because he suffers the pains of his sins and the pains of his enemies' harassment of him, so he urges God to answer him. He feels his weakness and unworthiness, but his hope is the mercies of God.

2- From the intensity of his remorse David entreats God not to hide His face from him, as he feels that he is very sinful and does not deserve God's love and care, but feels that sin has bound him and he needs God to loose him from it, and set him free, indeed redeem him, that is, take his sins away from him. He believes in Christ the Redeemer who was to come in the fullness of time, and he is also confident that God knows everything, his sins and his enemies' harassment of him. So he asks Him in faith to intervene and have mercy on him and lift all these pains from him.

3- These verses are about Christ, who bore our sins on His cross, and asks the Father to take them from Him, expressing the hideousness of sin and His distress over it, as He asked in the garden of Gethsemane that the cup of suffering pass from Him.
20- Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none.
21- They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.
Gall: a very bitter plant.

1- David expresses his suffering from the shame that came upon him when Absalom drove him out, and even lay with his wives on the roof of his palace in front of all the people, and this shame was so heavy upon David that he became sick. David waited for a retreat from Absalom, but found even his counselors such as Ahithophel standing against him, so he found no comfort and no tender feelings; because of all these pains he asks God's mercies.

2- As for Christ, the shame of the cross was heavy upon Him, and He passed through the winepress alone and found no comfort and no tender feelings from anyone; indeed, even in His thirst they gave Him vinegar mixed with bitterness and gall.
