This verse (v. 21) applies to Christ, and applies symbolically to David, as he bore sufferings like the bitterness of gall.

Sin binds your life, so do not be dazzled by its beauty, and do not slip running after its pleasure, and if you fall into it hasten to God with self-abasement, for He is merciful, and a tender Father ready to accept your repentance and free you from it, so that you return to your first sonship to God. Hold fast to your prayers and readings, and above all the sacraments of the Church, and you will remain steadfast in the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
22- Let their table before them become a snare, and a trap for the secure.
Trap: a snare or a trap.

1- The wicked caused the righteous man many troubles and gave him bitter drink and vinegar (v. 21); therefore he says here a prophecy of what will happen to them, meaning the Jews who rose up against Christ and crucified Him, that their table will become a snare. That is, their goods occupy them and keep them away from God. And as the hunter puts out food so that the animal falls into his net, so the devil uses their table and their material preoccupations to keep them away from God, and God permits this because they persisted in their sin, which is the torturing of the righteous man, by whom is meant Christ, or David who is a type of Him. And while they are secure and at ease they fall into the trap.

2- The Jews sought the help of the Romans and their authority and crucified Christ, but the Romans became a snare for them, and besieged Jerusalem and destroyed it in AD 70. St. Paul the Apostle made clear that these verses are a prophecy about the Jews who crucified Christ (Rom 11:9, 10).

3- The Holy Bible is the spiritual food, and the Jews did not understand the Holy Bible and all its prophecies about the Messiah, so they rejected Jesus Christ; that is, the word of God became a snare for them, so they rose up against Christ and crucified Him. They continued offering sacrifices after Christ had completed the redemption on the cross, so their table, that is, their altar on which they offer their sacrifices, became a snare that keeps them from faith in Christ, the true Sacrifice for us, to whom these sacrifices point.
23- Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not; and make their loins continually to shake.
Loins: their backs.

1- If the righteous man's eyes grew weary from waiting for the Lord because of all he suffers from the wicked (v. 3), God punishes the wicked by darkening their eyes so that they do not see, that is, they lose the ability to discern. The Jews did not discern that Jesus is the awaited Messiah, although after Christ not one prophet appeared among the Jewish people; for the prophets were preparing the way and prophesying about the awaited Messiah, indeed their eyes were darkened at the hour of the cross when darkness came over all the earth.

2- When a person is tired from work he feels pains in his back and needs sleep and rest, but the wicked have backs that remain in continual pain and trembling; because their inner anxiety causes them bodily pains, and these wicked, like the Jews who scourged Christ on His back and crucified Him, lived afterward in turmoil.

3- These verses may seem to be wishing evil on the wicked, but David here states truths and prophecies about the Jews who would crucify Christ. It is a warning hundreds of years before the event, perhaps that they might repent.
24- Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them. 25- Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents.
Indignation: thy intense anger.

David prophesies about the Jews who crucified Christ and about Judas Iscariot, and about the wicked on the day of judgment, so he asks God to punish them with His intense anger and to lay waste their houses so that they have no rest and no stability. This is what happened in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and also in the death of Judas by a hideous death. As for the day of judgment, the punishment cannot be imagined from its dreadfulness. All this is to put the fear of God into the hearts of all, that they may repent and return to God, and He lift His anger from them.
26- For they persecute him whom thou hast smitten; and they talk to the grief of those whom thou hast wounded.

1- God permitted David to be smitten, that is, to suffer pains, so that he would be strengthened and become strong and able to govern and lead his country as king. But Saul rose up against him, and pursued him and tried to kill him, so Saul by his evil carried out the will of God, which was the smiting of David, yet he is called to account and punished for his evil. Those who shared with David while he was driven out from the face of Saul also were exposed to the same troubles of being driven out from the face of Saul and attempts to kill them, so they speak with grief, that is, with sorrow, of all they met from Saul's pursuit of them.

2- This verse applies to Christ, whom it pleased the Father to bruise with grief (Isa 53:10), so He smote Him with the bearing of the bitter sins of the world on the cross. And the Jews drove Him out from among them by trying to ensnare Him with a word, and by the attempt to kill Him that ended with His crucifixion. And the disciples of Christ and all His followers were exposed to many pains and persecutions from the Jews, and they tell us with grief of all these persecutions, as appears from the Book of Acts and the history of the Church.
27- Add iniquity unto their iniquity: and let them not come into thy righteousness. 28- Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.
1- David asks God to gather the iniquities of the wicked who persecute the righteous. For the wicked persisted in their evil, and wronged not only the righteous man, but his followers.

2- David also asks that these wicked be punished by not entering into the righteousness of Christ, that is, they receive His redemption, and consequently do not enter the Kingdom, but are cast into eternal torment. So their name is not written in the book of life, that is, they have no portion with Christ, and consequently are deprived of the communion of the saints.

Do not be lax with evil, for your God is long-suffering and of great mercy, and He is also just, and repays for every evil thought, word and deed. Do not defy God with your sins, but on the contrary return to Him with repentance and humility and He will receive you. And do not be troubled by your weakness, for He loves the weak and supports them, and rescues them from every sin.

entries.section: (5) Praise of God the Savior of His children

paragraphs.text: 29- But I am poor and sorrowful: let thy salvation, O God, set me up on high.

After all the sufferings that David met, he did not answer them with any wrong; he did not meet violence with violence, but bore them with humility and spiritual poverty, and the signs of pain and depression covered his face. And when he accepted these sufferings for the sake of God, He blessed him with many spiritual blessings. The first is mentioned in this verse, and it is his salvation that lifts David from his sufferings; that is, David believed in God the Savior, so his heart was lifted up and he lived in hope. And indeed God saved him from the hand of Saul, then from the hand of Absalom, and from the hand of everyone who wanted to wrong him. David's greatest hope was in Christ who was to come in the fullness of time to lift him from hell to Paradise. David lived in hope, so his heart was lifted up in joy.

entries.section: (5) Praise of God the Savior of His children

paragraphs.text: 30- I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. 31- This also shall please the Lord better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs.
Shall please: becomes a good offering with which God is pleased.
Hoofs: nails.

The second blessing that God gives to His righteous children who endure sufferings for His sake is that they praise Him, magnify Him, and thank Him for His salvation. This praise has great value in God's sight, because it is praise despite the sufferings they endured, and because they tasted and experienced fellowship with God through the affliction, so they praised Him and glorified Him. The value of this praise in God's sight is greater than all animal sacrifices and offerings, even if the sacrifice is as great as an ox.

entries.section: (5) Praise of God the Savior of His children

paragraphs.text: 32- The humble shall see this, and be glad: and your heart shall live that seek God. 33- For the Lord heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners.
1- The third blessing that God gives to the righteous who endure sufferings is joy, for their hearts rejoice in fellowship with God and His work in them, and His rescuing them from their enemies.

2- As for the fourth blessing, it is life with God, while they are on earth, then eternal life in the Kingdom. He gives it to everyone who suffers pains and takes refuge in God with many requests, for He regards their requests and answers them, and frees them from the slavery of the world if they were enslaved, and from the slavery of sin, so they live with Him and enjoy fellowship with Him, and from the captivity of the body, so they put it off, and depart in the spirit, and rejoice in heaven. Also everyone who clung to God and became a prisoner of His love, like St. Paul the Apostle (Phil 1:1), to enjoy life with God.

entries.section: (5) Praise of God the Savior of His children

paragraphs.text: 34- Let the heaven and earth praise him, the seas, and every thing that moveth therein. 35- For God will save Zion, and will build the cities of Judah: that they may dwell there, and have it in possession. 36- The seed also of his servants shall inherit it: and they that love his name shall dwell therein.

1- The fifth blessing is the praise of the whole creation to God, sharing with the righteous man who endured sufferings for God, so he sees all creation around him sharing his praise: the heavens and all that is in them of angels, and the earth and all that is on it of human beings, animals and plants, and likewise the seas and all the animals that move in them; all these walk in their order in submission to God, and are led after man, the greatest creature, the leader of the praise of God.

2- The sixth blessing is the gift of salvation for Zion and Judah and those who dwell in them, and that is through the salvation accomplished in the fullness of time by Christ the Redeemer, when He founds His Church in every place, so His children find a dwelling and stability in her, and live to God, not only in one temple in the world, that is, in Jerusalem, but in every place. For Christ, although His salvation went out from Jerusalem, spreads His churches throughout the world, and the righteous who endured sufferings with thanksgiving and continued seeking God, and all the prisoners of His love, dwell in them, as we mentioned in the previous verses (vv. 32, 33). The righteous who walked in the way of their righteous fathers also enjoy life in the Church, which is the icon of heaven, or the new Zion, and the heavenly Jerusalem.

God's gifts to you are renewed every day, so the least you can do is thank Him and praise Him, and your heart will rejoice and you will enjoy fellowship with Him, and your heart will cling to the Kingdom of Heaven.

The salvation of the righteous and the shame of the wicked. To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance. "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O Lord" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet.
2- When was it written?
When David was exposed to a severe trial, perhaps it was Saul's pursuit of him, or Absalom's driving him out, or any other trial.
3- We see in the title the phrase "to bring to remembrance," that is, reminding God to intervene for David's great need of Him.
4- This psalm suits every person in distress, so that he may be strengthened and his adherence to God may increase.
5- This psalm is liturgical, that is, it is prayed in communal prayer, and most likely at the time of offering incense in the sanctuary.
6- In terms of meaning, this psalm is considered an extension of Psalm 69 and an introduction to Psalm 71; these three psalms ask for salvation from God because of severe distress.

7- There is a strong similarity between this psalm and Psalm 40, for the five verses of Psalm 70 are repeated in the verses (Ps 40:13-17) with a few verbal differences that do not change the general meaning of each verse.
8- This psalm is found in the Prime prayer of the Agpeya, because the one praying begins his day by asking God's help, so that he may face any afflictions he may meet.
Note: refer to the commentary on (Ps 40:13-17) found in Volume Ten of the Church Encyclopedia. And we offer you, dear reader, here a brief commentary on each verse.

entries.section: (5) Praise to God who saves His children

paragraphs.text: 1- Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O Lord.

David was in severe suffering in his trial, so he asked God for deliverance, indeed for haste in helping him. This shows his faith in God, his feeling of his great need of Him, and his hard suffering which he could not bear; therefore he asked God for swift help.

entries.section: (5) Praise to God who saves His children

paragraphs.text: 2- Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt.

David believed that God would save him from the hands of his enemies, and consequently shame would cover them. Likewise, those who desire David's harm and destruction will fear and turn backward before the power of God who rescues David.

entries.section: (5) Praise to God who saves His children

paragraphs.text: 3- Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha.

When those who want to destroy David are put to shame, and those who desire his harm draw back, then all who gloated over David will also be put to shame and draw back, those who mocked him when he was suffering in his trial and raised their voices against him in derision, saying, "Aha, aha."

entries.section: (5) Praise to God who saves His children

paragraphs.text: 4- Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let the Lord be magnified.

On the other hand, David calls all the righteous who cling to God to rejoice and be glad in the salvation of God which they have received, and then to glorify God and magnify Him. Thus the children of God spend their days, rejoicing in salvation and glorifying the name of the holy God.

entries.section: (5) Praise to God who saves His children

paragraphs.text: 5- But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O Lord, make no tarrying. At the end of the Psalm David declares his humility and his need before God, so he asks for God's help and His constant salvation for him; because the enemy, Satan, never rests, but repeats his attacks and stirs up the wicked against the one who walks in God's commandments, so David needs God's constant protection.

Be sure that your God is waiting for your prayers in order to answer you; for He loves you and died for you on the Cross. So do not be slack in asking for His help, and when afflictions increase upon you, cry out to Him, confident that He will keep you and deliver you, and you will glorify Him.
"Thanksgiving to God the Refuge"
"In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: a- This Psalm is one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those whose writer is not named in the title; but many of the Fathers attribute this Psalm to David.
b- Some see that its writer is the prophet Jeremiah, because its style is similar to Jeremiah's style, and also the events that Jeremiah went through (v. 20).
2- When was it written?
If its writer is David, then it was at the end of his life, when Absalom drove him out, or any other afflictions that met him in his old age.
3- For whom was it written?

In the Septuagint, the title of the Psalm reads, "Of David. A Psalm sung by the sons of Jonadab." This Jonadab is the son of Rechab, that is, the descendants of the Rechabites who held fast to the teachings of their father not to drink wine, nor build houses, nor plant vineyards (Jer 35:5-10); that is, they lived relying on God.

4- The title of this Psalm in the Septuagint also contains "and of those who were led into captivity", which means that the Psalm prophesies about the period of the captivity and the sufferings that the people of God endured as they went into captivity (v. 20).
5- This Psalm resembles Psalm 31 in its beginning, and resembles Psalm 35 in its ending. Thus we find (vv. 1-3) resembling (Ps 31:1-3), and also the verses (vv. 23, 24) resembling (Ps 35:26-28).

6- This Psalm is full of feelings of faith in the power of God who supports His children, and it calls whoever says it to thanksgiving and praise. It is therefore suitable for every person passing through affliction, so that his faith and his love for God may be strengthened.
7- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 1- In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion.

The writer of the Psalm speaks from an experience of faith: he asked for God's protection, found great help, and consequently was lifted up above his enemies. He was not put to shame, that is, God did not neglect him; on the contrary, his enemies were put to shame. This confirms the strength of his faith by which he lives all his life. This verse also shows the fatherhood of God and His care, who does not forsake His children forever; He keeps them in this life and gives them joy in the life to come.

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 2- Deliver me in thy righteousness, and cause me to escape: incline thine ear unto me, and save me.

1- Having become sure of the power of God which supports him, David asked Him to rescue him from the affliction he was passing through. David asked God to rescue him by His justice, and this shows David's reliance on the justice of God, and his innocence of the accusations that his enemies direct at him.
2- David's asking God to incline His ear to him shows two things:
a- David's declaration of his weakness, since his voice is feeble.

b- David's confidence in God's tenderness and humility, that He inclines His ear and condescends and draws near to him. This was fulfilled in the Incarnation of Christ in the fullness of time, when He came down to us from heaven to redeem us and give us life.

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 3- Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress.

1- David asks God to be a fortress for him, that is, a very strong place which he enters and takes refuge in, so that no one can harm him. This shows David's faith in the power of God, and at the same time his great need of Him.

2- What is wonderful is David's faith after this petition, for he trusted that God had heard him and would answer him, save him and protect him. So he said in the past tense, "Thou hast given commandment to save me", that is, he believes that God has answered and commanded, and only the carrying out of His divine command remains, which must surely be accomplished, and no one can resist it.

3- This verse also speaks of the rock that accompanied the people of God in the wilderness and gave them water to drink, which is a symbol of Christ as the New Testament has declared to us (Deut 8:15).

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 4- Deliver me, O my God, out of the hand of the wicked, out of the hand of the unrighteous and cruel man.

David asks God to rescue him from the wicked one, who is Satan; from the evildoer, who is everyone who obeys the thoughts of the devil and harms others; and from the unrighteous man, who is he who seizes the right of another and behaves selfishly at the expense of others. For David trusts in the hand of God, able to save him from the grasp of the wicked, because the hand of God is stronger than all men; therefore he asks with confidence, and so receives reassurance.

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 5- For thou art my hope, O Lord God: thou art my trust from my youth.
All of David's petitions to God rest on two things:
a- That God is his hope, and not men or material things; therefore he asks Him for all his needs and never despairs, however much things press upon him.
b- That he has relied on God since he became aware and understood, that is, when he was a boy; so he has a long experience of relying on God, which gives him reassurance in the midst of afflictions.

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 6- By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise shall be continually of thee.

Here David makes clear that God is his support even while he was an unborn child, and at his coming out of the womb. For God is the One who formed him in his mother's womb, and the One who brought him out of his mother's womb as a newborn, and then consequently takes care of him throughout his life, and therefore he relies on Him. For God knows his origin, so He is able to lead him and guide him in all his steps. And for all this care he praises Him and thanks Him at all times. The verses (vv. 5, 6) in this Psalm resemble (Ps 22:9, 10) and also resemble the words of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:5).

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 7- I am as a wonder unto many; but thou art my strong refuge.

David endured many sufferings and passed through afflictions, but God rescued him, so he became an example and a model, and a wonder of the great work of God among men; that is, he became a light for the world to be imitated by the righteous, so that they take refuge in God, the strong refuge in every affliction, to enjoy His wonderful work in them. And David here is a symbol of Christ, who fulfilled all righteousness and bore the sufferings alone on the Cross for our salvation, and all His children walk after His likeness, as the Apostle Paul said, "we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men" (1 Cor 4:9-13). That is, as Christ was the light of the world, so He also commanded His followers to be the light of the world.

entries.section: (1) God my fortress and my rock

paragraphs.text: 8- Let my mouth be filled with thy praise and with thy honour all the day.

After the Psalmist tasted the work of God in afflictions, his heart clung to the love of God, and he forgot the pains of the afflictions, and his chief occupation became the glorification of God throughout his day. Thus he passed from sorrow to joy, and this is one of the most important blessings of praise.

If you meet with afflictions in your life, hasten and look to God your refuge, and ask for His help, and He will bring you through the midst of afflictions, and you will rejoice in His fellowship, and your heart will be lifted up in praising Him and thanking Him.
9- Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth.

1- David asks God to keep protecting him and supporting him in his old age, because old age is accompanied by weakness of the body and inability to fight enemies, and this proves that David wrote this Psalm at the end of his life, that is, in his sixties. David died at the age of seventy, and it is well known that David was a man of war from his youth, and was a military commander in the army of Saul, and then after he became king. But when he grew old, the commanders of his army asked him to rest so that he would not be exposed to the dangers of war (2 Sam 21:17).

2- The time of old age, from the spiritual side, is a period of lukewarmness and spiritual weakness, and therefore the spiritual person asks God not to leave him in his weakness and spiritual old age, but to raise him up and encourage him.
10- For mine enemies speak against me; and they that lay wait for my soul take counsel together,
11- Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him.

1- David's enemies seized the opportunity of his weakness because of his old age, for they were always watching him, and they said that he was weak and could be attacked, and then they falsely claimed that God had forsaken him and would not rescue him from their hands. In this they deceived themselves, and tried to make David think that he was weak and without support so that he would be afraid. But David remained firm in his faith until the end of his life; indeed, at the end of his life, when his son Adonijah tried to seize the kingdom, he issued a decree making Solomon king as his successor, and this was indeed done (1 Kgs 1:29).

2- These two verses apply to Christ in His last sufferings and His crucifixion, especially when He cried out on the Cross, saying, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Mt 27:43). All this Satan said against Christ, and the wicked Jews repeated it after him; but Satan was surprised after the death of Christ that He seized Satan and bound him, and released the believers from Hades and brought them up to Paradise; for Satan thought that he would seize the spirit of Christ and put it in Hades, like the rest of men. So Satan always tries to fight the children of God through their weak points, whether in their old age or at any other time, to draw them away from God.
12- O God, be not far from me: O my God, make haste for my help.

David, in the weakness of old age, with the claims and threats of his enemies, had nothing before him but to take refuge in God. So he asked Him not to be far from him, but to keep supporting him and helping him, and when the enemies see that God is near him, they fear and flee.

13- Let them be confounded and consumed that are adversaries to my soul; let them be covered with reproach and dishonour that seek my hurt. Because of David's confidence in God, he believes that He will support him in his weakness, so that the falsehood and claims of his enemies are exposed, and indeed shame, disgrace and dishonour cover them, and they become liable to destruction, that is, God scatters them because of their evil.
14- But I will hope continually, and will yet praise thee more and more.
1- David's faith increased, so he had a continual hope in God that does not waver, whatever the afflictions or threats.

2- Also, before the wonderful works of God and His protection of David, his praise and his thanks to God increased. For through praise the eyes of the one who praises are enlightened, so he sees everything new in the works of God with him, and thanks Him for them, and then God increases His mercies and support to this thankful person, so that his thanks and praise increase as well.
15- My mouth shall shew forth thy righteousness and thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers thereof.

1- When David sees the works of God in a world full of injustice, he speaks and proclaims the justice of God who rejects all injustice; and though He is long-suffering toward the unjust, and the righteous endure sufferings for a time, yet He delivers them from the hands of the wicked and saves them. And His kindnesses to them are hard to count because they are very many. This is what David experienced; for he met many afflictions from Saul and Absalom and from many others, but God rescued him from their hands and was glorified.
2- David speaks of the justice of God all the day, that is, he praises God throughout his life, and thanks Him in affliction and in ease.
16- I will go in the strength of the Lord God: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.
Strength (jabarut): great power.

1- After all this praise David feels great confidence in himself, and a power by which he overcomes all his enemies. He expresses this power with "strength" (jabarut), but he ascribes this power to God; so he glorifies God and declares his humility before Him, that is, he does not steal the glory of God, and to the humble God gives power without limit.

2- David praises none but God alone, for He alone is righteous, perfect in His righteousness, and he does not ascribe glory to himself, nor to any pagan god, nor to any power in the world, but the cause of every blessing and virtue in his life is from God, and all his good works also are from God.

The more you thank God and ascribe the glory to Him, the more your heart rejoices in God, and God rejoices in you, and your life delights in fellowship with God, and many mercies overflow upon you; indeed your eyes are enlightened and God reveals to you His secrets which surpass the mind.
3- Thanksgiving and proclamation of the great things of God (vv. 17-24):
17- O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works.

David declares God's care for him, for He taught him how to walk in his way from his youth, so he enjoyed fellowship with God from the beginning of his life, and learned how to pray and praise God, and once he tasted the sweetness of praise he was no longer able to leave it, so prayer and praise became his life, until he said, "But I give myself unto prayer" (Ps 109:4).
18- Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come.

David repeats his request for God's presence with him in the time of old age and grey hair, not only to help him in the weakness of old age, as mentioned in (v. 9), but also that he may remain strong in his faith and his love for God, so that he can serve and preach to those around him, that is, tell them about the mighty God, who is able to support His children with His strong arm, and teach every child and youth who has come into the world how to live with God. In this David shows his concern for being discipled at the hand of God to the end of his life, and also his concern for discipling all those around him so that they may know God.
19- Thy righteousness also, O God, is very high, who hast done great things: O God, who is like unto thee!

1- David describes the righteousness of God as being high and exceedingly lofty; it is above all the gods, because they are demons, which the pagans think to be gods; He does great things with His children, and there is none like Him. For if the first Adam fell when he wanted to become, like God, a knower of good and evil, David, who is a symbol of Christ, the second Adam, declares that there is none like God.
2- The righteousness of God is His love and His faithfulness in caring for His children, from Adam until today, and it is also His Incarnation and His giving of Himself for the redemption of mankind.
20- Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.

1- The writer of the Psalm here prophesies about the children of Israel in the land of Egypt, who endured bitter slavery and many labors, but God gave them life anew by their crossing of the Red Sea and their going up to the wilderness of Sinai, and their deliverance from Pharaoh and his army who were drowned.

2- This verse is also a prophecy about the captivity that the people of Israel suffered, but God revived them anew by bringing them back from the captivity and taking them up to Jerusalem to build the Temple.

3- This verse likewise prophesies about Christ in His sufferings and crucifixion, but He returned to life by His Resurrection and ascended into the heavens. It also applies to every person who repents and suffers the pains of leaving sin, and then returns to life, and so ascends and rises above every sin and evil desire.
21- Thou shalt increase my greatness, and comfort me on every side.

1- David affirms the work of God with His children, whose example is David himself, for God gives him many blessings, so he becomes very great and his heart is comforted by the work of His Holy Spirit in him, to compensate him for all that he endured of afflictions. Thus after David endured the pursuits of Saul, then Absalom, God returned and magnified him, and he triumphed over all his enemies around him.

2- This also is what happens with every believer in Christ, for after he was condemned to death he enjoys the redemption of Christ, and regains his greatness as a man, and the Holy Spirit dwells in him to comfort him all his days.
22- I will also praise thee with the psaltery, even thy truth, O my God: unto thee will I sing with the harp, O thou Holy One of Israel.

23- My lips shall greatly rejoice when I sing unto thee; and my soul, which thou hast redeemed. 24- My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness all the day long: for they are confounded, for they are brought unto shame, that seek my hurt.

1- David ends the Psalm with the praise of God, using musical instruments such as the psaltery and the harp. This is what God deserves from the man whom He created, for all His righteousness and holiness, indeed His gifts and His support of His children and their deliverance from their enemies, so that the enemies receive shame and disgrace. And the children of God lift up not only their tongues and their lips, but their souls as well, in praise and thanksgiving to God.

2- If thanksgiving to God was a duty in the Old Testament for all His great works with His children, how much more does He deserve thanks and glorification in the New Testament, for His redemption, which saved them from Satan and gave them life with Him, and then the Kingdom of Heaven.
How great is the praise of God! It is not only a duty toward Him, but it also gladdens our hearts, so that we live in constant joy and attachment to eternal life.
The Kingdom of God, for Solomon: "Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: a- King Solomon, and he may have had in mind the instructions of his father David to him when he made him king.
b- There is another opinion that its writer is the prophet David, and that he addressed it to Solomon his son when he made him king, that he might be a true king as God wants.
2- This Psalm tells us about the kingdom of God, its characteristics and its blessings, and it is an example and model for all states and kingdoms in the world throughout the generations.
3- This Psalm speaks clearly about Christ, for it is a Messianic Psalm, and because Solomon is a symbol of Christ, there are verses that cannot apply except to Christ (vv. 8, 11, 17).
4- This Psalm is liturgical, and it was recited in the Church anciently on the feasts of the Nativity and the Baptism.

5- With the end of this Psalm the second book of the Psalms ends, as the Jews divided it, which includes (Ps 42-72). Therefore the reader notices that the last verses of this Psalm end with the word Amen, then Amen, Alleluia. Then after the end of this Psalm it adds and says, "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended", because the writer of most of the Psalms in this part is the prophet David, like the rest of the five books of the Psalms. It does not mean that David did not write the following books, but it only means the end of the second book.
6- There is a resemblance between this Psalm and the last part of the Book of Exodus (Ex 25-40), where it tells us of God's kingship over His people through the Tabernacle of Meeting.
There is also a resemblance between this Psalm and the Book of Isaiah (Isa 11:1-5; 60-62).
7- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 1- Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son.

1- The writer of the Psalm, who is Solomon, or David, asks for the king and the king's son at the same time, and this applies to Solomon, and not to David or Saul who preceded him. And he asks for him two things:

a- "Thy judgments", that is, wisdom, because of Solomon's young age, and God praised this request because he did not ask for riches, or power over enemies, but asked for something that benefits him and his people spiritually and administratively.
b- "Thy righteousness", and what is meant by righteousness is justice and goodness, that he may be saved and live with God, and be an example to his people.
2- This verse also applies to Christ, who is the king's son, because He is of the offspring of David. For Christ is the hypostasis of Wisdom, and in Him is the perfection of justice.

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 2- He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment.

1- From this verse the writer of the Psalm begins to list the characteristics of the king, meaning King Solomon, or Christ. The first two characteristics are justice and truth, for he uses them in his rule over his people. This people is the Jews, who are characterized by humility before God, and therefore he calls them the poor, that is, the poor in spirit.

2- The king judges his people, who are the Jews, and also the poor, and these may be meant to be the Gentiles, that is, he rules the Jews and the Gentiles with justice and truth. This is a prophecy about Christ, in whom the Gentiles believe, so He judges and rules the whole world, that is, all people who have believed in Him, whether from the Jews or the Gentiles.

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 3- The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness.

1- The third and fourth characteristics are peace and righteousness. By the mountains that bring peace are meant the spiritually great, whose lives are lofty like high mountains. These are full of peace, and at the same time an example to the rest of the people. As for the little hills, they are also the spiritual people who are lower in rank than the mountains. These are full of righteousness and goodness, and they too are an example to others. The meaning of this is that the reign of Solomon was a reign of peace, and gave the spiritual people an opportunity to live with God and to be elevated in their lives.

2- This verse also applies to Christ, who is the God of peace, and gave peace to His disciples and His people, and likewise is the Righteous and Holy One, who said, "Which of you convinceth me of sin?"
3- The mountains also symbolize the angels and the saints in heaven, who are the Church Triumphant, while the little hills symbolize the saints living on earth, that is, the Church Militant.

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 4- He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor.

1- The fifth characteristic of the king is that he is a judge, so he gives justice to the wronged and punishes the oppressor. So he saves the poor and the needy, that is, the weak and the helpless, and at the same time he punishes the oppressor by breaking him in pieces, that is, destroying his power and his domination over the poor.

2- The poor and the needy are the humble; these Christ saves by His blood on the Cross, while the oppressor, who is Satan, He breaks in pieces by binding him, and after this, on the Day of Judgment, He casts him into eternal torment.

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 5- They shall fear thee as long as the sun and moon endure, throughout all generations.

1- The sixth characteristic of the king is fear, that is, his people fear him, revere him and respect him. Solomon had great awe because of his power and his justice and his keen intelligence. He managed the country in the best way, and no one could stand before him; even his opponents fled, or were bound and unable to overcome him. And what is meant by the sun and the moon is day and night, that is, all through the night.

2- This verse applies to Christ more than to Solomon, for He is the Sun of Righteousness rising upon His Church, which is the moon, and the fear of Him is in the hearts of all because of His authority, for He spoke with authority and not as the scribes and Pharisees (Mt 7:29). In addition, the fear of Him and His kingdom endure throughout all generations, that is, forever, as the angel declared to the Virgin Lady (Lk 1:32).

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 6- He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth.
Fleeces (jazaz): plural of fleece (jazza), which is a piece of wool taken from sheep.
Showers (ghuyuth): plural of ghayth, which is rain.
Watering (dharifa): that which flows and runs.

1- The seventh characteristic of the king is spiritual consolation. Solomon was successful in managing his country, and he had authority, so the surrounding nations feared him, and not only his people but also his neighbors cooperated with him. So his country became rich, so much so that the Holy Bible declared that gold and silver were like stones in Jerusalem (2 Chr 1:15). So he poured out good upon the fleece, that is, Jerusalem, and also upon the earth, which is all the land of the children of Israel.

2- By the redemption of Christ He gave salvation to everyone who believes in Him from the whole world, so He poured out the blessings of salvation by the Holy Spirit upon the fleece, who are the Jews who became Christians, and upon the earth, which is the Gentiles who believed in Him.

3- The fleece is the Virgin who received the glad tidings of the divine conception for the salvation of the world, and the earth is the whole world which received the good news of salvation by means of the showers, who are the Apostles, the priests and the servants.

entries.section: (1) Characteristics of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 7- In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth.
Endureth (yadmahill): passes away.

1- The eighth characteristic of the king is that he is the giver of joy; because the days of Solomon were peace, they gave the righteous an opportunity to grow spiritually, so they enjoyed fellowship with God, and remained occupied with God, worshiping Him in His Temple and clinging to Him until the moon passed away, which is Solomon, that is, until the end of Solomon's life.

2- And when we apply this verse to Christ, it means that the righteous grow strongly in the New Testament because of the blessings of salvation which they receive through Christ, and they rejoice, indeed they shine upon others and are a light for the world, as Christ commanded them, and the righteous remain shining throughout the life of the Church on earth, which is symbolized by the moon.

Enjoy the characteristics of the kingdom of God in His Church, and care about attending the Church and receiving her sacraments, so that you live with the heavenly saints while you are on earth, and rejoice at all times in Christ who dwells in you.

entries.section: (2) The extent of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 8- He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.

1- The ninth characteristic of the king is that he has great authority. God granted Solomon to be the greatest of the kings of his age, and his kingdom extended from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth, that is, his kingdom was very wide, for the kingdom of the children of Israel reached its widest extent in the days of David and Solomon. Perhaps what is meant by from sea to sea is from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Red Sea in the south, and perhaps what is meant by the river is the river Euphrates, and to the ends of the earth, that is, a vast extent of Solomon's kingdom because God blessed him.
2- And if we apply this verse to Christ, what is meant is that He is the King of kings who reigned over the whole earth; for many from the different peoples of the earth believed in Him (Acts 4:4).

entries.section: (2) The extent of the kingdom of God

paragraphs.text: 9- They that dwell in the wilderness shall bow before him; and his enemies shall lick the dust. 10- The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. 11- Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him. Bow (tajthu): kneel and prostrate. Tarshish: an important commercial city in the south of Spain, and it is the last famous commercial center in the ancient world, since it lies in the far west of the world.
Sheba and Seba: countries lying in the south of the Arabian peninsula.

1- King Solomon became so great that the nations around him submitted to him, and tried to appease him by presenting him with gifts; for he was strong, and rich by the blessing of God, so that the kings feared him. And the queen of Sheba came with many gifts, and marveled when she saw his great glory, while those who tried to stand against him were unable to resist him, and submitted to him, as the verse (v. 9) expresses it, that they lick the dust, that is, his authority extended over the whole earth by the submission of the kings to him.

2- This verse clearly applies to Christ, who is the King of kings, and the kings of the earth and its rulers submitted to Him, such as the Magi, who came from the East and worshiped Him and presented gifts, and many of the rulers and kings of the earth submitted to Him by faith.

If you hold fast to God's commandments, He gives you awe in the eyes of those around you, and they see God in you and so submit to you, that is, they respect you and learn from you without your knowing it, so do not give up your great position by submitting to the lusts of the world, and be always a light to the world.
12- For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper.

1- The writer of the Psalm shows the characteristics of the loving king, and makes clear his love for his people through many characteristics, the first of which is the deliverer. He cares for the poor and for their cries to him, so he provides for them and delivers them from all the effects of poverty, such as the feeling of deprivation. And he protects them from falling into theft, murmuring and rebellion, and so gives them peace.
2- And the second characteristic of the king is that he is the helper of the weak and the poor, so he supports them in all their spiritual, psychological and bodily needs.

These are the characteristics of King Solomon to a great extent, but their perfection appears in Christ the King of kings, who cared for and supported everyone in need, especially those who have no one, like the sick man at the pool of Bethesda (Jn 5:1-15).
13- He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the needy.

1- The third characteristic of the loving king is compassion for the poor and the needy. His heart is full of tenderness, and he not only helps them, but is gentle with them and patient with them, as a mother bends over her nursing child, and in this he encourages them and gladdens their hearts.

2- The fourth characteristic of the loving king is that he is the savior, so he saves the poor from poverty, and satisfies them, and also from its effects in their lives, so that they live reassured, with strong spirits, and thankful to God.
14- He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight.

1- The fifth characteristic of the loving king is that he is the Redeemer, who redeems his people from injustice and the greed of others toward them, who snatch away their small possessions. This is because the king is just, strong and able to protect his weak people. And this characteristic is perfected in Christ, who redeemed His people by His death for them on the Cross and by giving them new life in Him, and delivered them from the oppressor, who is Satan.

2- The sixth characteristic of the loving king is that he honors those who endured hardships and afflictions, and died unjustly, so he cares for their bodies and their tombs, and shows their righteousness and goodness. And the greatness of this characteristic appears in Christ, who honors the bodies of His saints, making some of them not decay, and encourages His people to hold their feasts and hymns of praise, and to name His churches after their names.

I wish you would show your love for those around you, especially the needy, the weak and the helpless, and not be content with helping them, for your smile and your kind words are what they need most. And those in need of the kind word may be the people of your own household, so do not forget them.
15- And he shall live, and to him shall be given of the gold of Sheba: prayer also shall be made for him continually; and daily shall he be praised.
1- Here he speaks of God's blessings to the king, so He grants him to live and have life, and this is a greeting offered to the king even until now: "Long live the king."

2- And God enriches the king, so the people present to him precious offerings, such as the pure gold taken from the land of Sheba. Solomon became very rich, and became the richest of the kings of his age. And gold symbolizes heavenly life, that is, the people presented to him not only material gifts, but their hearts and their lives which live by God's commandments, and so became exalted.

3- Likewise the people loved King Solomon, so they prayed for him continually because of his great characteristics mentioned above, and this gladdens the heart of God, that the king loves his people, and the people love the king, and pray for him.
4- God gives the king a constant blessing all his life, so that everything he does prospers. Solomon's trade and works and his relations with the surrounding nations prospered.

5- When we apply this verse to Christ we find that He is the One who lives forever, and the Magi presented gifts to Him: gold, frankincense and myrrh. And the Father showed His love and His blessing to the Son, so that those who believe in Christ pray in His name continually, and bless Him.
16- There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon: and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth.
Handful (hufna): the fullness of the palm.
Corn (burr): grains of wheat.

1- The writer of the Psalm shows God's blessing with His children, for they are like a handful of grains of wheat cast on the mountains, which grow and yield ears even on the tops of the mountains where it is hard to farm because of the strength of the wind, and the harvest is plentiful like the trees of Lebanon filled with fruit, swaying with the winds, and the fruits are many in the city and in the field and everywhere, that is, God's blessing includes all the possessions of His children, who labored to prepare them, and everything is blessed by God.

2- This verse applies to the Church, which is the grain of wheat, or the grain of mustard seed, which grew and became a great tree (Mt 13:32), and it came to have fruits everywhere, in the city and on the mountain by the grace of God, although it began small, but Christianity spread throughout the whole world in the first century.
17- His name shall endure for ever: his name shall be continued as long as the sun: and men shall be blessed in him: all nations shall call him blessed.

1- God's blessing to the king also appears in that his name remains forever, that is, the immortality of Solomon's soul forever in the Kingdom, because of his goodness. And also the news of his greatness spreads throughout the whole earth in his days, that is, wherever the sun rises and shines. In addition to this, King Solomon becomes a cause of blessing to everyone who deals with him. And in the end everyone who knows him blesses him, and magnifies him, and glorifies him.

2- This verse clearly applies to Christ, whose name from eternity to eternity is great, and extends over the whole earth, and He is the source of blessing for the whole world. And in the end everyone blesses Him and glorifies Him.
. 18- Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things.

At the end of the Psalm he declares that God deserves that we glorify Him, for He is blessed because of the great works He has done, whether in the creation of man, or with all mankind, or with His people the children of Israel. He is the only God, worthy of blessing, and not the gods of the pagan nations, which are demons.
. 19- And blessed be his glorious name for ever: and let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen. The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended.

1- He closes the Psalm by giving glory to God forever, that is, to eternity, for He is glorified by His children on earth, and also by the heavenly ones, indeed the writer of the Psalm hopes that the earth will be filled with His glory, so that hearts and tongues are lifted up everywhere glorifying God. And this was indeed accomplished at the faith in Christ, for many of the Gentiles returned to God who created them, and glorified His holy name by their lives and by their lips.

2- Many of the Fathers and commentators see that the last two verses of this Psalm (vv. 18, 19) are a glorification of God placed at the end of the second book of the Psalms according to the Jewish division, which is from (Ps 42) to (Ps 72), that is, these two verses are not part of Psalm 72, but a general conclusion of the second book.

3- We see that (v. 19) ends with the word Amen, then Amen, as the rest of the books of the Psalms (the first, the third and the fourth) are concluded; as for the fifth, it is not written thus in it, because of the lack of need for it, since it is clear that it is the end of the whole Book of Psalms.

The blessing of the Lord is wonderful for His children, for it makes you need nothing of all that is in the world; it is enough for God to be with you, and you find that the little you have satisfies you and gladdens you, and if you need much He gives you. So hold fast to His commandments, and if you sin return quickly by repentance, and you will keep the blessing with you always.
God's dealings with the wicked and the righteous: "Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart" (v. 1). Introduction:

1- a- Its writer is Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David, and he is of the tribe of Levi, and he was assisted by two of the chiefs of the singers, Heman the Ezrahite and Ethan (who is also called Jeduthun) the Ezrahite (1 Chr 15:17). Asaph led the praise before the Ark of the Covenant in Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:4, 5, 7, 37), while Heman and Ethan led the praise before the Tabernacle at Gibeon (1 Chr 16:41).
b- There is an opinion that the writer of this Psalm is David, and he gave it to Asaph to sing. And Asaph was called the king's seer (1 Chr 25:5), (2 Chr 29:30, 35:15).

2- When was it written? In the days of the prophet David, when Asaph was exposed to a personal trial in which he nearly fell into sin, but God rescued him from it, so his faith in God was established. This shows Asaph's courage in mentioning this matter about himself, like David his teacher who mentioned his fall into sin and his repentance.
3- This Psalm may be a prophecy about a great trial that befell the people of God, namely the captivity, and then the return from it.
4- Asaph wrote twelve Psalms (Ps 5, Ps 73-Ps 83).
5- This Psalm resembles Psalm 37 and Psalm 49 in speaking of the success of the wicked and the afflictions that meet the righteous, just as Job and Jeremiah were exposed to the same subject.
6- The Psalm tells us of three important matters:
a- The success of the wicked is temporary.
b- Eternal destruction awaits the wicked.
c- The joy of the righteous in fellowship with God.
7- With this Psalm begins the third book of the books of the Psalms according to the Jewish division, which ends with Psalm 89.
8- Asaph cares about worship of the heart offered to God, and not outward worship, limited to offering sacrifices, and therefore he mentions the word heart six times in this Psalm.
9- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
1- Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart.
Imma: a conditional particle of emphasis, in his saying "imma" (truly).

1- The writer of the Psalm declares and affirms that God is good, that is, there is no evil in Him. And this goodness of His appears to Israel, that is, His people who believe in Him and hold fast to His commandments. And Israel in the Old Testament is a symbol of the new Israel, that is, the Church.

2- This goodness also appears to the pure in heart, who are able to see God by their purity, and love Him, and obey His commandments, so His goodness appears to them, and they accept from Him all His dealings, even trials for their purification. But the impure, that is, those far from God, do not see His goodness because of their rejection of God, although God is good to all.
2- But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.
Gone (tazill): fall.
Slipped (zaliqat): slid.
The writer of the Psalm confesses that he almost fell into sin, and slid down into it, and lost his spiritual balance. And this shows the following:
1- His concern for repentance and confession, so much so that he confessed openly before everyone who reads the Psalm.

2- His courage and his holding fast to the faith, for he saw that exposing Satan by declaring his sin enables him to resist sin by the power of God, and to reject the thoughts that almost made him fall into an evil deed. As for the heretics, they did not resist their thoughts, so they fell into heresies, and likewise the atheists.

3- The necessity of being careful in all our steps lest we fall suddenly into one of the snares of the devil. It may begin with a slip, that is, a small fall, or a sudden great one, and it may be the beginning of sliding and sinking into a great sin, and a pit from which it is hard to rise.
3- For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

The writer of the Psalm makes clear that he fell into the sin of envy, and probably after this the sin of murmuring, when he saw that the wicked enjoy outward peace, and probably also success in their work and their lives, although he knows that God blesses His righteous children. And here he forgot that they have no inner peace; because sin creates disturbance in the soul. Many men of God have wondered at the success of the wicked, like the writer of this Psalm, and among them Job and Jeremiah (Job 21:7; Jer 12:1).
4- For there are no pangs in their death, and their body is fat. 5- They are not in the toil of men, neither are they plagued like other men.
The writer of the Psalm adds that the wicked not only enjoy outward peace, but also:
1- They are not exposed to hard afflictions at their death, and this may be the result of their riches, and their use of money to treat their illnesses and their problems.
2- Their health is good, as he expresses this by saying that their bodies are fat, and not lean like the poor.

3- They are not exposed to the troubles of poverty, sickness and ignorance, for they learn, and know what benefits them in their business, so their riches increase, and the trials that meet them are few.

6- Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them as a garment. 7- Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish. 8- They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. 9- They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.

1- The writer of the Psalm shows the secret of the wickedness of the wicked, which is pride, which made them mock their righteous brothers, who may be poorer than they, or less healthy, and they spoke against them arrogantly, exalting themselves over them as if they had the authority of heaven, judging the people of earth, likening themselves to the angels and the inhabitants of heaven, although they are rejected by God because of their wickedness.

2- As a result of the pride of the wicked they also fell into the sin of injustice, for they wronged those around them, whether by mockery and harsh words, or by coveting the possessions of others, because the wicked are selfish, and were not ashamed of their sins, but put them on like a garment, so they persisted in their wickedness.

3- Since they were immersed in greed and lusts, the writer of the Psalm depicts their rush to eat and the desire of their bellies by the fullness and stuffing of their bodies until their eyes bulged outward. This affected their sight, and at the same time their insight grew weak, so they lost discernment because of their distance from God, and persisted in being occupied with material things beyond all imagination, for they became slaves of lusts.
10- Therefore his people return hither: and waters of a full cup are wrung out to them.

When the people of God look at the success of the wicked, and come hither, that is, to this reality, which is this success, they grow weary and remain in the suffering of pains, and they drink them to the end, as a man drinks the waters of a full cup that fills his glass. And God allows this for the benefit of His children, and their approval, so they receive great blessings, and He helps them at the right time and supports them, and they overcome the thoughts of doubt and envy at the success of the wicked. This is as God allowed His people to drink the cup of captivity for long years until they repented and returned to God, and He gathered them and brought them back to their land, and they returned to worshiping Him in His Temple.
11- And they say, How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?

1- The wicked said that God knows nothing about what we do on earth, and this in turn made them regard sin as permitted, for no one will punish them; because God does not see them. This is the mistaken and foolish notion into which the wicked fell.

2- There is another opinion on this verse, which is that when the righteous were exposed to sufferings, and their time and their suffering grew long, they said, Where is the God whom we sought? For He did not rescue us and restore to us our rights; so from the excess of their suffering they said that God does not know nor understand, for how can God's tenderness and fatherhood agree with our suffering and our pains? How can He neglect us and leave us? Yet God left them to suffer for a time for their benefit.
12- Behold, these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase in riches.

The writer of the Psalm concludes this part by saying that the summary is the ease of the wicked in material respects, and their increase in gathering money by lawful and unlawful ways, so their success and their ease appear outwardly, although they suffer inwardly, and eternal torment awaits them, especially since they have been enslaved in their thinking, so their consciences no longer prick them, and they persist every day in their wickedness.

Remember always that God is before you and sees hidden things, and knows your thoughts and the feelings of your heart, and therefore do not accept evil lest you anger Him, and if you fall, rise quickly, and if an evil thought fights you, ask for His help, and then you will receive inner peace and enjoy true happiness in fellowship with God.
13- Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency. 14- For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning.

I have cleansed my heart: I purified it and made it good and clean. When the writer of the Psalm saw the success of the wicked and the pains of the righteous, he said to himself, I have labored much in purifying my heart and cleansing the works of my hands; because the result of it is sorrows, and on the contrary those who walked in evil have prospered, especially as he noticed that the pains do not end all the day, that is, all his life, since divine chastenings and daily sorrows meet him.
15- If I say, I will speak thus; behold, I should offend against the generation of thy children.

The writer of the Psalm also felt that if he declared his murmuring and his doubt about the rightness of his conduct in righteousness and uprightness, he would stumble by this both himself and his sons if they were weak in faith. So that he would not make them stumble he kept silent, and kept his distress inside him, which increased his pains.
16- When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me;

Finally the writer of the Psalm discovered that discussing all these thoughts mentioned above is wearying and futile, and consequently there is no need to continue in these thoughts. Thus human wisdom declares its inability to understand God's purposes, and man returns to God with prayer and praise so that He may give him rest and make him understand what he is able to accept from the hand of God.

17- Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. 18- Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. 19- How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors. 20- As a dream when one awaketh; so, O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image.
The sanctuary of God: the Temple of God, or heaven.
Destruction (buwar): ruin and devastation.
In a moment (baghta): suddenly.
Terrors (dawahi): plural of dahiya, which is calamity.

1- When the writer entered the sanctuary of God, that is, returned to God by prayer before the Ark of the Covenant, or in the Temple of Solomon, and asked for God's help, God made him attentive and guided him to see that the end of the wicked is destruction, because they walked the way of lusts, and slid down immersed in them, so they affected their lives, and brought upon them troubles and calamities and ruin, such as the lust for women, or wine, or any evil lusts that lead a man to many troubles while he is on earth. Indeed, calamities, such as diseases and problems, come upon the wicked suddenly, when they are unaware or on guard against them; because they are immersed in their lusts, so the terrors strike them.

2- The sanctuary of God also means heaven, that is, when the writer of the Psalm reached heaven and learned of the glories of the Kingdom awaiting him, he rejoiced greatly, but he discovered that the conduct of the wicked led them to destruction and eternal torment. And death took hold of them suddenly, so while they were immersed in the lusts of the world they fell and died, and their riches or their strength did not benefit them. And it appeared clearly that the immersion of the wicked in lusts, and their dazzling life in all the material things they acquired, ended suddenly as if it were a dream, and they awoke from it and found themselves in Hades and destruction. Thus God mocked and despised the reliance of the wicked on lusts and material things, and they received the recompense of their evils, which is eternal destruction; for he who dreams of something great discovers when he awakes that it was merely a dream, and returns to his miserable reality. This is the end of the wicked.

Be faithful in holding fast to God's commandments and your upright principles, however much the wicked around you stray from the truth, and even mock you and try to draw you away from righteousness; do not let them, and persevere in your striving, for your crown in eternal glory awaits you.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

paragraphs.text: 21- Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins. 22- So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.
Was grieved (tamarmara): tasted bitterness and suffered greatly. I was pricked in my reins: I was pained as by a goad struck into my kidneys.

When the writer of the Psalm murmured against God, as appeared in the preceding verses of this Psalm, his heart was grieved like one who drank bitterness, and he was pained like one pricked in his reins, so he was in great pain, and therefore he decided in the end to keep away from all murmuring, and to rely completely on God, declaring his ignorance before the wisdom of God, and his complete submission to Him, and leaving Him to lead his life according to His divine will, as a beast is led behind the one who drives it, because the beast does not care about the hardships of the road or its straightness, for its leader is the one responsible; that is, man submits to God, and relies on Him, and leaves Him to arrange his life for him, and does not weary himself with thoughts of murmuring.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

paragraphs.text: 23- Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand. 24- Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory.

1- When the writer of the Psalm surrendered and relied on God, and rejected all the thoughts of doubt that attacked him because of the success of the wicked and the distress of the righteous, he enjoyed God's leadership, for He guided him to the right way by His counsel. And God's counsel is His commandments and His word in the Holy Bible, and indeed He held him by his right hand, that is, strengthened his works; because the hand symbolizes work, and He supported him with His divine power; because the right hand symbolizes strength. Thus the writer of the Psalm enjoyed fellowship with God, and experienced His great work in him.

2- God brought the writer of the Psalm to great glory, by which he means the heavenly glory that awaits him after the striving of this life, or the rest he enjoyed after God brought him out of his trial, so he received the blessings of endurance.

3- These two verses may be a prophecy about the affliction of the captivity, during which the people returned to God with repentance and faith, so God held them and led them to their land, and they enjoyed the building of the Temple, and the glory of worshiping God in His Temple.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

paragraphs.text: 25- Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.

Since the writer of the Psalm experienced fellowship with God, and enjoyed Him, he felt that he needed nothing on earth except the Lord, and then in heaven he desires nothing but to see God and enjoy Him; for God has become his chief occupation, the delight of his heart, and his desires forever, and in this he declares his faith and his longings for the heavenly Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

paragraphs.text: 26- My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.

1- The writer of the Psalm declares that if his flesh and heart fail, that is, he grows weak in body and soul under the pressure of the trials he passed through, he believes that his support is God his rock, and his portion, that is, that God is his refuge in whom he settles, and is his satisfaction who compensates him for all that he lost in the world, and therefore he does not fear trials, but they are his way to know God his rock and his portion, and in this he grows spiritually and enjoys fellowship with God.

2- The writer of the Psalm also feels that in order to experience God and know Him, and for God to become his life and his portion, he must give up the material things of the world, and so become stripped and humble until he almost perishes, and then he knows God. And the beautiful thing is that he will enjoy God for ever, that is, he longs for a permanent existence in eternity.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

paragraphs.text: 27- For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that go a whoring from thee.

The writer of the Psalm declares at its end that those far from God, that is, the wicked, however much they succeed in the world, or delight in the lusts of fornication and every evil lust, and reject God, which is spiritual fornication, nothing awaits them but annihilation and destruction in eternal torment, that is, they are deprived of all rest and of seeing God as a result of their evils.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

paragraphs.text: 28- But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord God, that I may declare all thy works.

1- And he decides in conclusion that he will draw near to God, keeping away from every sin, and that he is not disturbed by the success of the wicked, so he enjoys fellowship with God on earth, and then in heaven.

2- The second decision is his feeling of the necessity of preaching to others who are far from God, so that they may believe in Him, and love Him, and live for Him, and not be drawn to evil. He does all this preaching while he is in the embrace of God his refuge, that is, living with God, so by His power he is able to preach to all those around him to keep away from sin and return to God.

When you see the success of the wicked, pray for them that they may awake from their heedlessness, and thank God who made known to you your way, so your holding fast to His commandments will increase, and you will even strengthen your brothers and establish their faith, so that they live with God always. A prayer that God not reject His people: a poem of Asaph, "O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever?" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: a- Asaph, who is the leader of the singers, that is, all the choirs in the days of David (1 Chr 16:5).
b- David, and he gave it to Asaph to sing.
2- When was it written? In the days of David, but it is a prophecy about:
a- The destruction and burning of the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar in the days of the Babylonian captivity.
b- Or the days of King Antiochus (the Greek), when he destroyed and plundered the Temple in the time of the Maccabees (1 Macc 1:20-28).
c- Or the destruction of the Temple by Titus the Roman commander in the year 70 AD.

3- This Psalm is suitable for every person who meets a great affliction, and during it may feel that God is late in intervening to solve the problem. And it is suitable for the whole Church when a great affliction meets her.

4- There is a resemblance between this Psalm and Psalm 79, and both are by one writer, Asaph, as their titles mention. And they speak of the same subject, which is the affliction that befalls the children of God.

5- This Psalm was written in the past tense to affirm the certainty of the occurrence of this prophecy, which was fulfilled literally when the enemy defiled the Temple by the entry of the Gentiles into the Temple of God, whether in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, or Antiochus, or the Romans.
6- This Psalm is a symbol of Satan's destruction of man by making him fall into sin, but by the redemption of Christ He brought him back to life with Him.

7- This Psalm is considered a lament for the Church, or the people of God, or the human soul, which is affected by God's separation from it; it does not doubt Him, but with sorrow it shows how weary it is at losing God.
8- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 1- O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?

1- The writer of the Psalm reproaches God, because He allowed a severe affliction for His people, and by this it appears that He has rejected His people, and when the trial grew long the writer said, with sorrow, that he feels the affliction continuing and extending as if it were for ever. And God does not reject His people except because of their sins, for He allows the affliction to chasten them so that they repent, and if they repent He forgives them and lifts the affliction from them.

2- And the writer asks with sorrow, as if saying to God, Why do You show Your anger against Your people, who are the sheep You shepherd? And the anger of God is a consuming fire from which black smoke comes out and covers the people of God, as a warning to them so that they repent, otherwise the fire will consume them and they will perish. But the beautiful thing is that he says "the sheep of thy pasture", that is, You are the One responsible for us, confident of the love of God which does not neglect His children.

entries.section: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 2- Remember thy congregation, which thou hast purchased of old; the rod of thine inheritance, which thou hast redeemed; this mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt.
In his need the writer of the Psalm did not demand his needs from God, but reminded Him of His love for His people, and pointed to important matters in God's relationship with His people:
1- The people of God are His congregation belonging to Him, and not to another.
2- God is the One who purchased His people, and called His name upon them.
3- God's relationship with His people is very old, from the days of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

4- God redeemed His people when He brought them out of the land of Egypt, for He killed the firstborn of Egypt, but when He looked at the blood smeared on the doors, the angel passed over, and did not kill the firstborn of Israel, that is, He redeemed them by the blood of the lamb, which is a reference to the blood of Christ.

5- Israel comprises twelve tribes, which the writer gathers here by saying "the rod of thine inheritance", that is, they are all God's inheritance on earth, since they are the only people who believed in God at that time.

6- God Himself dwelt in the midst of His people in Jerusalem, that is, Zion, and blessed this people. By all these remembrances the writer moves the heart of God to compassion on His people, to deliver them from the trials they are passing through.

entries.section: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 3- Lift up thy feet unto the perpetual desolations; even all that the enemy hath done wickedly in the sanctuary.
Lift up thy feet: hasten.

1- The writer of the Psalm calls upon God to intervene quickly for the sake of His Temple which has been destroyed, and because of the horror of the destruction he describes it as perpetual desolations, that is, that it was severely ruined, that is, that it will not be rebuilt for ever, but of course God is able to rebuild it. And he describes what the enemies did as destruction of the whole, that is, a total destruction, by his saying "all that the enemy hath done wickedly", so the need for God's intervention is great. All this is a prophecy about the destruction of the Temple, as we mentioned in the introduction, in the days of Babylon, or the Greeks, or the Romans.

2- The enemy is Satan who destroys the human soul, and therefore the Psalm calls upon God to hasten to the help of man, and this was accomplished in the fullness of time by the Incarnation of Christ, to restore man as a temple of the Holy Spirit after Satan had destroyed him.

entries.section: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked
