paragraphs.text: 4- Thine enemies roar in the midst of thy congregations; they set up their ensigns for signs. 5- A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees. 6- But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers. Thy congregations (ma'hadak): thy dwelling, that is, the Tabernacle of Meeting. Hammers (ma'awil): plural of mi'wal, a strong iron tool with which rock is broken, or the ground is dug, or things are smashed.

1- The writer of the Psalm likens the voices of the enemies who will attack the Temple to lions, and their voices are the roaring of lions, that is, their voices are loud, proclaiming their victory over Your people, as if they had done great signs; because they forgot that Almighty God is long-suffering, and although He chastens His people by the destruction of the Temple, He will take vengeance on the enemies, and will rebuild the Temple.

2- He describes their cruelty in smashing and destroying the Temple as if they carried axes and cut down thick trees; because they broke all the carved woodwork that adorned the Temple (2 Kgs 25:8-17; Jer 52:12-23).

entries.section: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 7- They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground. 8- They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.

The synagogues of God (ma'ahid): the Jewish synagogues which the Jews established from the second century before Christ in the various countries to read the Holy Scriptures in them and explain them and pray. They continued until the days of Christ, and in the apostolic age. As for the sacrifices, they were offered only in the Temple in Jerusalem.

1- The enemies entered the Temple of God, and defiled it with their feet; because it is not permitted for pagans to enter the Temple, and their wicked hand stretched out to burn the Temple with fire, and they tried to kill the Jews. This is what happened at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar at the Babylonian captivity in 587 BC, and it was repeated at the hand of Antiochus the Great in the second century before Christ, who burned the doors of the Temple, while in 70 AD Titus the Roman destroyed the Temple completely.

2- The hand of the enemies stretched out to destroy the Jewish synagogues spread throughout the whole earth. All this shows the cruelty of the enemies toward the people of God, and God kept silent over all they did; because He intended to chasten His people so that they would repent.

entries.section: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 9- We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long.

1- The Jews became in the darkness of sin and went far from God, and the chastenings mentioned in the previous verses came upon them, besides that they did not see the signs of God, nor prophets declaring the voice of God to them, although there were prophets and signs, but the Jews did not understand them, and did not obey the prophets, but considered them wicked, and rose against them and killed them, like Isaiah whom they sawed asunder, and Jeremiah whom they stoned, and Ezekiel whom they killed.

2- This verse may be a prophecy about what would happen after the crucifixion of Christ and His redemption, for from that time until now the Jews have seen no signs, nor prophets. And they are still waiting for the Messiah, and do not know when; because they rejected the awaited Messiah when He became incarnate and died to redeem them.

If you see afflictions passing over you, examine yourself instead of murmuring or despairing, for your sins may be the cause, and hasten to repentance and you will receive God's blessings and mercies; because He loves you.
10- O God, how long shall the adversary reproach? shall the enemy blaspheme thy name for ever? 11- Why withdrawest thou thy hand, even thy right hand? pluck it out of thy bosom.

1- The writer of the Psalm asks God, and says to Him, Do You not see the adversaries, and the enemies insulting Your name, and reproaching us, because we are Your people! Why do You keep silent, and prolong Your longsuffering? And how long will You hide Your hand and Your right hand, or Your power? For I believe that You are able to destroy all the power of the enemies. And You are jealous and do not accept this reproach and this insult. And it is clear that the writer of the Psalm is appealing for God's mercies, that He may have compassion on His people, and intervene, and accept their repentance, and rescue them.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about the burning of the Temple and the Babylonian captivity, or the assault of Antiochus, or the Jews' resistance to Christ. So the writer of the Psalm asks God to rebuild His Temple, and declare the truth, and the only Son be glorified as happened in the Resurrection.
3- Every human soul that suffers from the wars of the devil calls upon God with these two verses, that He may intervene and rescue it, and lift it up from its weaknesses.
12- For God is my King of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.

1- The writer of the Psalm relies on his relationship with God that He is his King all his life, so he always trusts in Him, and He is the One who protects him and supports him, and not only in his life, but also from of old with his fathers and forefathers; for God has shepherded His people from the days of the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and He alone is able to save him and his people from the hard afflictions they are passing through. So he speaks with God with boldness that He may have mercy on him, and rescue him as He did from of old with His people, such as bringing them out of Egypt by the ten plagues, then dividing the Red Sea, and the crossing of His people, and the drowning of the Egyptians.
2- Perhaps the writer of the Psalm speaks in the spirit of prophecy about the salvation of Christ in the fullness of time, which He will accomplish in Jerusalem, in the midst of the earth.
13- Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters.
Dragons: ancient sea monsters that became extinct, and they used to attack ships and their passengers.

Thou brakest in pieces (radadta): thou broke. Leviathan: a sea monster that has heads, and is very ravenous, and has become extinct, and some say that it may be the crocodile found at the sources of the Nile.

1- The writer of the Psalm reminds God of His former works with His people, for He is the One who divided the Red Sea so that His people crossed on dry land in the midst of the sea, and broke the heads of the dragons, by whom he means the great soldiers and heroes in Pharaoh's army. And Pharaoh was drowned with all his mighty men, and He broke in pieces the heads of leviathan, by whom he means Pharaoh, so he was drowned, and the corpses of his army came up on the shore of the wilderness of Sinai, and instead of his devouring the people of God, the people devoured him, that is, they triumphed over him, and he became food for the people of the wilderness, who are the wild beasts of the wilderness.

2- The dragons and leviathan are also the demons whom Christ breaks in the water of Baptism, and strips of their authority over His children, so that the baptized are freed from the nature inclined to evil, and are born with the new nature that is inclined to life with God. For Christ the Savior by His redemption divided the waters, and broke the power of the demons, and gave His children victory and authority over serpents and scorpions, and all the power of the enemy.
15- Thou didst cleave the fountain and the flood: thou driedst up mighty rivers.

1- The writer of the Psalm also reminded God of His ancient works when He cleaved the fountain of water, and the waters flowed from the rock when Moses struck it. And this was repeated many times in the wilderness of Sinai. And he reminded God also that He dried up the river Jordan when the priests in the days of Joshua the son of Nun entered with the Ark of the Covenant, and the waters dried up under their feet, and the people of God crossed over and entered the land of Canaan. So God, who is able to cleave the waters and dry up the rivers, is of course able to rescue His people from their enemies.

2- The gushing waters and floods symbolize the souls of the Gentiles who believed in Christ, and from whom gifts and works overflowed because of the Holy Spirit in them. And at the same time God dried up the flowing rivers, which symbolize the Jews who refused to believe in Christ, so the works of God in them dried up because of the hardness of their hearts.
16- The day is thine, the night also is thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun.
Borders (tukhum): boundaries.

1- The writer of the Psalm addresses God, and reminds Him that He is the Creator of day and night, and the sun, and all the planets, and the One who orders the succession of day and night, and likewise the succession of summer and winter, and all the seasons of the year, and He is the One who sets the boundaries of nature in the movement of the sea, and the whole earth, and all the planets. For God sets boundaries and order for all His creatures; and consequently His power is great, and He is able to rescue His people; because everything is in His hand.

3- Day and light symbolize the righteous and those who fear God, and night symbolizes those far from God, occupied with sin, for which darkness is fitting. But the sun symbolizes the Sun of Righteousness, that is, Christ who shines upon the whole world, so He lights the places that were dark, and makes them light, that is, God works in all, those near Him and those far, so that all may believe, and those far may repent, and live with Him, and so be saved.

Meditate every day on the power of God in whose hand is the authority over all creation; so that your heart may be reassured, and that you may fear Him, and keep away from sin, and then God will reveal His beauty to you, and you will enjoy fellowship with Him.
18- Remember this, that the enemy hath reproached, O Lord, and that the foolish people have blasphemed thy name.
Reproached ('ayyara): showed his faults and attributed ugliness and deficiency to him.

1- The writer of the Psalm calls upon God, showing the impudence of the enemies who reproach His people, and attribute weakness to their God, and even insult the name of the holy God, and consequently he asks Him for quick intervention, to defend His great name, and rescue His people from the hands of their enemies; for the enemies from of old have boasted of their pagan gods, and spoken arrogantly against the name of the God of Israel.

2- This verse also applies to what happened with Christ, whom the Jews insulted, and whose rulers insulted Him, and accused Him of wicked accusations, that He deals with the prince of the demons, and that He is a blasphemer and an evildoer, and a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and harlots.
19- O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked: forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever.

1- The writer of the Psalm continues to appeal for God's mercies and compassion, and likens the people of God, or His Church in the New Testament, to the dove which cannot defend itself, and which loves quietness and peace, and likens Satan and all the wicked to the beast that attacks the children of God.

2- And he also likens the people of God to a flock of the poor, that is, a whole company of the poor and weak, unable to defend itself. But the beautiful thing in the matter is that he calls them "thy poor", that is, that they belong to God, and God cannot forget the one who has relied on Him, so He defends him and saves him from his enemies.
20- Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty.
Dark places (muzlimat): the places that are dark.

He also reminds God of His covenant with His people which He made with the fathers of old, and which He sealed with blood in the days of Moses; that He would be a God to His people, and they would obey His commandments. That is, that He is the One responsible for defending His people and caring for them. And at the same time he shows God that the earth has been filled with injustice, and much injustice is known in the darkness, and by this he means every injustice that has befallen the people of God; therefore God's quick intervention is needed to lift this injustice from His people.
21- O let not the oppressed return ashamed: let the poor and needy praise thy name.

As a result of God's intervention and His rescue of His people, His children praise Him and glorify Him, because He gave them victory over their enemies, and they trampled shame underfoot. And to obtain God's mercies, contrition, that is, humility, is necessary, and the feeling of need as the poor and needy feel. For this is the shortest way to the heart of God, to obtain His mercies.

22- Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily. 23- Forget not the voice of thine enemies: the tumult of those that rise up against thee increaseth continually. Thine enemies (adhdadak): plural of thy adversary, and the adversary is the opponent and the resister.
Tumult (dajij): a loud and disturbing noise.

1- He closes the Psalm with the request for God to arise after His silence for a period, to plead His cause, by which he means the cause and the complaint of His people before Him; that He may do them justice. And he said "thine own cause" because the people of God belong to Him, so their cause is His cause. For He is the judge and the defender at the same time of His people.

2- What calls God to quick intervention is the enemies' continuing to reproach His holy name, and showing this with impudence, cruelty and violence, which he expresses by tumult. These enemies deserve punishment for the following:
a- That they are fools, that is, pagans, refusing to know God.
b- That they resist God (thine enemies).
c- They speak with violence and pride, raising their voices with tumult.
3- And the writer of the Psalm does not mean to take vengeance on the enemies, but asks with humility for the glorification of the name of God which the enemies have insulted.
When you speak with another, show your concern for him, and not for yourself, and you will win his love and sympathy, and he will be ready to feel for you and help you.

God the Chastener and Rewarder: to the chief Musician, Al-taschith, a Psalm of Asaph, a song. "Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: a- Asaph, as the title mentions.
b- David wrote it, then gave it to Asaph to sing before the Temple.
2- When was it written?

a- There is an opinion that David wrote it when the angel stood in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and stopped the plague. So he thanked God who is just and merciful at the same time (2 Sam 24:1-17).
b- And there is another opinion that David wrote the Psalm after the death of Saul, and his becoming king.
3- This Psalm glorifies the just God, the Controller of all, who by His power punishes the wicked and rewards the righteous.

4- There is a completion between (Ps 74) and (Ps 75), for the first reproaches God for the delay of His intervention to rescue His people, and in this Psalm he thanks God for His intervention, and the rewarding of His children.
5- There is a resemblance between this Psalm and the Psalm that follows it, and also the prayer of Hannah the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 2:1-10), for both speak of the just God.
6- This Psalm calls every person to beware of sin because of its severe punishment (v. 8), and alerts him to prepare for eternity (vv. 9, 10).
7- This Psalm in its title has "Al-taschith" (Do not destroy), which was a musical tune known at that time.
8- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) Glorifying God for His justice and His power

paragraphs.text: 1- Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare.
1- The Psalm begins with thanksgiving to God, and repeats the word "we give thanks" to show the heart's attachment to God, and its thanks to Him for His many works with His children.
2- The wonders of God on earth with His children made Him near to their hearts, and they were bound to Him as a God of their own, and therefore they glorify Him and give thanks to Him.

entries.section: (1) Glorifying God for His justice and His power

paragraphs.text: 2- "For I appoint a set time; I judge uprightly.

1- God speaks and says to those who cry out to Him, that He may take vengeance on the wicked, that He has appointed a set time for their destruction, and He now gives them an opportunity to repent. And He judges uprightly, so He rewards the righteous, and is long-suffering toward the wicked, that perhaps they may repent, but if they do not repent He will punish them and destroy them. He has also appointed a set time for the whole world at which He will judge it, which is the great Day of Judgment, and He now gives an opportunity to the righteous to be approved before Him, and to the wicked to turn back from their sins.

2- He reassures His children who await His salvation that He has appointed a set time for the salvation of mankind by Christ the Redeemer, and that all the words of the prophets will be fulfilled in Christ, so He asks His children to await His salvation with faith, and even if they die in hope, Christ will lift them up from Hades to Paradise after He completes the redemption.

entries.section: (1) Glorifying God for His justice and His power

paragraphs.text: 3- The earth and all its inhabitants melt. I have weighed its pillars. Selah.

1- God assures those who are hasty for His judgment that the earth will melt and come to an end, it and all its inhabitants, and that is on the Day of Judgment, and by its inhabitants he means earthly people, occupied with the lusts of the world, but God is long-suffering toward these earthly people that perhaps they may repent.

2- He reassures the righteous who ask for the speed of His judgment that He is the Creator of the earth and its Ruler, and He is the One who weighed its pillars; for they used to believe anciently that the earth was fixed on pillars, so what is meant by the pillars is stability. And God knows the extent of the stability of this earth, and when He will end this stability, that is, on the Day of Judgment, and the earth and all material things will change.
3- Since God judges uprightly, the earthly, sensual people fear and melt trembling, but would that their fear were turned into repentance and return to God.

4- He ends these three verses with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditation on our God, the Controller of all, and Ruler of our life, that we may be reassured and be occupied with His love until He takes us to Himself in His heavenly Kingdom.

When you accustom yourself to thanking God you feel His nearness to you, and He also reveals Himself to you, so that your heart clings to Him and rejoices, and your thanks, your thanksgiving and your praise increase.

entries.section: (2) A warning to the wicked of the wrath of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 4- I said to the boasters, Do not boast; and to the wicked, Do not lift up the horn.

The writer of the Psalm calls to the wicked, and warns them against continuing to resist the Lord; this is a divine warning from God on the tongue of the writer of the Psalm so that the wicked do not persist in their wickedness, but repent and return to God. And he warns them of two things:
1- Pride, which he likens to the wild animal's lifting its horn and getting ready to resist and fight in defense of its evil.
2- Stubbornness, which he likens to the animal that stiffens its neck so as not to submit to the one who leads it on the way, for it refuses obedience and submission.
The insistence of the wicked on pride and stubbornness keeps them in constant distance from God, and consequently they walk in the way of destruction.

entries.section: (2) A warning to the wicked of the wrath of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 6- For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the wilderness of the mountains. 7- But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.

1- The writer of the Psalm completes his speech about the wicked in his warnings to them, and tells them to fear God only; because He alone is the Judge who rewards the righteous and lifts them up, or puts down the wicked and punishes them.
2- He asks the wicked to take into account: a- Let not people coming from the east, or the west, or from the wildernesses amid the mountains frighten you, that is, do not fear all men.
b- Fear God alone, from whom there is no escape, whether in the east, or the west, or even in the wildernesses among the mountains.
c- Do not pretend and please the people who are in any place.

entries.section: (2) A warning to the wicked of the wrath of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 8- For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.
The writer of the Psalm shows God's punishment of the wicked, and likens it to a cup in the hand of the Lord, and we note in this cup several things:
1- That its wine is "fermented", that is, strong in effect, so whoever drinks it becomes drunk with it, that is, the divine wrath is severe, and strong in its effect on the wicked.

2- "Full", that is, its wine is plentiful, so the wrath of God will pour out abundantly on the wicked, to each according to his evil, that perhaps they may repent, and if they refuse chastening nothing awaits them but destruction.

3- "A mixed drink", that is, it is a mixture of different kinds of wine so that its effect is stronger, and it means that the divine wrath will have varied punishments; so that its effect is severe, and pricks the wicked and distresses them that perhaps they may repent.

4- "He poureth out of the same": God will pour out from the cup of His wrath on the wicked according to their evil; that they may forget the pleasure of lusts, and return to Him, and awake from their heedlessness.

5- "The dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them": the dregs of the wine (the sediment) is what is at the bottom of the cup, and sucking and drinking it has a stronger effect and is more painful, and it means that the Lord in the end shows His wrath severely to the wicked as a last opportunity for repentance.

And by "sucks it" he means that he drinks it to the end and not a drop remains of it, that is, that the wicked who insist on their wickedness, God will give them complete wrath which they drink to the end in the hope that they may repent.

When you meet an affliction, know that God is alerting you by it to return to Him, and He does not want your destruction, but because of your immersion in evil He was compelled to awaken you strongly, that you may return to His embrace.
9- But I will declare for ever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.

1- After the writer of the Psalm has spoken of the punishment of the wicked he returns to himself, and looks at God, and his heart is filled with joy at His love and His tenderness toward His children, so his heart is quieted and he enjoys fellowship with God.

2- From the greatness of the writer's joy he began to sing and praise God, and tell of the work of God in him and preach to all around him, and draw those far away, in addition to establishing the righteous.
10- All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted. Cut off (a'dab): break.

1- He closes the Psalm with the declaration of the strength of the righteous, for the righteous by the power of God breaks the power of the wicked which seems to dominate on earth, but the righteous in his quietness and reliance on God triumphs and lives in peace.

2- In heaven, that is, the Kingdom, all the powers of evil are broken so that they no longer exist, and are cast into eternal torment, while the righteous receives very great power, which he expresses by horns, and not one horn. So the righteous lifts his head with strength and rejoices for ever, as the animal lifts its head and its horn is raised, declaring its strength.
If you look to Christ your heart is filled with joy, then you praise Him, and so you remain in this joy, and can then preach joy to others, and lead them to the spiritual life.
"God the great and mighty"
To the chief Musician on stringed instruments (Neginoth), a Psalm of Asaph, a song. "In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: a- Asaph, as appears from the title, and he is the chief of the singers in the days of David.
b- There is another opinion that its writer is David, and that Asaph is the one who sang it.
2- When was it written?
a- After David's victory over the Philistines in the valley of Rephaim (2 Sam 5:17-25).
b- On the occasion of the enthronement of one of the kings, or at one of the feasts of the children of Israel.
c- After a great victory over the enemies, and some see that it is a prophecy about the victory over Sennacherib king of Assyria.
3- This Psalm is sung accompanied by a stringed instrument called Neginoth (stringed instruments).
4- This Psalm is considered a "song", that is, praise of God who gave His people victory over their enemies, and thanks to Him.
5- This Psalm resembles the preceding Psalm in that their purpose is to show God as the just Judge of the whole earth.
6- This Psalm is among the group of songs of Zion which speak of Jerusalem the holy city, and of this group are Psalms (48, 87).
7- This Psalm is suitable for every person, when he triumphs in any spiritual war, to repeat it to thank God who supported him and gave him victory in his life over sin.
8- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, because it speaks of Christ who came from the tribe of Judah, victorious over Satan (vv. 1, 3).
9- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
1- In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel.

1- God is known among His people who believe in Him, who know Him not as a name only, but as One acting in their lives and leading their journey. He is known in Judah, the tribe from which the kings came, David and his descendants, and known among all the tribes of the children of Israel; and if the nations have heard of Him, yet He is known by experience among those who believe in Him.

2- God has been known from eternity; because He created the world and ordered it, and the life of man, but He declared Himself and became known by His Incarnation in Bethlehem, in the tribe of Judah, and among all the Jews in the tribes of Israel, and became known in the lives of His children in the New Testament, where He revealed His secrets to them, because they loved Him with all their hearts.

3- God is great in Himself, and perfect, but His people Israel knew Him through His care for them, and His great works in them, which made them triumph over their enemies, such as their triumph over Sennacherib.
2- In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion.
Salem: its meaning is peace, and what is meant is the city of Jerusalem, that is, the city of peace.
Zion: the most important of the five mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built. The name Zion is used to express Jerusalem.

1- God settles and rests in Salem, that is, peace, for He rejects sin and disturbance, and He also settles in Zion, that is, in the midst of His people who believe in Him, and declares His greatness and His glory to them.

2- The tabernacle of God which is in Jerusalem is the Tabernacle of Meeting by which He overshadows His people, and cares for them because of His dwelling in their midst. This happened in the days of David, and afterward the tabernacle became the Temple of Solomon. And in the fullness of time He presented the true tabernacle in Jerusalem, which is His Cross on which He died for the salvation of mankind.
3- There brake he the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah.
The bright bows (al-qisiy al-bariqa): the bows (qisiy) is the plural of bow (qaws) and bright (bariqa) means gleaming.

The shield (al-mijann): it is the large buckler, and the buckler is a defensive implement consisting of a piece of wood with a loop at the back into which the soldier puts his hand, and moves the buckler in front of his head and body to protect him from the arrows of the enemy.

1- There in Jerusalem, or among His people who believe in Him and hold fast to peace, God declared His glory, and gave them victory over their enemies whatever their weapons were; whether bows and gleaming arrows, or swords, or any defensive implements they had, all this God broke. That is, the enemy cannot stand before the power of God, and this indeed happened before Jerusalem with the army of Sennacherib, and then at the Cross when Christ bound Satan.
2- At the end of these three verses there is the word "Selah", which is a musical pause for meditation on the greatness of God and His power.

If you meditate on the power of God, the fear of Him stirs in your heart, and at the same time you are reassured because He protects you from all the wars of the demons, so you remove your sins from you and live in peace, occupied with His love, and not disturbed by any troubles that surround you.

entries.section: (2) The glory of God and His power

paragraphs.text: 4- Thou art more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey. 5- The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands.
Their sleep (sinatuhum): the beginning of their sleep, when their sleep is deep.

1- The writer of the Psalm speaks to God and says to Him that You are greater and more splendid than all the great ones of the world, whom he likens to mountains, and those able to plunder and rob others, that is, they have great power and authority. Perhaps here he means the Assyrians in the days of Sennacherib.

2- The writer of the Psalm describes the great ones of the world, that is, the Assyrians, as having, instead of plundering others, slept a deep sleep, and lost their ability to do anything, for he says they "found not their hands". By all this he means how the angel of the Lord killed them, because they besieged Jerusalem, and in pride transgressed against the name of the Lord. And so everyone who defies God, if he thinks himself victorious and triumphant, is defeated and becomes the spoil of God, and of His children.

3- What is meant by the mountains of prey may be the demons, since they are great in their power like mountains, but they use their greatness in evil, for they want to plunder the purity and righteousness of the children of God, but by His power His children were able to trample the demons, and make them lose their ability to act, so they were silent and still like sleepers, and the children of God will plunder the demons, taking their places in heaven which became empty by their fall, so they enjoy in the Kingdom inexpressible glories.

entries.section: (2) The glory of God and His power

paragraphs.text: 6- At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep.
Cast into a dead sleep (yusabbakh): sleeps a deep sleep.

1- God's rebuke of the proud, such as Pharaoh and all his army, as these enemies slept with their horses and horsemen in the bottom of the Red Sea; that is, they died, because they spoke arrogantly against God and His people.

2- Christ our God on the Cross rebuked Satan and all his power, which is symbolized by the horse and the horsemen, which is the strongest ancient military force, and bound Satan, and brought out Adam and his sons, and brought them up from Hades to Paradise.

3- On the Day of Judgment God, that is, the God of Jacob, will rebuke all the powers of evil symbolized by the horse and the horsemen, that is, the demons and all the wicked, and cast them into eternal torment.

entries.section: (2) The glory of God and His power

paragraphs.text: 7- Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry? 8- Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, 9- When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. Selah.

1- The writer of the Psalm declares the greatness and awesomeness of God, in whose hand is all authority, and consequently no one can stand before Him, but God issues His judgments against him from heaven, and they fear and tremble, for He is long-suffering, but He is just, so He judges the wicked, and sentences them to destruction, as He did with Pharaoh and all his army when He drowned them in the Red Sea, and with the Philistines who were defeated before David, and likewise with Moab and the children of Ammon and Edom and Aram in the days of David. And at the same time He keeps and saves His meek children who believe in Him, as He saved His people in the days of Moses and Joshua, and in all generations when they held fast to His commandments.

2- The awesomeness of God and the fear of Him appear clearly on the Day of Judgment when all the wicked are terrified before Him, and keep silent, since there is no opportunity for repentance or resistance, and He casts them into destruction, but the meek He saves and glorifies in His Kingdom.
3- These verses end with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditation on the greatness of God and His authority, so that all our hearts fear Him and keep away from every sin.

entries.section: (2) The glory of God and His power

paragraphs.text: 10- Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou gird upon thee.
Gird upon thee (tatamantaq biha): He wears it as a girdle (mintaqa), which is what is worn on the waist and downward.
1- The wrath of man praises God in four cases:

a- The holy wrath of man, that is, his rejection of the evil around him, so he praises and thanks and glorifies God, as Phinehas the priest did, who killed the fornicators and cleansed the house of God (Num 25:7, 8).

b- The wrath of the wicked man which God turns to good, such as the brothers of Joseph who were angry with him, and sold him as a slave, and God turned that to good, and raised him to the throne of Egypt; to store up wheat, and preserve the life of his father and his brothers, and all the world around him.

c- The wrath of man when he suffers from God's chastenings of him, but he accepts afterward, and endures these pains with contentment, so they are turned in the end to his good, and he receives a place in eternity, and he praises God, like Job the righteous.
d- The wrath of man against himself if he falls into sin, so he repents of it and praises God, as David did when the prophet Nathan alerted him to his sin.

2- The remainder of man's wrath God girds upon Himself, and he means here the wrath of the wicked, so God is long-suffering toward them, but continues to chasten them that perhaps they may repent. And if they insist on sin God punishes them with destruction, as God struck Pharaoh and the Egyptians with the ten plagues, and in the end when they refused to submit to Him He drowned them in the Red Sea.

3- The wrath of man in its strongest form was against Christ, whom the Jews insulted, and then crucified, and God turned their wrath into a salvation offered to all mankind, and it is the greatest praise that rises to heaven, and which all the believers enjoy, while the remainder of the wrath God girds upon Himself, and with it chastens the wicked throughout the generations. But if they do not believe and repent He casts them into eternal torment.

If God is great and awesome, then, O my soul, you should repent every day, and keep away from sin by every means, and live for Him, and not be troubled, for He is the Possessor of authority, and no one stands before Him, so do not be disturbed any more by the changes of life, or the threats of men; because God is able to protect you in all circumstances.
11- Vow, and pay unto the Lord your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared.

1- The writer of the Psalm calls all those around God, who love His name, to worship Him faithfully, and to vow vows to God, and pay them, that is, that their hearts cling to God, who leads all their lives, and to bring Him presents which are their repentance and their love and their prayers and their service. And they bow down before our awesome God, who was crucified on the Cross for our redemption and salvation, and who is awesome in His Resurrection, and in all His power and His work with us.

2- Our awesome God is the Judge on the Day of Judgment, to whom those who believe in Him bring their presents, which are their faith, and their faithfulness, and their virtues, and all the works of mercy they have done. And the common vow that every believer needs is to dedicate his heart to God, and believe in Him, and live for Him.
12- He shall cut off the spirit of princes: he is terrible to the kings of the earth.

1- God has authority over all men, so however great the rulers and kings of the earth become before Him, their spirits are in the grasp of His hand, and He cuts them off when He wishes, as fruit is gathered from a tree, such as the death of Herod, for the worms ate him while he was alive, and the death of Belshazzar the Babylonian king who grew proud and drank wine from the vessels of the house of the Lord (Dan 5:3), and consequently we are not disturbed by the domination of men and their persecutions of us, for their life is temporary, and they quickly return to the dust from which they were taken.

2- God is awesome to every spiritual person who rules over himself, controlling his thoughts and his words and his conduct, and lives for God, indeed God reigns over his heart, so he lives reassured and hopes for eternal life.

Cling to God who loved you, and died for you, and care about worshiping Him in many prayers and fasts, for they are very precious in His sight. In this you hold fast to His commandments and submit to Him, and He reigns over your heart for ever. God the Savior of His people: "To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, a Psalm of Asaph. I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: a- Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of the prophet David, and he is of the tribe of Levi, and he headed all the companies of singers at the official feasts.
b- There is an opinion that its writer is Jeduthun, who is also a leader of the singers under Asaph, and is also called Ethan the Ezrahite.

2- It is considered a prophecy about a period in which the people of God will suffer pains and the feeling of God's distance from them, which is the period of the captivity. And some see that it is a prophecy about the period before the reign of King Josiah, when the people went away from God in the days of the two kings Manasseh and Amon.
3- This Psalm resembles the prayer of the prophet Habakkuk (Hab 3), and it is likely that Habakkuk quoted from this Psalm, or was influenced by it; therefore this resemblance appeared in his prayer.
4- This Psalm focuses on the wonderful work of God in the crossing of the Red Sea in the days of Moses (Exodus 14, 15).

5- This Psalm is suitable for every person who suffers affliction and God's distance from him, so that he remembers God's former works with him and with His people, and his heart is reassured and his hope in Him is established.
6- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 1- I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me.

1- The psalmist felt great distress within himself and a strong need for God, so he cried out from his pain to God to rescue him. This shows his faith first of all, because he spoke with God and asked Him to rescue him; then the fervor of the prayer increased, and he cried out to Him. After this his faith also appears in his confidence that God gave ear to his prayer.

2- Perhaps the psalmist felt his weakness and the multitude of his sins, so he cried out to God because he had drawn away from Him, and he asked for His swift help, His mercy and His forgiveness; and God listened attentively to his prayer. This shows God's love and His care for those who pray to Him.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 2- In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord; my hand was stretched out in the night and did not grow numb; my soul refused comfort. Grow numb: that is, it became as if under the effect of an anesthetic, so that it lost sensation (became numbed) and the ability to work. "And did not grow numb" means that it did not cease to work.
1- When the psalmist was exposed to distress, he turned at once to God, that He might rescue him and support him, for he knows no one besides Him.

2- In spite of the distress the psalmist continued to work, that is, to pray, to do every good thing, and to be faithful in his responsibilities, even in the night, that is, the time when everyone else rests; but the distress drove him to constructive work. And if the night is a symbol of sin, then he did not surrender to the wars of sin, but continued to strive, and his hands did not stop working.

3- The writer continued in prayers that God might rescue him from the affliction, and his soul refused to be comforted by the words of loved ones and of all the people around him, because he was seeking comfort from God alone. In addition to this, he held fast to prayer until God should solve his problem; for he does not want comfort only, but also asks for the affliction to be lifted.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 3- I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah.
My spirit was overwhelmed: I fainted.

1- The psalmist expresses the extent of his distress by saying that when he prayed and remembered the name of God in order to glorify Him, his heart would open and he would tell God all his pains; he would suffer within himself and groan from the pain of soul and body, and then he would rely on God and lean upon Him.

2- But when he does not pray and thinks about his circumstances between himself and himself, his spirit, or his inner self, cannot bear his pains, and he faints, that is, his body cannot bear the memory of the severity of his pains. This shows that they were very intense and beyond his endurance, were it not for the support of God that he receives through prayer.
3- He ends these three previous verses with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for thinking and meditating on God, who supports us in the time of affliction.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 4- Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.

Because of the great anxieties of the psalmist over his severe affliction, he holds the lids of his eyes, that is, he did not sleep, but kept thinking about his problems; his heart was disturbed and he was unable to speak with people, yet his conversation with God continued, as we mentioned in the previous verses. He affirms that his only comfort in affliction is in prayer. In this we see that when the psalmist thought about the affliction between himself and himself, he was troubled, because it had become beyond his endurance. This is a period of suffering he went through, or a war from Satan that made his distress of soul increase. What, then, will he do? We shall see in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 5- I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times.

The psalmist found the way out of his affliction, which is remembering the work of God with His people in days of old and the ancient years, that is, the former years, and how He preserved the first fathers, delivered His people from the bondage of the land of Egypt, brought them across the Red Sea, and sustained them forty years in the wilderness... In addition to remembering that God has loved him since before the foundation of the world and orders all things for his good, including afflictions. So his heart was reassured and accepted the affliction.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 6- I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search.

1- When he remembered the works of God and His love, he began to sing praise, not only during the day but also at night when he was thinking, and his distress turned into joy. The night also symbolizes affliction, so his affliction was turned into rest and delight. He also remembered his happiness in God's former works, for which he sang praise and rejoiced in God.

2- When affliction came upon the psalmist, he was not vexed with those around him who had wronged him, but he began to think and to review his feelings; as for his spirit, which believes in God, it was searching for God to intervene, that is, he was praying, asking for God to act quickly and rescue him. Thus his heart was occupied with God, so he was comforted and forgot the affliction; for solitude and meditation on God satisfy and lift a person's pains from him.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 7- Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? 8- Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth his promise fail for evermore? 9- Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah. Shut up his tender mercies in anger: that is, because of His wrath He closed in upon His mercies and withheld them from us, as if they were confined in a cage.

1- The psalmist asks: Does God reject me and become angry with me because of my sins? The proof is the presence of this affliction. But he believes that God is compassionate and merciful, and cannot forget His children and those who seek Him; so it is a rhetorical question, because he is confident that if God withdrew for a time in order to discipline us, He returns and floods His children with His love, for His mercy is limitless and never ends, and He cannot deprive His children and those who seek Him of it, and He cannot hide His voice from His people through His prophets and His righteous men, whatever their sin may be.
2- He ends these verses with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on God's mercies that overflow upon His children.

entries.section: (1) A cry at the stopping of the mercies of G

paragraphs.text: 10- And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High.
My infirmity: what makes me sick, that is, ill and in pain.

1- The change of the right hand of the Most High, that is, God's mighty work with me, meaning that He shepherds me and cares for me, and then forsakes me in order to discipline me, causes me severe pain; for I have no rest or stability except in God's care for me and His mercy upon me.

2- The change of the right hand of the Most High means the Incarnation of Christ for the redemption of mankind, and the right hand is a symbol of power, and Christ, in whom is the fullness of God's power, became incarnate to save us. But when the psalmist learned this by the spirit of prophecy, he became sick and in pain, because he also learned that his people the Jews would reject Christ and crucify Him, and consequently the hardness of heart of his people that exists now would continue until the Incarnation of Christ and would cause God to forsake them and cause them to enter into many afflictions such as the captivity.

If affliction comes upon you, hasten to God, and remember His past mercies and His provisions for your life, so that your heart may be at peace; indeed, accept the affliction that is for your good, and increase your prayers and your awareness of God, and so you will rise above the affliction.
11- I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old.

1- If God is great in His love and His gifts, then a person ought to remember His works of old, whether His marvelous ordering in His creation of man and the whole world, or His special care for His people, and His protection and care for them. All this produces reassurance and joy in the heart.
12- I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings.

The spiritual person is not content with remembering God's works, but also meditates on them, repeats them, and thanks God for them with all his feelings, that is, he communes with Him, and so delights in His fellowship.
13- Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary: who is so great a God as our God?

1- The sanctuary is the mountain from which Moses received the commandments and the Law, and it is also the Tabernacle of Meeting where the commandments and the Law were placed. But above all this, the sanctuary is the heart of the person who loves God and keeps His commandments; there God rests and finds His way, and works freely in the person, sanctifying him, satisfying him, and revealing to him the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven.

2- After experiencing God in the heart, the psalmist declares that there is no God like Him, not only in His creation of the world and man, or His care for His people, but even more in His dwelling within the heart of those who love Him, to satisfy them and make them glad.
14- Thou art the God that doest wonders: thou hast declared thy strength among the people. 15- Thou hast with thine arm redeemed thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah.

1- God's wonders were not only among His people, but appeared among all the peoples of the world, because they were great and astonishing works: He freed His people from the bondage of Egypt, then divided the Red Sea, and His people passed through it, while Pharaoh and all his army He drowned in the Red Sea; and this news spread throughout the whole world, so that after forty years Rahab the harlot, who was in Jericho, declared that she had heard of the great God of Israel, who dried up the Red Sea beneath the feet of His people (Josh 2:10).
2- The arm of God that freed His people points to the Incarnation of Christ in the fullness of time, to free those who believe in Him from the bondage of sin.
3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on the greatness of God and His wonderful works.
16- The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled.

1- When God intervened to rescue His people at the Red Sea, when He divided it so that His people might cross through the midst of the waters on dry ground, the waters and the waves were afraid of Him and withdrew to the right and to the left to make room for the crossing of God's people; and likewise the waters of the River Jordan were afraid of God when He stopped the waters so that His people might cross in the days of Joshua, with the Ark of the Covenant.

2- The waters and the depths are a symbol of people, who, when they beheld Christ the incarnate God, believed in Him, whether they were from the Jews or the Gentiles. And the crossing of God's people between the waters of the sea that were divided is a symbol of Baptism, in which the one baptized passes through, then comes out and is freed from his sins.
17- The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad.
18- The voice of thy thunder was in the whirlwind: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook.

1- The psalmist adds details of what happened at the dividing of the Red Sea, and then when Pharaoh and his army entered after the children of Israel; he mentions that clouds appeared and rained water, and there were thunders, lightnings and an earthquake, so that the earth shook, to the point that the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots were taken off (Ex 14:25). These are additions that the psalmist declares to us, showing that God's arrows flew and sped forth, which are all these natural phenomena, to frighten Pharaoh and all his army; but he did not believe and did not fear God, and so in the end he deserved to perish and be drowned in the Red Sea.

2- The voice of the clouds, the thunders, the lightnings and the earthquake is the voice of the Apostles and the priests of the New Testament who preached the name of Christ, so that hearts trembled before the power of the word of God, as Felix the governor trembled before the words of St. Paul the Apostle (1 v. 24:25).
19- Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known.

1- The One who divided the Red Sea and the River Jordan is God, but the waters returned as they were, as if there had been no road or trace of God's work; yet all the peoples heard of these great events. All this was done with God's people under the leadership of Moses and Aaron, and God freed His people from the bondage of Egypt and brought them into the land of Canaan.

2- So also throughout history God does great works, but they pass, and people forget them, like the Jews who did not realize that Christ is God, and who still do not know the footsteps of God, and His Incarnation and redemption which were preached by the Apostles, who led the believers, and who are symbolized by Moses and Aaron.

3- Moses is the leader of the people, that is, the king and ruler, and Aaron is the priest, and they are a symbol of Christ the King and Priest who leads His people and His Church in the New Testament.

I wish that every week you would remember the works of God that He has done with you, and remember also His former works in your life and thank Him for them; then your faith will be established, your confidence in yourself will increase, and your heart will be filled with joy.
God's care and man's betrayal. A psalm of Asaph: "Give ear, O my people, to my law) "... v. 1) Introduction:

1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David; he was of the descendants of Levi, and was head over all the choirs of praise that the prophet David organized for singing before the house of the Lord.
2- When was it written?
a- In the days of David or immediately after him, before the division of the kingdom; because the events of this psalm stop at the age of David.

b- Some see that this psalm was written after the transfer of the Ark of the Covenant of God which was in Shiloh, which the Philistines took and which then returned to the land of the Jews, and David brought it back to Jerusalem; that is, God was pleased with His people and accepted to dwell in the midst of the holy city Jerusalem.
3- This psalm is considered one of the historical psalms, along with Psalms 105, 106, 107, 135 and 136.
4- This psalm is considered the second in length, after Psalm 119, the longest of the psalms.

5- The aim of this psalm is to show God's care and concern for His people, from the time He brought them out of the bondage of the land of Egypt, then how He took care of them in the wilderness of Sinai, and took care of them in the land of Canaan until the great David reigned over them. In contrast, it shows the extent of the betrayal of God's people and of their servants toward Him, and their forgetting of His commandments and His worship, so that they deserved punishment.
6- The New Testament quoted from this psalm, as in:
c- v. 37: Acts 8:21
7- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
(5) The necessity of keeping the commandments (1-8:)
1- Give ear, O my people, to my law: incline your ears to the words of my mouth.

1- God addresses His people, the children of Israel, and asks them to give ear, that is, to listen attentively, and to incline their ears humbly to His words and His Law; for the words are the words of God which He gave to Moses and the prophets, and therefore they are the most important words and need to be heard with humility, so that we may receive and understand the word of God.

2- This verse speaks by the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who calls His Apostles, His priests, His servants, and indeed all His people, to hear the words of the New Testament which complete what was said in the Old Testament, as He declared in the Sermon on the Mount (Mt 5-7).
2- I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old:

1- God informs His people through the psalmist, speaking by way of parables, because a parable makes the idea clear in a practical way, so that it is close to the heart, as Christ did in the New Testament; in addition to God's making His prophets a means of declaring and clarifying His word through what they do, that they may be an example before their people, as happened with Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea... A parable is hard for a person to reject, whereas direct speech may be rejected, because it shows the faults of its hearers plainly.

2- God also declares His word in dark sayings, meaning that in addition to the simple, understandable speech given by way of a parable, God will also give deep speech, hard to grasp in all that it contains, so that a person grasps some of the meanings of God's word; for he finds himself before dark sayings, and as he reads them he gradually discovers new meanings, and so he lives by them and is satisfied. The word "dark sayings" written here means, in the original Hebrew, the mysteries; that is, God's word is full of deep meanings like mysteries, which He reveals to a person gradually.

3- Which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us. 4- We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done. 5- For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children: 6- That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:

1- The reports that the psalmist wants to declare to us, he heard and knew from the first fathers of God's people, and the fathers told them to their children, and the children in turn taught them to their own children, until they reached the generation of the psalmist. And these reports contain the teaching of praising God and worshiping Him, and glorifying Him for His mighty works and His wonders with His people.

2- God set up the Tabernacle of Testimony, that is, the Tabernacle of Meeting that contains the Ark of the Covenant of God, in the midst of His people, the descendants of Jacob, and He also gave them His Law that they might live by it. When he mentions "Jacob", he means the one who took hold of his brother's heel and held him, and it is a symbol of spiritual striving. And when he mentions "Israel", he means the one who saw God at Peniel (Gen 32:31). So he calls his people to hold fast to striving, and then they receive the grace of seeing God. For God loves His people and reveals Himself to them and dwells in their midst in the Tabernacle of Meeting, and wants to show them Himself if they strive spiritually and hold fast to His commandments and laws. All this was fulfilled in the New Testament when Christ became incarnate and was born in the midst of His people the Jews, and showed them Himself by great signs and teachings, that they might believe in Him and be saved.

3- The psalmist makes clear that believers in God are responsible to tell their children, that is, the following generations, and to make known to them who God is, and His commandments and His laws, so that they too may tell their children and teach them these things, until the fullness of time comes and Christ becomes incarnate and accomplishes our salvation on the Cross, and the Apostles go out, and all their successors, the priests and servants, to preach to the world and to hand on the faith from generation to generation until today. This teaching and handing on is what we call Holy Tradition, that is, the oral teaching of the faith and how we live it, which we received from the Fathers and give to our children after us, and which St. Paul the Apostle calls the deposit (2 Tim 2:2.)

7- That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments: 8- And might not be as their fathers, a straying and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful to God.
1- If the children receive the faith and sound teachings from the fathers, this draws them to rely on God and not on themselves, and they hold fast to God's commandments and live by them.
2- The children guard themselves against the evil conduct that their fathers followed, as follows:
a- "A straying generation": that is, apostate from the faith, as the fathers did by their worship of the golden calf (Ex 32:4).
b- "And rebellious": that is, murmuring and rebelling against God, as the children of Israel murmured many times in Sinai.
c- A generation that set not their heart aright: that is, they betrayed God and tried to kill Moses and Aaron several times (Num 16:42) and tried to return to Egypt (Num 14:4).

d- "Whose spirit was not faithful to God": that is, their intention was not pure and their heart was not sincere, but they were hypocrites who pretended to follow God while their hearts were attached to the lusts of the world.
In sum, he means that the children should be obedient to God and submissive to His commandments, walking with Him with a pure heart and worshiping Him faithfully.
Remember God's past works with you, that your faith may be established and you may rely on Him, and the lusts of the world cannot entice you, and so you will be with Him with all your heart.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: . 9- The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle. 10- They kept not the covenant of God, and refused to walk in his law;
Armed (literally "drawers of the bow"), carrying bows: those who pull the string of the bow in order to aim their arrows.

1- He speaks of the sons of the tribe of Ephraim, famous for their large number and their strength in war, who relied on themselves and not on God. These turned back in the war and did not stand firm before the Assyrians, who took them captive as slaves. The captivity of the tribe of Ephraim took place before the other tribes. And what may be meant by Ephraim is the whole kingdom of Israel, since it was the largest in number, so it was a symbol of the whole northern kingdom of Israel, which worshiped idols and departed from the worship of God in His temple in Jerusalem.

2- Ephraim did not keep God's covenant and Law, and did not obey His commands to drive out the Canaanites, the original inhabitants of the land, when they entered the land of Canaan and took possession of it in the days of Joshua (Josh 16:10).

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 11- And forgat his works, and his wonders that he had shewed them. 12- Marvellous things did he in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan. 13- He divided the sea, and caused them to pass through; and he made the waters to stand as an heap.
Zoan: an ancient Egyptian city that was called Tanis, where Pharaoh used to reside; it is in the Sharqia governorate, that is, east of the Delta, and its place now is the village of "San el-Hagar".
Nad (heap): a like and a counterpart.

1- What caused the breaking of Ephraim, or Israel, was their forgetting of God's deeds and His power with their fathers when they were in the land of Egypt, when Moses met Pharaoh in Zoan, and God brought the ten plagues upon Pharaoh. And when his heart was hardened and he went out after God's people and caught up with them at the Red Sea, Moses struck the sea and divided it, and the waters of the sea stood to the right and to the left like a wall, and the children of Israel crossed into the wilderness of Sinai; but Pharaoh and his army, when they followed God's people, were drowned in the Red Sea.

2- The waters also stood like a heap in the River Jordan in the days of Joshua when the Ark of the Covenant of God entered the river, and the people crossed to the other bank, into the land of Canaan.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 14- In the daytime also he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a light of fire.

1- After the ten plagues with which God struck the Egyptians, and they allowed the children of Israel to leave Egypt, God did many miracles with His people, the first of which is that He appeared to them by day in a pillar of cloud that shaded them, so that the sun did not burn them. At the same time the pillar of cloud moves in front of them, and they move with it and it leads them, and this is a symbol of God's work in protecting His children from the trials that the sun symbolizes, and His guiding them in the way of life by His Holy Spirit.

2- And the rest of this wonder is that the pillar of cloud by day turns at night into a pillar of fire stretching from the earth to heaven, and goes before the people to light their way, to dispel the darkness of the night, and to guide them to the way that God wants for them. The pillar of fire is a symbol of the work of the Holy Spirit who enlightens and guides the children of God to the way of the Kingdom, dispels the darkness of sin, burns up all evil, and protects them, as He separated between them and the army of Pharaoh when they crossed the Red Sea.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 15- He clave the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths. 16- He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.
Depths: much water

1- The second miraculous work that God did with His people is that He gave them water to drink in the dry wilderness, the wilderness of Sinai, by making water burst out from the rock, so that much water came out and gave drink to all the people.

2- He mentions the coming out of water from the rock twice because God repeated the bringing out of water from the rock in the wilderness many times, whether the people thanked Him, or doubted Him, or murmured against Him. We notice that the two words for rock mentioned differ in their Hebrew origin, and the text of the word for rock mentioned in v. 16 is the same as that mentioned in (Num 20:1-11), when the people doubted God and murmured against Him, but by His love and care He gave them water in abundance.

3- The rock is a symbol of Christ, as St. Paul the Apostle said (1 Cor 10:4), and the rod with which he struck it is a symbol of the Cross, and the coming out of much water is a symbol of the Holy Spirit who gives drink to believers; in addition, the striking of the rock is a symbol of the piercing of Christ while on the Cross and the coming out of blood and water from His side.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 17- And they sinned yet more against him by provoking the most High in the wilderness.

The rebellion of the children of Israel against God was repeated in the wilderness of Sinai in spite of His great care for them through great miraculous works, the first of which was the ten plagues, then the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, and after that the dividing of the Red Sea, in addition to feeding them with manna and giving them water to drink from the rock. All this happened in very hard circumstances, that is, in the dry land, which is the wilderness of Sinai.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 18- And they tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust. 19- Yea, they spake against God; they said, Can God furnish a table in the wilderness? 20- Behold, he smote the rock, that the waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed; can he give bread also? can he provide flesh for his people?
They spake against God (literally "fell upon God"): they doubted God and rebelled against Him
1- The children of Israel fell into two sins in their dealing with God in the wilderness of Sinai, namely:

a- Disobeying God, that is, not obeying His commands in refusing to enter the land of Canaan, and then their daring to enter the land of Canaan against the command of God, who had forbidden them because of the weakness of their faith, so their enemies defeated them, as appears in (v. 17).

b- Their tempting God, as appears in (vv. 18-20), because they doubted His ability to feed them meat, although they had seen His miracles and His ability to give them water to drink and then to feed them with manna.
2- The sin of doubting God and tempting Him began in the heart, and then appeared in their words and their insolence against God.
3- It is the right of the children of Israel, as children of God who believe in Him, to ask Him for food or for any need of theirs, and He will of course give it to them, but the sin was in:
a- Their doubting of God.
b- Their lust and attachment to the meat and the foods which they used to eat in Egypt (Num 11:4-6).

4- The children of Israel doubted God and His power when they said that He gave us water from the rock, for this water comes from the underground water in the earth, but can God give us meat?! That is, of course He cannot.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 21- Therefore the LORD heard this, and was wroth: so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and anger also came up against Israel;

God was greatly angry with them as a result of their ingratitude, and fire was kindled at the edge of the camp because of their murmuring, but the compassionate God heard the prayers of Moses for them and put out the fire (Num 11:1-3). Then after that He fed them much meat when flocks of quails came upon them.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 23- And he commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven, 24- And had rained down manna upon them to eat, and had given them of the corn of heaven. 25- Man did eat angels' food: he sent them meat to the full. Doors: plural of misra' (the leaf of a door). Corn: wheat. Meat (zad): food. In spite of the murmuring and doubting of the children of Israel toward God, He poured His grace upon them and gave them manna from heaven, which is the bread of heaven, and therefore it was called "the corn of heaven." And this food He also called angels' food, because it came down from heaven, and St. Paul the Apostle even said of it that it was spiritual food (1 Cor 10:3), because it carries a special blessing, so that it satisfied the children of Israel not only bodily, but gave them reassurance that God was with them, and they rejoiced that they were eating from the hand of God, and so were satisfied spiritually.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 26- He caused an east wind to blow in the heaven: and by his power he brought in the south wind. 27- He rained flesh also upon them as dust, and feathered fowls like as the sand of the sea: 28- And he let it fall in the midst of their camp, round about their habitations. God did a great miraculous work with His people in the wilderness of Sinai in order to feed them meat, although their number was great, for they were about two million souls, since there were 600 thousand men besides women and children (Ex 38:26), to answer their murmuring and doubts, in that there were flocks of the quail bird (like the small quail) migrating from Africa northward, heading to Egypt and Sinai, and God sent upon these flocks an east wind coming from the Arabian Gulf that held them back from completing their journey, and also sent a south wind which collided with these flocks and drove them toward the children of Israel walking toward the wilderness of Sinai, and weakened the movement of these flocks, which numbered in the millions, so they flew close to the ground, at a height of a meter (Num 11:31). So it became easy for the children of Israel to catch these birds, which fly slowly, being weak as a result of the wind's colliding with them. And the Holy Bible describes their huge number as being like dust and like sand, and they flew around the tents in which the people dwelt.

entries.section: (2) The works of G in Egypt and Sinai

paragraphs.text: 29- So they did eat, and were well filled: for he gave them their own desire; 30- They were not estranged from their lust. But while their meat was yet in their mouths, 31- The wrath of God came upon them, and slew the fattest of them, and smote down the chosen men of Israel. God proved His power to His murmuring, doubting people when He gave them meat in abundance, as the flocks of quails fell around their tents and they caught them easily, but they were not ashamed and did not repent of their sins; rather they rushed with their lusts to eat much of the meat greedily for a month (Num 11:20-22). And while they were immersed in their lusts and refusing to repent of their sins, the poisonous serpents attacked them and killed many of them, especially the fattest of them, that is, those who went furthest in their lust, and likewise the chosen men of Israel, that is, the strongest and the proudest and most self-exalting, for they are not those chosen by God, but those chosen in the eyes of the people. So the divine punishment attacked the people while the food was still in their mouths (Num 11:33, 34). And perhaps some of them killed themselves by eating too much, that is, by gluttony, so that they suffered indigestion and died, because they seized the opportunity of there being much meat which they might be deprived of and not find afterward in the wilderness because of their unbelief, and these are the ones he describes as the fattest.

God is able to do all things, and can give you everything you wish for, but I wish you would be occupied with His spiritual gifts more than the material ones. Enjoy being with God, and trust that He will give you all your material needs.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 32- For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works.

God gave His people many wonders as we mentioned: He brought water out of the rock, manna came down from heaven, and the quails covered the camp where they lived, and in spite of this they sinned against God by their murmuring, their doubting, and their many lusts.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 33- Therefore their days did he consume in vanity, and their years in terror.

1- God punished His people by making them wander in the wilderness forty years, so He wasted their time, and all the people who murmured against God died, so their journeying was in vain because they rejected God and murmured against Him. It was also in vain because of their disobedience, and their not benefiting from God's work with them, and their immersion in their vain lusts and their unbelief in God.

2- God also consumed His people with terror because of their unbelief in Him and their fear that they would not find food, so they ate the quails greedily, and then the poisonous serpents attacked them, and they were very afraid, and indeed many of them died, but whoever believed in God and looked at the bronze serpent was saved from death. Then He consumed their life with terror when they continued in their unbelief, and so perished in eternal torment.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 34- When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned and enquired early after God. 35- And they remembered that God was their rock, and the high God their protector.

When God punished the children of Israel for their lust for meat and killed them with the poisonous serpents, they were very afraid of Him and returned to Him, and prayed, and asked to submit to Him, for they knew that He was their strength (their rock), their protection and their shepherd (their protector). They even hastened to Him in prayer early in order to appease Him, but not with all their hearts, as will appear in the following verses.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 36- Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues. 37- For their heart was not stedfast with him, neither were they faithful in his covenant.

1- The return of the children of Israel to the Lord was outward, that is, their prayers were words from their mouths and not from their hearts, because lust remained in control of them and the love of God was far from them, and they forgot that God is the searcher of hearts and reins, and no one can deceive Him.

2- So also in every generation we find these deceivers, like the heretics and innovators, who to this day lead people astray with their honeyed words, while they do not love God and do not submit to His commandments, and they draw the simple into their evil way.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 38- But he, being full of compassion, forgave their iniquity, and destroyed them not: yea, many a time turned he his anger away, and did not stir up all his wrath.

1- In the face of man's evil, his rebellion, his doubting, and even his deceiving of God, we find on the other hand that God is compassionate and has pity on man; He is a father who is tender toward His children, so He forgives them their sins and stops His anger, and does not punish man, and if He is angry He punishes partially so that they may repent; for if His anger were kindled He would destroy man. And He makes excuses for man, because man is weak and his life is short like the wind that goes and does not return, that is, fades away; therefore when man sins God is long-suffering, giving him an opportunity to return to God.
2- The teachers of the Jews consider (v. 38) to be the pivot of the whole Book of Psalms. For it lies in its middle, and shows God's love for man and His care for him.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 40- How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness, and grieve him in the desert! 41- Yea, they turned back and tempted God, and vexed the Holy One of Israel.
Vexed: that is, wearied Him and made Him suffer and bear their insults.

1- God's long-suffering appears in His bearing His people's rebellion against Him many times in the wilderness of Sinai, for they grieved His heart.
