And they tempted Him many times and wearied Him by their rebellion (Num 14:22, 23), instead of delighting in His fellowship, since they are the only people in the world on whom God bestowed the favor of dwelling in their midst and caring for them on every side.

2- All these insults the children of Israel directed to the holy God, forgetting His holiness and treating Him like an evil man, and rebelling against Him, and in this, without knowing it, they showed His holiness, which bears with rebellious sinners.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 42- They remembered not his hand, nor the day when he delivered them from the enemy. 43- When he set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Zoan.

1- The children of Israel did not remember God's work with them when He rescued them from the bondage of Egypt with great power, when Moses met Pharaoh in the city of Zoan, which is Tanis, which is in the Sharqia governorate. And God struck Pharaoh with the ten plagues at the mouth of Moses. These are great works that the whole world heard of, so how could God's people forget them, and return and rebel against Him, especially since God warned His people lest they forget His works with them (Deut 4:9).
2- The hand of God that freed His people from bondage is a symbol of the Incarnation of Christ, who freed His children by His Cross from the bondage of sin.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 44- He turned their bays into blood, and their streams, that they could not drink. 45- He sent gnats among them, which devoured them; and frogs, which destroyed them.

Their bays: bays, plural of bay, which is a waterway that opens onto the sea from one side, so it differs from a canal that is open from both sides. What is meant by bays here is the branches of the Nile and the canals branching from it. Here he mentions some of the plagues with which God struck Egypt in order that His people might leave it, and the first of these plagues is the turning of the Nile into blood (Ex 7:17). The second plague is the frogs (Ex 8:2), and the third plague is the gnats (Ex 8:17).

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 46- He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller, and their labour unto the locust. 47- He destroyed their vines with hail, and their sycomore trees with frost. 48- He gave up their cattle also to the hail, and their flocks to hot thunderbolts.

Caterpillar (jardam): one of the stages of the locust, which is the one that has not grown wings sufficient for flying, and it is very voracious in eating, and therefore its harm is very great in eating crops.
Hail: slabs of ice that fall from heaven with force and wound and kill the people and beasts that they meet, because they fall abundantly.

He also mentions a violent plague with which God struck the Egyptians, namely the plague of locusts, the eighth plague (Ex 10:12), then the plague of hail which killed people, beasts, trees and plants, which is the seventh plague (Ex 9:18). These two plagues were crushing for Egypt, for the locusts ate everything green, and the hail destroyed the trees of the rich, which are the vines, and those of the poor, which are the sycamores, in addition to the fact that sycamore wood was used in making the coffins in which the bodies of the dead were placed, and the Egyptians were very concerned with embalming and burying the dead.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 49- He cast upon them the fierceness of his anger, wrath, and indignation, and trouble, by sending evil angels among them.
50- He made a way to his anger; he spared not their soul from death, but gave their life over to the pestilence;

The psalm tells us about God's discipline of the Egyptians, for He showed them His severe anger in the ten plagues, which showed them the weakness of their gods, and God's anger against them because of their evils. And the ten plagues were carried to them by evil angels; they are not evil in themselves, but on the contrary pure, but they carry harsh plagues, which the Egyptians consider an evil that befell them. The first nine plagues were a preparation for the tenth, harsh plague in which their firstborn were struck, and many died in the nine plagues, whether by pestilence or by the other various plagues; and He gave the plagues gradually, increasing in their severity, so He made a way for His severe anger that would appear in the tenth plague; all this so that the Egyptians might repent and believe in God and reject their weak gods. And some of them were affected and accompanied the children of Israel, and the Holy Bible called them the mixed multitude (Num 11:4).

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 51- And smote all the firstborn in Egypt; the chief of their strength in the tabernacles of Ham:

At the end of the plagues came the harsh plague, which was the plague of killing all the firstborn of Egypt, of people and beasts. The firstborn are the first born, when the health of the parents is strong and their capacity for begetting is high, in addition to the fact that the firstborn is a pride to his parents; so the angel killed the strongest and proudest in Egypt, who are the descendants of Ham the son of Noah, and father of Mizraim (Gen 10:6).

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 52- But made his own people to go forth like sheep, and guided them in the wilderness like a flock. 53- And he led them on safely, so that they feared not: but the sea overwhelmed their enemies.
Feared: were greatly afraid.

After the Egyptians were struck with the ten plagues they were very afraid, so they begged the children of Israel to go out from their midst, and God led His people out from among them, and brought them across the Red Sea, and led them, and sustained them in the wilderness of Sinai. And so the strong, who are the Egyptians, became fearful, while the weak, who are the children of Israel, became safe; because God's power is with them, protecting them and caring for them.

entries.section: (3) The betrayal of the people of G in the wilderness and their forgetting His works

paragraphs.text: 54- And he brought them to the border of his sanctuary, even to this mountain, which his right hand had purchased. 55- He cast out the heathen also before them, and divided them an inheritance by line, and made the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.
Border: boundaries.

1- After God had sustained His people in the wilderness of Sinai, He brought them in to possess the land of Canaan, and drove out from before them seven peoples stronger than His people, and settled His people in the cities and tents of these pagans, and He also called the land of Canaan the mountain of His sanctuary, because it was sanctified by God's presence among His people in it, and He also called it the mountain which His right hand had purchased; because the land of Canaan is full of mountains (Josh 14:12), among them the five mountains on which the city of Jerusalem was built and in which His holy temple dwelt. And He divided the land of Canaan among the twelve tribes, and areas of land were anciently measured by the line; all this was by God's power with His weak people, and God expresses His power by His right hand.

2- In the New Testament Christ settles those who believe in Him in the place of the demons who fell from heaven, and their places were emptied, so that after the striving of this life the believers reign with Christ forever in heaven.

When you see those who wrong you being strong, do not be troubled by your weakness; for God's power is glorified in weakness, but hold fast to your prayers, and trust that God will protect you, and will even give you peace and joy in the midst of afflictions.

entries.section: (4) Turning away from G in the age of the Judges

paragraphs.text: 59- When God heard this, he was wroth, and greatly abhorred Israel: 60- So that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he placed among men; 61- And delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand.
Shiloh: a place called Shiloh where the Tabernacle of Meeting settled in the land of Canaan for about three hundred years, after it had moved from Gilgal, and after that it settled in Jerusalem.

In the face of the ingratitude of God's people and their provoking Him by the worship of idols, God abandoned them and rejected them for a time until they should repent, and even refused to be in their midst, so the Philistines took the Ark of the Covenant of God, which was in Shiloh (1 Sam 4:1-11). And so God delivered His strength, which is the Ark of the Covenant of God, to the Philistines, and departed from His people.

entries.section: (4) Turning away from G in the age of the Judges

paragraphs.text: 62- He gave his people over also unto the sword; and was wroth with his inheritance. 63- The fire consumed their young men; and their maidens were not praised. 64- Their priests fell by the sword; and their widows made no lamentation.

God continued His discipline of His people who worshiped idols and fell into many lusts, and He disciplined them by stirring up against them the original inhabitants of the land, when the children of Israel were negligent in driving them out and did not obey the word of God by the mouth of Joshua the son of Nun. So these peoples arose and occupied and enslaved the children of Israel, and killed many of them by the sword (1 Sam 4:10). And so the fire of God's anger consumed His people, and many of the men died in the fire of wars, so the maidens did not find anyone to marry them, and were not praised as they had been accustomed anciently to praise the bride on her wedding day. The priests also, many of them died, such as the two sons of Eli the priest, Hophni and Phinehas (1 Sam 4:11), and the widows also saw the calamity of the people, and the shock and fear came upon them, and they could not weep for their husbands, since the calamity of the people was too great for them to bear, so there was no room for receiving consolation or lamenting their husbands. The Book of Judges, and likewise First Samuel, is full of the disasters that came upon God's people.

God is long-suffering and gives you an opportunity to repent, so hasten and make use of it lest He abandon you, and many afflictions come upon you that are hard to bear. He loves you, so do not waste the opportunity of repentance, that you may enjoy His care.
65- Then the Lord awaked as one out of sleep, and like a mighty man that shouteth by reason of wine.
Shouteth: crying out and calling aloud.

The psalm likens God to a man asleep from drinking much wine, who then awakes like a mighty man who shouts in a loud voice at the enemies of his people. The sleeper does not feel the time and thinks it short; so also God abandoned His people for a little while in order to discipline them, and then arose to discipline their enemies. All this shows God's love and care for His children. For He desires their repentance, and then defends them and protects them.
66- And he smote his enemies in the hinder parts: he put them to a perpetual reproach.

1- After God declared His anger against the enemies who wronged His people, He struck them a severe blow, so that they became a disgrace and a reproach among the peoples. This is what happened with the Philistines who struck the children of Israel, and God allowed this to discipline His people, and they stole the Ark of the Covenant of God, so God struck them with hemorrhoids (1 Sam 5:6, 7).
2- When Christ rose like a mighty man from the dead He declared that Satan is bound, and freed those who believe in Him, and opened to them the Paradise of Joy.
67- Moreover he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim: 68- But chose the tribe of Judah, the mount Zion which he loved.

1- God honored the tribe of Ephraim, for He made its number large, since Ephraim is the son of Joseph. And He honored it also in that spiritual leaders came out of it, among them Joshua the son of Nun, and Gideon. But they did not keep His commandments, and became proud and rebelled, so He was angry with them and refused to dwell in their midst. So the Philistines took the Ark of the Covenant of God which was in Shiloh, which is situated in the tribe of Ephraim, and then the Ark returned from the Philistines to the village of Kiriath-jearim which is in the tribe of Judah, and then David moved it to Jerusalem. So God chose the tribe of Judah, from which would come Christ the Savior, and in it was the temple, and the tribe of Judah was more steadfast in the worship of God than the rest of the tribes.

2- The Ark of the Covenant of God dwelt in the land of Canaan first in the city of Gilgal for a short period, then was moved to Shiloh in the tribe of Ephraim, and after this it was moved to Jerusalem, where the temple was built and the Ark placed in it, but the temple was burned by Babylon at the captivity, and then was destroyed in AD 70 by the Romans. And perhaps the moving of the Ark from Ephraim to Judah is a prophecy of God's rejection of the worship of the kingdom of Israel, which would separate from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and His acceptance of the worship offered in His temple in the tribe of Judah.
69- And he built his sanctuary like the heights, like the earth which he hath established for ever.

After God moved the holy Ark to Jerusalem by the hand of David, He built there by the hand of Solomon a temple for Himself, like the holy heights in heaven where the angels are around the divine throne. And the building of Solomon's temple was a symbol of the Church, which is the earth that God established forever; because those who believe in God will live forever, and God will glorify them with Him in heaven.

70- He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds: 71- From behind the nursing ones he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance. 72- So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands. God chose David from among the tribe of Judah for his spiritual readiness, and he lived with God in perfection, after being tried in shepherding sheep, for it mentions that God took him from behind the nursing ones, that is, the mothers who care for their young attentively among the ranks of the sheep. So David was therefore able to shepherd God's people. And he shepherded them with skill and fatherhood, and with a perfect heart like the heart of God. He shepherded God's people Jacob, who is Israel, and was a symbol of Christ the Good Shepherd, who lays down His life for the sheep, and redeems His people on the Cross, to acquire them for Himself as sons in the Kingdom.

Obey God's commandments so that He may choose you from among His sons and work through you, and so that you may care for all who are around you, to draw them to Him, and you will enjoy His fellowship and His work in you.
The supplication to God the Deliverer "O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance) ".. v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David, and it may be that David himself is the writer, and he gave it to Asaph to sing.
2- Why was it written?

A prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian captivity, or the devastation of the temple by Antiochus the Great in the days of the Maccabees, or the devastation of the temple by the Romans in AD 70.
3- This psalm is a cry to God to rescue His people and His temple that was destroyed, and it is suitable for the Church and every believer to say if they pass through affliction.
4- This psalm resembles Psalm 74, which speaks about the same subject, and one may refer to its introduction.
5- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The destruction of Jerusalem and the temple

paragraphs.text: 1- O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps. The psalm prophesies about the entry of the pagans into Jerusalem, God's inheritance, since they are His only people who worship Him in the Old Testament; and they defiled His temple by entering it, and burned it, and made it and Jerusalem a ruin like heaps of stones and dust. And although this was a dreadful thing in the eyes of the Jews, since they thought that the temple would remain firm until the end of the world, they were shocked by its destruction, and forgot that they had broken God's commandments and worshiped idols, so the natural result was that God departed from them and let His temple be ruined, which they had already ruined by their deeds.

entries.section: (1) The destruction of Jerusalem and the temple

paragraphs.text: 2- The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth.
3- Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.

The psalm describes the multitude of the slain in Jerusalem at its destruction, showing that the corpses were cast down everywhere, and blood flowed from them, and the Jews could not bury the corpses because of their great number, so the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth ate them. All this was because they rejected God's commandments, so God rejected them. And the enemies were hard of heart, so they killed the Jews and cast their corpses inside Jerusalem, and likewise they shed the blood of everyone who tried to flee, around Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) The destruction of Jerusalem and the temple

paragraphs.text: 4- We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us.

By the destruction of Jerusalem it became a disgrace and a mockery in the eyes of its neighbors, such as the Edomites who gloated over it and seized the Jews who were fleeing and handed them over to their enemies (Ps 137:7), noting that the neighbors of the Jews had been enslaved to them in the days of David and Solomon, so they seized this opportunity to gloat over them.

When any affliction comes upon you, examine yourself lest your sins be the cause, and return to God with repentance, and trust that He is able to heal you, build you up, and compensate you for all that you have missed.

entries.section: (2) Turning G's anger away from His people

paragraphs.text: 5- How long, LORD? wilt thou be angry to the uttermost? shall thy jealousy burn like fire?

The psalmist pleads with God to stop His anger and His jealousy toward His people. The anger meant is the discipline of the people, that they may repent. As for jealousy, it is God's love for His people, who does not want them to turn aside from Him to the worship of idols and evil; for God has no passions like human beings. And this verse shows the extent of the suffering of God's people, and at the same time their hope in God who rescues them and lifts His disciplines from them.

entries.section: (2) Turning G's anger away from His people

paragraphs.text: 6- Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name.
7- For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place.
Pour out: to pour abundantly; it is from the verb "to overflow".
The psalmist also asks God not only to cease from disciplining His people, but to turn His anger upon the Gentiles, for two reasons:
1- That the Gentiles do not know God and do not worship Him.

2- That they wronged God's people violently and destroyed them, as he says "devoured". So he cries to God to save His people, to drive the enemies away from them, and to take vengeance on them, that they may know the corruption of their evil, perhaps they will return to God.

Do not be troubled by God's disciplines of you, for they are temporary and are for your good. And do not doubt when those who wrong you gain power, because God hates their evils and will punish them. Do not gloat over them, nor be filled with rage against them, but correct their faults with repentance, and pray for those who wrong you that they may return to God.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

paragraphs.text: 8- O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low. The psalmist comes to God with humility and lowliness, and asks Him for two things:

1- That He not remember the sins of their fathers, for they are many, and He has promised that every person bears his own guilt, so the children are not punished for the sin of the fathers (Ezek 18:2-4).
2- He asks for God's forgiveness and mercies for the present sins of the people.
And in this God quickly lifts His anger from His people; because they are in severe affliction and were almost perishing.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

paragraphs.text: 9- Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and forgive our sins, for thy name's sake.
1- The psalmist asks three blessings of God, which are:
a- His divine help to bear the sufferings.
b- That He deliver them from the hands of their enemies.
c- That He forgive them their sins that caused them these disciplines.

2- The people do not deserve these blessings, but the people ask for them for the sake of God's name. And what is meant by the name of God the Savior is Christ, incarnate in the fullness of time. This verse shows the humility of the people and their confidence that salvation is from the hand of God alone, and that every blessing they need is a divine gift.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

paragraphs.text: 10- Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed.
Shed: poured out, that is, that which flows on the ground.

The writer asks God not to leave the pagan Gentiles believing in their strength and their gods and despising You, the great God, when they say, Where is our God? Why did He not rescue us from their hands? Therefore we ask that You avenge the blood of Your people that has flowed on the ground, so that they may know that You alone are the great God, and that their gods are nothing, perhaps they will believe and return to You.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

paragraphs.text: 11- Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou the sons of death;

1- In humility again the writer asks God to accept the prayers of the captives, who are the Jews taken captive by Assyria and Babylon, because they are in humiliation, indeed counted among the dead, since they have no freedom or ability to move and return to their land to worship God. And he asks also that He preserve His children, who from the severity of the enemies' pressure and humiliation of them have become as good as dead.

2- The arm of God is a symbol of the Incarnation of Christ, for He is the Word of God and His power, which is very great, so he asks God to hasten to save His people who are dead, not only because they are in the humiliation of the bondage of captivity, but also because they will go down to Hades, but by the Incarnation of Christ He saves them and moves them from Hades to Paradise.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

paragraphs.text: 12- And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord.

1- The psalmist asks God to show His justice, and take vengeance on the wicked enemies of His people according to their cruelty to His people, punishing them sevenfold for what they did, so that they may know the hideousness of evil and turn back from it, and know the power of God who is above all gods, and so disgrace and shame come upon the enemies.

2- Perhaps what is meant by the enemies of God's people is the demons who try to draw God's people away from faith and the worship of God, so he asks for vengeance on them sevenfold, that is, in eternal torment.

entries.section: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

paragraphs.text: 13- So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: to generation after generation we will shew forth thy praise. The psalm ends with a great hope that the writer saw by faith, which is that God will rescue His people and bring them back to their land, and they will build the temple and worship Him, and then their voices will rise in thanksgiving and praise to God for the greatness of His works. And this praise continues from generation to generation, that is, forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

How great are God's works with you, for He is ever caring and watching over you; therefore He deserves from you constant thanksgiving and praise. And this thanksgiving and praise fills your heart with joy; for He bestows on you His fellowship, so you pass through afflictions without weariness, because you feel His presence with you.
The right hand of God restores us and shepherds us. To the chief Musician upon the Lily. A testimony. Of Asaph. A psalm. "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel) "... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: Asaph, the head of the singers in the days of David.

2- Why was it written? It is a prophecy about the Jews taken captive in the Babylonian captivity, who ask God to bring them back from the captivity, and to care for His people and His temple that the enemies burned.
3- This psalm is said to the accompaniment of a musical instrument called the lily, as appears in the title of the psalm. It is an instrument resembling the lily flower.
4- The title of the psalm declares that it is a testimony; that is, it bears witness to the faith of God's captive people, their suffering, their prayers, and their hope of returning from captivity.
5- The title declares that it is a psalm; that is, it is sung to the accompaniment of the pipe.
6- This psalm speaks about the Church, or the suffering human soul, which believes in God and so prays and pleads to Him to lift its sufferings from it and to take care of it with His care.
7- This psalm longs for God to become incarnate and redeem mankind, and to take care of His children who believe in Him, and shepherd them forever.
8- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like sheep; thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth.

1- The psalmist pleads with God, and describes Him as the Shepherd of Israel, that is, God's people before the division. And he reminds Him that He is the leader of Joseph, who bore many troubles from his brothers and remained steadfast in his chastity. And he is poor like the sheep, that is, the weak lamb before wolves. So he needs Your care and Your leading, O God, especially since You are the great God, able to do all things, who sits upon the cherubim who are full of eyes, and praise You continually. So You are the mighty God, and the tender one, the Shepherd of Your people at the same time.

2- When the psalmist calls upon God who sits upon the cherubim, he reminds Him that He created His people with a heavenly nature, when He created the spirit in them, that they might know Him and praise Him like the angels; therefore the psalmist asks God to shepherd His people, and lead them, and free them from their captivity, that they may glorify Him.
2- Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh awaken thy might, and come and save us.

The psalmist calls upon the mighty, powerful God to awake; for he considered His silence over the humiliation of His people as if He were a sleeping person. So he asks Him to move and awake from His sleep, and to save His people. And he mentions these three tribes, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, to symbolize all the people of Israel, and these three tribes used to march before the Ark of the Covenant of God when the tribes moved on their march during their stay in the wilderness of Sinai; because they are strong tribes, but now they are enslaved in captivity and weak, so the psalmist implores God to rescue His weak people and restore them to their strength, as these three tribes once were.
3- Turn us again, O God, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved.

1- At the end of this passage he asks God to return to the care of His people whom He neglected by disciplining them in the period of captivity, that is, return to Your care for Your people to bring us back from the captivity, so that we regain our freedom and dignity.

2- He also asks God to cause His face to shine upon His people, so that they may receive salvation. For the appearing of God's face, or His dwelling in the midst of His people, is the life that He grants them, so that they leave the darkness of sin and live a spiritual life in Him, filled with righteousness and virtues, and this is salvation, not only from the bondage of captivity, but it is freedom and the enjoyment of fellowship with God.

3- This verse is a refrain that is repeated in this psalm three times, in (vv. 3, 7, 19); because this is the aim of the psalm, that God bring His people back from captivity and let them enjoy His light and His salvation.
I wish this verse would be a constant petition for us; that God may bring us back from our sins into His embrace, so that we are enlightened by His light and enjoy His salvation in His Church.
4- O LORD God of hosts, how long wilt thou smoke against the prayer of thy people?

The writer reminds God that He is the God of hosts, that is, the mighty One, able to do all things. And he asks Him, why do You smoke against the prayer of Your people? That is, why do You reject it, neglect it, and not respond, so that they remain in the humiliation of the bondage of captivity?! Is not the discipline that they have received enough, that You might forgive them and bring them back from their captivity?!
5- Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure.
1- The psalm describes the state of the captive people and how God allowed their food to be mixed with their tears; tears of pain, and tears of repentance.

2- The tears that God allowed to His people were very many, so they were by measure, but at the same time they were by measure; that is, in a fixed amount that does not exceed it lest they be swallowed up by despair. And their amount may differ from one person to another according to his need for discipline and tears. And the purpose in the end is the salvation of His people.
6- Thou makest us a strife unto our neighbours: and our enemies mock among themselves.

1- The enemies of God's people are the nations surrounding them, that is, their neighbors, who are the Moabites and the Ammonites on the east, the Edomites in the south, and the Philistines in the west. These contended among themselves over who would take vengeance on the Jews and hand them over to the Babylonians when Nebuchadnezzar attacked them; that is, they contended and took counsel together to destroy them.

2- This is also a prophecy about those who believe in Christ, whom their enemies mocked, namely the Jews, the Greeks and the Romans, because of the Christians' faith in a crucified person who had died; since these enemies did not know that He is God, our Redeemer.
7- Turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved.

This verse is repeated, for it is the refrain found at the end of each group of verses, and it was already explained in (v. 3). And it means here the hope of returning from captivity, and salvation from all the sufferings that God's people endured in captivity, which are mentioned in (vv. 4-6).

If you are passing through afflictions by which you suffer and your soul is crushed, trust that God has allowed them to you so that you may repent of your sins, and that your prayers may grow, and you may experience new depths in your relationship with God, and so your heart is comforted.
8- Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it.

1- The psalm likens God's people to a vine because it is a weak plant that needs care. And when it is cared for it gives sweet and abundant fruit. So God brought His people out of Egypt when He brought them out with a high arm from the bondage of Egypt by the ten plagues, and divided the Red Sea, and brought them across the wilderness of Sinai, and brought them to the land of Canaan, and drove out the nations living in the land, and settled them in their place. Because they were the only people who believed in God, unlike the rest of the pagan world, God therefore cared for them, led them, sustained them, and settled them in a land flowing with milk and honey.

2- The Church is also called the vine for the same reasons as above. For the Church is the new people of God, and therefore in the hymn "O Lord, God of the Powers" we give the Church the title of the vine.
9- Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land.

God prepared the way before His people, so He troubled the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, and they feared God who walks in the midst of His people, because they had heard of the dividing of the Red Sea, in addition to the dividing of the River Jordan. And this helped His people to be victorious over their enemies, and they dwelt in their place after they had driven them out. And they became established as the vine is established by stretching its roots in the earth, that is, its roots took root, and the roots spread in the earth and filled it; that is, the people were victorious and continued driving out the pagan peoples, and this happened in the reign of David and Solomon.
10- The hills were covered with the shadow of it, and the boughs thereof were like the cedars of God. 11- She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river.

1- The psalm continues its speech about the vine, and declares that it extended to cover the mountains, that is, the people settled and spread over the mountains of the land of Canaan. And it likens the people also to cedar trees, that is, the people became strong, and firm in the land, and rising up to heaven. And it declares also that it extended from the sea, meaning the Mediterranean Sea, to the river, meaning the Euphrates River, and the River of Egypt, which fills seasonally in the winter season and is found in the wilderness of Sinai.

2- These two verses are a symbol of the spread of Christianity in the whole world across the seas and rivers, while the mountains are a symbol of rising toward heaven in the life of believers. In sum, believers in the New Testament live a heavenly life, raised above earthly things, like those who dwell on the mountains, and become strong like the cedars of Lebanon, and live by the streams of waters, that is, the work of the Holy Spirit overflows in their lives.
12- Why hast thou then broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her? 13- The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it.

1- The psalmist asks, and says to the Lord, why have You broken down the walls of this vine? That is, Your people, and by this he means the pulling down of the walls of Jerusalem, and burning it and its temple, and the attack of the Assyrians, then the Babylonians, and their taking possession of its good things, and after them Antiochus the king came in the days of the Maccabees, and attacked Jerusalem and Judea.

So the pig of the wood and the wild beast of the field are symbols of Assyria and Babylon, and those who pass by the way are symbols of the enemies of the Jews who lived around them, who are the pagan peoples; Moab, the sons of Ammon, Edom, and Philistia. All these gloated over the fall of Jerusalem and all the land of the Jews, and seized the Jews who were fleeing, and handed them over to Assyria and Babylon.
2- The enemies of God's people are the demons in every generation, who gloat over the believers if they fall, and humiliate them by sin.
14- Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine;

1- The psalmist calls upon God and gives Him the title God of hosts. It is noticed that the expression "God of hosts" is repeated four times in this psalm; because God is the Almighty, the strong, who governs the whole world with its four corners.
2- The psalmist asks four acts of God, which are:
a- "Return": that is, go back to Your fatherhood and Your love and Your first concern for Your people, after You had forsaken them for a time to discipline them.

b- "Look down": that is, look with care and calm, and this looking is from heaven, and means a pure spiritual look, which pours tenderness and love upon the people and raises them up to heavenly things.

c- "Behold": that is, look closely and concentrate Your care on Your people because they are weak and in need of all Your concern; it is a pleading and a hope that God will give the people all His love.
d- "Visit": that is, shepherd Your people and care for their growth, and remove everything that hinders them from You, as the sower takes care to fertilize the plant and to resist harmful pests.
15- And the plant which thy right hand hath planted, and the son whom thou hast chosen for thyself.

1- Here he describes God's people as a plant that God planted, which is therefore firm and strong, since God's right hand and His power are what planted His people. And he likens it also to the son, because God cares for it as a father, and He chose it from among all the peoples, and brought it out of Egypt to live to Him in the right faith.

2- This verse is clear about the Incarnation of Christ, whom the Father planted among human beings by His Incarnation, and He is the Son of God whom He chose from among all human beings, because He alone is able to redeem us; God who became man.
16- It is burned with fire, it is cut down: they perish at the rebuke of thy countenance.

1- The vine that symbolizes God's people, when it turned aside to the worship of idols, God allowed it to be burned and cut down, and this was done at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar who burned the temple and Jerusalem. And so God used Nebuchadnezzar to rebuke His people and discipline them, so many died and the rest lived in bondage and humiliation; that they might return to God.

2- By the Incarnation of Christ He rebuked evil, and destroyed sin so that it had no power over Him, and when the Jews refused to believe, the Romans rose against them in AD 70, and burned and destroyed Jerusalem and its temple.
17- Let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand, upon the son of man whom thou hast chosen for thyself.

This verse focuses fundamentally on the incarnate Christ, so it asks the Father that His hand be upon the man of His right hand, who is Christ, and the son of man whom the Father chose, and the hand of the Father is upon the Son, that is, the divinity works in Christ in the following:
1- Giving Him strength, so that the Jews could not lay hold of any fault in Him, and could not seize Him before the time (Jn 8:59).
2- Glorifying Him with miracles and mighty teachings (Jn 17:4).
3- Raising Him from the dead.
4- Sending His Holy Spirit to pour out the results of salvation and Christ's redemption upon the Church through the Sacraments, the gifts, and the fruits of the Holy Spirit.
18- So will not we go back from thee: quicken us, and we will call upon thy name.

1- If God takes care of His people He keeps them and establishes them in the faith, so that they do not turn back from Him, and gives them the grace of life in Him, keeping away from the death of sin, and then they glorify Him, praise Him, and thank Him for His works.

2- This is also a prophecy about the incarnate Christ the Redeemer, who establishes believers in the faith, makes them alive from the death of sin, and raises them to eternal life, so that they glorify Him not only on earth, but also in heaven forever.

19- Turn us again, O LORD God of hosts, cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved. This verse is the refrain repeated here for the third time, and it was already contemplated, see (v. 3). And God's shining upon us concerns eternity, where believers enjoy the luminous, exalted, perfect life.

Ask God every day to take care of your soul and shepherd it, that it may grow in His love. And seek Him in every difficult situation, then your heart will be at peace whatever difficult circumstances confront you. And do not reject His voice if He calls you to any spiritual work, whether by a voice inside you or one you hear around you.
The people's call to repentance. To the chief Musician upon Gittith. Of Asaph. "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David. It may be that David is the writer, and he gave it to Asaph to sing.
2- When was it said?
At the new moons, the feast of trumpets, the feast of Passover, and in the feasts in general, because it offers glorification to God.
3- It is mentioned in the title of this psalm that it is said upon Gittith, which is a musical instrument taken from the Philistine city of Gath..
4- The idea of the psalm is a call to God's people to repent of their disobedience, that they may regain their position as a people who believe in God, and so glorify Him.
5- This psalm is suitable for every person to repeat at all times, to repent and regain his strong relationship with God, and so return to his strong prayers and his praises.
6- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob.

1- The psalm calls God's people to express their love for the mighty God, who supported His people and saved them with great power, and who is the only strength of the people that relies on Him. So it does not lean on weapons, or its own human strength, or its relations with strong surrounding nations; all this is nothing before the power of God. This singing declares the faith of the people and establishes them in it, and even gives them joy, delight, and fellowship with God.

2- From much singing to God the hearts of the people were filled with joy, so the psalm called them to shout aloud, because shouting is loud voices showing the heart's attachment to God, and they sing to the God of Jacob, because Jacob relied on God, so Esau was not able to harm him, but on the contrary the two brothers embraced in love (Gen 33:4). So the people shout to God, their mighty God who protects them and keeps them.
2- Raise a song, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant lute with the rebab.

Timbrel: a wooden frame over which a thin skin is stretched, and on the sides of the frame there are small cymbals to give strong sounds for keeping rhythm. To play it one strikes the stretched skin with the hand, and it is now called the "riqq".
Lute: a stringed musical instrument known to this day by the same name, consisting of a wooden box over which a number of strings are stretched.
Rebab: plural of rababa, a stringed instrument over which twelve strings are stretched and it is played with the fingers, or with a plectrum like the lute.

The psalm calls the praising people to sing to God with high notes, accompanied by musical instruments such as the lute, the timbrel and the rebab, to express joy and to praise God who gives them victory over their enemies, especially since the people had been accustomed to singing with musical instruments since their departure from the land of Egypt, when Miriam led the people in their praise and glorification.
3- Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, at the crescent, for the day of our feast. 4- For this was a statute for Israel, and a law of the God of Jacob.
Trumpet: a musical instrument resembling the horn of an animal, with a narrow opening at one end and wide at the other, and it is blown for playing.

The psalm also calls the people to use trumpets, and it was the priests who blew the trumpets, for blowing the trumpet is a priestly work, because the trumpet is a symbol of the word of God. And trumpets are used at the new moon, at the appearing of the crescent, and at the Feast of Trumpets which is the head of the seventh month, and is the beginning of the year. It calls people to repentance and a new beginning, and reminds them of the power of God that gave them victory over their enemies, so it fills the hearts of the people with zeal to begin a strong spiritual life with God. And blowing the trumpets is a divine command, and a statute that God's people fulfilled at the head of every month to renew feelings of repentance, hope and strength. And the Church holds prayers and Liturgies at the head of the year, to call her people to repentance and hope.
5- This he ordained in Joseph for a testimony, when he went out over the land of Egypt. I heard a language that I knew not:

1- God made the feast, meaning all the religious feasts, in which trumpets and spiritual memorials are used, a testimony in the midst of His people, declaring their faith in God and their worship of Him. And he chose the name Joseph as a symbol of all God's people; because Joseph was the cause of bringing his brothers into the land of Egypt and honoring them, but the Egyptians enslaved them and humiliated them after this, and so the children of Israel lived as slaves among the Egyptians, who have a language that God's people do not know, but their consolation was their knowing God, and God's knowing them, which was manifested in the religious feasts and seasons, and in every worship they offered to God.

2- Joseph is a symbol of Christ, for Christ bears witness through Joseph in the land of Egypt to the work of God; because Joseph was sold as a slave, and bore sufferings for thirteen years, and then was raised to the throne of Egypt, and Christ became incarnate, and took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and bore sufferings, and was obedient unto death, even the death of the Cross, and then rose in great glory, conquering all the powers of darkness, and bound Satan; so Joseph bore witness by love and forgiveness to his brothers, as Christ forgave humanity, and died for it and redeemed it on the Cross. And humanity heard a new language that it had not known, which is the love poured out on the Cross, love without return, and giving unto death so that humanity may change and be renewed in Christ.
6- "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were turned from the basket.
Basket: it is the basket (sall), and its plural is baskets, in which vegetables or fruit, or earth, or sand are put...

This verse tells us about God's work with His people in Egypt, for He freed them from the forced labor with which the Egyptians forced them, for they used to carry heavy loads on their shoulders to build cities, and no longer carried the baskets full of the clay needed for making bricks, and they went out to the wilderness of Sinai and lived in freedom. So also Christ freed us from the bondage of sin, and its burdens, and its consequences by His redemption of us on the Cross
7- Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah.

1- God reminds His people that when it was distressed as Pharaoh and all his army pursued it, and it was hemmed in between Pharaoh's army and the Red Sea, it cried out to God and He delivered it from the hands of the Egyptians, for He sent an east wind over the Red Sea, and divided the sea, and the children of Israel crossed, when Moses struck the sea (Ex 14:21), and they reached the wilderness of Sinai, while Pharaoh and all his army were drowned in the Red Sea; so God's answer to the prayers of His people was mighty, and beyond human imagination. For God's work was hidden behind the sound of the storm, or the thunder, that divided the Red Sea; this was a miraculous work of God by which He rescued His people from death and freed them from the bondage of Egypt, so they feared God and His servant Moses.

2- But after crossing the Red Sea God sustained the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai with water, manna and quail, and kept them from enemies, and in spite of this they doubted Him, and tempted Him at the waters of Meribah, and murmured against Him, so God was angry with them, and forbade Moses and Aaron to enter the land of Canaan.
So God punishes them for the weakness of their faith in spite of His many miracles with them.
3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on God's power, care, and love for His children.
Look at God's care for you throughout your life, and thank Him and praise Him until your heart is filled with joy, and God's mercies overflow upon you more and more.
(8- Hear, O my people, and I will warn thee: O Israel, if thou wilt hearken unto me;

God calls His people, who tempted Him and doubted Him at Meribah, and says to them "O my people"; to remind them that they are His children, and He is their Shepherd and their heavenly Father. And He named them "Israel" because they obey Him and hear His word. But if they disobey Him and refuse to obey Him they lose their sonship and God's care for them. So He speaks here decisively and warns them, lest they turn aside from Him to the worship of idols and all the evil lusts connected with them.
(9- There shall no strange god be in thee; neither shalt thou worship any strange god. 10- I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.

Open wide: open. God forbids His children to worship idols and all strange gods; because they believe in God their one God who is able to satisfy them with great abundance, if they open their mouths and ask Him to sustain them. For this shows their need and their faith. And here He affirms the first commandment of the Ten Commandments (Ex 20) which the people sometimes forget, as their fathers did when they worshiped idols and left God. And this happens to this day when a person relies on the powers and lusts of the world, and does not trust in God, for by this he worships other gods and forgets God.
11- But my people would not hearken to my voice; and Israel would none of me.

1- God speaks with sorrow about the children of His people who refused to listen to His commandments, and walked after their own thoughts and the evil thoughts of the world, so they moved away from God, although they have the name of being God's people, and they in truth reject Him; by this God does not please them, and they are not content with Him, and prefer the world and its lusts to Him. This is ingratitude, and a hardness of heart into which God's children fell, and fall to this day.
2- This rejection of Him by God's people happened when Christ became incarnate, and preached among the Jews, His own kin, and they rejected Him and crucified Him.
12- So I gave them up unto the hardness of their hearts, to walk in their own conspiracies.

1- When God saw the people's insistence on evil, and the hardness of its heart, that is, its pride and refusal to hear the voice of God, He forsook them, and left them to taste the result of hardness of heart, and the evil conspiracies they devise, perhaps if they suffer from their results they will repent, and if they persist in evil like Pharaoh they will perish in the Red Sea. And God does not harden anyone's heart, but leaves him to the hardness of his heart.

2- God left the Jews to the hardness of their hearts and their evil conspiracies, and because they said we have no king but Caesar, and crucified Christ, Caesar sent Titus the Roman commander who destroyed Jerusalem and killed the Jews in AD 70.
13- Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! 14- I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries.

God makes clear that the cause of His people's suffering is their refusal to hear His word, and to walk in His ways, that is, His commandments. But if the people had submitted to God, He would have intervened and given them victory over their enemies quickly, and turned back upon their heads their transgression against His people. So God shows here:
1- His concern for man's freedom, for it is necessary for his salvation..
2- The importance of human striving "hearkened, walked" to obtain God's grace and victory.

3- The affirmation of the well-known truth that whatever a man soweth, that shall he also reap (Gal 6:7). If a person hears and walks in God's commandments he is victorious over his enemies, and if he does not hear and do, many afflictions befall him, and he should not blame God but blame himself if affliction comes upon him.
15- The haters of the LORD should have submitted themselves unto him: but their time should have endured for ever.

1- The wicked who hate God and refuse to obey Him, if God allows afflictions for them, and they humble themselves in them but persist in the hardness of their hearts, are cast into eternal torment, that is, they live and all their time is in torment, and if they pretend to humble themselves in order to deceive God, then of course God is not deceived and repays them for their evil with eternal torment.

2- This verse can be interpreted in another way, namely that the haters of the Lord, if they humble themselves in repentance and return to God, then their time and their life forever will be with God in eternal happiness.
16- He would have fed them also with the fat of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock would I have satisfied thee.

1- God continues His speech about His children, if they obey His commandments, He pours His blessings upon them, so He gives them wheat in abundance, and it satisfies them, and he expresses that by saying "fat". And likewise He waters them with water from the rock, and because of their thirst they feel the sweetness of the water as if it were honey, that is, God sustains His people with riches and great abundance.
2- The wheat and the rock are Christ, and He gives us His Body and His Blood, which is the fat of the wheat, and His words that water our souls and are sweet like honey.

Hold fast to God's commandments carefully at the beginning of your day; that He may lead your life in the straight way, and satisfy you, and fill your heart with peace, and so you will live in joy all the days of your life.
God the just Judge "God standeth in the congregation of God" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David.
2- This psalm is among the psalms of Asaph that make clear the evils of the children of Israel, and Asaph tries to remedy them.
3- This psalm calls the judges to judge with justice, and to do justice to the wronged, and to imitate the just God.

4- This psalm was repeated in Jewish worship on Tuesday, as the Jewish liturgy mentions, and it is considered part of the Jewish Law because Christ referred to it and said about it to the Jews that it is written in your Law (Jn 8:17)
5- This psalm points to the unjust judgment that the Jews passed on Christ, so it is a prophecy of what the Jews did to Christ, and in this respect it is considered one of the Messianic psalms.
6- This psalm resembles the psalms (Ps 50, 75, 81) in that their writer is Asaph, and we also see in them God Himself speaking as a just Judge.
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
1- God standeth in the congregation of God; he judgeth among the gods.

1- God standeth in the congregation of God, and he means heaven where the angels and the saints stand before Him. And He also calls them gods: because they took of His Spirit, and He is the living God. So it is an honoring and exalting of His creation by Him. And all are subject to Him, and He judges with justice. This is an example of true judgment for the judges of the earth to follow.

2- The congregation of God is also His people to whom He gave His commandments and His Law, and He called them the congregation of God; because they alone believe in Him in the midst of the world. And He also called them gods as a kind of honor to them, as Christ interpreted in the New Testament and declared that God calls the children of His people gods to honor them (Jn 10:34). And what may be meant by the gods is the leaders in the children of Israel.
3- The word God here is originally, in Hebrew, Elohim, which is plural, and of course means the Holy Trinity.
2- How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.
Unjustly: wrongfully

1- God rebukes the judges of the children of Israel who judge with injustice, that is, they wrong the innocent and do justice to the wicked wrongdoers, that is, He calls them to stop this unjust judgment, and to return to divine justice and upright judgment. And the act of injustice is an evil thing, but worse than it is judging with injustice; because it is the codifying and establishing of injustice, for the wicked goes further in wronging the innocent, and encourages others to fall into the sin of injustice, and the seizing of the rights of the innocent.
2- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for a person to review himself concerning the injustice into which he falls, or the unjust judgments, that he may repent of them.
3- Judge for the lowly and the fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. 4- Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.

1- God requires the judges to have compassion on the weak person, such as the lowly, the orphan and the poor; for what he suffers of troubles in life is enough for him, and he needs the judge who does him justice and delivers him from the hand of the wrongdoer, so it is never right that we add to the troubles he suffers also injustice in judgment. And because the weak has no support, the judge is to be the image of God supporting this weak one and doing him justice.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; that is, He had the appearance of weakness, but sadly the judges of the children of Israel, and its priests and its leaders wronged Him, and condemned Him to death, although He is righteous and holy.

Do not hasten to judge others, and do not be emotionally influenced by the words of those around you so that you honor those you love at the expense of others. Be just and speak what pleases God, and then God will also judge justly for you, and will not let people wrong you. For God has mercy on the one who has mercy on others, and forsakes the unjust, so people wrong them.
5- They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.

1- The unjust, wrongful judges have immersed themselves in their sins, and walk in them like one who lives in darkness, and consequently sees nothing, so he does not know and does not understand. And he is ignorant by his own will, for he refuses to be with God so as to be enlightened and judge with justice. And by this injustice with which the wicked judges rule they shake the foundations of the earth; because the wronged will cry out to the just God who founded the earth on justice, and they by their evil have changed the divine order.

2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ whom the Jews condemned unjustly, so they crucified Him and were immersed in spiritual ignorance, so they did not know and did not understand the truth declared to them, and did not take notice when the earth shook and quaked during the crucifixion of Christ.
6- I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.

1- God rebukes the judges and says to them, I called you gods and sons of the Most High, that is, I raised you to a high position, so that you do the work of God, for God alone is the Judge of the whole earth: that is, I gave you the authority of judging people, and called you My sons, so how do you judge an evil judgment and wrong people and show partiality?

2- If God honored the judges and leaders, and called them gods and sons of the Most High, then it was strange that the Jews were troubled by Christ because He declared that God is His Father. For if the judges are gods and sons of the Most High, then all the more Christ, who appeared as a teacher with authority, and a worker of miracles that no one had done with such power.

3- Christ became incarnate to lift us up to Himself, for He took what is ours, that is, our body, and gave us what is His, that is, the blessings and works of His divinity, such as judging, and so we all became gods who offer the sacrifices of our lips before God in prayers and praises, and sons of the Most High by our spiritual conduct, and He even gave us authority over the world to judge it by our upright conduct without our knowing it, and authority also in some situations, as Moses was a god to Pharaoh (Ex 7:1), that is, he commands him with God's commands and Pharaoh submits.
7- But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.

If the judges forget their great position that God gave them, and do not judge with truth, they die in their sins, and fall in humiliation like the leaders who fell, and died the worst of deaths, among them King Saul, upon whom an unclean spirit came and who died in the war with the Philistines, and likewise Pharaoh in the days of Moses who was drowned in the Red Sea, and also the angels who fell from heaven, that is, the demons, who were leaders of the rank of the cherubim.
8- Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.

1- Since the judges left the truth and passed unjust judgments, there was no solution left but for God Himself to intervene and arise, after having been silent, to judge their unjust judgments and their evils; because God is the Owner of the whole earth, so He rescues His wronged children and restores their rights to them. And the stories are many of God's intervening to do justice to the wronged, such as His bringing the children of Israel out of Egypt, and rescuing David from the hand of Saul.
2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who rises from the dead after completing the redemption, and then comes to judge the whole earth on the great Day of Judgment.
Remember that you are a son of God by adoption; that you may walk well according to God's commandments, and so be a light to the world, and salt of the earth.
God destroys the wicked. A song. A psalm of Asaph. "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God) "... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David the prophet.
2- When was it written?
a- In the days of David, and it speaks of the peoples who rose against David, but he was victorious over them by the power of God.

b- It was written in the days of David, but it is a prophecy about the peoples who attacked the king of Judah (2 Chr 20), and they are mentioned here in this psalm among the peoples hostile to God's people, and they are Moab, Edom and the children of Ammon (vv. 6, 7).
3- This is the last of the twelve psalms that Asaph wrote, and they are (Ps 50, 73-83).

4- We find in the title of this psalm the word song; because it is a communal lament that shows the suffering of God's people from the peoples hostile to it, and its crying out to God to rescue it from them.

5- If the previous psalm speaks about internal troubles in the midst of God's people through unjust judgment, then this psalm speaks about external troubles from the surrounding peoples hostile to God's people.
6- This psalm is suitable for the Church, or any human soul that the wicked or the demons attack, so it flees to God to rescue it from their conspiracies.
7- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God.

1- The psalmist speaks here in the voice of God's people who see the plots of the enemies surrounding them. So he says to Him: Though I in my weakness am silent, You do not be silent, but speak, for one word from Your mouth drives all the wicked away from me.

2- The enemies are not only the peoples surrounding God's people, but this psalm is a symbol of the enemies who fight God's people in the New Testament, whether those who live alongside them from among non-Christians or those who are in their midst such as the heretics..
2- For, lo, thine enemies roar: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head. 3- They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy protected ones.
Roar: they make loud noises like the sound of waves dashing in a troubled sea. Protected ones: those whom You protect.

1- The enemies of God's people gathered to wrong them; therefore he said "have lifted up the head", for they have one head, who is Satan and evil, and they make loud, unintelligible noises, that is, they have no argument in their agitation against God's people, but it is something that has filled their hearts against the innocent people of God, and we see in these enemies many evils, which are:
a- They gathered in great numbers to fight God's people.
b- They were proud toward God's people; for they lifted up the head.
c- They were malicious, so they devised plots with cunning in secret against God's people.
d- They held many consultations and plots in order to inflict great harm on the children of God.

2- The psalmist evokes God's mercies, for he says to Him that these wicked are Your enemies and haters; so that God may arise and defend His people, especially since they were bold and made light of God in wronging His people.

4- They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance. 5- For they have consulted together with one heart: they are confederate against thee:

1- These enemies united together to destroy God's people, and to remove its name from among the peoples. And they made a covenant among themselves on this; that is, they are insistent on their evil, and forgot that they are defying God, before whom no one can stand.
2- These verses are a prophecy of what happens from the demons and the wicked against the Church, but all their plots fail because God protects His Church and His children.

6- The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes; 7- Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek; the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre; 8- Assur also is joined with them: they have holpen the children of Lot. Selah. Asaph mentions a number of peoples hostile to God's people, showing their multitude, and consequently the difficulty of their wars, but because God protects His children, David was able to be victorious over all the peoples around him. And these peoples are:
1- Edom: they are the descendants of Esau, and they dwell on the mountains of Seir which extend from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba, and they lived in tents.
2- The Ishmaelites: the descendants of Ishmael the son of Abraham by Hagar, and they are tribes that move in the desert between Egypt and the Persian Gulf.
3- Moab: they are the descendants of Lot and dwelt east of the Dead Sea.
4- The Hagarenes: tribes attributed to Hagar who live east of Gilead, which lies east of the River Jordan.
5- Gebal: these are the mountain tribes that lived in the northern part of the mountains of Seir where the Edomites lived.
6- The Ammonites: they too are descendants of Lot and lived east of the River Jordan and north of Moab.
7- Amalek: tribes that lived in the regions between the north of the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean Sea.
8- The Philistines: they lived east of the Mediterranean Sea along the coast.
9- Tyre: the greatest commercial city in the world, situated on the northeastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea.

10- Assyria: a great state whose capital was Nineveh, situated on the River Tigris in northern Iraq, but it gradually weakened, and Babylon took its place, and the children of Lot, who are the two peoples Moab and the children of Ammon mentioned above, sought its help to fight God's people.

Do not be troubled by the multitude of enemies and the wars of the demons, for they are worthless before the power of God who protects you. Only hold fast to your prayers, and be steadfast in your Church and your Holy Sacraments.

entries.section: (2) A request for the intervention of G

paragraphs.text: 9- Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: 10- Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth. 11- Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna: 12- Who said, Let us take to ourselves the habitations of God in possession.
Dung: the droppings and waste of beasts.

Asaph asks God to destroy the enemies of His people, as He did of old in the age of the Judges when He destroyed the Midianites by the hand of Gideon (Judg 7, 8), and as He destroyed Jabin king of Canaan and the commander of his army Sisera at the River Kishon, which lies in the north of the land of the Jews toward Galilee. And these enemies fled in the region of En-dor, which is near Megiddo, which lies south of the Sea of Galilee. And their corpses became fertilizer for the earth. And he asked also that God destroy the leaders of the enemies, as He destroyed of old the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, and likewise the kings of Midian, such as Zebah and Zalmunna. These were those who tried to occupy and possess the land of the children of Israel. In sum, he believes in God and His power able to destroy the enemies, and as He did of old He does today.

entries.section: (2) A request for the intervention of G

paragraphs.text: 13- O my God, make them like the jall, as the stubble before the wind. 14- As the fire burneth the rugged ground, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; 15- So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm.
The jall: it is straw mixed with the droppings of beasts, formed into discs and dried in the sun, and it is used for burning for heating and for lighting ovens.

Asaph asks God to put an end to the enemies, and make them nothing by His great power, like the jall, and to scatter them like stubble before the wind, and burn them with the fire of God, like the rugged ground and the mountains. And by rugged ground he means rocky places on which wild trees grow, and likewise the mountains planted with dry plants, all this burns with the flame of God. And they are also scattered by the power of God, which he likens to the tempest and the storm, so that the enemies may feel their weakness before God and His overwhelming power.

entries.section: (2) A request for the intervention of G

paragraphs.text: 16- Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD.

When the enemies are put to shame and are ashamed of their weakness before God, this calls them to believe in the power of God and to return to Him and leave their sins. And this shows the compassion of Asaph, or of the children of God, toward the enemies, for they seek their salvation through divine discipline; they do not hate them and want vengeance on them, but wish their return to God by faith and repentance.

entries.section: (2) A request for the intervention of G

paragraphs.text: 17- Let them be confounded and troubled for ever; yea, let them be put to shame, and perish: 18- That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth. But if the enemies refuse to believe in God and to turn from their sins, nothing remains for them but eternal shame and torment, and then they will know that God alone rules over all things, and they will live in their weakness and humiliation forever.

Satan wants to possess your heart and make you completely subject to him, so do not make peace with him or accept any of his evil lusts, but drive him away, by prayer, humility, and faith in God who dwells in you and is able to protect you. Dwelling in the house of the Lord. To the chief Musician upon Gittith. For the sons of Korah. A psalm. "How sweet are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!"
Introduction:
1- Its writer:

a- The sons of Korah, who did not die with their father Korah when the earth split open and swallowed the rebels (Num 26:11), and they served as doorkeepers of the Tabernacle of Meeting, and then the temple. And they wrote ten psalms, which are (Ps 44-Ps 48) and (Ps 84-Ps 88), and all of them are psalms that call to joy and enjoyment of fellowship with the Lord. So while divine punishment fell upon their father Korah because of his rebellion, God rewarded the sons of Korah and gave them the joy and peace which appear in these psalms that they wrote; because they did not take part in the rebellion against God.

b- David the prophet, who fled from the house of the Lord because of Saul's pursuit of him, and who longed to return to it, and was joyful on his return to worship, and even longed to build a house for the Lord.

2- This psalm used to be said to the accompaniment of the Gittith, a musical instrument resembling the zither, which was known in the city of Gath, one of the five great Philistine cities, and the Gittith may have been a musical tune that was famous in Gath.
3- We see in the title the word psalm, which means that these words are accompanied by a pipe.

4- This psalm is suitable for every person who longs to worship in the house of the Lord and rejoices to be in it. It is an encouragement to the hearts of those who love God and are attached to His house.
5- This psalm is a prophecy about the captives taken by Assyria, then Babylon, who are far from God's temple and long to return to it.

6- This psalm gives hope to everyone whose circumstances are difficult and whose family is far from God, for in spite of the destruction of Korah, his sons were attached to the service of the house of the Lord, and wrote this psalm full of longings for the worship of God.
7- This psalm gives longings for God's eternal dwellings, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, which is higher than all our earthly life.
8- This psalm expresses the longings of all those who are prevented from reaching the house of God because of their particular circumstances, such as illness.

9- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Sixth Hour in the Agpeya, in which the soul expresses its longing to dwell with God in His house, after Christ completed the redemption and reconciled the heavenly beings with the earthly, by His crucifixion at the time of the sixth hour.

entries.section: (1) The sweetness of the house of G

paragraphs.text: 1- How sweet are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!

1- The psalmist expresses his feelings toward the house of the Lord by saying how sweet; that is, he cannot describe the sweetness of the house of the Lord; because God Himself dwells in it, and so whoever comes to the house of the Lord meets God Himself, and enjoys His fellowship, and receives His blessing. He also feels his weakness before the greatness of God; therefore he describes Him as the Lord of hosts. And so a person is reverent and humble before God.

2- He said the tabernacles of the Lord of hosts and did not say tabernacle; because in the days of David there were two tabernacles, one in Jerusalem in which was the Ark of the Covenant, and the other in Gibeon, in which were the remaining contents of the Tabernacle of Meeting. And this verse can be a prophecy about the churches of the New Testament, for they are tabernacles and not one tabernacle, as it was in the Old Testament. And it may be a prophecy about the hearts of believers in the New Testament, which become temples of the Holy Spirit, and likewise it is a prophecy about eternal life, where there are many mansions, or dwellings.

entries.section: (1) The sweetness of the house of G

paragraphs.text: 2- My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God.

1- The feelings of the spiritual person move toward the house of the Lord because God dwells in it, and even faint, that is, long intensely to reach the house of the Lord to enjoy seeing Him. And this means that the heart has been freed from the attachments of the world and its enticements, so that what controls the heart is the love of God. And it also means a person's faith that there is a special blessing in the house of the Lord, and a divine indwelling and grace not found outside this place, and this is our faith to this day that there is no salvation outside the Church, as St. Augustine said, and a person cannot substitute for the Church any other place such as the private chamber; for in the Church a person receives the Holy Sacraments, and knows God and is united with Him.

2- Then the person moves with his whole being, that is, his heart and his body (his flesh) to enjoy fellowship with God. After the spiritual person believed that God is the only Being who lives forever; since the pagan gods are all dead idols, and also all the powers of the world are passing away.

entries.section: (1) The sweetness of the house of G

paragraphs.text: 3- Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God.
Swallow: a small bird with two large wings and a beautiful voice, swift in flight.

1- The psalmist expresses his wandering in the midst of the world, and his need for settledness, and he finds no comfortable and settled place for himself except the altars of God, and by this he means the bronze altar and the altar of incense in the Tabernacle of Meeting, and then in Solomon's temple. And it is a prophecy about the churches and their altars in the New Testament, where a person enjoys partaking of the Holy Mysteries that are on the altars. And he likens himself to small birds, such as the sparrow and the swallow which search for nests or houses to settle in, and at last found a place for themselves in the house of the Lord and its courts around it; and the sparrow and the swallow are among the clean birds in the Law of Moses, and they are a symbol of the souls that dwell in and draw near to the house of the Lord, which must be pure to enjoy its blessings.

2- The writer feels that God is his King and his God, and this shows the boldness of sonship that he has, which draws his heart to the house of the Lord. And these words are a prophecy about Christ the King and the true God of the soul that believes in Him, who gives it enjoyment in His Church of all spiritual blessings.

entries.section: (1) The sweetness of the house of G

paragraphs.text: 4- Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be ever praising thee. Selah.
