1- 1- After the psalmist has expressed the sweetness of God's house and the longing for it, he shows the great happiness that those who dwell in the house of the Lord receive, and it is noticed that in the Tabernacle of Meeting and Solomon's temple there was no dwelling of people in it, but he prophesies about the Church where believers settle in it by their attachment to the Holy Sacraments, and then by their continued steadfastness in the Church in its prayers and praises they become worthy of the eternal dwelling in the Kingdom of Heaven, where they praise God forever, sharing with the heavenly beings in the praise of God.
2- These verses end with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on the sweetness of the house of the Lord, being satisfied by fellowship with God, and praising His holy name
Hasten to the Church to meet God in His house. He is waiting for you to embrace you and satisfy you, so that your heart rejoices, and your prayers and praises increase.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 5- Blessed are the people whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of thy house.

1- The psalm shows the happiness of those who believe in God, and calls them blessed because their strength is God, and that is by keeping His commandments in their hearts and lives, for these are the ways of the house of the Lord in their hearts, so that the feelings of their hearts lift them above earthly things, attached to God, so they long not only for the house of the Lord that is on earth, but also for the heavenly house which is the Kingdom of Heaven.

2- The psalm calls blessed the believers who boast in God; because they loved Him more than everything in the world, so that material things and honor have become passing in their eyes, and nothing greater than God remains for them to boast in, and they remain in their love for God by keeping His commandments, these are the ways of God's house that are in their hearts, and by this they love everyone around them too.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 6- Passing through the valley of weeping, they make it a spring; yea, with blessings they cover Moreh.
Moreh: the early rain that falls in the autumn. It is necessary for watering the crop at the beginning of its life.

1- The psalm shows the means by which believers receive God's blessings. It declares that this takes place through their passing through the valley of weeping, which is one of the roads leading to Jerusalem, and it was very dry; so that whoever walked in it was exposed to death by thirst. Therefore they used to dig pits around it which filled with rain water; to help the one walking on the road to drink from them. That is, whoever passes on the road to Jerusalem to worship and bow down to God bears sufferings and prays and his tears flow, but if he perseveres on the road his heart becomes a spring of water full of blessings; because God pours out upon him many graces as the early rains pour upon the crop, so whoever strives and bears sufferings the Holy Spirit pours out upon him many blessings, like the rains of Moreh, and even more, so blessings are given him from every side.

2- The valley of weeping is the tears of repentance that become like a spring of water welling up from the heart of the penitent, turning the dryness of his heart into abundant waters, and his life is filled with divine blessings. So here he calls the penitent blessed and promises them all God's blessings.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 7- They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God.

1- Then the psalm declares a new blessing for the striving believers, that they advance from strength to strength, that is, they are not only strong, but their strength increases gradually through their spiritual striving and their victories, so they receive more and more grace, and likewise acquire virtue after virtue. And more than this, when they show their faithfulness in spiritual striving on earth, and receive divine strength supporting them, they are lifted up after this to heaven; to receive great strength, so they are propelled into a strong relationship with God that makes their souls rejoice forever.

2- And after this a new blessing that believers receive, which is that they are seen before God in Zion, and he means Jerusalem where the house of the Lord is, so they enjoy not only the worship of God, but God sees them, and he did not say that they see God; for their seeing God gives them enjoyment of the sweetness of His fellowship, but God's seeing them gives them care, love, and inexpressible joy, which is a pledge of what they receive in the Kingdom of Heaven.

The heavenly Kingdom is available to you here on earth if you draw near to God in His house to behold His glory through His Holy Sacraments. And when you lift up prayers before Him, His mercies and blessings pour out upon you. Take care lest the devil hinder you from being constantly in His Church.
8- O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer: give ear, O God of Jacob. Selah.

1- After the believer has received blessings in the house of the Lord, he asks Him to hear his prayer. And he gives God the title Lord of hosts, that is, the mighty One, able to do all things, and consequently He can answer all his requests. Then he advances to a higher degree, and asks that God give ear to him. And he gives Him here the title God of Jacob; because He is the God who appeared of old to Jacob on the ladder reaching up to heaven. So the believer rises above his material and spiritual requests to ask to see God Himself, as Jacob saw Him. And God is the same yesterday, today and forever, so He is not only with Jacob, but with all his descendants who walk with God as he did. And by this the psalm lifts us from material worship such as sacrifices to spiritual worship that requires seeing God, and enjoying being in His presence.
2- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical extension for a person to meditate on the sweetness of seeing God.
9- Behold, O God our buckler, and look upon the face of thine Anointed.

Our buckler: the buckler is the large shield. And the shield is a wooden piece with a loop at the back in which the soldier puts his hand, and he moves this wooden piece before his face and his body to protect him from the arrows of the enemy. So it is a defensive instrument of war to protect the soldier.

1- Believers look to God as their protection, for He is not only a shield for them but a buckler, that is, a large shield, representing complete protection. So they call on God and give Him the title "our buckler" and ask Him to look upon them; because they are confident of His love, so when He looks upon them, He stretches out His hand and protects them from all enemies. And this shows that they feel wars surrounding them, and need God to protect them.

2- If the writer of the psalm is David, he asks God to look upon him; because he is the anointed king over his people, and he asks merely for God's turning to him, for this gives him all the protection he needs. And this verse is also a prophecy about Christ who speaks to the Father as in His intercessory prayer (Jn 17), and asks for the turning toward Him during the sufferings He endured at His arrest and crucifixion; to declare that they were real sufferings. And it is also a prophecy about the believers in the New Testament who ask God to turn to Christ who dwells in them, as they are anointed with the Myron for the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in them, and they are members of the Body of Christ who is the Head and the face. And they intercede through Christ in all their petitions; because without Christ they have no acceptance before the Father.
10- For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I have chosen to stand at the threshold in the house of my God rather than dwell in the tents of the wicked.

1- The psalm declares that spending one day in the house of the Lord, that is, in prayer, worship, and enjoyment of fellowship with God, is better than a thousand days that a person spends in the midst of the passing pleasures of the world far from God. And the one day is the day of the Resurrection, which surpasses the thousands of days in the Old Testament in which humanity awaited the salvation of God. And the one day is the last day of the Lord, in which the believers enter into the glories of eternal life, which is better than a thousand days in earthly life. And the one day is eternity itself; because eternity is day without night, so it is one day better than a thousand days on earth.

2- The psalm also declares that standing at the threshold of the house of the Lord is better than sitting and settling in the tents of the wicked, and by this he means the places of the world with all its lusts. Because standing at the door of the house of the Lord gives a person enjoyment of God's blessing and the sense of His presence. And perhaps the sons of Korah, who were charged with guarding the doors of the house of the Lord, felt the greatness of their position and its blessing; because they stand always before God, and this is better than any other place in the world, indeed this is true settledness; because being in the presence of God is life and being far from Him is death.
11- For the LORD God is a sun and buckler: the LORD will give mercy and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.

1- The psalm describes God as a sun, that is, He is the One who shines upon His children, and upon the whole world, to give them an illumined way that brings them to Him. For He guides everyone who desires to live with Him, for He is the Sun of righteousness. And He is also the buckler, that is, the Protector of His children from all the wars of the devil.

2- And God gives mercy to His children by forgiving their sins and accepting their repentance, and also grants them the glory of life with Him, so they are adorned with virtue. And this glory that they enjoy on earth is a pledge of the eternal glory that cannot be expressed. And God by nature is good, that is, the source of all good in the world; therefore He does not withhold good from His children, but pours it out upon them, to satisfy them and draw them to His Kingdom.

12- O LORD of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee. The psalm ends with the blessing of the person who trusts in God, that is, the one who repents of his sins; so that he received God's mercies and forgiveness, and then enjoyed His glories, and the highest glory is seeing God, and enjoying His fellowship. And God, the Lord of hosts, is strong and able to keep those who trust in Him in constant enjoyment of Him on earth as long as they hold fast to Him, and then forever in His heavenly Kingdom.
I wish you would give priority to going to church over all your ties in the world. Then you will enjoy the sense of God's presence, and receive blessings without end.
The mercies of God. To the chief Musician. For the sons of Korah. A psalm. "LORD, thou hast been favourable unto thy land) "... v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: the sons of Korah, who did not take part in the rebellion of their father Korah against the priesthood, so they lived and God blessed them.
2- When was it written? It was written after the first return from the captivity, and before the completion of the return of the following groups of returnees.

3- This psalm recalls God's former mercies to His people, and asks the completion of His mercies in the present for the return from the captivity, and the completion of the building of the temple and Jerusalem and its walls. And it hopes for the continuance of God's mercies in the future.
4- This psalm is a prophecy about the liberation from the captivity and bondage of the devil by Christ the Redeemer; and therefore it is considered one of the Messianic psalms.
5- This psalm is suitable for the soul that has begun repentance and received God's forgiveness, so it asks His help to complete its repentance and live a new life with God.
6- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Sixth Hour in which we remember the crucifixion of Christ and His cry that frees us from the captivity of Satan and binds him.
1- Lord, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob.

1- After the people of God tasted the humiliation of bondage in captivity, they repented and returned to God, so God was pleased with them, and consequently was pleased with the land He had given to His people, the land of Canaan, for they had defiled it with their sins, and the Assyrians and Babylonians destroyed it. But it was sanctified by the repentance of His people and by His consequent pleasure in their land. The writer of the Psalm says “thy land” because God is the Creator of the earth and of the whole world, and He is also the Giver of the land of Canaan to His people, and it was He who sanctified it by the presence of His temple in it.

2- The Psalm thanks God, who began to bring His people back from captivity at the hand of Zerubbabel, which was the first return. It thanks Him for gathering His people from the dispersion and bringing them back by the authority of the king himself, to dwell in their land and to build the temple of God. The Psalm says “the captivity of Jacob” and not Israel, because Jacob was the righteous one, of whom the Scripture bore witness that he was a perfect man dwelling in tents (Gen 25:27). Then God blessed him by the hand of Isaac and appeared to him on the ladder reaching up to heaven, then spoke to him many times, and appeared to him afterward at Penuel, and rescued him from the hand of Esau. He is beloved by God, and therefore his offspring return to the land that was promised to Jacob, that is, God brings back the captivity of Jacob.

3- This verse is a prophecy of God's good pleasure in the world, and of His redemption by the Cross so that His children who believe in Him might return from the captivity of Satan after He bound him.
2- Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah.

1- When the people of God repented in captivity, God forgave them all their iniquities and sins, for God longs for His people to return to Him. He covered all their evil deeds and blotted them out, so that they did not appear to men, for He is a compassionate God who desires not only the salvation of His people but also to glorify them before the rest of the peoples, while hiding their sins.

2- Although God forgave His captive people, it was in the hope of their redemption by the Cross, so the forgiveness was not completed except by Christ, who forgave and covered, and still covers and forgives the sins of His people when they repent.
3- The word “Selah” is a musical pause for meditating on the mercies of God and His forgiveness.
3- Thou hast taken away all thy wrath: thou hast turned thyself from the fierceness of thine anger.

God is holy and just, and He is repelled by and angry at any sin. Repentance stops the wrath of God and looses all the bonds of indignation, which is the intense anger, so that man enjoys the peace of God, His love and His care. This is what happened to the repentant captives, and it was completed by the redemption of Christ.

How great you are, O repentance, you who break all the shackles of sin and release those who believe in you into the new life with God, so that they enjoy His fellowship. Therefore, O my soul, do not let repentance leave you all your life, every day and every hour, for it is your helper and it opens the arms of God.

entries.section: (2) Asking for the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 4- Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease. 5- Wilt thou be angry with us for ever? wilt thou draw out thine anger to all generations?
“Cause to cease” (anf): make it banished, that is, put it far away.

1- The fatherly feelings of the writer of the Psalm appear, for he rejoiced in God's mercy in the return of some of the people, and he asks God to forgive the rest, that is, to move them to repentance, and to forgive them and bring them back to Him, and consequently His anger is lifted from them, for God is merciful and does not wish His anger to last from generation to generation and for ever.

2- If God's anger, which appears in disciplining His people with afflictions such as captivity, is a very heavy matter, how much more severe must His anger be in eternal torment! Therefore today we cry out with all our hearts that God may accept our repentance and lift His anger from us, so that we may return to our sonship to Him and enjoy His care.

entries.section: (2) Asking for the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 6- Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee? 7- Shew us thy mercy, O Lord, and grant us thy salvation.

After God lifts His anger and accepts the repentance of His people, He gives them life with Him, which is true happiness and joy. This is the divine salvation and mercy, which was completed in Christ the Redeemer, who raised us to fellowship with Him and to joy in Him on earth, after He removed our sins from us by His blood, that we might enjoy the earnest of the heavenly Kingdom. This salvation and this mercy are what we receive today through the Holy Sacraments in the Church of the New Testament.

1- David prayed for his enemies, but his prayer returned to his bosom, that is, God rejoiced in David's prayer and blessed him with good, but did not answer his prayer, because of the evil of his enemies.

2- The return of the prayer to David's bosom moved his heart to pray again, and thus he lived in what is called constant prayer, so that he said of himself, “but I give myself unto prayer” (Ps 109:4).
3- Christ prayed for those who crucified Him while He was on the Cross, that God might forgive them, but they did not benefit, because of their insistence on evil and their unbelief.

Enjoy true joy in being with God in prayer and meditation, for life is in Christ, while the joys of the world are vain and passing. And abide in His Church and its Sacraments, and you will live in salvation for ever.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 8- I will hear what God the Lord will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly.

1- The writer of the Psalm hears the voice of God through the prophets who speak to the people, especially to those among them who fear God, so that they may remain firm in faith and in the fear of God and not return to the foolishness of sin and to conduct that turns away from God in the worship of idols, or any evil conduct. The condition for hearing the voice of God and benefiting from it is the fear of God, which keeps man away from sin.

2- The voice of God is Christ, who became incarnate in the fullness of time to proclaim salvation to all mankind, especially to those who fear God, whether Jews or Gentiles, so that they believe in Him and do not return to the folly of sin.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 9- Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land.

1- Whoever fears God keeps His commandments, therefore God draws near to him and grants him His salvation, that is, saves him from his sins and pours His blessings upon him, and even is glorified in him, and this glory dwells and settles in the children of God, because it is manifest in their works and in their lives, which glorify God.

2- Salvation is accomplished by Christ, and it is near to those who fear God and await the expected Messiah. The writer of the Psalm saw, in the spirit of prophecy, that the Incarnation of Christ had become near, and that He would come and give salvation to those who fear the Lord, and thus glory dwells in our land through the Incarnation of Christ upon it.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 10- Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

1- In Christ Jesus mercy and truth, which is justice, were fulfilled. For truth requires the death of the sinner, and mercy requires that death be lifted from him. So Christ died and rose from the dead, to remove our sins from us, and that we might receive mercy in Him.

2- Likewise in Christ righteousness and peace kissed each other, that is, each accepted the other and they were united, and Christ even gave them to everyone who believes in Him. So the believer has peace, and an inclination toward righteousness, that is, toward doing good and what is right.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 11- Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven.

1- The Truth is Christ, who springs out of the earth by His Incarnation. And Christ is God who came down from heaven, or He is the righteousness that dawned on us from heaven. So the One who is on earth is at the same time the One who is from heaven.

2- Our faith in the Truth, who is Christ, springs up within us, that is, we live the faith in Christ, and then righteousness looks down on us, that is, by faith we are able to live righteousness and to live as heavenly beings on earth, walking in the Spirit and adorning ourselves with virtues.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 12- Yea, the Lord shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase.

God is the Giver of good to His children, that is, He gives them the inclination to do good, for God renews the nature of His children in the Sacrament of Baptism, so that it has an inclination to become like God, to keep His commandments, and to serve others. And thus the good increase of the land appears, that is, the spiritual fruits; that is, unless God gives the inclination to do good we cannot bear spiritual fruits. And God gives all people this gift and waits for our response to Him.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercies of God

paragraphs.text: 13- Righteousness shall go before him; and shall tread in the way of his steps.

1- Righteousness here is repentance, which goes before Christ so that He may dwell in the hearts of His children. And by this He tramples every evil in the believing soul, and Christ dwells in the heart and fills it with peace and joy.

2- Righteousness is also Christ, who walks before the Father and tramples sin and its consequence, which is death. By His death He trampled death on the Cross, and rose and ascended into the heavens, and opened the way for those who believe in Him, that they may enter heaven.

Repentance is your way to eternity, so live in it every day and you will receive the blessings of heaven and feel Christ in your life, and taste the sweetness of eternity while you are on earth, and live in a joy that lasts for ever. A prayer and thanksgiving. A prayer of David. “Bow down thine ear, O Lord, hear me ...” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet.
2- When was it written? When David was pursued from the face of Saul, or from the face of Absalom his son.
3- It suits the soul that needs God, or that is in distress but whose faith in Him is strong; this prayer supports it and gives it hope.
4- This Psalm is liturgical, and it used to be chanted by the Levites and the people on the great Day of Atonement, which is a type of Good Friday.

5- This Psalm is a comprehensive prayer, that is, it includes petition, repentance, thanksgiving and praise. It is many-sided, showing that David is a man of prayer, and encouraging everyone who loves prayer, as it covers the different aspects of his life.

6- This Psalm is found in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ was crucified, because it is full of prayers and supplications from a needy, repentant heart, looking to Christ the Redeemer to answer him, save him from his enemies, and gladden his heart. This Psalm also represents the prayers of the suffering Christ on the Cross, who by His death triumphed over Satan and bound him, and trampled death by His death.
1- Bow down thine ear, O Lord, hear me: for I am poor and needy.

1- David asks God to condescend and incline His ear, because He is the great God, exalted above all His creation. And David declares that he is poor and needy, because he is weak, a sinner, and driven out of Jerusalem. Consequently he does not enjoy the worship of God in His house, and he feels his need of God. Therefore he asks Him to listen to him and incline His ear, that is, to take interest in his prayer and answer him. This shows David's humility and his declaration of his great need.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, humble and suffering on the Cross, who declares before the Father that He took the form of poverty and misery for the redemption of mankind, and asks the Father, as a man, to condescend, to listen to Him and to answer Him.
2- Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee.

1- David declares that the reason for his godliness is his trust in God, and because he fears God and trusts in Him, he asks God to preserve him from the wicked who want to destroy him. At the same time he defends himself before the wicked who accuse him of evil and pursue him, so he says to God: I fear You and revere You, and I am not as they accuse me, and I am Your servant, submissive to You and trusting in You.

2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ the godly, or the righteous, who trusts in God, who took the form of a servant by His Incarnation, and asks the Father to preserve Him before the cruelty of the wicked who crucified Him, in order to confirm His humanity.
3- Be merciful unto me, O Lord: for I cry unto thee all the day.

This verse shows the extent of David's suffering, for afflictions surrounded him all day long and for a long period, so he cried out to God asking for His mercy, for He was his only hope and the compassionate heart able to embrace him however great the evils of his enemies. Thus David continued to cry out to God for many years until prayer became habitual, and his whole life became prayer, and the responsibilities of kingship did not keep him from God. He was anointed king since he was a boy, and Saul pursued him, and then after he reigned Absalom drove him out; through all this he continued to cry out asking for the mercy of God.
4- Rejoice the soul of thy servant: for unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.

David trusts in God not only to preserve him during the affliction but also to gladden his heart. And David strove and struggled by lifting his heart to God, that is, he rose above the preoccupations of the world, its desires and its cares, seeking the vision of God that gives him joy.
5- For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.
David concludes this part of his prayer by showing the attributes of God that encouraged him to make the preceding petitions. These attributes are:
1- That He is good, so He is not pleased with the evils directed against David.
2- That He is forgiving, which encourages David to draw near to God, who is able to forgive his sins, and this shows David's confession that he is a sinner in need of forgiveness.
3- That He is plenteous in mercy, so He cares for David the poor, driven out by the wicked and in need of the mercy of God.

The mercies of God encourage you to draw near to Him however great your sins, and however great your weakness, He cares for you, keeps you and protects you from every evil, and even gives you peace and gladdens your heart, so rejoice and do not hesitate, for He loves you.
6- Give ear, O Lord, unto my prayer; and attend to the voice of my supplications.

David draws near to God with humility, asking Him to hear his prayer and his supplications. And out of his great need he says “give ear” and “attend,” because his sufferings are many, and he needs God to listen to them carefully and rescue him from them. It is clear that he prays many times, since he says “supplications,” because his sufferings are successive, but his hope in God is confident.
7- In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me.

David experienced God's support in his life and was assured in taking refuge in Him, so when trouble comes upon him he calls on God quickly, and He answers him. He has learned and become accustomed to seek God in every trouble, and He rescues him from it.
8- Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works.

God's intervention to rescue His children in the hour of trouble is a very powerful intervention, because He is God, able to do all things, and He is of course higher than all the pagan gods, who are demons. And His works are greater than any works, as He saved His people from the hand of Pharaoh of Egypt, and later from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria.
9- All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name.
10- For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone.

The power of God manifested in His people before the rest of the peoples draws these peoples, that is, the Gentiles, to faith, and they declare their faith by coming to Jerusalem and worshiping God, who is great and does wondrous things. His greatest wonders are His Incarnation, His redemption and His Resurrection, in addition to His many miracles, which strengthen the faith of His people and of the Gentiles who believe in Him, and thus the Church is formed of the Jews and the victorious Gentiles.

If the works of God are mighty and wondrous, do not be troubled if any affliction or problems face you, for your God is able to do all things; He will rescue you and keep you, and even grant you a peace that surpasses all understanding.
3- Thanksgiving to God (vv. 11 - 13):
11- Teach me thy way, O Lord; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name.

1- David asks God to teach him His way. And the way is Christ, that is: give me, O God, Your knowledge, especially since God cannot be known without His support, and when I know You I will be able to walk in Your truth, which is to keep away from sin and to acquire purity of heart, and on the other hand to walk in the different virtues, which is the spiritual life as it is lived.

2- David also asks God to unite his heart to fear Him, so that it is not a heart divided between the love of the world and the love of God, but his aim is the fear of God, so he rejects all evil, and then he is enlightened spiritually and enjoys fellowship with God.
12- I will praise thee, O Lord my God, with all my heart: and I will glorify thy name for evermore.

When David's heart was united in the fear of God, his heart and all his feelings were released to praise God, and since he delighted in it on earth, he longed to remain in it for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven.
13- For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell.

David saw, in the spirit of prophecy, the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption, so he declared that God's mercy toward him is great, which he will receive in the fullness of time, when Christ will bring him up from the lowest hell, for Hades has degrees. So Christ delivers His children from all their sins, even if they were in the depths of Hades, that is, its hardest degrees.

Do not forget to thank God every day for His gifts, for this fills your heart with joy and increases your enjoyment of His gifts, in addition to the abundance of new gifts that God pours out upon you.
4- God the Helper (vv. 14 - 17):
14- O God, the proud are risen against me, and the assemblies of violent men have sought after my soul; and have not set thee before them.

1- David's enemies rose up against him to destroy him, and because they left God they lost the fear of Him, and consequently it became easy for them to wrong others and even kill them, and therefore there was no chance of escape from their hands except by the power of God, for they were tyrants, proud, and persistent in evil.

2- The Jews who rose up against Christ are the proud and the tyrants, who sought the help of the Roman authority and crucified Christ, because they did not fear God, so they killed Christ, but by His power He rose from the dead. The demons also do likewise in their wars against men, but God delivers His children and gives them victory over the demons.
15- But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth.

If the demons and all the wicked who follow them are hard of heart and want to destroy the righteous, because the fear of God is not before them, then God intervenes with His mercy and compassion to protect His children, and even is longsuffering toward them however great their sins, and gives them an opportunity to repent, especially since He fulfilled truth and mercy in the Cross of Christ, for by His redemption He paid the debt of sin, and in His mercy offered salvation to His people.
16- O turn unto me, and have mercy upon me; give thy strength unto thy servant, and save the son of thine handmaid.

1- David asks God to look at him, have mercy on him, and rescue him from the hands of his enemies. And he asks with boldness because he is the servant of God, and the son of His handmaid, that is, one who belongs to Him and was born in His house, and consequently he can enjoy the care and protection of God.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the crucified Christ, who cried out while on the Cross, “My God, my God ...” (Mt 27:46), because He humbled Himself as a man and took the form of a servant, and He is the Son of the Virgin, the handmaid of God, that is, His female servant. He is Son by nature, not like the rest of mankind, who are children by adoption.
17- Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, Lord, hast holpen me, and comforted me.

1- David asks God to work with him a good sign that those around him who hate him may see, so that they are ashamed and confounded, by rescuing David from their hands and glorifying him, and this is what actually happened. And it was repeated with Christ, to whom the Father turned, and in whom the greatest sign in the world appeared, which is His Resurrection from the dead, and the demons were put to shame.

2- Although the whole Psalm asks for God's mercy and help, David declares at the end of the Psalm, with faith and confidence, that God gave him great help and comforted his heart, and after this the grace of God to David was completed after the killing of Absalom, when David returned to his throne with great honor.
Ask with humility everything you want from God, and He will answer you, for He loves the humble and hastens to them, and rescues them from every evil.
Jerusalem, the city of salvation. By the sons of Korah. A Psalm, a song of praise. “His foundation is in the holy mountains ...” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer:
a- The sons of Korah, who did not take part in the rebellion of their father Korah, as we mentioned in the introduction to (Ps 84).
b- David the prophet, who gave it to the sons of Korah to chant.
2- When was it written?

a- In the days of King Hezekiah, when this king took care to restore the temple, especially since Babylon had begun to become famous in those days, and was even close to seizing the world and dominating it, and at that time Egypt was called Rahab, as Isaiah the prophet mentions (Isa 30:7).
b- In the days of David, when he brought the ark of the covenant of God back to Jerusalem and prepared the materials for building the temple that his son Solomon would build.
3- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms that speak to us clearly about the Incarnation of Christ.
4- This Psalm is one of the “Songs of Zion” that glorify Jerusalem, the city of God, such as (Ps 48, Ps 76).
5- This Psalm speaks clearly about the salvation of the Gentiles in Christ Jesus.
6- This Psalm speaks not only about Jerusalem, but about the Church of the New Testament, and the heavenly Jerusalem.

7- The Church chants this Psalm in the greatest of her prayers, the Divine Liturgy, in the days of the Great Fast, immediately before the absolution of the servants, and says it in the Coptic language, “Nef Sinti.”

8- This Psalm is found in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, because in this hour Christ was crucified to save mankind, Jews and Gentiles, and so that the New Jerusalem, that is, the Church, might be open to receive everyone who believes from mankind.
1- His foundation is in the holy mountains.

1- The foundation of God He laid in the holy mountains on which the city of Jerusalem was built, and in which the temple of God was built by the hand of Solomon. God's foundation is faith in Him, or His teachings, or it is Christ Himself, the foundation on which the building of His Church stands, or on which the life of His children who believe in Him stands. The mountains are holy because God sanctified them by dwelling in His temple, and the foundation in the New Testament is also the teaching of the Apostles, and their successors the bishops and priests, and all the servants.

2- Mountains signify steadfastness, and also loftiness and elevation above material things, and on them the temple was built. And the Church of the New Testament is steadfast in Christ and lifted above the world.
2- The Lord loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.

1- The gates of Zion are the gates of the temple, and God loved them more than all the gates and dwellings of Jacob, that is, the dwellings of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, because the kingdom of Judah, in which the city of Jerusalem and its temple lie, was the one that continued to worship God. As for the ten tribes, they worshiped idols after they split and separated, after the reign of Solomon, under Jeroboam the son of Nebat. So God loved Jerusalem because He dwelt in its temple and rejoiced in the worship of His children offered in it. And in Jerusalem godly kings appeared, such as David, Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah, who led their people in the worship of God.

2- The gates of Zion are the Church, which God loved because He founded her with His blood on the Cross, and she is better than all the dwellings of the world, and the gates of Zion are also the Christian virtues.
3- Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah.
1- The glories of the city of God spring from the temple of God that is in it, in which He dwells by His Holy Spirit, blessing the place and everyone who comes to it to worship God.

2- The city of God is the Church, and her glories are Christ, who gives His Body and Blood to His children, and likewise the angels and saints who fill her, for the Church is the house of the angels and the place of the saints, and she is also the heavenly Jerusalem whose glory cannot be expressed.

3- The city of God is also the Virgin Mary, whom the Holy Spirit sanctified, and in whom Christ was born, and to whom God gave many glories which the Midnight Praise expresses in various forms every day in the Theotokia.

4- This passage ends with the word “Selah,” which is a musical tone that gives the chanter and the hearer an opportunity to meditate on the greatness of the Church, in which God dwells by His Spirit, with His angels and saints around Him.

If Jerusalem is holy through its temple, and is a symbol of the Church and of the Virgin, then it is also a symbol of your soul, my brother, in which God has dwelt by His Holy Spirit. If God loves your soul and prefers it to many souls, it is because He dwells in it. And the more you respond to His dwelling by prayer and meditation, He rejoices in you, works in you, and fills you with many blessings.

entries.section: (2) Jerusalem, the salvation and joy of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 4- “I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to them that know me: behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there.”
Rahab: a word meaning pride, and what is meant by it is Egypt.
Tyre: a city on the northern coast of the Mediterranean, and it was the greatest commercial city in ancient times, and was distinguished by wealth.
Cush (Ethiopia): Abyssinia.

The Psalm shows the different peoples of the world at that time, namely Babylon, which became an empire, and Egypt, which was a great empire, and likewise Philistia with its five cities lying on the coast of the Mediterranean, and Tyre, the most important commercial city in the world at that time, and Cush, distinguished by the strength of its men in war. What is meant is that the different countries of the world, with all their distinctions, are where faith in Christ was born, and churches were established in them, and they followed Christ and left their idols and sins. This is the new Jerusalem, the Church of the New Testament, and she is what is meant by the phrase “this man was born there.” So God mentioned all these countries, that is, all the Gentiles in addition to the Jewish people, and in the fullness of time He became incarnate and redeemed them, and gave them salvation, and established His Church everywhere.

entries.section: (2) Jerusalem, the salvation and joy of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 5- And of Zion it shall be said, “This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her.”

The Psalm speaks about Jerusalem, the city of God, and calls it Zion, which is the most important of the mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built, so the name Zion is applied to the city of Jerusalem. This Psalm speaks to her, and says to her that many sons will be born in her one after another, for God the Most High has established her, so birth in her continues. What is meant by Zion is the Church, in which many sons will be born through the baptismal font, and become Christians who live for ever with God in the heavenly Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) Jerusalem, the salvation and joy of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 6- The Lord shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah.

1- The Lord counts, as one who writes the names of His children in the Book of Life, and He writes the names of those who believe in Him from the peoples, that is, the Gentiles who were born in Baptism and became Christians.
2- The Lord Jesus Christ was enrolled and counted in the books of the peoples through Caesar Augustus in Bethlehem.
3- “This man was born there” means Jesus Christ our Lord, who was born in Bethlehem.
4- This verse ends with the word “Selah,” a musical tone for meditating on the humility of Christ in being born as a man, and His greatness in His love for mankind.

entries.section: (2) Jerusalem, the salvation and joy of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: 7- As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee.
1- All the worshipers who chant in Jerusalem rejoice, accompanied by musical instruments, and this happened in the days of David, Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah, and there was great joy in the city.
2- In the Church all her members sing hymns of thanksgiving and praise to God after receiving the Body and Blood of the Lord, for they have become one in Christ, gathered by one love.
3- In the heavenly Jerusalem they sing great hymns, as if they were playing musical instruments in unspeakable joy, in which all the heavenly ones share.

The greatest place in the world is the Church, where Christ dwells by His Holy Spirit and His most holy Body and Blood. So do not be slow to take part in her, that you may be united with Christ and rejoice, and then go out to rejoice and call everyone to enjoy it with you.

Pains and supplications. A song of praise. A Psalm for the sons of Korah. To the chief musician, upon the lute, for singing. A poem of Heman the Ezrahite. “O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee ...” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer:

Heman the Ezrahite, who was one of the three chief singers, and used to stand at the right hand of Asaph the chief. He was of the clan of Zerah the son of Judah, that is, of the tribe of Judah, and he was counted among the prominent wise men after King Solomon (1 Kgs 4:31).

2- This Psalm shows severe pains that the writer suffered, yet he still prays even though he feels no consolation, but his hope is in God. It is a personal lament resembling the laments of Job and Jeremiah.
3- This is the only Psalm that goes through sufferings to its end, and does not announce, even at its close, God's intervention and the solution of the problem.
4- This Psalm is considered a prophecy about the sufferings of Christ on the Cross.
5- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya, and it suits every person who suffers pains, and calls him to continue in prayer and not despair however great his sufferings.
6- This Psalm gives reasons for the petitions it makes to God, to stress the importance of its petition, and this is in the verses (vv. 1, 2, 3, 7, 12, 17).
1- O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee:

The writer of the Psalm feels severe distress, so that he cries out all day, by day and by night, because the pain is continual. But at the same time he has hope in God his Savior, and indeed he has no salvation except in Him, so he says “God of my salvation,” that is, the only One responsible for his salvation.
2- Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;

1- Heman pleads with God that his prayer reach Him, that is, that He take care to hear his prayer, and also his cry, which may be inward, heard by no one, but a strong and painful groaning within his soul. He trusts that God is a compassionate Father who will care for him and rescue him from his troubles. And the inclining of the ear means great humility on God's part, and a special care that supports Heman and encourages him to bear the sufferings. For the feeling of God's presence within the affliction is very consoling and comforting.
2- These two verses (vv. 1, 2) are a prophecy of the cries of Christ and His sufferings on the Cross, which He expressed by His saying, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46).
3- For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave.
Draweth nigh: approached.

The writer of the Psalm expresses his sufferings, saying that they are so many that his soul is full of them, like one who eats food and is filled and cannot eat any more; so his soul cannot bear other calamities. And he also feels that he has come near to death (the grave), and almost loses his hope of deliverance from the sufferings.
4- I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength:
The pit: a deep, wide hole.

1- He feels that he is about to die, thrown into a pit whose bottom he does not know, and he also feels that he has lost all strength to resist the sufferings, because they are so severe. Perhaps he remembers Joseph the righteous, who after bearing the sufferings of slavery in the house of Potiphar was cast into prison, after he had endured being thrown into the pit by his brothers, who wanted to kill him, while he had no strength.
2- These verses also (vv. 3, 4) and those that follow are prophecies about the sufferings of Christ on the Cross.
5- Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand.

1- From the severity of the pain the writer of the Psalm felt that he was near death, as if he had already reached the grave, and his bed, or resting place, was there among the slain, and he no longer enjoyed God's care and attention, that is, he felt forgotten and abandoned by God, and this is a very hard feeling, for he is suffering not only physically but even more psychologically.

2- All these sufferings are a prophecy of what Christ felt on the Cross, as He was approaching the tomb to lie there, like those who sleep and the slain, forgotten by God, so that He felt that God had forsaken Him.
6- Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps.

1- The writer of the Psalm feels that God has put him in the depths of a great and deep pit, where the darkness is intense. All this expresses his hard sufferings, so that despair almost closes in on him.

2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ on the Cross, for He feels that He is nearing death to go down to the depths of Hades, but to save His children and bring them up from it, and not to remain in it.
7- Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah.

1- The writer of the Psalm felt that the sufferings were severe as a result of the wrath of God that lay upon him, that is, became fixed and settled, as if he were in the depths of the sea, covered with water and its currents, until he became utterly abased. And God allowed all this so that he might be humbled, repent and be purified.

2- This verse also shows how Christ bore the sins of the whole world, and endured the divine wrath that ought to have come upon man, so Christ bore it for him, and likewise on the Cross, to redeem mankind.

3- The verse ends with the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditating on the extent of Christ's suffering of pains for us to redeem us, that we may repent of our sins and offer Him constant thanks.
8- Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth.
An abomination: filthy and unclean, and what is meant here is that he became a shame.

1- The psychological distress of this speaker increased as his loved ones and friends kept away from him, for they saw him as a shame and did not want to come near him, and this shame closed in on him with the psychological pains it carries, and he cannot come out of them. And this represents the extreme of psychological pain.

2- This is what happened to Christ when everyone left Him at the Cross, and thought Him an evildoer deserving death, and thus He suffered psychological pains, and not only physical ones, in addition to spiritual pains, for He bore the sins of the whole world, and He cannot come out of these pains because He wants to complete the redemption.
9- Mine eye mourneth by reason of affliction: Lord, I have called daily upon thee, I have stretched out my hands unto thee.

1- The eye of this sufferer also grew weak from the severity of the humiliation that came upon him, but he continued to call on God and did not lose his hope, so he continued in his prayer, stretching out his hands, asking for the help of God, who still loves him and whom he calls upon.

2- Likewise Christ, from the severity of the pains, showed humiliation in the look of His eyes, because He bore all the sins of the world, but He remained with His hands stretched out on the Cross, praying and calling on the Father with many words.
When your sufferings increase, lift your heart in prayer to God, and trust that He hears you and rewards you, and turns that into glory, and blesses your life.

10- Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. 11- Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction? 12- Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

1- Since the writer of the Psalm felt that he had come near to death, he said to God: why do You not rescue me from these pains and from that death? For after death a man cannot worship You, nor can the shades, that is, the souls that have fallen asleep, do anything, nor do the graves hear any glorification of God or proclamation of the truth. And from the dark grave or the dead who have left life there comes no magnifying of God.
2- The grave and the darkness signify the death of sin, for whoever is immersed in sin cannot glorify God.
3- The only person who was able to glorify God while in the tomb is Christ, because He was able to do the greatest wonder, which is the Resurrection.
4- He ends the tenth verse with the word “Selah,” which is an invitation to meditate on what comes after death.

Do not lose your hope in your Christ however much troubles increase upon you, for He is able to bring life out of death, and to bring out of affliction many blessings that gladden your heart and fill you with happiness.
[3] The prayer of one who meditates (vv. 13 - 18):
13- But unto thee have I cried, O Lord; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee.

The early morning (al-ghadat): the early morning. Despite all the pains the writer of the Psalm suffers, he continued in his prayers, and from the beginning of the day, in the early morning, he offered many prayers before God, and expressed his cry as if God were walking in a procession while he offers these prayers and cries to Him, that He may rescue him from his troubles. He presses God and awaits His answer, that is, his hope is still firm in God.
14- Lord, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?

From the severity of the writer's suffering, and God's not intervening to lift the pains from him, he reproaches God with the boldness of love and hope, because He is slow to rescue him, and says to Him that Your silence means Your rejection, and the turning away of Your face from me despite my great need, that is, he asks that God intervene quickly.

15- I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted. 16- Thy fierce wrath goeth over me; thy terrors have cut me off. 17- They came round about me daily like water; they compassed me about together. 18- Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness. Thy terrors: great calamities.
Thy fierce wrath: your intense anger.
They compassed me about: surrounded me on every side.

1- The writer of the Psalm continues his reproach of God with boldness and hope, saying to Him: You know the extent of my suffering since my youth. I am poor and weak and resigned to the afflictions and pains that You permit. Indeed, O Lord, You allowed me great afflictions when You were angry with me. He likens the afflictions to the waters of the sea into which he fell, and which surrounded him on every side, and he became unable to come out of them, and they continued all day, that is, all his life, and all his loved ones were scattered from him, and he lived in the darkness of affliction.
2- These verses are prophecies about the sufferings of Christ and His affliction on the Cross, as we explained before in the preceding verses.

When you enter into afflictions and suffer much, know that this is by God's permission, that you may feel for those who suffer, and as God brought you out of the affliction, help others with all you can to lift their sufferings from them.
The mercies of God and His promises. A poem of Ethan the Ezrahite. “I will sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever ...” (v. 1). Introduction

1- Its writer: Ethan the Ezrahite, who was one of the three chief singers in the days of King David. He used to stand at the left hand of Asaph, the highest chief of the singers, while Heman the Ezrahite used to stand at the right hand of Asaph, in the great religious celebrations. And Ethan was chief of six companies of singers, and his six sons were chiefs over these companies (1 Chr 25).
2- This Psalm is a prophecy about the condition of the people of God during the captivity, when they were exposed to attack by enemies, and the humiliation of the king, the rulers and the people.
The writer of the Psalm may be from the descendants of Ethan the Ezrahite, and wrote it in the days of the captivity.

3- This Psalm is different from the other Psalms, because they begin by crying out to God and asking for His mercies, and end with thanksgiving and praise. But this Psalm begins with thanksgiving, then asks for the mercies of God, and this is the thought of the Church to this day, for she begins all her liturgical prayers with thanksgiving, then asks for what she needs, to teach us that our spontaneous prayers should be in the same manner.

4- This Psalm is the last in the third book of the Psalms according to the division of the Jews, for this section begins with Psalm 73 and ends with Psalm 89, and so we notice that this Psalm ends with “Amen, and Amen.”

5- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms because it prophesies about the sufferings of Christ (vv. 50, 51), and the Psalm tells us of God's promise to David to establish his throne for ever, but the descendants of David were exposed to deposition, captivity and sufferings, and the solution was the Incarnation of Christ, who is the offspring of David who reigns for ever. By this the mercies of God appeared, for which the writer of the Psalm praises and gives thanks.
6- There is a similarity between this Psalm and Psalm 73 in the sufferings that face the righteous, godly man and the importance of standing firm in faith.
7- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- I will sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations.

1- The writer feels that because of the multitude of his sins he needs many mercies from God, and when God declared His mercy to him his mouth was loosed in praise, glorifying God who forgave him; indeed, out of the intensity of his joy he declares that he will keep praising and singing to God for ever, that is, all his life, and from generation to generation, that is, in this life and in the eternal life.

2- After the writer of the Psalm thanked God for His mercies, he also proclaims the truth of God, that is, His justice. God is perfect in His justice, but God's mercy came first in the person of Christ the Redeemer, for He paid the debt on our behalf, had mercy on us, and forgave us our sins.
2- For I have said, “Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens.”

1- This verse is the purpose of the whole Psalm, which is the glorifying of God's mercy that is increasing on the earth, and the children of God feel it piled up, being built and rising higher and higher until it almost reaches heaven. The writer of the Psalm discovered this truth about God's mercy through his life with God; therefore he said, “I have said.”

2- If God's mercy is built up on earth, His truth is firm in heaven, where the angels are subject to Him and praise Him. That is, God has mercy on those on earth and forgives them, so that they may reach heaven and be established in His truth for ever; for people on earth are changeable and liable to fall into error and need God's mercy, but in heaven they are established in the justice of God, His fear and the glorifying of His holy name.

3- God's mercy on His children is built up on earth and rises, and its foundation is God's truth and justice. For He is perfect in His truth and justice, which appeared and were fulfilled in the fullness of time in Christ Jesus.
3- I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, 4- Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah.

1- God's mercy appears in its perfection when He makes a covenant with His righteous son David, whom He chose to live with Him and also to make king over His people, and from whose offspring Christ would come. And He directs this covenant of His to every person who believes in Him and lives for Him, so that he becomes chosen by God, and He blesses him for ever, and establishes his throne in heaven, and also blesses his offspring who live as he does with God.

2- These verses apply to David and his offspring, who is Solomon, who sat on his throne after him (2 Sam 7:12-14), and indeed many kings from the offspring of David sat on the throne of the kingdom of Judah, but the carrying out of these verses is completed by Christ, who reigns on the throne of David for ever, and it says “thy seed” and not “thy seeds,” because it means Christ, as St. Paul the Apostle said (Gal 3:16).

3- The kingship of Christ from generation to generation means His reign over the Jews and the Gentiles who believe in Him. And Christ also reigns from generation to generation, that is, over the hearts of His children who are on earth, and then in heaven.
4- These two verses end with the word “Selah,” which is a musical tone for meditating on the mercy of God that appeared in Christ Jesus.
5- And the heavens shall praise thy wonders, O Lord: thy faithfulness also in the congregation of the saints.

1- The heavens are the angels who saw the Incarnation of Christ, and then His Resurrection and redemption, and they praised and glorified Him. The heavens are the Church and the believers on earth who glorify the wondrous works of God and His care for His children. We call the believers on earth heaven because they repent of their sins and accept the commandments of God, and so become sons of heaven, and call God their heavenly Father.

2- The truth of God, that is, His justice, appears in the congregation of the saints who are on earth, for because they held fast to the commandments of God and left evil, He gives them peace and blessing in their lives. And God's truth also appears in the congregation of the saints who have reached heaven, for He compensates them for what they endured on earth with glories in heaven.

6- For who in the heaven can be compared unto the Lord? who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the Lord? 7- God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about him.

Assembly: gatherings, that is, congregations. God is not only great on earth, but in heaven also, for He is the One who created all the heavenly beings. And there is none like Him in heaven and among the sons of God who are the angels, all of whom are His servants. They are all sons by adoption, but Christ is the only heavenly Son of the Father in essence, and all fear Him, glorify Him and revere Him; all hold Him in awe, and in the assembly of the saints in heaven God is fearful, great and glorified.

Meditate on the mercies of God in your life and His longsuffering toward you, so that you may thank Him and praise Him, and your mind will be enlightened and His beauty will be revealed to you, and you will rejoice in Him.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 8- O Lord God of hosts, who is a strong Lord like unto thee? or to thy faithfulness round about thee?

1- The writer of the Psalm glorifies God in His power, for there is none like Him in power among all the pagan gods and among all the powers of the world, because He is their Creator. So Miriam the sister of Moses sang before the people of God when they came out of the Red Sea and said, “Who is like unto thee, O Lord” (Ex 15:11), and so the Church praises God every day in the First Hoos with the same words of Miriam.

2- And God, besides His power, is just, and His truth is round about Him, radiating from Him, for He is the source of truth, and it is manifest in His angels who are in heaven and His believing children who are on earth.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 9- Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them.

1- The power of God appears in His dominion over the high waves of the sea, and over all its might. This happened when He divided the Red Sea before Moses (Ex 14) and the river Jordan before Joshua (Josh 3:16), and also the Book of Job bore witness to the power of God and His authority over the sea (Job 38:8, 9).

2- This verse is a prophecy about the authority of Christ over the sea when He rebuked the stormy winds and the raging sea, and they obeyed Him and were silent at once (Mk 4:39). The sea signifies the world and its turmoils, that is, God, the Creator of the sea and the world, has authority over all the turmoils of the world and controls them for the sake of His children, for He is the Controller of all.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 10- Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces, as one that is slain; thou hast scattered thine enemies with thy strong arm.
Rahab: what is meant by it is Egypt, which was a great and dreaded state in ancient times, for it was the first empire that appeared in the world.

1- The power of God appeared in crushing Egypt with all the power of its gods by means of the ten plagues to bring His people out of it, and He even drowned Pharaoh and his army, the greatest army at that time, and freed His people from the bondage of Egypt, and cast the bodies of the Egyptians on the shore of the Red Sea, and by this God scattered His enemies, that is, the enemies of His people, so that they became nothing before the power of God.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the crucified Christ, for it said “with thy strong arm,” a reference to His Incarnation, who by His death bound Satan, scattered his power, freed His children who believe in Him, and brought them up from Hades to Paradise.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 11- The heavens are thine, the earth also is thine: as for the world and the fulness thereof, thou hast founded them.
12- The north and the south thou hast created them: Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in thy name.

1- The heavens that He created belong to God, and they are the angels who praise Him, and likewise the earth in which those who believe in Him dwell and also glorify Him. Indeed all who dwell on earth through the generations and in every place, in the north and the south, and also the east (Hermon) and the west (Tabor): all praise, shout for joy and glorify God.

2- The north may signify what is opposed to God, for from the north came the many attacks on the people of God in ancient times, such as Assyria, Babylon, the Medes and Persia. What is meant is that God is the Creator of all, even those who turn away from Him and are hostile to Him, and He does not allow them to fight His people except to the measure suitable for His people, and He gives His children strength to resist the enemies.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 13- Thou hast a mighty arm: strong is thy hand, and high is thy right hand.

1- The writer of the Psalm glorifies God because He has ability and power over the whole world, and perhaps when he says “arm” and “thy hand” he means the Incarnation of Christ. For Christ, by His redemption, has authority over all, and He also bound the demons.
2- The right hand of God is high, and the right hand signifies glory, so His glory is above all the glories of the world.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 14- Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face.

1- God is perfect in His justice and judgment, which is the foundation of His throne, but He is longsuffering, so this justice does not appear in its fullness except on the Day of Judgment. And wise is the one who fears God today, so that he is glorified with God on the Day of Judgment.

2- God's mercy and His faithfulness in His promises go before Him now, and we see them in His care for His children. And they appeared clearly in the New Testament by the redemption of Christ. And whoever benefits from the mercy and the promises of God that go before Him enjoys happiness in the end in eternal life.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 15- Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O Lord, in the light of thy countenance.

1- When those who believe in God saw His wondrous light their hearts were illumined, and they left everything behind to walk in the life of light, that is, by the commandments of God they walked in the way of righteousness, rejoicing in seeing God and His face that looks upon them with His care and love, and He lifts them above all the desires of the world, and they express their joy by shouting and praising His holy name. They behold God because they are pure in heart, and for this the writer of the Psalm calls them blessed, because of their enjoyment of the vision of God and their walking in light.

2- The face of God that shines upon His children appeared clearly in the Incarnation of the only-begotten Son, and those who believed in Him and walked with Him in a life of righteousness enjoyed seeing Him, and shouted joyfully for the new life. They are the blessed Apostles and all the followers of Christ who were discipled at His hands.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: 16- In thy name shall they rejoice all the day: and in thy righteousness shall they be exalted.

1- Remembering God and repeating His holy name makes a person feel the presence of God and so he rejoices, and continuing to remember the name of God all day gives man constant joy. What is meant by the day is the whole life. As for sin, it gives only a temporary pleasure, and after it sorrow and distress take over.

2- God's justice rewards the righteous who remember His name, so He lifts them in this life above the sin that abases man, then lifts them in heaven and glorifies them and compensates them for all the toils of the earth.

entries.section: (2) The Almighty God, the glory of His people

paragraphs.text: (17- For thou art the glory of their strength: and in thy favour our horn shall be exalted. 18- For the Lord is our defence; and the Holy One of Israel is our king.

Our shield: the shield is the large buckler, a defensive instrument consisting of a large piece of wood with a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand, and he moves it in front of his face and body to ward off arrows.

1- The writer of the Psalm here shows the reason for the exaltation of the children of God mentioned in the previous verse, saying: because God is the cause of the strength of His children, in which they glory, and indeed when they walk in His commandments they obtain His favour, so their horn is exalted, that is, their strength appears, which frightens their enemies the demons.

2- Also God is the shield, that is, the defender of His righteous children, and more than this, God the Holy One, the God of Israel, is the One who reigns over the hearts of His children and keeps them from every evil, so that no one can harm them, that is, He keeps them in righteousness and holiness, enjoying His fellowship, rejoicing at all times.

Your God is strong above all the powers of the world, so hold fast to His commandments, take care to please Him, and remember His name at all times, and God will rejoice in you and protect you, and your heart will rejoice.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 19- Then thou spakest in vision to thy holy one, and saidst, I have laid help upon one that is mighty; I have exalted one chosen out of the people. 20- I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: 21- With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him.

1- The writer of the Psalm speaks in these verses about David the prophet and king, to whom Nathan the prophet spoke in a vision (1 Chr 17:15) concerning the building of the house of God, which David wished to do. And God said to him that his son would be the one to build the house, and God gave strength and help to David the strong and great, so he increased in strength upon strength, and He chose him from among all the children of Israel to anoint him king, and established his kingdom, so he triumphed over all the surrounding enemies, and God quelled the revolt of Absalom, and kept David all the days of his life because he was righteous and his heart was like the heart of God.

2- These verses are also a prophecy about Christ the only-begotten Son, who became incarnate and was the second Adam, and the perfect man who feared God in His conduct, so He did not sin in anything, and the Father upheld Him by the Holy Spirit and chose Him from among all mankind, and anointed Him with the Holy Spirit when He was baptized in the Jordan, and He triumphed over all the devices of Satan in the temptation on the mountain, and in the Jews' opposition to Him, and then completed His victory in the redemption of mankind on the Cross and bound Satan.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 22- The enemy shall not exact upon him; nor the son of wickedness afflict him.
Exact upon: force him

1- As for the enemies, none of them was able to compel David, or seize him, humiliate him, and force him to any evil deed, but on the contrary God was protecting him from the pursuit of Saul, and likewise Absalom, and in the end God crushed his enemies, so Saul died in the war, and Absalom also. And David triumphed over his enemies in the surrounding lands, so they submitted to him and offered him gifts. As for Saul, he fell into David's hand twice and David forgave him, but David never fell into anyone's hand.

2- All of the above happened with Christ, who proclaimed the truth everywhere, and Satan could not humiliate Him, but on the contrary He said to the crowds, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Jn 8:46). And in the end Christ bound Satan at His death on the Cross

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 24- But my faithfulness and my mercy shall be with him: and in my name shall his horn be exalted.

1- God speaks and says that He takes care of David with all faithfulness and fulfills the promises to him, and has mercy on him, so He forgives him all his sins. Then in the name and power of God, David is strengthened, and he expresses this strength by the raising and exalting of his horn.

2- The Father gave all authority to the Son in faithfulness, and mercy was completed in Christ who redeemed the world. And in His holy name His horn was exalted when He defeated the demons and bound them by His Cross.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 25- I will set his hand also in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers.

1- David's authority extended over the sea and over the rivers, for he triumphed over all the surrounding enemies and subdued them to himself. The sea signifies the world, that is, the pagans, and the rivers signify the believers, so David had authority over his people, that is, the rivers, and over the surrounding nations, that is, the sea.

2- Christ had authority over the sea and the rivers, that is, the Gentiles and the Jews, and He spoke as one having authority and not as the scribes and Pharisees, and after His Resurrection and Ascension believers of Gentile and Jewish origin believed in Him.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 26- He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation. 27- Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.

1- God showed His love and fatherhood to David, so that David said in the second Psalm, “The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee” (Ps 2:7). And David also felt the power of God supporting him, so he called Him “the rock of my salvation,” and God chose David from among his brothers, and gave him the blessing of the birthright when he anointed him king in his father's house by the hand of Samuel, and he became firstborn in his relationship with God, so that God testified that his heart was like the heart of God (Acts 13:22).

2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ the only-begotten Son, who called God His Father sixty times in the Holy Bible. And Christ, in respect of His humanity, calls God the rock of His salvation, that is, His strength, and He is of course the firstborn among many brethren, for He is the firstfruits of those who slept, who rose from the dead to raise by His Resurrection those who believe in Him.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 28- My mercy will I keep for him for evermore, and my covenant shall stand fast with him. 29- His seed also will I make to endure for ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.

1- God's mercy keeps and forgives David and his seed for ever, as long as they walk in righteousness like their father David. And God establishes His covenant with them by caring for them and saving them, and the days of David's seed before God are like the duration of the heavens, that is, unshakable. And the seed of David is not only those who reigned over the tribe of Judah, but even more it is fulfilled in Christ the Son of David who reigns for ever.

2- If we apply these two verses to Christ as a prophecy about Him, then God's mercy and covenant are for ever, because He is God who reigns for ever. And the divine mercy appears to the seed of Christ, that is, those who believe in His name, who are the Church His Body, so God has mercy on them and cares for them with His care, not only on earth but for ever in the heavens.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 30- If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments; 31- If they break my statutes, and keep not my commandments; 32- Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes.

The justice of God with His children appears, whether the seed of David or those who believe in Christ, for He does not show partiality to them if they sin by leaving His commandments and teachings, and likewise the ordinances and rites of His worship, but disciplines them with a rod and stripes, that they may repent and return to Him, and that they may know that when sin is committed He forsakes them, so they face problems that perhaps they may return to Him.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 33- Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. 34- My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. 35- Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David.

God's mercy remains upon the seed of David and those who believe in Christ because He wants their salvation even if He has to use discipline. God remains faithful in His promises to David and His mercy to his seed, for God is unchanging, with Him there is no variation, so He does not break His promises in caring for His people. If they sin He is longsuffering toward them, for He kept the seed of David as kings over the kingdom of Judah even the wicked among them. For God swore that the seed of David would remain kings for ever, and this was fulfilled in Christ. As for the wicked seed of David who persisted in being far from God, God punished them with eternal destruction.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 36- His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me. 37- It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven. Selah.

1- The faithfulness of God is fulfilled in His promises to David to establish his kingdom as the sun and moon are fixed in nature. And in heaven Christ, who is of the seed of David, reigns for ever over the hearts of His children, and all the seed of David who believe in God reign with Him, and they are witnesses to the truth of God's promises.
