2- This passage ends with the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditating on the love of God and His care for His children.

Trust in the promises of God and His fatherhood, which cares for you even if you are weak and fall into sin, for He is longsuffering toward you. He may discipline you and forsake you for a short time, then return and forgive you and compensate you for what has passed. [4] The annulling of God's promises (vv. 38 - 45)

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: (38- But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. 39- Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground.

1- God gave great promises to David and his seed, but the condition for the continuance of these promises was holding fast to a life of righteousness, otherwise God is ready to break His covenant. This is what actually happened in the days of David, when his son Absalom rose against him and drove him from the kingdom, and David went out running barefoot in humiliation. And people asked why God rejected David the Lord's anointed, that is, the one anointed king by Him? And why was his crown profaned, that is, why was he removed as king from his throne? And the reason of course is God's discipline so that David's repentance for his sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite might be realized.

2- God's rejection of His anointed was carried out in His rejection of the seed of David who sinned, such as Rehoboam, in whose days the kingdom was split, and the Jews almost killed him, so he fled from them. And this was repeated with many kings because of their sins.

3- The rejection of the Lord's anointed was carried out in the greatest person of the seed of David, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom the Jews arrested, despised, scourged and tortured, and then in the end crucified to die. And He endured all this for the sins of all mankind, but He was able to rise from the dead to raise all His children who believe in Him

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: (40- Thou hast broken down all his hedges; thou hast brought his strong holds to ruin. 41- All that pass by the way spoil him: he is a reproach to his neighbours. 42- Thou hast set up the right hand of his adversaries; thou hast made all his enemies to rejoice.

1- This Psalm continues its reproach of God for rejecting His anointed, saying to Him: why did You leave the enemies of Your anointed to tear down the walls of his houses? And even his strongholds have become ruins, and also the neighbors of Your anointed have mocked him and he has become a shame to them, and has shared with the enemies in the ruin of his country. And at the time when You rejected Your anointed You raised up his oppressors and enemies, and they rejoiced in the ruin of his cities. This happened many times with the seed of David, when Assyria, Aram and Babylon attacked him, but the ruin was completed for Jerusalem and its temple at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and the Babylonian captivity took place, beginning in the year 605 B.C.

2- These three verses were a prophecy about what happened with Christ when they tore down His body, and His glory, and humiliated Him on the Cross. And His enemies mocked Him. And He endured all these pains for our salvation

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 43- Thou hast also turned the edge of his sword, and hast not made him to stand in the battle.

1- The writer of the Psalm reproaches God because He forsook His people, so He was no longer a strength against their enemies, that is, they lost the power of their weapon, which is the sword, and did not triumph. All this of course is because the people turned away from God and worshiped idols.

2- This verse also applies to Christ, for the sword of Christ is His word, which was no longer effective on the people, who rejected His word, and even asked Pilate to crucify Him. And Christ did not fulfill the wishes of the Jews that He become king over them and free them from the Romans, but on the contrary was crucified in humiliation and shame, for they did not understand that He came to reign over them spiritually and to free them from the death of sin.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 44- Thou hast made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground.

1- The glory of the Jews departed and they lost their kingdom when they went into the Assyrian captivity, then the Babylonian, and became humiliated slaves, and this was to discipline them that they might repent.
2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ who lost His glory, that is, His earthly glory, by the Crucifixion, and did not reign as an earthly king over the Jews.

3- With the coming of Christ the Jews lost their glory in respect of the Law and circumcision, which were a type of the New Testament, and they were no longer the chosen people of God, and they lost their dominion and distinction by their refusal to believe in Christ.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 45- The days of his youth hast thou shortened: thou hast covered him with shame. Selah.

1- This verse applies to the kingdom of Judah, which lost its strength and vitality, that is, its youth, through the Babylonian captivity, after the kingdom of Israel its sister lost its strength and youth through the Assyrian captivity, and it was covered with shame by the bondage of captivity.
2- This verse also applies to Christ, who died young on the Cross, and was covered with shame and disgrace before men, but in truth by His death He trampled death.

3- This verse was fulfilled in one of the stages of the Babylonian captivity on King Jehoiachin, who was young in age, who reigned only three months, then was taken captive to Babylon, that is, shame covered him, but after he had been imprisoned for a long time the king of Babylon returned and freed him and seated him at his table.
4- This verse ends with the word “Selah,” which is a musical tone for meditating during it on God's discipline of us so that we may repent and return to Him.

God seeks your salvation by every means; if He allows you a trial, trust that He loves you and wants your repentance so that you may obtain your salvation, and then He gives you the joy of fellowship with Him and you rejoice with Him on earth, and then in eternity.
[5] Pleading for the mercies of God (vv. 46 - 52):

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 46- How long, Lord? wilt thou hide thyself for ever? shall thy wrath burn like fire? The writer of the Psalm felt that God's wrath and discipline had lasted long upon his people, so he pleads with God to stop this wrath, for the people know their sin and will repent, but God of course knows when the repentance of His people will be complete, and then He will lift His wrath and bring them back from captivity with great honor.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 47- Remember how short my time is: wherefore hast thou made all men in vain? 48- What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death? shall he deliver his soul from the hand of the grave? Selah.

1- The writer of the Psalm reminds God that the life of man on earth is short. He is passing and vain, that is, he does not remain on earth for ever. All mankind will die and go to Hades (the grave), because redemption has not yet been accomplished, and therefore he pleads with God to lift His discipline, so that they may rest a little before their lives end in the bondage of captivity and humiliation.

2- These two verses end with the word “Selah,” which is a musical tone during which man meditates on how he is a stranger on earth, and sees that his only hope is God, so he prays, and his heart clings to Him.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 49- Lord, where are thy former lovingkindnesses, which thou swarest unto David in thy truth? 50- Remember, Lord, the reproach of thy servants; how I do bear in my bosom the reproach of all the mighty people; 51- Wherewith thine enemies have reproached, O Lord; wherewith they have reproached the footsteps of thine anointed.

1- The writer of the Psalm asks God about His promises to David and his seed of many mercies; for if the people had sinned, the divine discipline is enough, and they have repented and need the mercy of God, especially since the people of God have borne much reproach within them from the pagan nations, that is, Assyria and Babylon which humiliated them. So he pleads with God to lift from them this shame and humiliation, which befell the seed of David, that is, the footsteps of His anointed; for David is the Lord's anointed and his footsteps are his offspring.

2- The fatherhood of the writer of the Psalm and his love for his people appear, for he feels that the shame, disgrace and sufferings of the people of God have come upon him, indeed he carries them in his bosom and suffers for them; therefore his prayers rose in this Psalm that God might stop His wrath and have mercy on His people.

3- These verses apply to Christ, who cries out to the Father that the cup of sufferings, the sufferings of the Cross, pass from Him, because He bore in His bosom all the sufferings of mankind and its sins, and bore the shame of the Cross; for Christ is the seed of David, that is, the footsteps of His anointed. For David is the Lord's anointed, and Jesus Christ is the footsteps of David who bore all the shame and redeemed His people.

4- The footsteps of Christ are the believers in Christ who endure the wars of the demons and the shame of humiliation for the sake of Christ, and ask God to lift from them trials and afflictions, and He gives them His mercies which He promised His children.

entries.section: (3) The promises of God to David and his seed

paragraphs.text: 52- Blessed be the Lord for evermore. Amen, and Amen. He ends the Psalm with this verse that glorifies God, for He deserves blessing and honor for ever; because this ending is not only the end of this Psalm, but the end of the third part of the Psalms according to the division of the Jews, for the Jews divide the Psalms into five books, and Psalm 89 is the end of the third book, and it is noticed that this verse is repeated at the close of the first four books only.

Your repentance and your humility before God every day open for you the door of God's mercies so that they flow over you; for God is compassionate and gives generously to the humble who ascribe the glory to Him, and thus you live reassured, and walk with wide steps in the way of the Kingdom.
Asceticism is the way to the knowledge of God. A prayer of Moses the man of God. “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations ...” (v. 1). Introduction:

1- Its writer is Moses the prophet, as is mentioned in the title of the Psalm, and the similarity is noticed between this Psalm and the Book of Deuteronomy which Moses the prophet wrote, especially the Song of Moses (Deut 32). And the title mentions that Moses is the man of God, and this description is mentioned more than 4 times in the Holy Bible for godly men of God.

2- When was it written? Most likely Moses wrote it in the wilderness of Sinai after the exodus from the land of Egypt, when he was angry with his people who murmured against him, who wanted to return to Egypt, refusing to enter the land of Canaan, so He made them wander in the wilderness forty years until they died, and their sons entered the Promised Land, as God's anger appears in (v. 7).
3- This Psalm speaks about asceticism in worldly matters, and leaving the cares of the world so that man may live with God.
4- This Psalm speaks about God's creation of man, then his fall, then his hope of rising from this fall, which will be accomplished by Christ who rose from the dead.
5- This Psalm is the beginning of the fourth section, that is, the fourth book according to the Jews, which begins with Psalm 90 and ends with Psalm 106.
6- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The eternal God and transient man

paragraphs.text: 1- Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.

1- God is a refuge for the children of His people throughout the ages; when they meet various afflictions and trials, they hasten to Him, and He supports them. He kept them from the days of their father Abraham in the land of Canaan, then in Egypt, and brought them out and freed them from the bondage of Pharaoh with an uplifted arm, and drowned Pharaoh and all his army.

2- When man becomes a stranger to the desires of the world, he is able to feel God, and hastens to Him as a refuge instead of the passing and changing things of the world. Then he experiences God's help, care and protection.

entries.section: (1) The eternal God and transient man

paragraphs.text: 2- Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

1- God, who is a refuge for His people, is the One who created the whole world with its greatest things, that is, the high mountains, for He has existed from eternity, and He lives for ever, and He is steadfast and does not change throughout the generations.

2- If God is steadfast and exists before all creatures, then He is the greatest refuge, and there is no other protection like Him; therefore His people live in tranquility with Him, and He will take them with Him for ever in the Kingdom.

entries.section: (1) The eternal God and transient man

paragraphs.text: 3- Thou turnest man to dust; and sayest, “Return, ye children of men.”

God's anger at man is because of man's separation from Him, when Adam and Eve fell, and by this man came down from his rank and became dust, that is, earth, and this is what God declared to man after his fall (Gen 3:19). But at the same time God gives man hope by calling him to return to Him by repentance, so that He may accept him and raise him to his first rank. And this shows the extent of God's compassion and longsuffering.

entries.section: (1) The eternal God and transient man

paragraphs.text: 4- For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.

1- Even if the people of God live a thousand years in sin, God is longsuffering toward them, and when His people repent He rejoices in them, and even counts the thousand years as one day. And this shows God's longsuffering and His forgiveness of man.

2- God shows His love in that He considers the period of His people's disobedience, even if it extended a thousand years, as a watch of the night, and the night is divided into four parts, so a watch is about three hours. God says this to confirm His love and forgiveness for His children however long they continue in their sins; what matters is that they return to Him by repentance, and He wipes the sin away from them as though it had not been.

entries.section: (1) The eternal God and transient man

paragraphs.text: 5- Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: in the morning they are like grass which passeth away. 6- In the morning it flourisheth and passeth away; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth.
As a sleep: like slumber. Morning: the early morning

1- He likens the life of man to being short and passing like a period of sleep and like a dream that man sees during the night and it ends quickly. Therefore man must hasten to repentance, and not be occupied with sins or the desires of the world, but renounce them in order to live for God.

2- He also likens the life of man to grass that grows with vitality in the period of youth, then flowers in the period of manhood, but after this withers in the period of old age, which is referred to by the evening, and this grass is cut down and passes away. That is, however great man's life may appear, he is weak, so he should not be occupied with the prosperity and positions of the passing world, because all this is perishable, and man should live for God, and hasten always to repentance, and prepare for his eternity.

If our life is short and changing, and everything in the world is passing, then we ought to look to God, who is lasting and remains for ever, and from whom, through whom and for whom is our life. And if we sin, let us hasten to Him with repentance, for He is merciful and accepts us and brings us back to His arms, and we enjoy His love for ever.

entries.section: (2) The wrath of God and the shortness of man's life

paragraphs.text: 7- For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled. 8- Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance.

1- Moses comes forward on behalf of his people to offer repentance for them, and by this he pleads for the mercies of God, and implores Him because the people are in terror and almost perish from the wrath of God upon them, for they sinned and deserved punishment when they asked to return to Egypt instead of entering the land of Canaan, so God made them wander in the wilderness of Sinai forty years, so that all the adults would perish and only their sons would enter.

2- What exposed the evil of the people before God was that God looked at them with His shining face, which uncovers secret things, even if they are not apparent to people, or even to the sinning man himself, for God reveals them, that man may repent of them.
3- The light of God's countenance was completed in the incarnate Christ, who revealed the secret sins of men, and paid the debt for mankind and redeemed us on the Cross.

entries.section: (2) The wrath of God and the shortness of man's life

paragraphs.text: 9- For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told.

1- Moses feels that God's wrath continued a long time upon his people, forty years, until all the days of those who came out of Egypt were ended, with God angry at them, and they all died in the wilderness; even Moses himself did not enter the Promised Land, but saw it from afar, and only the children entered, who grew up, and with them Joshua and Caleb, who obeyed God when they were sent to spy out the Promised Land.

2- Moses shows that the life of man is short and limited, and he likens it to a story that is told, which has an end, and therefore man should not cling to earthly things, but renounce the world and look to God, to whom he will go and with whom he will live for ever.

entries.section: (2) The wrath of God and the shortness of man's life

paragraphs.text: 10- The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.

1- Moses affirms that the life of man is short, for it generally does not exceed seventy years, and may reach eighty, and most people die before this age. And whatever the blessings of God to man, the pains of life do not leave him, from the toils of the body, diseases, and the various problems of life. And thus the life of man ends quickly, as straw flies with the wind.

2- If Moses lived more than eighty years, for he lived a hundred and twenty years, this is a gift from God which He gives to some people to fulfill divine purposes, such as leading the people of God to the borders of the land of Canaan, and if life ends quickly for those who believe in God, their spirits fly and ascend to heaven.

entries.section: (2) The wrath of God and the shortness of man's life

paragraphs.text: 11- Who knoweth the power of thine anger? even according to thy fear, so is thy wrath.

1- God's anger is very severe and frightening beyond all imagination, for if God is unlimited then His anger is also unlimited; therefore every person must think of God's anger when Satan tries to draw him into sin, so that he may quickly keep away from it.
2- When man fell in the Garden of Eden, and his falls followed one another, God was very angry at Satan, and decided to become incarnate to redeem man and bring him back to His arms.

entries.section: (2) The wrath of God and the shortness of man's life

paragraphs.text: 12- So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

1- If our days and their number are limited, that is, our life is short, then we should walk with care and wisdom. And this wisdom is not from the earth but from God; therefore Moses the prophet asks God to teach us wisdom so that we may walk well and keep away from sin, for the wise heart keeps away from sin because it lives with God.

2- The heart of wisdom is feelings filled with wisdom, that we may live by them in the midst of our troubled world. And true wisdom is the most upright wisdom, that is, the incarnate Christ; this is what he asks of God, for Moses awaits in hope the Incarnation of Christ, who redeems mankind and gives it wisdom to walk in the way of the Kingdom.

I wish, my brother, that you would seize the opportunity of this short life to live with God and keep away from every sin, and let it not entice you with its beauty and its desire, for all this is passing, and what remains is God alone.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercy of God

paragraphs.text: 13- Return, O Lord, how long? and let it repent thee concerning thy servants. 14- O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.

1- Since life is short, all hope is in God. Therefore Moses the prophet calls on behalf of mankind, asking God to come quickly and have compassion on mankind, so that He redeems it from sin and satisfies it with His love, and He declares this early, that is, at the dawn of Sunday by His holy Resurrection.
2- The Incarnation of Christ gladdens the hearts of all who believe in Him, not on earth only, but rather in heaven for ever.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercy of God

paragraphs.text: 15- Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil.

1- When we were immersed in sin God was angry and forsook us, so we were in great humiliation. But when we repent God compensates us for the humiliation of sin with great joy, which is a divine gift that God grants to His repentant servants, and they call on God and glorify Him. And their offspring also see it and continue to glorify Him and keep away from every sin.
2- In order for us to repent and reject sin we need the work of God in us, so that He pricks us and convicts us to repent.

entries.section: (3) Hope in the mercy of God

paragraphs.text: 17- And let the grace of the Lord our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it. At the close of the Psalm Moses the prophet asks that the grace of God come upon him and upon all who believe in God. And for the grace of God to come it is necessary for man to show his response to God by spiritual striving, which he repeated in this verse twice to confirm its importance. And he says “the work of our hands,” which is our striving, and by it he means love, whether the love of God or of others, so he does not say the works of our hands but the work of our hands, because love is the bond of perfection.

Whatever your sins, and however much the problems around you increase, do not be troubled, for God your Father sees you and hears your requests, and trust that He will intervene and give you rest, and even joy, and His grace will come upon you.
The shelter of the Most High. “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (v. 1). Introduction:

1- Its writer is one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those for which no writer is mentioned, and some think its writer is David, and some that it is Moses, because it was placed in the order after Psalm ninety, which Moses the prophet wrote.

2- This Psalm speaks about the power of God, His fatherhood, and His care for His children, so that they do not fear the wicked, because God rescues them from their hands, so it is a reassuring Psalm for the children of God; therefore many repeat it throughout their day.

3- It is one of the Messianic Psalms, because it speaks about the life of Christ in His trials and sufferings, and indeed Satan quoted part of this Psalm (vv. 11, 12) (Mt 4:6) and Satan did not complete the Psalm, because it contains a prophecy about the crushing of Satan by the Cross (v. 13).
4- The name of God is mentioned with four titles, to reassure His children in this Psalm, and they are (the Most High - the Almighty - God - the Lord).
5- This Psalm is found in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ passed through the sufferings alone and crushed Satan by His Cross, because Christ was crucified in this hour.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 1- He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Secret place: a hiding place.

1- The writer of the Psalm calls God the Most High because He is higher than all the powers of the world, so whoever takes refuge in His shelter and hides in it, no one can harm him. And he also calls Him the Almighty, because He is able to do all things, and no one can stand before Him.

2- The children of God dwell between the hands of God, and also abide in His shadow, that is, His protection, so they settle reassured and are not disturbed by any turmoil in the world, that is, they continue in peace in the care of God.
3- The shelter of the Most High, as St. Athanasius says, is the commandments of God, so whoever keeps them, God keeps him from all dangers.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 2- I will say of the Lord, “He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.”
1- Because of the multitude of enemies the writer of the Psalm flees to God, who is a refuge and fortress for him, and he finds protection from all enemies however strong they may be.

2- Because of the writer's confidence in God he trusts in Him, and does not trust in himself or in any other power in the world. And in order to trust in God he must be repentant and rejecting every sin, that is, walking uprightly, and then God accepts him and protects him. Just as the killer in the Old Testament used to take refuge in God, represented in the cities of refuge, on condition that the killing was unintentional, but if he was a deliberate killer the elders of the city of refuge did not accept him, and consequently whoever regards sin as permissible and clings to it, God does not accept him if he tries to take shelter in Him.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 3- Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence.
Pestilence: a disease that spreads quickly and infects people by contagion.

1- The fowler is Satan and his snares are his tricks, deceit and thoughts, and all his evil works into which he makes men fall, but however great Satan's power, it is nothing before the power of God, who is able to deliver His children from all the snares of the demons, and uncovers the hidden snares, and gives discernment to His children, so that they keep away from every evil.

2- The pestilence is sin, for it spreads quickly among people, and many fall into it, but God is also able to deliver His children from it, whether this sin is lusts, or heresies, or doubts, or anything that draws us away from God.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 4- He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
His feathers: the small feathers found under the wings of a bird.

Buckler: the large shield, and the shield is a piece of wood with a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand and moves the shield in front of his head and body, to protect him from the arrows of the enemy.

1- The writer of the Psalm likens God to a bird that has wings with large feathers, and under them small feathers with which it shades its young, as the eagle does, so God shades His children, and protects them from the blows of the enemy Satan, and becomes for them a refuge and fortress, and consequently they no longer fear Satan. And this is what Christ declared when He likened Himself to the hen that gathers her chicks and shades them with her wings (Lk 13:34), so the chicks are hidden from the face of the enemy and he does not snatch them.

2- He also likens God to the shield and buckler with which the soldier protects himself, so God's truth, that is, everyone who believes in God, this faith becomes for him a shield that protects him from the thoughts of Satan and his snares.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 5- Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day;
Darkness: thick darkness.

1- Whoever trusts in God is not disturbed by the wars of Satan that come in the night, and all the fears of that time, and what is meant by the night is the hidden wars concealed in the darkness, while the arrow that flies by day is the open wars, where Satan or the wicked appear and show their evil to the righteous man in order to harm him.

2- He also adds regarding the wars of Satan that they spread quickly in the darkness, which represents obscurity and mystery; in addition to the wars of Satan at noonday, when man is occupied with food and rest, and Satan attacks him and destroys him because of his slackness and lack of attention, and this means that the wars of Satan are continuous night and day, so constant attention and watchfulness against them are necessary.

3- These two verses declare God's continuous care for His children night and day, to protect them from all the wars of the devil, which reassures them and even encourages them to resist these wars and triumph over Satan.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 7- A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.
Ten thousand: plural of ribwa, which is ten thousand.

1- Since God protects His children who are joined to Him, He helps them in their striving, and strikes the demons who fight them, whether from the right side or from the other side, which is the left, so the demons cannot come near or defeat the children of God.

2- The left side includes the wars of falling into various sins, when the spiritual man is in lukewarmness and weakness, and exposed to falling. As for the right, it represents the state of the spiritual man who is joined to God in spiritual practices, and thinks his state is good, though he is negligent in many matters, so more demons, whose number reaches tens of thousands, fight him to try to make him fall, and if they find him in a state of weakness and negligence he responds to the wars of the demons, but if he holds fast to his striving, then tens of thousands of satanic wars are worthless, and God protects him from them.

entries.section: (1) God protects His children and rescues them

paragraphs.text: 8- Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked.
1- God encourages His children, if afflictions meet them, to bear them, because in the end God will punish the wicked for all their sins, but His children He will justify.

2- This verse is a prophecy about what will happen on the Day of Judgment, for Christ in His first coming endured much injustice, and His children also endured toils and persecutions even to death, but Christ in His second coming will recompense all the wicked and cast them into eternal torment.

If you strive and bear the pains of striving and the afflictions from the wicked, do not be troubled by them because they are temporary; be confident of the righteousness in which you walk, but evil will not endure.

entries.section: (2) The strength of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 9- Because thou hast said, “Thou, Lord, art my refuge.” Thou hast made the most High thy habitation;

1- The writer of the Psalm addresses the righteous man, and says to him that you have declared that God is your refuge, then the writer of the Psalm continues his speech, and says to the righteous man that you have made God the Most High a dwelling for yourself. That is, the righteous man chose God as his refuge, and consequently no one can harm him, but he has settled and dwelt in God the Most High, who is above all, and no one can reach Him, so the righteous man is in complete protection.
2- This verse is a confirmation of the meaning declared in (v. 2).

entries.section: (2) The strength of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 10- There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling.

1- The writer of the Psalm offers new promises to the righteous man, namely that no evil will meet him in his life; because God does not allow him anything that harms him, and turns evil into good; for all things work together for good to them that love God (Rom 8:28).

2- Also a new promise he offers, which is that no plague will come near the tent of the righteous man, that is, his place of settlement and peace; for God may allow him a trial, but the plague is a punishment and harm that befalls man, and this does not happen to the righteous man, but he keeps his peace even within afflictions and trials. And that is because of his faith in God, which remains steadfast. For righteous Job was exposed to harsh trials and not plagues, so he learned and benefited from his trials, and remained with God, but what befell Pharaoh is called plagues and not trials, because they were a punishment for him, and a warning of the nearness of his destruction.

entries.section: (2) The strength of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 11- For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. 12- They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.

1- A new promise to the righteous man: that God sends His angels to keep him in all his ways; that is, the angels guard him at every step, and this is a clear scriptural declaration of the guardian angel who accompanies each one of the children of God.

2- This verse shows the ministry of the angels to men (Heb 1:14), and indeed in their tenderness they bear up the righteous man so that he does not stumble by striking against any stone, that is, afflictions do not trouble him, but they lift him by the command of God above them, and by this his heart is lifted to heaven, and he feels God within the trial more than at any other time, and enjoys the company of the angels.

3- Satan tried to use this verse in the temptation of Christ on the mountain, but Christ exposed his deceit and rejected the pride that Satan intended. And it is noticed that Satan did not complete the words of the Psalm (v. 13), which says “the lion and adder shalt thou tread upon,” because it declares that Christ will trample Satan, who is the lion and the adder (the serpent).

entries.section: (2) The strength of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 13- Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the serpent shalt thou trample under feet.
The adder: a vicious kind of snake.
The young lion: the little lion.

1- Another promise given to the righteous man, which is that he will tread upon, have dominion over, and triumph over Satan, who is symbolized by the lion and the young lion for his strength (1 Pet 5:8), and is also symbolized by snakes, that is, serpents, for their cunning (Lk 10:17-19).

2- The authority that God gives to His children is over every sin, and He gives them power to reject sin, and if they fall into it they rise with hope, confident that with God they are stronger than the wars of the demons, and they are not troubled by the plots of the wicked; for God will bring them through all afflictions, and bring them in peace to the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) The strength of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 14- “Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name.

1- God promises the righteous man who obeys His commandments that He will deliver him from any affliction, and lift him above the trial; because he clung to God, that is, was attached to Him and loved Him very much. And because he knew God closely, and realized that He is the only God able to satisfy all his needs, and because he knew the great God exalted above all creatures, so when the righteous man knows Him he rises to Him, and is lifted above material things.

2- This divine promise is for the whole Church if she clings to Him and knows His name, for He delivers her and raises her to true spirituality, until He brings her to the heavenly Kingdom. For God will allow afflictions, but afterward He delivers her from them.

entries.section: (2) The strength of the children of God

paragraphs.text: 15- He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and honour him. 16- With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation.

1- The righteous man who obeys God, if he takes refuge in Him and prays, God cares very much for his prayers and supplication, which come from his heart because he is in affliction, so He answers him, and rescues him from falling into sin, and indeed the righteous man experiences the fellowship of God, and enjoys Him, and receives the earnest of the Kingdom within the affliction, and rejoices. And by this God glorifies him in the midst of affliction, as He did with the three youths in the fiery furnace.

2- After this God grants the righteous man who endured affliction and took refuge in God a grace than which no grace is greater, which is that He gives him long days without end, and complete salvation, in the heavenly Kingdom.

3- This verse applies to Christ, who while crucified prayed to the Father, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46), and He answered Him and rescued Him and glorified Him by the Resurrection from the dead; then He ascended to the heavens, and prepared a place for all His children who believe in Him, who call on Him, and He answers them.

God awaits your prayers when any affliction comes upon you, in order to rescue you from it, and He gives you a peace that surpasses understanding, then brings you out of it, and rewards you with a great reward in the heavens for your endurance of the trial.
The greatness of those who praise God. “It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord ...” (v. 1)
Introduction:
1- Its writer:
The writer is not mentioned in the title, so it is considered one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those whose writer is unknown. But it is thought to be:
a - David the prophet, with the purpose that it be chanted on the Sabbath day in the temple.
b- Moses the prophet.
2- When was it written?
After David triumphed over his enemies, and God gave him rest from wars, he wrote this Psalm to praise God.

3- This Psalm used to be chanted by the Levites and the people on the Sabbath day inside the temple to glorify God, and by this it is understood that it is a liturgical Psalm offered in congregational worship.

4- This Psalm shows the greatness of praise and the blessings of God to His righteous children, for it is thanksgiving to God, and at the same time an encouragement to a life of righteousness and keeping away from evil.
5- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High:

1- At its beginning the Psalm declares the importance of thanking God, praising Him and confessing His greatness, and this in turn moves the heart and the tongue to sing to His holy name, because He is God, high above all creatures, for He is their Creator, and therefore man, the leader of creation, should praise Him and glorify Him at all times.

2- The Church takes care to begin all her liturgical prayers with praise of God, so she prays the prayer of thanksgiving. It is noticed that this verse and the one after it are prayed by the Church every day in the piece found in the prayer of Sleep, which begins “Vouchsafe, O Lord,” for these two verses are at the end of this piece. St. Athanasius the Apostolic composed and arranged this piece.
2- To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night,
Morning: early, that is, the dawn of the new day.

1- Whoever thanks God and sings to His holy name, God grants him His mercy all his life, that is, in the morning and throughout the day. And as long as we are alive, that is, in the day, we have an opportunity to praise God, because in death there is none who remembers God and thanks Him. Also in the day, that is, throughout life, man can repent of his sins, and so obtain God's mercy and make it known, that is, thank God and call people to faith and repentance to enjoy God's mercy. So the day is the opportunity to enjoy God's mercy, care and love, and man's thanks to God increase. And the day is the times free from trials, in which there is an opportunity for spiritual growth and a relationship at rest with God.
3- Upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon the psaltery, upon the playing of the lute.

1- The writer of the Psalm is not content, in calling people to thank God and sing to Him with their mouths, but calls them to be accompanied in the hymns by musical instruments, and mentions here three kinds of stringed instruments that accompany praise. And this means variety in the instruments, which signifies the variety of kinds of thanksgiving, because God's works are very many, and their kinds are countless.

2- The ten strings signify the Ten Commandments, and also the five outward senses, that is, the bodily ones, and the five inward senses, that is, the psychological ones. And this means that man praises with the spirit and with the body, and whoever keeps the commandments of God and lives by them can thank God, and his heart longs to praise Him.
4- For thou, Lord, hast made me glad through thy work: I will triumph in the works of thy hands.

Whoever loves God, and his tongue is loosed in praise and thanksgiving, his heart is enlightened, and God's love for him is revealed through His works, so his heart rejoices and exults. And the more his thanksgiving increases, his enlightenment and his seeing of the works of God increase, so he thanks more and rejoices.
5- O Lord, how great are thy works! and thy thoughts are very deep.

1- At the end of this passage, the writer of the Psalm, before the multitude of God's works and their variety and His care for His children, declares that His works are very great, so that he expressed it by his saying, “how great are thy works,” that is, he is unable to know and appreciate this greatness. For they are greater than any works that men do. And consequently they deserve constant thanksgiving.

2- And when the writer of the Psalm contemplated the thoughts of God that are behind His works he found them very deep, and indeed he was not able to express how deep they are, so he said “very deep,” as St. Paul the Apostle said, “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33), and since the thoughts of God are very deep, man must submit to God and obey His commandments and praise His greatness.
Take care to thank God at the end of every day for His providence so that your heart may be enlightened and you see God, and enjoy seeing His works, and your heart is filled with joy.

entries.section: (2) The weakness of the wicked before the strength of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 6- A brutish man knoweth not; neither doth a fool understand this.

1- The fool and the brutish are the two who neither know nor keep the commandments of God, and consequently they have no spiritual enlightenment, so they do not see the greatness of God's works, and do not glorify Him or thank Him. And on the contrary, in pride they claim knowledge and understanding, and walk in evil, and make light of God.

2- The fool and the brutish, having lost the inward senses, that is, understanding and wisdom, walk in an animal, instinctive manner, and interpret God's judgments wrongly, and become vexed with God and murmur against Him. They do not submit to the will of God nor trust in Him, so their conduct is foolish and leads them to destruction.

entries.section: (2) The weakness of the wicked before the strength of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 7- When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever:

1- Here the writer of the Psalm decrees that the end of the wicked is eternal destruction, and consequently we should not be preoccupied with their success in this life, for it will pass, and we should not be troubled by their pride and boasting in this success, for it is temporary, and even if it lasts it is not for more than this life, but the other life is eternal torment for them.

2- Since life is temporary, and our life resembles the grass and its flowers, which even if they appear beautiful quickly wither, all this leads us to repentance and to preparing for eternal life, so we live with God on earth, that we may have a place in heaven, and be rid of all our evils.

entries.section: (2) The weakness of the wicked before the strength of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 8- But thou, Lord, art most high for evermore.

1- The wicked cling to earthly desires and so descend downward, but the righteous cling to God the Most High, and to all the spiritual things that lift them to Him, so they rise every day to heavenly things.

2- God is most high for ever, and everyone who lives with God enjoys eternity with Him, but the wicked exalt themselves in this life, and their greatness ends with death, so they enter the lowest parts of the earth, that is, Hades.

entries.section: (2) The weakness of the wicked before the strength of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 9- For, lo, thine enemies, O Lord, for, lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.

1- Here the writer of the Psalm affirms that whoever commits sin is an enemy of God; if he repents God accepts him, but if he persists in sin he is a true enemy of God, and a follower of Satan who is hostile to God, and is a worker of iniquity, that is, persists in iniquity and clings to it in his heart.

2- These wicked who cling to sin perish, because they clung to the perishing world and so perish with it, that is, go to eternal destruction. And they are scattered like chaff before the wind, that is, they have no value however they appear in greatness and authority in this world, because they are empty as regards God, and their hearts are full of evil.

entries.section: (2) The weakness of the wicked before the strength of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 10- But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of a wild ox: I am anointed with fresh oil. 11- Mine eye also shall see them that watch for me, and mine ears shall hear of them that rise up against me with evil.
On the other side God gives the righteous many blessings, which are:
1- They receive strength, symbolized by the upraised horn, and no sacrifice was offered to God except one with an upraised horn, because it signifies Christ the strong, crucified to redeem us.
2- They receive vitality, symbolized by the fresh oil, so they move with energy and do their spiritual and material works with zeal, and prosper in all they do (Ps 1).

3- They receive discernment, so they know the plots of the enemy and Satan and all that follows him, and they are on guard against him by taking refuge in God through all the spiritual practices. Those who watch them are the wicked who want to snare them and make them fall into errors, so God gives them sight, hearing and knowledge of everything that is plotted against them, and delivers them from the hands of the wicked, and they live in tranquility.

Trust in the power of God that supports you and works in you so that you are not troubled by the plots of the wicked around you, and on the contrary have compassion on them and pray for them, that God may give them repentance so that they know God and live with Him.

entries.section: (3) The blessings of God to the righteous

paragraphs.text: 12- The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.

1- The writer of the Psalm likens the righteous man to the palm tree that rises toward heaven, and it signifies elevation above earthly things and preoccupation with heavenly things, and likewise the cedar tree that grows in Lebanon, for it rises toward heaven.
2- The palm tree needs a long time to grow, a reference to the spiritual striving by which man reaches God. As for the grass that also flourishes (v. 7), it is quick to grow and quick to pass away.

3- The palm tree's roots extend to great depths to feed the tall trunk, a symbol of the importance of spiritual depth, and it gives sweet fruit, the dates, in their different colors, which signify the spiritual fruits, and its branches rise toward heaven like one who lifts his hands in prayer.

4- The cedar is a tree whose wood is strong and which lives hundreds of years, a reference to the strength of the life of believers, and their remaining for ever in the Kingdom. And the cedar grows in Lebanon, which is of the Gentiles, a prophecy of the Gentiles' faith in Christ.

entries.section: (3) The blessings of God to the righteous

paragraphs.text: 13- Those that be planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God.

The planter who plants these trees is the Lord, so He plants His children in His house, that they may grow and flourish. And everyone who is rooted in the house of the Lord, that is, in holy worship, brings forth flowers and spiritual fruits on earth and they are completed in heaven. And as long as they are planted in the house of the Lord, God satisfies them and makes them grow and cares for them, so Satan cannot draw them away from God.

entries.section: (3) The blessings of God to the righteous

paragraphs.text: 14- They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;

1- The righteous are full of vitality and spiritual satisfaction, “fat and flourishing,” and consequently they have spiritual fruits. These fruits do not leave them, not only in the days of their youth, but even in their old age, so they glorify God and draw the souls of others to Him, and satisfy them from the overflow of the satisfaction with which they are filled. For the righteous are a light to the world by their righteous life.

2- The body weakens when man reaches old age, but the spirit is renewed as the eagle's youth is renewed (Ps 103:5), for the righteous are in a constant spiritual youth, like the palm tree that gives its sweet fruit in its old age; and likewise the cedar becomes strong wood when the tree grows old.

entries.section: (3) The blessings of God to the righteous

paragraphs.text: 15- To shew that the Lord is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him. When the righteous bear fruit throughout their lives they glorify God, and declare by their works that God is upright and just and wrongs no one. For He rewards the righteous with good fruits, but as for the wicked, their flourishing and greatness are short-lived like the grass (v. 7); for the true, complete fruit is in eternity, so the righteous are blessed in the Kingdom, but the wicked are tormented in eternal destruction.
Be patient in your striving, confident of the grace of God that supports you and pours spiritual fruits over you, so that you live in happiness on earth, and in unspeakable glory in heaven.
God the Almighty, the Holy, the Glorified. “The Lord reigneth, he is clothed with majesty ...” (v. 1)
Introduction:
1- Its writer: there are two opinions:
a - The Holy Bible does not mention a title for it, so it is considered one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those whose writer is not mentioned.

b- In the Septuagint translation there is a title for this Psalm, which is “A blessing, a song of praise of David, for the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was inhabited.” From this we learn the following:

That its writer is David the prophet, as evidenced by the similarity of the verses of this Psalm to the song that David repeated when he moved the ark of the covenant of God to Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:30-33).

It announces the redemption of Christ that was accomplished on Friday, before the Sabbath, so the earth was inhabited by believers in the New Testament from the Jews and the Gentiles, that is, from all the earth, and the Jews refused to put this title, because it points clearly to Christ the Redeemer on the Cross.
2- When was it written? When David moved the ark of the covenant of God from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem, and they were praising with this Psalm while it was being moved.

3- This Psalm is considered one of the royal Psalms, that is, those that speak about the Lord the King, and some consider it an introduction to these Psalms, which begin from Psalm 95-100 and they call them the “theocratic” Psalms, that is, those that speak about God the King.

4- This Psalm is also one of the Messianic Psalms, for it speaks about Christ risen from the dead by the power of His divinity, His majesty and His might, and it does not mention anything about the sufferings of Christ.
5- This Psalm is also one of the liturgical Psalms, that is, those which the people used to repeat under the leadership of the Levites on the eve of the Sabbath and at the feast of harvest.

6- The priest in the New Testament repeats this Psalm when he puts on his priestly vestments to begin the service of the Liturgy, so that he remembers that he represents Christ the King in the Liturgy with all His glory and greatness, and so is reverent before Him, and comes forward with the fear of God to the service of the Holy Mysteries.

7- This Psalm is found at the end of the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which we remember the crucified Christ, who reigned on the wood of the Cross to redeem us, so we glorify Him, for He condescended from His greatness to lift our sins from us.
1- The Lord reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the Lord is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself: the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved.
Girded himself: wrapped it around his waist like a belt.

1- Christ hid His divinity by His Incarnation and did not appear as a king of great majesty except in His miracles, and His teaching with authority, but His power and greatness appeared clearly in His Resurrection from the dead, and His appearing in a luminous body to His disciples, then He ascended to the heavens in great glory.

2- The Lord reigned on the Cross when He bound Satan, and brought those who believe in Him out of Hades, and brought them up to Paradise, and reigned over the hearts of those who believe in Him, and thus He girded Himself with strength in delivering His children from the bondage of Satan in Hades, and lifted them to Paradise, to reign over them for ever. And in the Kingdom His complete and eternal reign appears.

3- The earth, “the world,” God established in its rotation on itself and around the sun, and it also signifies the steadfastness of believers in Christ despite the changes of life around them and the wars of the devil, for God establishes them in faith in Him, and as for the new earth and the new heaven, that is, the new world and the Kingdom of Heaven, God establishes them for ever.

4- When God girds Himself with strength He declares that He is the leader of the war against Satan, and this reassures His children who believe in Him that He protects them, so they are filled with hope however much they fall or are weak, and they are strengthened to resist the devil and triumph over him by the power of God.
2- Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting.

1- In this verse the writer of the Psalm declares the eternity of God, for although He became incarnate in the fullness of time to redeem mankind, He has existed from eternity before all creatures, because He is their Creator.

2- The throne of God signifies His Incarnation, for it was in God's mind to become incarnate from the beginning and from eternity, and He accomplished it in the fullness of time when He was born of the Virgin.
3- The throne of God is also a symbol of those who believe in Him, in whom He dwells and over whose hearts He reigns.

4- On Good Friday, in the Church of the New Testament, at the burial of Christ in the twelfth hour, we remember the greatness of God and His throne that has existed from eternity, so we say the Psalm “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever,” with its well-known long melody.
God wants to reign over your heart to give you tranquility, and to gladden your heart by His dwelling in it, so make room for Him by many prayers and by reading His holy word in the Bible every day.
3- The floods have lifted up, O Lord, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves.
Their roaring: the sound of the crashing of their waves, and it is a loud sound.
1- Nature glorifies God, so the floods (rivers) come forward as representatives of it and their waves crash, to praise God their Creator.

2- The voice of the rivers signifies the Apostles who preached the name of Christ in the whole world, and also signifies the men of God and the prophets in the Old Testament who proclaimed the divine truth, and also the priests and servants through the generations until now who proclaim the name of God, in addition to the martyrs who proclaimed with a loud voice their love for God by shedding their blood for Him, and likewise the ascetics who inhabited the deserts and sent up voices of praise and glorification to God. This is the effect of the Holy Spirit who flows like living rivers in the hearts of those who believe in Him.
4- The Lord on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea.
Mighty: many waters that flood what is around them, that is, cover it.

1- Nature also represents the seas, which glorify God by their voices and the abundance of their waters, and are able to flood the dry land; all this is a declaration of their power, but God their Creator is mightier than they and more able without limit. So the power of the seas is merely a small expression of the power of God the Creator.

2- The seas signify the lives of believers and servants through the generations, which flood the dry land, that is, paganism, so the waters cover the hearts far from God, and draw them to Him, to declare that God is mightier and more able than the hardness of the hearts of men, and by His love He draws these hearts to Himself.

Trust in the power of God that is in you to live by His commandments, and offer your love to all around you however much they wrong you, for love is strong as death, and cannot be resisted if it comes from your heart, so continue in it in every way.
5- Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O Lord, for ever.

1- The testimonies of God are all the prophecies and types that were mentioned in the Old Testament about Christ. And all of them have been fulfilled, for of God's word not one letter can pass away, and consequently we should hold fast to the promises of God, because they are sure.

2- If God is true in every word He says to us, then we should enter His holy house, which remains holy not only on earth, represented in the temple of Solomon, and after it the Church in the New Testament, but also in the Kingdom of Heaven. And if holiness becomes the house of God, then we must purify our hearts by repentance and by love for everyone when we enter the Church, and for this reason the priest repeats this Psalm when he puts on the priestly vestments to begin the prayers of the Divine Liturgy, to remember the holiness of the house of God in which he will stand and raise his voice in prayer before Him.

Take care to pray and repeat the Psalms while you are on your way to the Church, so you say the Psalm “I was glad when they said unto me” (Ps 122). And when you reach the Church you pray at the door and repeat the Psalm “How amiable are thy tabernacles ...” (Ps 84) and you prostrate before the sanctuary and say “But as for me, in the multitude of thy mercy ...” (Ps 5). And you stand in reverence before God the Holy asking His forgiveness for all your sins, and you attend to the prayer to share with the heavenly ones in praising His holy name.
God, the Deliverer of the righteous and the Avenger of the wicked. “O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: there are two opinions:
a - This Psalm has no title in the Beirut version, so it is considered one of the orphan Psalms, that is, those without a title.
b - In the Septuagint translation there is a title for this Psalm and it mentions that it is David's.

2- In the title of the Septuagint translation it is mentioned that this Psalm is for “the fourth day,” so it used to be recited on the fourth day in the tabernacle of meeting, or the temple of Solomon. And perhaps this Psalm is a prophecy about God's vengeance on Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Christ and conspired with the Jews to deliver Him on the fourth day.

3- The subject of this Psalm is the distress of the people of God from those who oppress them, and they ask God to rescue them, for they are peaceable and do not take revenge on those who oppress them, but ask for God's intervention.
4- It appears from this Psalm that God does not keep trials from His children, but He listens attentively to their prayers, comforts them, and punishes those who oppress them.
5- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 1- O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself.

1- The psalmist repeats the expression “God of vengeance” twice, meaning by it the just God who repays everyone according to his works. This is evidence of his great need for God’s intervention, because he is wronged. This repetition may also be a prophecy of the coming of Christ twice: the first in His Incarnation, to take vengeance on Satan and bind him on the Cross; and the second coming, to judge the world and cast Satan and all his wicked followers into eternal torment.

2- He calls on God to shine forth because He is the Sun of Righteousness, and he asks Him to light the world with His justice, so that the righteous may appear and be rewarded, and the wicked be punished. This shining forth is also a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ, that He might light the world with His holiness and His redemption.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 2- Lift up thyself, thou judge of the earth: render a reward to the proud.

1- The psalmist asks God, the only Judge of the whole earth, to lift Himself up; that is, to show His exaltation and greatness as a Judge to whom all peoples are subject. Then all the proud will fear, and God will repay them for their pride, and all the righteous who are wronged will be reassured that God the Judge will intervene and vindicate them against the proud wicked who trouble them.
2- The lifting up of God the Judge is a prophecy of the Cross, for when Christ was lifted up on the Cross He repaid the proud, that is, the demons, and bound them by His death.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 3- LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked triumph?

Those who are wronged feel the length of the time of their oppression, and they reproach God for His long-suffering toward the sinners who gloat over them when they see the wronged in distress. The wronged forget that God is also long-suffering toward them, and they rejoice in this. So this verse is an expression of the great and urgent need of the wronged for God’s help. And God, of course, will lift the affliction from them; and if He delays for His wisdom, He comforts them and gives them peace.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 4- They utter and speak hard things: and all the workers of iniquity boast themselves.
“They utter”: they speak much; what is meant here is that they speak much evil talk.

1- The wicked speak evil words without manners, that is, with insolence, against the righteous and against God Himself. All this is because they are proud and are not ashamed of their sins; on the contrary, they boast of them. Therefore the psalmist cries to God to stop this evil.
2- This verse is a prophecy of what the Jews would do to Christ when they accused Him with false accusations and reviled Him with pride, and He endured all this for our sake.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 5- They break in pieces thy people, O LORD, and afflict thine heritage.

The wicked persist in their evil, so they crush the children of God, that is, the righteous, breaking them and weakening them until they lead them to despair, and the righteous are unable to resist them. Then they humble them by making them fall into lusts, and then by reproaching them for having become wicked, so that they despair. All this is directed at God personally, for Satan offends God through His children, because he says “thy people … thine heritage.” By this the psalmist stirs God to draw out His mercies, so that He may intervene and rescue His children.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 6- They slay the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless.
1- The enormity of the wicked’s evils appears in their exploiting the weakness of some people, such as the widow, the stranger and the fatherless, in order to kill them; this is an excess of evil.

2- These wicked people are the heretics, who exploit some people symbolized by the widows, since they have no support or reliance on God, so it is easy to make them fall into evil lusts. As for the stranger, he is the one who has no stability in fellowship with God, that is, his relationship with God is weak, and it is easy to kill him spiritually by drawing him away from God and making him fall into heresy. And finally the fatherless, who is a symbol of the newly converted in the faith, who can be made to doubt, so that he wavers and departs from God. This is what the scribes and Pharisees did, and Christ rebuked them for it in (Mt 23) that they might repent.

entries.section: (1) A cry to God to take vengeance on the wicked

paragraphs.text: 7- Yet they say, “The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it.”

When the wicked commit the sins mentioned above and God does not punish them, they accuse Him of not seeing and not regarding, forgetting that He is long-suffering and gives them an opportunity to repent. And when they deceive themselves with this, they persist in their sins, so that in the end they deserve the divine punishment.
Do not persist in your negligence and your sins, and be careful, for God is long-suffering but just. Return to Him in repentance, for He is compassionate and will forgive you.

entries.section: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 8- Understand, ye brutish among the people: and ye fools, when will ye be wise?

The brutish and the fools are the wicked who forget the existence of God and so persist in their sins; to them are added the righteous who are weak in faith, who because of the many trials doubt their faith in God. So the psalmist stirs them to understand and believe and submit to God.

entries.section: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 9- He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?

The psalmist offers simple examples that children and the simple can easily understand, to prove that God knows everything about man and observes everything that happens in the world. He says: Does the One who creates the ear and gives it the power to hear not Himself hear? And the One who creates the eye and gives it the power to see, does He not see, and see everything!

entries.section: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 10- He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct? he that teacheth man knowledge, shall not he know?

1- Then the psalmist offers another logical proof of God’s power and of His seeing everything. He says: if God disciplines the Gentiles who are far from faith in Him, will He not rebuke the ignorant among His people, to call them to repentance! For if He is long-suffering toward wicked men, it is so that they may repent, and, from another side, to complete His discipline of His children by means of these wicked men, so that His children may repent. From this it appears that God watches over and cares for all people, whether Jews, or Gentiles, believers or unbelievers, for all are His creation.
2- God teaches man knowledge in the following ways:
a- He teaches His people His commandments, that they may know Him and be firm in their faith.
b- He teaches those who do not believe in Him the knowledge of Him through the conscience, which is the voice of God within them, until it leads them to faith, and they leave their sins.

entries.section: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 11- The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity.

God knows that most people do not believe in Him, or even that many of His children are occupied with material things instead of Him, and consequently their thoughts are tied to earthly lusts. These are vain thoughts that do not lead them to the Kingdom. Nevertheless God is long-suffering toward them that they may repent, and He may discipline them to return to Him, so that they change their thoughts, rise from material things to spiritual things, and seek God and being with Him.

entries.section: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 12- Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law; 13- That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit be digged for the wicked.

On the other side, the psalm blesses the righteous man whom the Lord disciplines by allowing him trials, so that he learns the law of God, holds fast to his faith, and keeps away from evil. By this God protects him from the days of evil, that is, eternal perdition, which is the pit, or the abyss into which the wicked fall, that is, hell and the abyss. So the temporary discipline that the righteous man endures in this life keeps him from sin, binds him to God, and brings him to the Kingdom. In addition, God supports him during the afflictions of life and comforts his heart.

entries.section: (2) The One who hears the complaint of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 14- For the LORD will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance. 15- But judgment shall return unto righteousness: and all the upright in heart shall follow it.

From the foregoing appears the justice of God, who does not leave His children in afflictions and neglect them, but supports them, comforts them, and compensates them afterward in the Kingdom. By this the perfection of justice appears after this life, when the righteous pass to the paradise of delight, and then the Kingdom of Heaven. And these are the effects of justice that the upright enjoy, that is, the joys of the Kingdom.

Do not let your heart be troubled by the afflictions that pass over you, for they are necessary to straighten your life and prepare it for the Kingdom. Trust in God’s support for you, for He protects you from Satan, gives you the victory in the end, and compensates you with what eye has not seen, that is, the glories of the Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) The Comforter of the righteous and the Punisher of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 16- Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity? 17- Unless the LORD had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence.

1- The righteous man in his distress cries out for help and rescue from the hands of the wicked who do him wrong, and he finds none, because in distress people scatter from the one in affliction. But he sees his hope in God, who does not leave him even if everyone leaves him, and sends him someone to help him, as He sent Jonathan to David to rescue him from the hands of Saul (1 Sam 19:1-7), and also sent Ebed-melech to Jeremiah to rescue him from the pit so that he would not die (Jer 38:7-13). And if God does not send a person, He gives strength to the one in trial, and inner peace, and strengthens him, as He did with Paul.

2- God the Helper appears in the Incarnation of Christ the Redeemer, to save those who believe in Him from the hands of the evildoers and workers of iniquity, that is, the demons. And He frees His children from the land of silence, that is, the graves and death. He did not leave His children to go to eternal death, but freed them and raised them from hell to paradise.

entries.section: (3) The Comforter of the righteous and the Punisher of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 18- When I said, My foot slippeth; thy mercy, O LORD, held me up.

The righteous man is assured that, although he is weak as a human being and exposed to falling into sin, however great or serious, through his faith in God he trusts that God’s mercy supports him, for it calls him to repentance and then forgives him his sin. This means two things:
1- The righteous man’s declaration, in humility, of his weakness and his need of God.
2- His faith in God’s wide mercy, which supports him and rescues him from any sin.

entries.section: (3) The Comforter of the righteous and the Punisher of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 19- In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul.

The righteous man continues his speech and declares that if the cares and afflictions that come upon him increase and become very many, God does not leave him alone, but comforts his heart with sweet consolations that not only give him peace but delight him and make him enjoy fellowship with God until it makes him forget his pains. Indeed, these consolations surpass all the consolations of the earth and of men. And in proportion as the believer takes refuge in God in his distress with humble prayers and importunity, in that proportion he receives very great consolations, and in proportion to his faith he receives blessings that surpass the mind, as happened with the three youths in the furnace of fire when they saw God, and as John enjoyed the Revelation while exiled on the island of Patmos, and likewise Stephen, who saw Christ in His glory while he was being stoned.

entries.section: (3) The Comforter of the righteous and the Punisher of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 20- Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law? 21- They gather themselves together against the soul of the righteous, and condemn the innocent blood.

The psalmist asks a rhetorical question, saying to God: Is it reasonable that the wicked who hold power in the world would agree with You and make a covenant with You? They sit on the seat of government, authority and power, but all their deeds are corrupt and evil, and from the abundance of their corruption they make evil a statute and a law, and judge by this law against the righteous, as they did with Christ and crucified Him, and as they sentenced the Apostles to scourging and death. The answer, of course, is no: these wicked do not agree with God. In their pride they feel their authority in the world and forget God, so they walk quickly on the road to eternal perdition. Indeed, in this pride of theirs, even if they remember God they defy Him and stand as His equal and refuse to repent of their corruption and their injustice toward the righteous. By defying God they refuse God’s covenant, or submission to Him, and instead they oppose Him.

entries.section: (3) The Comforter of the righteous and the Punisher of the wicked

paragraphs.text: 22- But the LORD is my defence; and my God is the rock of my refuge. 23- And he shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness; yea, the LORD our God shall cut them off.
“Defence” (literally, a lofty citadel): a great, high building.

1- The psalmist concludes his speech by saying that God is his fortress and his great refuge in which he shelters from the wicked and from all the afflictions that pass over him. He also affirms that God will punish the wicked and destroy them by casting them into eternal torment. And He brings the consequences of their evil upon their heads; that is, they are punished for every evil they have done.

2- Christ our God, by His Incarnation and redemption, is our refuge and our strong rock, who rescues us from every evil and every affliction, lifting us above the pains, so that we feel peace and rest within the affliction, and then lifts us up to the glories of heaven.

3- The psalm began with God as the God of vengeance in (v. 1) and ends with His destroying the wicked in (v. 23); He is a just God. And at the same time, by His justice He rewards His righteous children with sweet consolations (v. 19), and then with glories in heaven (v. 15).

Let your heart be at peace when you see injustice spreading around you, or when wrongs come upon you though you have done nothing wrong. God is just and compensates you for all your toils if you persevere with contentment, thanksgiving and steadfastness in your relationship with Him, and He supports you and then gives you joy in His fellowship forever.
Thanksgiving to God and obedience to Him: “O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation … v. 1”
Introduction:
1- Its author: there are opinions on this matter
a- It has no title in the Beirut edition, that is, its author is unknown, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms.
b- St. Paul the Apostle attributes this psalm to David (Heb 4:7), and likewise in the Septuagint translation the title of this psalm says that it is David’s.
2- When was it written? Perhaps when David moved the ark of the covenant of God from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite to Jerusalem and went before the ark with singing, dancing and sacrifices.

3- This psalm is liturgical; it was repeated by the congregation before the Temple, especially at the dedication of the new Temple after the return from the captivity in the days of Zerubbabel and Jehozadak the high priest, and in the days of the prophets Zechariah and Haggai.
4- This psalm is considered one of the royal psalms that speak of God the King and glorify His holy name; these psalms are (Ps 95-99), and (Ps 93) is added to them.
5- There is a similarity between this psalm and Psalm 81 in the call to sing to the Lord, in addition to the warning against not obeying Him.
