6- This psalm was repeated when the procession moved from a holy place, such as Gihon and the Kidron Valley, which is an area east of Jerusalem, and they headed north until they entered through the gate of Jerusalem into the Temple and bowed down before it. The people would repeat the first two verses of this psalm, and the chorus, that is, the rest of the singers, would answer them with the verses (vv. 3-5); then the people would return and repeat the verse (v. 6), and the chorus would answer them with the verse (v. 7).
7- This psalm does not occur in the prayer of the Agpeya.
1- O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. 2- Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.

1- No one can sing but the penitent. So here is a call to the penitent who believe in God to sing to Him; indeed, to lift up their voices in praise and thanksgiving with a joyful shout, because He has offered a mighty salvation, firm like a rock, and has offered it to the whole world. He alone is the Savior of the world, and this is a clear prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ, the Redeemer of mankind.

2- The joyful shout means inward faith and a raised voice to call those who are far off. So this verse is a call from the believers to the unbelievers to believe and share in singing and praising God the Savior. This sharing is in a spiritual joy, not like the passing joys of the world.

3- Singing to the Lord and the joyful shout, that is, praise in a loud voice to God our Savior, surely gladdens our hearts and affects those around us. It draws them to thanksgiving, singing and sharing in the joy, as happens in the feasts of the Church in which we praise God, and the feasts of the saints, in which we come before God with praise and hymns and cry out, not only with our voices but with our hearts rejoicing.
3- For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods.

1- In glorifying God, the psalmist declares that God is a great God, not like the pagan Gentiles, these weak gods. He is higher than all gods, and spiritual, whereas the gods of the Gentiles are demons that incline to sins and base lusts.
2- The Lord is a great King above all gods, and these gods are:
a- The angels in all their ranks, including principalities, powers and lords.
b- The rulers and kings of the world.
c- The Gentiles and their pagan gods, which they claim are gods although they are demons.
So the Lord is a King who reigns over all these forms of power and authority, because He is greater than all.
4- In his hand are the deep places of the earth: the strength of the hills is his also. 5- The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land.
“The deep places of the earth”: the deep parts of the earth.
“His hands formed”: made and shaped it, as metals are shaped after being heated.

1- God has authority to know everything in the depths of the earth, and also all the treasures hidden in the mountains, and He made the great sea that carries mighty ships and overturns them if He wills. God is also the maker of the earth on which man lives, which rises between the seas and oceans.

2- God knows everyone who strives toward the depth while he lives on the earth, and everyone who strives to acquire the treasures of the mountains when he goes up on them and struggles spiritually in solitude, prayers and meditations, seeking spiritual elevation. He knows all that is in the earth and the sea; that is, all secrets are open before Him, even if a man were to rise above the mountain peaks or hide in the belly of the seas. This shows the greatness of God and His knowledge of everything, and therefore all mankind must submit to Him and offer Him glory.
How beautiful it is to contemplate God and His greatness, so that we glorify Him and praise Him, for praising Him fills the heart with joy and spreads joy to all who are around.

6- O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker. 7- For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice, 8- Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness. “Let us kneel”: let us bow down and bend.

“Massah” is a word meaning trial, and “Meribah” is a word meaning contention. The two words recall a place at the beginning of the journey of the children of Israel, in Rephidim, an area in western Sinai (Ex 17:7). Then Meribah is mentioned again at the end of the journey at Kadesh-barnea, which lies east of Sinai and south of the land of Canaan (Num 20:13). In these two places the people murmured against God and fell into doubt, so God was angry with them and with Moses and Aaron

1- In the joy of exultation and praise, the psalmist calls for submission before God, and he expresses this submission by bowing down, kneeling and bending before Him. For He alone is our Creator, so submission, worship and glorification are due to Him; and He is also our Shepherd and we are His sheep, who follow Him and submit to Him and find in Him their salvation and life. He has prepared for them pasture, water and rest, for He is responsible for them, so they are bound to Him and submit to Him at all times lest they go astray.

2- Prostration, with kneeling and touching the ground, is a man’s declaration before God of his weakness and the multitude of his sins, and an offering of repentance for them. Then he rises and stands upright to glorify God, who forgives his sins, and to praise Him and glorify Him for all His blessings.

3- After speaking of the greatness of God and the necessity of glorifying Him and submitting to Him, the psalmist warns the people of God not to murmur against Him or refuse to obey Him, as happened of old at Meribah and Massah, because the people of old were hard of heart. But “today” means the present span of man’s life and his life on earth, in which submission to God and obedience to Him are required.

9- When your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my work. 10- Forty years long was I grieved with that generation, and said, It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways. 11- So I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

1- God gave very great care to His people in the wilderness of Sinai. Despite the harshness of conditions in that wilderness, God gave them, in a miraculous way, food and drink, led them by the pillar of fire and the cloud, preserved their clothes and sandals for forty years, and protected them from all the tribes hostile to them. But they refused to obey Him, and strayed from Him in their hearts and minds, and refused to enter the Promised Land, the land of Canaan, so God deprived them of it.
2- Everyone who now murmurs against God and does not obey His commandments, God deprives of His rest, that is, eternal life.

Hold fast to God’s commandments and obey His word, even if it seems hard. Trust that He will support you and help you to carry out His commandments; indeed, your heart will delight in His fellowship, and then in the end you will rejoice with an inexpressible joy in the eternal Kingdom.
A call to glorify God: “O sing unto the LORD a new song … v. 1”
Introduction:
1- Its author: there are two opinions:
a- It has no title in the Beirut edition, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms, that is, those whose author is unknown.
b- David the prophet, according to what the Septuagint states.
2- When was it written? There are opinions:
a- When the ark of the covenant of God was brought back from the house of Obed-edom the Gittite to Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:23-33).
b- A prophecy of the glorification of God in the Temple that Solomon would build.

c- A prophecy of the praise of God and the offering of sacrifices to Him after the building of the Temple by Zerubbabel, that is, after the return from the captivity, as the title of this psalm in the Septuagint states.
3- This psalm is a call to mankind to glorify God, not the Jews only but the Gentiles also. This was not clearly fulfilled until the New Testament.

4- This psalm is considered a call to glorify God in the heart of man. And the heart of man is also a temple of the Holy Spirit. So it is the return of the penitent man to God and the glorification of His holy name.
5- This psalm is a call to the Church of the New Testament to praise God alone and not be occupied with the cares of the world, which are the many gods.
6- This psalm is one of the royal psalms, which begin with Psalm 95 and run to Psalm 100, in addition to Psalm 93, which is an introduction to them.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya at the beginning of the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ completed the redemption of mankind and died for it; therefore the whole earth glorifies Him, because He alone is its Savior.
1- O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth.

1- David the prophet calls the Jews and the Gentiles, that is, all the earth, to praise God, for with the eye of prophecy he sees Christ the Savior, who redeems mankind, so that all the earth praises Him.

2- The praise of God is a new praise, that is, in spirit and in truth, where we rise above the lusts and the old man and praise in the Spirit. This is the praise of the Church, which she began after the Resurrection of Christ and the descent of the Holy Spirit, and this praise is the joy with which she has evangelized the whole world.
2- Sing unto the LORD, bless his name; shew forth his salvation from day to day.

1- The psalm calls us to sing and bless the name of the Lord, because the name of the Lord is great, and He is the One who arranged salvation for His people in the Old Testament and completed His redemption in the New Testament; therefore calling on the name of Christ is a powerful prayer that protects His children and overcomes the demons.

2- Proclaiming the salvation of Christ is the aim of believers who praise God, through their lived life and through every word that comes out of their mouths, “from day to day”; that is, the Old and the New Testament, and it also means constant proclamation throughout life.
3- Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.

1- The psalm calls the believers to speak of the glory of God and not of their own glory; that is, the servant hides himself and shows Christ, and the proclamation of Christ is to every person, for it says “among the heathen”; that is, the speaking is not limited to the Jews but includes the whole world.

2- Speaking of the wonders of God means His great works that He did with mankind, the summit of which is His Incarnation from a virgin without the seed of man, to redeem mankind. And the works of God are wonders that take place every day to draw souls to Him and to do all that helps them to live with Him.
4- For the LORD is great, and greatly to be praised: he is to be feared above all gods.
This verse mentions three attributes of God that distinguish Him from the rest of the pagan gods and from all the powers of the world that exist to this day. These attributes are:
1- “Great”: that is, all perfection is in Him, and He is exalted above everything man knows.
2- “Greatly to be praised”: that is, He is worthy of praise and glory at all times, because there is none like Him in all the earth.
3- “To be feared”: that is, fearful, because He is able to do all things and no one can stand before Him, and in His hand is the life of all people, and He has authority of judgment.
5- For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens.

Here the psalmist declares the truth about those called gods among the Gentiles. There are, of course, no gods other than God, but these gods are demons that deceive people with their false power so that they worship them, yet these demons have no power before God. The true God is the only God who created everything in the world, and created the heavens and created in them the angels, some of whom fell, and these are the demons. So He is the Creator of the demons, and how can they stand before Him?!
6- Glory and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.

1- He continues to describe God, saying that glory and majesty, that is, greatness and splendor, go before Him to prepare His way, and those who prepare His way are the angels, the prophets, the Apostles, and all the priests and servants of the New Testament. These are clothed in righteousness and declare the glory of God by their lives and their teachings.

2- But in the sanctuary of God, that is, His place (for since He is holy, His place is holy), we find strength and beauty in it. Strength is blessing and goodness, and in it are all the treasures of knowledge and love. Beauty means all the perfections of God, and it is unlimited, and everyone who enters into it in a relationship of love is satisfied and rejoices. These are God’s gifts to those who believe in Him, who love Him.
How beautiful it is to contemplate the attributes of God and to praise His holy name, for it fills the heart with joy, keeps sin away from man, and fills him with love of good for every person.

entries.section: (2) The worship of the Lord is fear and joy

paragraphs.text: 7- Give unto the LORD, O ye kindreds of the people, give unto the LORD glory and strength.

The psalmist calls the Gentiles, that is, the unbelievers, to believe in God and give Him glory and honor, because He deserves glorification, and to Him all power is ascribed. And if a man believes in Him, all the powers and glories of the world become small before him.

entries.section: (2) The worship of the Lord is fear and joy

paragraphs.text: 8- Give unto the LORD the glory due unto his name: bring an offering, and come into his courts.

He adds also, in the worship of God, that the Gentiles should repeat the holy name of God and glorify Him, for His great name crushes all the power of Satan. Then, as man’s love for God grows through many prayers, he offers Him offerings in His holy Temple, whether in the Temple of the Old Testament among the Jews, or in the courts of the Lord, that is, the churches of the New Testament. The offerings are not sacrifices but the good works that we add to the divine praises. Thus we see from (vv. 7, 8) a clear prophecy of the faith of the Gentiles and their offering of worship to God, and this is what was fulfilled in the Church of the New Testament.

entries.section: (2) The worship of the Lord is fear and joy

paragraphs.text: 9- O worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth.

1- The psalmist continues his speech about the worship of God and asks those who believe in Him to worship Him in submission, represented by prostration before Him in His house. He sets a condition for worship, that it be in holy adornment, and this means the following:
a- We wear modest clothes that befit reverence before God in His house.
b- We adorn ourselves with spiritual virtues.

2- He demands that the inhabitants of the earth, that is, all people, fear God and tremble before Him, so that they leave the worship of idols and all their sins and come forward in faith and purity to worship Him, just as the heavenly angels cover their faces and their feet before God the awesome when they stand before Him and praise Him.

entries.section: (2) The worship of the Lord is fear and joy

paragraphs.text: 10- Say among the heathen that the LORD reigneth: the world also shall be established that it shall not be moved: he shall judge the people righteously.

1- The psalmist proclaims to the Gentiles that the Lord has reigned, and in the Septuagint “reigned from the tree”; that is, the crucified Christ is the Redeemer of mankind. So he proclaims to them salvation from sin and enjoyment of fellowship with God. Then they live in assurance in His churches spread throughout the world, which establish the believers in the whole inhabited earth. For the world is established by the salvation offered in the churches of the New Testament.

2- Whoever does not believe in God and persists in his sins has nothing before him but the judgment that Christ will carry out at His second coming, when He will judge and destroy the wicked, and at the same time glorify His children who believe in Him and are firm in His commandments.

entries.section: (2) The worship of the Lord is fear and joy

paragraphs.text: 11- Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof.
“Let roar”: the roaring is the sound of crashing waters, and it is a loud sound.

1- The psalmist calls the heaven to rejoice; that is, he calls all the angels to rejoice in the salvation of God which He offers on the Cross to mankind. Then he returns and calls the earth also to be glad in this salvation that it receives in the Church by the Holy Spirit, and so heaven and earth share in joy in the salvation of God. And as the angels came down to earth with joy to proclaim Christ, so also the righteous went up to heaven to see its glories, like Paul and John the Seer.

2- The sea is a symbol of the world, and by it is meant all the Gentiles, and he calls them too to rejoice and to declare this with sounds of joy, symbolized by the crashing of its waves, that is, their clapping and praise. For the Gentiles share in the Church of the New Testament in the worship and glorification of God.

entries.section: (2) The worship of the Lord is fear and joy

paragraphs.text: 12- Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice 13- Before the LORD: for he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth: he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth. “Be joyful”: be glad.
“The wood” (literally, rugged places): difficult places; the trees of the wood mean the Gentiles.

1- The psalmist calls the plants of the field, that is, the land that the farmer tends, to grow and bear fruit and so rejoice in their fruits, and by the plants of the field he means the Jews, whom God cared for as His own special people that they might grow in faith. In addition to the Jews, he also calls the trees of the wood, which are unfruitful trees, to bear fruit too by the power of God. By the trees of the wood are meant the Gentiles who believe in Christ and so bear spiritual fruits. Thus the whole world, Jews and Gentiles, rejoices in the salvation of Christ.

2- This joy is lived by the believers before God, and they enjoy His coming in the fullness of time, that is, His Incarnation and His death on the Cross, which condemned sin and freed His children from its bondage that they might rejoice with Him. Then he repeats the word “judge,” saying He shall judge the world with righteousness, and this will be fulfilled at His second coming on the last day of judgment, when the evil of the wicked will appear and they will be punished with perdition, because they saw God’s faithfulness toward them in His care for them and His call to them to believe, and also His faithfulness that appeared in the lives of His children who lived among them. And these children of His, who believe in Him, He glorifies in His Kingdom at the same time that He punishes the wicked.
This life is an opportunity to worship God and walk in good works, so our hearts rejoice in His fellowship, and then complete eternal joy awaits us in the Kingdom of Heaven.
The Lord, the great King: “The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof … v. 1”
Introduction:
1- Its author: there are two opinions:
a- There is no title for this psalm, and consequently it is considered one of the orphan psalms, that is, those whose author is unknown.
b- In the Septuagint it is stated that its author is David the prophet.

2- When was it written? The Septuagint states in the title of this psalm that it is “of David, when his land was restored to him,” that is, when David triumphed over all his enemies, and the land submitted to him and paid him tribute, and he rested from his wars, and that was at the end of his life.
3- This psalm is also among the group of royal psalms that speak of the Lord the King, and they are the psalms from (Ps 95 - Ps 100), in addition to Psalm 93, which prepares the way for them.

4- This psalm is considered one of the messianic psalms that prophesy about Christ the awaited Messiah, who reigned from the tree, which is the Cross, and bound Satan, and the earth was restored to Him, that is, the believers in Him, and He raised them from hell to paradise.

5- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ reigned on the Cross, condemned Satan, and gave joy to His children who believe in Him, who were in hell, and raised them to paradise.
1- The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.

1- The Lord is King over the earth because He is its Creator, and He is King from eternity, but He is King also in the fullness of time when He was lifted up on the Cross, and then the earth rejoiced, that is, mankind, at His salvation, which freed them from bondage to sin and opened to them the door of paradise.

2- The many isles are the churches of the New Testament, which have spread throughout the whole world. And the isles are firm like the churches that are firm in the faith, and surrounded by the sea on every side, which symbolizes the world. So the isles are strong by Christ who dwells in them, even if the world surrounds them with all its evils on every side.
2- Clouds and darkness are round about him: righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne.

1- The cloud and the mist are around God because He is great and awesome and His depths cannot be comprehended, just as what is behind the mist and the cloud cannot be seen. The mist has appeared around God many times in the Old and New Testaments: it would settle around the tabernacle of meeting, and the pillar of cloud led the people of God in the wilderness; the mist also appeared on the mountain when Moses was given the commandments and the Law, and the mist also appeared at the Transfiguration of Christ … The cloud and the mist symbolize the body of Christ, in which He hid His divinity. And the Virgin is the cloud that carried Christ in her womb, as Isaiah mentioned (Isa 19:1). The angels also are the cloud and the mist surrounding God, and likewise the believers in God are the cloud and the mist by their deep, luminous lives, bearing witness to God by their conduct.

2- And God also has perfect justice, and therefore judgment and condemnation belong to Him alone. By His Incarnation He condemned sin when He was crucified for us, and at His second coming He will judge and condemn the whole world. And the believers in God in their lives show His justice and His judgment, for they are a light to the world, calling others to repent and follow their example, otherwise they will be judged before God.
3- A fire goeth before him, and burneth up his enemies round about.

Fire goes before God to declare His power, for He is a consuming fire that punishes the wicked and destroys them on the last day, that is, in eternal torment. Fire also purifies those who believe in Him and burns up their sins. Likewise the divine fire kindles love in the hearts of His servants, as the Holy Spirit descended as tongues of fire on the heads of the Apostles gathered in the upper room on the day of Pentecost, and drove them by love to preach to the whole world. Fire may also symbolize the angels who prepare the way of God, and also John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ by proclaiming the truth and calling the crowds to baptism and to change their lives.
4- His lightnings enlightened the world: the earth saw, and trembled.

1- Lightning shines and appears to the whole world, for it flashes from the east and reaches to the west, and it symbolizes the redemption of Christ and the preaching of the Apostles and all the ministries offered to this day, for they enlighten the hearts of believers and draw them to God to live with Him. But the wicked, who are symbolized by the earth because their thoughts are earthly and carnal, do not obey and submit to the light of God, but it exposes their sins and they tremble and do not return to Him.

2- Lightnings also symbolize the promises of God, which must be fulfilled, and they are bright and give hope to man, and lightning is followed by the falling of rain, which symbolizes heavenly blessings.
5- The hills melted like wax at the presence of the LORD, at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth.

1- The mountains that melt easily like wax before the face of the Lord, who is Lord of the whole earth, are the Roman Empire, which turned to Christianity not only as individuals but also its head, King Constantine, who permitted freedom of the Christian religion and the turning of the pagan temples into churches. The Roman Empire symbolizes the authorities and powers in the world, which God turns and subjects to Himself, just as the Soviet Union collapsed in the present generation and the authority of Communism weakened, so that Christian worship returned to the churches there.

2- The mountains also symbolize the forces of evil, which fear the power of God, Lord of the whole earth, and melt and have no existence or power before Him, and this of course reassures the believers, so that they do not fear the wicked.
6- The heavens declare his righteousness, and all the people see his glory.

1- The heavens declared the justice of God, who comes to take away the sins of the world and free mankind by His Incarnation, through the announcement of the angels that Christ was born, so the shepherds rejoiced and went to the manger; and the heavens also declared His justice when He was baptized in the Jordan River by John the Baptist, and heaven bore witness to Him that He is the beloved Son (Mt 3:17).
2- All the peoples saw the glory of God through the preaching of the Apostles of the redemption and Resurrection of Christ, and many of the Gentiles believed.

May all the movements of nature and the events of life that show the fear of God call you to repent and keep away from sin, so that you draw near to God and are enlightened by His light through prayer and reading His word.

entries.section: (2) The Lord exalted above the gods

paragraphs.text: 7- Confounded be all they that serve graven images, that boast themselves of idols: worship him, all ye gods.

1- When God is glorified and all creation submits to Him, those who worship idols and boast of them feel that they are in shame, for their pagan gods appear very weak before God. So also everyone who relies on and clings to the material things of the world and its lusts, and every power in it, feels that he is nothing before the power of God, and is put to shame, especially when he loses this power, such as money, health or relationships, and God alone remains the strong One, able to do all things.

2- When the glory of God appears, not only the human beings who believe in Him submit to Him, but also the gods, who are the angels, and they glorify Him. And the demons also, who work in the idols, cannot stand before the power of God, as the weakness of the god Bel appeared before the power of God in His prophet Daniel (Additions to Daniel 3:

entries.section: (2) The Lord exalted above the gods

paragraphs.text: 8- Zion heard, and was glad; and the daughters of Judah rejoiced because of thy judgments, O LORD.

When the gods, that is, the angels, worshiped God, and Zion heard, and also the daughters of Judah, that is, the believers in God, they rejoiced and exulted and praised God, because He is the true God and not the idols. If the pagans bow down and boast of the idols, the believers in the Old or New Testament rejoice and exult and glorify God.

entries.section: (2) The Lord exalted above the gods

paragraphs.text: 9- For thou, LORD, art high above all the earth: thou art exalted far above all gods.

1- The psalmist declares that God is higher than all the pagan gods that the Gentiles worship, that is, that He is the only God, and He is above all the powers and material things with which the people of the world are occupied, because He is the Creator of all. Therefore He ought to be exalted in the hearts of men above everything else, so that they worship Him faithfully with all their hearts.

2- When Christ was lifted up on the Cross He became higher than the powers of Satan when He died, and Satan was bound, and His love, which surpasses all understanding, appeared, and the Jews and the Gentiles were called to salvation by faith in Him.

Always remember your only goal in life, which is the love of God and eternity, so that you always strive toward Him and leave behind everything that hinders you from Him, and so grow quietly in His love and advance toward blessed eternity.

entries.section: (3) The joy of the righteous in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 10- Ye that love the LORD, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked.
1- Whoever loves the Lord must hate evil, because the love of the Lord cannot agree with the love of evil, and hatred of evil is considered a virtue, because it means love of righteousness.
2- God blesses those who love Him with two things:
a- He preserves their lives from evil, though not from the pains of this life, and gives them peace during trials, and then eternal life.

b- He delivers them from the wicked, that is, the demons, so that they do not have dominion over them, and He nullifies their wars and exposes their deceit, so that those who love the Lord do not fall into the deceit of the demons.

entries.section: (3) The joy of the righteous in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 11- Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.

1- Among the blessings that God gives to His righteous lovers is that He enlightens their lives to know Him and sows this knowledge in the depths of their hearts so that they remain firm in Him, and from this enlightenment comes a joy that lasts in their lives as long as they hold fast to uprightness of heart.

2- The light that is sown for the righteous is Christ our God, who became incarnate in the fullness of time and gave them salvation. And from this salvation came joy in all their lives, because their hearts are upright before Him.
3- The light that is sown for the righteous is the Holy Bible, that they may eat of it and be satisfied, and their upright hearts rejoice at all times and forever.

entries.section: (3) The joy of the righteous in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 12- Rejoice in the LORD, ye righteous; and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.

1- This verse is a call to the righteous to rejoice in the knowledge of God and His salvation, and not in the lusts of the world, and also to rejoice in the faith of many and their enjoyment of the salvation of Christ.

2- The righteous express their joy by thanking God and praising Him, so they mention His holy name often to enjoy Him, and thank Him for all His gifts, and contemplate His gracious person and His holiness, and so they live in heaven while they are on earth.
Seek Christ in prayer and meditation so that you may be satisfied with Him and be repelled by sin and all that causes it, and then you will remain firm in the love of God and His commandments.
Joy in salvation. Psalm “O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things” .. v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: there are two opinions:
a- It is one of the orphan psalms, in whose title there is no name of the author.
b- In the title of this psalm in the Septuagint it is said to be David’s.
2- Why was it written?
a- To glorify God, who gave salvation by the hand of David through his victory over the nations surrounding the Jews.
b- It may be a prophecy of the return from the captivity, deliverance from its bondage, and the rebuilding of the Temple.
c- It is a prophecy of the salvation of Christ, who became incarnate in the fullness of time and gave salvation by His Cross.
3- This psalm is the only psalm whose title is “A Psalm,” and the word psalm means that it was sung with the accompaniment of a musical instrument, which is the pipe.
4- This psalm is among the royal psalms, which we said before are (Ps 95-Ps 100), in addition to (Ps 93), which is a preparation for them.
5- There is a similarity between this psalm and Psalm 96, for both speak of the Lord the King and His praise.

6- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Agpeya, in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ completed redemption by His death on the Cross, so He reigned on the wood of the Cross, and over the hearts of His children to whom He gave salvation.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the salvation of God

paragraphs.text: 1- O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory.

1- David the prophet calls all the believers to sing to the Lord a new song to thank Him and praise Him for His wonders that He did with His people in the Old Testament, and then in the New Testament, and which were completed by the wonder of the Cross, in which He offered salvation to everyone who believes in Him in the whole world.

2- The salvation that Christ offered on the Cross He accomplished by His right hand, that is, His power, and His arm, that is, the only-begotten Son incarnate, as Isaiah the prophet pointed to this (Isa 51:9; 53:1). The right hand and the arm also symbolize the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church. In sum, Christ bore our sins alone on the Cross, and died and raised Himself by the power of His divinity.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the salvation of God

paragraphs.text: 2- The LORD hath made known his salvation: his righteousness hath he openly shewed in the sight of the heathen.

Christ declared His salvation by His Resurrection, and this appeared to the whole world, to the Gentiles as to the Jews, and He opened the door for everyone who accepts this declaration and believes in Him to receive salvation.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the salvation of God

paragraphs.text: 3- He hath remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel: all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.

1- God gave many promises and prophecies in the Old Testament about His Incarnation and redemption, and in the fullness of time He remembered all these promises and fulfilled them by the Cross. For all the children of Israel who knew these prophecies, the way was made easy before them to believe in Christ, but the hardness of their hearts stood as an obstacle between them and faith, and they rejected the mercy of God and His salvation.

2- The love of God appeared in delivering the good news of Christ the Redeemer to the whole world, even the lands far from Judea, and perhaps those far away at the ends of the earth are more concerned about faith and receiving salvation than many who are near, even the chosen people of God, who are the Jews who rejected faith.
May you praise God and sing to Him every day a new praise, for His works with you are renewed. So thank Him for His care and His keeping of you and His limitless love.

entries.section: (2) How we rejoice in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 4- Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise.

David the prophet calls all the earth, Jews and Gentiles who have believed in Christ, to shout to the Lord for His salvation that He offered on the Cross, and he even encourages them to express their joy with all their abilities: they call out with loud voices, which is the joyful shout, and they sing words set to melody with their voices. And they also chant, that is, they proclaim melodious words accompanied by musical instruments. For he wants us to express our joy in God by every means and to glorify His wonderful salvation.

entries.section: (2) How we rejoice in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 5- Sing unto the LORD with the harp; with the harp, and the voice of a psalm. 6- With trumpets and sound of cornet make a joyful noise before the LORD, the King.
“Cornet”: a kind of trumpet.
David calls the believers to express their joy, using musical instruments and every means of expressing joy, which are:
1- The harp: a musical instrument with a set of stretched strings, and it symbolizes readiness, and the joining together of all a person’s powers and abilities to express thanks to God.
2- The psalm: strong words that express a person’s joy, and it symbolizes zeal and spiritual earnestness.

3- The trumpets and the sound of the cornet: these are instruments with loud sounds. The cornet is the horn of an animal that rises above its head, so it symbolizes the necessity of rising above bodily lusts in order to be free to praise God. The trumpets and the cornet symbolize the proclamation of the salvation of Christ and of the Holy Bible. All these praises and shouts we offer before the Lord the King, whom we want to reign over our hearts and purify us and satisfy us with His love.
Express your love for God by meditating on Him and by words of praise and by works of good, so that you declare your thanks to Him at all times.

entries.section: (3) The joy of nature in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 7- Let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
“Let roar”: the roaring is the loud sound of the waters of the sea.

1- Nature shares in the praise of God its Creator, so the sea makes loud sounds as its waves collide, to declare its joy in God, and in this it joins the human beings who dwell in the whole earth, the believers in God who glorify His salvation.

2- The sea symbolizes the world and those who dwell in it, who formerly made loud sounds to glorify lusts and evil, but now that they have believed they make praises and glorifications to Christ the Savior.

entries.section: (3) The joy of nature in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 8- Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together

1- The rivers also join with the seas in rejoicing in God the Savior, for when the waters of the rivers crash they make sounds as if they were human hands clapping, declaring their joy. And the rivers symbolize the Apostles, servants and believers who overflow upon others with spiritual teachings and example by the power of the Holy Spirit, who flows from their bellies like rivers of living water (Jn 7:38).

2- And the high mountains stand to sing without a voice; that is, by their appearance rising toward heaven they seem to praise God with the rest of creation. And the mountains symbolize the Apostles and the believers advanced in their spiritual lives, and the great servants who by their lives glorify the Savior.

entries.section: (3) The joy of nature in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 9- Before the LORD; for he cometh to judge the earth: with righteousness shall he judge the world, and the people with equity. All the displays of joy that men declare, and nature declares, are an offering before the Lord, who will judge the whole world on the day of judgment. So all the wronged, that is, the righteous who endured many pains for the sake of Christ, have their hope in the day of judgment, in which God judges with justice, and glorifies and compensates His righteous children with the glories of the Kingdom, and stands as a judge to judge with uprightness all the peoples of the earth.

Do not forget your goal, which is blessed eternity, where you will receive every blessing and God will compensate you for all your pains. So endure for His sake the toils of spiritual striving and service, and live in self-restraint and keep far from every evil, for God looks upon you with concern and never forgets your labor.
The Lord, the holy King: “The LORD reigneth; let the people tremble … v. 1”
Introduction:
1- Its author: this psalm is considered one of the orphan psalms, that is, it has no title and its author is unknown, though some attribute it to David.
2- This psalm is among the royal psalms, which are (Ps 95-100), and (Ps 93) is a preparation for them.
3- There are three psalms that begin with “The LORD reigneth,” and they are (Ps 96, 97) and this psalm.

4- This psalm tells us of the greatness of God, who reigned over His people in the Old Testament, and then in the fullness of time reigned on the Cross over the hearts of all who believed in Him in the whole world.

5- This psalm prophesies about the Lord the Judge, who reigns on the day of judgment, and the peoples who did not believe in Him tremble before Him, because He punishes them, and at the same time He glorifies those who believe in Him.

6- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ completed redemption on the Cross, because the psalm makes clear the reign of God over those who believe in Him and worship Him, whether from the Jews or the Gentiles, when He reigned on the wood of the Cross.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of the awesome Lord

paragraphs.text: 1- The LORD reigneth; let the people tremble: he sitteth between the cherubims; let the earth be moved.

1- When the glory of God appeared in His ministry on earth, that is, in His teachings and miracles, the hearts of many trembled and they repented and believed in Him; and when He was lifted up on the Cross and died to redeem us, the demons who lead the peoples astray through the pagan gods trembled. And at the end of days, when the Lord the King and Judge appears, the unbelieving peoples will tremble, because He will punish them with eternal perdition.

2- The Lord the King sits upon the cherubim, who are the angels full of eyes and knowledge; He is eternal and established and sits upon those who know Him, who are the cherubim, and likewise upon everyone who believes in Him and knows Him and loves Him. And when the demons working on the earth see the King, God, sitting upon the cherubim, who became incarnate and redeemed us on the Cross, their kingdom, which leads astray those on the earth, is shaken.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of the awesome Lord

paragraphs.text: 2- The LORD is great in Zion; and he is high above all the people.

1- God is great in the midst of His people, that is, Zion, throughout the Old Testament; He is known, His works are many, and His miracles are mighty among them. And He is exalted above all peoples, that is, above all the pagan gods that the Gentiles worship, for they are nothing before Him, because those in them are demons. On the other hand, every humble heart enjoys God’s reign over it, but as for the one who is proud, God exalts Himself over him to make him feel his weakness.

2- The Lord is great in His Temple in Jerusalem, and His worship is holy and higher than all the evil pagan worship spread among the Gentiles in their unclean temples and all the defiled lusts connected with it.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of the awesome Lord

paragraphs.text: 3- Let them praise thy great and terrible name; for it is holy.

When believers become accustomed to thanking God and praising His holy name, their hearts are moved by love for Him and they feel His greatness, and then their hearts are filled with fear of Him, so they keep away from sins, which encourages them to cling to God and to thank Him and praise Him. Thus praise encourages them to the fear of God, and the fear of God encourages them to praise.

Contemplate the holiness of God and His righteousness, so that your heart is lifted up to Him and you cling to Him in prayers and praises and meditations on His word, and then it becomes easy for you to leave your sins and the enticements of evil, and this in turn helps you to lift your heart to God, so that you always grow in His love and always keep your peace.
4- The king’s strength also loveth judgment; thou dost establish equity, thou executest judgment and righteousness in Jacob.

1- The King, who is God, has as His glory and greatness that He loves truth and justice, whatever the price of justice. And man’s sin deserved eternal death, so Christ became incarnate and redeemed him, to fulfill divine justice and save man.

2- In God is perfect uprightness, and He showed uprightness in the conscience of man whom He created, and then in the commandments and the Law of Moses. And finally He showed the perfection of uprightness in the Law of the New Testament. So He establishes uprightness forever.

3- God gave an example to the whole world in judgment and justice when He chose His people in the Old Testament, and gave them the commandments and the Law, and judged them by it, so He honored the righteous such as Abraham and David, and punished the wicked such as Achan son of Carmi, and Hophni and Phinehas; indeed, He blessed and rewarded all His people by their possessing the land of Canaan and punished them with captivity.
5- Exalt ye the LORD our God, and worship at his footstool; for he is holy.

1- Believers in God ought to exalt Him in their sight and their prayers above every power in the world, for He is the only God, and they worship at His feet, declaring their submission to Him and to His perfect holiness. This helps them to worship God and receive spiritual enlightenment, so that they know Him and discover His secrets and enjoy Him.

2- “Exalt the Lord” was fulfilled when they lifted Him up on the Cross. And worshiping at His footstool means worshiping in His Temple in Jerusalem, or worshiping in the New Testament at the foot of the Cross, and it is worship in purity and holiness, because He is holy.

6- Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name; they called upon the LORD, and he answered them. 7- He spake unto them in the cloudy pillar: they kept his testimonies, and the ordinance that he gave them.

1- The salvation accomplished by the Cross was spoken of by the prophets in the Old Testament, and by well-known men of God such as Moses, Aaron and Samuel. And because Moses, Aaron and Samuel prayed and interceded for the people of God, and the basic function of the priest is to intercede for his people before God, Moses was called a priest, as was Samuel, although they were not priests, but they prayed for the people of God, as Moses prayed for the people when he fought Amalek (Ex 17:8-16) and as Samuel prayed much for his people (1 Sam 7:8, 9).

2- God showed His love and care for His people by the pillar of cloud, from behind which He spoke from inside the tabernacle of meeting, and He cared for them because they held fast to His commandments and submitted to Him.

3- The pillar of cloud symbolizes the Incarnation of Christ, for God was hidden behind the pillar of cloud, and likewise Christ hid His divinity in His body. And Moses, Aaron and Samuel offered animal sacrifices as a symbol of Christ, the true Sacrifice on the Cross.
8- Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their deeds.

1- God rejoiced in the prayers of His children Moses, Aaron and Samuel and all the prophets and men of God in the Old Testament. And He answered their prayers and gave care to His people, and took vengeance on their enemies such as Amalek, and those who murmured against the priesthood such as Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and the Philistines, and the enemies of the people of God, who submitted to David the prophet.
2- The Lord’s answer to His devout men was fulfilled in His Incarnation and redemption, and His vengeance on Satan when He bound him on the Cross.
9- Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy hill; for the LORD our God is holy.

1- The psalmist concludes his psalm with the glorification of God the King and worship on His holy mountain, by which he means the places that God sanctified by His dwelling, such as Mount Sinai, and he affirms here the importance of honoring God and submitting to Him in order to receive His salvation.

2- He affirms the importance of the Cross, by which we receive salvation, which was lifted up on the mountain of Golgotha, so when we worship it we declare our submission to His holiness and so receive His salvation.

To the extent that you submit to God and His will you give yourself an opportunity to receive God’s blessings and salvation from your sins; indeed, you can intercede for others, caring for the salvation of all.
Thanksgiving for God’s mercies: “Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands” v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: there are two opinions:
a- The author is not mentioned in the title of this psalm, so it is one of the orphan psalms.
b- David the prophet, as is stated in the title of this psalm in the Septuagint.

2- This psalm is liturgical; that is, the people sang it with the chorus of the Levites to praise God and thank Him. It was sung during the offering of worship in the Temple of God, especially at the offering of peace offerings, that they might thank God.
3- The purpose of this psalm is to declare that joy moves man to worship God and thank Him, just as praise generates joy within man.
4- This psalm is considered one of the messianic psalms, since it calls the whole earth, and not only the Jews, to praise God, because Christ offered salvation to the whole world.

5- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Agpeya among the psalms of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ completed redemption by His death on the Cross; therefore the believers in God thank Him and praise Him for the salvation offered to them.
1- Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands.

1- David the prophet, in the spirit of prophecy, calls all the inhabitants of the earth, not only to believe in God but to thank Him and praise Him in a raised voice, which is the joyful shout, declaring their following of Him, their love, and their joy in their relationship with God.

2- The reason for the joyful shout is the victory of Christ over Satan by the Cross, for He bound him; this psalm, as we said, is messianic and prophesies of the redemption that was accomplished in the fullness of time, by which mankind gained victory over Satan.
2- Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.

1- Drawing near to God and worshiping Him fills the heart of man with joy, because the best place is the presence of God, and therefore the Church is considered the icon of heaven on earth. So the worship of God gives man joy and delight, and it is a pledge of the glories of the Kingdom of Heaven.

2- Entering into the presence of God is worship in His Temple and His worship, and it is also worshiping God in the Church, and likewise enjoying His presence in the inner room. And before the glory of God and His beauty the heart of man exults and sings, because he has been freed from his sins by repentance and has cast them out before entering into the presence of God. And the sense of God’s presence shines forth in the sacraments of the Church, for God is present in the sacrament of confession and the sacrament of Communion, which man practices often in the New Testament, and he rejoices in the presence of God.
3- True joy is in the worship of the Lord, and not in the joys of the world and its passing lusts, which leave behind sorrow and deprivation, whereas the joyful worship of God gives lasting peace.

May you understand the words of prayer so that you speak them with your tongue and your heart, and God will give you joy during worship and make you feel His presence, so that you rise above all your pains.

entries.section: (2) God the Creator and the Faithful

paragraphs.text: 3- Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.

1- Here he speaks of the Lord Jesus Christ and declares that He is God, and that out of His love for His creation He endured sufferings and bore sins in its place in order to redeem it. And no one can offer this infinite love except God alone.
2- If God is our Maker, then our life is His property, and if He is our Shepherd who provides for our needs every day, then we must live for Him and serve Him faithfully and praise Him at all times.

entries.section: (2) God the Creator and the Faithful

paragraphs.text: 4- Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
David repeats the call to believers in God to worship Him, praise Him and thank Him, and to enter His courts through His gates. And what are the gates?
1- Faith in God and confession of His holy name.
2- Repentance from all sins.
3- The sacrament of Baptism, by which we enter into sonship of the Church.
4- Prayer, which brings us into the presence of God in heaven, and we enjoy meeting Him.
5- The Holy Bible, for it is the door of the great treasure, and we eat and are satisfied from its word and meditate on it.

6- Communion from the Holy Mysteries, which is the door of union with God and abiding in Him. For the courts are not only the porticoes of the Temple in the Old Testament, but are a prophecy of the churches of the New Testament, which are completed in the glories of the heavenly Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) God the Creator and the Faithful

paragraphs.text: 5- For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations.

1- The goodness of God appears in His many kindnesses to His people, not only in the Old Testament but even more in the New Testament, when He died on the Cross for our salvation; therefore praise is due to Him at all times.

2- The second attribute that this verse mentions to us is His mercy, for He loves His children when they fall into sin, and forgives them when they repent, however often their sins are repeated, so there is no God who is merciful to this extent.

3- The third attribute in God is His faithfulness in His promises to His children, and His perfect care for them through the days, that is, “from generation to generation,” and this means His care in the Old Testament and the New Testament, and His care for His children on earth and in heaven. For all this He deserves praise, thanksgiving and glorification continually, because the goodness of God, His mercy and His faithfulness continue, and consequently thanking Him and praising Him lasts forever.

Contemplate God’s mercy in your life and how He forgave you all that you did wrong toward Him, and toward His children, mankind, and toward yourself also because you are His child. And thank Him for His forgiveness, and let the divine mercy turn your life into a positive launch in His love, to make up for what you have missed and to enjoy new depths in His love.

I will sing of mercy and judgment: unto thee, O LORD, will I sing.

1- Divine mercy precedes God’s judgment and condemnation, for God wants everyone to be saved. For this reason David sings and chants that mercy precedes judgment; indeed, God is merciful in His judgment, as He stopped the plague with which God punished David for numbering the people (2 Sam 24:15, 16). And God is also wise in His mercy, for He allowed the child born of the adultery of David and the wife of Uriah the Hittite to fall sick, that David might know that the result of adultery is hateful to God; He forgave David, but the child died (2 Sam 12:13-15).
2- God’s mercy is in this life, to give us an opportunity to repent, while judgment is on the last day of judgment.

3- God’s mercies are many, and it is natural for David to sing of them, but the wonder is that he also sings of God’s judgment and justice. He sings of the justice of God that would be accomplished in the fullness of time, when Christ paid the debt owed by mankind on the Cross. And David sings of God’s judgment and condemnation by which He punishes the demons and destroys them in eternal torment.

4- If God’s mercy precedes His judgment, then the children of God ought to let mercy precede judgment in their feelings and their deeds toward others, so that they seek the salvation of everyone’s souls like God.
I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.

1- David declares his course in life by his promise to God that he will walk in perfection and with wisdom; that is, he will understand all that he does, and be exact in it, and walk according to the commandments of God. And he walked in perfection not only before men but also in the midst of his house, in dealing with his family and his servants, and in all his personal affairs. And his walking in perfection comes from his heart, and is not outward, superficial behavior.
Psalm one hundred and one

2- When David mentioned his striving to walk in perfection he remembered his weakness and shortcoming, so he asked God to come to him, to support him in carrying out His commandments. He also entreats God, declaring his longing that He come to him and bless him, as He promised Moses of old (Ex 20:24). And likewise his asking that God come is a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ to redeem mankind.
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.

On the path of perfection David declares that he does not set before his eyes as a goal any wicked thing, because he hates it and does not want to cleave to it. Although as a human being he is liable to fall into any sin, he does not set sin as the goal of his life, but keeps away from it and hates it, because he wants to cleave to God and walk in His commandments.

Set God as your goal at the beginning of your day, that you may hold fast to His commandments, and please Him in your thoughts, your words and your deeds, and keep away from evil, even if everyone around you walks in his own way, and remain cleaving to God, and you will always enjoy your peace.
(2) Keeping away from the wicked and cleaving to the faithful (vv. 4-8:)
A froward heart shall depart from me: I will not know a wicked person.

David continues his speech about perfection, and affirms that he keeps away from the crooked, that is, those whose hearts are twisted away from God, and from all the wicked. He does not want to mix with evil lest he fall into it, and this shows his exactness and his purity. In this he is a symbol of Christ the righteous and holy, who is repelled by evil.
Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.
“Slandereth”: judges another in his absence. David adds to his pure conduct that he keeps away from the wicked who commit two great sins:

1- Judging and slander: because they are against love of the other, and also wound him, and are a stumbling block to the hearers, and the loss of peace of the one who judges; so it is an evil from every side, with many offenses.
2- Pride: whether in the heart, or in conduct by the look, or in speech, or in behavior.
So David the prophet could not bear these two sins, and he shunned anyone who walked in them.
Mine eyes shall be upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me: he that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me.

In order that King David might keep away from injustice in his judgments and decisions, he shunned the wicked, and at the same time brought near to himself those faithful to God and those who walk in perfection. For the just ruler is not content only to shun the wicked, but must surround himself with the faithful and the perfect, as David befriended Jonathan, and as Christ drew near to Himself the twelve disciples and the seventy Apostles, and loved Lazarus and his two sisters Mary and Martha.
He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight.

1- David continues his speech about the purity of the atmosphere around him, and declares that whoever acts with deceit or lies does not settle inside his house. Even if the liar and the deceiver try to slip into David’s palace, he drives him out and does not let him settle with him in the house.
2- If thoughts of deceit or lying try to enter the heart of the spiritual man, he rejects them and does not let them settle within him.
Psalm one hundred and one
I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the LORD.

1- David concludes the psalm with his hatred of evil, so he destroys it from his city Jerusalem, and hastens to this by rising early to rid himself of evil, in order to preserve the purity of the city and of all who are around him.

2- The city symbolizes the heart of the spiritual man, and the Church, which ought to remain pure, as St. Paul the Apostle did and separated the sinner in the church of Corinth until he repented (1 Cor 5:

Examine yourself every day so that you rid yourself of your sins by repentance, and indeed cut yourself off and keep away from the sources of evil, that you may live in peace and purity and enjoy fellowship with God.

The sufferings of the poor man and his hope. A prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD: “Hear my prayer, O LORD, and let my cry come unto thee … v. 1”
Introduction:
1- Its author: there are several opinions on this matter:
a- The name of the psalm’s author is not mentioned in the title, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms, since it says that its author is a poor man and does not mention his name.
b- David the prophet, who was poor in spirit, that is, humble before God, and endured many pains, so he lifted up his prayer to God.
c- Ezra the priest and scribe wrote it at the end of the captivity, and it expresses the pains of the captives and their longing to return to Jerusalem.

d- Nehemiah, who returned from the captivity to Jerusalem in the third return, and saw the wall of Jerusalem broken down and the stones scattered, so he prayed and God supported him, and he built the wall and cared for Jerusalem and its inhabitants spiritually and materially.
2- When was it written?
There are two opinions:
a- When David was driven out from the face of Absalom his son.
b- At the end of the period of the captivity and the beginning of the return to Jerusalem.
3- This psalm expresses the pains of the poor who believe in God and are humble before Him, and their hope in His salvation.
4- In a large part of this psalm he speaks in the voice of the congregation, for it expresses the pains of the people of God and their supplication to Him to rescue them.

5- This psalm is one of the messianic psalms, and this poor man symbolizes Christ, who endured sufferings for our sake and prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane that the cup of sufferings might pass from Him.
6- This psalm is considered one of the liturgical psalms, for it was used in public worship, being offered as a prayer on the days of God.
7- This psalm is considered one of the seven penitential psalms, which are (Ps 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).
8- St. Paul the Apostle quoted a part of this psalm, which is (vv. 25-27), in his Epistle to the Hebrews (ch. 1:10-12), and this confirms that the words of the psalm prophesy about Christ.
9- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: Hear my prayer, O LORD, and let my cry come unto thee. Hide not thy face from me in the day when I am in trouble; incline thine ear unto me: in the day when I call answer me speedily.

1- The supplication of the psalmist shows his need of God, and he asks Him to hear his prayer, indeed that his cry, which expresses the extent of his need, enter into the presence of God. He does not cry with a loud voice, but rather his heart cries, because he is in great pain. And in the intensity of his need he entreats God not to hide His face from him or forget him. Indeed, he hopes that God will incline His ear and hear him, for he trusts in God’s love and humility. Although the voice of the poor man is low because of the intensity of the pains, his hope is that God will condescend, incline His ear, and listen to him. And because of his great need he wishes for God’s speedy answer.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about the crucified Christ, from whom the face of the Father was hidden, so He cried “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46) as an expression of the difficulty of bearing all the sins of the world, for He had to drink the cup of sufferings to the end and die to complete our redemption.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: 3- For my days are consumed in smoke, and my bones are dried up like firewood. 4- My heart is scorched like grass and withered, so that I neglected to eat my bread. 5- By reason of the voice of my groaning my bone cleaveth to my flesh.
“Firewood”: the dry branches with which fire is kindled.
“Scorched”: a hot wind blew on it and made it dry.
“Neglected”: forgot.

The psalmist describes the effect of the pains on him, until they made his life like smoke that quickly scatters and ends; that is, his life is almost consumed by the intensity of the pain, and likewise his bones have become like sticks of firewood used to kindle a fire. The bones are the strong part in man that supports the body; these have become very weak and have begun to burn, and the bones that support man have been turned into a cause of fire being kindled within him, that is, the cause of his violent pains. Then he likens his life to a plant on which a hot wind has blown and made it dry.

And the scorched plant loses its vitality and becomes firewood for kindling fire, unless the divine waters come to its aid to water it and restore its vitality. So also the heart of the poor man dries up from the intensity of the pains. And in the end he no longer has ability or desire to eat food, but has forgotten it, and so has become liable to die of hunger; in addition, his sighing and constant groaning because of the intensity of the pains made his flesh cleave to his bones, since the whole body has become dry and liable to perish.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: 6- I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am become like an owl of the ruins. 7- I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.
“Pelican of the wilderness”: a kind of bird, some of which live in the wilderness, and which makes sounds like the cry of one who suffers and mourns. It feeds on poisonous animals such as snakes.
“Owl of the ruins”: a kind of bird that makes sad sounds and lives in tombs and ruined places, and the Arabs consider it an omen of ill fortune.
“I watch”: I keep awake.

1- The psalmist likens his painful state to the birds that make sad sounds, such as the pelican and the owl. And because of the intensity of his pains he has kept away from loved ones and suffers from isolation; therefore he likens himself to a lone sparrow on the roof of a house, with no one with him and no one aware of him, especially since this sparrow means the house sparrow that stands alone on the roofs of houses in the cold weather.

2- These two verses symbolize Christ, who trod the winepress alone and bore all the pains for us on the Cross, like the pelican and the owl, which are among the unclean, sorrowful birds, because He bore our uncleannesses and our sorrows, and He was alone in the sufferings and everyone left Him, so He was like the lone sparrow.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: 8- Mine enemies reproach me all the day; and they that are mad against me are sworn against me.
“Mad”: intensely enraged.
“Are sworn against me”: have banded together against me; that is, they agreed to do me harm and swore to it.

1- This poor man also endured reproaches from enemies, and many of those who were enraged at him because of his righteousness conspired against him. And they continued like this all the day; that is, they continually troubled him with hard words, and affirmed that they would do him harm.
2- This verse applies to Christ, who endured many reproaches from the Jews, and they were enraged at Him, and did Him harm by scourging and crucifixion.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: 9- For I have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping. The psalmist expresses the extent of his pains and his humiliation before God, for he put ashes on his head as was the custom of the ancients, and when he ate food the ashes fell from his head and mixed with his food; that is, he was in great austerity and humiliation. And when he drank water, or any other drink, in his intense sorrows, his tears would flow and fall into his drink, and he would drink his drink mixed with his tears. All this shows the extent of his pains.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: 10- Because of thine indignation and thy wrath: for thou hast lifted me up, and cast me down.

All the pains that passed over the psalmist, he felt were by God’s permission. God was greatly angry with him, so He lifted him up and cast him down, and he suffered pains as a result of being thrown on the ground. And this shows the extent of his faith and his acceptance of the pains from the hand of God, for he felt that they were a discipline for him, that he might repent and renounce the world. And God raised David to the throne of the kingdom, but allowed his son to rise against him, who drove him out and tried to kill him, but when David prayed God restored him to his throne.

entries.section: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

paragraphs.text: 11- My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass.

1- The psalmist feels his weakness, and likens his life to a shadow that declines on the ground. This shadow grows longer the nearer the time of sunset, that is, man grows older, but after the sun disappears it vanishes completely, that is, life ends, so he sees that his life will end. And he also expresses his pains by saying that he is near perishing, so he likens himself to grass uprooted from its roots in the earth that has begun to dry, and so is near losing its vitality, that is, becoming firewood; such is the life of the psalmist.
2- This verse applies to Christ, whose life on earth was short and ended with His crucifixion, and who endured all the pains out of love for us.
If you suffer pains, be faithful to God, holding fast to His commandments, and trust that your pains are very precious to God, and He will reward you for them in the Kingdom.
12- But thou, O LORD, sittest for ever; and thy memorial unto all generations.

1- The psalmist is a weak human being and his life is short, but God is great and glorified, sitting on His throne, and the heavenly ones remember Him, and His children on earth from generation to generation glorify His name. So although man is suffering and weak on earth, he will be made happy by seeing God and will glorify Him in the heavens. And this shows the psalmist’s faith in eternal life and its glories, and this helps him to bear the temporary pains of the earth.
2- Though the life of Christ on earth was filled with pains and He died a terrible death by crucifixion, He is glorified in the heavens for ever and ever.
13- Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come.
“Zion”: the most important of the five hills on which the city of Jerusalem stands, and it symbolizes the holy city.

1- The psalmist shows his hope in the mighty God who sits for ever on His throne, who will have compassion at the set time when the times are fulfilled and bring His people back from captivity. He arises to help His people after they have endured discipline, to free them from their bondage and return them to their land, that they may build the Temple and worship Him in it; thereby fulfilling the words of the prophecies (Isa 40:2; Jer 29:10; Hab 2:3).
2- This verse points to the redemption of Christ in the fullness of time, and His Resurrection, that He might raise His children in Him and save them from their sins.
3- This verse also points to the final resurrection after the day of judgment, when He will have compassion on His believing children and compensate them for all their toils on earth.
14- For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof.

1- The servants of God are the Jews who believe in God and hold fast to His worship, who went into captivity, but still long for the stones of the ruined Temple in Jerusalem, that they may build it anew. And they also yearned for the dust of Jerusalem to restore it to its former splendor, and by this they draw out God’s mercies and compassion, that He may help them to build the Temple and Jerusalem anew.

2- In this verse the “servants of God” symbolize the Apostles who took pleasure in the stones of the Church, that is, the believers, and yearned for her dust, that is, for those who are far off and walk in an earthly, dusty way of life, to preach to them and draw them to the Church.
15- So the heathen shall fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth thy glory.

When the Gentiles see God’s care for His people in bringing them back from captivity and helping them to build the Temple and Jerusalem, they believe in the power of God, the God of Israel, and fear Him, they and their kings, and indeed turn to faith, and this is what happened in Christianity when the Gentiles believed and became strong churches at the hands of the Apostles, especially St. Paul the Apostle.
16- When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory.
1- The psalmist believed that Zion would be built, and so the glory of God who built it by means of His children who believe in Him would appear, and this great work draws the Gentiles to faith.
2- God’s work in building up His believing children glorifies God, so many of those who are far off believe. This is what happens in the Church every day.
17- He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.

Here the psalmist speaks in the past tense of God, that He regarded the prayer of the destitute, who is the believer in God who is in distress and has nothing before him but to take refuge in God, and He took heed of his petition and did not neglect it, and helped His captive children and brought them back to Jerusalem, and they built the Temple and the city. This shows the extent of the psalmist’s faith in the answer of God that will take place.
18- This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.

In the spirit of prophecy the psalmist declares a great truth, that not only will the people of God return from the captivity and build the Temple again in Jerusalem, but a people will be created who will praise the Lord in the following generations, that is, the generation to come, and he means in the fullness of time when Christ redeems mankind and establishes His Church by His Holy Spirit, and she praises Him with a new praise, around a new sacrifice, which is the sacrifice of Himself (His Body and Blood.)
19- For he hath looked down from the height of his sanctuary; from heaven did the LORD behold the earth; 20- To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to

loose those that are appointed to death; God the compassionate has been occupied since eternity with His children who fell into sin but who believe in Him and await His salvation, and in the fullness of time He looked down and beheld from heaven, that is, He cared for His children and showed His love toward them by His Incarnation and redemption, for He heard their groaning and their pain at the dominion of the devil over them, and the sentence of death that had been passed upon them, indeed their distress at hell, which they had entered, so He stretched out His hand and saved them, and raised them up to paradise, after He had completed their redemption on the Cross.
21- To declare the name of the LORD in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem; 22- When the people are gathered together, and the kingdoms, to serve the LORD.

After many in the whole world believed in Christ the Redeemer, they offered praises to God in Jerusalem, or the new Zion, that is, the Church. And the name of the Lord Jesus Christ was declared, and praises were offered to Him, when the peoples who believed in Him gathered around Him.

God is ready, however much you have sinned, to forgive your sins and rebuild your spiritual life, so you return and offer Him thanksgiving and praise, and enjoy not only your first fellowship with Him but also experience new depths in His love.
23- He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days. 24- I said, O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days: thy years are for ever and ever.
“Weakened”: made weak, that is, made it feeble.

The psalmist expresses the pains he suffers as a human being, which make him weak, and he feels that his body is not strong enough to complete his days on earth; therefore he asks God to lengthen his days and not to let the pains shorten them, for he longs to see the salvation of God that would be accomplished in the fullness of time, which God promised by the mouth of the prophets, that is, the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption. And he says to God: You endure for ever, so lengthen my life and grant me to live before You, that I may see and enjoy this salvation. So it is clear that all the believers in the Old Testament longed for the salvation of Christ, as St. Paul the Apostle expressed this in his Epistle to the Hebrews by saying that they “saw them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them” (Heb 11:13), that is, they were longing for them.

25- Of old hast thou laid the foundation of the earth: and the heavens are the work of thy hands. 26- They shall perish, but thou remainest: and they all shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed. 27- But thou art he, and thy years shall not end. 28- The children of thy servants shall dwell, and their seed shall be established before thee.

1- In these verses the psalmist declares that God is the Eternal One who created heaven and earth and all that is in them. And that all the material things in the world will perish, but human beings God will change into spiritual bodies that will live forever with their spirits. And although material creatures perish, God their Creator endures forever, and with Him endure His children and servants who believe in Him, and all their descendants who lived a spiritual life like them with God. All these are immortal and enjoy the Kingdom of Heaven from God.

2- And so we see that at the beginning of the psalm the author speaks of the pains that people experience, even believers in God, but he concludes the psalm with a great happiness that the children of God receive in return for all their toils on earth, because they believed in God and loved Him.

May your eyes be lifted to heaven every day, even for minutes, to remember that your only goal in this life is to reach heaven, so that you live with uprightness of heart and purity on this day, and keep away from what makes you stumble, and if you fall you return quickly in repentance to God, so that you keep your eyes raised toward heaven.
A call to all to praise the Lord: “Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name … v. 1”
Introduction:
1- Its author: David the prophet, as the title of the psalm states.
2- When was it written? At the end of David’s life, that is, in his old age, so he praises God and blesses Him with all his heart for His works with him and with his people.
