2- As God saved His people the children of Israel from the slavery of the Egyptians by their crossing the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh and his soldiers; so also He saves His children in the New Testament from the slavery of Satan by their crossing through the water of Baptism, so they receive the new nature and the freedom of the children of God.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 13- They soon forgat his works; they waited not for his counsel: 14- But lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tempted God in the desert. 15- And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.

1- Three days had not passed since their crossing the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh when they murmured because of their thirst when they reached the region of Elim, and they did not seek God's counsel by prayer and supplication because the waters were bitter. But Moses prayed, and God guided him to throw a tree into the water, and it turned into sweet water (Ex 15:22-24). And they murmured also after this asking for meat, so He gave them quails and they were satisfied with them, for they ate greedily, but God struck them with serpents and their bodies and souls fell into leanness. And when they cried out to God, Moses made the bronze serpent, and saved them from death when they looked at it (Num 11).
2- The tree is a symbol of the cross, which turns bitterness into sweetness, and the bronze serpent is a symbol of the crucified Christ, who saves us from the death of sin and lust.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 16- They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord. 17- The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. 18- And a fire was kindled in their company; the flame burned up the wicked.

1- Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and two hundred and fifty men who followed them, envied and murmured against Moses and Aaron for their being singled out for the priesthood and speaking with God, so God was angry with them, and the earth was split open and swallowed them, and the fire also burned them; that God might show the greatness of His children and that all the people might revere the priesthood.

2- Moses was a type of Christ as the leader of His people, and Aaron also is a type of Christ our greatest High Priest. And the splitting of the earth and the swallowing of the wicked shows the providence of God, who established the earth for the sake of His children but it shakes, and splits and swallows the wicked. And the fire shows God's wrath, because our God is a consuming fire, and it is a symbol of the eternal fire.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 19- They made a calf in Horeb, and worshipped the molten image. 20- Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass.
Horeb: a mountain in Sinai.

Although the people of God in Sinai asked to see God, and God appeared to them on the mountain in a great sight, and they were very afraid, and said to Moses: You go up and speak with God and tell us. And after he went up and was absent forty days with God, they thought that he had died, or that some strange thing had happened to him, so they turned back from the worship of God, and asked for another god. So Aaron made them a golden calf to worship. And instead of worshipping God who dwells in heaven they debased themselves and made an image of an animal that eats the people; that is, the calf. It is a very strange rebellion and debasement of thought, and they resembled the surrounding nations in the worship of idols, such as Egypt.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 21- They forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt; 22- Wondrous works in the land of Ham, and terrible things by the Red sea. 23- Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them.
The land of Ham: Ham the son of Noah settled in Egypt and the surrounding countries in Africa, and what is meant here is the land of Egypt.
Stood in the breach: interceded and prayed.

The rebellion of the people of God in Sinai by worshipping the golden calf is a forgetting of all the great works of God that He did with them to bring them out of the land of Egypt, whether the ten plagues, or the parting of the Red Sea, and their crossing and the drowning of Pharaoh. So it is a terrible rebellion that deserves that God punish them severely and destroy them, had not Moses stood praying and interceding for his people, so God forgave them (Deut 9:25-29), and this shows the faith of Moses and his boldness before God, for he stood praying for a stubborn people, standing before God who was angry with his people.
So God's love and long-suffering appeared, and His great esteem for intercession, and He forgave the people.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 24- Yea, they despised the pleasant land, they believed not his word: 25- But murmured in their tents, and hearkened not unto the voice of the Lord. 26- Therefore he lifted up his hand against them, to overthrow them in the wilderness: They murmured: grumbled, rebelled and cried out.

When the children of Israel came out of Egypt Moses sent twelve men to spy out the land of Canaan, and they reported that the land was fertile and pleasant, but that its inhabitants were giants who could not be overcome, that is, they did not believe in God, so they refused to enter the pleasant land of Canaan. And none of these wicked spies was an exception except two, Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, so the people were influenced by the words of doubt because of their unbelief in God, and refused to enter the land of Canaan. So God swore (lifted up His hand) that all those who rebelled would not be permitted to enter and possess the land of Canaan, but must perish in the wilderness of Sinai (Num 14:21-23). And He made them wander forty years in the wilderness until all who had rebelled died, and only their sons, who were children at the time of this rebellion, entered.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 27- To overthrow their seed also among the nations, and to scatter them in the lands.

But when this generation that entered the land of Canaan rebelled, God commanded that they go into the Assyrian captivity, then the Babylonian, so He dispersed them and scattered them far from their country throughout the Assyrian kingdom, then the Babylonian; until they repented, and then He brought them back to their land.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 28- They joined themselves also unto Baalpeor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead. 29- Thus they provoked him to anger with their inventions: and the plague brake in upon them. 30- Then stood up Phinehas, and executed judgment: and so the plague was stayed. 31- And that was counted unto him for righteousness unto all generations for evermore.
Baal: the name of a pagan god well known among many nations in the East.
Peor: a mountain in Moab, and what is meant by Baalpeor is: the Baal whose worship is found on Mount Peor and who is worshipped by the Moabites.
The sacrifices of the dead: the sacrifices offered to dead idols.
Executed judgment: that is, judged and decided and intervened to punish the licentious; the Jewish man and the Midianite woman.

Balak king of Moab tried - by means of Balaam the prophet the son of Beor - to curse the people of God, but God refused and blessed them. So Balaam advised Balak to throw Moabite girls to the children of Israel to commit fornication with them, so that God would be angry with them and forsake them, and it would be easy for Balak to defeat the children of Israel. And this actually happened, for the children of Israel committed fornication with the Moabite women, and bowed down to their pagan god Baalpeor, and ate of the sacrifices offered to him. So the Lord struck them with the plague, and twenty-four thousand of them died. And Moses and the elders of Israel hurried to the door of the tent of meeting with prayer and supplication and much weeping, but there were some Jews immersed in fornication, so that an Israelite man named Zimri took a pagan Midianite woman before all the people and went into the tent to commit fornication with her. So Phinehas the priest was jealous with the jealousy of God against evil, and took a spear and killed the two adulterers with it, so God's wrath was calmed because of the prayers of Moses and those with him and the zeal of Phinehas, and He stopped the plague, and God blessed Phinehas the priest and his seed (Num 25). From this appears God's hatred of evil and His punishment of it, and on the other hand the power of prayer and the zeal of the righteous, especially those in positions of responsibility.

entries.section: (2) Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness of Sinai

paragraphs.text: 32- They angered him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes: 33- Because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips.

Meribah (the waters of strife): a place where there is a rock near the city of Kadesh-barnea, which lies north of the Gulf of Aqaba and south of the Dead Sea and Beersheba; that is, south of the land of Canaan.
They angered him: they made him very angry.
Spake unadvisedly with his lips: spoke without wisdom.

1- The people of the children of Israel were much given to murmuring and rebellion; until they made Moses very angry when they reached the region south of Kadesh-barnea. So Moses was troubled and uttered words in which there was something of hesitation and doubt, for he said, "Must we fetch you water out of this rock?" Then he struck the rock twice instead of once (Num 20:10). So God was displeased with him and prevented him - and Aaron, who shared with him in this act - from entering the land of Canaan, so the two died before entering Canaan, and Joshua entered with the people as God commanded him.
2- The Psalm here mentions a group of the rebellions of the children of Israel against God, which are:
a- Their rebellion when Pharaoh pursued them before they crossed the Red Sea (v. 7).
b- Their rebellion because there was no meat in the wilderness of Sinai (v. 14).
c- Their rebellion against Moses and Aaron because of their being set apart for the priesthood (v. 16).
d- The worship of the golden calf (v. 19).
e- Their refusal to enter the land of Canaan because of the words of the spies (v. 24).
f- Fornication and idolatry (Baalpeor) (v. 28).
g- Murmuring because there was no water at Meribah (v. 32).

Do not hasten to murmur against God if you do not find what you want, but be patient and persevere in your prayers, and the Lord will give you at the right time your needs, and even pour out upon you more than you ask or think.

entries.section: (3) Rebellion in the land of Canaan

paragraphs.text: 34- They did not destroy the nations, concerning whom the Lord commanded them: 35- But were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works. 36- And they served their idols: which were a snare unto them.
A snare: a trap and a net.

After God brought His people into the land of Canaan He commanded them to destroy the pagans, the inhabitants of the land, because of their evils (Ex 23:32, 33). For God had been very long-suffering toward them and they did not turn back from their evils.

But the children of Israel were negligent and did not obey God, so there happened to them what God had warned them of, for they mingled with these pagans, and learned their evil works, that is, their sins, and took part with them in the worship of idols. So their mixing with these pagans became a snare for them that took them far from God. They are rebels against God, who do not obey His commandments but their own whims and desires.

entries.section: (3) Rebellion in the land of Canaan

paragraphs.text: 37- Yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto idols, 38- And shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood. 39- Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions.
Shed: caused to flow; that is, they made the blood of their sons flow on the ground.
Innocent blood: blameless blood, that is, the blood of the innocent and not of the wicked.

The mingling of the people of God with the pagans made them imitate them in the most horrible deeds, so that they slaughtered their sons who had done no evil. Although murder is a very great sin, and killing the wicked is easier than killing the innocent, they killed the innocent, and also their beloved sons, to please the ideas of Satan through the pagan gods; thus they left God and His commandments and clung to the wicked; that is, they fell into spiritual fornication, and became unclean. This is the result of rebellion against God.

Do not neglect, my brother, God's commandments because of any thought that comes to you and you think it is from your own mind; as long as it is a destructive and disturbing thought, trust that it is from Satan; because God's thoughts and commandments give peace and build up your life. Do not rush into evil, for this is spiritual fornication, but cling to God and you will enjoy His love, His care and His peace.

entries.section: (4) God's punishment and deliverance of His people

paragraphs.text: 40- Therefore was the wrath of the Lord kindled against his people, insomuch that he abhorred his own inheritance. 41- And he gave them into the hand of the heathen; and they that hated them ruled over them. 42- Their enemies also oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their hand.

When the people of God persisted in evil as a result of their mingling with the pagans, God was angry with them in order to discipline them so that they would repent, so He forsook them, and lifted His protection from them. Then their enemies, with whom they had mingled and shared in evil, ruled over them and humiliated them, and God permitted this; so that by this punishment they would take heed of the seriousness of evil and repent.

entries.section: (4) God's punishment and deliverance of His people

paragraphs.text: 43- Many times did he deliver them; but they provoked him with their counsel, and were brought low for their iniquity. 44- Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry: 45- And he remembered for them his covenant, and repented according to the multitude of his mercies. 46- And he gave them grace before all those that carried them captives.
Brought low: they came down from their rank as children of God and became like the wicked.
Repented: ceased to discipline them.

God did not continue to punish His children, but His discipline was temporary so that they might repent, for God looked with His fatherhood and love upon His people and heard their prayers and their cry to Him when their enemies humbled them, so He saved them by His power; because they are His children with whom He made a covenant to protect them. For although they had broken the covenant, by their repentance they returned to God, so He had mercy on them, and even gave them grace before those who had humbled them, so they were lifted up and found rest by the grace of God. As happened in the Babylonian captivity, for when they repented and cried to God He moved the heart of Cyrus king of Media and Persia and he sent them back to their land, and they built the temple of God. And as happened with Daniel and the three young men, for Nebuchadnezzar raised them to be rulers of the kingdom. And likewise when Pharaoh raised Joseph from prison to be ruler over Egypt.

entries.section: (4) God's punishment and deliverance of His people

paragraphs.text: 47- Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto thy holy name, and to triumph in thy praise. 48- Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting: and let all the people say, Amen. Praise ye the Lord.

1- At the end of the Psalm the people of God cry out to Him, rejecting all rebellion, and declaring their need of Him by saying: save us from every evil and humiliation into which we have cast ourselves. And this is also a prophecy about the request of the captive people of God that He save them and gather them from among the nations. And the aim of the salvation is not only liberation from the humiliation of slavery, but rather life with God, and thanking Him for rescuing them, then praising Him, and even glorying in their sonship to God in the midst of the evil world, and they continue to bless Him throughout their life, indeed for ever.

2- These two verses declare the desire of the children of God in the Old Testament who long for the salvation of Christ and life with Him in the Church of the New Testament. And they are also the feelings of the Church in the New Testament, longing for deliverance from the prison of the body and for rising to the glories of the Kingdom, where there is continual praise.
3- This Psalm is the end of the fourth book of the five books of the Psalms according to the Jewish division. And the fourth section begins from Psalm ninety to Psalm one hundred and six.

And we notice the conclusion of this section with (v. 48), which is repeated at the end of each of the four sections. As for the fifth section, this sentence is not written at its end, because it is the end of all the Psalms.

Wonderful is Your long-suffering, O God; for You give me successive opportunities for repentance, and bear my disobedience of Your commandments and my immersion in sins. But my hope is Your mercy, O Lord, for I have no Savior but You, so have mercy on me; for I need Your fatherhood, indeed I long to live for You, and praise You and enjoy fellowship with You, for this is the true life, and not the evil desires of the world.

God's care for His children: "O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever. Let the redeemed of the Lord say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy" (vv. 1, 2) Introduction:
1- Its writer: It has no title, so it is counted among the "orphan" Psalms whose writer is not known. And some attribute this Psalm to David.
2- When was it written? There are two opinions:
a- That it was written a little after the return from the captivity, and they rely on the words "the redeemed of the Lord"
(v. 2), that is, those returning from the captivity, whom He redeemed from slavery.

b- That it was written before the captivity by David or another, and it speaks of God's redemption of His people in all the circumstances of their life, and a prophecy of the return from the captivity. And this opinion is the more probable.

3- This Psalm is thanksgiving and praise to God, so it suits every believer who feels the hand of God, especially in the afflictions from which He rescues him, so he lifts up his heart in thanks to Him.

4- There is a relation between this Psalm and the two Psalms before it. The three Psalms speak of the history of the people of God and His work with them, so we see that Psalm 051 tells us of God's care for His children and His carrying out His covenants with them. And Psalm 106 tells us of the rebellion of the people of God against Him and His long-suffering toward them. As for Psalm 107, it tells us of His care for His people and His bringing them out of the various afflictions, even if it was the heavy captivity.

5- This Psalm is the first of the fifth and last book of the Psalms, which begins with this Psalm (107) and ends with Psalm (151). And this fifth book tells us of the living word of God, and among the most important things this book contains:
a- Psalm 119, which is David's experiences with the word of God, and it comes in twenty-two parts.
b- The Psalms from (120-134), which are called the Psalms of Ascents, which the people of God used to repeat when they went up the mountain in Jerusalem to the temple of God.
c- Psalm 136, which the Church calls the Second Hoos. It is a Psalm of thanksgiving to God who cared for His people and cares for them in every generation, and the Church repeats it.
d- The Psalms from (148-150), which the Church repeats every day and calls the Fourth Hoos, that is, the fourth praise, and they contain much rejoicing, thanksgiving and praise to God.
6- This Psalm does not occur in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The redeemed give thanks to God

paragraphs.text: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.

1- Giving thanks to God means two things: the confession of sins and thanksgiving for kindness. And they go together in prayer, and they confirm that He is good, and that His goodness is constant throughout life and for ever. And there is much evidence of this from the history of the people of God, for it is He who freed them from the slavery of Egypt, and it is He also who saved them from their enemies in the age of the Judges, and after this brought them back from the captivity in which they were scattered to Jerusalem. All this confirms the continuing care of God for His children however much they sin, as long as they repent and return to Him.

2- The giving of thanks to God is fulfilled in the Church of the New Testament when we confess our sins, and thank Christ the Redeemer who freed us by His cross, and gave us the new life that extends to eternity. So this verse is a prophecy about the Church of the New Testament and the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (1) The redeemed give thanks to God

paragraphs.text: 2- Let the redeemed of the Lord say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy; 3- And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the sea.

Those whom God redeemed from the hand of their enemies share in giving thanks to God, that is, His people who were in the slavery of Egypt, and He brought them out of it by the ten plagues, and they crossed the Red Sea. As for Pharaoh, from whose hand He redeemed them, he was drowned with his army in the sea. And He redeemed them also from the hand of their enemies in the age of the Judges, and killed their enemies. And from the Babylonian captivity He redeemed them and brought them back to their country, while their enemies the Babylonians He destroyed at the hands of Media and Persia. For God gathered His people whom the Babylonians had scattered throughout the world, He gathered them from the east and the west; that is, from every place, and brought them back to live in peace and worship Him in Jerusalem.

I wish, my brother, that every day you would take care to give thanks to God, that is, to confess your sins and thank Him for His care of you throughout the day. So you humble yourself before Him because you offend Him by your sins, while He puts you to shame by His mercy and kindnesses. His love is wonderful, surpassing the mind.

entries.section: (2) God's care for those wandering in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: 4- They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in.

1- The Psalm tells us of the wandering of the people of God in the wilderness of Sinai for forty years. There was no food or drink in the wilderness, but God permitted this because of their murmuring against Him and their refusal to enter the promised land, so He commanded that they should not enter this land but die in the wilderness. But at the same time in His fatherhood He was guiding them and leading them by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, and gave them manna and quails as food, and gave them water to drink from the rock, and kept them in the wilderness from all their enemies. So this shows the sins of mankind, and the mercy of God that keeps man and leads him to repentance, and teaches the sons who would enter the land of Canaan how to obey God, so that they might enjoy His overflowing love.

2- This wandering in Sinai is a symbol of the wandering of mankind away from God before Christ and the inability of philosophy to satisfy it or bring it to God; until Christ became incarnate in the fullness of time.

entries.section: (2) God's care for those wandering in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: 6- Then they cried unto the Lord in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses. 7- And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.

1- When the people of God wandered in the wilderness of Sinai they felt their sin, and repented, and cried out to God during the forty years, so He forgave them and guided them to return to Him and keep His commandments. Then He brought their sons into cities to dwell in them in the land of Canaan, which flows with milk and honey. So crying out and prayer to God is always the only solution that draws out the mercies of the tender God, and so He shows His love and care for His children.

2- In the Old Testament the prophets cried out for the nations that were wandering far from God; until in the fullness of time He guided them to the right way, which is faith in Christ, who declared that He is the way, the truth and the life (Jn 14:6).

3- Verse six is repeated four times in this Psalm to confirm the necessity of crying out to God at all times, and especially in afflictions, for then God's tenderness and His love, which surpasses every mind, appear, and His forgiveness of all sins.

entries.section: (2) God's care for those wandering in the wilderness

paragraphs.text: 8- Oh that men would praise the Lord for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men! 9- For he satisfieth the longing soul, and filleth the hungry soul with goodness.

1- In the face of the greatness of God's love the Psalm calls to the confession of God's love, and thanks to Him for it. For this is the meaning of giving thanks. God's wonders and miracles are many, and His miracle appears here in satisfying two million souls with food and drink in a dry wilderness in which life is very difficult.

2- (Verse 8) is repeated four times in this Psalm to confirm the importance of giving thanks to God, which binds the soul to His love, and protects it and keeps it from sin and makes its life happy, so it delights in fellowship with God.

If affliction is something you do not like, trust that it is by God's arrangement to awaken your soul, so you pray fervently and seek God's help. Cry out to Him, and you will receive His mercies and return to hear His voice and rejoice in fellowship with Him.

10- Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron; 11- Because they rebelled against the words of God, and contemned the counsel of the most High: 12- Therefore he brought down their heart with labour; they fell down, and there was none to help.
Contemned the counsel of the most High: rejected the word of God.
Fell down: fell.

1- The Psalm here speaks of those imprisoned in slavery when the people of God were in Egypt, and the Egyptians humbled them and forced them to labor. And this humiliation was repeated in the age of the Judges when they were negligent toward their enemies and mingled with them, so they rose against them and humbled them.

2- This prison and these fetters mean falling into sins and desires. And this happened to the people of God when they mingled with the pagans and worshipped idols. And it happens today when a person is negligent and falls into sin, and Satan humbles him, especially in the sin of pride, so God forsakes him, and Satan humbles him and God does not help him; because he does not repent and return to God because of his pride, which delays repentance.

3- These verses tell us of the humiliation of mankind condemned to death in the Old Testament. And all, even the righteous, used to go to Hades; until Christ accomplished redemption on the cross, and brought up those who believe in Him to Paradise.

13- Then they cry unto the Lord in their trouble, and he saveth them out of their distresses. 14- He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder. 15- Oh that men would praise the Lord for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men! 16- For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder.

The verses are repeated here (vv. 13, 15) as the people of God cry out to Him, and He frees them from their slavery however strong it is, like iron and brass; because some sins are difficult, such as pride, the return of sin, and despair. But the power of God works miracles and wonders, so He frees His children and brings them back to enjoy life with Him.

Do not be troubled by the multitude of your sins, or their ugliness; because your God is strong and able to free you from them. And however much your circumstances bind you to sin, He is able to change the circumstances, or to support you, so you rise above evil and are delivered from it. Only take refuge in Him with humble and persevering prayer, and you will receive your freedom and regain your joy.
17- Fools because of their transgression, and because of their iniquities, are afflicted. 18- Their soul abhorreth all manner of meat; and they draw near unto the gates of death.

1- The fools are those who go far from God, so they fall into many sins that humble them, and put them in distress and despair; until they lose their appetite for food and drink. And diseases may strike them as a result of their thoughts and their agitation, which contribute to the loss of appetite for food, which increases their weakness, so they become perplexed and anxious.

2- These fools fall into sins that increase their distance from God; until they lose their spiritual appetite, that is, they lose their longing for prayer, for reading the word of God, and for being in the house of the Lord.
Although the spiritual food is before them, they do not benefit from it; until they almost die spiritually, that is, they fall not only into coldness but into spiritual dryness.

19- Then they cry unto the Lord in their trouble, and he saveth them out of their distresses. 20- He sent his word, and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions. 21- Oh that men would praise the Lord for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men!
22- And let them sacrifice the sacrifices of thanksgiving, and declare his works with rejoicing.
Declare his works: recount His works one by one.

1- Here, as we mentioned, the two verses (vv. 19, 20) are repeated, which show the people of God taking refuge in Him, then God's answering them with great miracles. And we see the tenderness of God who heals His children of the disease of sin, and also of bodily diseases if need be, that is, He forgives them and gives them spiritual health and vitality, so they come to Him and worship Him with joy, and offer Him the sacrifices of thanksgiving, that is, the praise of the lips, and thank Him for His works with them.

2- The word of God that God sends is a prophecy about the Incarnation of Christ, who heals the diseases of mankind that believes in Him, and transfers it from death to life, so it praises Him and thanks Him for ever, and they enjoy the sacrifice of thanksgiving, which is the sacrament of Holy Communion of the Body and Blood of the Lord.

How great are Your works with me, O Lord, which are manifested in Your receiving me while I am fallen in sin and unable to rise from it, so You stretch out Your hand, and accept my repentance and turn me from death to life, so I rise and praise You, and enjoy being with You.

entries.section: (5) God's care for those traveling on the sea

paragraphs.text: 23- They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; 24- These see the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep. 25- For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof. 26- They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths: their soul is melted because of trouble. 27- They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and all their wisdom is swallowed up.

1- The Psalm speaks of the merchants traveling on the sea, and the sailors, and the suffering they meet in traveling through the sea. And it shows that God is the mover of nature and the Upholder of all, for it is He who commands, and the winds are stirred up, and the waves rise. So the ships are lifted up toward heaven. Then they go down toward the depth, and the passengers of the ship reel violently like a drunken man, and face death, and their hearts melt with fear, and they lose their ability to control the ship, and surrender to the hand of God, as happened with Jonah and the passengers of the ship when they were traveling on the sea (Jon 1:4).

2- The merchants and sailors are a symbol of the spiritual person who crosses the sea of this world, and God permits him afflictions, which are the winds and waves, and he faces joys and sufferings, which are the rising to heaven and the going down to the depth, and his soul is pressed, and he faces death, or is exposed to severe psychological pressure, and finds nothing before him but to surrender into the hand of God.

3- The merchants and sailors are also a symbol of the prophets, Apostles, priests and servants in every generation who proclaim God, so they face many afflictions and troubles, and during them they experience God, who lifts them to heaven. And they also face psychological troubles by their going down to the depth, and they have nothing before the afflictions but to commit their souls into the hand of God.

entries.section: (5) God's care for those traveling on the sea

paragraphs.text: 28- Then they cry unto the Lord in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses. 29- He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still. 30- Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven. The haven that

they desire. 31- Oh that men would praise the Lord for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men! 32- Let them exalt him also in the congregation of the people, and praise him in the assembly of the elders.
The haven: the port.

1- Those who suffer in their travel within the sea have nothing before them but to cry out to God to rescue them, so He intervenes in His fatherhood and calms the storm, and they regain their peace, and even thank God, and tell of His wonders everywhere among the peoples, and in the gathering of the rulers and the great.

2- The spiritual people and the servants cry out to God in their afflictions, so He intervenes and rescues them from them and their souls grow calm, and they feel the power of God who protects them, so they praise Him for His wonderful works with them, whether in the gathering of peoples and nations, so they guide them to faith, or in the gatherings of the servants and the spiritual teachers, so their faith is confirmed, and they glorify God.

Afflictions are permitted by God not to trouble you, but to awaken your soul, so you move in fervent prayers, and experience the work of God and rejoice, and your zeal for praise and thanksgiving increases all the days of your life.
33- He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watercourses into thirsty ground; 34- A fruitful land into barrenness, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein.
Wilderness: dry deserted land without water or life.
Thirsty ground: land in which there is no water, but in which every man, animal and plant is thirsty.
Barrenness: ruined, unfit for farming or dwelling.

The Psalm shows the seriousness of the evil that people walk in, for it angers God, so He permits them distress in the hope that they will repent, so He makes places with much water, such as rivers and watercourses, completely dry, and the fertile land ruined, to the degree that it is fit for nothing. So when the wicked see their material distress they return to God whom they angered and neglected.

35- He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings. 36- And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation; 37- And sow the fields, and plant vineyards, which may yield fruits of increase. 38- He blesseth them also, so that they are multiplied greatly; and suffereth not their cattle to decrease.
Standing water: a small river whose waters run quietly.

1- These verses show God's work with the humble believers, for He blesses them and gives them the water that gives life to them, and to their animals so they multiply, and to their land so they sow it, and reap many fruits and crops.

2- To the poor in spirit who repent with humility God gives many spiritual blessings, so the Holy Spirit works in them, who is symbolized by the waters, and bestows on them the fruits of the Holy Spirit, which are symbolized by the fruits of the earth, the produce and the cattle, so they rejoice and thank God.

39- Again, they are minished and brought low through oppression, affliction, and sorrow. 40- He poureth contempt upon princes, and causeth them to wander in the wilderness, where there is no way. A wandering place: a place in which a person wanders because there are no roads, like the deserts.

1- If God blesses people, then they return to being immersed in their sins, He removes His grace from them, and their good things decrease, water, fruits and cattle, so they grow weak and many of them die, so they are fewer in number, because of their evils, and their souls that are troubled by the scarcity of their material resources, and He even permits the humiliation, disgrace and straying of their guides and rulers who lead them. So they all go astray because they follow their rulers, that is, God forsakes them so they face many afflictions; that they may take heed and repent.

2- Afflictions meet the spiritual people; so that they hold fast to God. And God permits the humiliation of their rulers, that is, their minds that go astray, and their feelings that err, so they humiliate their bodies. And when they see their calamity they return to God with repentance. As happened with David the prophet.

41- Yet setteth he the poor on high from affliction, and maketh him families like a flock. The poor is the humble one, who takes refuge in God in repentance; for if the righteous have faced afflictions because of their falling into evil, yet when they repent He lifts them up and blesses them, so their tribes multiply like flocks of sheep in their abundance. And God shepherds them all in His love, so they are in unity. And this shows the extent of God's long-suffering and mercy, who is long-suffering toward His children, so He blesses them if they keep His commandments, and permits them afflictions if they go far from Him, but if they repent He returns and lifts them up, and blesses them a second time, as happened with Job, who was a righteous man whom God blessed, then permitted him afflictions, to be freed from self-righteousness, and when he repented He blessed him again greatly, that is, He gave him double what he had had.
42- The righteous shall see it, and rejoice: and all iniquity shall stop her mouth. 43- Whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the Lord.

The Psalm ends with these golden words, calling the believers and the upright in their lives to understand God's care for His children from the beginning of the Psalm to its end. And especially in this last part; that they may keep away from evil and hold fast to God, and that every wicked person may fall silent after the Psalm has exposed the end of evil (vv. 33, 34, 39, 40). And it calls the upright to keep these words not only in their hearts but in their conduct. And to understand, and always meditate on God's mercies and His care for mankind; that they may thank Him and praise Him.

Be watchful so that you live with God with exactness, and hasten to repentance if you sin, so you always enjoy God's care, and His mercies overflow upon you, and the blessings of the Holy Spirit work in you, and you taste the sweetness of fellowship with God.
The praise of God the Victor is His praise. A Psalm of David: "O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, as the Psalm mentions.
2- When was it written?

When David was fighting Aram, Edom took this opportunity, united with Moab, and they attacked the south of the land of the children of Israel, so David sent Joab the commander of his army, and he fought Edom and defeated it.
3- This Psalm is made up of two parts borrowed from the previous Psalms. And these two parts are:
a- The verses (vv. 1-5) are those found in (Ps 57:7-11).
b- The verses (vv. 6-13) are those found in (Ps 60:5-12).
4- This Psalm is full of hope and suits every person who needs hope, whether he is passing through an affliction, or has come out of it, so it confirms his hope.
5- This Psalm was repeated in the communal worship of the Jews, especially after victory in wars, for it is a liturgical Psalm, that is, the congregation prays it together in worship.

6- Those who compiled the Psalms took this Psalm from the two mentioned Psalms (Pss 57, 60), which David wrote; so that they would be a Psalm of praise and thanksgiving to God and give a feeling of victory over the enemies.
7- There are no differences between this Psalm and the Psalms taken from, except in very few words that do not affect the meaning, and they are:
a- Verse (1) "even with my glory" and in (Ps 57:8) "awake up, my glory".
b- Verse (2) "Awake, psaltery and harp" and in (Ps 57:18) "Awake, O psaltery, and O harp".
c- Verse (4) "great above the heavens" and in (Ps 57:10) "great unto the heavens".
8- The title of this Psalm shows the importance of man's praising God with his whole being, for the title says "his praise".
A Psalm of David. Praise belongs to the mind, and the tongue expresses it. And "Psalm" means what is accompanied by a musical instrument, which is the pipe, and the mouth and the hands share in it.
9- The first part of this Psalm (vv. 1-5) is found in Psalm number 56 in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, as we praise God crucified for us; that He may save us from our sins.
(1) The praise of God (vv. 1-5):

1- O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory. 2- Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early. 3- I will praise thee, O Lord, among the people: and I will sing praises unto thee among the nations. 4- For thy mercy is great above the heavens: and thy truth reacheth unto the clouds. 5- Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: and thy glory above all the earth.

See the interpretation of Psalm 57 in the Encyclopedia, Volume Eleven. In general this part tells us of the steadfastness of the spiritual person in praising and glorifying God; so that he wakes early, with his musical instruments, to praise God for His many mercies.
(2) God the helper of His people (vv. 6-13):

6- That thy beloved may be delivered: save with thy right hand, and answer me. 7- God hath spoken in his holiness: I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth. 8- Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the helmet of my head; Judah is my sceptre.

9- Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe; O Philistia, shout aloud over me. 10- Who will lead me into the fortified city? who will bring me into Edom? 11- Is it not thou, O God, who hast cast us off? and thou goest not forth, O God, with our armies?
12- Give us help in trouble: for vain is the salvation of man. 13- Through God we shall do valiantly, and he shall tread down our enemies.
See the interpretation of this part in Psalm sixty, which is in the Encyclopedia, Volume Eleven.

And it is to be noted that this part speaks to us of the intervention of the mighty God to rescue His people, and give them victory over their enemies, and it returns the power to God, and not to weak man.
God rescues the righteous and punishes the wicked. To the chief Musician. For David. A Psalm: "Hold not thy peace, O God of my praise" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: David the prophet, as the title of the Psalm mentions.
2- When was it written? After David reigned over all the tribes of the children of Israel, and took Ahithophel as a counselor and a friend to him.

3- This Psalm expresses David's sufferings from the betrayal of those close to him, and asks for deliverance from God to save him from their hands. So it is the cry of one who suffers and at the same time with the eye of prophecy he saw God's punishment of them. This reassured him, and confirmed his faith in the just God, who keeps him and protects him.
4- This Psalm suits everyone who is exposed to offenses or betrayal from those close to him, for it gives him hope in God who is able to protect him and compensate him for what he lost.

5- This Psalm is Messianic because it prophesies about Christ, who was exposed to many sufferings for our salvation, and speaks clearly of the betrayal of Judas Iscariot, and the punishment that will come upon him.

6- In the title of this Psalm in the Septuagint it says "to the end", and by it he means the wicked's completing their evil, and Christ's completing the salvation by His death on the cross, as David, who is a type of Christ, completed his endurance of the wicked, and their betrayal, and God's rescue of him.
7- The Book of Acts quoted from this Psalm, and confirms that its writer is David, and this Psalm was fulfilled in the betrayal of Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:15-20).
8- This Psalm does not occur in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The hatred of the wicked for the righteous

paragraphs.text: 1- Hold not thy peace, O God of my praise, 2- For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me: they have spoken against me with a lying tongue. 3- They compassed me about also with words of hatred; and fought against me without a cause.

1- David was accustomed to prayer every day and to praising God, even when troubles came upon him, because his life was prayer. But here he asks God to intervene to rescue him from the affliction through which he is passing, for Ahithophel counseled Absalom and helped him to kill his father David.
2- David describes his enemies with three characteristics: wickedness, deceit and lying. All this expresses their hatred of him, although he had not wronged them.

3- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, the only-begotten Son, whose life is prayer and continual conversation with the Father, and who at the same time faced betrayal by His disciple Judas, the fury of His Jewish nation against Him, and the hatred of the priests, the scribes and the Pharisees for Him, together with their wickedness, their deceit and their lying, by which they tried many times to trap Him in a word but were unable; so they fabricated many charges against Him, and in the end they crucified Him unjustly.

entries.section: (1) The hatred of the wicked for the righteous

paragraphs.text: 4- For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer. 5- And they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.

1- David loved all those around him, even those who were hostile to him, such as Saul. But the wicked rose up against him, not only Saul and those with him, but also his son Absalom and David's counselor Ahithophel. They repaid David's love with betrayal and evil, and this shows how deeply they were immersed in evil, for they hated him though they knew that he was innocent and loved them. On the other hand, David continued to love them and to pray for them always; therefore he said, "but I give myself unto prayer."

2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who loved His disciples and all the multitudes, worked many miracles with them, and cared for them with varied teachings. But they rose up against Him with the help and betrayal of His disciple Judas Iscariot, while Christ continued to pray for them and to warn Judas to turn back from his evil.

May you look to the love of Christ, so that you learn love and become accustomed to it in all your relationships. And if anyone wrongs you, continue to pray for him and love him, that perhaps he may repent, so that you continue throughout your life in prayer, praise and love.

"Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand." The wicked one whom God sets over him is Satan, who stands at his right hand; that is, the wicked man receives his strength from him, because the right hand represents strength. These words are a prophecy of what would happen to Ahithophel, David's counselor, or to the Jewish nation, or to Judas Iscariot. The right hand of the spiritual man is in God's hand, as it was with David (Ps 16:8). But if a man rejects God and persists in rejecting Him, Satan takes God's place, because God forsakes him and hands him over to Satan, who takes his strength and his gifts. Judas was a disciple close to Christ; he went out with the disciples, healed the sick and cast out demons, and saw at close range the works of Christ and heard His words; then Satan came to be at his right hand, because he rejected God, and Satan became his adversary, tormented him and led him to suicide.
"When he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let his prayer become sin."

1- David continues his prophecy about Ahithophel, or the Jewish nation, or Judas Iscariot, and declares that if he comes forward for trial on the day of judgment he will be found guilty and will be punished with eternal perdition. And if he cries out to God at that time, his prayer will not be accepted, because the time has passed.

2- If this wicked man, in his life, judges himself before his conscience, he will discover that he is guilty. And if he prays while persisting in sin, he gains nothing from his prayer. As for Judas, when he repented after betraying Christ, his remorse appears to be prayer, but it was despair, and it led him to hang himself.
"Let his days be few; and let another take his office."

1- David prophesies about this traitor that the days of his life will be short; for Ahithophel and Judas each hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23; Mt 27:5), and the Jewish nation was destroyed by the Roman Titus in AD 70, when he laid Jerusalem waste and killed a million and a half of the Jews.

2- The office of this wicked man was a great office, which another takes. In place of Ahithophel came Hushai the Archite (2 Sam 17:14), and in place of Judas Iscariot came the Apostle Matthias (Acts 1:
26), and in place of the Jewish nation came the Church of the New Testament, which has spread everywhere.

9- Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow. 10- Let his children be continually vagabonds, and beg: let them seek their bread also out of their desolate places. 11- Let the extortioner catch all that he hath; and let the strangers spoil his labour. 12- Let there be none to extend mercy unto him: neither let there be any to favour his fatherless children. 13- Let his posterity be cut off; and in the generation following let their name be blotted out. 14- Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered with the LORD; and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out. 15- Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth.

1- Evil and ruin come upon the followers of this wicked man, although no source mentions that Judas Iscariot had a wife or children. But if he had a wife and children who walked in evil, having learned it from him, all these curses come upon them, so that his wife becomes a widow, because Judas hanged himself, and his children become orphans through the death of their father. His sons become poor and so beg, and ruin comes upon them. The extortioner who catches their labor is Satan, and the strangers are the demons. No one has mercy on his offspring or shows them kindness, because they are wicked. His offspring die, and no one is left to perpetuate his memory. And his wicked parents, who taught him evil, are punished.

2- If Judas had no wife and children, then his offspring are his deeds and his thoughts, or all who walk in evil as he did, and so all the curses mentioned before come upon him. This applies also to Ahithophel.

3- And if we apply this to the Jewish nation, then the extortioner and the strangers are Titus and the Roman soldiers, who destroyed Jerusalem and killed the Jews, and everyone who has persecuted the Jews throughout the generations, such as Hitler the German.

16- Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart. 17- As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing, so let it be far from him. 18- As he clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment, so let it come into his bowels like water, and like oil into his bones. 19- Let it be unto him as the garment which covereth him, and for a girdle wherewith he is girded continually. 20- Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the LORD, and of them that speak evil against my soul.

The cause of all the calamities and curses that may come upon the wicked man is his oppression of the poor and needy and his depriving them of all strength or help; this means Christ, or David. So did Judas, or Ahithophel, or the Jewish nation. So the curses which they desired came upon them, because they desired evil. And evil is joined to cursing, so they put on evil like a garment, indeed they put it on also as an outer robe like a cloak, and girded themselves with it, that is, they braced themselves to do evil. So it entered into their bowels and their bones, that is, they held fast to evil from within, which is their thoughts and feelings, and from without, which is their deeds. And the curse came upon them, that is, they were tormented within and without, and nothing awaits them in the end but eternal torment. This is the reward of him who clings to evil, so that it becomes part of his nature and it is very difficult for him to leave it; even if his inner being is pained by turmoil and anxiety, he rejects the voice of God and persists in evil until death, as Judas and Ahithophel each hanged himself; for they loved evil, so the curse came upon them, which is the inevitable result of evil, and consequently the blessing of God was far from them, for they rejected Him by their own will and did not love Him. Ahithophel rejected his great position as David's counselor, and Judas rejected the greatest thing, which was his discipleship to Christ and his apostleship.

Do not be careless and accept evil, even if it is small, lest it creep into your inner being and the devil deceive you, so that you love it and it gradually gains mastery over you, until you can no longer hear the voice of God, and you continue to drift away from Him and lose your life.
21- But do thou for me, O GOD the Lord, for thy name's sake: because thy mercy is good, deliver thou me. 22- For I am poor and needy, and my heart is wounded within me.

1- Although David spoke by the spirit of prophecy about what would happen to Ahithophel, or to Judas Iscariot, he is not occupied with evil and its recompense, but comes humbly before God and prays, asking for mercy and deliverance from the hand of the wicked. Two things appear in David's prayer:
a - His humility, for he says "for thy name's sake," and describes himself as poor and needy, and wounded within.
b - His faith in the merciful God, who is able to deliver him.

2- These two verses are a prophecy about the sufferings of Christ and His cross, because David is a type of Christ. Christ speaks as the Son of Man, that is, on behalf of humanity, and He speaks to the Father, asking for mercy and deliverance; for in His human form He is poor and needy and His heart is wounded, because He will bear all the sins of the world upon Himself, and everyone has forsaken Him, and His disciple has betrayed Him, and He will endure all the torments for the sake of our salvation. So He asks for the Father's help and mercy in His sufferings, as He expressed the harshness of the sufferings by saying in the garden of Gethsemane, "remove this cup from me" (Lk 22:42).

23- I am gone like the shadow when it declineth: I am tossed up and down as the locust. 24- My knees are weak through fasting; and my flesh faileth of fatness. 25- I became also a reproach unto them: when they looked upon me they shaked their heads.
"Shaked": they shook their heads in mockery and scorn.

1- David likens his life, with all the hardships he endured, to a shadow, short and passing; indeed David died at the age of seventy. He likens himself also to a locust, a light insect that is tossed about before the wind that carries it. So David too suffered in his soul, as if he were trembling within.

David also declares that he took refuge in God with many fasts, and that he ate vegetable food cooked with oil. From the many fasts his body grew weak and his knees trembled, and his body, which had been full and fat, became lean and thin, so that his enemies mocked him, and he became an example of shame and ridicule. David mentions all this to show his weakness with humility before God, asking for His help.

2- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who appeared in the flesh as weak as a locust and trembled in His soul from the multitude of sufferings; His life passed swiftly, and He died young, at about thirty-three years of age. His body grew weak and became lean from the fasts, and also from the sufferings and the scourging, and He became an example of shame when He was hung on the cross, and the Jews mocked Him and shook their heads (Mt 27:39; Mk 15:29). All this He bore for our sake, and He asks the Father's help to complete the redemption.
26- Help me, O LORD my God: O save me according to thy mercy: 27- That they may know that this is thy hand; that thou, LORD, hast done it.

1- David asks for God's help according to His abundant mercy, for he trusts in God's limitless mercy. And when his enemies see God's power which protects him, they will learn the importance of walking in righteousness and of God's care for the righteous, that perhaps they may repent of their evil and return to God.

2- These two verses also are a prophecy about Christ, who speaks in the voice of humanity as He approaches the sufferings of the cross, and asks for the Father's help and mercy, so that those who persecute Him may know that He is the Son of God, the awaited Messiah, so that they may believe in Him and understand that the sufferings and the crucifixion are God's will for the salvation of humanity.
28- Let them curse, but bless thou: when they arise, let them be ashamed; but let thy servant rejoice.
29- Let mine adversaries be clothed with shame, and let them cover themselves with their own confusion, as with a mantle.

1- David declares that his enemies curse him while he blesses them, as Saul and Absalom did to him, whereas he forgave Saul and had compassion on his son Absalom. So he was in peace and joy with God because of his love. And perhaps God's dealing with David and His protection of him will shame his enemies, so that they are abashed and put to shame, that perhaps by this they may repent. For David did not ask for their destruction, but only for their shame, that they might turn back from their evil.

2- The Jews persecuted Christ and tried many times to kill Him; then they seized Him, tortured Him and crucified Him, whereas He cared for them, healed their sick and fed them. And when they had completed all their evil by crucifying Him, they were put to shame when they saw that He had risen from the dead. Perhaps this would have led them to repent and believe in Him, but they were put to shame because of their evil, while He was in joy for the accomplishment of redemption on the cross: they hate Him, and He loves them and dies for them.
30- I will greatly praise the LORD with my mouth; yea, I will praise him among the multitude. 31- For he shall stand at the right hand of the poor, to save him from those that condemn his soul.

1- At the close of the psalm David thanks God and praises Him, not only in his chamber but in the midst of the congregation of the Jews during the worship of God, because God stood by his side and delivered him from the hand of Saul and Absalom and all his enemies.

2- Christ, by His death and His redemption of humanity, offers through the sacrifice of Himself the greatest praise before the Father, and as the Son of Man He thanks Him because He stood by His side, and triumphed over all the demons who were trying to stop the redemption.
Therefore the Church, which is the mouth of God on earth, praises God always for His care and His love.
And if, for a wicked man like Judas, Satan stands at his right hand, here we find the Father standing beside the Son, and Christ standing beside every believer who suffers hardships on earth.

Be sure that God is beside you when sufferings surround you, even if all those around you rise up against you. Know that God is stronger than all, and able to deliver you from their hands, so that your heart is filled with joy and praise, while they are put to shame, that perhaps they may repent.
Christ, the victor on behalf of David. Psalm "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand) "..(v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states, and as Christ declared in the New Testament (Mt 22:44).
2- When was it written? After David's victories over the nations surrounding him.
3- This psalm is one of the greatest Messianic psalms, because it speaks entirely of the awaited Messiah, and the Jews agree on this, as appears from Christ's words with them (Mt 22:41-46).
4- The psalm tells us of the attributes of Christ: He is the Lord, the King, the Priest, the Judge, and the Conqueror of His enemies.
5- This psalm was sung at the coronation of the kings of the kingdom of Judah, that is, the kings who were of the seed of David.

6- This psalm is among the psalms most quoted by the New Testament: Christ Himself used it (Mk 12:35-37), Peter mentioned it in his sermon on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:34), and the Apostle Paul drew on it in his epistles to the Corinthians and the Hebrews (1 Cor 15:

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, because in it Christ appeared triumphant over Satan; for He paid the debt by His death and bound Satan by the sacrifice of Himself, for He is the Great High Priest.
"The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."
1- "The LORD said unto my Lord" declares that the Lord the Father speaks to "my Lord," who is the Son, Jesus Christ.
That King David calls Christ "my Lord" confirms the divinity of Christ, for David was a great king, and who could be the one he calls "my Lord," that is, his master, except God?
2- In the Hebrew original of this psalm the word "LORD" is "Yahweh" and "my Lord" is "Adonai."

Yahweh is the name of God the Father in the Old Testament (Ex 6:3), and Adonai means Lord, or Master, and this is the name of Christ by which He was addressed on earth. This confirms that the verse tells us of a dialogue between the Father and the Son.

3- This verse was fulfilled after Christ died on the cross, paid the wages of men's sins, and bound Satan. For after He completed the redemption, the Father calls the Son within the Godhead, to show His glory by His sitting at the right hand of the Father, that is, to show the fullness of His power and divinity, which appeared to men in His resurrection. By this He shows His authority over the demons, His enemies, and also over their wicked followers who crucified Christ and insulted Him, and who submitted to Him and declared their faith in Him, like Longinus who pierced Him with the spear.

4- We cannot understand the equality of the Son with the Father in essence except by the Holy Spirit; it is the Spirit who revealed this truth to David (Mt 22:43). And because of this equality, the sitting of the Son at the right hand of the Father, that is, the declaration of His equality with the Father because they are one in essence, is an equality that is constant from eternity to eternity. Although it was hidden from the eyes of men in the Incarnation of Christ, His sufferings and His death, the Holy Spirit declares it to David and to all believers, especially after He showed His power in His resurrection.

5- The sitting of the Son at the right hand of the Father is the sitting of Christ, God incarnate, that is, in His divinity and His humanity, to reign forever, triumphant over His enemies the demons. By this He declares to all humanity that believes in Him that He gives it authority and victory over all the wars of the demons, through Him and by His power.

And after humanity completes its striving on earth, the triumphant Christ grants it to ascend to heaven to live with Him forever, and to enter through the closed doors, the doors of the Kingdom, so that He permits humanity that believes in Him to enter and live in heaven.
"The LORD shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies."
1- The rod is the rod of the king, and this appeared on the cross, for Christ reigned from a tree (the psalm of the Ninth Hour of the Agpeya: "The Lord hath reigned from the tree").

2- If the first verse showed a dialogue between the Father and the Son, this verse completes for us the work of the Trinity, for it tells us of the work of the Holy Spirit, who sends out the preaching of Christ the King and Savior from Zion, that is, Jerusalem, to the whole world, that it may believe in the salvation of Christ.
3- By the reign of Christ on the cross He rules over His enemies, that is, the wicked who opposed Christ and crucified Him. It says "rule," not "destroy," and this rule appears in two forms:
a - These wicked people believe in Christ and submit to Him.
b - They do not believe in Christ, but they fear Him, so He restrains their evil from harming His children except to the extent that He sees to be for their benefit.
"Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth."
"Willing": it means that they are volunteers and have come to the Lord of their own freedom.

1- "Thy people shall be willing": the Father addresses the Son, saying that He offered salvation on the cross and many believed in Him, and these are His people. They submitted to Him of their own freedom, and even went out preaching in His name to the whole world. In the Septuagint translation, in the Agpeya, it says "With thee is the principality," that is, thy people of their own freedom submitted to thy lordship in their faith and their preaching.

2- "In the day of thy power": the day of Christ's power is the day of the cross, on which He gave salvation to His people, and the day of salvation extended through the life of the believers throughout their lives, so that they lived in the power of Christ, defeated the demons, stood firm in their faith, and walked in the virtues. In the Agpeya it says "in the day of thy strength," that is, thy power.

3- "In the beauties of holiness": the beauties of holiness are the virtues with which the people of God adorn themselves, that is, they walk in the virtues they have acquired by the power of Christ, so that He is glorified in them. In the Agpeya it says "in the splendors of the saints," that is, the virtues of the saints, and so lived all the children of God.

4- "From the womb of the morning": that is, before the dawn comes forth, and this tells us of the eternity of the Son, who became incarnate in the fullness of time. What takes place in the womb is hidden and secret, so the eternity of Christ is a mystery that rises above the mind, how He exists from eternity and became incarnate in the fullness of time, to shine like the dawn upon all who sit in darkness, enlightening by His salvation all who are subject to sin and death, and they are all mankind, and giving them His salvation that they may live anew.

- The birth of Christ from the womb before the dawn, besides signifying His eternity in His begetting from the Father and His equality with Him in essence, also signifies His birth in the fullness of time from the womb of the Virgin, and this actually took place at night before the dawn. In the Agpeya it says "before the morning star have I begotten thee," that is, before the sun and the moon the Son was begotten of the Father, because He is eternal and has the same nature. At the same time He was born of the Virgin at night before the morning star, that is, before the rising of the sun.

5- "Thou hast the dew of thy youth": the dew is the moisture of the morning; Christ has the dew, and it means the many who believe in Him, who are like drops of dew falling from heaven. They are heavenly by their faith in Christ and their spiritual conduct. "Thy youth" means youthfulness, vitality and strength. The believers in the early Church, in the apostolic age, were full of vitality and of love for Christ.
And in every generation there are believers full of vitality.

May you live in spiritual youth, that is, take care of your prayers and your readings so that you feel Christ, and He gives you zeal and opens your heart with love for doing good and for loving every person, even the one who wrongs you.
"The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

1- The psalm speaks here about Christ, and the Lord, that is, the Father, has sworn that Christ is the priest after the order of Melchizedek; that is, He is priest and king forever. Among the Jews the priesthood and the kingship were not joined in one tribe, for the priesthood was from the tribe of Levi and the kingship from the tribe of Judah. Yet David and his son Solomon, the kings, practiced the priesthood in part, for David put on the priestly garments when he brought the ark back to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:14).

2- "The Lord hath sworn," for He alone has the right to swear, since He has complete power to fulfill what He swears by, whereas men are weak and cannot fulfill what they swear, so an oath is not fitting for them. And "will not repent" means that He will not go back on His word, because His command is protected and established forever, that Christ is priest and reigns forever. And if it is said of God that He repented, that is a divine expression for the possibility of God relenting from His word if man repents, as in the repentance of the people of Nineveh.

3- The priesthood of Christ is eternal, therefore it says "after the order of Melchizedek," who is the king of Salem, that is, the king of peace, and of whom no beginning or end is known. The priesthood of Aaron, however, is given to limited men who die; the priesthood of Christ is after the rite of Melchizedek and not of Aaron.
We note that Melchizedek offered his sacrifice of bread and wine, as Christ did, and Melchizedek was a type of Christ (Gen 14:18).

5- The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath. 6- He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill the places with the dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries.
"His wrath": his severe anger.

1- This verse shows the equality of the Father with the Son, for it says to the Son, "The Lord at thy right hand," as was mentioned in (v. 1) that the Son sits at the right hand of the Father; and the sitting at the right hand does not mean a place, because God is without limit and has no right or left. What is meant by the right hand is power and glory.

2- The two verses show the authority of Christ, who strikes through, judges and crushes all who oppose Him, meaning the demons and all the wicked who follow them; for everyone who opposed God and His Church throughout the generations was broken and became humbled, like Nebuchadnezzar who became like the beasts (Dan 4:33), and Holofernes whom Judith killed (Jdt 13:10), and Antiochus the Great who was eaten by worms and died in the days of the Maccabees (2 Macc 9:9), and like Diocletian and the emperors who stood against the Church, and other kings of the earth who were broken, while the Church remained strong until now.

3- The judgment of Satan was accomplished on the cross when Christ bound him by His death on the cross, and on the last day of judgment He will cast him into eternal torment, together with all the wicked who follow him.
"He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head."

1- Christ the Son drank from the river of sufferings, bore all the hardships of the cross, and died to redeem us, and by the power of His divinity He lifted up His head in the resurrection, to raise us up in Him from the death of sin.

2- Every spiritual man in the hour of affliction drinks from the river of the Holy Spirit, to whom he flees for refuge, so his heart is comforted and he stands firm during the trial, so that at its end he lifts up his head by the power of God and triumphs over the wars of Satan.

When any affliction meets you, be sure that it is by God's permission for your good, so do not let your heart be troubled. But seek God in prayer and humility, offering repentance for your sins, and you will be purified, and God will lift up your head, glorify you and bless you with many blessings.
Thanksgiving to God the fortress "Alleluia. I will praise the LORD with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: unknown.

2- When was it written? There is a title in the Septuagint translation of this psalm, which is "For the return of Haggai and Zechariah." So the time of its writing would be after the return from the captivity.
3- This psalm speaks of the works of God, their greatness and their attributes, and it calls man to thank God and praise Him while remaining steadfast in faith in Him.
4- There is a relation between this psalm and the one that follows it, in that the first speaks of the attributes of the works of God, while Psalm 112 speaks of the attributes of those who fear God.
5- This psalm is liturgical, and it used to be chanted at the feast of the Passover, as St. Augustine tells us.

6- This psalm and the one that follows are arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet. This psalm is divided into twenty-two parts (a verse may contain two or three parts), and each part begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It is noted that these two psalms contain verses similar to those in the books of Psalms and Proverbs.

7- Because Psalm 110, which precedes this psalm, speaks of the Ascension of Christ, this psalm and the two psalms that follow it each begin with the word Alleluia. These three psalms express joy at the Ascension of Christ.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ died on the cross and completed our redemption; therefore we glorify the great works of God by which we obtained our salvation and redemption.

entries.section: (1) Thanks to God for His works

paragraphs.text: "Praise ye the LORD. I will praise the LORD with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation."

1- The psalm begins with rejoicing, praise and thanksgiving to God for all His benefits. This praise is from the whole heart, that is, with all the feelings, and not only with the tongue; that is, the whole being of the psalmist thanks God and praises Him, for he is not occupied with the desires of the world or its cares, but his only occupation is the praise of God. In this he fulfills God's commandment to love Him with all his heart (Deut 6:5).

2- He is not content with thanksgiving and praise in his chamber, but also praises God in the assembly and congregation of the upright, that is, those who believe in God and are upright in His worship. He is encouraged, and encourages those around him, to praise God, and this confirms that this psalm is a liturgical psalm.

entries.section: (1) Thanks to God for His works

paragraphs.text: "The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein."

1- The works of God are great and show the extent of His wisdom and power in creation, and in His ordering of the universe and keeping it in balance. Indeed His greatness appears also in making creatures act contrary to their nature for the glory of His name and for the salvation of His children; so He makes the fire not burn the three youths, and the hungry, ravening lions not harm Daniel. And on the contrary hail and fire come together to destroy the Egyptians, and the sun and the moon do not shine in the plague of darkness.

2- The believers seek out the works of God; that is, they meditate on them and behold God their Creator, so their hearts are gladdened and they praise God for His greatness, and indeed they always seek to meditate on the works of God in order to discover the God hidden behind them, and to remain in constant glorification and praise of Him.

entries.section: (1) Thanks to God for His works

paragraphs.text: "His work is honourable and glorious: and his righteousness endureth for ever." Honourable: greatness.
Glorious: goodliness and beauty.
Endureth: is established.

1- The works of God are very great and beautiful, not only in huge beings such as the sun and the moon, but in the smallest creatures, such as insects, or microbes invisible to the naked eye. All of them were created in wisdom and have an order in life that preserves them, however weak they appear or whatever conditions oppose them. All this God created for the sake of man; how much greater, then, is His work in creating man, caring for him, and ordering his life.

2- God is perfect in His justice, and His justice is everlasting, but He is long-suffering toward the wicked to give them an opportunity to repent. Therefore man should not be disturbed if he suffers injustice, because God is just and will compensate him partly on earth and without limit in eternity. On the other hand, no one should rush to wrong another even if he has the opportunity. For God will surely punish him, whether in this life or, still more, in the next life if he refuses to repent.

entries.section: (1) Thanks to God for His works

paragraphs.text: "He hath made his wonderful works to be remembered: the LORD is gracious and full of compassion."

1- It is important for man to remember the wonderful works of God, so that his faith may be strengthened and they may move him to praise and thanksgiving. Therefore God commanded His people to keep a portion of the manna in a pot inside the ark of the covenant throughout their lives, and also Aaron's rod that budded, and above all the tables of the commandments. And God commanded His people to sanctify days as feasts in which to remember God. And to this day the Church takes care to remember the works of God through the feasts and fasts, and above all through the living, tangible memorial of His Body and Blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist.
