2- Remembering the works of God reveals to the one who takes care to do so the graciousness and mercy of God, and by this those who thank God become attached to His person and love Him with all their hearts, so more abundant mercies overflow upon them, until they are filled with love and mercy toward others, and serve them and honor them.

May you set aside even a few minutes every day or every week to meditate on the works of God, whether in nature, or its ordering, or your creation, or His care for you, so that your heart may be calmed and filled with love for Him, and your tongue may be loosed to praise Him.
"He hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant."

1- God remembered His covenant with the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so He cared for His people in the wilderness of Sinai and gave them manna as food for forty years, because they believed in Him and feared Him. He fed them in a barren wilderness, the wilderness of Sinai, as He fed His children throughout the generations, such as Elijah, whom He fed by means of the raven (1 Kgs 6:17), and as Christ fed the multitudes with the two fish and the five loaves (Mt 14:13-21).

2- The meat means the Passover, and therefore this psalm is chanted at the feast of the Passover, as we mentioned in the introduction. The Passover is a type of the sacrifice of Christ, that is, His Body and Blood, which He gives in His Church every day to those who fear Him as an everlasting covenant, that is, He feeds them spiritually forever. And God does not forget His covenant, and He wants His believing children also not to forget His covenant, so they partake of His Body and Blood always for the forgiveness of their sins, and that He may give them a strong spiritual life. Just as He commanded His people in the days of Moses to put manna in the golden pot inside the ark of the covenant, that they might always remember how He fed them, remembering His covenant with Abraham, so that they might rely on Him and thank Him.
"He hath shewed his people the power of his works, that he may give them the heritage of the heathen."

1- God showed His people the children of Israel, who were enslaved in Egypt, the power of His works, not only by promises and words, but in deed, through the ten plagues, the dividing of the Red Sea and their crossing it, and the drowning of Pharaoh and all his army.

2- After God sustained them in the wilderness of Sinai for forty years in a miraculous way, giving them water from the rock, manna from heaven, and also quail, and keeping their clothes and sandals from wearing out, and protecting them from enemies, so that they triumphed over them, such as Amalek, and finally brought them to a river and divided it so that they might cross over, then He destroyed the pagans who dwelt in Canaan because of their wickedness, and gave the children of Israel their land because of their faith in Him.
7- The works of his hands are verity and judgment; all his commandments are sure. 8- They stand fast for ever and ever, and are done in truth and uprightness.

1- The works of God are sure; that is, certain and true, meaning that they are for the good of man, and likewise all His commandments are steadfast; even if man does not understand them at the time and endures afflictions, he discovers in the end that the narrow gate and the hard way is what leads to eternal life. God is long-suffering toward evil, but He will surely reward those who do good.

2- The commandments and works of God are steadfast and cannot change even if the whole world changes, and all of them are truths however much Satan tries to cast doubt on them. They alone are upright, and their opposite is deviation, however tempting the matter may be, like the desires of the world. Therefore the believer must hold fast to his faith and to God's commandments, and reject every doubt even if the words of Satan are convincing; for his deceit will be exposed after this.
"He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name."

1- God sent redemption to His people Israel, who were enslaved in Egypt, so He freed them and brought them out of Egypt and across the Red Sea, and Pharaoh and all his army died in their place. And God established His covenant with His people, to be their God and to have them as His people, so He kept them and sustained them in the wilderness of Sinai, gave them the land of Canaan as a possession, and showed His holiness to them when He dwelt in His house in the tabernacle of meeting, after He had appeared in His might on the mountain, and the people offered Him sacrifices and feared Him and worshiped Him, so they enjoyed His care and His fellowship.

2- All that God did with His people in the Old Testament was a type of the redemption of Christ on the cross, and then He established His covenant in His Church by the sacrament of the Eucharist. So the Holy One dwelt among His children and sanctified them by the Holy Myron and by partaking of His Body and Blood.

3- The name of God is holy, for in it is all righteousness and goodness, and it is also reverend and fearful, and exceedingly great, and so it deserves glorification and praise. At the same time His name is very fearful to the wicked, especially on the day of judgment when He casts them into eternal torment.
"The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever."

1- "The beginning of wisdom," that is, its start, its root and its first source, is the fear of the Lord, and there can be no wisdom without the fear of the Lord; for the fear keeps man away from evil and leads him to humility, so that he is able to behold God, who guides him in all his spiritual and material affairs.
2- And wisdom is good not for him who knows it in theory, but for him who lives it, that is, carries out God's commandments and clings to Him, so he fears Him and loves Him and lives in peace.

3- When man knows God through wisdom he rejoices greatly and praises Him continually. He keeps praising God throughout his life, and the praise even extends into eternity. So the psalm ends with praise as it began with it, with the word Alleluia. And although this verse is the close of this psalm, it is the beginning of the next psalm, which speaks of those who fear God.

If God has worked many works in your life that show His fatherhood and care, you must believe in Him, so that you live at ease, relying on Him, and your heart is free to love Him and praise Him, and you taste the sweetness of the Kingdom while you are still on earth.
The one who fears the Lord and loves others "Alleluia. Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD, that delighteth greatly in his commandments" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: not mentioned, so it is one of the orphan psalms, and some attribute it to the prophet David.
2- When was it written?
Because there is a title for this psalm in the Septuagint translation, which is "For the return of Haggai and Zechariah"
its time of writing could be after the captivity, or in the days of David if David is its author.

3- There is a similarity between this psalm and the one before it, that is (Ps 111); if the previous psalm blesses God and His works, this psalm blesses the one who fears God and shows his attributes and blessings.
4- This psalm is considered one of the wisdom psalms, as appears from its beginning.

5- This psalm, as we mentioned in the introduction to the previous psalm, is one of the psalms that begin with the word Alleluia, and it is among three psalms (Ps 111, 112, 113) full of the glorification of God who ascended into heaven, as Psalm 110, which precedes these three psalms, tells us.
6- This psalm is divided into twenty-two parts and arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, each part beginning with one of the letters of the alphabet in order, like the psalm before it.
7- This psalm resembles the books of Proverbs and Psalms, for there are some verses common to them.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ completed the redemption, and the Righteous One died on the cross for us sinners. This psalm tells us of Christ the Righteous One, whose righteousness endures forever.

entries.section: (1) The attributes of him who fears the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Praise ye the LORD. Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD, that delighteth greatly in his commandments."

1- The psalm begins with rejoicing, that is, the praise of God, and at the outset it blesses him who fears the Lord, who, as we learned at the end of the previous psalm, is the wise man, and who is therefore able to praise God continually, to rejoice before Him, and to walk in His commandments.

2- The demons fear God, and so do the wicked, but they do not love His commandments or walk in them; therefore he continues his words in this verse, saying that the true fearer of the Lord is the one who delights in His commandments, who loves them and desires them with all his heart, and is indeed greatly delighted in them. Thus the love of God and the fear of Him are mingled, and are united in a wonderful way that only he knows who has experienced it through keeping God's commandments.

entries.section: (1) The attributes of him who fears the Lord

paragraphs.text: "His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed."

1- God blesses not only those who fear Him but also their offspring on earth, in addition to the blessings of heaven that He gives them. The might of the offspring does not mean the multitude of their number or their bodily or material strength, but rather their spiritual strength, so that they too live in the fear of God and enjoy His blessings in their lives.

2- God's goods are many, and He gives them to His upright children, that is, those who fear Him and keep His commandments, and they are the blessed offspring, and not only the bodily children of those who fear the Lord but also the spiritual children. The patriarchs, bishops, monks and celibates, whether in the Old Testament, such as Elijah and Jeremiah, or in the New Testament, such as Paul, had many spiritual children, far more than any bodily children of any pious men.

entries.section: (1) The attributes of him who fears the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever." Wealth: ample provision and great riches.

1- God blesses those who fear Him and gives them not only their material needs but gives them abundance and ease in material things, so that they are not preoccupied with them and their only concern is life with Him. And to the extent that they are occupied with God, He grants them material things, and they distribute these to the needy, as the believers used to lay their gifts at the feet of the Apostles, so that the Apostles were in plenty, to satisfy the Church with their spiritual teachings and also their material needs.

2- One of the most important attributes of him who fears the Lord is that he is righteous, that is, he lives with God and loves Him and walks in His commandments, loves the virtues and longs for the heavens, so that he lives spiritually until he enters the Kingdom. The righteous one here is not only the one who is righteous on earth, but rather it means Christ, the Righteous and Holy One.

3- By this we see that the righteous man enjoys material wealth in his house, that is, he is settled in this wealth, in addition to his enjoyment of righteousness, that is, the spiritual life; so he receives a material portion on earth in addition to a righteousness that endures forever in heaven.

entries.section: (1) The attributes of him who fears the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Unto the upright there ariseth light in the darkness: he is gracious, and full of compassion, and righteous."

1- He speaks here of God, who has made His light arise upon His righteous children, upright in their spiritual walk, who were in the darkness of affliction, so that their hearts were comforted, as He did with the three youths in the furnace and Daniel in the lions' den. And this light illumined the souls of His righteous children, so that they too became light to those around them through their righteous lives which they received from Him, just as the moon draws its light from the sun.

2- God is also gracious and full of compassion, so He has pity on His children in their afflictions, and if they sin He accepts their repentance, but at the same time He is righteous, that is, just, so He rewards them for all their labors, and disciplines them if they turn away from Him, as He disciplined His people with the captivity. And the righteous children of God learned these attributes from Him, so their hearts were filled with graciousness and compassion toward all those around them, but at the same time their justice and firmness appear toward the careless and the licentious, so they discipline them that they may repent, as Paul excommunicated the sinner of the city of Corinth.

Remember God, and set Him before you at all times by repeating His holy name, so that you protect yourself by the fear of Him and reject evil however small, and hasten to Him with repentance if you sin, so that your heart is purified and His secrets are disclosed to you, and you cling to Him and He pours out His mercies upon you, and you praise Him with joy.
"A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion."
Lendeth: gives them loans.

1- The righteous man imitates God, so he becomes merciful, has compassion and pity on the poor and lends to them, so he gladdens their hearts and in turn becomes happy himself. He is compassionate: he gives the poor gifts, and also gives them loans, and helps them in every way so that they may be able to continue their lives.

2- This righteous man orders his affairs with justice; that is, without malice or evil purpose, because his heart is pure, and at the same time his management is just, that is, balanced, so that he does not go to excess in his loans to others to the point that he himself is in need and enters into hardships (2 Cor 8:14), nor does he reduce his help to the poor very much, so that he becomes hard. And this merciful righteous man, because he helped the poor on earth, will have rest and happiness in heaven; because "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again" (Prov 19:17), so God rewards him in heaven.
"Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance."

1- He who fears the Lord, the righteous man, is not moved from his principles, but remains holding fast to his righteousness and to the fear of God, for he is a man of principles and values. Nor is he moved from the work of mercy and compassion toward the needy. So he is established in God, and God establishes him with Himself forever.

2- This righteous man or just man is remembered after his death, indeed forever, where he is rewarded in eternity. And just as the works of God are remembered forever (Ps 111:4), so also His righteous children's works, which they did by the power of God, are remembered forever, and they are works of righteousness and mercy.
7- He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD.
"See his desire upon his enemies": he sees the punishment of those who trouble him.

1- He who fears the Lord is not afraid of the evil tidings that Satan stirs up against him, but his heart remains steadfast in faith, because he trusts in God, and God gives him this steadfastness which surpasses the mind; for the mind alone is troubled, but faith surpasses it and gives steadiness to man's feelings, so that he goes on living and walking in tranquility and does all his works successfully. The righteous man is liable to hear or to meet with evil tidings, and God permits this to test his faith and steadfastness and spiritual growth.

2- The heart of him who fears the Lord and is merciful to the poor remains steadfast throughout his life, until at the end, that is, in eternity, he sees the punishment of the demons who troubled him in eternal torment, in addition to his victory over the demons who troubled him in life, in his repentance, his striving and his service, and his ability to do mercy to the needy.

"He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honour." His horn shall be exalted: the horn is the strongest part of an animal's body, and its being exalted, that is, standing in defiance in readiness to attack the prey, means a declaration of its strength. What is meant is that God declares the strength and glory of the righteous man before all.

1- He who fears the Lord is distinguished by giving and by compassion toward the poor, and by this he brings about justice in the equality of all, when the poor man receives his right and lives, for this is his right, like the right of the rich man to life.

2- God rewards the merciful righteous man, giving him strength and glory by the exalting of his horn in this life in part, that is, in some situations, and gives him victory over Satan, and then in the eternal life he will have true glory. For he who honors the brethren of the Lord will surely be honored by the Lord and rewarded in heaven.
"The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish."
"Gnash with his teeth": he grinds and presses his teeth together as an expression of his intense rage.

1- The wicked man cannot bear to see virtue and the doing of good; the wicked man is Satan, or every man who walks in evil, who is enraged when he sees good and is troubled within, and his conscience pricks him, and he is in sorrow. The writer of the psalm expresses the wretched state of the wicked man, not in gloating over him, but in grief for him and an attempt to warn him, that he may repent and be saved from this severe distress.

2- All the evil desires in the heart of the wicked man are in vain, for they pass away, that is, they do not benefit him in life, and in addition they end in eternity, and after them come the gnashing of teeth and rage in eternal torment. All this is because the knowledge of God and fellowship with Him do not exist among the wicked, neither on earth nor in the other life.

If mercy gives all these blessings, hasten to it; that is, seek out every needy person, whether materially, psychologically or spiritually, and offer him your love in any form, for it is very precious to God, and it gladdens Him, and gladdens you also.
Praise of the God of the humble "Alleluia. Praise, O ye servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: the psalm has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms and its author is unknown, although some attribute it to David.
2- When was it written: if David is its author, it was probably written toward the end of his life, after he had sat on the throne of the kingdom of Israel.

3- This psalm is one of the Hallel psalms, and we have already said that Psalms 111-113 magnify God, of whom it was said in Psalm 110 that He ascended into heaven, and all of them begin with the word Alleluia.
4- Psalms 113 and 114 were said before eating the Passover "and then Psalms 115-118 were said after eating the Passover.

5- This psalm is a liturgical psalm, that is, it is sung in communal worship at the three great feasts, which are the Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, in addition to the feast of the Dedication mentioned in the books of the Maccabees (1 Macc 4:36-49; 2 Macc 10:1-8).
6- This psalm resembles the prayer of Hannah, the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 2:2), and the canticle of the Virgin (Lk 1:47-55).
7- In the Book of Psalms there is a group of psalms called the Hallel psalms, and they are three groups:
a - The Egyptian Hallel psalms (Ps 113-118).
b - The Great Hallel psalms (Ps 120-136), which include the psalms of ascents.
c - The concluding Hallel psalms (Ps 146-150).

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime and the prayer of the Ninth Hour, because it contains praise and glorification of God, with which we begin our day, and we also glorify Him at the Ninth Hour because He accomplished our redemption on the cross. And God in His humility cares for the humble, and this encourages everyone who begins his day with the remembrance of God, and shows His humility on the cross at the Ninth Hour.
(1) Longings and praise (vv. 1-7:)
1- Alleluia. Praise, O ye servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD.

1- The writer of the psalm calls all the servants of the Lord to praise Him. The servants of the Lord are those who have been freed from material things and have become servants of the Lord, because servitude to God is freedom from the material things of the world, and so man is able to be released and praise God, not only with the tongue but with thought and feelings and his whole being and with works also.

2- The praise is for the name of the Lord, and the name of the Lord means His person, and this means the attachment of the hearts of those who praise God to Him, so that they repeat His name, remember Him always and glorify Him. This praise and glorification begins now and continues throughout life, and even extends forever in the Kingdom.
"From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD's name is to be praised."

1- The name of the Lord is praised from the rising of the sun to its going down, that is, throughout the day, and by the day is meant the whole of life. Continual praise is a natural, or spontaneous, duty of the children of God.

2- By the rising of the sun to its going down is meant the Jews who are in the east and the Gentiles who are in the west; all of them praise Him. This verse is a prophecy of the Church of the New Testament, where the Jews and the Gentiles in the whole world believe in Christ and establish churches in every place, in which they raise praises to God at all times, for worship is no longer confined to one place as it was among the Jews.

If the praise of God is constant in the heavens, then we should strive on earth to praise God, so that we know Him and enjoy fellowship with Him and love Him, and our heart grows more inflamed and our praise increases.
(2) The greatness of God who lifts up the humble (vv. 4-9:)
4- The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens. 5- Who is like unto the LORD our God, who dwelleth on high,

1- The greatness of the Lord rises above all men, because He is their Creator, and His mercies overflow upon all, and He deserves continual praise. And if the Lord is above all nations, and they believed in Him, they will feel that He is their God and will praise Him; how much more should the Jews, who knew God before the Gentiles, praise Him and glorify Him, because He humbled Himself, became incarnate and redeemed them on the cross.

2- The loftiness of God and His greatness are above the heavens, because He is the Creator of all the angels, and there is none like Him in greatness, and the mind of man cannot comprehend the extent of His greatness, nor can even the angels comprehend God. Therefore all His works deserve praise. And this praise benefits those who praise; as for God, He is perfect, but He rejoices in the praise of His children and blesses them.
"Who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth!" The things that are humble: the lowly.

God, the All-Great, is loving and very humble, indeed He loves the humble and looks upon them with care and tends them, whether in the heavens, that is, the angels, or on the earth, that is, men. Christ showed His humility by His Incarnation, and asked us to learn humility from Him (Mt 11:29) so that we may have compassion on all around us.
7- He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill; 8- That he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people. Princes: great men and rulers.
1- The poor is man, who by his sin went down to the dust after he was driven out of Paradise.

And man is also the needy one who dwelt in the dunghill, which is the dunghill of his sins. And Christ became incarnate to live among sinful men, and to receive them to Himself, and to show His love for them in His teachings, the healing of their diseases, the feeding of them, and then in their redemption on the cross.

2- The aim of the Incarnation and redemption is to raise man from the dust and the dunghill, to be exalted to an honorable place that befits him, that is, to become a son of God. For Christ, by His death and resurrection, has become the firstborn among many brethren, that we may rise in Him from our sins and enjoy the honor of sonship to God. And this has happened in the lives of many, such as David the shepherd of sheep who became a king, and the fishermen who became apostles and preached to the world.
"He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children. Praise ye the LORD."

The barren woman is the Church of the Gentiles, far from God, and when she believed she had many children who believe in Christ. This verse was fulfilled in many women who were barren, such as Sarah the mother of Isaac, and Rebekah who bore Esau and Jacob, and Hannah the mother of Samuel, and Elizabeth who bore John the Baptist.

The humility of God is wonderful, who makes me, the lowly, a son to Him, and raises me from the dust and the dunghill, that I may share with the saints in the enjoyment of fellowship with Him. This impels me to greater humility at His feet, and at the feet of all His children, that I may serve them all the days of my life.
God the Almighty Savior "When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: unknown, because it has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms.
2- When was it written?
This psalm tells us of the crossing of the Red Sea and then of the river Jordan, and therefore the time of its writing is one of these possibilities:
a - At the entry into the land of Canaan, at Gilgal, immediately after crossing the river Jordan.
b - After David's victories over the nations, in glorification of the mighty God.
c - After the return from the captivity, in glorification of God who brought back His people, and as an encouragement to the people to build the temple in Jerusalem.

3- Since the psalm tells us of the crossing of the Red Sea and the Jordan, it encourages the soul that repeats it to come out from under the authority of the devil and his sins, to repentance and the beginning of a new life with God.
4- This psalm is liturgical and was prayed before eating the Passover, which is the most important of the feasts of the children of Israel.

5- This psalm is mentioned in the Laqqan (the washing of the feet) of the feast of Epiphany; it is read before the Gospel, and its mention is repeated during the Liturgy of the Laqqan, to declare the authority of God over the waters. And although Christ was immersed in the waters to fulfill all righteousness for us, He is the Creator of the waters, and all nature is subject to Him.
6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: 1- When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language, 2- Judah was his sanctuary, and Israel his dominion.
Strange language: foreign in speech.

1- The psalm shows that when the people of Israel went out of Egypt, and then took possession of the Promised Land, the tribe of Judah, in which Jerusalem and the temple are situated, was the holy place of God; for in Judah worship was offered in the temple, which was the holiest place in the world at that time. And they worshiped God and thanked Him because He brought them out of Egypt with great power by the ten plagues, from among a people who spoke a language strange to them. By Judah is meant not only the great tribe of Judah in which the temple stood, but the whole kingdom of the children of Israel, because God dwells in their midst.

2- By Israel also is meant the whole kingdom of the children of Israel, and not only the ten tribes. The authority and power of God appeared in settling His people in the place of the wicked Canaanites in a land flowing with milk and honey, and in His protecting them from the surrounding nations when they held fast to Him, as in the days of David and Solomon. God's authority and protection are bound up with the submission of His people to Him and their holding fast to His commandments and Law. In sum, the people of God enjoy holiness and God's protection of them as long as they worship Him faithfully in His temple and live by His commandments.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: "The sea saw it, and fled: Jordan was driven back."

1- God's authority over nature appears in the fleeing of the waters of the sea before the power of God represented in the rod of Moses, so the sea was divided and the children of Israel crossed over. The river Jordan also turned back, to make a way for the people of God to cross into the land of Canaan. These two events, at two different times, represent God's authority over nature for the benefit of His people.

2- The sea is a symbol of the world, of evil and of the demons, all of which flee before God, and the river is a symbol of the love of material things, which retreats before the believer's love for God; indeed the river is also a symbol of death, which retreated before the authority of God who rose from the dead, and before the saints who raised the dead. In sum, the believer in Christ has authority over nature, the demons and all evil if he holds fast to God.

entries.section: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

paragraphs.text: "The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs."
Little hills: the hills.

1- The mountains and the little hills are the greatest things on earth, and they are firm and solid, yet they move before God and skip like rams and lambs, and tremble before the power of God, as the mountain quaked when God appeared on it to Moses and to all the people of Israel, when He gave Moses the commandments and the Law (Ex 19:18). The mountains also move before the power of God in His children, as Mount Mokattam was moved by the prayer of Simon the Tanner with the Pope and the people.

2- The mountains are a symbol of the saints, such as the prophets and the Apostles, and all the saints who rejoice and skip with all their hearts praising God. And when the prophets and the Apostles moved from place to place proclaiming the word of God, they were like one who skips before God in zeal to declare His voice.

If God has all authority over the world, do not be troubled by changes in nature, or by the power of the rulers and the mighty of the world; all of them are in the grasp of God, the Ruler of all, and He moves them for your benefit if you hold fast to your faith and to God's commandments and His worship.

5- What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back? 6- Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs? The writer of the psalm marvels at the mighty authority of God over nature, so that the seas and rivers flee and fear Him, and the mountains and hills also move as if they were children in their father's hands, for lambs are the young of the sheep and the rams. And he asks nature the reason for this movement of hers, and she answers only that she is subject to her God and Creator. This repetition, which was mentioned in (vv. 3, 4), is a confirmation of the greatness of God and His authority.
7- Tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob; 8- Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters.
Standing water: pools, that is, a small river.
Flint: a very hard rocky stone called granite.

1- Here the writer of the psalm answers his question in (vv. 5, 6): that nature, when she saw the fearful Lord, trembled. The Lord is the God of Jacob, so the earth trembled before the people of God when the Lord appeared on the mountain to Moses, as we mentioned. It also trembled when the archangel Michael announced the resurrection of the Lord Jesus from the dead. And in the wilderness of Sinai, when Moses struck the rock, it poured forth water like a river, and the people drank and glorified God (Num 20:11).

2- These verses are a symbol of the trembling of man before the power of God in Baptism, when the old man dies and the new man is born, and then rivers of living water flow from his belly by the Holy Spirit.

And man's heart had been hardened by sin, but by faith it recovers its vitality, and indeed the Holy Spirit pours out of it the waters of grace, so that it is satisfied and satisfies others, for he is transformed into a light for the world and salt for the earth.

The Holy Spirit is ready to work in your heart however great your sins, so that your heart is softened and you are bound to the love of Christ, and are satisfied with Him, and indeed overflow upon others with giving and generosity.
The living God and the dead idols "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory ..." (v. 1) Introduction:

1- Its author: unknown, for there is no title for this psalm, and it is considered one of the orphan psalms whose author is unknown. There are many opinions about the author of this psalm; some think that he is:
a - The prophet Moses.
b - The prophet David.
c - Mordecai.
d - The three youths.
e - King Hezekiah.

2- When was it written? It could be in one of the earlier times, that is, the days of Moses, or David, or during the captivity. Some think that it was written after the return from the captivity to be prayed in the temple as an encouragement to the returning Jews.
3- There is a similarity between this psalm and the one before it in that they both speak of God who is able to do all things, and who protects His people and blesses them.

4- There is a relation between this psalm and the psalm that follows it, in that this psalm asks for God's help, relies on Him and calls for His praise, whereas in the next psalm the victorious people of God praise Him.
5- It is fitting for everyone in affliction to take refuge in God by repeating this psalm, and to rely on Him.
6- This psalm is fitting for the children of God when they are exposed to affliction, so that they rely on God and ask for His blessing, that He may give them victory over their enemies.
7- This psalm is considered liturgical, for the people used to chant it in alternation with the Levites and priests.
8- Parts of this psalm, namely (vv. 16-18), are prayed in the funeral services of men and women, because they express the importance of praise throughout life.
9- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
"Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake."
1- The writer of the psalm declares in humility his unworthiness of any grace or blessing because of the multitude of his sins.
2- He shows that the reason for God's care and concern for His people is due to two things:
a - His limitless mercy toward all men, and especially His believing children.
b - His faithfulness in His fatherhood and His promises to His people.
"Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is now their God? But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased."

1- The Gentiles cast doubt on the existence and power of God for the children of God, as Rabshakeh the Assyrian did to King Hezekiah (Isa 36:18-20; 37:1-13), and more dangerous still is for a man to doubt, within himself, the power of God. All these are attempts of Satan to separate us from God, so that we do not enjoy His protection of us.
And he also makes us doubt by saying that He is in heaven, far from us, and does not feel for us.

2- (v. 3) declares the truth of the faith of God's children in Him, that our God is strong and rises above all creatures on earth, and is able to do all things, so He does what He pleases, and therefore He is able to protect His people. This is what the prophet Isaiah reassured King Hezekiah with, and the angel of God killed the army of Sennacherib, and the rest fled (Isa 37:33-38).

Meditation on the greatness of God and His power, and His many works with His children, and even in our own lives, establishes our faith, so that we are not disturbed by the changes of life or the false doubts of Satan.
"Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

1- These idols which the pagans worship, whether images, or statues made of stone and wood, or even made of silver and gold, are all the work of men's hands, and therefore they are not gods but things made by men, and are less than any creature that God created.
2- The idols in our life now are what we cling to in life of material things, such as money, possessions and relationships .. and all of them pass away.

3- The images of the saints, made of silver or gold or any material, are holy, because their subjects had holy lives, and we remember them by these images in order to honor them for the sake of God, for whom they lived faithfully, and to imitate them, and this gladdens God's heart.

"They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not: They have ears, but they hear not: noses have they, but they smell not: They have hands, but they handle not: feet have they, but they walk not: neither speak they through their throat."

The idols are portrayed in the form of men or animals, but they are far weaker and baser than they: though they have the form of mouths, they are unable to speak, and they have the form of eyes but are unable to see, and the look of ears does not give them the ability to hear, and though they have noses, they cannot smell. And though they have the form of hands and feet, they are unable to touch or walk, and they do not speak though they have throats; the smallest animal is able to make sounds, or walk, or make movements that the idols are unable to make, so of course they cannot be gods.
"They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them."

1- If the idols are helpless, weak and base, then everyone who clings to them, whether he who makes them or worships them and trusts in them, becomes like them, weak and base, and indeed passing away like them, and becomes hard of heart like these stone idols. Thus man is degraded and separated from God by the worship of idols.
2- On the contrary, he who worships God becomes like Him in purity, love, perfection, holiness and immortality.

Do not cling to the passing material things of the world and its desires, lest they take your heart captive and enslave you and take you away from God. You are greater than they, so use them for the glory of God, and your God is able to provide them for you as much as you need them.

"O Israel, trust thou in the LORD: he is their help and their shield. O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD: he is their help and their shield. Ye that fear the LORD, trust in the LORD: he is their help and their shield."

Their shield: the shield is the large buckler. It is a defensive instrument consisting of a piece of wood with a handle behind, into which the soldier puts his hand and moves it before his head and body to protect him from arrows.

1- The writer of the psalm calls all the people of God to trust in Him, because He is their help in all their afflictions, and defends them before their enemies, so that they triumph over them. And he singles out especially the priests and servants when he says "house of Aaron," and then he affirms that God is the help and defender of those who fear the Lord, that is, who fear Him; meaning that all the people of God are called to trust in Him, and the priests and servants even more, and then the one who enjoys God's help and defense more than all is he who fears Him and reveres Him.

2- Some interpreters think that those who fear the Lord are the Gentiles who feared God and believed in Him and joined His people; these God helps and defends like His people, and even more than His people, in proportion to their fear and faith in Him.

3- God is the helper of His children in every generation in their wars against the demons, and He is also their defender, so He repels many attacks against them without their feeling it, and increases His protection of those who serve Him, and above all those who fear Him and revere Him, so that they live in peace and tranquility however great the wars of the demons.

Trust in the Lord is the ship in which we cross the sea of this world, however high its waves and strong its winds, so that inside the ship you enjoy fellowship with God, who protects us. And although we see with our eyes the wars of the demons, they are unable to hinder us from God, and indeed God uses them for our spiritual growth.

"The LORD hath been mindful of us: he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron. He will bless them that fear the LORD, both small and great. The LORD shall increase you more and more, you and your children."

1- God loves His people and remembers them because they are always in His thought, so He blesses them, as He gives a special blessing to His servants who are the house of Aaron, and above all to those who fear Him, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles joined to them. And He increases His blessing to them, and also to their children, to gladden the hearts of the fathers; for our God is generous in giving and blessing, and His generosity is in proportion to His children's holding fast to His commandments, their fear of Him, and their love which appears in their service of His holy name.

2- God remembers His children even if they are few and weak, as they were during the captivity, or at their return from the captivity, so He blesses them and increases their number and strength. So also in their wars with their enemies, as it was with Gideon, Jephthah and Samson in the age of the Judges, and as it was with David and Solomon, and also in the days of the Maccabees. And still to this day He protects His Church and blesses her with His power however few the believers in Him may be, but they are strong by His strength. For He blesses and increases everyone who fears Him, small and great, and indeed cares for the weak who rely on Him more than for the rest.

3- The priest used to repeat these three great verses when offering the sacrifices in the tabernacle of meeting, or the temple of Solomon, so that the blessing would embrace all the people, and especially the priests and servants and those who fear the Lord.
"Ye are blessed of the LORD which made heaven and earth."

This blessing which God gives to His children affects them and draws them to love Him, so they are blessed of the Lord, and live for Him and worship Him faithfully and thank Him, and indeed serve Him with all their hearts, especially since they believe that their God has everything in His hand because He is the Creator of all, heaven and earth. And Melchizedek mentioned this blessing to Abraham when he blessed him, declaring that the blessing was for him from God, Creator of heaven and earth, that is, He in whose hand are all blessings (Gen 14:19).

"The heaven, even the heavens, are the LORD's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men. The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence. But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and for evermore. Praise the LORD."

1- God is the Creator of heaven and earth, and He is exalted above all things; therefore the writer of the psalm expresses God's loftiness by saying that He dwells in heaven, and He created the first man in Paradise, but after the fall He gave him an opportunity to live on the earth, to show his faithfulness and his love for God, so that He may bring him back to heaven, where he enjoys freedom with the angels in fellowship with God and praises Him forever.

2- The earth is an opportunity for the believing man to live with God and praise Him, not only with his tongue but with his heart and his good works; for he whose life ends and who dies and goes down to Hades (the land of silence), as used to happen in the Old Testament, has no opportunity to praise or to do good works.
3- Those who live on earth while dead in sins do not praise God, nor live for Him, and so they lose His blessing which helps them to live with Him, and consequently do not reach the heavens.

Thank God every day for His blessings and His help and His protection of you, and lift up your heart in praise of Him, so that you taste the sweetness of fellowship with Him, until you come nearer every day to the life of the angels and the blessings of heaven.
Thanksgiving to God the Savior "I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: unknown, because the psalm has no title, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms.
But there is an opinion that its author is the prophet David.
2- When was it written? If David is its author, he wrote it during, or after, his flight from the pursuit of Saul, or the pursuit of his son Absalom.
3- This psalm is considered a psalm of thanksgiving to God, fitting for every believing man who passes through affliction, or whose affliction has ended, so that he praises God.
4- The previous psalm (Ps 115) speaks in the spirit of the congregation with God, whereas this psalm speaks in the singular, and this makes it more affecting to the soul.
5- This psalm is Messianic, because it speaks of the sufferings of Christ, His death and His victory.
6- This psalm is liturgical, because it is used in worship in the Church of the New Testament, since the first part of it (vv. 1-9) is prayed in the funeral service of men.
7- In the Septuagint translation this psalm is divided into two psalms (vv. 1-9), (vv. 10-19).

8- This psalm is found in the prayers of the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, because it speaks of the sufferings of Christ, His death, and His victory over Satan, whom He bound by the cross at this hour.

entries.section: (1) A request for deliverance from affliction

paragraphs.text: "I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications. Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live."
"The sorrows of death compassed me,"

1- When the writer of the psalm experienced God's concern to hear his prayers and supplications, he loved Him and loved prayer, so he continued to pray all day and every day, enjoying fellowship with God.

2- God is a tender Father, therefore He inclined His ear to hear my prayer, and this is also humility on God's part, and great concern, especially since I am a sinner and a weak man and am ashamed to raise my voice, yet even so He loves me and comes down to me to hear me. This is a clear reference to the Incarnation of Christ, who came down to us from heaven to redeem us because He loves us so much; and so it becomes natural for us to love Him with all our heart.
3- Prayer and calling upon God "as long as I live" does not mean only continuing in prayer throughout life on earth, but also continuing in prayer in the Kingdom forever.

entries.section: (1) A request for deliverance from affliction

paragraphs.text: "and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow."
Compassed me: surrounded me and clung to me.
I found: I suffered.

1- The prophet David faced severe afflictions in his flight from the pursuit of his enemies, and was exposed to death many times. And he says "the cords of death," because cords are used in dividing land, as if his portion were death, and it surrounded him to the point of clinging to him, so he was in great sorrow and distress.

2- The wars of the devil can be severe, surrounding the children of God and trying to make them fall into sin. And in their striving against them they bear much suffering and hardship, but it is precious in the sight of God.

entries.section: (1) A request for deliverance from affliction

paragraphs.text: "Then called I upon the name of the LORD; O LORD, I beseech thee, deliver my soul."

1- The severity of the affliction drove the prophet David to call upon God. And "O" means taking refuge in God and entreating Him, for he has no deliverer in his affliction except God, and this comforted his heart and gave him rest.

2- When David called upon the Lord in his affliction, and the effects of this prayer appeared on him in his calm and peace, this was a silent proclamation to those around him, that they might follow his example in their afflictions and seek God the deliverer from distresses.

God is very near to you, and He loves you, so do not be troubled if afflictions draw near to you, and even cling to you. For God is nearer to you than they are, and He is able to deliver you from them, so that you come out safe, and even benefit from the trial and grow strong spiritually.
"Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; yea, our God is merciful."
Righteous: just and upright.

1- God is gracious to His children, for He feels their weakness as human beings, and helps them to live with Him. But at the same time He is just, so He holds them to account for their sins, and we must therefore keep in mind His justice and enjoy His graciousness which encourages us. God declared Himself to Moses in this sense in one of his meetings with Him (Ex 34:6).
2- He returns to affirm that God is merciful; for man has many sins, but God's mercy is wide, and by this He encourages him to repent, and whoever repents enjoys God's graciousness and mercy.
"The LORD preserveth the simple: I was brought low, and he helped me."

By the simple are meant little children, as in the Septuagint translation, for God preserves His children who feel their need of Him like children. David knew the way to God when he was brought low, that is, humbled himself, and became like children, as Christ asked in the New Testament (Mt 18:3), and He delivered him from all his afflictions.
"Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee."

1- David expresses his joy, and asks his soul to return to her rest, because the Lord dealt bountifully with him when He delivered him from his enemies, and delivered him also from all turmoil and distress of soul, so he regained his peace. For the natural state of the spiritual man is to live in peace, and any turmoil is foreign to him, and if he takes refuge in God through prayer and spiritual striving, God gives him His rest.

2- The rest mentioned points to the eternal rest, which is the greatest divine benefit that God gives to His children who believe in Him, who sought Him in humility and not out of any merit of their own; therefore this psalm is read in the funeral prayers, to recall the eternal rest into which the departed, over whose body the prayer is made, has entered.
"For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling."
1- David makes clear the reason for the rest which he received from God, which is:
a - That He delivered his soul from death as a result of his enemies' pursuit of him.
b - He dried his tears and comforted his sorrowful heart by lifting the affliction from him.
c - He kept his feet from slipping into various sins, such as taking vengeance on Saul, or any other sins. So God's protection was both material and spiritual.

2- This verse applies to the person who has died, over whom we pray at the funeral, that God has delivered him from eternal death, and from the tears of anguish in Hades, and also from slipping into the desires that lead him to perdition.
3- This verse is fitting for everyone who passes through afflictions and thanks God who keeps him during them.
"I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living."

1- Verses (8, 9) were mentioned in Psalm 56:13. And the verse here means that since God has delivered me and kept me in all that went before, I must walk before Him in the land in which we live, that is, throughout our lives. Walking before God means pleasing Him with a pure life and keeping away from sin, in preparation for eternity, in which are the new earth and the new life.

2- The repentant man who takes refuge in God in humility thanks God who delivered him, and returns to life with Him, and promises Him that he will walk in the fear and love of God, and please Him all the days of his life.

Life is an opportunity for repentance, so hasten to return to God if you fall, and be sure of His love; for He welcomes you and supports you to live with Him, and indeed you will make up for all that you have missed with a pure life that pleases Him, and so enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "I believed, therefore have I spoken: I was greatly afflicted: I said in my haste, All men are liars."

1- I believed that I would please God and walk before Him as in (v. 9). And this faith must be a practical faith, not only theoretical, and humility before God results from this faith, especially since the afflictions through which David passed brought him low, so he humbled himself before God that He might have mercy on him and deliver him.

2- David felt that all men are liars, that is, vain, of no use, indeed that the whole world does not support him, and he too is vain and cannot support himself, and the only solution is faith in God and humility before Him.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the LORD."

1- The prophet David marvels at the multitude of God's benefits to him, so that he finds himself unable to repay God what is due, or to respond to Him and answer Him, for whatever David offers, the love of God is nothing before His many benefits. And he does not give God love as a favor from himself, but he only answers and responds to the divine love with which God began toward him.

2- David feels that the least response to God is to share in His worship, and to drink the cups which were appointed at the feast of the Passover, which were cups of wine, a sign of joy, in addition to prayer, whether by reciting the psalms or any prayers.

3- The cup of salvation which he takes is a clear symbol of the sacrifice of the New Testament, and of partaking of the Blood of Christ, in addition to His Body, and all this is accompanied by the prayers of the Liturgy, which are full of thanksgiving to God.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people."

1- If God has fulfilled His covenants and delivered me from my enemies and from every affliction, I must respond to Him and fulfill my vows which I promised Him during my affliction, as an expression of thanks and love to Him.

2- These vows include prayers and the offering of sacrifices to God, and sharing the needy in eating of them, so they become love and thanks to God, and also love for others. And all this is done before the people of God, not for boasting, but to spread the spirit of thanksgiving among the people and to confirm the response to the divine love, and the necessity of fulfilling vows. All this used to happen in the Old Testament, and it can also happen in the New Testament, according to the kind of vow and what my lips have uttered, which must be fulfilled.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints."

1- He who reveres God and fears Him, so that he cares for His worship, drinks the cup of joy, calls upon the name of the Lord and pays his vows, this man, if he dies, his death is precious and honorable in the sight of the Lord, and He prepares for him a place of rest and joy in heaven.

2- By the saints is meant Christ, the martyrs, and all who die in the service of the Lord, such as the Apostles, the priests, and everyone who serves the Lord. The death of Christ was precious in the sight of the Father, because by it the redemption of humanity was accomplished. And the death of the martyrs, and of all who fall asleep in the Lord, is precious in His sight, and He gives them rest from the labors of earth and rewards them with the glories of heaven.

3- If Christ died for me and offered me the cup of salvation, which is His Blood on the altar of the New Testament, it is natural for me to respond to His love and die to sin that I may live for Him, and when I die in the body, this will be precious in His sight.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "O LORD, truly I am thy servant; I am thy servant, and the son of thine handmaid: thou hast loosed my bonds."
Thine handmaid: thy female servant.

1- The prophet David declares his submission to God and his faith in Him, saying "I am thy servant" and also "the son of thine handmaid," from which it is understood that David's mother was a pious woman who brought him up with a spiritual upbringing. So because of his faith and the faith of his mother, God blessed him and loosed his bonds, that is, brought him out of his afflictions.

2- This verse applies to Christ, who was in the flesh in the form of a servant, and is the son of the handmaid of the Lord, the Virgin Mary, who declared this to the angel who brought her the good tidings (Lk 1:38); and for this reason the Father loosed His bonds by His resurrection from the dead.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and will call upon the name of the LORD. I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people, In the courts of the LORD's house, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Praise ye the LORD."

The verses mentioned before in (vv. 13, 14) are repeated here to affirm his longing to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving to God accompanied by prayers, with the fulfilling of vows before all the people, and in front of the house of the Lord. And the sacrifices are not limited to animal sacrifices, which are thanksgiving to God, but also include sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving. The meaning of this is that David was far from Jerusalem, but his heart was attached to God and to worship before His house.

May you take care to thank God for His works with you, especially after afflictions. Do not be content with asking for your needs, or for deliverance from the affliction, but also thank Him, to prove your love for God and to increase your sense of His love.
A call to all to praise God "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: the psalm has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms whose author is unknown. There is an opinion that its author is the prophet David.
2- When was it written? There are two opinions:
a - It was written in the days of David when the Jewish nation was in its strength and extent, so David calls the whole world to believe in God and praise Him.
b - It was written after the captivity, at the return of the people to Jerusalem, with its writer longing that the nations among whom he had lived would believe and praise God.
3- This psalm calls the whole world to praise God for His many mercies, His faithfulness, and His care for men. It encourages every believer to praise, and to encourage those around him to do so.
4- It is a Messianic psalm which speaks of the Church of the New Testament, which includes all nations and peoples.
5- Christ referred to this psalm after His resurrection, when He called His disciples to preach and to make disciples of all nations (Mt 28:18-20; Mk 16:15-16).
6- The Apostle Paul quoted from this psalm in his epistle to the Romans (Rom 15:11).
7- This psalm is fitting for every believer when he begins his day, so that he repeats this psalm to encourage himself and those around him to praise God, as Pope Kyrillos VI used to do.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya at the beginning of the prayer of Vespers, because the salvation of Christ included not only the Jews but also the Gentiles, who are symbolized by those of the eleventh hour, that is, the hour of sunset, whom Christ received and gave them salvation and a place in His Kingdom.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people."
1- This verse represents the longings of the prophet David, and of all the pious in the Old Testament, who wished that all nations and peoples would believe, and praise God and thank Him.
2- It is a clear prophecy of the Church of the New Testament, which includes all nations and peoples, many of whom believe and praise God in His churches.
3- The praise is completed by all peoples in heaven, where there is neither Jew nor Gentile, but all believe in Christ and praise Him forever.

entries.section: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

paragraphs.text: "For his merciful kindness is great toward us: and the truth of the LORD endureth for ever. Praise ye the LORD."

1- God's mighty mercy appeared in offering salvation to the whole world, which had been hinted at in the Old Testament by the acceptance of a few of the Gentiles into the faith, who even came to be in the lineage of Christ, such as Rahab the harlot and Ruth the Gentile. But it became perfectly clear in the salvation offered on the cross, which the Apostles proclaimed in the whole world, and many believed and praised God.

2- God's faithfulness appeared in His fulfilling His promises, for He promised Eve that her seed would crush the head of the serpent, and her seed is Christ who bound Satan on the cross. And all His promises which the prophets uttered were fulfilled in the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption of the whole world, and the acceptance of faith by the Gentiles.

May you pray for all those around you, that they may share with you your love for God and praise Him with faith and joy, so that you rejoice and gladden the heart of God, and He works in the hearts of many.
Rejoicing in the blessings of salvation "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: there are two opinions:
a - The prophet David, for he expresses his attachment to the worship of the Lord in His house, and the power of God which supported him against his enemies.
b - An unknown writer who wrote it after the return from the captivity; because the psalm has no title, that is, it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is unknown.
2- When was it written? There are two possibilities:
a - Toward the end of David's life, after the moving of the ark of the covenant of God and his victories over his surrounding enemies.
b - After the return from the captivity and the rebuilding of the house of the Lord.

3- This psalm expresses the salvation of the Lord however severe the afflictions, so it is fitting for every believer who is exposed to afflictions, so that he prays it to be strengthened and to make his faith firm.
4- It is the last of the Egyptian Hallel psalms (Ps 113-118), which the Jews chant after eating the Passover, rejoicing in the salvation of the Lord.
5- This psalm is the prayer of Christ with His disciples after eating the Passover (Mt 26:30).

6- This psalm is prayed at the feast of Tabernacles, since it mentions in (v. 24) that this is the day which the Lord has made. And because of the importance of the feast of Tabernacles, it used to be called the feast, or the day, and it is understood to be the feast of Tabernacles (Neh 8:14; Ps 81:3). And the refrain that was repeated at the feast of Tabernacles is (v. 26), and the palm branch that was used at the feast of Tabernacles they call "Hosanna." In addition, at the feast of Tabernacles the rite of the lights was very important, as (v. 27) mentions. And this psalm was prayed each day of the six days of the celebration of the feast of Tabernacles, and prayed seven times on the seventh day of the feast.

7- This psalm is a liturgical psalm, for we understand that it was chanted at the feast of the Passover and the feast of Tabernacles, and the king, the priest and the people shared in chanting it. Each group chants a part of it, and the other group responds. And when Christ chanted it after the Passover, He would say a part of it and the disciples would respond.
8- This psalm is one of the strong Messianic psalms, because it speaks of Christ, who is the Righteous One who bore many afflictions and lived in righteousness, and He is the chief cornerstone.

9- This psalm is used in the rite of the Church, as a part of it is chanted every Sunday at the offering of the Lamb (v. 24), and it is said in the psalm of the feast of the Resurrection (vv. 24-26). And it is prayed on the second day of the feast of the Cross (vv. 15, 16, 28).

10- The New Testament quoted much from this psalm: the Jews chanted (vv. 25, 26) when they welcomed Christ as He entered Jerusalem (Mt 21:9). And Christ quoted from it (vv. 22, 23) in His dialogue with the Jews (Mt 21:42). In addition to the quotation by the Apostle Paul (Heb 13:
6) and Peter quoted from it in (Acts 4:11; 1 Pet 2:7).

11- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, in which they took down the body of Christ from the cross, so we remember the sufferings of Christ which He completed for us, to grant us salvation, as this psalm makes clear.
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever.
The writer of the psalm, and this verse may have been said by the king or the high priest, calls upon everyone, without distinction, to praise and thank the Lord for two things:

1- That the Lord is good, that is, He does good things and bestows many blessings on mankind, and at the same time He is perfect in His virtues, shining upon humanity with His light so that it may learn from Him.

2- That His mercy is great and continues for ever. He is tender and forgives sins, and not only at a particular time but throughout our whole life on earth; and in eternity also His mercy continues in the form of His gifts and His great blessings, which we do not deserve.
Let Israel now say, that his mercy endureth for ever.

1- The psalm calls Israel, who are the people of God, to contemplate the greatness of God and to praise Him for His goodness and His continuing mercy toward them. He did many good things for them: He fed them manna and gave them water to drink in the wilderness, and He gave them the land of Canaan, which flows with milk and honey. His mercy also continued with them: He rescued them from the bondage of Egypt, from the bondage in the age of the Judges, and likewise from the Assyrian captivity and the Babylonian captivity...

2- In this verse the specification begins. It singles out Israel, the people of God, because the first verse was an invitation to the whole world; and it singles out Israel because they believe in God, so they know His goodness and mercy, and therefore it is natural that they should praise Him and thank Him.
Let the house of Aaron now say, that his mercy endureth for ever.

The specification in the praise increases, and it calls the house of Aaron, that is, the priests, because God singled them out with the blessing of the priesthood, and destroyed those who opposed them and murmured against them, namely Korah, Dathan, Abiram and those with them. He also granted them to draw near to Him in His service. And God proclaimed the greatness of the priesthood when Aaron's rod budded.
Let them now that fear the LORD say, that his mercy endureth for ever.

1- The fourth group that the psalm calls to praise God is those who fear the Lord, that is, those who revere Him. By this it means the believers among His people who fear Him, and also those among the Gentiles who fear Him and will join His people and believe. These feel the goodness of God and His favors more than others do, and also His mercy that lasts for ever.

2- It called four groups to praise in the four verses, and these signify the four corners of the world, that is, a prophecy about Christianity, which spreads throughout the whole world. The believers praise God from the four corners of the world.

3- In the verses (vv. 2-4) it begins with the word "let ... say", whether for Israel, or the house of Aaron, or those who fear the Lord; that is, they declare praise and thanksgiving to God so as to move the hearts of those around them, that they may join them in the praise.

Praising God and thanking Him makes you feel God's love for you, and it gladdens the heart of God, so His gifts and blessings to you increase, and joy spreads in the hearts of those around you. May you not forget praise every day, even if only with a small part of the Midnight Praise, or one psalm of praise.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place.
A large place: spaciousness.

1- David, or every person in distress, or Christ in the midst of His sufferings as a representative of mankind, cries out and asks God to bring him out of his distress. And because God is unlimited, that is, He has all spaciousness, He is able to loosen my distress and make room for me, so that I do not feel the distress though it is present; He grants me peace and strength and gives me rest, so I walk with success and vigor.

2- When the sufferer calls on God while in the midst of afflictions, God hears him and gives him peace, and then promises him complete rest and release, and the enjoyment of fellowship with Him in eternity, where there is complete spaciousness.

3- If I am suffering in my distress, I cannot ask a human being, because he is limited like me and lives in the midst of the afflictions of the world. But the only One who has all spaciousness is God, because He is unlimited, and therefore He alone is able to give me rest in the midst of the affliction, as the holy Fathers said: "Do not place your hope in a human being, but in God."

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?

When the sufferer feels that the Lord is on his side, that is, he has gained by faith the perfect God in His spaciousness, he no longer fears any human being, meaning that no human being can trouble him, because he has gained peace and rest within himself. Even if he suffers in the body, he is in inner peace and fears no man. David was pursued by Saul for many years and was not disturbed, because God was with him.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: The LORD is with me among my helpers, and I shall look upon my enemies.

If I have any resources, such as money, health or relationships, I thank God for them because He gave them to me, but I hold fast to God my helper and boast in Him, for He is my true support, and He is able to use whatever resources He has given me. In this way I see the weakness of my enemies, the demons, whom God will drive away from me and give me victory over them.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man. It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes.
1- Here the psalm states an important truth: that reliance and refuge are in God alone, and not in any human being, because God alone is able to do all things, while human beings are weak.

2- Even if human beings are rulers, they are also weak and cannot be relied upon. Despite King Artaxerxes' support for Nehemiah, this did not prevent Tobiah, Sanballat and Geshem from opposing him. And despite King Darius' friendship with Daniel, this did not prevent the princes of the kingdom from rising against the king and threatening him with death, and taking Daniel and casting him into the lions' den for six days; but God preserved him and sent him food by the hand of the prophet Habakkuk (Dan 14:36).

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: All nations compassed me about: but in the name of the LORD will I destroy them. They compassed me about; yea, they compassed me about: but in the name of the LORD I will destroy them. They compassed me about like bees; they are quenched as the fire of thorns: for in the name of the LORD I will destroy them. Compassed me: surrounded me closely and clung to me.

1- David, or Christ, or every suffering believer declares that the wicked and unbelievers surround him and try to harm him, come very near to him, besiege him and even kill him. He likens them to bees around the honeycomb, that is, their numbers are great and they are able to strike and sting the one they surround. He likens them also to a fire blazing in thorns, which spreads quickly through them; but by the power of God he is able to overcome them and destroy them.

2- The believer's reliance on the name of the Lord protects him and takes vengeance on his enemies, the demons. And he repeats the name of the Lord three times, after the likeness of the Holy Trinity.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: Thou hast thrust sore at me that I might fall: but the LORD helped me.
Thrust sore at me: pushed me forcefully so that I would fall.
Helped me: supported me.

Though the afflictions were very severe and pushed me to fall, the Lord supported me with power, so the demons did not prevail. So I do not fear the force of the wars as long as God is with me, protecting me from any blow of the enemy. And I am not disturbed if the affliction increases upon me, for in the end God must intervene as long as I have taken refuge in Him. And if God permits afflictions, He gives peace during them, so that a person may benefit from them.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: The LORD is my strength and song, and is become my salvation.
1- When I see the wonderful work of God within afflictions, and His power, I sing and praise His holy name, because He always saves me from every affliction.

2- Because of the greatness of this verse, we find that it is taken from the song of Moses (Ex 15:2) and was repeated by Isaiah (Isa 12:2), and the Church repeats it on Great Friday in the hymn "Thine is the power and the glory."
3- "Is become my salvation" speaks of the salvation of Christ, which He accomplished by the Cross, and I obtain it by faith through the Holy Sacraments and the means of grace.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tabernacles of the righteous: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly. The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly.
Valiantly: with might.

1- From the dwellings of the righteous and the just there rise hymns and praises to God their Savior. The tabernacles refer to the booths in which they used to dwell during the Feast of Tabernacles, at which this psalm is recited. This singing continues throughout their lives, and grows stronger in the eternal life.

2- The right hand of the Lord refers to His power, which appeared in His Incarnation in the fullness of time. For it speaks of the right hand, which represents the body, and it is mentioned three times to signify the Holy Trinity. And this power of God is exalted above all the powers of the demons who fight me, and of the wicked who follow them.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the LORD.

Though I meet severe afflictions that almost cost me my life by their harshness, God rescues me with great power, so I live with Him during the afflictions and come out of them, and I even speak of the wonders of God with me, so I preach to all who are distressed and strengthen the righteous in the faith. This is what happened with David, whom Saul pursued and often tried to kill, yet he reigned over the children of Israel and was the greatest of its kings. And Christ suffered to the point of death, and then rose from the dead. And this is repeated with every believer who holds fast to God, so he comes out of afflictions with abundant blessings, and tells of the works of God with him.

entries.section: (2) Trusting in the Lord the Savior

paragraphs.text: The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death.

The afflictions that come upon me, even if they are harsh, are chastenings from God my Father who loves me, and He uses these chastenings to save me from my weaknesses and my sins. And I also choose fellowship with Him during the affliction, so I live and the death of sin does not overcome me, but I enjoy the life of righteousness.

Do not be disturbed by the multitude of afflictions, for they are your way to the Kingdom. Even if they are many, you will experience in them abundant blessings that you cannot taste outside of afflictions, and your heart will rejoice more than all those around you.

entries.section: (3) Worship is thanksgiving to the Savior

paragraphs.text: Open to me the gates of righteousness: I will go into them, and I will praise the LORD: This gate of the LORD, into which the righteous shall enter. I will praise thee: for thou hast heard me, and art become my salvation.

1- The gates of righteousness are the gates of the Temple through which the believer wants to enter in order to offer his worship to God, and when he is permitted to enter he praises God and thanks Him. In the New Testament they are the gates of the Church into which he enters, and he receives the greatest gift from God, which is His Body and Blood and all the sacraments of the Church, and he enjoys prayer in the presence of God, so he praises Him and glorifies Him.

2- The one who asks for the gates of righteousness to be opened is Christ, whose spirit ascends after His death to enter Paradise and the Kingdom, after He completed the redemption of mankind, proclaiming the possibility of man's return to heaven, as stated in (Ps 24:7, 9). And He praises the Lord on behalf of all mankind; that is, mankind thanks God who restored to it the grace of entering heaven after the redemption of Christ.
3- Those who enter the Temple and the Church are the righteous, that is, the just, who are the believers who want to live with God and enjoy fellowship with Him.

4- The one who calls for the gates of righteousness to be opened is God, who wants to enter the hearts of His children who believe in Him and love righteousness. Then His children rejoice and thank Him for His humility in dwelling within them, and because He answered their requests in (v. 19), opened to them the gates of righteousness and virtue, and gave them strength by dwelling in them, that they may enjoy all that He accomplished on the Cross for their sake.
