3- This psalm is a prophecy about the feelings of those returning from captivity to Jerusalem to build the temple and restore worship in the house of the Lord, of which they had been deprived throughout the period of captivity.
4- The house of the Lord in Jerusalem is a symbol of the Church of the New Testament, and also of the heavenly Jerusalem.
5- This psalm is prayed on the third step at the ascent to the house of the Lord.
6- This psalm shows the importance of common prayer and worship (v. 4).

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, where the worshiper remembers the house of the Lord and the worship in it, that his heart may be lifted up to heaven, where the eternal home with God is. For when the day draws near its end, we remember that we are approaching eternal life, and so we prepare with many prayers and praise.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: I was glad when they said unto me, "Let us go into the house of the Lord."
1- A person rejoices in the one who encourages him to go to the house of the Lord, if he is repentant, or loves God and wants to be present before Him in His house to praise Him and thank Him.
2- God's angels rejoice over us when we desire to go to the house of the Lord as they do.
3- The joy of going to the house of the Lord is a longing for common prayer, and a faith in God's blessing in His house, which is distinguished from His blessing in every other place.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Our feet shall stand within your gates, O Jerusalem.

David imagines that he has completed the ascent to Jerusalem and stands before its gates, and this gives him a joy surpassing every joy, because he has reached the city of God and its temple, that is, he will enter into the presence of God and enjoy being in His hands. There he offers his repentance for all his sins, shows his love in songs of praise, and shares with his brethren in worship.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem is built as a city that is compact together.

1- David feels that Jerusalem is like a city joined together, one part to another, meaning the unity of the believers who worship God in the temple of Jerusalem, so that they pray before Him with one heart.

2- This is a prophecy about the oneness of the believers in the Church of the New Testament, where they become members in the Body of Christ, and He is the Head. This oneness appears even more clearly in the heavenly Jerusalem, where the believers are united in praising the risen Christ in their midst.

entries.section: (1) Joy in the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the Lord, unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the Lord. For there are set thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David.
"Set": established, or erected, or seated.

1- The tribes of Israel, that is, all the believers, come to worship in Jerusalem, especially at the three great feasts: the Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. All are believers who love to worship God, and each tribe is distinct from the others, yet in unity they stand before God. Also in Jerusalem they go to law before the judges who know the Law, who sit on the thrones of judgment, and King David and his descendants sit among these judges.

2- Here he prophesies about the gathering of the believers in the Church to worship and give thanks to God, and to submit to its teaching and the guidance of its priests, who sit on the thrones of guidance and judgment.

3- He also prophesies about the gathering of the believers in the Kingdom of Heaven and on the day of judgment, when the twelve disciples will sit on twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes who did not believe in Christ, and to live with Him.

4- The thrones may mean the hearts of the believers in which God sits and rests to lead their lives, and to warn them by the Holy Spirit to keep away from sin, and He judges them, rebukes them and convicts them so that they may rise from it.
And so He leads them in the way of life to the Kingdom.

How beautiful it is to be present before God in His house! So take courage with your brethren to be before Him as much as you can, that you may enjoy not only His presence, but also partaking of His Body and Blood.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: may they rest that love you. Peace be within your towers, rest within your palaces.

1- Since judgment was established in Jerusalem by the Law of God, discipline and peace pervaded the city, and consequently those who love Jerusalem gained rest for dwelling in it and worshiping God; rest for all, whether those dwelling in it on towers in the mountains, or those dwelling in Jerusalem in palaces, that is, great houses.

2- Here he prophesies about the Church of the New Testament, and asks peace for it, as we now pray and ask in the litany for the peace of the Church in the Divine Liturgy. The towers are the saints, for they are like towers in their high spiritual rank, and are like towers also in their security, because they are under God's protection. The palaces are the true believers, who are temples of the Holy Spirit and palaces in which God the King dwells. And the palaces are a symbol of the abundance of good things in them, just as Christ gives abundant spiritual and material good things to His children.
For my brethren and companions' sakes, I will now say, "Peace be within you." Because of the house of the Lord our God I will seek your good.

1- David asks peace for Jerusalem for the sake of his relatives and friends, that is, all the Jews who dwell in Jerusalem and those who visit it, so that they may enjoy worship in a tranquil atmosphere. Indeed he also asks goodness and blessings for Jerusalem, because the house of the Lord is in it, for God sanctifies His city by dwelling in it.

2- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who asks peace for His Church for the sake of His brethren, since He is the firstborn among many brethren, and asks good for it, because it is His house in which He dwells.

May you pray for the peace of the Church, and the peace of all around you, that they may live with God in holy worship; and do not forget yourself, but ask for your own inner peace, so that you may be able to behold God.
Taking refuge in God in affliction. A song of ascents: "Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its author: it is one of the orphan psalms in which the name of the psalmist is not mentioned.

2- The words of the psalm show the author's faith in God and his taking refuge in Him, especially as he is exposed to distresses from those around him. It suits every believer who suffers distresses, for the psalm is a prayer of supplication to the merciful God.
3- This psalm is prayed on the fourth of the steps of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

4- This psalm may be a prophecy about the feelings of Nehemiah when he visited Jerusalem and saw the walls broken down and the gates burned; he began to rebuild them, and his enemies around him rose against him, mocked him, and tried to oppose him by every means.

5- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, because it suits the worshiper at the end of the day as he implores God to deliver him from the wars of the demons that confronted him throughout the day, so that they may quiet down for him at the end of the day and during the night.
Unto You I lift up my eyes, O You who dwell in the heavens.

1- The writer of the psalm lifts his eyes, while on the earth, to God who dwells in the heavens, and by this he declares his humility and his need of God, the High and Exalted. He entreats God and seeks His mercies.
2- Lifting the eyes to God confirms the psalmist's faith in God and his confidence that He is able to help him and rescue him from all his troubles.
Behold, as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress, so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until He have mercy upon us.

1- The psalm declares that we lift our eyes toward God like servants and maidens, who belong to their master and lift their eyes to him to ask of him whatever they request; perhaps he will have pity on them and give to them, or perhaps he will see fit not to give to them, and they accept; for their master sees what is suitable. And although men may err, the Lord is good, and He knows what is good for us, and gives us all that is suitable for us.

2- Lifting the eyes toward God that He may have mercy on us shows our trust in Him and our love for Him, and our faith in His mercy and tenderness. We keep our eyes lifted until He has mercy on us, and even after this we keep looking to Him all our life, because He is a tender God, ever merciful.
Trust in God's tenderness, and ask of Him what you need, and may you remain persevering until He gives to you and fills you with peace.
Never leave Him, for we have no one but Him.

Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us, for we are exceedingly filled with contempt. Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorn of those that are at ease, and with the contempt of the proud.

1- He asks for mercy and repeats it, confirming his great need and also the abundance of mockery and contempt from his enemies, and he expresses this by saying “we are filled” and “filled.” The writer of the psalm suffers great bitterness in his soul and a hard affliction, so he entreats the merciful God to lift it from him.

2- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who bore all our sins on the Cross, and who asks the Father to take away from Him the cup of suffering, and declares that He has been filled with contempt and mockery for the sake of our redemption.
3- These verses express the feelings of the penitent whom the devil has wearied by mocking him.

Turn your suffering and your pains in affliction, or in falling into sin, into prayers and supplications to God your Father, who loves you and longs to have mercy on you and take away your pains; indeed, He has already lifted them on the Cross, and He desires to support you in all your troubles.
God the Savior. A song of ascents. Of David. “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, let Israel now say” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states.
2- When was it written? Late in David's life, after God had delivered him from the hands of his enemies and he had triumphed over them all.

3- Perhaps this psalm is a prophecy about those returning from captivity after God had delivered them from the hands of the cruel Chaldeans, and they returned to Jerusalem at the beginning of the kingdom of the Medes and Persians.
4- Perhaps this psalm is also a prophecy about Nehemiah and the Jews of his time, whom God delivered from the hand of their neighbors who opposed them: Tobiah and those with him.
5- This psalm shows the feelings of the penitent believer who has triumphed over Satan, who thanks God and glorifies Him because He delivered him from the hand of his enemies, the demons.
6- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms because it prophesies about Christ, especially in (v. 7).
7- This psalm is prayed on the fifth of the steps of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.
8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, where we thank God for His love and care, by which He rescued us from the devil's wars all day long and brought us to its end.
“If it had not been the LORD who was on our side,” let Israel now say, “if it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us,

1- David shows his faith in God and his boldness before Him when he says “the LORD who was on our side,” for He is the only protection from the enemies surrounding us. He speaks in the plural, because the wars of the demons are against all who believe in God; indeed, he calls his people Israel to declare this faith, that the God who is ours is our protection from the enemies.

2- These are the feelings of the penitents who return to God, whom He delivered from the snares of the devil, and who rose from their falls. They are also the feelings of the captives who returned to Jerusalem and built the temple despite the opposition of the enemies around them, because the Lord was with them.

3- These two verses are the feelings of Jacob, the patriarch, which he declared to his uncle Laban when he left him and Laban tried to bring him back by force, but God appeared to Laban and rebuked him, so he did not lay a hand on Jacob (Gen 31:42).
Then they had swallowed us up quick, when their wrath was kindled against us. Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul. Then the proud waters had gone over our soul.
Overwhelmed us: the waters carried us and flung us far away.
Proud (swelling): overflowing, that is, covering us completely.

1- David likens the enemies to waters rushing violently like a torrent, which carry us and fling us far away, and we die from the violence of the waters. He also likens the enemies to many waters, able to flood us so that we die, as the great army of Pharaoh was able to kill all the children of Israel or return them to slavery, and as the waters of the Red Sea were able to drown the people of God. But God rescued His people and drowned the enemies.

2- These two verses signify what happened with Christ, against whom the Jews rose up and crucified Him, and He died on the Cross; but by His death He triumphed over death, and went down to Hades, and brought Adam and his children up to Paradise. So the waters flooded Him and the torrent covered Him, but He was drowned, that is, He died on the Cross, and then rose triumphant and also rescued the humanity that believes in Him.

If you hear threats, or fears from the wicked, do not be alarmed, for they have no power before God who protects you. Hold fast to God by repeating your psalms and your prayers, and you will enjoy His fellowship within His strong fortress.
Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth.

He likens the enemies to ravenous beasts with sharp teeth and fangs, but they could not come near us and devour us because of God's protection of us; therefore David calls all believers to bless God, praise Him and glorify Him for His protection and care for them.
Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we are escaped.

1- Here he likens Satan to the fowler, meaning by the fowler cunning and deceit. Satan sometimes fights with violence and fears, as he likened them to sweeping waters or ravenous beasts. But here Satan appears setting a snare for the man who believes in God, whom he likens to a small, weak bird, and he throws into the trap the grains that lure it. If a person rejects the lusts of the world he will not fall into the snare; and if he falls through ignorance and seeks God with faith, He breaks the snare for him, and the bird escapes and flies and gets far from the fowler. God's grace breaks the snare, while the striving lies in seeking God, and then escaping and flying far away from the snare.

2- The bird signifies Christ, who fell into the hand of the devil on the Cross and died, but by His death He trampled death and seized Satan, that is, He broke the snare, in order to give power to His believing children, that they may escape the snares of Satan.
Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

In this last verse David summarizes the psalm: God is the Savior, the Deliverer and the Help in every step of our life, and therefore we ought to rely on Him in everything, because He is our help and is able to help us, since He is the Creator of all things: heaven and what is in it, and earth and what is in it.

May you thank God every day for His works and His help and His care for you, so that your heart may rejoice and your faith be established, and you rejoice the heart of God, and He gives you spiritual and material gifts without measure.
The blessings of the righteous. A song of ascents. “They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion”... v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown. This psalm is considered one of the orphan psalms because the name of its writer is not mentioned in the title.

2- This psalm speaks of God's care for His children in the Church, that is, His care for those who believe in Him and their great eternal future, and on the other hand the punishment of the wicked. It is a psalm that helps the one praying to stand firm in faith, and it carries the meaning of thanksgiving to God.
3- This psalm is prayed on the sixth step in the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

4- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Agpeya, in the prayer of Vespers, to help the one praying to stand firm in faith until the end of the day, indeed throughout life, and to warn him against negligence, lest the punishment of the wicked come upon him.
They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed, but abides for ever.

1- The writer of the psalm likens those who trust in the Lord to mount Zion, which rises toward heaven higher than its surroundings, and so it signifies inclination toward spiritual and heavenly things.
2- It is also great and firm, signifying strength and continuance.
3- It is also lasting, that is, it remains for ever, because those who trust in God have a portion in the eternal Kingdom.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about His people from henceforth even for ever.

The city of Jerusalem is surrounded by mountains on its four sides; so also God surrounds it with His care. These mountains signify the holy angels who love God and His children, whom God sends to serve His children, and who always intercede for them. So Jerusalem, that is, all the believers in it, are in the care and providence of God and in the company of the saints, now in their life on the earth, and then the enjoyment of the vision of God and His care, and the communion of the saints, will be complete in the age to come.
For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity.

1- Although the believers are in God's care, He permits trials for them, to which he refers here as the rod of the wicked; so He permits the enemies of His people to trouble them for a time, but not for ever. For if the trials increase, they may lead the righteous to despair, and if the trials lessen, they may lead to negligence and falling into iniquity. For this the Scripture says that “God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it”

(1 Cor 10:13). And God disciplines His children in a spirit of fatherhood to lead them to the straight way, as He disciplined Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, with leprosy, as a father, that she might repent and not judge Moses or murmur against him, declaring His fatherhood toward her by saying “If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days?” (Num 12:14).

Trusting in God gives you rest and peace, and establishes you in faith, and even gives you an opportunity for spiritual growth. So firmly drive away all the anxious thoughts that Satan stirs up against you, for they are foreign to you, so that you may enjoy the embrace of God.

entries.section: (2) The recompense of the righteous and of the wicked

paragraphs.text: Do good, O LORD, unto those that be good, and to them that are upright in their hearts. As for such as turn aside unto their crooked ways, the LORD shall lead them forth with the workers of iniquity. But peace shall be upon Israel.
Such as turn aside unto crooked ways: those who are changed and deviate into crooked ways.

1- The psalm ends by declaring the recompense of the righteous, which is divine goodness on the earth and in heaven, and in general they enjoy God's peace continually, because they believed and trusted in Him and lived with Him.

2- On the other hand, the wicked who deviate from God's way and walk in the crooked ways of evil receive the punishment of their deviation and crookedness and distance from God, that is, they receive the natural result of the evil in which they lived, which is of course eternal torment; and they do not enjoy peace within them, but on the contrary are in constant turmoil and disquiet.

Look at the grace of the peace that is within you, and also at the greatness of the eternal good things, so that you may bear the toils of spiritual striving and reject the temporary pleasure of sin, and so walk in the straight way that leads to the Kingdom.
The joy of the strugglers. A song of ascents. “When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion”... v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is not known.
2- The time of its writing: at the return from captivity, whether a short time after the captivity in the days of Zerubbabel, or a long time after it in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah.
3- This psalm is considered a song of the captives returning from captivity with joy to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, to return to their worship and to offer sacrifices to God.
4- This psalm suits every penitent and every striver on the path of the spiritual life, who remembers God's comforts and thanks Him, and so is strengthened to complete his striving.
5- This psalm resembles Psalm 85 and the thirty-first chapter of the Book of Jeremiah.
6- This psalm is prayed on the seventh step on the way of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, so that the spiritual striver may remember God's work with him throughout the day, to be comforted and to complete his striving and his spiritual vigilance for the rest of the day and during the night.
When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream.

1- When the children of Israel returned from captivity to Jerusalem, they were in joy and incredulous wonder, so that they thought they were in a dream during the night. This is an expression of the intensity of their joy, because God's work was beyond imagination, not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles who heard of their return.
2- Likewise the penitent who returns to God, after He removes his sin and he returns to his purity and lives in fellowship with God, is in inexpressible joy.

Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing. Then said they among the Gentiles, “The LORD has done great things for them.” The LORD has done great things for us, whereof we are glad.
The children of Israel rejoiced at the decree of Cyrus, the Persian king, that they should return to Jerusalem to build the temple.

They began to regain their longing for worship in the house of the Lord, and even began to sing the spiritual songs that their fathers had been accustomed to say before the house of the Lord. They were in great joy, which the nations around them witnessed, and they marveled at God's wonderful work, and the joy of the children of Israel became a preaching without words to the nations, that they might believe in the mighty God, who is above all gods.

Ask the Lord to help you in your striving to be rid of your sins, so that you praise Him and glorify Him and live in joy amid the pains of this life, and so become a light to the world, which suffers many afflictions.
Turn again our captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south.

1- About 50,000 persons of the captives returned with Zerubbabel in the first return, then about 4,000 in the second return with Ezra, while the third return, with Nehemiah, was a very limited number. The rest of the Jews in captivity were occupied with trade and their business and projects, so their hearts were not moved to worship God in His temple. Therefore the writer of the psalm prays to God to bring back the rest of the captives, whose hearts had dried up from the love of God, like the streams found south of Jerusalem, at the end of watercourses that are dry throughout the summer; but in the winter season the warm winds coming from the south move the clouds, and the rains fall and fill the water channels, and the streams flow.

2- The captives occupied with trade and business in Babylon signify the believers in every generation who are occupied with the lusts of the world, whose hearts have dried up like dry watercourses; so we ask that God move their hearts to return to Him, like the streams of the south.
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goes forth and weeps, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

1- The farmer toils in preparing the ground, sowing the seeds and caring for his crop until it grows, bearing many toils, so that his tears flow from the great effort he makes, but in the end he rejoices when he reaps this crop and gathers it in sheaves.

2- This sower signifies the spiritual striver who toils in his striving against sin and his pursuit of acquiring the virtues, and perseveres many days, but in the end he will surely rejoice when he receives God's spiritual blessings in his life, and so enjoys purity and peace and the spiritual virtues, and above all fellowship with God, which is the pledge of the everlasting heavenly joy. Whoever toils in his spiritual striving on the earth will surely receive God's grace in the joys of the Kingdom.

God has prepared for you a great crown in the heavens, so may you look to it at the beginning of every day, that you may fight the good fight; and if you fall, rise quickly and continue your striving, and be confident that God's grace will help you to receive your crown.
The blessings of God. A song of ascents. Of Solomon. “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.) “.. v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its writer: Solomon, as stated in the title of the psalm, and there are two opinions about Solomon as its writer: a- Solomon the well-known king who built the temple.

b- Solomon is a title of Zerubbabel, who returned with the first company of the captives, and he was called Solomon because he was of the seed of Solomon, since Zerubbabel was of the royal line. This is the more probable opinion, because in the days of Zerubbabel there was opposition to the building of the temple, but God made the Jews prosper, and they built the temple and Jerusalem and its walls.
2- When was it written? After the return from captivity.
3- This psalm suits every believer who prays and suffers afflictions, and so trusts in God's power and relies on Him.
4- This psalm speaks of the two prophets, and the next psalm speaks of the wife and the prophetess; therefore these two psalms are considered psalms of the family and of God's work in it.
5- This psalm used to be chanted for the woman after her childbirth, as thanksgiving to God and a blessing for the mother who had given birth.
6- This psalm is prayed on the eighth step on the way of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, to confirm an important truth, namely that the Lord is the foundation of life and the supporter of the believer in all his steps; so it lifts the heart in thanksgiving to God and establishes it in relying on God.

entries.section: (1) The blessing of those who love Him

paragraphs.text: Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman wakes but in vain.

1- In this verse Solomon shows that God is the foundation of success in everything that is for building, and also in guarding our life and keeping it, so that those returning from captivity are not disturbed when the enemies oppose them; for as long as God is with them they will succeed in building the temple and Jerusalem and renewing its walls and gates.

2- This verse shows the work of the supporting grace in the spiritual striving, for man's abilities are limited and few before the power of Satan. But God's supporting grace makes man stronger than Satan, and this calls the striving man to faith in God and reliance on Him, with caution against negligence, because it angers God, and also because relying on human strength alone must lead to failure.

3- Although Satan opposed Christ and made the Jews crucify Him, and still opposes the Church of God in the New Testament to this day, he is helpless before the grace of God that has established the Church until today, and she will remain established for ever through the power of the faith of God's children, their reliance on Him, and their continual self-giving for the sake of His love.

entries.section: (1) The blessing of those who love Him

paragraphs.text: It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of toils. But
gives His beloved sleep.

1- When a person is occupied with material goods, and rises early for them to work a long time, and does not sit down to rest, and finds no opportunity for prayer or reading in the word of God, his heart is filled with worry, and he eats his food with troubles and psychological distress. On the contrary, whoever relies on God and does his duty in life is happy, and God gives him peace in his steps and during his sleep, so he lives in constant joy.
2- God gave His beloved sleep when Christ slept on the Cross, that is, died for our redemption, and then rose on the third day.

Relying on God gives peace, and even makes a person active and able to accomplish greater works. Therefore do not weary yourself with worry and too much thinking, but do your duty and leave God to complete every weakness and lack in you.

entries.section: (2) Children are a blessing from the Lord

paragraphs.text: (Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is a reward.
1- From ancient times, and even now in many parts of the world, a multitude of children is considered a blessing from God, and the Law of Moses declares this (Deut 28:4, 11).

2- If a multitude of children is a blessing from the Lord, then all the more the spiritual children born of the font of Baptism in the Church of the New Testament are a blessing from the Lord, and new members in His body, which is the Church, that He may be glorified in them when they live with Him and keep His commandments. For Christ paid His blood as the price for acquiring His children who are born of the font of Baptism; they are His reward, because He bought them with His blood.

entries.section: (2) Children are a blessing from the Lord

paragraphs.text: (As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man, so are children of the youth.
The youth: young age.

1- When a young woman gives birth, her children are physically strong; so the children of youth are strong, but their true strength is that they are in the hand of a mighty man, who is God. An arrow, however strong and sharp, reaches its target when it is placed in the hand of a mighty man. So also the spiritual children of God, who declared His name in the Old and New Testaments, that is, the prophets and Apostles and all the priests and servants.

2- Youth signifies strength, for Christ accomplished His redemption on the Cross with power, and freed Adam and his children and brought them up to Paradise, and gave power to everyone who believes in Him, so that he overcomes Satan.

entries.section: (2) Children are a blessing from the Lord

paragraphs.text: (Happy is the man that has his quiver full of them; they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate.
Happy: how blessed and joyful he is. Quiver: the quiver is the pouch, that is, a leather bag in which arrows are placed.

1- He who has strong sons, when the enemies come, does not let them into the city, but they stand at its gate, and the sons confront the messengers sent by the enemies with strength, and reject their threats or their deceit.

2- The strong sons who are the arrows signify spiritually the words of God with which a person confronts the wars of Satan, as Christ did in the temptation on the mountain; and the arrows also, that is, the strong sons, are the spiritual weapons in general, such as faith and truth and righteousness) ... Eph 6:13-17), and likewise the spiritual virtues; all of these can repel the attacks of the devil and overcome him.

May you fill your mind with spiritual thoughts, and your heart with feelings toward God, so that you may fight and overcome Satan; for the power of God gives you victory always, however great the devil's cunning or power.
The blessings of the godly. A song of ascents. “Blessed is every one that fears the LORD; that walks in His ways) “... v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is not known.
2- This psalm is distinguished by its speaking of the spiritual family in the home, of the wife and the children and the grandchildren.
3- This psalm encourages the one who prays it to fear the Lord, that he may enjoy blessings in his life and in his home.
4- This psalm is prayed on the ninth step on the way of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

5- This psalm encourages those who returned from captivity in small numbers, that as long as they fear God, and have returned to build His house and worship Him, He will bless them and multiply their offspring, and they will live in God's good things.

6- This psalm signifies Christ, for He is the man who fears the LORD, and his wife is the Church, and his children are the believers in Him throughout the generations; in this respect it is considered one of the Messianic psalms.
7- The Church reads part of this psalm in the rite of the Crowning prayer.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, because it promises the man who fears the LORD, who has lived in the fear of God all day long, many blessings that encourage him to continue his life in the fear of the Lord for the rest of his days.
Blessed is every one that fears the LORD; that walks in His ways.

1- The psalm shows the happiness of him who fears the LORD, for he receives spiritual and material good things, in addition to the eternal good things; because he fears God, he keeps His commandments, and walks in the ways of the Lord, which are the commandments and the means of grace.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the salvation of the Gentiles, and everyone who fears the LORD, so believes in Him and lives with Him and joins the people of God and walks in His ways; for reaching God has many forms in life, such as marriage, or monasticism, or serving virginity.
3- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who lived in godliness all His days on the earth, and walked in the ways of the Lord and did not commit a single sin, and fulfilled all righteousness.
For you shall eat the labour of your hands; happy shall you be, and it shall be well with you.

1- This verse shows the importance of work and spiritual striving; whoever toils, God gives him blessings and good things. Work is necessary, since Adam was working in the garden to till the ground and to name the animals with their names. And Paul tells us of the importance of work, saying “If any would not work, neither should he eat) “(2 Thess 3:10)

2- The good things received by him who works or strives spiritually, he receives their recompense partly on the earth, and then a great, inexpressible reward in heaven. All this is for him who toils and so receives; but beware lest anyone wrong another and take his toil, that is, take the reward of another's toil.
Your wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of your house; your children like olive plants round about your table.
Extended blessings (vv. 4-6)
(Behold, thus shall the man be blessed that fears the LORD.

1- All the previous good things and blessings that the psalm mentioned come upon the man who fears the LORD, and God loves those who fear Him, because they believe in His name and walk by His commandments, so He blesses them with countless spiritual and material blessings. The world cannot take away these blessings, because they are from God, unlike the temporary, passing good things of the world. All these blessings are accompanied by peace in the heart of him who fears God, and great joy; all this is a prelude to the blessings that surpass the mind, which he receives in heaven.
(The LORD shall bless you out of Zion, and you shall see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life.
1- The blessings that come upon him who fears the LORD come to him from Jerusalem, that is, from the temple of the Lord; so they are blessings from God, and not from the passing world.

2- The one who fears the LORD sees the good of Jerusalem, not only the material good things, such as rebuilding the temple after the return from captivity, or its renewal in the days of King Herod, or material good things for the holy city of God, but rather the spiritual good things, which appear in the fullness of time through Christ the Redeemer, who offers in Jerusalem salvation to the whole world. Blessings overflow from the Church of the New Testament in the whole world, while the fullness of blessings and good is in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Remember God's previous works with you, that your faith may be established and you may rely on Him, and the lusts of the world may not be able to lure you, so that you are with Him with all your heart.
(Yea, you shall see your children's children. Peace be upon Israel.

1- He gives a new blessing to him who fears the LORD, which is length of days of life on the earth, so that he sees his grandchildren; for he who fears the LORD enjoys peace and joy, and so lives in quietness a long life. As in ancient times a multitude of children was a blessing from God.

2- The children's children are the spiritual children whom the priests and servants in the New Testament, and all who spoke in the name of the Lord in the Old Testament, such as the prophets, enjoy seeing, that is, those who are taught at the hands of these and the hands of their children, as appears in the life of the monastic fathers and the bishops and the celibates consecrated to the service of God in the world.
3- The psalm ends by invoking peace upon all the people of God, filled with the godly who live in God's blessings, the most important of which is inner peace.

Good things await you as much as you fear God; so remember God's justice, and walk in repentance at all times, and keep the commandments of the Lord, and enjoy confession and Communion, and you will live in peace all your days.
The Lord delivers the afflicted. A song of ascents. “Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say) “.. v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is not known.

2- There is a great similarity between this psalm and (Ps 124), which is also one of the psalms of ascents, “If it had not been the LORD”.... so that some believe that their writer is one, the prophet David. We see in both psalms that the first and second verses are repeated, and each presents the suffering of God's children, and then shows God's love that keeps them and delivers them.

3- Although those who fear the LORD receive many blessings, as appears in the previous psalm, Satan also fights them much, and God delivers them and takes vengeance on the wicked, as appears in this psalm.
4- This psalm suits everyone who suffers afflictions, for it strengthens him and gives him hope in God's protection and His rescue of him.
5- This psalm is prayed on the tenth step on the way of the ascent to the temple.

6- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, to encourage the spiritual striver who has borne many toils all day long that God is with him, and will deliver him from the hands of his enemies, and even take vengeance on them.
“Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth,” let Israel now say, “many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.

1- God's children are exposed to afflictions from the wicked from their youth, that is, from their childhood until the end of their life, but what encourages them to endure is that their enemies are not able to prevail against them, because God is with them.

2- All the righteous bore afflictions even when the number of people in the world was very small: Cain afflicted Abel, and Noah was mocked by the whole world when he built the ark, and he may have endured much even from the hired workmen who made the ark; and the people of Israel bore at the beginning of its life severe afflictions in Egypt, then in the wilderness of Sinai and the war of Amalek, and afterward in wars with the inhabitants of Canaan, and was exposed to the humiliation of the Assyrian and Babylonian captivity, yet they enjoyed God's dwelling among them and His blessings. And if David is the writer, he bore many afflictions from Saul, then Absalom, but God was with him and delivered him from their hands and made him king over his people and gave him the joy of His fellowship.
(The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows.”
Their furrows: plural of furrow, which is the line dug in the ground that the plow makes as it passes over the ground.

1- The writer of the psalm makes clear the extent of the suffering he bore from the wicked, who struck him and scourged him and left cruel marks on his back, and his blood flowed. And as the plow passes through the ground and splits it, making deep lines in it, so also the wicked plowed upon his back, that is, they scourged him, and split his back with deep lines (furrows), that is, he bore and suffered much for the sake of God. For the purity of the righteous rebukes the wicked, so they mistreat them violently.

2- Although the plow splits the ground, afterward the seeds are placed in these deep lines and the plants grow and give fruit; so also bearing sufferings gives the soul strength, and a blessing from God, so it grows in righteousness and virtue, and bears the fruits of the Holy Spirit.

3- Christ bore the scourging on His back and the Crucifixion and gave us salvation. So also the priests and servants bear many troubles from the flock, and carry their burdens, so that they may know God with a true knowledge, and their harsh natures may change.
Bear with those around you for the sake of Christ who bore with you, and know that this endurance proves your life, so you become worthy of many blessings on the earth and in heaven.
(The LORD is righteous; He has cut asunder the cords of the wicked.
The cords of the wicked: the cords are the ropes by which the yoke is fastened, which is a piece of wood fixed on the necks of the two animals and tied at the neck, so that the yoke rests upon them.

1- God intervenes when He sees the cruelty of the wicked toward His children, and He likens the burdens they place on His children to the yoke that is tied on the necks of animals; if these cords are cut they are freed from the cruelty of the wicked, and go far away from them. So God lifts the trial and gives rest to His children, and even blesses them with many comforts. This gives hope to the suffering that the trial is temporary, and God will surely end it.

(Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion. Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withers before it grows up, wherewith the mower fills not his hand, nor he that binds sheaves his bosom.
Zion: the most important of the five hills on which the city of Jerusalem was built, and by Zion he means Jerusalem, in which the believers in the Lord live.
The binder: the one who gathers plants into sheaves.

1- God declares that the wicked who hate His children will be overtaken by shame, and even be turned back, and leave off harming His children. He also likens their evils against His children to the grass of the housetops, that is, the small plants that grow on the roofs of village houses in a thin layer of soil, so the roots of these grasses have no depth, and they dry up from the heat of the sun and die quickly. Before these grasses grow, and the farmer gathers them and puts them in sheaves to feed his cattle, they dry up and are thrown far away to be burned, because there is no use in them. So also the evils of the wicked are superficial, with a strong appearance, but they end quickly.

2- All the persecutions directed against the Church throughout the ages are brought to nothing, and the demons are put to shame and turn back, because all their evils are superficial, since God dwells in His children, so they are not disturbed by the persecutions, and they end quickly, and even His children grow in their love for God.
(Neither do they which go by say, “The blessing of the LORD be upon you; we bless you in the name of the LORD.”

1- It becomes clear before all people who pass by the wicked, whom he previously likened to the grass of the housetops, that the wicked have no power, and receive no blessing from God, for they dry up and are burned, as a pointer to their destiny, which is eternal torment in the blazing fire.
2- On the other side, God's children receive a blessing in the name of the Lord, because of their walking in righteousness and their bearing persecution from the wicked for the sake of the Lord.

The success of the wicked seems great but it is temporary and passing, so do not heed it, and stand firm in your faith in God and His commandments, and you will live in peace on the earth, and then in inexpressible happiness in heaven.
H Forgiveness and redemption. A song of ascents. “Out of the depths have I cried unto You, O LORD) “... v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer's name is not mentioned in the title; but there is an inclination that he is the prophet David.
2- When was it written? In the days of David, because Solomon quoted from it in his prayer (v. 2; 2 Chr 6:40-42).
3- Perhaps Nehemiah quoted from this psalm in his book and in his prayer (v. 2; Neh 1:6, 11)

4- This psalm is also similar to the Epistles of St. Paul the Apostle, especially (Rom 7, 8). This confirms the unity of the Holy Bible, for the Holy Spirit is the inspirer of all the books of the Old and New Testaments.
5- This psalm suits the penitent person who asks forgiveness from God, for it develops his hope and his reliance on Him.
6- This psalm suits those returning from captivity, for it gives them hope in the new life with God.
7- This psalm is one of the well-known penitential psalms mentioned before, which are seven psalms: (Ps 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143)
8- This psalm shows God's concern for the depths of man, that is, his heart and his feelings, more than his outward appearance.
9- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks to us of Christ the Redeemer (vv. 6-8).
10- This psalm used to be prayed on the eleventh step on the way of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

11- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, for we offer repentance before God and ask His forgiveness for all our sins, in preparation for a new day, not only on the earth, but for the day that has no end, that is, eternity.
Out of the depths have I cried unto You, O LORD.

1- After the one ascending to the temple has passed through the suffering of many pains during the ascent, as appears from the previous psalms, he reaches the point of crying out to God from the depths of his heart. A cry of the heart may not need a cry of the lips, like the cry of Abel's blood from the ground (Gen 4:10), and the heartfelt cry of Moses before the Red Sea (Ex 14:15), and the cry of the silent one, the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 1:13). This shows two things:
a- The extent of his suffering from lusts, or problems, or afflictions.
b- The extent of his faith in God, who is able to rescue him.

2- The depths may be the depths of God, that is, the spiritual man has reached the depths of God and from there cries out to Him; for whoever enters into the depths, his longings toward God increase, and his faith in Him and his hope in Him.

3- These words may be a prophecy about Christ, who went down to the depths of Hades before the Cross, and cried out to the Father, declaring the accomplishment of the redemption by which Adam and his children ascend from Hades to Paradise.
Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications.
1- David asks God to hear his voice and to open His ears to his supplications. This shows two things:
a- His humility and his great need of God.
b- His faith in the power of God, who is able to rescue him from all his troubles.
If You, LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? For there is forgiveness with You. That
be feared of you.

1- David shows the justice of God and the sin of man, for there is no man without sin, and therefore no one can stand before God to be judged or to defend himself; because all have gone astray and become corrupt, there is none who does good (Ps 14:3).

2- The just God is also the merciful One who forgives. Forgiveness comes from the Son who is with the Father, for it is He who will redeem humanity, and with this hope the believing penitent can stand before God, who is just and merciful at the same time.

3- If a person receives forgiveness, he thanks God and does not become negligent, but remains holding fast to the fear of the just God, or else he loses forgiveness, that is, he works out his salvation with fear and trembling (Heb 2:3).

However many afflictions meet you, take refuge in God and cry out to Him, for He awaits you in His love. And however great your sins, He will forgive them for you. But hold fast to His commandments and His fear, and you will live in repentance and in peace all your days.
I waited for You, O LORD; my soul waits, and in His word do I hope.

1- In his affliction David looked to God, and was not occupied with his sins or his weakness, or the difficulty of the affliction, but in faith he waited for God, that is, he was not disturbed by the delay of God's answer.

2- David concentrated on waiting for the Lord, and confirmed this by repeating the word “wait” twice in this verse, and then a third time in the next verse. All this was in hope of God's promise that He would rescue him from all his afflictions. For God's word confirms to him God's care and help; therefore he was reassured, and even his love and faith in God grew, for the affliction pushed him a step forward in his attachment to God.
My soul waits for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning; I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
1- David waits for the Lord with longing and concern more than the night watchman who waits for the dawn to break.

He confirms his longing by repeating the phrase twice in this same verse, and this signifies the difficulty of patience throughout the night, and the increase of longing to see the light of dawn. So everyone who passes through affliction, or wants to be rid of sin, awaits this hope with intense longing.

2- The Jews used to set guards for the temple who watched in the night for the dawn to break, and waited for it with great concern, so that when they saw the dawn they hastened to offer the morning sacrifice, which is the burnt offering. So David's waiting for the Lord is with intense longing to offer Him holy worship, thanksgiving and praise.

3- The waiting for the dawn that David awaited signifies, in the spirit of prophecy, the waiting for the Resurrection of Christ, which took place at the dawn of Sunday, to proclaim the salvation of all humanity that believes in Christ.
(Let Israel hope in the LORD; for with the LORD there is mercy, and with Him is plenteous redemption. And He shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
Let hope: that is, let them hope.

1- At the close of the psalm he calls the people of God who believe in Him, Israel, to place their hope in the Lord; for His mercies are many, or with Him is infinite mercy, and therefore He is ready to forgive them and support them, however great their sins and however hard their afflictions.

2- God has redemption for His people from all their sins and their problems; His power is great and He has many means to save them. His redemption is complete to lift from them all their troubles; therefore let God's children be reassured, and hope in Him always.

3- The redemption for which David and all the believers in the Old Testament hoped is the redemption of Christ, which was accomplished in the fullness of time, and it is the pledge of the complete redemption when Christ lifts them up to the Kingdom and compensates them for all their toils on the earth.

Look to God's mercy and His promises so that your heart may be strengthened, and depression may not strike you because of afflictions, or the sins into which you fall, but hasten to repentance and prayer, indeed to every good work, relying in this on God's mercy and His redemption.
Humility, striving and hope. A song of ascents. Of David. “LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty) “.. v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states.
2- When was it written?
There are two opinions:

a- When David went down to visit his brothers who were fighting the Philistines, and his eldest brother Eliab rebuked him, accusing him of pride, so he wrote this psalm, declaring his humility before God (1 Sam 17:28).

b- David wrote it when the servants of Saul accused him that he ought to seize the kingdom when he was a military commander, or one of the bravest commanders under Saul, to declare that he was not seeking this kingdom, although the prophet Samuel had anointed him king years before.
c- When Michal despised her husband David for his dancing before the ark of the covenant of God, he declared that he would make himself even smaller than this before the Lord (2 Sam 6:22).
3- This psalm suits everyone who flees from the glory of the world, and humbles himself and hopes in God.

4- Perhaps this psalm is a prophecy about the feelings of the captives in Babylon, or those returning from captivity, in humility before God, and they entreat Him to help them in building the temple and the acceptance of their worship.

5- This psalm shows the feelings of the spiritual man who believes in God, so he humbles himself, and it exposes the sin of Satan the proud, who fell through his pride and his attempt to raise his throne and his position like God (Ezek 28:16-17). So also it rebukes the pride of the first man, Adam and Eve, who tried to become like God (Gen 3:5).
6- This psalm is prayed on the twelfth step on the way of the ascent to the temple.

It is noticed that as one ascends and approaches the temple, one prays this psalm that calls to humility. The higher we rise toward God, the more humility we need, and the spiritual striving and hope in the Lord increase.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, so that in it a person may declare his humility before God, hoping for his salvation after a whole day has passed, that He may forgive him all his sins and give him quiet sleep and a place in eternity.
LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor my eyes lofty; neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me.
Lofty: not exalted and not proud.

1- David declares that he did not fall into pride in his feelings, and did not look with his eye to the kingdom, or a position higher than the one he was in; not in order to boast of his humility, but to thank God for the grace of humility that He gave him, whether in his heart, or in the look of his eyes, or in his conduct and works.

2- David did not desire to sit on the throne and remove Saul, although he had been anointed by the hand of Samuel, and God had rejected Saul because of his sins, but he remained subject to Saul. Indeed, when Saul fell into David's hand twice, he said how could he stretch out his hand against the Lord's anointed (1 Sam 24:6), and he did not kill him, although Saul tried many times to kill David.

3- Here David resembles Christ in his humility, for David is a type of Christ, and therefore God blessed David when He said of him, “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after My own heart” (Acts 13:22).

entries.section: (1) David desires to build the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: LORD, remember David, and all his afflictions: how he swore unto the LORD, and vowed unto the mighty God of Jacob:
The mighty God of Jacob: that is, the great God, the God of Jacob.
1- David entreats God to remember his humility and weakness, for he declares that he is nothing before God, that He may have compassion on him and bless him.

2- If the writer is Solomon, he reminds God that He has fulfilled what He promised his father David, who humbled himself before God and vowed to build a house for Him. And that You, O God, said to him that your son Solomon is the one who will build the house, and I have built it; so bless it, and bless everyone who enters it to worship.

3- David also shows his love in his oath and his vow to God that he would build a house for Him, because David was living in a great house made of cedar wood, while God dwelt in a tent; this shows David's love for God, although he had no power to build the house without God's permission. God did not permit David to build it, but David is the first to declare his love for God in his desire to build for Him a great house in place of the moving tent.

entries.section: (1) David desires to build the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: “Surely I will not come into the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed; I will not give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids,
Slumber: drowsiness.

1- David spent all his effort to find a dwelling for the Lord and to build Him a house; he did not rest from searching and preparing the building materials all day, and also at night he did not tire of praying that God would fulfill his longings and permit the building of the house. He gave his body no rest to achieve his goal.

2- David worked with perseverance to build the house, because Satan opposes the works of God and searches for a gap through which to enter, and David gave him no opportunity by continuing in striving and prayer. David represents seriousness in work, and once he has begun he must complete it.

entries.section: (1) David desires to build the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob.”
Mighty: great.

David wanted to find a place, a dwelling and a rest for the Lord, who in his sight is more important than any man. How could David rest in his house and his palace while God has no place of His own? By “place” he means a great place suited to the glory of God. He did not say “I will build Him a house,” because he knows that God is the Builder, and David longs only that there be a place in which God is pleased to dwell.

entries.section: (1) David desires to build the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah; we found it in the fields of the wood.
Ephratah: a Hebrew word meaning fruitful, and it is Bethlehem, which lies southwest of Jerusalem at a distance of 8 km.

Fields of the wood: the wood means wilderness places, or places of forests. What is meant here is the village of Jearim, which lies southwest of Jerusalem at a distance of 18 km. The word Jearim means forests.

1- David heard that the ark was in the region of Ephratah, so he searched for it until he found it in the village of Jearim, in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, and he moved it with great celebration to Jerusalem (2 Chr 1:4). This shows David's diligence and seriousness in searching for the ark of the covenant of God because of his heart's attachment to God; for the ark of the covenant represents the presence of God.

2- This verse is a prophecy about the Incarnation of Christ, who was born in Bethlehem, which is Ephratah (Gen 35:19), and He came to save the whole world; for the fields of the wood signify the Gentiles. He was born of the tribe of Judah in Bethlehem, but He also came to save all humanity.

entries.section: (1) David desires to build the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: “We will go into His tabernacles; we will worship at His footstool.”

1- When David found the ark of the covenant he moved it with great celebration to Jerusalem, and called all the people to worship before it, that is, to submit to His commandments and His Law, and to surrender life to Him. This shows David's submission to God and acceptance of His will in all his life.
2- This worship in Ephratah happened with Christ, born in the manger, by the shepherds, and then by the Magi. And God's footstool signifies His Incarnation.

Weary your body in spiritual striving and in fulfilling your responsibilities, and your spirit will rest; for the more the body is pressed, the stronger the spirit becomes, and then God is pleased to dwell in it, and this is God's dwelling, and the greatest place He seeks, that is, your heart, that He may reign over it and satisfy you with His love.

entries.section: (2) Bringing back the ark of the covenant

paragraphs.text: Arise, O LORD, into Your rest; You, and the ark of Your strength.

1- David calls on God to arise from Jearim, that is, the ark of the covenant of God, and be moved to Jerusalem to settle there, for he knows that God is the mover of the whole world, and He permitted Himself to be among His people by means of His ark of the covenant. Therefore he says to Him, arise and move, and his heart is full of joy that God will dwell in Jerusalem beside him, or more precisely, David will be beside God who dwells in Jerusalem. And David feels that the ark of God's strength is the ark of pride and glory, because God is above all gods.
2- Moses used to repeat this verse when the ark journeyed in the wilderness of Sinai (Num 10:35-36), and Solomon also said it after building the temple at its dedication (2 Chr 6:41-42).
3- This verse applies to the captives returning to Jerusalem, whose feelings repeated this verse after the rebuilding of the temple.

4- In the spirit of prophecy David calls Christ to arise from the bosom of the Father and condescend and become incarnate for the redemption of His people. And he also calls Him, while He is in the tomb after His death on the Cross, to rise from the dead, declaring His victory over death for the benefit of His people, to give resurrection to everyone who believes in Him.
5- The rest of the Lord is also the Church, in which God arises and dwells in the midst of His people, and the ark of strength is also the womb of the Virgin from which Christ was born.

entries.section: (2) Bringing back the ark of the covenant

paragraphs.text: Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let Your saints shout for joy.

Since the ark has settled in Jerusalem, the psalmist calls on the priests to live in righteousness and purity, so that they may stand before God to serve Him. As for His people, let them be in great joy, and praise God with continual shouting and glorification. This is fulfilled, in the spirit of prophecy, more clearly in the Church of the New Testament.

May you, my brother, call on God, whose Holy Spirit dwelling in you you have neglected, to arise and be kindled within you, and may you give Him a greater place in your life and hold fast to His commandments, so that He always finds His rest in you and works freely in all your thoughts and words and deeds.

entries.section: (3) The promise to the offspring of David

paragraphs.text: For Your servant David's sake turn not away the face of Your anointed.

1- The prophet David says in the spirit of prophecy, entreating God, who promised to set his son Solomon as king after him and that he would build a temple for the Lord, and David asks Him not to turn away the face of His anointed, that is, Solomon, anointed king, and to help him build a temple for Him.

2- If the writer of the psalm is Solomon, he entreats God, interceding by his father David, who had died by then, that He not turn away the face of His anointed, that is, Solomon himself, and bless him to build and dedicate the temple. And this verse is found with the same text in Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple (2 Chr 6:42).

entries.section: (3) The promise to the offspring of David

paragraphs.text: The LORD has sworn in truth unto David; He will not turn from it: “Of the fruit of your body will I set upon your throne. If your children will keep My covenant and My testimony that I shall teach them, their children shall also sit upon your throne for evermore.”

1- These two verses are God's promise to David that He will put his offspring on the throne of David, that is, the throne of the kingdom of Judah, for ever (2 Sam 7:12-13). And indeed this was fulfilled until the Babylonian captivity, and was completed in Christ, who comes of the offspring of David, to reign for ever.

2- The condition for the offspring of David to sit on his throne for ever is their keeping God's covenant and His testimonies. Some of this offspring lived in righteousness and the worship of God, and some did not keep His commandments, and therefore God permitted the captivity as a punishment for them. And when they returned to repentance before God, God's promise was renewed in Christ, incarnate in the fullness of time. So the angel declared to the Virgin that the Lord would give the One born of her the throne of His father David (Lk 1:31); Christ sat on the throne of His father David, and He will continue to reign over the hearts of those who believe in Him for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

Ask the intercession of the saints and God will have mercy on you, as Solomon interceded by David his father (v. 10), because intercession is precious to God, for it declares your love for His children, and your longing for God, and your humility before Him, and so He grants you abundant blessings.
For the LORD has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His habitation: “This is My rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it.
1- God chose Zion, that is, Jerusalem, because His temple is in it, and He found rest in its being His dwelling.
And God's rest is in the prayers of His children and their praises lifted up to Him, for He rejoices in the faith of His children and His love for them.

2- He says that His rest is in Jerusalem for ever, and of course He does not mean the city of Jerusalem in Judea, because it was destroyed in AD 70 by the hand of Titus the Roman. But He means the Jerusalem that is the Church of the New Testament, which extends for ever into the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

3- The writer of the psalm called on the Lord and said to Him, “Arise, O LORD, into Your rest” (v. 8), and the Lord answers in (v. 14) and says that My rest is in Jerusalem, that is, in the prayers of My children and their praises.
4- Jerusalem is the soul that believes in God, in the Old Testament and the New Testament, and He rests in it for ever, because this soul is immortal with Him in the Kingdom.
I will abundantly bless her provision; I will satisfy her poor with bread.
1- As long as God dwells in the midst of His people, He blesses their material needs and satisfies all the poor in it, so that all are content materially and thank God.
2- Christ in His Church satisfies His poor children in spirit, that is, the humble, and gives them their spiritual needs, in addition to the material, and gives them above all His Body and Blood.
3- The food of the Church (or her catch in the Septuagint translation) is her children and those who join her and believe in Christ; He blesses them and satisfies them spiritually and materially.
I will also clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints shall shout aloud for joy.

1- God gives a special blessing to His children the priests, because they serve in His temple and lead His people in the spiritual way, so He grants them salvation, that is, deliverance from sins and the preoccupations of the world, that they may enjoy fellowship with God. As for all the godly believers, they praise God, and even shout with all their hearts, rejoicing. These blessings for the godly priests He gives them in the Old Testament, and all the more in the New Testament from the abundant blessings of the Holy Spirit.

2- In the ninth verse the writer of the psalm calls on the Lord and asks Him to clothe the priests with righteousness and make the godly shout for joy. And God answers in (v. 16), responding to the call of the writer of the psalm, and confirms that He will clothe the priests with salvation and make the godly shout aloud.
There will I make the horn of David to bud; I have ordained a lamp for My anointed. His enemies will I clothe with shame, but upon himself shall his crown flourish.”
1- The horn of David that God makes to bud is Christ, who comes of the offspring of David. And “I have ordained a lamp for My anointed”
what is meant by it is David's prophecy about Christ, in addition to the prophecies of the prophets, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah ...
Then John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, who prepared the way for Him.

2- The ordaining of the lamp for Christ is the Body of Christ that He took from the Virgin, because Christ is the light of the world. And by the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption, shame came upon the enemies of Christ, that is, the demons. And the flourishing crown of Christ is the Church, and the head of this flourishing crown is Christ.

3- Christ, who is the lamp of the world, a light whose divinity appeared through His life on the earth, through His words and His miracles, and His holiness appeared in that He did not sin, and His holiness and His light appeared still more in His Transfiguration on the mountain, and then in His Resurrection and Ascension.

4- Although the psalm began with humiliation in (v. 1), it ends with glory and light and holiness in Christ who comes of the offspring of David, who enlightens the whole world and all who believe in Him.

God wants to enlighten your life, so He drives all the darkness of sin from you when you repent and adorns you with virtues, so that you are a light to the world and the salt of the earth, and He supports you in your spiritual striving until you reach the glories of heaven.
Brotherly love. A song of ascents. Of David. “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.
2- When was it written? After David became king over all the children of Israel, to call them to love and brotherhood in their worship of God.
3- This psalm is a prophecy about the feelings of the Jews returning from captivity with joy, to dwell together in Jerusalem and Judea and build the temple, to worship God in it with one heart.

4- This psalm is liturgical, because it was chanted at the three great feasts of the Jews, which are the Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, in which all the males of the children of Israel come before the temple of God to worship Him, and bring their families with them.

5- This psalm declares the importance of brotherly love and of brethren dwelling together, so it is fitting for every believer to chant it in the midst of the Church in every spiritual atmosphere, or in a setting where the believers gather.

6- This psalm declares the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church among the brethren who are members of the one body and are bound by love and unity. If the previous psalm tells us of the saving work of Christ and His rest in His Church, this psalm declares the work of the Holy Spirit in the salvation which He pours out on the Church.
7- This psalm used to be prayed on the fourteenth of the steps of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, to remind the believers of the importance of brotherly love among them, so that if there are any differences, or distress in hearts, they give them up and forgive one another, so that they find rest in the hands of God.
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together!

1- The best thing in the relationship between people is for brethren to dwell together; what is meant is not dwelling in houses, but spiritual dwelling, that is, unity in worship, so that they worship God with one heart. This used to happen in the temple, as the priests and Levites chanted this psalm when they entered for worship and the practice of their service. This was also the feeling of those returning from captivity to build the temple and restore the worship of God with one heart, since they had become one people and were no longer divided into a northern and a southern kingdom as they were before the captivity.

2- For brethren to be able to gather and dwell together, each one must be purified from his sins, and believe in God and live with Him, and then he can love the brethren. Worship in unity is made easy in the Church of the New Testament when the Holy Spirit begets the believers from one womb, which is Baptism, and unites them in the sacrament of Communion from the Body and Blood of the Lord, so that it becomes natural for them to worship God with one heart, as the Apostles continued in worship with one accord (Acts 1:14).
It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard, that went down to the skirts of his garments.

1- David likens the love of brethren for one another to the perfume, or oil, that Moses poured on the head of Aaron when he anointed him high priest. This oil ran down from the head and descended upon the beard, then ran from the beard to the neckline of the robe, and it was a beautiful sight.

2- Aaron the high priest signifies Christ, the High Priest of our New Testament, and He is the head of the body upon whom His Holy Spirit is poured, and it runs down from Him to the beard, which signifies the Apostles; for the beard grows on the mature, the grown and the full-grown, and the beard signifies the Apostles because it is attached to the head, who is Christ. Then the oil runs from the beard to all His garments, even to their skirts. The garments signify the believers, and the skirts signify all the believers, and so they are all united through the pouring out of the Holy Spirit upon them.

3- And the oil that runs down upon the beard comes from the head and carries the fragrance of the head, which belongs to Christ, so all the believers receive the sweet fragrance of Christ (2 Cor 2:15).

4- The Holy Spirit used to be poured on certain persons in the Old Testament, such as the high priest, the prophet and the king, but in the New Testament He is given to all the believers and dwells in them permanently, and not temporarily as in the Old Testament. And for the Holy Spirit to work in the believers, constant repentance is needed and attachment to the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace.
As the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion; for there the LORD commanded the blessing, life for evermore.
1- Mount Hermon is in eastern Lebanon, and its summit is high, rising 9,200 feet above sea level.

The summit of the mountain is covered with snow, and abundant dew flows from the summit and descends the mountain to the small hills adjoining it, such as the hill of Sion, or Zion, which is different from the hill of Zion on which Jerusalem in Judea was built. This dew makes forests and vineyards grow, and the dew tempers the air in the heat of summer.

2- The dew of Hermon, descending abundantly on the mountain and the surrounding hills, signifies the pouring out of the Holy Spirit on the believers in the Church. And as the dew of Hermon gives life to the plants and trees, so it gives the believers spiritual growth, and fruits, which are the virtues.

3- If the writer of the psalm likens the love of brethren to the dew of Hermon, which signifies the pouring out of the Holy Spirit on the Church, then all of these give a growing spiritual life to the believers, and extend with them for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven. For the love of brethren grants them a pure life with God, and overcomes all the devil's cunning of strife, or divisions, and by this love prepares them for the Kingdom of Heaven.

4- As the dew of Hermon tempers the plants and trees growing on the mountain and at its foot, so also the love of brethren tempers the relationship between them, and supports them before trials, which are signified by the intense rays of the sun, and gives them a beautiful feeling that makes them happy in their life, and makes them grow in their love for God.

If Satan tries to disturb you with the mistakes and offenses of those around you, hasten to prayer with humility, and the Holy Spirit who dwells in you will give you calm, and even turn you from distress to pity for them, so that you pray for them.
The night prayer in the sanctuary. A song of ascents. “Behold, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD ...” v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms, because the name of the writer is not in the title of the psalm.
2- When was it written? Not known precisely, and it may be:
a- In the days of David, or Solomon, to encourage the priests and Levites and the believers to worship and praise God in His temple.
b- The days of Nehemiah, who took care to restore and organize the service in the temple of the Lord, and he encourages the priests and Levites to praise.

3- This psalm is a call to the priests and Levites to offer the evening worship, which is the evening burnt offering, and the prayers and praises offered in the temple, and that is in (vv. 1, 2). And the high priest answers them in (v. 3) and gives them the blessing from the Lord. It is therefore a liturgical psalm offered by the company of the priests and Levites, and the believers.

4- There is a relation between this psalm and the one before it, which tells us of the work of the Holy Spirit in the believers, while this psalm tells us of the final effect of the Holy Spirit, which is the love of praise and being with God.

5- This psalm is offered and prayed on the last of the steps of the ascent to the temple of the Lord, which is the fifteenth step, where they reach the temple and enter it and offer prayers and praises.
6- This psalm suits the believers at every time, and especially in the nights, to encourage them to prayer and praise.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, and as the introduction to the prayer of Midnight, where it calls the worshipers to praise God and to enjoy being before Him after the preoccupations of the long day.
Behold, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who by night stand in the house of the LORD.

1- The psalm addresses the servants of the Lord who love His house and stand before Him for prayer and praise and blessing the Lord, in the night when people are quiet and asleep. But the priests and Levites and the believers who love God offer the evening burnt offering, which expresses their love for God, since the whole sacrifice is burned to please Him, and the offering of the sacrifice is accompanied by prayers expressing their love for God.
