And prayer in the night declares that these worshipers loved God more than sleep and the rest of the body, so they spent part of the night in prayer because their hearts were attached to Him, like David who said, “At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto You because of Your righteous judgments” (Ps 119:62).

2- If in the Old Testament a person had to be clean when entering the temple, then all the more in the New Testament a person must be penitent and pure in order to share in the prayers of the Church and her praises, whether in the Liturgies or the other prayers.
3- Some people loved God and prayer and praise in His house, so that they lived their life night and day in praise, like Anna the daughter of Phanuel (Lk 2:36-37).
Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD.
1- Lifting the hands in prayer means:
a- Declaring repentance, and asking purity and forgiveness from God.
b- Supplication to God, and this means need and humility.
c- Faith in God to whom we lift our hands, for He is our Deliverer and our only support.
d- Joining prayer with the lifting of the hands means our readiness to act, and not only to speak, that is, we strive and do all we can to be rid of our sins and to acquire every virtue.

e- Lifting the hands means the sign of the Cross, as Moses lifted his hands, and the children of Israel prevailed over Amalek (Ex 17:11). So lifting the hands is holding fast to the Cross that gives us spiritual victory.
Therefore St. Paul the Apostle in the New Testament calls us to lift up holy hands before God in prayer (1 Tim 2:8).

2- The believers used to pray lifting clean hands and looking toward the sanctuary of the tabernacle of meeting, or the temple of the Lord, that is, looking toward the holy place, as Daniel did (Dan 6:10), and as we pray toward the sanctuary which is in the east in the Church of the New Testament.
3- Lifting the hands and looking toward the sanctuary is accompanied by blessing the Lord, that is, praise and thanksgiving for all that God has done with us all day long, or all our life.
The LORD bless you out of Zion, He who made heaven and earth.

1- If the writer of the psalm is calling the priests and Levites and the believers to bless the Lord, they receive a blessing after this in (v. 3). And if the high priest is the one who calls to bless the Lord in (vv. 1, 2), they answer him in (v. 3). In sum, this psalm closes with a blessing that comes from the Lord to the worshipers standing in the sanctuary in the nights. And this blessing means:
a- The divine forgiveness and the purity granted by God to the priests.
b- Inner renewal and being filled with God.
c- The person himself becomes a blessing to those around him.
2- The Law commanded Aaron and his sons the priests to bless the people who believe in God (Num 6:23-26).

3- This blessing comes from God, the Maker of heaven and earth, that is, He in whose hand is everything, and He gives this blessing from Zion, that is, from His temple, or from the Church, or from heaven. It is a great blessing, indeed the highest gift in the world. This means that there is a special blessing in the Church, but God blesses His children also in every place, because He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

May you take care of your prayer every night, to declare your love for God, and to thank Him for His care for you all day long, and to offer repentance for your sins, and to ask for quiet sleep in His hands, so that you wake for praise and prayers. Praising the mighty, blessed God. “Alleluia. Praise the name of the LORD; praise Him, O you servants of the LORD) “... v. 1. Introduction:
1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms whose title does not mention the name of its writer. But some incline to the view that the writer is the prophet David.

2- This psalm calls to the praise of God, and suits everyone who loves God and grows spiritually. We should enjoy being in His hands, and thank Him for His works with us. Therefore this psalm calls to praise three times at its beginning (vv. 1-3) and to blessing God four times at its end (vv. 19-21).

3- This psalm resembles the one before it in praising God, but it is distinguished in that it gives the motives of this praise, which are God's works with His children and the weakness and baseness of the worship of idols. It clearly declares the rejection of pagan worship, and the praise of God alone.

4- This psalm is considered one of the great Hallel psalms that praise and glorify God, together with the psalm after it. The two were chanted in the morning service on the Sabbath and at the feast of the Passover. It is therefore a liturgical psalm. It was also chanted after the return from captivity, and also during the captivity, so that the believers might reject the worship of idols.
5- This psalm begins with the word “Alleluia” and also ends with it, like Psalms (106, 113, 146, 148, 149, 150).
6- This psalm is similar to the ninth chapter of the Book of Nehemiah in that both call the Levites to bless God and thank Him for His great works with His people.
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
Alleluia. Praise the name of the LORD; praise Him, O you servants of the LORD.

1- The writer of the psalm calls the servants of the Lord to praise Him, since he has experienced the sweetness of praise; therefore he wants all who believe in God to enjoy praising Him. The sign that declares the faith of the servants of the Lord in Him is that they love Him, and feel His grace, and so thank Him and praise Him.

2- If the servants of the Lord lift their hearts in praise to God, they cling to Him, and God gives them the grace of sonship, which was clearly declared in the New Testament; for Christ, the Only Son in essence, by His redemption of us became the firstborn among many brethren, so we became sons of God, attached to Him, striving to praise Him, like the angels who praise Him at all times; indeed some people have consecrated their lives to praising His holy name, and they are the monastic fathers.
3- Praising the name of the Lord means His person, and this contains all the beauty of the Lord, of virtues and blessings, which His children see and experience.
You that stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God.

1- Here the writer of the psalm calls those who stand in the house of the Lord, who are all the believers who offer worship in the house of the Lord, and especially the priests and Levites who stand for long periods to offer worship and prayers and praise to the Lord.

2- “Those who stand” means spiritual vigilance and attention, and it also means reverence in the presence of the great God. It likewise means uprightness in faith before God. All this draws the hearts of God's children to live with Him in holy worship in His temple, and therefore keeps them entirely away from the temples of idols.
Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing praises unto His name, for it is pleasant.

1- The writer of the psalm, who has experienced the sweetness of praise, calls the priests and Levites to praise God, and what encourages them to praise is that He is good. And whoever comes forward to praise the good God ought to be striving in the way of goodness.

2- When the believers praise the good God, they praise Him for His goodness; He treats them according to His goodness and blesses them. And they praise Him also not only for the benefit and the answer to their requests, but because He is sweet and worthy of praise.
For the LORD has chosen Jacob unto Himself, and Israel for His own possession.

1- God chose Jacob, or Israel, the father of the tribes, and all the people of the children of Israel, because of his faith, and his pursuit of the way of perfection, and his love for God, so He shepherded him and cared for him, that this people might be a light to the world and an example to the rest of the peoples; and as God is glorified in His people, He calls the rest of the peoples to believe in Him.

2- God's choice of His people is a great pride that makes this people distinct from the rest of the peoples, as the Law declared (Deut 7:6). And it calls the people to hold fast to the Law and the commandments, that they may enjoy the fellowship of God and His increasing work in them. And all the more in the New Testament, the Christians in the Church are distinguished by God's choice of them, and this makes them hold fast to His word, and unite with Him through the Holy Sacraments, and acquire His virtues, and so enjoy His constant presence with them.

God is sweet, and therefore it is natural for us to praise Him, and it is unnatural for us to neglect praising Him; for praise expresses our faith in Him, and our love for Him, and our appreciation of His gifts, for which we thank Him. Therefore may we take care to set aside a time, even if small, every day for praise.

entries.section: (2) The power of ... with His people

paragraphs.text: For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods. Whatsoever the LORD pleased, that did He in heaven, and in earth, in the seas, and all deep places. He causes the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth; He makes lightnings for the rain; He brings the wind out of His treasuries.
Deep places: waves.

1- The writer of the psalm declares his experience with God, and says that He is great, indeed greater than all the pagan gods that the peoples of the world follow. And that He is able to do everything in every place, whether in heaven, or on earth, or in the sea; because He is the Creator of all, and therefore He alone is worthy of prayer, glorification and worship.

2- The writer of the psalm gives examples of God's power: He alone is the One who makes the clouds ascend from the end of the earth to its end. And it is laden with many good things, which are the rains that He pours out on people in God's wisdom in the suitable measure. And He gives light to the sky, which is the lightnings, and likewise He moves the winds in their various directions. These examples signify God's power that sends the Apostles and priests and servants into the world to pour out on it the blessings of God's word and His sacraments, and they are the clouds. As for the lightnings, they signify the spiritual enlightenment that God gives His children. And the winds signify the manifold work of the Holy Spirit in every direction to meet the needs of the Church and the believers.

entries.section: (2) The power of ... with His people

paragraphs.text: Who smote the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and beast. Who sent tokens and wonders into the midst of you, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh, and upon all his servants.
1- God struck the Egyptians with ten plagues to show them the weakness of their gods whom they worshiped, so that they would take heed and return to Him and know that He is the one God.

2- The plagues were gradual so that they might return to Him, but because of the hardness of their hearts the force of the plagues increased until it reached the tenth plague, which is the hardest, in which the firstborn of men were struck, and also the beasts; for the beasts are a blessing from God, so if man deviates God withdraws His gift from him.

3- All these plagues came upon the Egyptians, and did not come upon the children of Israel, for they lived in peace and divine blessings; all this so that the Egyptians would take heed and know the power of God, who shepherds His people and protects them, that perhaps they would believe, and repent, and return to Him.

entries.section: (2) The power of ... with His people

paragraphs.text: Who smote great nations, and slew mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan; and gave their land for an heritage, an heritage unto Israel His people.

1- After the liberation of the people of God from the slavery of Egypt, and their crossing the wilderness of Sinai, they reached the land of Canaan, and faced at its front, east of the Jordan River, strong peoples of giants, who are the Amorites, headed by Sihon, who signifies pride and haughtiness, and Og, who signifies reliance on blessings and material strength. The children of Israel killed them by the power of God, and crossed the Jordan River, and also triumphed by the power of God over all the kings and kingdoms they faced in the land of Canaan, and possessed their land.

2- The children of Israel triumphed by the power of God over the Canaanite peoples, and killed them because of their evil, and they signify the demons, because they are wicked and worship idols, and they possessed their land in their place; because the people of God believe in Him and walk by His commandments and His Law. And if the people of God go away and walk in evil, God disciplines them with afflictions and captivity. And the cause of all the blessings is faith in God, and walking by His commandments.

The power of God with you protects you and reassures you, and even fills your heart with joy as long as you strive in the way of His commandments, and repent if you sin; but beware of negligence lest God abandon you and you suffer many troubles and lose your eternal place.

entries.section: (3) The blessed ... and the corruption of the idols

paragraphs.text: Your name, O LORD, endures for ever; Your memorial, O LORD, throughout all generations.

God is eternal and everlasting, so He is different from all the weak pagan gods, and because of His great works with His people, they ought to remember Him and thank Him. This establishes their faith, and develops their love for Him, and then He gives them new blessings, and they live always in joy, reassured, because their God is strong and firm for ever, not only in this generation, that is, the lifetime they spend on the earth, but also in the coming generation, which is eternal life.

entries.section: (3) The blessed ... and the corruption of the idols

paragraphs.text: For the LORD will judge His people, and He will have compassion on His servants.

1- God judges the wicked of His people for their sins, since He is just, and disciplines them that they may return to Him. But if they repent He has compassion on them, and blesses them and compensates them for what is past, as He disciplined His people in the captivity, then supported them and blessed them and brought them back from the captivity.
2- God judges the wicked of His people that they may repent, and has compassion on His servants who believe in Him and keep His commandments, and keeps them from all evil.

entries.section: (3) The blessed ... and the corruption of the idols

paragraphs.text: The idols of the Gentiles are silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, but they speak not; eyes have they, but they
see not; they have ears, but they hear not; neither is there any breath in their mouths. They that make them are like unto them, and so is every one that trusts in them.

These verses are found in (Ps 115:4-6, 8), and this psalm is in this same book, and they have already been explained, so may the reader refer to them. In summary of the explanation, the idols, that is, the pagan gods, are statues made by people with their hands, and they are unable to speak or see or hear or breathe; they are lifeless statues in the form of a man or an animal, and they are cursed and a dwelling for demons, and likewise their makers are wicked, cursed, and tools in the hand of Satan, that is, they lack the ability to speak and see ... what is meant is spiritual speech and insight; their makers are alive in body, dead in spirit, and have no eternal life.

entries.section: (3) The blessed ... and the corruption of the idols

paragraphs.text: Bless the LORD, O house of Israel; bless the LORD, O house of Aaron; bless the LORD, O house of Levi; you that fear the LORD, bless the LORD.

1- The psalm closes with a call to bless the Lord and glorify Him, calling first all the people of God, then the priests, the leaders of the service, and after them the Levites, the servants of the temple, and finally those who fear the Lord, that is, the righteous and the just; so all the classes of the people praise God.

2- He mentions these different classes, and calls them to praise, because each class differs from the other in praising God, and God in His love accepts all spiritual levels. In addition, He singles out the priests and Levites because they are an example to the people. As for those who fear the Lord, it is a call to them to increase their praise and blessing of God, since they have loved righteousness and godliness.

3- There is a resemblance between these two verses and Psalm 115 (vv. 9-11); in Psalm 115 He calls these classes to trust in God, and here He calls them to bless God. These two verses also resemble Psalm 118 (vv. 2-4), in which He calls them to thank God.

entries.section: (3) The blessed ... and the corruption of the idols

paragraphs.text: Blessed be the LORD out of Zion, who dwells at Jerusalem. Alleluia.

1- God is blessed from Zion, that is, from His holy temple, for from the temple many praises ascend, more than ascend in the houses of the believers. And those who enter the temple express their blessing of God by offering many sacrifices and prayers.

2- God is blessed in the midst of His people Israel, because He dwells among them. And this moves the hearts of all the people to reassurance and joy and pride, and finally praise; indeed it is a call to constant praise, because God dwells always in their midst. And he expresses this praise when he ends the psalm with the word Alleluia.

God dwells in your heart because you receive His Body and Blood, indeed He is united with you; does this not call you to glorify Him and to constant prayers to God from your heart and your tongue, whether by repeating the psalms or the hymns, or the Jesus Prayer?
Why do we thank God?
“Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good, for His mercy endures for ever” (v. 1). Introduction:

1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms, that is, those whose writer's name is not known in their title. But there is an opinion that its writer is David, on the evidence that he said of God, “for His mercy endures for ever,” when he moved the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:41). Then his son Solomon repeated it after him at the dedication of the temple (2 Chr 5:13). And after them Ezra prayed it on the day of the rebuilding of the second temple (Ezra 3:11).
2- This psalm is one of the most important psalms of thanksgiving to God and is called the Great Hallel, that is, the great rejoicing, together with its companion, the previous psalm.
3- This psalm is liturgical; it was chanted daily in the praise of God, in addition to the New Year and the feast of the Passover.
4- The manner of repeating this psalm was in different forms:
a- Repetition by all together.

b- One group repeats the first part of every quarter (verse), which is the part whose words differ from the other quarters, and the other group repeats the repeated part, which is “Alleluia, for His mercy endures for ever.”
c- One chanter says the different part of the verse, and the company of chanters repeats the repeated part.
5- This psalm suits everyone who loves God and wishes to praise Him and glorify Him, so he stands firm in his faith, and his joy increases, and even his delight in life.
6- This psalm is repeated in the Church daily and is called the Second Hos, that is, the Second Praise.

7- This psalm was chanted in the Old Testament and also in the early Church; the history of the Church in the fourth century tells us that Pope Athanasius the Apostolic was in the church chanting this psalm with the people when soldiers attacked to arrest him by order of the king, and in his calm he signaled to all to continue the praise in their loud voice, so the soldiers stopped before this powerful celebration, and he withdrew quietly through the back doors, and they could not arrest him.
8- The repetition of the last part of every verse 26 times in this psalm is not a vain repetition, but is because of:
a- The greatness of God's mercy, which has no limit, and the mind cannot grasp its extent.
b- To establish in the heart thanksgiving to God for His mercies, so that man's attachment to God increases.
c- To repel all the attacks of the devil with doubt and murmuring.
9- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
O give thanks unto the LORD, for He is good, for His mercy endures for ever.

1- The writer of the psalm calls all the believers in the whole world, throughout the generations, to give thanks to God because He is good, and it is His nature to do good with all His creatures, and especially those who believe in Him, so He supports them in their weakness and rescues them from their enemies and satisfies them with His good things.

2- The writer of the psalm reminds those who praise that God's mercy is not only on the earth, as appears from this psalm, but extends for ever in the Kingdom of Heaven with gifts and blessings that surpass the mind, which the tongue cannot express.
O give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy endures for ever. O give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy endures for ever.

1- The writer of the psalm calls the whole world to thank and give thanks to God, the God of gods. What is meant by gods is everyone whose strength and authority people feel, whether of men such as kings and rulers (Ps 82:6; Jn 10:34) or those who claim to be gods, which are the idols (Dan 2:47); He is above all power and authority, and He alone is the true God, able to show mercy on the earth and for ever.

2- Thanks is also offered to God because He is Lord of lords, and what is meant by lords is all the great creatures in heaven, that is, the great ranks of angels who have authority; God is also their Creator and their Lord, that is, their master and father, and He alone is able to show mercy on the earth and in heaven.

God's good things toward you are many, so it is natural for you to thank Him for them. And when you become accustomed to thanksgiving every day, God will open your spiritual eyes, and you will see and discover His works, His care, and His love for you more clearly, and your joy will increase.

To Him who alone does great wonders, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him that by wisdom made the heavens, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him that stretched out the earth above the waters, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him that made great lights, for His mercy endures for ever. The sun to rule by day, for His mercy endures for ever. The moon and stars to rule by night, for His mercy endures for ever.

1- God alone is the Creator, and He made everything of the creatures great and small, and here he recounts a group of His great works, which are the heaven and the earth, the sun, the moon and the stars, as examples of His creatures, and from their creation the extent of His greatness appears. The psalm calls them wonders because God's power and His plans appear in them, which surpass the human mind, and by this the psalm protects the person chanting from deviating after any pagan gods, all of which are worthless, because God alone is able to create.

2- The heavens and the creatures in them, that is, the angels, are above man's comprehension, and he knows only a little about them. All of these God created by understanding, that is, by wisdom that surpasses the mind.

3- God's wonderful work in spreading the earth upon the waters, as the oceans surround it on every side. For the earth, although it turns on itself and around the sun, is firm, to give stability to the life of man.

4- God also created the sun to declare the hours of the day on the earth, because the earth turns once on itself every day, so it is lit by the light of the sun for about half the day, or more, while the other half, which is called night, it is lit by the light of the moon and the stars. Therefore the sun rules and arranges the hours of the day, and the moon and stars rule and arrange the hours of the night. All this by the arrangement of the great Creator, God alone.
5- All that is mentioned in these verses is mentioned in the Book of Genesis in the order of the days of creation (Gen 1:6-18).

If you meditate on nature you will feel the greatness of God who created everything for your sake, so you glorify Him and thank Him at the same time for His love for you, and your heart is reassured, because God, who is able to do everything, loves you and protects you.
3- Thanksgiving to the victorious Savior (vv. 10-26:)

To Him that smote Egypt in their firstborn, for His mercy endures for ever. And brought out Israel from among them, for His mercy endures for ever. With a strong hand and with a stretched out arm, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him who divided the Red Sea into parts, for His mercy endures for ever. And made Israel to pass through the midst of it, for His mercy endures for ever. But overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red Sea, for His mercy endures for ever.

1- After God showed His work in which He is alone, which is creation, he speaks here of His rescue of His people the children of Israel from the slavery of Egypt. And here appears His making men and angels share with Him in His great works, to the end of the chapter; for God loves His creatures and encourages them, and even ascribes to them some of His glories.

2- He refers here to His wonders in Egypt for the rescue of His people, which are the ten plagues, and he concentrates on the tenth plague, which is the killing of the firstborn of the Egyptians, because of which Pharaoh yielded and permitted the children of Israel to go out of Egypt, though this yielding was temporary, because he returned in the hardness of his heart and went out after them to bring them back again to slavery, so God destroyed him.

3- God rescued His people from Pharaoh by dividing the Red Sea into parts, that is, sections, and we understand from the Holy Bible that He opened a way in the Red Sea (the Sea of Suph). The waters were on both sides like a wall on the right and on the left, and this is a wonderful work the like of which had not been heard before. And when Pharaoh dared to follow the children of Israel, God drowned them in the Red Sea after His people were saved and went out to the wilderness of Sinai.

4- The crossing of the Red Sea signifies Baptism, and the rod of Moses with which he struck the sea signifies the Cross. And by the children of Israel crossing the Red Sea they were rid of the slavery of Pharaoh, who signifies Satan. And the drowning of Pharaoh and his soldiers signifies the death of the old man, that is, the nature inclined to evil, in the waters of Baptism.

5- God's power was not only in dividing the Red Sea, but also in supporting His children, for He gave them courage to cross through the water to the other shore, that is, the wilderness of Sinai. And the pillar of fire protected them from behind and separated them from Pharaoh and his soldiers.

To Him who led His people through the wilderness, for His mercy endures for ever. To Him who smote great kings, for His mercy endures for ever. And slew famous kings, for His mercy endures for ever. Sihon king of the Amorites, for His mercy endures for ever. And Og the king of Bashan, for His mercy endures for ever. And gave their land for an heritage, for His mercy endures for ever. Even an heritage unto Israel His servant, for His mercy endures for ever.

1- The psalm tells us in these verses of God's care for His people in the wilderness of Sinai, and He brought them into the land of Canaan; He Himself was their leader, and walked with them in the wilderness forty years, and He led them by the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, and God sustained them with food and drink, and kept them from their enemies such as Amalek, until He brought them to the east of the land of Canaan.

2- On the way of the children of Israel to Canaan they met great kings and killed them by the power of God, and he mentions among them as examples Sihon and Og, who were distinguished by strength and the fortification of their cities and their wealth, and they are the ones who opposed the children of Israel during their crossing. These kings signify Satan who opposes God's children, and God gives them victory over him.

3- God gave the land of the pagan kings to the children of Israel, to be an inheritance for them. What is meant by the land is the souls that worship paganism, which believed in Christ in the fullness of time and became the people of God, that is, the Christians; and what is also meant is the places of the demons who fell from heaven, which are received by the human beings who believe in Christ, and so become an everlasting possession for them in the Kingdom of Heaven.
Who remembered us in our low estate, for His mercy endures for ever. And has redeemed us from our enemies, for His mercy endures for ever.

God's fatherhood and tenderness appear in His feeling for His people, whom Pharaoh humiliated and enslaved and forced to work cruelly, so they cried out to God in humility, asking His help, and He intervened and rescued them and brought them out of Egypt by the hand of Moses. The one who humiliates man is Satan and sin, but repentance and prayer rescue man from every affliction.
Who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy endures for ever.

The psalm closes with thanks to God who feeds all people, Jews and Gentiles, and also the righteous and the wicked. He cares for all, to establish the righteous in their righteousness, and to call the wicked in His love to repentance and faith in Him. Indeed He also feeds the animals and birds and plants and trees, for He is the source of life for all His living creatures.
O give thanks to the God of heaven, for His mercy endures for ever.

And at the end he calls everyone to thank the God of heaven, so as to lift their eyes to their eternal future, that they may live with God in His fear, and believe in Him and keep His commandments, and so His mercies toward them increase all their days.

Lift your eyes, my brother, toward heaven every morning, that you may walk this day in a manner worthy of the heavenly ones, and so enjoy God's care and fellowship, and prepare for the Kingdom of Heaven with energy and zeal.
The longing of the captives for Jerusalem. “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down ...” (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its writer: there is more than one opinion:
a- It is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is not known, because the name of the writer is not mentioned in the title of the psalm.
b- It is David, as is found in the title of the psalm in the Septuagint translation; he wrote it in the spirit of prophecy about the Babylonian captivity and its end.

c- It is written in the title of the Septuagint translation “Of David, for Jeremiah,” that is, David wrote it for Jeremiah to repeat it at the destruction of Babylon. Some see that its writer is Jeremiah himself, who lived at the time of the Babylonian captivity and its end.
d- It is one of the Levites of the captivity who returned to Jerusalem in the first return with Zerubbabel.
2- When was it written? There is also more than one opinion:
a- The days of David if the writer is David, and he wrote in the spirit of prophecy about the events of the captivity and the destruction of Babylon.
b- It was written during the Babylonian captivity, and the last part of the psalm (vv. 7-9) was written in the spirit of prophecy about what would happen to Babylon of destruction.
c- It was written a short time after the return from captivity.
3- This psalm suits everyone who feels his exile in the world and his longing for the heavenly Jerusalem. It also suits every penitent who rejects the slavery of sin and longs for life with Christ.
4- This psalm can be considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it prophesies about Christ in the last verse.
5- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, to lift our longings to the Kingdom of Heaven.
By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down; yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.

1- These are the feelings of the captives in Babylon, who sat on the banks of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and all the canals branching from them. They remembered Jerusalem and the temple of God, and wept for the loss of worship in the temple. Although their appearance was restful on the banks of the rivers, their sorrow of heart was great, for the loss of the most important thing, which is being with God and worshiping Him, especially since Babylon signifies evil throughout the history of the Holy Bible, because of its being filled with many lusts, and that from the days of the tower of Babel (Gen 11:9) to the end of the Holy Bible in the Book of Revelation (Rev 17:1-6).

2- Sitting on the rivers, that is, their banks, signifies those attached to the world, but they are better than those who went down into the rivers to swim in them, who signify those immersed in lusts.

3- Perhaps those sitting on the rivers who remembered the temple also remembered their brethren the captives, who forgot Jerusalem and were occupied with trade and building houses and left God, indeed entered into the worship of idols, so they wept for them, asking God to awaken them to return to Him.
We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst of it.

Willows: trees widespread in Syria that grow along watercourses, and they are shade trees, that is, they have leaves and many branches, and have no fruit, and their leaves are pyramid-shaped and their edges are serrated like a saw.

1- The captives sat in the shade of the willow trees on the rivers of Babylon, and hung their harps on these trees. Although they had brought them out of Judea because of their attachment to singing to God, they could not praise in a foreign land, and their slavery to Babylon made them aware of their bondage, so they hung up the harps because of their lack of desire to praise away from the temple, of which they were deprived, and they did not break the harps because of their hope of returning to Jerusalem, that is, Zion.
2- The willow is a tree without fruit, so it signifies the person without spiritual fruits, who is unable to praise God, and one who is in the slavery of sin, his tongue is not loosed in praise.
For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song, and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, “Sing us one of the songs of Zion.”

1- The captives were in sorrow and weeping because of their distance from Jerusalem, and the Babylonians asked them to sing the songs of Zion, famous for their beautiful melodies, and the captives were very astonished, and felt that they could not sing in a foreign land, because the worship of God by singing is offered only in the temple of Jerusalem. In addition, their souls were in sorrow, and utterly far from delighting in beautiful melodies, and their whole feeling was longing to return to Jerusalem.
2- The penitent who grieves over his sins finds it hard to take delight in the joys of the world and its lusts, for weeping over his sins and rejecting evil suit him.

3- The Babylonians who enslaved the children of Israel and tormented them humiliated them when they asked them, while they were in sorrow and weeping, to sing songs of joy, but this humiliation increased the captives' longings for Jerusalem to offer worship there, as appears from the following verses (vv. 4-6).

Take care to examine yourself every day to repent of your sins and to discover the sources of evil that made you fall, and keep away from them. And when you offer repentance before God and confess your sins before the priest you receive peace, and an inclination to a new beginning with God.
How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?
1- The captives could not sing to God in a foreign land, because the songs of worship are offered only in the temple of Jerusalem.

2- Singing in Babylon refers to offering holy things and speaking of them in the council of mockers, or before those who do not appreciate their value; we ought not to cast holy things and pearls before any stranger, for he does not understand them, and may despise them for his lack of understanding.

3- Jerusalem signifies the deep spiritual life, and the foreign land signifies distance from God. And one who is far from God cannot praise Him, even if he has the instruments of praise such as harps, that is, even if his voice is beautiful and his ability to perform songs is outstanding, yet he does not feel the feelings of praise to God, so his praises are a superficial outward performance, and do not reach God.
If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget! Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, if I remember you not, if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy!

1- The captive says that if he forgets Jerusalem his right hand will forget, that is, his hand will be unable to play the musical instrument, and also if his tongue does not repeat what expresses his love for Jerusalem, his tongue will be unable to speak ordinarily with people, and therefore cannot sing to take delight in melodies with worldly delight. And this shows the extent of his heart's attachment to Jerusalem and the worship of God in His temple, so he cannot be occupied with the lusts of the world and its pleasures.

2- Although the captive, as a man, has what gladdens him of the material things of the world, that is, food and clothing and possessions, his joy in God and His worship rises very far above the joys of the world; his joy in God is greater than everything, and his whole heart is occupied with God.

Remember with every morning the words of Christ, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” so that you give yourself a great opportunity for prayer and being with God, and remember Him also during your many works and preoccupations.
Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who said, “Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation of it.”

1- The captive felt in his weakness and humiliation that he had no hope but God, so he lifted his eyes to Him, asking Him to deal with those who torment him. He did not mention Babylon only, but asked still more for Edom, who are the neighbors of the Jews living south of their land, and they are the descendants of Esau, that is, relatives of the Jews.

These were in intense enmity with the children of Israel, and gloated over them at the attack of Babylon on them, and during their demolition of Jerusalem and its walls they were encouraging the Babylonians to demolish the walls, until the foundation was torn up so that Jerusalem would be utterly ruined, its temple and its palaces and its walls.

2- Edom signifies the demons who rejoice and fight the righteous, and want to destroy them completely, and remove their foundation, which is Christ, from their hearts. And Edom means red; therefore it signifies Satan, the shedder of blood.
O daughter of Babylon, who are to be destroyed, happy shall he be that rewards you as you have served us!

1- Here he calls on Edom, which helped Babylon in seizing the Jews and selling them as slaves during the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem. And he calls her the daughter of Babylon, for she is her daughter in evil, and he asks God to declare His justice, so that Edom receives her recompense, so that the righteous may stand firm in their faith, and the wicked repent, and not be dazzled by the power of evil; it is not gloating on the part of the Jews, but holding fast to divine justice.

2- The spiritual man calls on his wretched soul, the daughter of Babylon in evil, which made him fall into sin and took him far from God, and he repays it with fasting and spiritual striving. And as it took him far from God, he repays it with the same recompense, that is, he brings it back forcefully to God in repentance, that it may live with Him anew.
Happy shall he be that takes and dashes your little ones against the rock!

1- The writer of the psalm continues his words about Edom, and blesses those whom God used to punish Edom, who are Abishai the commander of the army in the days of David, who threw the Edomites from a high rock in the Valley of Salt, and they perished (1 Chr 18:12). And also King Amaziah killed 10,000 of the Edomites and took another 10,000 of them and threw them from the top of Selah, and they fell and were broken (2 Chr 25:11, 12).

2- The children of the Edomites signify the sins of God's children who repent, so they dash their lusts and evils against the rock, who is Christ, that they may be broken and removed from them, and they live in purity by the power of Christ the Savior.

Do not keep company with the wicked, or walk in their way, lest you be defiled and fall into their sins, but cut off your relationship with them firmly, whatever the cost, and hasten to repentance, for your Christ awaits you to purify you, and you will live in purity and peace with Him.
Thanksgiving to God for His fatherhood to David. “I will praise You with my whole heart; before the gods I will sing praises to You” (v. 1). Introduction:

1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears in the title of the psalm in the Hebrew text that is in our hands. It is noticed that in the Septuagint translation the title mentions “Of Haggai and Zechariah” or “Of Zechariah” after the name of David. This means that Haggai and Zechariah used to repeat this psalm after the return from captivity, but the meaning of this is that the writer is David. And the words of this psalm resemble the psalms of David.
2- When was it written? After David's great victories over the surrounding enemies, that is, it was in the last part of David's life.
3- This psalm expresses David's deep feelings toward God, and his experiences of God's power in afflictions.
4- This psalm suits everyone who loves God, or thanks Him for His gifts, so his faith increases and is established during afflictions.

5- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms that speak clearly of the Incarnation of the Word, which is the greatest declaration and manifestation of God to people, to make Himself known to them and save them from their sins.
6- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Compline, to encourage us to thank God for His works with us all day long, and especially in distress.
I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee.

1- David thanks God not only with his tongue but with all his feelings, that is, from his heart, and praises Him at all times, even in the midst of troubles, especially since God accepted him in spite of his sins and weakness and brought him into His presence, so that he stood before Him giving thanks. This also means that there is nothing in David's heart but God, since he praises Him with his whole heart. He had already lived out the words of Christ, who declared, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart" (Mt 22:37).

2- David sings with joy before the gods, that is, the angels, as the Septuagint translation mentions. David rose above earthly things to heavenly things and stood before God, who is surrounded by the angels, who give thanks to God and praise Him continually. Among the angels he imitates them, leaves aside earthly concerns, and occupies himself with heaven and its spirituality. When he feels that he is among the angels, he not only rises up to them, but they also condescend and share the praise with him. For this reason the Church is called the house of the angels, and many angels and saints have appeared and shared the praise with those on earth, in many apparitions. He also sings before the gods, that is, the kings, the rulers of the world. He bears witness to God boldly everywhere, even before the great ones of the world.

3- By the gods may be meant the pagans and their gods. David boldly gives thanks to God before the pagan nations with their gods, which are not gods but mere idols. He praises the true God, who is God, and gives Him thanks with all his heart.
I will worship toward thy holy temple, and praise thy name for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name.

1- David praises God for His mercy, because He accepted him and forgave him his many sins, and he also thanks Him for His truth, because God showed the truth by rescuing him from the hand of Saul and Absalom, rescuing him also from the hand of his enemies and giving him victory over them. He declares his thanks and his submission to God by worshipping in His holy temple, meaning the tabernacle of meeting before the ark of the covenant, especially after David fell into his great sins, repented of them, was forgiven by God, and was permitted by Him to worship before His temple.

2- David's thanks to God for His mercy and truth is a type of our thanks for His redemption of us on the Cross, in which mercy and truth met: mercy in taking away our sins, and truth in satisfying divine justice through the death of Christ on our behalf.

3- God magnified His word above all His name. The name of God means His person; that is, the God known in the Old Testament to His people declared Himself with a great declaration in His commandments and His law, which He gave to Moses, and then His greatness increased as He declared Himself in His Incarnation and redemption. Although God was hidden and humbled in the form of human flesh, it is the greatest declaration that we see God walking among us in perfection as an example for us, then taking up our sins on the Cross, and after this rising from the dead by the power of His divinity. By this Christ was exalted above every name in heaven and on earth when He declared His divinity by His Resurrection (Phil 2:9).
In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul.

1- David declares his daily experience with God, that He answers his requests. This of course gladdens him and reassures him. And not only this, but God encourages him with a divine power within him, so that he may move, bear all responsibilities and succeed, and God also guides him in all his circumstances, whether to rise up and fight or to withdraw and flee.

2- God's answer to David is a type of His answer to the human race by His Incarnation in the fullness of time and by His giving of the Holy Spirit as a permanent gift dwelling in the new man, giving him strength for life with God and for service, however great his weakness, as happened with the Apostles, to whom He gave strength to endure and courage to face every situation and to preach everywhere (Acts 5:41).

How beautiful it is to feel heaven while you pray, and the presence of God and His angels who praise Him, so that you rise above every sin by repentance, cast off the cares of the world, and your heart is drawn to the person of God, so that you praise Him and enjoy being in His hands.

entries.section: (2) The Most High, who loves the humble

paragraphs.text: All the kings of the earth shall praise thee, O LORD, when they hear the words of thy mouth.

1- When the kings of the earth praise God, this means that they have heard His word and believed in Him; this is a prophecy of the entry of the Gentiles into the faith. The kings of the earth are the kings of the pagan nations, and this is a prophecy of the spread of Christianity throughout the whole earth.

2- The kings of the earth are all the spiritual believers who have controlled themselves against the lusts of the earth, and God reigns over their hearts; they have heard His commandments, kept them and lived by them, and so they were then able to praise Him.

entries.section: (2) The Most High, who loves the humble

paragraphs.text: Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the LORD: for great is the glory of the LORD.

Those who praise will sing in the ways of the Lord, that is, His commandments, because they have kept them, and they have worked in their hearts and appeared in beautiful praises to God. They have even felt the greatness and glory of God and so humbled themselves before Him, whatever their position; and the more they repent, the more their humility grows and their praise rises.

entries.section: (2) The Most High, who loves the humble

paragraphs.text: Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off.

1- Despite the perfection of God's virtues, and although He is higher than all men and angels, His heart is full of love, so He is tender toward the humble, while the proud He keeps far from Him, for they do not love God but themselves. The humble person feels his need of God and loves Him, so God pours out His mercies and blessings upon him. The proud person, however, deprives himself of God's gifts.

2- The humble one is David, who loves God and feels His loftiness, so God sees him, condescends to him and embraces him with His blessings. But David's proud enemies, such as Saul and his servants, God keeps far from Him because of their pride.

Humility is the shortest way to the heart of God; by it you obtain all your requests, and His mercies are poured out upon you beyond what you ask or think. Be sure that your sins do not hinder you from enjoying God as long as you repent of them. God loves the weak, supports them and has compassion on them, and for this reason He blessed them, saying, "Blessed are the poor in spirit." [3] The one who delivers from troubles (vv. 7, 8):

entries.section: (2) The Most High, who loves the humble

paragraphs.text: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me.

1- One who believes in God and praises Him is not disturbed by troubles, for God is able to give him a peaceful and happy life despite the troubles around him. It is not necessary that God remove the trouble, but He gives His children a life full of joy in the midst of troubles (Jn 16:33).
2- If the enemies rise up in anger to harm me, they cannot, because Your right hand, O Lord, saves me from their plots and their evil, as God saved David from the hands of Saul and Absalom.

3- The right hand of God is a type of the incarnate Christ, who saved us from the wrath of the devil, who accuses us and wants to destroy us, and by His Cross He not only saves us but gives us life, even in the midst of troubles.
Our life on earth is the trouble from which we are delivered, if we live heavenly lives on earth.

4- One who lives with his eyes toward heaven is not distressed by the troubles of the earth, for he sees the vastness of God's love and lives heavenly by the Spirit, so that he rejoices at all times while he is on earth, the earth of troubles.

entries.section: (2) The Most High, who loves the humble

paragraphs.text: The LORD will plead for me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands.

1- David concludes the psalm by declaring his faith and the secret of his peace of mind, which is God's protection of him, who repels from him all the attacks of enemies and protects him if he walks in the midst of them.

2- David also trusts that God's mercy is what keeps him throughout his life, for He forgives his sins and pours out His blessings upon him. This mercy continues with him on the day of judgment, so that God does not condemn him, because of his faith and repentance, and God's mercy toward him grows greater in the blessings of eternity.

3- David's peace is built on his trust in God, who protects him and continues in His protection of him. Even if men forsake him and become enemies as well, God cannot forsake him, even if the whole world stands against him, for God is with him, as happened with St. Athanasius the Apostolic.

How beautiful is peace of mind in the hands of God! Rely on Him and accept His will in your life, even if it seems difficult, because He is able to bring you through in peace in the midst of sufferings and to make your heart rejoice at all times.

The Psalm The Psalm The One Hundred and Thirty-Ninth The Eighty-Ninth God's perfect knowledge For the choir director. Of David. A psalm: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me" (v. 1). Introduction
1- Its author: the prophet David, as the title of this psalm states.
2- Many commentators consider this psalm the crown of the psalms, because it declares David's practical spiritual experience of God and speaks about it in detail throughout the psalm.
3- This psalm suits the one who prays, who loves God, wants to live in His embrace, and rejects evil.
4- The psalm calls us to examine ourselves and review ourselves in the light of God's word and commandments (v. 23).
5- This psalm speaks in detail about the attributes of God, His knowledge of hidden things, His presence everywhere, and His authority over everything.
6- The psalmist rebukes the wicked and calls them to repent quickly, because persisting in evil will inevitably lead them to destruction (vv. 19, 20).
7- There is a similarity between this psalm and the Book of Job (Job 10).
8- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.
Compassest (dharayta): spread out or scattered.
Lying down (marbad): the place where animals rest, and what is meant is my place of rest.

1- David declares to God, as he speaks with Him in private conversation: You, O God, know everything about me by complete examination and scrutiny, like one who winnows grain to separate it from the chaff. You know the good and the evil that is in me and in all my inclinations, and not only my deeds and my words; You know my character; You know me in my rest and in my distress, and You even know what I intend to do or say. You see from afar all that is in me, and You do not need to associate with me as men do in order to know me, because You are my Creator, and You have complete knowledge of all that is in me.

2- These verses are a type of the voice of Christ in the flesh in His converse with the Father, and since the two are of one essence, the Father knows all that is in the Son and knows His love for mankind, how He humbled Himself in His Incarnation, and how He would suffer and bear all the evil of humanity on His shoulders when He is crucified and dies for the sake of redemption.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me.

You know everything about me, O Lord: what has passed in my life, recently or long ago, and what will happen in the future. You also know where I go, what I will succeed in or fail at, what I will grow in spiritually and what I am unable to do. Your hand is upon me, protecting me and keeping evil away from me as long as I seek You. You are the Controller of all; to You I flee for refuge, and I trust in Your hand that protects me. And if I think of evil, You declare to me Your fear so that I repent. I rest and am at peace in Your hand; even if You allow troubles to come upon me, they are for my benefit and to protect me from many evils.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.

You, O Lord, know everything about me, while I can know only a little about You, because You are unlimited and I am limited. You are wonderful; I cannot contain You, but You contain me, and You make Yourself known to me as much as I can bear, and Your knowledge of everything about me is beyond my understanding and is wonderful in my eyes.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me.
1- David shows that he cannot flee from God, even if he turns in any direction in the world, for God is present and sees him and is able to take hold of him and do two things with him:

a - He guides him and brings him back to Himself and to the spiritual life with Him, however much he has been occupied with other things or has gone far away on a wrong path. This shows God's love, which gladdens the heart of man.
b - He restrains him by His justice and judges him, and this produces the fear of God within the heart, so that it makes him keep away from evil and remember always that God is before him.
2- God appears in His Holy Trinity in (v. 7): "Thy spirit," that is, the Holy Spirit, and "thy presence," that is, the incarnate Son, while the Father is the One whom David addresses.

3- The vertical direction appears in (v. 8) in ascending to heaven, the place of the righteous, or making one's bed in Hades, that is, lying in the grave and in death. This is what David imagined: by rising up to heaven, or going down below, he would find God, who is everywhere, to glorify the righteous in heaven and to judge the wicked in Hades. On the other hand, if he goes horizontally with the beginning of the morning, to reach the uttermost parts of the earth, God is present everywhere. The vertical direction and the horizontal direction are a type of the Cross on which Christ was crucified to save all, everyone who believes in Him in every one of the four directions, for He is the Savior of all humanity.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me. Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee.
Shall cover me (taghshani): shall envelop me.

1- A man may feel that he is in darkness where no one sees him, so that he may do evil in the darkness of the night, but he forgets that God is light and lights up the night with His light; it is He who created the sun to give light to the day, and the moon and stars to give light to the night, and He is the searcher of hearts and reins. So even if the wicked man hides himself in the darkness of the night, God sees all his deeds, his thoughts and the feelings of his heart.

2- If the children of God walk in the darkness of the night, let them not fear evil, because God lights up their lives and keeps them from their enemies the demons and from every temptation. If sins attack them to darken their thoughts, God warns them by His light so that they reject all evil, and if they fall into the darkness of sin, God pricks them by His Holy Spirit so that they hasten to repentance.

3- "The night shineth as the day." If darkness is the nature of the night, and at the same time God's nature is light and brightness, so also the dark temptation appears harsh and difficult to a person.
But with God it is bright, and for the benefit and good of the person, and He makes it bright and comforting to him, that is, He turns feelings of distress into rest and peace, and even joy.
4- "The night shineth as the day" is a prophecy of the Resurrection of Christ, the true Light, who rose from the darkness of the tomb in the light of His great glory.

5- "The night is light about me" means the turning of elements into the opposite of their nature: the night is dark and the day is bright, but the night shines, just as God made the fire gentle for the three young men although it burned the Babylonians who threw the three young men into the fire (Dan 3:27).

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb. I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.

1- God possessed my reins, that is, He possessed my feelings, because above the kidney lies the adrenal gland, which is responsible for a person's emotions. What is meant is that God possessed me wholly, with all my abilities and affections, and it is He who made me, as a craftsman makes a woven fabric, and formed me gradually in my mother's womb. By this, God is the One who knows everything about me, and He contains me and leads me in the way of righteousness if I walk with Him.

2- The making of man is distinguished from the rest of creation in his body and spirit. This calls for thanksgiving and glorifying of God, and indeed every person is distinguished from other human beings, which shows God's special love for every person. This gives a person confidence and strength because of God's care for him personally.

3- The works of God the Creator in me and in the rest of creatures are beyond my mind, but by faith my soul understands this wonder that God has made. And as knowledge advances, it discovers something of God's wonderful works in the creation of man and of the rest of creatures.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth. Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.

1- God formed in His mind an image of man; that is, in secret man was in the thought of God, and this from eternity. At the proper time He created him with precision, so that each bone of man, however small, had a number with God, that is, it was known and counted. And because God created man from dust, he says, "curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth." God formed the members of man, which were in God's book, that is, written in His mind, and He even knows their past, present and future. So everything is known to God from eternity, and all that will happen to him. All this shows God's love and care, which surpass the mind; there is no one who cares like Him, not even man cares for himself as God cares for him.

2- God sees man with his shortcomings and rejoices in him as he grows and matures, and this gives hope to every person who is weak and lacking in understanding and maturity, for God loves him, accepts him and makes him grow until he is perfected.

entries.section: (1) The One who knows all and is present everywhere

paragraphs.text: How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them! If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee.

1- The thoughts of God, His plans and His love for His creation are so many that they cannot be counted, because God is unlimited, and His love and care for man are unlimited; how great is the sum of them, and they are more than the sand. This makes a person thank God at all times, and it is not possible to comprehend the preciousness and greatness of God's thoughts, but a person believes in God's infinite love for him.

2- God loves man before he is born, so when a person awakes, that is, is born, he finds God with him, caring for him. And if a person sleeps every day and awakes, he finds God's care surrounding him in his sleep and in his waking.
And if a person neglects himself or his spiritual life, then is roused by the action of the Holy Spirit of God, he finds God's love with him always.

Look at God's love and care for you from the time you were born until now, so that your heart may be at peace, and you may thank Him, trust in your soul that relies on God, go forth in works of love for God and people, and gladden God at all times.

Surely thou wilt slay the wicked, O God: depart from me therefore, ye bloody men. For they speak against thee wickedly, and thine enemies take thy name in vain. Do not I hate them, O LORD, that hate thee? and am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee? I hate them with perfect hatred:
I count them mine enemies.
Grieved (amqut): I hate intensely.

Since David loved God, he also loved the good and lived in it, and consequently could no longer bear evil, and was distressed by the wicked because of their evils. Although he wishes for their repentance and salvation, why does David hate them?
1- He hates their evil because it is against God, and they are God's enemies.
2- Because the wicked are deceivers who pretend to piety but cling to evil, so they deceive themselves and may deceive others.
3- David fears that he may be affected by their evil, even partially, and stumble and fall into one of the evils they do.
4- David was moved and utterly hated the wicked's contempt for the lives of the righteous and their killing of them.

5- David was also distressed by the wicked's abuse and their killing of others morally, that is, they directed to them hard words that a person cannot bear, so David was moved because of the humiliation of the righteous.
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: and see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.

After David showed his rejection of evil, he draws near to God with humility, asking God to search him and to test his thoughts, lest there be any evil within him, or any negligence however small, so that God may cleanse him from it. The wicked way is anything that has no benefit and does not bring a person nearer to God, but on the contrary, with time, a person may fall into great evils. This shows David's carefulness and his concern for his purity, and also his concern for his eternal life, for he does not want to be hindered by any evil, and so we are assured that he did not reject evil out of pride, but out of aversion to evil and love for righteousness. He loves the wicked and hates their evil, which he mentioned in (v. 21), and this hatred is not considered a wicked way but is the love of God and purity of heart toward the wicked, for he wishes for their repentance.

Be careful in your relationships, and in the places where you sit, so that you keep away from sources of evil; this will help you toward a life of righteousness and a growing relationship of love with God.
God who delivers from evil For the choir director. Of David. A psalm: "Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states.
2- When was it written? When David was driven from the presence of King Saul.
3- This psalm suits everyone who suffers from the wicked and asks for God's deliverance.

4- There is a similarity between this psalm and the three psalms that follow it, all of which show the suffering of the righteous man and his request for deliverance from God, and it is also similar to Psalms 58 and 64.
5- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man; which imagine mischiefs in their heart; continually are they gathered together for war.

1- David asks God to deliver him from the wicked and the unjust, especially since they may not show their evil at first, or may be hypocrites who show the opposite of what is within them, but they certainly think evil in their hearts. This evil appears in wronging others and fighting them, so David asks God to deliver him before the evil happens. This shows David's need and humility, in addition to the evil surrounding him and his need for help from God, and it certainly shows his strong faith in the power of God.

2- The wicked are the demons and all who follow them among men. These are selfish people who think only of themselves and wrong others, but they unite only in evil, gathering to fight the righteous and wrong them, yet the power of God is able to deliver the righteous, even if all the demons gather against them.
They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. Selah.
Adder (al-ufu'an): the male of the venomous snake.
Poison (hummah): the venom of a snake or scorpion.

1- David likens these wicked people in their cunning and evil to the serpent, which keeps its venom, so they keep the venom under their tongues and lips; that is, the tongues of these wicked people are harsh and sharp and want to kill whoever meets them. The Apostle Paul repeated this verse to show the evil of the wicked (Rom 3:13).
2- These wicked people whose tongues kill others are the heretics and the malicious servants who proclaim any teachings foreign to the mind of God and of the Church.

3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause, so that the psalmist may reflect on this psalm, guard against the wicked, and ask for God's help. The word Selah is repeated three times in this psalm. It appeared often in the first part of the Psalms, but in the last part, in which we now are, this is the first time.

Keep me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the violent man; who have purposed to overthrow my goings. The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah. Overthrow my goings: they make me fall into a stumbling, that is, they make me fall into sin and keep me away from God.
Gins (ashrak): plural of sharak, which is a trap or snare.

1- Here he appeals to God in a supplicating prayer to deliver him from the wicked and violent man who think of making him fall, using all cunning and malice, which he likens to the cunning of the hunter who uses snares, cords, nets and traps. This shows the variety of the warfare of the devil and of the wicked who surround David, since Saul made various attempts to seize David and destroy him, but God delivered him from his hand.
2- Nets and snares are set beside the way; if the righteous man walks in the way of God, nothing makes him stumble, but if he turns aside from the way, he falls into the hand of Satan.

3- The Way is Christ, as He said of Himself (Jn 14:6), and He is humble and wants His children to be humble like Him. But the demons are the proud, so if the righteous walk humbly in the way of God, the demons are unable to fight them.
4- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for reflection on the importance of prayer, which delivers us from all the snares of the demons.
Hold fast to God's commandments, and remain in the Church and her sacraments with humility, and Satan will be unable to fight you.
I said unto the LORD, Thou art my God: hear the voice of my supplications, O LORD. O GOD the Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle.

1- Before the various snares of the demons David was not disturbed, but looked to God and felt his boldness before Him, so he said to Him, You are my God. He made supplication to Him, that is, he asked Him with humility, and he even attributed power to Him, saying to Him, the strength of my salvation. All this made him calm and encouraged, and increased his clinging to God.

2- He thanked God, who covered him in the day of battle. The covering here is the protection of his head from the arrows of enemies; that is, God became to him like a helmet protecting him from the wars of the wicked, and consequently David advanced and was victorious over the enemies, because God protects him; that is, David recalled his experience with God by thanking Him, so he was reassured and became strong. The helmet of salvation is affirmed to us by the Apostle Paul (1 Thess 5:8). And God covered His people in the wilderness of Sinai with the pillar of cloud, that is, He protected them from the scorching sun in the wilderness, as He now protects us from the temptations of the devil.
Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; further not his wicked device; lest they exalt themselves. Selah.

1- David asks God not to give the wicked man his desire, that is, the destruction of David, but to bring to nothing his evil purposes of harming the righteous, and to show the emptiness of his pride and exaltation and his hatred of the righteous. By this He gives the wicked man an opportunity to review himself and repent, and at the same time He confirms the faith of the righteous in God.
2- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for reflection on the emptiness of evil and the power of God that brings his evil to nothing, and this through prayer.
As for the head of those that compass me about, let the mischief of their own lips cover them.

1- The wicked spoke with deceitful and false lips in order to destroy the righteous man, but God intervened and turned their evils upon their own heads. The misery they wished with their lips for the righteous man turned back upon them and harmed them. Thus the venom under their lips mentioned in (v. 3) appeared upon their heads; that is, God openly showed their cunning and evil before the people. This is what happened with Saul, who pursued David, for he fell twice into David's hand, but David forgave him; and the brothers of Joseph sold him as a slave, and they became slaves to him; and Absalom tried to kill his father David and rose against him with a great army, and Absalom died a shameful death.
2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom Satan rose up, and He was nailed to the Cross and died, and by His death He paid the debt on our behalf and bound Satan.

Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again. Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him.
Deep pits (ghamarat): much deep water.

David continues his explanation of what will happen to the wicked, saying that fire will fall upon them from heaven and they will perish, as happened to the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, and likewise to the murmurers who followed Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Num 16:32), and this fire that burns them leads them to the eternal fire. And he describes what happens to them as being drowned in water and perishing, as happened to Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, and as happened to the wicked in the Flood. All this happens to the wicked man of harsh tongue and to the unjust man, whose injustice leads him and makes him fall into destruction.
I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor. Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence.

1- If the wicked, as appeared in the preceding verses, will suffer pains resulting from their evils, being tormented as by fire and drowning waters, then on the contrary God, the Controller of all, cares for the poor and the afflicted, that is, the humble who have relied on Him, and He gives them just judgments, that is, He rewards them with peace in their hearts, so that they praise God and dwell in His presence, that is, they enjoy His company and rejoice; all this on earth.

2- If the end of the wicked is eternal torment, then God the just Judge executes a just judgment for the poor and afflicted, and rewards them with the Kingdom of Heaven, where they continue their praise and thanksgiving to God forever, and enjoy sitting in His hands in His Kingdom.

Look at the glories that God has prepared for you so that you may endure the sufferings of the earth, and do not be dazzled by the temporary success of the wicked, for it will come upon their own heads. Only hold fast to your faith and know that God supports you and will never leave you.
The Lord keeps and delivers His children "LORD, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee" v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states.
2- When it was written: during Saul's pursuit of David.
3- It suits every person who wants to live with God and keep away from evil, who faces tests and temptations, and who is preparing for his eternity.
4- This psalm is liturgical; it was prayed in the evening at the offering of the evening burnt offering.
5- It is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, because at the end of the day a person reviews himself and asks God to keep him from evil and deliver him.

entries.section: (1) A cry to be kept from evil

paragraphs.text: LORD, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee.
1- David cries to God and asks Him to hear him attentively, and even to hasten to his help, and this shows:
a - his severe distress, and his urgent need of God's intervention.
b - David's boldness before God, and his sonship to Him, so he says, make haste and give ear.
c - his continuing to cry out, and consequently his constant need that God hear him. This is what happens in the life of believers in the Old Testament and in the Church of the New Testament.

2- Crying out means prayer not only with the lips, but with the mind and all the feelings of the heart, and sometimes the cry is from within a person and is not accompanied by words from outside, as Moses did when he was before the Red Sea with Pharaoh's army behind him (Ex 14:15).

entries.section: (1) A cry to be kept from evil

paragraphs.text: Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.

1- David offers his prayer and wishes that it be like the incense that burns before God, giving off a sweet fragrance that pleases God. And he likens the lifting up of his hands to the evening sacrifice, which is the burnt offering that the Jews offered every evening on the bronze altar to please God. The hands always signify works, and lifting them before God means offering the good works that David did throughout the day, and he offers them to God.

2- He mentioned incense before the sacrifice, because incense is offered in the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, while the sacrifice is offered on the bronze altar outside the Holy Place. The evening sacrifice is burned entirely before God, so that God may smell a sweet savor, and likewise the incense is burned entirely before the Holy of Holies to satisfy divine justice.

3- Incense is placed on burning coals so that it burns and gives off its sweet fragrance; so also the heart, if it is kindled with the love of God, is inclined to give and sacrifice in order to please God, and its prayers are fervent and rise quickly to heaven.

4- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who offered Himself at evening time on the Cross, and lifted His hands nailed to the Cross, and died for us; He is the burnt offering offered by the High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, He offered Himself on the Cross, and ascended as the fragrance of incense, and His good Father smelled it at evening time on Golgotha (the Sunday Midnight Praise).

5- In the Church of the New Testament the priests offer the true sacrifice on the altar, which is the Body and Blood of the Lord. But all believers are also priests in the general sense of the priesthood, and not in the particular sense of the priest, the steward of God for the completion of the sacraments, for every believer offers his prayers, his praises, his service and all his good works as a sacrifice and incense before God every day.

entries.section: (1) A cry to be kept from evil

paragraphs.text: Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.
