1- The tongue is a very important member of the body, for from it comes the speech that expresses the person, whether in good things or in evil; therefore David asks God to keep his mouth and his lips, which stand before the tongue like a door, for they represent the control of the tongue, and the Apostle James affirms the seriousness of the tongue (Jas 3).

2- David asks for a watch for his mouth, that is, an external warning so that the tongue may not err, such as the occurrence of some event that stops speech, or the interruption of another person... He also asks for the keeping of his words, that is, an inner control from the person, so that he is careful and does not speak evil.

3- David asks God for a watch and keeping of his tongue, so that he may speak what pleases God and be silent from evil speech, in addition to his silence for the sake of conversation with God, and so that he may listen to others and understand them, and ask for God's guidance and speak what he is permitted.

entries.section: (1) A cry to be kept from evil

paragraphs.text: Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties.

1- After asking for the control of his tongue, David moves on to the source of blessings or of evil, which is the inner heart, and he asks God not to allow his heart to incline to evil, but to incline always to good, and consequently his tongue will speak good things. For what is asked is not merely the control of the tongue while the heart is left to incline to evil, because the evil would then be suppressed within the person and would later burst out and appear; rather what is asked is the purifying of the heart, so that good speech comes out spontaneously (Lk 6:45).

2- David also asked that his heart not persist in evil and support its evil with corrupt thoughts, and that he not agree with the workers of iniquity in their evils, nor mingle with them so as to sit in their assemblies and eat of their dainties, that is, their delicious foods that could arouse his desires, in addition to their evil words and deeds; what is meant is excessive mingling with the wicked, and consequently being affected by their conduct. In sum, he asks for his restraint with the wicked and for his not sharing in their evil deeds.

Remember that your goal in life is to be with God and praise Him, and to offer your life as a sacrifice of love for God and care for others. Do not share with the wicked in their evils, but keep your heart and your tongue in purity for God's sake.

entries.section: (2) The salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked

paragraphs.text: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities.
Shall not break (la ya'ba): does not refuse, that is, accepts.

1- So that David may keep the purity of his heart and tongue, he accepts not only the direct chastisements of God, but also the chastisements and blows of the righteous, that is, the just. He considers this a mercy to him, for it keeps him from evil.

And the reproofs of the righteous prick him so that he does not fall into sin, and he even regards them as oil that anoints his head; for the ancients, when receiving their guests at banquets, used to anoint their heads with perfumed oil, so David regards the reproof of the righteous as perfumed oil on his head, which he accepts, because it will heal him of his sins, just as he accepted the reproof of Nathan the prophet for his sin; and out of David's love for the righteous he prays for them if calamities come upon them.

2- In the Septuagint translation it says, "let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head"; on the other hand, David does not accept the oil with which sinners anoint him, since the sinners' care for him is hypocrisy. David prays that God may deliver him from their calamities, that is, their hypocrisy, and he prays that the sinners may take heed and repent and return to God, as he used to pray for his son Absalom, the hypocrite who sought to take the kingdom from him and drive him out.

entries.section: (2) The salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked

paragraphs.text: When their judges are overthrown in stony places, they shall hear my words; for they are sweet.

1- The overthrow of the judges of the wicked, that is, their great ones, from the rock: this is what happened to Saul and the great ones of his army, for they were killed in the war with the Philistines. But David did not kill Saul when he fell into his hands, but reproached him with sweet words that carried love and submission, and also after Saul's death he cared for his offspring, Mephibosheth, and this love is regarded as sweet words.

2- The judges, that is, the great ones of the proud wicked, were overthrown because of their pride, while the humble, such as David, God granted sweet words, and he was exalted and sat on the throne of the kingdom.

3- This verse applies to Christ, when the great ones of the world, of the Jews and the Gentiles, rose up against Him and crucified Him, and fell into a great sin, and collided with the Rock, who is Christ, and Satan himself, who moved them, was bound by Christ with the Cross. This verse also applies to the heretics who resisted the teachings of Christ, so they fell under His judgment, and in the Septuagint translation it says that these great ones "were swallowed up near the rock," that is, Christ drew them and others, and they believed in Him, as happened with Saul of Tarsus, that is, the Apostle Paul.

entries.section: (2) The salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked

paragraphs.text: Our bones are scattered at the grave's mouth, as when one cutteth and cleaveth wood upon the earth.

David likens what happened to him and his men when they fled before Saul to the earth that is scattered when the farmer breaks up the ground with the plow; so also the souls of David's men were scattered at the mouth of Hades, that is, they came near to death from the severity of the hunger, thirst and exhaustion they suffered as a result of running and fleeing. He expresses the severe suffering he endured in the face of Saul's pursuit.

entries.section: (2) The salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked

paragraphs.text: But mine eyes are unto thee, O GOD the Lord: in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute. Keep me from the snare which they have laid for me, and the gins of the workers of iniquity. Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape. Gins (ashrak): plural of sharak, that is, a snare or trap.

1- David concludes the psalm with hope in God, to whom he lifted his eyes with humility, so that He may protect him from the wicked, and not leave his soul destitute, that is, leave him to perish, or that his soul be emptied of faith and courage, so that he becomes weak and goes away from God.

2- He also asks God to keep him from the snares of the wicked that seek his destruction, but on the contrary let the sinners fall into their own nets and snares, while David alone escapes completely, and this is what happened, for Saul and his sons died in the war, and David escaped and reigned over the children of Israel.

3- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane to the Father, and the Jews set up the Cross for Him as a snare and killed Him, but He escaped by His Resurrection, while they perished in AD 70 at the hand of Titus the Roman, who destroyed Jerusalem and killed a vast number of Jews.

If you humble yourself and accept God's chastisement and the reproof of those who love you, God will deliver you from every evil, whatever the plots of the wicked, and they will come upon their own heads, while you remain in your peace.
God who delivers from trouble A maschil of David, when he was in the cave: "A prayer"
"I cried unto the LORD with my voice; with my voice unto the LORD did I make my supplication" (v. 1) Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.

2- When was it written? When David was pursued by King Saul and was in the cave, which was either the cave of Adullam (1 Sam 22) or the cave of Engedi (1 Sam 24). In both cases he was fleeing before Saul, and with David were a number of people persecuted by Saul and fleeing in the wilderness.

3- There is a similarity between this psalm and Ps 57, for in both David was in the cave, as appears from their titles. But in (Ps 57) David appears strong and victorious by the power of God, while in this psalm David appears weak, taking refuge in God to deliver him from his enemies.
4- This psalm suits every one who prays who suffers troubles and persecutions, yet has faith and hope in God, so he prays to Him and asks for His help.
5- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of Christ persecuted by the Jews even to death.
6- This psalm is also a prophecy about the Church persecuted throughout the ages, yet her refuge and portion is God.

7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, where a person takes refuge in God at the end of the day and casts all his problems and troubles with confidence upon God, so that he may sleep in rest and have hope for the days that follow.

entries.section: (1) A cry to escape from the snare

paragraphs.text: I cried unto the LORD with my voice; with my voice unto the LORD did I make my supplication. I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.

1- David shows the extent of his suffering by four verbs: I cried, I made supplication, I poured out, and I shewed; in every way he shows his pains. The cry is from the depth of the heart. Supplication means humility, need and persistence. The pouring out shows the bringing forth of all that is within him, and this is evidence of his purity and his repentance from all evil. The showing means declaring his trouble in all its aspects, for he loves God, trusts in Him, and has the boldness of sonship, so he speaks with God with all his feelings.

2- The variety of David's prayer with God shows his persistence in prayer at all times and in every form. And it shows that God is his only refuge, and consequently his attachment to God, and by this he obtains peace, even in the midst of severe trouble.

entries.section: (1) A cry to escape from the snare

paragraphs.text: When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. In the way wherein I walked have they privily laid a snare for me.
Overwhelmed (a'yat): wearied.

1- David was greatly wearied by the weight of the trouble upon him, that is, his spirit was wearied within him. But he continued walking in virtue and righteousness, although the wicked laid a snare for him to make him fall, so that he would be hindered from righteousness and go away from God. But the trouble led him to fervent prayer and crying out to God. This shows David's love for God, for he did not murmur or show any evil in his heart.

2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane, with His sweat falling like drops of blood, as He declared to the Father the weight of the sufferings and asked that the cup of suffering pass from Him (Lk 22:44), yet at the same time He was submissive to the divine will, which was the accomplishment of redemption. In His humanity He suffers pains, but He is submissive to the divinity within Him, and He still walked in righteousness although Satan rose up against Him and the Jews tried to ensnare Him with a word, and even to kill Him.

entries.section: (1) A cry to escape from the snare

paragraphs.text: I looked on my right hand, and beheld, but there was no man that would know me: refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul.
Refuge (al-manas): shelter or escape.

1- When the trouble increased upon David he looked on his right hand, that is, to his friends, servants, followers and loved ones, and found no one to help him, for all were occupied with other things than him, and he found no one to take refuge in and lean on.

All acted as though they did not know him, and consequently he found no one to ask about him or care to bring him out of the trouble, and there remained only God, to whom he lifted his eyes toward heaven, and he cried out and made supplication to Him.

2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, from whom all His loved ones were scattered, even His disciples closest to Him, who slept and left Him to pray alone in the Garden, and fled when He was arrested, and no one supported Him in His trials, torture and crucifixion because of their weakness.

Hasten to God in every trouble, for He feels for you and loves you and is able to deliver you, and if God wills He will direct people to help you, and by this you live steadily and are not disturbed by anything that passes over you.
I cried unto thee, O LORD: I said, Thou art my refuge and my portion in the land of the living.

1- When people left David alone he found before him only God, so he cried out a second time and took refuge in Him, and found in Him the impregnable fortress that protects him with complete protection, even if he is alone and without a weapon or any earthly power.

2- David also discovered that the Lord alone is his portion after people left him, and He is his portion in the land of the living, that is, throughout his life and not only at the time of trouble, so he enjoyed fellowship with God and became peaceful and joyful despite the trouble. And he believed that the Lord would remain his portion in the coming land of the living, that is, eternal life, where there is the complete enjoyment of being with God.
Attend unto my cry; for I am brought very low: deliver me from my persecutors; for they are stronger than I.

1- David is still declaring his suffering to God, mentioning for the third time the word cry, and he begs God to take notice and attend to his cry, his plea being that he has been brought very low, that is, wearied greatly by the weight of the trouble upon him, but the useful thing is that he was brought low, that is, he humbled himself and clung to God, who has no helper but Him.

2- The second reason for which David asks for God's swift intervention is that those who persecute him are stronger and mightier than he, for they are the rulers of the world and have great power; Saul is the king, and with him is the whole army, but God is of course stronger than Saul and any other power, and this shows David's faith in God.
Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name: the righteous shall compass me about; for thou shalt deal bountifully with me.
Compass me about (yaktanifunani): surround me.

1- David finally asks God to bring him out of prison, that is, the trouble he is passing through, which is the pursuit of Saul, who wants to kill him. By the prison he also means the psychological distress he suffers as a result of the evil of Saul and those with him, in addition to the scattering of David's loved ones from him, so he asks for rest for his soul, so that he may continue to be occupied with his goal, which is praising God and thanking Him, since he sees no goal for his life except the love of God and the enjoyment of praising Him.
2- David also longs for his soul to be released from his body to rise to heaven and to live in continual praise to God in the Kingdom, where the saints surround him and praise God with him.

3- David sees with the eye of hope that God has delivered him from his trouble, so the righteous were confirmed in their faith, and surrounded him to rejoice with him at God's bountiful dealing with him. Thus he returns with all the believers to the worship of God before the house of the Lord, that is, the tabernacle of meeting.
May you thank God when He delivers you from any trouble or gives you a new gift, for this is the feeling of a son with his father, so that you rejoice and also gladden the heart of God.
God saves those who please Him "Hear my prayer, O LORD, give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me" v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.
2- When was it written? The title of this psalm in the Septuagint translation says that it is "of David, when his son was pursuing him," meaning Absalom.
3- This psalm is similar to the psalm before it, but the preceding psalm focuses on the leaving of David by his loved ones, while this psalm focuses on the evil of the enemies who surround him.

4- This psalm is the last of the seven penitential psalms, which are (Ps 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143). In this psalm there appears the joy of repentance and preparation for eternity, in addition to the remembrance of God's kindnesses, which stand over against man's sins.
5- This psalm suits every believer who passes through trouble and hastens to repentance, and obtains God's mercies, which strengthen his hope in eternal life.
6- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the feelings of Christ as He approached the Cross and the darkness of the tomb.
7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime, in which a person at the beginning of the day asks for God's help, remembers His kindnesses, and offers repentance for all his sins.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from enemies

paragraphs.text: Hear my prayer, O LORD, give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me, and in thy righteousness. And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified.

1- We note that the beginning of this psalm is like the beginning of the preceding psalm, where David lifts his prayers and supplications to God because he is in trouble and his enemies have risen against him, although he did not wrong his son Absalom, and so he asks for God's faithfulness and His promises to deliver those who believe in Him, so that He may deliver him from the hand of Absalom, who wants to kill him. This does not mean that David trusts in the perfection of his righteousness, or that he cannot bear that God should judge him, because it would reveal his weakness and sins, but he means that he did not sin against Absalom or the people, that they should rise against him and kill him.

2- David asks God to deal with him by His righteousness and faithfulness, but at the same time he is a sinner and cannot bear that God should judge him. The solution is Christ the Savior, in whom divine justice is fulfilled on the Cross, and by His mercy He delivers David and every wronged person who believes in God, in the Old and New Testaments.
3- The Litany of the Departed mentions that every person is a sinner even if his life on earth were one day; these words are taken from this psalm (v. 2).

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from enemies

paragraphs.text: For the enemy hath persecuted my soul; he hath smitten my life down to the ground; he hath made me to dwell in darkness, as those that have been long dead.

1- It shows the cruelty of Absalom, who persecuted his father and crushed his soul with grief when he rose up against him and gathered the army to kill him, so that David became like one dead in the darkness of the tomb, as happened to Adam and Eve when they were driven out of Paradise; this is what Satan did to them, and this is the feeling of every sinful person who has not completed his repentance and returned to God, or the repentant person's view of the period of his fall before he repented.

2- Christ bore the sufferings of the Cross and death for us, and Satan and all his followers among the wicked Jews persecuted Him, and humiliated Him by scourging and spitting, and all the sufferings of the Cross, until He died like one rejected, but He rose after this by the power of His divinity, to raise us up in Him.

3- If Christ suffered all these sufferings for us, let us not be troubled if trouble befalls us, and God permits Satan to persecute us and humiliate us and make us fall into the darkness of sin, but with God's help we rise from sin, repent, and recover our spiritual zeal.

entries.section: (1) A cry for deliverance from enemies

paragraphs.text: Therefore is my spirit overwhelmed within me; my heart within me is desolate. I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works;
I muse on the work of thy hands. I stretch forth my hands unto thee: my soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land. Selah.
Overwhelmed (a'yat): wearied.

1- David felt the weight of the trial upon him, until he was perplexed in finding a way out to deliverance, and here he returned to himself, and remembered God's works with him, and His works with His people, whom He delivered from the bondage of Egypt, brought out and sustained in the wilderness, and brought into the land of Canaan, which flows with milk and honey, so he thanked God and asked Him to deliver him, and even declared to Him his great need, and said that his soul had become like a dry land needing the divine water to water it; all this he said while stretching forth his hands in prayer.

2- Here appears the importance of knowing the works of God and remembering them at all times, especially in trouble, for it is what restored David's peace, confirmed his faith, and gave him a fervent prayer that delivered him from his enemies.

3- Stretching forth the hands does not mean only prayer, but also showing his need of God to quench his thirst, and it also means emptying himself of his own will, in addition to repentance and declaring complete inability to find a solution.

4- These verses apply to Christ, whose spirit was wearied as a man, and whose heart was perplexed by the many pressures and sufferings, for how could He who had no sin become sin for us, and He expressed the sufferings of the Cross approaching Him, while in the Garden of Gethsemane, by saying, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, and He stretched out His hands in fervent prayer, and His soul was in distress like a parched land, but He bore all this for our redemption.
5- This passage ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for reflection on the works of God and for prayer to Him, that He may deliver us, satisfy us and strengthen us.

When you face any trouble, remember what Christ bore for your sake, and that by accepting the trouble you share in Christ's sufferings, and remember the works of God in the Holy Bible so that your faith increases and you keep your peace.
Hear me speedily, O LORD: my spirit faileth: hide not thy face from me, lest I be like unto them that go down into the pit.
The pit (al-jubb): a deep hole, and it is a type of Hades and hell.

1- David calls to God, who is his only hope, and asks Him to hasten to his help and answer his request, because the trouble is severe and he cannot bear it, and his spirit is almost failing within him from the many threats and the intensity of grief. His asking God to hasten means his great need and his trust in God his deliverer.

2- He also asks God to look upon him with His shining face, for if He does not look upon him he will be like those who go down into the pit and die. The pit is also a type of eternal torment, and this means David's declaration of his attachment and hope in God's care for him. He considers fellowship with God to be life, and if he loses this fellowship he dies.
Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning; for in thee do I trust: cause me to know the way wherein I should walk; for I lift up my soul unto thee.
Morning (al-ghadah): early morning.

1- David begs God to pour out His mercies upon him, and would that this were soon, that is, in the early morning. The time of darkness has passed, which is the time of trouble that he likens to the darkness of the night, and he longs for the light of the morning. This is because he trusted in God, so his hope in God is firm and strong.

2- David also asks God to make him know the way of deliverance from his trouble, and he declares to God that he has lifted up his soul to Him, so he seeks Him alone and does not rely on earthly things or on any man.
3- The way that we need is Christ, and if we trust in Him, lift our hearts toward heaven and leave the lusts of the earth, it is easy for us to walk in the right faith in Christ our God.
Deliver me, O LORD, from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me.

When the enemies threatened David he took refuge in God to be fortified in Him, and asked Him to deliver him from these threats, for he suffers from the evil of the wicked, but he believes that God is a strong fortress. And if David had fled from God by falling into sin, now that he has repented he takes refuge in Him, and God protects him from his enemies.
Teach me to do thy will; for thou art my God: thy spirit is good; lead me into the land of uprightness.

1- David declares his allegiance and faith in God, for he says my God, so he is His follower, and he also seeks His good pleasure and will, and begs that God teach him how to please Him and do His will, because the word for good pleasure in Hebrew also means will. And learning how a person pleases God requires training and time. This means that David is ready to train and labor to please God his God. This shows his true love for God, and also his trust in the grace of God that will teach him.

2- He describes the Holy Spirit of God as good, and this confirms his faith in the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and this is against the heresy of Macedonius, which appeared in the fourth century and was condemned at the Council of Constantinople in AD 381.

3- He asks the Spirit of God to guide him and lead him to reach a level land, that is, an upright land in which there is no crookedness, meaning a life firm in God, and upright conduct by His commandments, and a level land free of dangers, that is, a life of peace in the hands of God. And after David's life on earth is completed he hopes for the land perfect in uprightness and truly level, which is the new earth, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

Quicken me, O LORD, for thy name's sake: for thy righteousness' sake bring my soul out of trouble. And of thy mercy cut off mine enemies, and destroy all them that afflict my soul: for I am thy servant.

1- David concludes the psalm, asking God to bring him out of the trouble he suffers and to give him life, because he is almost dying from the pressure of the trouble upon him. His hope for life is built on his faith in God and His holy name, which is able to give him life, and it is exalted above all the pagan gods known in the Old Testament, because God alone is the giver of life by His Holy Spirit.

2- David clings to God's righteousness, who promised to reward the righteous and punish the wicked, so David asks for God's righteousness and His promises to deliver him from his trouble, because he believes in Him and strives in the way of righteousness.

3- God's mercy, mingled with His righteousness, is manifested, that is, His mercy on His children who walk by His commandments, such as David, in cutting off his enemies and destroying those who afflict his soul, because David is submissive to God and to His commandments, and he declares to God that he is His servant. God's righteousness destroys the wicked as a punishment for them, and at the same time it is a mercy to the righteous, confirming them in faith and making them grow in every good work.

4- In Christ mercy and righteousness meet and are fulfilled, so these two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who bound Satan by His Cross, and at the same time gave salvation to those who believe in Him.

5- God's grace to the righteous appears in God's mercy that cuts off and destroys the wicked, but it requires of a person that he declare his submission to God and to His commandments, so he says that he is the servant of God. Grace together with spiritual striving gives a person salvation.

6- God's perfect mercy and perfect righteousness appear in eternity in the cutting off of the enemies and those who afflict the righteous, that is, He casts Satan and all his followers into eternal torment, and gives His righteous children everlasting joy in the Kingdom of Heaven.

Have a firm hope in God however much troubles rise against you, or you are wounded even in the house of your loved ones, for He is able to deliver you, keep you, comfort your heart and take away all your pains.
God delivers and blesses His people "Blessed be the LORD my rock, who teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight" v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.
2- When was it written? In the title of the psalm in the Septuagint translation there is "of David, against Goliath."

This means that it was written after his victory over Goliath. But in (v. 2) it mentions that God subdued his people under him, and this means that he had reigned over the children of Israel, and it mentions that God scattered his enemies (v. 6); from this it is concluded that David wrote the psalm after he became king and after his victories over the surrounding peoples, remembering his victory over Goliath.
3- This psalm is a psalm of thanksgiving to God, who gives us victory over our enemies the demons, and gives us many good things, and cares for us throughout our lives.
4- This psalm is a type of Christ, who triumphed over Satan, since David was a type of Christ.
5- It appears here that God is the One working in His children, to give them victory over their enemies the demons?
6- This psalm is classified as one of the psalms of battles, like Psalm 18, in which appears the power of God supporting His children.
7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
Blessed be the LORD my rock, who teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight.

1- David thanks the mighty God, who gave him strength in fighting against the enemies. And because God is firm and strong like the rock, He is able to make David firm and strong in the battles against his enemies.

2- God taught and trained David, so He gave him victory over a lion and a bear, and after this He gave him courage to triumph over Goliath, which qualified him for victory over all his enemies surrounding his country, so the kingdom expanded in his days, as God promised, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

3- God trained David for fighting so that he might defend himself and deliver his people from Goliath and the Philistines and all the enemies. By this training his faith in the mighty God who was with him was confirmed and he was filled with strength, and he triumphed over his sins and weaknesses.

4- Faith in God's power and obedience to Him make it easy for a person to learn from God victory over Satan gradually in the spiritual battles, so that the person grows and becomes strong, and even becomes firm and victorious always. This means that the cause of the strength and victory is God, who was with David and works in all who trust in Him.
My goodness, and my fortress; my high tower, and my deliverer; my shield, and he in whom I trust; who subdueth my people under me.
High tower (sarh): a lofty building, or a great tower.

Shield (mijanni): the mijann is the large shield, and the shield is an ancient defensive instrument that the soldier used; it is a piece of wood with a handle at the back into which he put his hand, and he moved it before his face and body to protect him from the arrows of enemies.

1- David describes God with many attributes: He is mercy, the refuge in which he takes shelter, and the high tower in which he fortifies himself, so that He delivers him from the hands of his enemies; He is the shield that protects him, and He is the one in whom he trusts, and who gives him strength and awe so that his people submit to him, and not only his enemies. He attributes every power in his life to God, who is the source of all blessings.

2- The people that submit to a person are his senses and all his abilities, his body and spirit, his mind and emotions; that is, God gives him a strong will that leads him in the way of righteousness and goodness, protects him from the demons and defends him, so that he lives at peace within God his strong fortress, and thanks Him every day for these great mercies.
(vv. 3, 4): LORD, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him! or the son of man, that thou makest account of him?
Man is like to a breath: his days are as a shadow that passeth away.

David marvels at God's concern for him, so he says that he is a weak man, and compares himself to a breath that a person breathes out, or the shadow of anything that passes with time. That is, he is something very small, so how does God care for him and think of him?

Here the divine knowledge means concern and care. And thinking means divine providence and care for all the needs of man. David marvels at God's humility and love in His concern for him and for every person.

Would that you, my brother, thank God every day for His care for you, for He is the source of every blessing in your life. So humble yourself before Him and before all His children, mankind, and your thanksgiving will increase, and God's gifts to you, and your inner joy.
Bow thy heavens, O LORD, and come down: touch the mountains, and they shall smoke. Cast forth lightning, and scatter them: shoot out thine arrows, and destroy them.
Bow (tati): condescend and bend down with humility.

1- David begs God to condescend from His heights to care for His children and deliver them from their enemies; as for the enemies, that is, the demons, however strong and great they are like mountains, He touches them with His power and they smoke, that is, they begin to burn. And He shines upon them with His mighty light, so they fear and are scattered and flee from before His face, and when they flee He directs His arrows at them and they are greatly troubled. All this shows David's faith in the mighty God, whom no one can resist, so the weakness of the enemies before Him appears.
David does not look at his weakness before the power of the enemies, but at the power of God that is with him, which is able to crush the enemies.

2- God's power appeared when He appeared to Moses and the people on the mountain, accompanied by smoke, fire, thunder, lightning and a thick cloud (Ex 19:16-19). These manifestations show the power of God and the weakness of man.
3- These two verses speak of the Incarnation of Christ, who condescended from His heights. Although He fills heaven and earth, He became incarnate, lived among us, died on the Cross, and bound Satan.
And Satan burned before Him like smoke, and fled and was troubled. The arrows are a type of the Apostles, who spread the teachings of Christ that caught souls.
Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children; whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.

1- David asks God, who is above all, on high, that is, in the heavens, to deliver him from the great waters, by which he means the enemies, who are strangers to him. And those who speak false words, and whose right hand is false, that is, their speech is against the truth and their deeds are wicked; these are the wicked and the heretics in every generation, and everyone who resists the truth.

2- The hand of God that was stretched out from on high is the incarnate Christ, who redeemed us from the great waters, that is, the demons who are strangers to us, and from their false speech and their vain deeds.
I will sing a new song unto thee, O God: upon a lyre of ten strings will I sing praises unto thee. It is he that giveth salvation unto kings: who delivereth David his servant from the hurtful sword.

1- When David saw God's delivering power for him he rejoiced, and praised God with a new song, because it is full of new joys on account of the experiences and wonderful divine works that happened to him. His song was accompanied by a musical instrument, the lyre of ten strings, which signifies the ten commandments that David believed in, and the senses of man and his inner abilities. And he sang giving thanks to God, who saves devout kings like him, however weak he is, so that He kept the hurtful sword away from him, by which he means the sword of the great Goliath, for David threw Goliath to the ground with a small stone, then cut off his head with his sword.

2- The new song is a type of the New Testament, and the ten strings are a type of the ten commandments. All the children of God in both Testaments sing with joy at His Incarnation and redemption; in the Old Testament they lived on hope and awaited the Messiah, and in the New Testament they saw the salvation offered on the Cross, so God's work in both Testaments is complete, because the whole Holy Bible speaks of Christ.

God, your God, is strong and able to deliver you from every evil, so take refuge in Him and do not fear Satan, his power and his wiles, for God will crush him and drive him away from you, so that you may continue your spiritual striving and enjoy fellowship with God.

Rid me, and deliver me from the hand of strange children, whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood: that our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; that our daughters may be as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace.

1- Here David shows the good things and blessings of God that He gives His children after delivering them from the hands of their strange enemies, and from all their false deeds. And these blessings are many: the first is that He gives them plants grown up in their youth, that is, they have spiritual and bodily strength, and continue to grow, so that they may afterward lead their families and defend them against every evil. As for the daughters, he likens them to corner stones polished in the temple of the Lord, and the corner stone is that which binds all the stones of the two walls, and by this he means that the daughter is the one who will become a mother and bind all the members of her family to one another in love and unity. And these pillars are polished, that is, refined, and he means that the daughter should have a good, refined upbringing, so that the family lives as a temple for the Lord and worships the Lord in holiness and purity. Strong sons and holy daughters full of love are the most precious gift that God gives His people.
That our garners may be full, affording all manner of store: that our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets:

1- The second blessing for the people of God is that their storehouses be full of different kinds of grain. This means that God blessed their farming, so it produced abundant crops, and they gathered them into their storehouses to satisfy them.
2- The storehouses of a person are his heart and mind, and God fills them with longing for Him, love of virtue, and every good thought and feeling toward God and people.

3- The third blessing is in livestock, specifically in sheep, that they be many, for they multiply abundantly until they fill the streets with their numbers, and they obtain their products of milk, meat and wool... The sheep are a type of spiritual possessions, that is, the many souls that they draw to the Lord.
That our oxen may be strong to labour; that there be no breaking in, nor going out; that there be no complaining in our streets.
Laden (muhammalah): carrying young in the womb.

1- The fourth blessing is in the cattle that God blesses, so they bear many young and are good cattle, and although they are desirable cattle, God keeps them from any breaking in, whether by predatory animals or by any attack of enemies, so they graze in the streets and the places around the houses in safety and peace. The laden cattle are a type of the spiritual blessings within a person, so that he is full of many graces.

2- The fifth blessing is the peace in which the people of God and all their possessions live, and no one troubles them. This is a type of God's protection of His children from the wars of the demons, so that they may live with Him and grow spiritually.
Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the LORD.

1- At the conclusion of the psalm David declares his blessing on the people of God, that is, how joyful and happy they are; not only because of material good things, but because their source is God, so the people enjoy fellowship with God who dwells in their midst, and thank Him at all times and praise Him.

God's blessings upon you are many, but the greatest blessing is God's dwelling within you, so enjoy speaking with Him, and rejoice in His presence within you, and you will taste the sweetness of the Kingdom while you are on earth.
Glorifying the greatness of the Lord A song of praise. Of David "I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever" v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.
2- This psalm is a praise of God, as appears from the title. And all its verses praise God.

3- This psalm and the psalms that follow it are psalms of praise, that is, from Psalm 145 to Psalm 150. The Book of Psalms ends with the praise of God, which is preparation for and entrance into eternity.

4- This psalm is arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, and each verse begins with one of the letters of the alphabet. And each verse consists of two parts, as will appear in the explanation of the psalm.

5- This psalm is liturgical, that is, it was prayed in the congregational Jewish worship. It is prayed twice in the day and once in the evening, that is, three times every day, to glorify God and praise Him.
6- The Divine Liturgy in the Church quotes from this psalm (v. 15), that is, it is prayed in the congregational worship in the New Testament.
7- This psalm begins with David's praise of God and ends with the praise of all creation to Him, for the psalm calls everyone to praise God.
8- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever. Every day will I bless thee; and I will praise thy name for ever and ever.

1- King David feels that God is the true King, and He is the King of kings; therefore he declares his submission to God in extolling Him, blessing Him and praising Him, and he even expresses his feeling continually every day, that is, throughout the days of his life, and indeed throughout the whole day, in his joys and his sorrows, in the time of rest and the time of trouble.

2- David feels a special relationship between himself and God, so he says my God, for he has the boldness of sonship and a strong love for God, and his continual praise continues forever. Having enjoyed praise on earth, he longs for continual praise after putting off the body, to rejoice forever with God. It is implicitly understood that whoever has not experienced praise on earth will not long for continual praise in heaven, or will have no share in the Kingdom of Heaven.

3- These two verses are read on the second day of the Feast of the Cross (18 Tut), because Christ reigned on the Cross; therefore we praise Him and bless Him because He is the Redeemer and Savior of mankind. It is understood from this that this psalm is liturgical in the Church, that is, it is used in the congregational worship.
Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
Unsearchable (istiqsa'): complete examination and investigation.
1- The praise of God is continual forever, because His greatness has no end; no man can search it out or reach its end.

2- When David magnifies God he lifts his eyes to heaven, so he clings to heavenly things and rises above earthly lusts, and humbles himself before God, whose infinite greatness he cannot fathom to its depths.

One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts. I will speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty, and of thy wondrous works. And men shall speak of the might of thy terrible acts: and I will declare thy greatness. They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness, and shall sing of thy righteousness.
I will speak (alhaj): I meditate and speak continually.
Utter (yubdun): make manifest.

The praise of God is from age to age, that is, from generation to generation, so it is continual throughout the generations, and even to the age to come, that is, in heaven, and that for many reasons, which are:
1- Your works: which are very many and appear in His creation, living and inanimate; man, animals and plants.
2- Your mighty acts: that is, Your great power, which is above every power in the world, which shattered the gods of Egypt, parted the Red Sea, and overcame all the gods of the pagan nations.
3- Your majesty and glory: praised by the heavenly and the earthly, and no man can bear to see it, as Moses felt when he pleaded to see God (Ex 33:20-23).

4- Your wondrous works: which appear in the order of Your creatures, whether in the body of man and his spirit, the arrangement of the system of the heavenly bodies, and the ecological balance between the various kinds of animals and the different plants.

5- Your terrible acts: God is very awesome and fearful, and this appeared on few occasions, because man could not bear it; it appeared to Moses and the people on the mountain with smoke and fire, the thick cloud, and the sound of the trumpet and thunder. And the fear of Him leads a person to leave sin and to live a pure life. And His terrible acts appear in many great works, such as the heavenly bodies, the wide sea, the thunders and lightnings.

6- Your greatness: which appears in the union of great awe with great tenderness, for although the angels cover their faces from the brightness of His glory, He at the same time cares for the smallest of His creatures, such as insects and small plants. He is perfection in everything.
7- Your goodness: that is, all good, who feeds all flesh and cares for all His creatures, and in Him is perfect purity, love and every virtue.

8- Your righteousness: You reject evil and are repelled by it, and despite Your great mercy, You are also great in Your righteousness. Righteousness and mercy were joined in Christ Jesus on the Cross.

How great and how sweet it is to meditate on the attributes of God and His many kindnesses, until the meditation turns into thanksgiving and praise that fills the heart with joy and spreads happiness in the whole atmosphere around it.
The LORD is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy. The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.

1- Although God is awesome, just and great, He is at the same time loving and merciful, and His love appears in His longsuffering and tenderness. God's mercy is mingled with all His works. When He is just and fearful and firm, He is also merciful, as He permitted the bondage of His people in Egypt, but brought them out with a great power. And as He permitted their humiliation in the age of the Judges because of their worship of idols, He had mercy on them when they cried to Him, and sent them judges who freed them from bondage.

2- The goodness of God and His mercy are over all men, righteous and wicked; His sun and His air and His gifts are for all, that they may know Him and live with Him, and He is good to all His creatures, feeding the wild beasts and the tame animals. He has mercy on and cares for the smallest of creatures.

All thy works shall praise thee, O LORD; and thy saints shall bless thee. They shall speak of the glory of thy kingdom, and talk of thy power; to make known to the sons of men his mighty acts, and the glorious majesty of his kingdom. Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations.

1- All the works of God, that is, His creatures, glorify Him through their submission to the divine order, so they walk in the order appointed for them, and this amazes men, so they praise God. As for the devout, they know God and utter His praise, so they enjoy fellowship with Him. And they speak of God's reign over all creatures, and praise Your great power.
2- As the devout praise by their words and deeds they proclaim to all men the greatness of God, which lasts throughout life, and even forever.
Your thanking God every day for His dealings with you is a quiet preaching of the great God, who gives blessings to all men. By this thanksgiving you quietly invite everyone to glorify God.

entries.section: (3) The mercy of the Lord to those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that be bowed down.
Upholdeth (a'id): supports.
Raiseth up (muqawwim): brings back to the straight way.

God's mercy appears in its first form, which is the support of those who fall, and of the bowed down, the repentant who return to God. God rejoices in the repentant, and is even tender toward those who do not repent, and warns them that perhaps they may repent. He is a tender Father who strives for the salvation of His children, and forgives them their falls if they repent.

entries.section: (3) The mercy of the Lord to those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing.

1- The second form of God's mercy is satisfying the needs of men, and indeed of all living creatures. He satisfies all, from the small insect to the predatory beasts, and above all man, the head of creation, and He gives man not only material satisfaction but also psychological, so that he is content and thankful to God, and above every satisfaction He gives spiritual satisfaction. He is satisfied with God's love the nearer he draws to Him.
2- We pray these verses in the Divine Liturgies in the Litany of the Airs of Heaven, the Waters and the Plants, and we also pray them at the end of the Second Hoos, which is (Ps 136).

entries.section: (3) The mercy of the Lord to those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: The LORD is righteous in all his ways, and merciful in all his works.

The third form of God's mercy is its association with righteousness. God's mercy is not for pampering man and spoiling him, but to lead him to righteousness and goodness. A person may need God's mercy to discipline him at times, or to withhold from him some of his desires, so that it may raise him up, and he may live in righteousness.

entries.section: (3) The mercy of the Lord to those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth. He will fulfil the desire of them that fear him: he also will hear their cry, and will save them.

1- The fourth form of God's mercy is His nearness to men, for He is not a God who exalts Himself and keeps away from His creation, but a loving Father who draws near to His children to give them His love.
2- Those who enjoy the feeling that God is near them are:
a - those who call upon Him in truth, that is, who make requests according to God's will, and He answers them.
b - they fear Him, so they walk uprightly and reject sin, and if they fall they hasten to repentance.

God is present everywhere, but everyone who draws near to Him feels His nearness, and calls upon Him in truth, and fears Him. And whoever draws near to God, God draws near to him and answers his requests. And whoever does God's will, God fulfils his desires and forgives his sins.

entries.section: (3) The mercy of the Lord to those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: The LORD preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy.

The fifth form of God's mercy is His preserving everyone who loves Him, so He keeps him from dangers and problems that exceed his ability, and brings him through in peace on the way of life. On the contrary, He is just, so He destroys all the wicked who trouble His children, and supports His children in all their steps.

entries.section: (3) The mercy of the Lord to those who fear Him

paragraphs.text: My mouth shall speak the praise of the LORD: and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever. He concludes the psalm with praising God with his understanding and heart, and by this praise he stirs the hearts of those who hear him, so God blesses them too, and thus the earth is filled with the praise of God.

Look at God's mercy upon you and meditate on it until it leads you to have mercy on those around you, so that you do not judge them or become angry with them, but find excuses for them, and if you can, pray for them and support them with your works of love, so that you draw their hearts to God.
Praise of God the Shepherd "Hallelujah. Praise the LORD, O my soul" v. 1 Introduction:
1- Its author: unknown, because this psalm has no title; it is one of the orphan psalms whose author is unknown, but there are two other opinions:
a - that its author is David.
b - there is a title in the Septuagint translation, "Prescribed with Hallelujah, of Haggai and Zechariah," so some see that the author is Haggai and Zechariah.
2- When was it written? According to what we mentioned about its author, there are two opinions:
a - the days of David.
b - after the return from captivity.

3- This psalm is among the Hallel psalms, which are the five psalms from (Ps 146 to Ps 150), and they are distinct from the Egyptian Hallel psalms (Ps 113-118) and from the two psalms of the Great Hallel (Ps 135, 136).
4- These Hallel psalms (Ps 146 to Ps 150) begin and end with the word Hallelujah, except (Ps 147), which begins with the word "Praise," which also means exultation.

5- There are some other psalms, apart from the Hallel psalms (Ps 146 to Ps 150), that begin and end with the word Hallelujah, and they are: Ps 106, Ps 113, Ps 135. (And there are other psalms that only begin with the word Hallelujah, and they are: Ps 111, Ps 112.) (And there are other psalms that only end with the word Hallelujah, and they are Ps 104, 105, 116, 117.)

6- This psalm and all the Hallel psalms are considered liturgical, for they were prayed after the return from captivity and were also prayed in the Jewish synagogues that spread in the land of Judea in the two centuries before the birth of Christ, and remained until the first century AD.
7- This psalm suits every believer who feels God's care for him in his needs and weaknesses, so he praises Him and thanks Him for His kindnesses.
8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, where a person thanks God and praises Him for His gifts throughout the day.
Alleluia. Praise the Lord, O my soul. While I live will I praise the Lord: I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being.
1- The psalmist calls himself to praise before he calls others to it, for the one who has experienced praise and loves it has words that are effective when he calls others.

2- The psalmist loved praise, so that he became accustomed to it, and came to praise throughout his life, as long as he is alive and present. And God supports him and encourages him, and encourages us all in the New Testament by His Holy Spirit continually.

Give yourself an opportunity to praise God in your prayer every day, by repeating a small portion of the Midnight Praise, or a psalm of thanksgiving, that you may taste a new sweetness in your sense of God during prayer.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

1- The psalmist makes clear the weakness of human beings, even if they are rulers and great men in the world, so that it is not possible to trust in them, because they are mortals subject to death and burial in the dust from which they were created.

2- Jeremiah emphasizes not trusting in human beings, saying: "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord" (Jer 17:5-75), and likewise (Isa 31:

1-3; 20:1-6.) For the material thoughts of a person, however great they may seem, can perish suddenly with the person's death, and the parable of the rich fool confirms the same meaning (Lk 12:16-21).
Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the Lord his God.

1- It is understood from the two preceding verses that God is the only One in whom one can trust; He is the true Helper and Support, and the only hope of the people who believe in Him, and therefore we praise Him at all times. And whoever becomes accustomed to praising God learns to trust in Him and in no one else.
2- The mention of the name of Jacob, who trusted in God, so that He blessed him and made him a great nation, which is the Jewish nation.
Do not be dazzled by the promises of people, and do not place your hope on words, for they are mortal human beings like you, but place your hope on God alone in everything.

Which made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all that therein is: which keepeth truth for ever. In this verse and the following verses the psalmist reviews the causes and reasons for trusting in the Lord, which are:

1- "Which made heaven, and earth, the sea": and He is eternal and everlasting, and these creatures are very vast when compared with the small human being, and this calls a person to trust in the Creator of all creation.

2- God's faithfulness in His promises, which continues throughout life and forever. But the promises of human beings are all shaky and not guaranteed, because they are subject to death, whereas God is constant, as proved by the fact that His vast creatures are constant, such as the heaven, the earth and the sea, and subject to the laws He set for them.
Which executeth judgment for the oppressed: which giveth food to the hungry. The Lord looseth the prisoners:
The psalm continues presenting the reasons for trusting in God, saying:

3- "Which executeth judgment for the oppressed:" By the oppressed is of course meant the one who has endured hardships without any fault of his own, so God shows their right, even if after a while, and blesses them and compensates them. For this He shows His tenderness and calls us to trust in Him.

4- "Which giveth food to the hungry:" For He feeds human beings and animals, even the smallest of them, namely the birds, and likewise the plants. He is a Father who feels for all His creatures, especially man, and above all this He cares for His children who trust in Him. And to His children who believe in Him He gives the greatest thing, which is spiritual food, that is, His Body and Blood, and nourishes them with His life-giving word.

5- "The Lord looseth the prisoners:" By the prisoners is meant every person who is confined and humiliated, for when he cries out to God, He rescues him and looses him, as happened with Lot and all the prisoners whom Chedorlaomer the king took (Gen 14:17). The prisoners are also the prisoners of sin, whom Christ set free by His redemption on the Cross.
The Lord openeth the eyes of the blind: the Lord raiseth them that are bowed down: the Lord loveth the righteous:
The psalm adds new reasons for trusting in God, which are:

6- "The Lord openeth the eyes of the blind:" God, who created the eyes, is able to heal them and give them light so that they see, as He opened the eyes of Tobit. But the matter is not limited to bodily eyes, but goes beyond them to spiritual eyes, for He grants insight and discernment to His children who trust in Him, such as the men of God in the Old Testament and the prophets. In the New Testament, Christ opened the eyes of many of the blind, and by the Holy Spirit gave enlightenment to the Apostles and the servants of the New Testament.

7- "The Lord raiseth them that are bowed down:" that is, He makes them upright and straight and strong. Those who are bowed down are all who fell under heavy pressures that made them unable to do their work or to continue their lives, like Judith and her people, who were exposed to death by thirst. In the New Testament, Christ healed the woman who had been bowed down by the devil for eighteen years (Lk 13:13).

8- "The Lord loveth the righteous:" they are the just who trust in Him, so He supported them and cared for them with His love, like the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And as Christ cared for His twelve disciples and the Apostles, and all His followers.
The Lord preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he turneth upside down.
And the psalm adds to the preceding reasons for trusting in God the following:

9- "The Lord preserveth the strangers:" The stranger is the person who has no settled place and does not find his needs, so He cares for him and blesses him, as He preserved Abraham in Egypt (Gen 12:17), and blessed Isaac in Gerar (Gen 26:12), and Jacob in Egypt (Gen 47:27).

10- "He relieveth the fatherless and widow": The fatherless is the one who has no father to care for him, and the widow is the one who has no husband to support her, so God took care of them, as He cared for the child Joash, whom Jehoiada the priest looked after and protected from the violence of Queen Athaliah until he sat on the throne (2 Kgs 11:17-21). And He blessed the widow of Zarephath of Sidon by Elijah's staying with her, and blessed the jar of oil and the barrel of meal throughout the famine (1 Kgs 17:14). And Christ had compassion on the widow of Nain and raised her son (Lk 7:11-15). And God cares for the fatherless and the widow in the spiritual sense, that is, those who have no strength or support, so God relieves them and supports them spiritually and in facing all the problems of life.

11- "The way of the wicked he turneth upside down:" God does not allow the ways of the wicked to be always successful, so He protects the righteous from them, and if He overturns their ways He gives them an opportunity to repent and return to Him, when they see their failure, as He showed Pharaoh his weakness by the ten plagues in the days of Moses, and as He showed the weakness of the pagan kings in the days of the Judges, and freed His people from under their authority, and as Christ bound Satan on the Cross; for the way of the wicked is Satan, just as the way of the righteous is Christ.

The Lord shall reign for ever, even thy God, O Zion, unto all generations. Alleluia. God the Shepherd of His children, as appeared in the preceding verses, reigns over their hearts and cares for them; not only in this age, that is, this generation, but in the coming generation, which is eternal life. And all aspects of God's care for human beings were manifested in Christ in the New Testament, as we indicated in the preceding verses. Therefore the children of God are reassured and trust in Him, and He supports them throughout their lives and forever.
In all your needs take refuge in God and trust in Him, confident of His love, and you will live reassured and will not be disturbed by the changes of the people around you.
Praising God who cares for His people: "Praise ye the Lord: for it is good to sing praises unto our God" (v. 1). Introduction:
1- Its author: unknown, since it has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms, but there are two other opinions:
a- David wrote it in the spirit of prophecy about the return from captivity and the building of Jerusalem and the temple.
b- In the Septuagint and Coptic versions it has the title "Ordained with Alleluia, for Haggai and Zechariah"
like the preceding psalm; that is, its author is Haggai or Zechariah.
2- When was it written? There are two opinions:
a- In the days of David.
b- After the return from captivity.
3- This psalm is one of the Hallel psalms, and it ends with the word Alleluia, and its beginning is the words "Praise ye", which resemble the word Alleluia.

4- In the Septuagint, that is, the Agpeya, this psalm contains two psalms, Ps 146 and Ps 147; that is, this psalm in the Septuagint consists of two psalms, while in this Hebrew version it is one psalm.
5- This psalm speaks about the return from captivity and the building of Jerusalem, which is a symbol of the Church of the New Testament.
6- This psalm suits every penitent who feels that God has turned the ruin within him caused by sin into a great and joyful spiritual building; therefore he praises God.

7- This psalm is liturgical, with the rest of the five Hallel psalms (Ps 146-150); it was prayed in the temple in the morning, and after the return from captivity, and likewise in the Jewish synagogues that were established about two centuries before the birth of Christ.

8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, and it includes, as we said, the last two psalms, where the worshiper thanks God for His care of him, and the acceptance of his repentance and his restoration as a living member in the Church.
Praise ye the Lord: for it is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely.

1- The psalmist calls the believers returning from captivity to Jerusalem to praise the Lord, because praising and singing psalms is good, for it lifts the soul to heavenly things and frees it from the bonds of earthly lusts.

2- Praise is also pleasant to the soul ("pleasant"), making it rejoice and enjoy. And on the other hand, it is fitting for the soul that believes in God and loves Him to express its love by praise and singing. But the soul that does not praise proclaims its neglect of God and the weakness of its love, especially if God has done a great work with it, such as gathering the dispersed Jews who were captives and bringing them back to their land to build the temple of the Lord and worship Him in it; and of course praise and thanksgiving are required.
The Lord doth build up Jerusalem: he gathereth together the outcasts of Israel. He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.

1- God's love appears in helping His children who returned from captivity to build their holy city Jerusalem. By this God gathered His people the children of Israel, who had been scattered in the lands of the world subject to Assyria and Babylon, and by this He heals the hearts of His people broken by humiliation and slavery, and binds up their broken souls, so that they are strengthened and become firm, and proudly glorify their God who rescued them and set them free, and favored them with the building of His temple and worship in it.

2- Christ the Redeemer built the Church of His Body by His death on the Cross, and gathered the Jews and the Gentiles who believed in Him, and united them in faith in Him, and healed their souls broken by the humiliation of sin, so they lifted up their heads in joy and glorification of Him.
He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names. Great is our Lord, and of great power: his understanding is infinite.

1- If God counts the vast and numberless stars and calls them by names, then His power is great and cannot be measured, nor can His understanding or knowledge be counted. If God is of such power and greatness, He is of course able to gather His scattered people and bring them back to Jerusalem and Judea to build the temple.
2- The stars are the pious and the saints who were broken under slavery, and God bound up their souls and supported them, so they praised Him and became saints by the power of God.

3- Christ is able to gather His children from the ends of the world, that they may believe in Him and become saints, that is, great stars, and to turn those who are far into those who are near, and opponents into apostles like Paul.
The Lord lifteth up the meek: he casteth the wicked down to the ground.

1- The meek are the children of Israel who were captives, and God lifted them up by bringing them back from captivity at the command of Cyrus the emperor, king of Media and Persia, to build their city Jerusalem and its holy temple. As for the wicked, they are the Babylonians who humiliated the people of God, so He casts them down to the ground and humbles them by means of Media and Persia. The same thing happened with Pharaoh of Egypt and his army, who were shattered by the ten plagues and drowned in the Red Sea, while the people of God He freed from the slavery of Egypt, and took them through the midst of the Red Sea, and provided for them in the wilderness of Sinai.
2- Christ humbled Himself and bound Satan the evil one, and raised up the Apostles, so they preached to the whole world, and cast down the opposing wicked, so they failed in resisting Christianity.

Thank God for the great works He has done with you throughout your life, and if you can, write them in a spiritual journal so that you do not forget them; all this establishes your faith and gladdens your heart.

entries.section: (2) God's care for His pious ones

paragraphs.text: Sing unto the Lord with thanksgiving; sing praise upon the harp unto our God:

1- After God favored His people with the return from captivity, it was natural for the psalm to call them to thank God, and even to accompany the thanksgiving with musical instruments, as an expression of intense joy and praise.
2- Praise is the highest and loftiest degree of prayer, because it is pure love for God without any request. And whoever loves God speaks to Him with the words that He loves, which is praise.

entries.section: (2) God's care for His pious ones

paragraphs.text: Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains. He giveth to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry.
What moves us to praise God is His care for all His creatures, which appears in:

1- "Who covereth the heaven with clouds:" God covers the high heavens with white cloud that gives a sense of mystery, yet God pours out rains from it upon the earth. So He covers the heavens with a beautiful sight, and satisfies man and the rest of creation by means of the rains.
And the cloud is a symbol of the saints, who are distinguished by spiritual radiance and pour out upon those around them an example and good teachings, as the rains come down from the cloud.

2- "Who prepareth rain for the earth": God does not leave the earth dry, especially the land far from the rivers, but satisfies it, and man, and the animals, and the plants upon it, with the rains that come down from heaven.
And so all creatures serve man: the rains come from heaven, and the earth bears the plants and animals.

3- "Who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains:" The mountains that appear dry and are hard to climb, when God sends rains upon them He makes grass grow on them, so their appearance becomes green and beautiful, and even sheep and cattle graze upon them, eat and are satisfied, and thank God. So the mountains that appear dry and barren God gives life, which is the grass, and the animals are fed. As God turns barren, parched souls into living, fruitful souls, which are even satisfied and serve those around them.

4- "He giveth to the beast his food": The beasts cannot speak, but they express their hunger with sounds that God hears, so He hastens to feed them with various plants. And you, whenever you humble yourself, become like a beast before God, as the psalm said (Ps 73), not only materially but spiritually as well.

5- "And to the young ravens which cry": God also feeds the young ravens that cry to Him, because when the raven's chicks come out of the eggs they are white, so he is afraid of them and their parents, the large ravens, are distressed, and fly far away and leave them. Then the chicks open their mouths and cry to God with weak voices, and He sends them large numbers of insects that are drawn toward the smell of their mouths, and they eat them, and the chicks grow, and the color of their feathers changes to black, so their parents the ravens become familiar with them and come to them to help them and care for them.

entries.section: (2) God's care for His pious ones

paragraphs.text: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man. The Lord taketh pleasure in his pious ones, in those that hope in his mercy.

God, whom we praise, rejoices in the humble who trust in Him and longs for their praise. He does not prefer the one who depends on the strength of military equipment, of which in ancient times the most important was the horse, and to it is added the bodily strength of the man, which appears in his legs able to run swiftly to attack and crush the enemies, but God takes pleasure in His pious ones who hope in His mercy with humility. For Satan calls human beings to depend on their strength and weapons and to leave God, and the remedy is the fear of God, forsaking sin, and humbling oneself before Him with many prayers, asking His mercy, and so we triumph over our enemies the demons however great their strength. For Solomon, who depended on the multitude of horses (2 Chr 9:25, 28), contrary to the Law (Deut 17:16), the kingdom was split after him; but Gideon, who feared God and depended on Him, triumphed over tens of thousands of enemies with three hundred men without weapons (Judg 7:7).

Do not be disturbed by the weakness of your resources, or the strength of those who attack you, because the power of God that is with you gives you victory over all the obstacles before you; walk in the fear of God and hope in His mercy, and you will receive all the blessings you need.

Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise thy God, O Zion. For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee. He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat. The bars of your gates: the posts of your gates, that is, the main boards of wood that make up the gates.
Your borders: your boundaries.
The finest of the wheat: the best kinds of wheat, full-bodied as if they were rich food.
1- From (v. 12) Psalm 147 begins in the Septuagint, and it is the last psalm of the prayer of Sleep.

2- For all the blessings mentioned above, the psalm calls Jerusalem, which is Zion, to praise the Lord her God, for He is a God special to her who loves her, because she is His holy city, and her inhabitants are His children, who worship Him in His great temple standing within Jerusalem.
3- The reasons for Jerusalem's praise of God are many, the most important being:

a- "He hath strengthened the bars of thy gates:" meaning that He made your gates strong and fortified, so they protect the believers dwelling within Jerusalem. And this proclaims the power of God who protects His children.

And the door is Christ, as He Himself declared (Jn 10:7). And the gates are also a symbol of a person's senses, for God strengthens them so that they become pure and clean, and everything that enters the person is pure.

b- "He hath blessed thy children within thee:" in that He multiplies the believing children, and also sanctifies them and fills them with His power. And the children are also a symbol of a person's senses and virtues, for God blesses the senses and multiplies the virtues.

c- "He maketh peace in thy borders": that is, God keeps the boundaries of the lands belonging to Jerusalem, which is the region of Judea, so its inhabitants live in peace, and He drives the enemies away from them, so Jerusalem and those in it are able to love God and praise Him.

d- "Filleth thee with the finest of the wheat:" God gives her material blessings and satisfying food, granting her the best kinds of wheat, so she eats and is satisfied abundantly, and this is from the grace of God, and not because of the quality of the land or the weather conditions. And the finest of the wheat is a symbol of the Body and Blood of Christ, which is the best spiritual food.
He sendeth forth his commandment upon earth: his word runneth very swiftly.

1- The word of God is His command to all His creation to serve man, and it is His commandments and His Law that were given to man to live by, and it is also His word on the lips of the prophets, and His living word in His pious men in the Old Testament, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

2- The word of God is Christ incarnate in the fullness of time, who gave salvation to mankind, and it is the word of God on the lips of the Apostles, who preached to the whole world. And likewise the Fathers, the bishops, the priests and the servants in every generation.
He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes. He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold?
Scattereth: strews.
Hoarfrost: ice.
His ice: His snow.
His cold: pointed slabs of ice that kill whoever they fall upon, as they fall in great numbers from a great height.
Other reasons the psalm presents for praising God, which are:

1- "He giveth snow like wool:" His ability to turn nature to work contrary to its purpose. The extremely cold snow becomes like wool that warms the one who clings to it, as the children of Israel passed forty years with their simple clothes in the wilderness of Sinai, bitterly cold at night, where water turns to ice, yet God gave them warmth like those covered with wool. And this is a symbol that God turns spiritual coldness into a warm, even fervent, spiritual life.

2- "He scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes:" The hoarfrost is cold, and ashes are the product of burning, that is, hot. And this is a symbol of God's turning spiritual coldness into repentance and contrition before God, so that sin is burned and becomes ashes, as the Holy Spirit burned sin within the believers when He came upon them, and burned in them every lust and sin by repentance.

3- "He casteth forth his ice like morsels:" The ice is the hard snow broken into small pieces. And this is a symbol of the crushing of stony, hard hearts so that they become like crumbs. Indeed the morsels are also a symbol of crumbs of bread, that is, that they become useful to others, and become food and spiritual satisfaction for those around them, like Saul of Tarsus, hard of heart, who became Paul the Apostle and laid down his life for Christ, to satisfy the hungry souls among the Gentiles, and became a sensitive heart that feels for all his children, for he said: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).

4- "Who can stand before his cold?" The cold represents God's justice and His punishment of the wicked, so whoever does not learn from all that has preceded and come to God, that is, persists in his evil, God's wrath comes upon him and destroys him. As happened with the pagan peoples who dwelt in the land of Canaan and whose evil increased, so God destroyed them (Josh 2:8), and as happened with Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:28).
He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, and the waters flow.

1- God is able by His word to command the creatures, so they act contrary to their nature; snow, hoarfrost, ice and cold are solids, but God is able to change them, so they turn into liquids that flow out upon people and animals, who drink from them, and it does not harm them but benefits them. As God changed the nature of the fire in the furnace with the three youths, so it did not harm them (Dan 3), and the ravenous lions became tame, gentle animals with Daniel (Dan 6:22), and the liquid water of the Red Sea became like a solid wall for the children of Israel to cross (Ex 14:22), whereas the dry ground under the feet of Dathan and Abiram became soft like the water of the sea, so they fell and the earth swallowed them (Num 16:31-33).
